Non-residential (Workforce Housing Program) 2026: office, commercial and hotel $3.69 per sq ft; industrial, warehousing and agricultural processing $3.80; retail and services $6.38; first 2,000 sq ft exempt. Both adjust each January 1 by the ENR Bay Area construction cost index.
affordability_requirement: On-site alternative for rental projects: at least 15% of units affordable to low and very low income, or 10% to very low and extremely low income; ownership projects 20% split between low and moderate income. Exemptions include ADUs, farmworker and agricultural employee housing, replacement of fire-destroyed homes within 10 years, and projects complying through other approved means (Code 26-89-045).
next_deadline: Compliance method must be selected with the first permit application; fee schedules reset every January 1 (2027 schedule due January 2027).
layering_notes: This is the revenue engine for CFH and the inclusionary rule that mixed-income rental developers in the unincorporated county must satisfy; a 100% affordable LIHTC project satisfies the requirement outright and pays no fee. Developers of market-rate or mixed projects can also meet it by land dedication or restricting existing units. The fee is separate from the traffic and parks impact fees that the Board waived for affordable projects in 2025-2026.

program_name: Traffic and Parks Impact Fee Waiver for Affordable Housing (2025-2026)
administering_agency: Sonoma County Board of Supervisors; administered through Permit Sonoma
typical_award_size: Waiver of County traffic mitigation and parks impact fees for affordable projects in the unincorporated area that received building permits from Feb 1, 2025 through Dec 31, 2026; staff estimated up to $19.5M in fees waived across 15 eligible projects (over 1,900 affordable units) with a $1.5M General Fund backfill.
affordability_requirement: Units reserved for moderate-, low- and very low-income renters or buyers; recorded deed restriction of at least 55 years for rental and 45 years for ownership units. Minimum affordable percentage not stated in the County release; confirm with Permit Sonoma.
next_deadline: Expires Dec 31, 2026 unless extended; the County is studying its fee structure and may adopt a permanent program. Permits must be issued before the sunset.
layering_notes: Worth several thousand dollars per unit in the unincorporated county and reduces basis for the CTCAC cost containment score. Labor Code 1720(b)(4) counts fees waived or forgiven by a public agency as public funds, so a waiver can itself trigger state prevailing wage unless the project is otherwise exempt; most LIHTC projects taking HCD money already pay prevailing wage. Does not cover the affordable housing in-lieu fee, school, water agency or sanitation district fees. Multi-family fee deferral (separate record) remains available after the waiver sunsets.

program_name: Multi-Family Development Fee Deferral Program
administering_agency: Permit Sonoma
typical_award_size: Deferral of County development fees (traffic impact and parkland dedication fees; not school, water agency or sanitation district fees) from building permit final until permanent financing closes, under a recorded Fee Deferral Agreement.
affordability_requirement: Affordable rental or ownership housing for low- or very low-income households, or special needs housing (elderly or disabled) with at least 20% of units for low-income households.
next_deadline: Rolling; request by letter with the permit application. Approval requires a Director finding that the fees are not needed for near-term programmed improvements; agreement signed before building or grading permit.
layering_notes: Bridges construction-period cash flow so impact fees are paid from permanent sources at conversion, a common pairing with CalHFA or bond-financed 4% deals. Deferral terms (interest, security) are not published; a deferred fee charged at less than market terms may be treated as public funds under Labor Code 1720(b)(4). Separate single-family ADU affordable-fee deferral exists for restricted ADUs.

program_name: Sonoma County Density Bonus Program (Code Chapter 26, Sections 26-89-050 and 26-89-060)
administering_agency: Permit Sonoma
typical_award_size: State Density Bonus Law (Gov. Code 65915 to 65917) applied directly: the County acknowledges its Chapter 26 provisions are out of date and states it will comply with current state law until Housing Element Program 15 amendments are adopted (adding lower-income student housing, 100% affordable bonuses, and updated bonus and incentive calculations). Affordable Housing Incentives under Section 26-89-060 also available to projects building inclusionary units on site.
affordability_requirement: State thresholds (5% very low, 10% low, 10% moderate for-sale, 100% affordable, senior, special populations); county inclusionary units may be counted toward the bonus.
next_deadline: Rolling with the entitlement application; code update timing not published (Housing Element 2023-2031 Program 15). Contact Permit Sonoma Housing at (707) 565-1391.
layering_notes: Because the local code lags the statute, rely on Gov. Code 65915 as amended (up to 80% bonus and unlimited waivers for 100% affordable projects, 3-story height bonus near major transit, reduced parking) and expect staff to process requests case by case. Pair with the inclusionary on-site option so the same units earn the bonus and satisfy the Affordable Housing Program with no in-lieu fee. Permit Sonoma also maintains Streamlined Housing Developments (SB 35 and AB 2011 style) and Rezoning Sites for Housing pages for by-right sites.

program_name: Welfare Exemption processing, Sonoma County Assessor
administering_agency: Sonoma County Clerk-Recorder-Assessor, Exemption Unit
typical_award_size: Exemption of the qualifying low-income share of assessed value from the roughly 1.1% to 1.2% property tax rate plus voter-approved debt in Sonoma County.
affordability_requirement: Per state law: nonprofit or eligible LLC owner, or limited partnership with a qualifying managing general partner holding an Organizational Clearance Certificate; recorded regulatory agreement or deed restriction; tax savings must maintain affordability or reduce rents; plus government financing, LIHTC, or at least 90% lower-income occupancy.
next_deadline: Annual claims Jan 1 to Feb 15 (next Feb 15, 2027). First filing on newly acquired property due within 90 days after the first day of the month following acquisition or by Feb 15 of the following year, whichever is first; property must be in exempt use or under construction within 180 days of acquisition. File BOE-267 with the OCC, regulatory agreement and the low-income supplemental affidavit. Exemption Unit (707) 565-1881, assessor@sonomacounty.gov.
layering_notes: Standard statewide rules (see Pass 1 BOE record). Sonoma's assessor page is unusually explicit about the 180-day use requirement and first-filing deadline, which matters for construction-period exemptions on land acquired mid-year. No county property tax abatement JPA exists.

program_name: Measure O Behavioral Health and Homelessness sales tax, housing category
administering_agency: Sonoma County Department of Health Services
typical_award_size: Quarter-cent countywide sales tax (approved 2020, 10-year term) generating about $30M to $33M a year across five categories, one of which is Transitional and Permanent Supportive Housing. Pathways to Sustainability NOFA (released Aug 14, 2025) awarded $10M in Measure O plus $2.4M HHAP to 26 projects on Feb 10, 2026; PSH awards went to Committee on the Shelterless ($392,034 Measure O and $196,017 HHAP) alongside city, shelter and services grants.
affordability_requirement: Transitional and permanent supportive housing for people with behavioral health conditions experiencing homelessness; awards to date are predominantly operating and services, not capital.
next_deadline: 2025-26 round awarded Feb 10, 2026. The County says it hopes applicants 'continue to submit proposals for future projects' but has not announced a 2026-27 NOFA; the February 2026 release noted doubts about future funding levels. Measure sunsets around 2030-2031.
layering_notes: Best viewed as an operating and services subsidy for PSH units rather than a capital source; pair with HCD Homekey+, MHP supportive units and PBVs. Sonoma's BHSA (Prop 1) housing interventions requirement (30% of BHSA funds, half for chronically homeless) begins July 2026 and is administered by the same department; no BHSA capital NOFA was found. County funds are public funds for prevailing wage purposes if used for construction.

program_name: Sonoma County Homeless Coalition (CoC CA-504) funding: HUD CoC competition and Homeless Services Consolidated NOFA (HHAP, ESG, HHIP)
administering_agency: Sonoma County Department of Health Services, Homelessness Services Division, as CoC collaborative applicant
typical_award_size: 2026 HUD CoC competition: about $4.9M in renewal funding; HUD had not announced CoC Bonus or DV Bonus amounts; local applications due July 21, 2026. Annual Homeless Services Consolidated NOFA (state ESG, one-time HHAP, DHCS HHIP and local sources): about $5.5M expected in the 2025-26 cycle (applications due Feb 7, 2025). HHAP rounds 1 to 5 brought $32.2M to the Sonoma area; HHAP Round 5 allowed one CoC Builds PSH construction project.
affordability_requirement: Homeless households via Coordinated Entry; CoC PSH rental assistance and services; HHAP permits permanent housing capital as an eligible use.
next_deadline: 2026 CoC round closed July 21, 2026 (new project categories offered were TH, SSO and DV Bonus only; no new PSH). Next Consolidated NOFA expected January 2027 with a February deadline, based on the 2025 cycle. HHAP Round 6 and 7 disbursements flow through the County.
layering_notes: Operating-side partner for PSH: CoC rental assistance or HHAP operating subsidy can replace or supplement PBVs on supportive units. HHAP capital for permanent housing is allowed but Sonoma has directed most HHAP to shelter, outreach and rehousing. Developers should engage the Homelessness Services Division early so a PSH project appears in the CoC's regional action plan and Coordinated Entry referral agreements.

program_name: RED Housing Fund (Renewal Enterprise District, PG&E wildfire settlement capital)
administering_agency: RED Housing Fund, a nonprofit capitalized with $10M each from the County of Sonoma and the City of Santa Rosa (PG&E 2017 fire settlement), affiliated with the Renewal Enterprise District JPA
typical_award_size: Round 1 (Jan 2022 NOFA): about $20,000,000 in subordinate gap loans, designed to cover roughly 10% of cost on four or five higher-density projects and leverage $180M to $220M (known award: $2.4M to Aviara in Santa Rosa). Round 2 (NOFA issued March 4, 2026, applications due April 1, 2026): up to $5,000,000 in loans, recommendations expected by May 18, 2026. Interest rate, term and per-project maximum are in the NOFA PDF, not on the site.
affordability_requirement: Infill, mid- to high-density residential or mixed-use projects in transit-rich or planned areas meeting RED criteria; income mix may be affordable (up to 80% AMI), middle income (80% to 120% AMI), market rate, or mixed.
next_deadline: 2026 round closed April 1, 2026 (recommendations by May 18, 2026). Rounds have run in 2022 and 2026 as capital is repaid; no 2027 date announced. Email apply@redhousingfund.org for a secure upload link when a NOFA is open.
layering_notes: Lender of last resort (recycling repaid settlement capital) for projects the County and Santa Rosa want built in downtown Santa Rosa and other priority development areas; it accepts market-rate and middle-income deals that cannot use CFH or LIHTC. Capital is public settlement money, so prevailing wage exposure depends on loan terms. The separate private Sonoma County Housing Fund ($10M, Housing Trust Silicon Valley with the Santa Rosa Metro Chamber, predevelopment and acquisition loans up to five years) belongs in Pass 4.

program_name: Napa County Affordable Housing Fund
administering_agency: Napa County Housing and Community Services (County Executive Office)
typical_award_size: Gap loans historically $500,000 to $2,000,000 per project: $2,000,000 requested for Burbank Housing Stoddard West (51 units, 2017), $650,000 plus $148,000 for Turley Flats in St. Helena (8 units, 2017-2018), $500,000 for SAHA Manzanita Family Apartments (51 units, 2019, with $750,000 HEAP), $200,000 for 963 Pope Street in St. Helena (5 units, 2025). The 2010 NOFA offered $5,000,000 plus $2,000,000 reserved for farmworker housing. By 2017 the fund had loaned $22,000,000 for more than 1,000 units since 1992; fee revenue runs about $2,000,000 a year and the fund also pays for farmworker centers, homeless services and fair housing.
per_unit_cap: No fixed cap. The joint City and County Multi Family Transaction Underwriting Guidelines (Jan 21, 2020) size the subsidy by gap analysis against comparable projects; developer fee for small projects capped at $25,000 per unit for units 1-10, $15,000 for units 11-30, $12,000 above 30.
affordability_requirement: 55-year affordability covenant for rental projects (40 years for County-assisted ownership). County preference for projects in the unincorporated area, deeper affordability, permanent affordability and local workers where allowed by law. Loans may be forgiven after 40 to 55 years by Board action.
next_deadline: Rolling since the 2010 NOFA; the County accepts applications year-round under the 2010 application and the 2020 joint underwriting guidelines. Requests go to the Napa County Housing Commission and then the Board of Supervisors; time them to the CTCAC round.
layering_notes: Capitalized by residential inclusionary in-lieu and impact fees and nonresidential housing impact fees under County Code Chapter 18.107 (Ordinance 1026, 1992); the October 21, 2025 fee overhaul (phased in from Jan 16, 2026) should raise annual revenue. Terms per the joint guidelines: 3.0% simple interest (lower if needed for feasibility), 55-year term from permanent loan conversion, 50/50 split of residual receipts between the City/County and developer, balance due at maturity, subordinate to senior debt, 90% maximum LTV on senior debt, monitoring fee $100 per unit for the first 40 units. Deferred developer fee may be repaid from cash flow within 15 years before residual receipts split. Most funded projects are inside the cities; the County obtains RHNA transfer credits in exchange (80% of County RHNA goes to the City of Napa under the Napa Pipe agreement through 2058), which limits funds for other jurisdictions. typical_award_size: State Density Bonus Law benefits summarized in the guide: 20% to 50% more units, up to five concessions, unlimited waivers on showing of physical infeasibility, parking caps of 1 space (studio and 1-bdrm), 1.5 (2 and 3-bdrm), 2.5 (4+ bdrm). 100% affordable projects get 80% bonus or no maximum within one half mile of a major transit stop. Guide cites the May 2025 HCD AMI for Solano County of $124,600.
affordability_requirement: Government Code 65915 set-asides: 5% to 15% very low, 10% to 24% low, 10% to 44% moderate (for-sale only); 55-year rental covenant.
layering_notes: No Solano County density bonus or inclusionary ordinance surfaced in Chapter 28 (Zoning) searches; recent Chapter 28 work has been ADU conformance (ZT-20-02, ZT-26-02) and the County defaults to state law where its code is silent. Unincorporated Solano is largely agricultural with limited sewer, so multifamily sites are rare outside the Homeacres area and County-owned parcels in Dixon. The guide is a two-page information sheet hosted by the City of Vallejo, which calls it the Solano County Density Bonus Guide; confirm with County Planning whether it is the County's document and whether a local ordinance exists. Municode and Vacaville pages returned 403.

program_name: Public facilities fee waiver or deferral for affordable housing (none adopted, Solano County)
administering_agency: Solano County Department of Resource Management (County Code Chapter 11, Article X public facilities fees)
typical_award_size: None. In Jan 2024 The Hampstead Companies asked the Board to waive $672,829 in public facilities fees for Prospera at Homestead, which would have cut the Housing Trust Fund loan to $2,500,000; the Board did not act and funded the full $3,200,000 loan instead.
affordability_requirement: Not applicable.
next_deadline: No waiver or deferral program exists; requests are handled case by case through the Board.
layering_notes: Negative finding. Budget the County's public facilities fees in full for unincorporated and Dixon deals and ask for a Housing Trust Fund loan instead. If a waiver were granted it would count as public funds under Labor Code 1720(b)(4). City fee waivers and deferrals are Pass 3.

program_name: Welfare Exemption processing, Solano County Assessor
administering_agency: Solano County Assessor/Recorder, Exemptions Division, 675 Texas Street Suite 2700, Fairfield, 707-784-6210, exemptions@solanocounty.gov
typical_award_size: Full exemption of property tax on qualifying low-income rental units under Revenue and Taxation Code 214(g) once the BOE issues an Organizational Clearance Certificate (BOE-277); the Assessor rules on property use.
affordability_requirement: Units occupied by households at or below 80% AMI (140% AMI over-income allowance on BOE-267-L3); regulatory agreement, LIHTC or public financing required; managing general partner a qualifying nonprofit or qualifying LLC.
next_deadline: File BOE-267 (first filing) or BOE-267-A (annual) with BOE-267-L, L1 and L2 supplements by February 15 each year; late claims through December 31 receive a partial exemption.
layering_notes: Standard statewide exemption (Pass 1 BOE record), recorded per county because the assessor administers it. Solano has no local property tax abatement JPA. The Assessor's page points to BOE Publication 149; office hours Monday to Friday 9 a.m. to 4 p.m.

program_name: Housing First Solano Continuum of Care (CA-518) and HHAP homelessness funding
administering_agency: Solano County Health and Social Services, Behavioral Health Division (County HHAP grantee); CAP Solano JPA (CoC collaborative applicant, HMIS lead and CoC HHAP administrator)
typical_award_size: County HHAP: Round 1 $1,256,129 (board and care beds), Round 2 $574,231 and Round 3 $1,607,846 (Fair Haven Commons and rental subsidies), Round 4 $1,470,396 ($873,703 to Abode Services for mental health rental subsidies), Round 5 $1,655,549 (accepted April 8, 2025, tenancy supports through June 30, 2029), Round 6 allocation $1,968,380.51 (awarded in the April 2026 batch with the CoC's $2,102,264.22, about $4,100,000 combined, for interim housing operations). CoC HHAP Round 5 $1,725,588.34. The 2026-27 state budget HHAP allocation gives the same pair about $4,070,000. CoC HHAP Round 4 permanent housing RFP offered $470,167.50 (2024). HUD CoC awards: $2,247,299 (FY 2024); FY 2025 round 1 $642,829 for STOP Plus. State dashboard: $13,600,000 HHAP rounds 1-5 to the Solano area, $6,500,000 direct to the County. State ESG 2024 via CA-518: $186,481 to Vacaville Solano Services Corporation.
affordability_requirement: HUD CoC and HHAP target people experiencing homelessness; HHAP allows PSH capital, operating subsidies and rental assistance (no cap on permanent housing uses per HCD's Dec 2025 memo), but Solano has programmed its rounds to rental subsidies, tenancy supports and interim housing.
next_deadline: CAP Solano JPA runs the HUD CoC local competition each summer and periodic HHAP RFPs; its site (capsolanojpa.gov) and housingfirstsolano.org blocked automated access, so check them directly for the 2026 CoC listing and any HHAP Round 6 or 7 RFP. HHAP Round 5 funds must be 75% obligated by June 30, 2026.
layering_notes: For PSH underwriting the usable pieces are County Behavioral Health rental subsidies and tenancy services (Abode Services contract, $26,142,891 for Dec 2023 to June 2026) and HHAP operating commitments, not capital. Solano has no housing sales tax measure. The 2026 PIT count was Jan 29, 2026. HHAP capital is state money and triggers prevailing wage.

program_name: Solano County Behavioral Health Services Act (BHSA) housing interventions
administering_agency: Solano County Health and Social Services, Behavioral Health Division (BH Housing and Homelessness 707-553-5525, bhhousing@solanocounty.gov)
typical_award_size: FY 2026-29 Integrated Plan approved by the Board June 9, 2026. Year one (FY 2026-27) Housing Interventions component allocation $9,636,071 (30% of $32,120,235) plus $1,415,984 carryover, $11,052,055 available. Solano's population exceeds 200,000, so it cannot claim the small-county exemption; up to 25% of housing funds may go to capital development, half must serve chronically homeless people. Current delivery is through Abode Services (outreach, navigation, rental subsidy administration, rapid rehousing, PSH services at Blue Oak Landing and Fair Haven Commons) and the BHSA-funded ARCH program; an interim housing placement RFP closed July 9, 2026.
affordability_requirement: Adults and transition-age youth with serious mental illness or substance use disorder who are homeless or at risk; County BH client eligibility required.
next_deadline: Integrated Plan in effect July 1, 2026 with annual updates; the Abode contract term ended June 30, 2026 and its successor was not located. Ask BH Housing whether capital development (up to about $2,400,000 a year at the 25% cap) or project-based operating subsidies will be offered to PSH sponsors.
layering_notes: Roughly $9,600,000 a year makes Solano's BHSA housing pot the largest county-controlled housing source after HHAP; most of it will fund rental subsidies and services, which is what a PSH operating budget needs. Pair with Homekey+ or HHAP capital and SCHA or city PBVs. Public funds, so capital triggers prevailing wage. Budget figures from Appendix A of the adopted plan (content.solanocounty.gov).

program_name: Contra Costa County Affordable Housing Program: HOME and CDBG-Housing (annual NOFA)
administering_agency: Contra Costa County Department of Conservation and Development (DCD), Housing and Community Improvement Division, 30 Muir Road, Martinez; Kristin Sherk, Principal Planner, 925-655-2889, dcd.housing@dcd.cccounty.us
typical_award_size: FY 2026/27 Board award (May 19, 2026): $4,294,840 CDBG-Housing and $3,500,000 HOME across five projects, including $2,000,000 HOME to Lakeside Recapitalization (RCD, Concord, 122 units) and $2,500,000 CDBG plus $1,500,000 HOME to Trinity Plaza (Eden and CHDC, Richmond, 65 senior units). FY 2025/26: $4,889,000 CDBG and $3,456,343 HOME plus $2,550,000 recaptured HOME-ARP. FY 2027/28 NOFA (released Sept 15, 2026) estimates up to $14,000,000 across CDBG-Housing, HOME and Measure X. FY 2026/27 Action Plan expected resources: CDBG $4,724,092 annual allocation plus $1,000,000 program income; HOME $2,927,850 plus $400,000 program income. ESG $384,307 (services and shelter only).
per_unit_cap: HOME maximum per-unit subsidy (effective Feb 13, 2024) sets County-assisted unit counts for all sources: 0BR $181,488, 1BR $208,049, 2BR $252,994, 3BR $327,293, 4BR $259,263. Performance retention of at least $50,000 (up to 10% of the loan) held by DCD.
affordability_requirement: 55-year County Regulatory Agreement (57 years from loan documents if the occupancy date cannot be established). County policy goal: 100% of County-assisted units at or below 50% AMI and 10% at or below 30% AMI; HOME units at HOME rent limits. 15% of Consortium HOME must go to CHDO-sponsored projects; CDBG new construction only through a qualified CBDO.
next_deadline: 2026-12-07 (FY 2027/28 applications due 5:00 PM via City Data Services). NOFA released Sept 15, 2026; application live Oct 15, 2026; TA meeting Oct 21, 2026; technical questions due Nov 23, 2026; AHFC meets April to May 2027; Board approves May to June 2027. Prior cycle: FY 2026/27 applications were due Dec 11, 2025.
layering_notes: County pages on www.contracosta.ca.gov refuse automated fetches (403); the same pages and DocumentCenter PDFs were opened on 2026-11-06 through the site's CivicPlus origin host (ca-contracostacounty3.civicplus.com), and Board reports were read through the contra-costa.legistar.com API. Standard terms: 3% simple interest, 55-year term, annual payments from residual receipts shared 75% to soft lenders pro rata and 25% to the borrower, special payment from 75% of cost savings, due on sale or refinance; the County will not cut its rate below the home city's rate. Davis-Bacon applies to HOME projects with 12 or more HOME-assisted units and CDBG projects with eight or more units; state prevailing wage is the developer's responsibility to determine but applies to County loans as public funds. Build America Buy America applies to CDBG and HOME projects over $250,000. The County is the HUD entitlement for the Urban County (all of the county except Antioch, Concord, Pittsburg and Walnut Creek, which have their own CDBG) and lead of the Contra Costa HOME Consortium, so HOME can be used countywide including inside those four cities. Awards are sized by the HOME per-unit subsidy table and used as gap money for 4% and 9% tax credit deals; the FY 2026/27 Trinity Plaza and Lakeside awards are both acquisition-rehab recapitalizations. HOME-ARP ($12,108,330 allocation) is closed to new applications. The County staff report notes awards are made contingent on other commitments by Dec 31 of the following year, with recapture if unmet.

program_name: Measure X Housing Fund (affordable housing development share)
administering_agency: Contra Costa County Department of Conservation and Development (75% share); Health, Housing and Homeless Services (H3) administers the 25% services share
typical_award_size: Measure X is a countywide half-cent sales tax (Nov 2020, 20 years, began April 1, 2021). The Board committed $10,000,000 in year one and about $12,000,000 a year after; the County's Measure X allocation table shows the Local Housing Trust Fund line at $12,600,000 (FY 2023-24), $12,902,400 (FY 2024-25), $13,156,577 (FY 2025-26) and $13,306,957 (FY 2026-27), with a 20-year total near $258,000,000. Capital share available through the housing NOFA: $9,707,500 in FY 2025/26 (including $2,000,000 recaptured from Anton San Ramon) and $7,880,690 in FY 2026/27. FY 2026/27 awards: $5,380,690 to 949 Moraga Road (SAHA and Sunflower Hill, Lafayette, 47 IDD units) and $2,500,000 to Rumrill Commons (Novin, San Pablo, 39 units). Earlier: $5,000,000 to El Cerrito Plaza Parcel A South (Related, 69 units), $4,968,158 to Choice in Aging Senior Housing (SAHA, Pleasant Hill, 82 units, matched with $2,963,384 state LHTF), $1,770,958 to Village of Hope Pittsburg (Hope Solutions, 15 PSH cottages). Minimums: $500,000 for capital projects, $250,000 for renovation and microhome projects, $25,000 to $500,000 for predevelopment with no more than $1,000,000 a year for predevelopment (Board, Sept 16, 2025).
per_unit_cap: None beyond the HOME per-unit subsidy table used to count Measure X-assisted units; recent awards range from about $72,000 to $118,000 per total unit.
affordability_requirement: Priority to households at or below 50% AMI (designated target population); up to 80% AMI eligible. Rental loans 55 years; homeownership 20 years or more (80% AMI, 81% to 120% allowed). Grants only for pilot, innovation and capacity-building projects.
next_deadline: 2026-12-07 (FY 2027/28 NOFA with CDBG-Housing and HOME, applications due 5:00 PM). Loan agreement required within two years of contingent award; work must start within one year of loan execution; grants spent within two years.
layering_notes: County pages on www.contracosta.ca.gov refuse automated fetches (403); the same pages and DocumentCenter PDFs were opened on 2026-11-06 through the site's CivicPlus origin host (ca-contracostacounty3.civicplus.com), and Board reports were read through the contra-costa.legistar.com API. Largest discretionary local source in the 12 target counties. Same 3% simple, 55-year residual receipts terms as HOME, but no federal cross-cutting rules, so it is the preferred fill for projects inside cities without their own gap funds and for IDD, senior and farmworker deals. Predevelopment loans are not forgivable and must be repaid even if the project dies. The County used Measure X as the local match to win a $2,963,384 state Local Housing Trust Fund grant (FY 2024/25) and as match for Homekey awards (El Portal Place, $5,200,000). The 25% H3 share (about $4,068,983 in FY 2026/27) funds services, prevention and legal aid through a separate two-year RFP and is not capital. Awards are contingent on other commitments (Dec 31, 2027 for FY 2026/27 awards) and executed loans by June 30, 2028; the County recaptured $2,000,000 when Anton San Ramon stalled and pulled Harbor Pointe's Measure X request in May 2026. Measure X is County General Fund money, so state prevailing wage applies.

program_name: Inclusionary Housing Ordinance In-Lieu Fee Fund (Chapter 822-4)
administering_agency: Contra Costa County Department of Conservation and Development
typical_award_size: FY 2026/27: $1,216,295 available; awards $1,000,000 to Orbisonia Village (Pacific West, Bay Point, 167 units) and $216,295 to Harbor Pointe (USA Properties, Discovery Bay, 168 units). FY 2025/26: $1,054,134 awarded. Fees come from unincorporated projects of five or more units that pay in lieu of building 15% affordable units; the fee is set annually by the Board (for rentals, the 55-year gap between average two-bedroom rent and the affordable rent; for sale units, the gap between the affordable price and the countywide median sale price).
per_unit_cap: Mixed-income projects are capped at an award based on the number of 80% AMI or 50% AMI units that exceed the inclusionary requirement.
affordability_requirement: New construction for households up to 80% AMI, unincorporated county only; preference for two-bedroom and larger units and for projects exceeding the inclusionary minimum. Cannot fund units required by density bonus or inclusionary obligations. Forgivable low-interest loan reconveyed after five years in service as affordable housing.
next_deadline: 2026-12-07 (included in the County housing NOFA when a balance exists; the FY 2027/28 NOFA names CDBG-Housing, HOME and Measure X, so confirm an in-lieu balance with DCD). FY 2026/27 awards required commitments by July 1, 2026 (Orbisonia) and Dec 31, 2027 (Harbor Pointe).
layering_notes: County pages on www.contracosta.ca.gov refuse automated fetches (403); the same pages and DocumentCenter PDFs were opened on 2026-11-06 through the site's CivicPlus origin host (ca-contracostacounty3.civicplus.com), and Board reports were read through the contra-costa.legistar.com API. Small and lumpy, about $1,000,000 to $1,200,000 a year, and limited to unincorporated areas (Bay Point, Discovery Bay, North Richmond, Rodeo, El Sobrante, Alamo). It was used as last-dollar construction money alongside Measure X and PLHA in Orbisonia Village, which also needed a July 1, 2026 close for its 4% credits. Public funds, so prevailing wage applies. The fee calculator and 2025 rent maximums are posted on the County ordinances page.

program_name: Summer Lake Affordable Housing Fund (east county)
administering_agency: Contra Costa County Department of Conservation and Development
typical_award_size: Balance of $913,438 as of 2026, fed by a $3,333 affordable housing fee on each new Summer Lake home collected by the City of Oakley and transferred to the County under the Cypress Corridor annexation Transition Agreement. FY 2026/27 awards: $413,438 construction loan to Harbor Pointe (Discovery Bay, 168 units) and $500,000 predevelopment loan to Casita Phase II (Hijas del Campo, Byron, 17 manufactured farmworker units) at 3% simple interest with a five-year term to start construction.
affordability_requirement: Affordable housing in east Contra Costa County; the agreement asks the County to consider reserving 20% for projects in Oakley. Awarded through the County Affordable Housing Program, so County loan terms (55 years, 3% simple, residual receipts) apply to construction loans.
next_deadline: 2026-12-07 (through the County housing NOFA when a balance exists). Casita Phase II predevelopment loan must be executed by June 30, 2028.
layering_notes: A geographic set-aside, not a standing program, but it is real money for Oakley, Brentwood, Discovery Bay, Byron and Bay Point projects and the County used it in 2026 to fill requests that Measure X could not. Public funds, so prevailing wage applies. Documented in the May 19, 2026 Board report (file 26-2203) read through the Legistar API.

program_name: Permanent Local Housing Allocation (PLHA), Contra Costa Urban County entitlement
administering_agency: Contra Costa County Department of Conservation and Development (HCD entitlement grantee for the Urban County)
typical_award_size: HCD 2024-2028 Formula Allocation NOFA: Contra Costa County CY 2024 $1,523,318 and CY 2025 $1,631,698; five-year estimate $13,021,068 per the amended Five-Year Plan (Resolution 2026-406, Oct 20, 2026). FY 2025/26 allocation $1,860,477 with $1,767,453 to projects after 5% administration; FY 2024/25 award $1,876,423 to El Cerrito Plaza Parcel A South; FY 2022/23 award $1,000,000 to Choice in Aging Senior Housing and $1,650,000 to Rumrill Commons. Earlier HCD awards: $3,373,129 (2022) and $2,170,178. Antioch, Concord, Pittsburg and Walnut Creek receive separate PLHA entitlements (Pass 3).
affordability_requirement: Activity 1: rental development for extremely low to low income households as low-interest deferred loans with a 55-year regulatory agreement, priority to units at or below 60% AMI, awards counted on units at 80% AMI or below. The 2024 HCD NOFA requires 40% of funds for affordable owner-occupied workforce housing (Activity 9: down payment assistance, homeowner rehab, 80% to 120% AMI).
next_deadline: Rental PLHA is awarded through the County housing NOFA in years with a balance; the FY 2027/28 NOFA (due 2026-12-07) lists CDBG-Housing, HOME and Measure X only, so ask DCD whether PLHA will be added. HCD formula allocations arrive annually.
layering_notes: County pages on www.contracosta.ca.gov refuse automated fetches (403); the same pages and DocumentCenter PDFs were opened on 2026-11-06 through the site's CivicPlus origin host (ca-contracostacounty3.civicplus.com), and Board reports were read through the contra-costa.legistar.com API. Roughly $1,500,000 to $1,900,000 a year, now split with 40% to homeownership under the state's 2024 workforce housing rule, so the rental share is under $1,000,000 a year. Used as a companion to Measure X in El Cerrito Plaza (7 PLHA units of 69) and Choice in Aging. State funds with County loan terms, so prevailing wage applies. State regulations require commitment and occupancy deadlines (Choice in Aging PLHA must be occupied by 2030). The County's PLHA Five-Year Plan narrative (Sept 2025) is attached to Resolution 2026-406 on Legistar.

program_name: Multifamily Housing Revenue Bonds, County of Contra Costa conduit issuer
administering_agency: Contra Costa County Department of Conservation and Development, bond administration (Kristin Sherk, 925-655-2889)
typical_award_size: Active issuer. Board approvals: El Cerrito Plaza Parcel A South, up to $35,700,000 tax-exempt plus $10,000,000 taxable (Res. 2025-383, Nov 4, 2025, JPMorgan private placement, 6.824% TIC); Lakeside Apartments, Concord, up to $30,000,000 for RCD's 124-unit acquisition-rehab (Res. 2026-59, March 3, 2026; CDLAC allocation in hand, sale resolution expected May 2026); Res. 2026-196, up to $15,075,837 for a 124-unit acquisition-rehab (May 19, 2026); Res. 2025-362, $29,238,977 tax-exempt plus $8,000,000 taxable (Oct 21, 2025); Res. 2025-196, up to $40,000,000 for an 84-unit development (June 10, 2025); Res. 2025-117, up to $50,000,000 for 70 units (April 15, 2025). Fees per the 2018 Debt Policy appendix: $2,500 application fee, issuance fee at closing, annual fee of 0.125% of outstanding principal (minimum $5,000, may be subordinated) for the 55-year regulatory agreement term.
affordability_requirement: CDLAC and Section 142(d) minimums; County regulatory agreement typically runs 55 years. Recent deals are 100% affordable at 30% to 60% AMI. Projects must be in the unincorporated area or in a city that approves the County as issuer (cities often use CMFA or CSCDA instead).
next_deadline: Tied to CDLAC rounds. The program web page still says the County is not currently accepting applications, but the Board approved six bond resolutions between January 2025 and May 2026; the FY 2026/27 guidelines (section 9.4) direct any County-funded project seeking CDLAC bonds to contact DCD bond staff about the County acting as issuer. Allow for a TEFRA hearing and inducement resolution before the CDLAC deadline.
layering_notes: County pages on www.contracosta.ca.gov refuse automated fetches (403); the same pages and DocumentCenter PDFs were opened on 2026-11-06 through the site's CivicPlus origin host (ca-contracostacounty3.civicplus.com), and Board reports were read through the contra-costa.legistar.com API. The County issues for projects it also lends to (El Cerrito Plaza, Lakeside), which keeps one regulatory agreement and one monitor; bonds are payable solely from project revenue with no County pledge and the sponsor reimburses TEFRA and approval costs. The 0.125% annual issuer fee is in line with CMFA and CSCDA. Tax-exempt bonds alone do not trigger state prevailing wage, but County, HOME or Measure X loans in the same deal do, and Davis-Bacon follows HOME and CDBG. Program overview and 2018 policy appendix are on the County DocumentCenter.

program_name: Project-Based Vouchers, Housing Authority of the County of Contra Costa (HACCC)
administering_agency: Housing Authority of the County of Contra Costa, 3133 Estudillo Street, Martinez; Tony Ucciferri 925-957-8055 (PBV), Robert Moore, Director of Development, 925-957-8025
typical_award_size: HACCC administers about 9,500 Housing Choice Voucher and CoC households and owns 963 public housing units plus two tax credit developments (2025 RFP). Most recent PBV invitation for proposals (REQ-12092025, released Dec 8, 2025, due Jan 8, 2026): up to 15 units for existing properties needing no more than $3,000 per unit of rehab, aimed at properties converting from CoC project-based rental assistance to PBVs. PBV waiting lists opened for partner properties in June to August 2025, Oct 27 to Nov 13, 2025 and March 2 to 19, 2026. Public housing repositioning underway (Las Deltas main campus developer RFQ due Feb 4, 2025; repositioning financial and legal consultant RFPs in 2025 and 2026).
per_unit_cap: HUD PBV caps (20% of authorized vouchers agency-wide, project cap of 25% of units or 40% in low-poverty or supportive housing projects). Rents at the lower of reasonable rent or 110% of FMR.
affordability_requirement: Households at or below 50% AMI at admission (75% at or below 30% AMI); HAP contracts up to 20 years with extensions. Awards subject to HUD PBV caps and long-term affordability. Jurisdiction is the whole county except Pittsburg; the Richmond Housing Authority and Pittsburg Housing Authority serve their cities (Pass 3).
next_deadline: No open PBV solicitation as of Nov 2026; the last closed Jan 8, 2026 and targeted CoC PBRA conversions. HACCC also offers a Mixed Finance capital loan with operating subsidy, sale of units to HACCC, and long-term Property Rental Assistance contracts for developer-owned units (competitive selection required for mixed finance). Register on the Housing Agency Marketplace e-procurement system for notices.
layering_notes: PBVs are the operating subsidy of choice for Contra Costa PSH and CoC-funded buildings, and the 2025 solicitation shows HACCC converting CoC rental assistance to PBVs to free CoC dollars. Underwrite PBV rents at the HAP contract rent; a PBV HAP contract is not a prevailing wage trigger, but Davis-Bacon applies to PBV new construction or rehab of nine or more contract units. HACCC is not a Moving to Work agency. Public housing repositioning (Las Deltas in North Richmond, El Pueblo, Bayo Vista) may produce RAD or Section 18 PBV units for partner developers. Sources opened: HACCC closed solicitations page and the Dec 2025 PBV advertisement PDF; the repositioning RFP PDF supplied the voucher and unit counts.

program_name: Inclusionary Housing Ordinance (Ch. 822-4) and Residential Density Bonus Ordinance (Ch. 822-2)
administering_agency: Contra Costa County Department of Conservation and Development, Community Development Division
typical_award_size: Inclusionary: 15% of units in unincorporated projects of five or more units must be affordable (rental: 20% of those at very low income, remainder lower income; for-sale: 20% lower, remainder moderate), 55-year rental term, with in-lieu fee, off-site units or land dedication as alternatives. Density bonus: up to 15% for providing the required inclusionary units (822-2.402), with state law bonuses under Government Code 65915 for units beyond the requirement, land donation and child care, and incentives or concessions per 65915(d)(2). Incentives for inclusionary compliance (822-4.418(c)) may include fee deferrals or waivers, housing set-aside funds, tax-exempt financing and zoning modifications at County discretion.
affordability_requirement: Inclusionary units: 55 years for rentals; for-sale units owner-occupied with resale controls and County recapture. Density bonus target units: 30 years or longer if required by financing (822-2.410); density bonus housing agreement recorded against the property.
next_deadline: Not applicable; applies by right to unincorporated projects at entitlement. Developer agreements are approved by the Board (for example Grayson Road and Walnut Estates density bonus and inclusionary agreements, April 2026). Confirm current code text with DCD; the County code is hosted on Municode (blocked to automated access), and the mirror read for this record was Zoneomics.
layering_notes: County pages on www.contracosta.ca.gov refuse automated fetches (403); the same pages and DocumentCenter PDFs were opened on 2026-11-06 through the site's CivicPlus origin host (ca-contracostacounty3.civicplus.com), and Board reports were read through the contra-costa.legistar.com API. The ordinance text itself was read on the Zoneomics mirror of the County Ordinance Code. In-lieu fees from this chapter feed the County's In-Lieu Fee Fund (separate record). A 100% affordable project is exempt from the inclusionary requirement and takes the state density bonus and concessions directly; the County's density bonus submittal checklist and 2025 rent maximums are on the County ordinances page. In-lieu funds cannot be used for units that satisfy inclusionary or density bonus obligations. Density bonus alone does not trigger prevailing wage.

program_name: Development fee waiver for affordable housing (no countywide program; discretionary under 822-4.418)
administering_agency: Contra Costa County Department of Conservation and Development
typical_award_size: None adopted. The County has no standing impact fee waiver or deferral program for affordable housing. Chapter 822-4.418(c) lists fee deferrals or waivers among incentives the County may offer to projects providing inclusionary units, and County loans may be used to pay permit fees. No fee waiver awards appeared in 2025 or 2026 Board records.
affordability_requirement: Discretionary; would follow the inclusionary or density bonus agreement for the project.
next_deadline: Not applicable. Request fee deferral in the inclusionary housing plan or density bonus application and ask DCD about paying fees from the County loan.
layering_notes: County pages on www.contracosta.ca.gov refuse automated fetches (403); the same pages and DocumentCenter PDFs were opened on 2026-11-06 through the site's CivicPlus origin host (ca-contracostacounty3.civicplus.com), and Board reports were read through the contra-costa.legistar.com API. Negative finding recorded so the county does not look thin. Budget full County and special district fees (Contra Costa Fire, East Bay Regional Park, school, traffic mitigation) in unincorporated deals. Labor Code 1720(b)(4) treats waived or reduced fees as public funds, so any waiver that is granted could itself trigger state prevailing wage.

program_name: Welfare Exemption (property tax), Contra Costa County Assessor
administering_agency: Contra Costa County Assessor, Gus Kramer, 2530 Arnold Drive Suite 100, Martinez, 925-313-7400
typical_award_size: Full or partial exemption of property tax on units occupied by households at or below 80% AMI (Rev. and Tax. Code 214(g)); worth roughly 1.1% or more of assessed value a year depending on the tax rate area (1% base rate plus voter-approved debt). File early; supplemental affidavits are required for every claim year.
per_unit_cap: Statewide $20,000,000 aggregate cap on exempted assessed value for limited partnership projects that qualify only through the managing general partner test without government financing (Rev. and Tax. Code 214(g)); projects with tax credits, bonds or government loans are outside the cap.
affordability_requirement: Nonprofit or LP with eligible nonprofit managing general partner holding a BOE Organizational Clearance Certificate; units restricted by recorded regulatory agreement or occupied by households at or below 80% AMI; BOE-267 first filing and BOE-267-L, L1 or L2 supplemental affidavits annually by Feb 15 (late claims receive a reduced exemption under Rev. and Tax. Code 270).
next_deadline: 2027-02-15 (annual claim deadline for the 2027-28 roll). First-year claims can be filed on acquisition; construction-period exemption is available under 214(g) once the OCC is in hand.
layering_notes: County pages on www.contracosta.ca.gov refuse automated fetches (403); the same pages and DocumentCenter PDFs were opened on 2026-11-06 through the site's CivicPlus origin host (ca-contracostacounty3.civicplus.com), and Board reports were read through the contra-costa.legistar.com API. Standard in every tax credit operating budget; underwrite the exemption only for the restricted units and confirm the managing GP's OCC before closing. The Assessor's site has no dedicated welfare exemption page; forms are under the Assessor's Forms link and the BOE county contacts page lists the office. The BOE's assessment practices survey of Contra Costa recommended tighter handling of late-filing provisions, so expect staff to apply the statutory late penalties strictly.

program_name: Richmond/Contra Costa County Continuum of Care (CA-505) and HHAP
administering_agency: Contra Costa Health, Health, Housing and Homeless Services Division (H3), CoC lead and HHAP grantee; Contra Costa Council on Homelessness is the CoC board
typical_award_size: HHAP Round 6: $6,708,895 (County $3,244,119 plus CoC $3,464,775), state agreement ratified May 12, 2026, term through June 30, 2030. HHAP Round 5: $6,683,382 (County $3,272,469, CoC $3,410,913), agreement approved March 11, 2025. State accountability site: $28,900,000 in HHAP rounds 1 to 5 awarded to the Contra Costa area, $18,300,000 spent by June 2025; Encampment Resolution Funding $5,700,000 to the County. HUD CoC program FY 2024 awards to CA-505: $11,522,492, including $8,638,557 for Contra Costa tenant-based rental assistance and $1,960,996 for ACCESS. State ESG CoC allocation $304,250 (2024). Homekey history: Delta Landing, Pittsburg (172 interim units, $21,500,000 Homekey), El Portal Place, San Pablo (54 PSH micro-units, $16,000,000 Homekey plus $5,200,000 Measure X). Homekey+: $1,500,000 standard agreement for five PSH units at County-owned Sherman Terrace, Pleasant Hill (Oct 6, 2026); $30,000,000 joint application with SAHA for Choice in Aging Senior Housing (June 9, 2026).
affordability_requirement: Households experiencing or at risk of homelessness per HUD and state definitions; CoC permanent housing requires Coordinated Entry referrals. HHAP Round 6 must obligate 75% and spend 50% by June 30, 2027.
next_deadline: 2026 CoC NOFO priority listing approved Aug 6, 2026 (HUD awards expected winter 2026-27); the Council on Homelessness runs the local competition each summer. HHAP is allocated by state round with no local NOFA; H3 contracts HHAP to operators (Delta Landing, Hope Solutions, BACS, Catholic Charities) through Board-approved contracts.
layering_notes: HHAP money in Contra Costa goes to interim housing operations, rapid rehousing and prevention, not capital, so treat H3 as the services and operating partner for PSH rather than a gap lender. CoC TBRA ($8,600,000 a year) is being converted to HACCC project-based vouchers where possible, which is how new PSH buildings get a long-term subsidy. Homekey and Homekey+ awards have run through H3 for County-owned sites and through DCD for developer sites. The Council on Homelessness agendas (contra-costa.legistar.com) carry the CoC NOFO schedule. Figures from the May 12, 2026 Board report (file 26-1970), HCD HHAP award lists, the HUD FY 2025 CoC award report and accountability.ca.gov.

program_name: Behavioral Health Services Act (BHSA) housing interventions, Contra Costa Behavioral Health
administering_agency: Contra Costa Health, Behavioral Health Services Division (CCBHS), with H3 and DCD for capital awards
typical_award_size: Integrated Plan FY 2026-29 approved by the Board March 17, 2026. Estimated housing intervention funding (BHSA plus MHSA carryover): $41,688,148 in FY 2026-27, $37,553,061 in FY 2027-28, $38,543,498 in FY 2028-29; planned housing expenditures $32,515,162, $35,491,761 and $36,458,704. Capital development share 14.1% in year one (about $4,600,000) then 3.8% and 3.7%; 50% of housing funds dedicated to chronically homeless people; no exemptions requested. First capital awards: $2,250,000 BHSA grant to Village of Hope Pittsburg (Hope Solutions, 15 PSH cottages for transition-age youth, approved June 23, 2026, documents Aug 11, 2026) and BHSA operating and development commitments for Sherman Terrace Homekey+ (five PSH units, Pleasant Hill). No Place Like Home: Legacy Court, Richmond (13 NPLH units, Community Housing Development Corp., MOU Oct 7, 2025).
per_unit_cap: Capital development limited to 25% of the housing interventions component by statute; the County planned 14.1% in year one.
affordability_requirement: Adults and transition-age youth with serious mental illness or substance use disorder who are chronically homeless, homeless or at risk; Housing First; CCBHS client eligibility and referral. Capital grants carry occupancy preferences (five of 15 units at Village of Hope) and no repayment if the project is completed.
next_deadline: No standing capital NOFA; the two 2026 capital awards were negotiated with CCBHS and brought to the Board. Annual plan updates each spring; ask CCBHS about year two and three capital (about $1,300,000 a year at the planned share) and about project-based operating subsidies and rental subsidies for PSH units.
layering_notes: Contra Costa's BHSA housing pot (about $32,000,000 to $36,000,000 a year in spending) is now the largest county-controlled housing source, but most of it is rental subsidies, operating subsidies and services. The capital slice was front-loaded into FY 2026-27 and mostly committed (Village of Hope, Sherman Terrace). The practical ask for a PSH sponsor is a BHSA operating or rental subsidy commitment plus services, layered on HACCC PBVs and Measure X or HOME capital. State funds, so capital grants trigger prevailing wage. Plan read from the Board attachment (CCC Integrated Plan 2.27.26) on Legistar.

program_name: Housing Successor Low and Moderate Income Housing Asset Fund and surplus land (former Contra Costa County Redevelopment Agency)
administering_agency: Contra Costa County Department of Conservation and Development, as Housing Successor
typical_award_size: Housing Fund balance about $8,700,000 at June 30, 2025, of which about $6,600,000 is pre-dissolution bond proceeds restricted to affordable housing; FY 2024-25 revenue $756,175 from loan payments, interest and land sales; $382,774 spent on monitoring and administration. The County holds former redevelopment land in Bay Point (near Pittsburg/Bay Point BART), North Richmond and Rodeo and solicits developers through RFPs (Heritage Point, 42 units, and Bay Point Senior, Eden Housing, 80 units, came from these parcels). No County loans between the Successor Agency and the County remain outstanding.
affordability_requirement: Health and Safety Code 34176.1: funds for households at or below 80% AMI with at least 30% for extremely low income over each five-year period; land disposed for affordable housing with recorded covenants (55 years rental).
next_deadline: Watch the County's Development Opportunities page and Board agendas for Bay Point and Rodeo parcel RFPs; the FY 2024-25 Housing Successor report (SB 341) was filed in 2026 and the next is due with the FY 2025-26 financial report.
layering_notes: County pages on www.contracosta.ca.gov refuse automated fetches (403); the same pages and DocumentCenter PDFs were opened on 2026-11-06 through the site's CivicPlus origin host (ca-contracostacounty3.civicplus.com), and Board reports were read through the contra-costa.legistar.com API. Land is the main asset: County-owned sites in Bay Point and Rodeo have been offered at nominal cost with the County as a co-applicant for state funds, and sale proceeds are recycled into affordable housing. The $6,600,000 in old bond proceeds is a one-time pot that could fund site work or gap loans on those parcels. Public land and funds trigger state prevailing wage. Report read from the County DocumentCenter (Contra Costa County Housing Successor Report 2024-25).

program_name: Orange County 2026 Supportive Housing NOFA (HOME, HOME-ARP, MHSA/BHSA, 15G Reserves, Housing Successor funds)
administering_agency: OC Housing and Community Development (OC Community Resources), 1501 E. St. Andrew Place, Santa Ana; Michelle Zdeba, Housing Development Manager, 714-480-2994; Sherluna Vien 714-480-2936; OCHCD.NOFA@occr.ocgov.com
typical_award_size: Up to $20,900,000 in loans authorized by the Board Feb 10, 2026 and released March 6, 2026 (OpenGov NOFA 2026-01), plus up to 100 Housing Choice, Mainstream or VASH project-based vouchers. Replaces the 2025 NOFA ($12,050,000 and up to 150 PBVs) and the 2023 NOFA ($67,100,000 authorized, $32,700,000 and 218 PBVs in Amendment 1). Maximum County subsidy per assisted unit: $137,500 (any bedroom size) in the unincorporated area and Urban County participating cities; $95,000 (0BR), $100,000 (1BR), $105,000 (2BR+) in all other cities. MHSA/BHSA capital limit $207,235 per regulated unit plus up to $207,235 per unit for a capitalized operating subsidy reserve. Minimum five assisted units; total development cost above TCAC's $650,000 per unit threshold needs justification.
per_unit_cap: $137,500 per County-assisted unit in unincorporated areas and participating cities; $95,000 to $105,000 elsewhere; HOME units also capped at HUD 221(d)(3) limits; MHSA/BHSA $207,235 per regulated unit (rises 4% a year, locked at application).
affordability_requirement: All County-assisted units restricted to households at or below 30% AMI who are experiencing homelessness, filled through the Coordinated Entry System, with a 55-year regulatory agreement from the qualified project period. MHSA/BHSA units serve adults with serious mental illness and may not exceed 49% of project units. Projects outside the unincorporated area must show host-city financial support at least equal to the County request (land, fee waivers and infrastructure count) and accept a RHNA transfer or credit to the County.
next_deadline: Open first come, first served until funds are committed or a new NOFA replaces it. Geographic tiers: March 6 to May 4, 2026 unincorporated area and Urban County cities only; May 5 to June 3 added entitlement cities except Santa Ana, Anaheim and Garden Grove; from June 4, 2026 any eligible location. Allow at least eight months from a complete application to Board approval. PBVs only for sites in OCHA jurisdiction.
layering_notes: The County's only capital program and it is PSH only: every assisted unit must be 30% AMI and CES-referred, so it fits a 4% or 9% deal with a PSH set-aside, not a general affordable project. Terms: 3% simple interest, 55 years, residual receipts split 50% to public lenders pro rata and 50% to the developer, monitoring fees of $500 setup plus $3,795 a year plus $22 per unit, replacement reserves $250 to $500 per unit, partnership management fee up to $25,000. Davis-Bacon applies at 12 or more HOME-assisted units or nine or more PBV units; projects using only MHSA/BHSA or Housing Successor money may avoid Davis-Bacon but state prevailing wage applies to public funds. HOME-ARP, 15G Reserves and Housing Successor dollars are pooled here rather than offered separately. OCHA PBVs can be requested with no capital. Homekey+ projects vetted through the County RFI skip the geographic tiers. NOFA, exhibits and sample loan documents are posted on the NOFA page (opened 2026-11-06).

program_name: HOME, CDBG and ESG, Orange County Urban County program
administering_agency: OC Housing and Community Development, Community Development Division; Craig Fee, Community Development Manager, 714-480-2996
typical_award_size: FY 2026-27 Annual Action Plan: CDBG $3,467,220 annual allocation plus $20,000 program income and $806,834 prior-year resources ($4,294,054 available); HOME $1,244,582.84 plus $135,000 program income; ESG $302,608. Five-year ConPlan FY 2025-29 expects about $12,900,000 CDBG and $4,100,000 HOME over the remaining years. HOME housing development dollars are awarded only through the Supportive Housing NOFA; CDBG goes mainly to public facilities, public services and housing rehabilitation through the annual Request for Applications (generally due in November under the Funding Allocation Policy and Process).
per_unit_cap: HOME subsidy limits per 24 CFR 92.250 apply through the NOFA.
affordability_requirement: HUD income limits (80% AMI, HOME rents); the County's NOFA restricts HOME-assisted PSH units to 30% AMI for 55 years. CDBG new construction only by a CBDO.
next_deadline: FY 2027-28 Funding Allocation Policy and Process posted Oct 2026; the RFA for CDBG, ESG and HOME public service and facility projects is generally due in November with the Action Plan draft out for 30-day comment in March and Board adoption in spring. Housing development applicants should use the Supportive Housing NOFA instead.
layering_notes: Small program for a county of 3.2 million because most cities are their own entitlements. Urban County members: unincorporated area plus Brea, Cypress, Dana Point, Laguna Beach, Laguna Hills, Laguna Woods, La Palma, Los Alamitos, San Juan Capistrano, Seal Beach, Stanton, Villa Park and the metro cities Placentia and Yorba Linda; Anaheim, Santa Ana, Irvine, Garden Grove, Huntington Beach and 15 other cities run their own CDBG and HOME (Pass 3). The County is not the HOPWA grantee. The County's HOME-ARP allocation was folded into the Supportive Housing NOFA rather than offered separately. Davis-Bacon and state prevailing wage apply. Pages and the FY 2026-27 Action Plan PDF opened on housing.oc.gov.

program_name: MHSA/BHSA permanent supportive housing capital and Capitalized Operating Subsidy Reserve (Orange County Health Care Agency through OC Community Resources)
administering_agency: OC Health Care Agency, Behavioral Health Services (MHSA/BHSA Housing Program), with OC Housing and Community Development administering loans
typical_award_size: BHSA Integrated Plan FY 2026-29 (Board May 19, 2026): Housing Interventions component $73,500,000 a year; planned capital development $18,375,000 a year (the 25% statutory maximum) plus about $990,508 from other sources; rental subsidies $14,000,000 a year; operating subsidies $6,787,829 a year; $36,750,000 a year reserved for chronically homeless people. Named capital pipeline: Mercury Senior Apartments (Brea), Lampson Workforce Housing (Los Alamitos) and projects to be determined in San Juan Capistrano, Anaheim Hills, Buena Park and Fountain Valley, 56 BHSA units of 416 at about $208,000 per BHSA unit. Since June 2018 the County has completed 476 MHSA units with 196 in the pipeline toward a goal of 2,396 PSH units by 2029; each MHSA dollar leveraged about $5.50. HCA also granted $20,500,000 of MHSA and General Fund to the Orange County Housing Finance Trust. Loan limit $207,235 per regulated unit for capital and another $207,235 for COSR under the 2026 NOFA.
per_unit_cap: $207,235 per MHSA/BHSA regulated unit (capital) plus up to $207,235 per unit COSR; BHSA statute caps the housing intervention share at $450,000 per unit.
affordability_requirement: Extremely low income (30% AMI) adults experiencing homelessness with a serious mental disorder (WIC 5600.3(b), BHSA eligibility under WIC 5830(a)), certified by HCA and referred through CES; rents at 30% of the 30% AMI limit or 30% of SSI; no minimum income where PBVs or COSR are provided; MHSA/BHSA units at most 49% of the project; units at least 450 square feet with full kitchens and furnishings; 55-year covenant.
next_deadline: Apply through the 2026 Supportive Housing NOFA (open since March 6, 2026) with an HCA review meeting before submission. The three-year plan runs July 1, 2026 to June 30, 2029 with annual updates; HCA moves money to OCCR under a three-year spending plan, so NOFA amounts rise when new BHSA allocations post.
layering_notes: Orange County's BHSA program is the deepest county PSH source in the 13 counties researched: $18,400,000 a year in planned capital plus a COSR that replaces PBVs when none are available (zero interest, forgivable over 15 to 20 years, sized to cover MHSA unit operating deficits). Pair the capital with 4% credits and OCHA or city PBVs; use COSR when PBVs are refused. MHSA capital alone can avoid Davis-Bacon but state prevailing wage still applies. Terms are in Attachment D of the 2026 NOFA (opened); budget figures from the Integrated Plan PDF on ochealthinfo.com (opened). HCA does not run its own developer NOFA.

program_name: Orange County Housing Finance Trust (OCHFT) permanent supportive and affordable housing loans
administering_agency: Orange County Housing Finance Trust, joint powers authority of the County of Orange and 27 cities (9-member board, 4 County and 5 city seats), administered by County staff
typical_award_size: 2024 NOFA (due March 15, 2024, availability extended by Addendum 2 through July 2026, now fully committed): $25,700,502 from County MHSA ($12,371,809), County General Fund ($1,000,000) and state Local Housing Trust Fund matching grants ($12,328,693), split in thirds across North, Central and South service planning areas, project cap $3,500,000. Awards 2020 to 2024: $55,035,131 to 32 project awards funding 441 Trust-restricted units in 2,477 total units (2024 round $22,143,076 for 152 units across 10 projects including Cypress Village Irvine $3,500,000 and Aspan Court Lake Forest $3,490,000). June 30, 2025 audit: notes receivable $25,013,554, net position $54,579,510; FY 2024-25 deposits $4,000,000 MHSA, $1,200,000 County, $3,000,000 CalOptima, $402,747 LHTF. $250,000 federal community project funding presented April 2026. Goal 2,396 PSH units by 2029.
per_unit_cap: 2024 NOFA: $126,000 (0BR), $140,000 (1BR), $154,000 (2BR+) for non-MHSA units; $191,600 per MHSA unit; $3,500,000 per development unless waived by the board.
affordability_requirement: Extremely low, very low and low income households and people experiencing homelessness; MHSA units for homeless adults with serious mental illness; LHTF-funded units at or below 60% AMI per state rules; 55-year covenant. Projects must be in the unincorporated area or a member city, and LHTF dollars only in cities compliant with state housing law; MHSA-only requests may be anywhere in the county.
next_deadline: No open NOFA as of Nov 2026; the 2024 NOFA has no funds remaining and no 2025 or 2026 round was posted. Watch the Trust's NOFA page and board agendas; rounds have opened each spring since 2020 when state LHTF matches were awarded. An Affordable ADU Loan Program is also offered.
layering_notes: Regional JPA recorded at county level because the County seeded it and sits on its board; it is the vehicle that captured $12,300,000 of state LHTF matches for Orange County. Terms mirror the County NOFA: 3% simple, 55 years from conversion, 50% residual receipts, TCAC developer fee limits, $25,000 partnership management fee cap. Awards are small ($500,000 to $3,500,000) and used as last-in gap money on 4% and 9% deals, often alongside County MHSA loans and OCHA PBVs. Member cities: Aliso Viejo, Anaheim, Buena Park, Costa Mesa, Dana Point, Fountain Valley, Fullerton, Garden Grove, Huntington Beach, Irvine, La Habra, Laguna Beach, Laguna Hills, Laguna Niguel, Lake Forest, Los Alamitos, Mission Viejo, Newport Beach, Orange, Placentia, San Juan Capistrano, Santa Ana, Seal Beach, Stanton, Tustin, Westminster and Yorba Linda. Public funds trigger state prevailing wage. NOFA page, developments page, member list and 2025 audit opened; the 2024 NOFA PDF is hosted on Squarespace.

program_name: Project-Based Vouchers, Orange County Housing Authority (OCHA)
administering_agency: Orange County Housing Authority (OC Community Resources), 1501 E. St. Andrew Place, Santa Ana, 714-480-2700; PBV requests through OC Housing and Community Development NOFA staff
typical_award_size: 26 PBV projects listed on the OCHA site total 693 PBV units (for example Stanton Inn 71, Oasis Huntington Beach 62, Tahiti 59, Ascent 57, Avon River 48, Casa Paloma 48, Crossroads at Washington 43, Salida Del Sol 40). The 2026 Supportive Housing NOFA offers up to 100 Housing Choice, Mainstream or VASH PBVs (150 under the 2025 NOFA; 218 under the 2023 NOFA Amendment 1). Pipeline as of Feb 2026: Cartwright Irvine (8 PBV, 60 units, May 2026), Avon River Costa Mesa (14 PBV plus 10 VASH, 78 units), Orion Orange (3 PBV, 166 units), Lincoln Avenue Buena Park (13 PBV, 55 units, Nov 2026), Casa Colibri Midway City (30 PBV, 71 units, Dec 2026). Total OCHA voucher count was not confirmed from an opened document.
per_unit_cap: HUD limits: 20% of authorized vouchers plus 10% for homeless, veteran, supportive services, low-poverty or FUP/FYI units; project cap 25% of units (no cap for supportive housing and elderly units). Rents at the lower of reasonable rent or 110% of FMR with OCHA utility allowances.
affordability_requirement: Extremely low income households experiencing homelessness referred through the Coordinated Entry System; VASH units need VA eligibility; many projects are senior (62 plus) or MHSA/NPLH restricted. Tenants pay 30% of income. HAP contracts up to 20 years with a 20-year extension option.
next_deadline: Request PBVs through the open 2026 Supportive Housing NOFA (OpenGov 2026-01); PBVs are available only for sites in OCHA jurisdiction (the county except Anaheim, Santa Ana and Garden Grove, which run their own authorities) and may be limited by federal funding changes. OCHA posts PBV waitlist openings per project; the 2027 payment standards were posted Nov 2026.
layering_notes: OCHA PBVs are the standard operating subsidy for Orange County PSH and are awarded with or without County capital under the same NOFA; the 2026 NOFA lets the County claim part of the NOI the PBVs create for services. A HAP contract is not a prevailing wage trigger but Davis-Bacon applies to new construction or rehab of nine or more PBV units, and PBVs bring NEPA and a HUD subsidy layering review. Four PHAs operate in the county (OCHA, Anaheim, Santa Ana, Garden Grove); their PBV pipelines are tracked by the CoC Housing Opportunities Committee. OCHA is not a Moving to Work agency. Sources opened: OCHA project-based page, 2026 NOFA Section III, Feb 11, 2026 Housing Opportunities Committee slides.

program_name: Apartment Development Revenue Bond Program, County of Orange conduit issuer
administering_agency: County Executive Office, Public Finance (Louis McClure, 714-834-5999, Luis.McClure@ocgov.com) with the Public Financing Advisory Committee (PFAC) and Board of Supervisors
typical_award_size: Tax-exempt multifamily bonds for new construction or acquisition-rehab anywhere in Orange County; a typical bond loan is $7,000,000 or more with issuance costs of about $300,000, 30-year amortization, credit enhanced (Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, bank letter of credit) or privately placed at County discretion. Borrower pays all issuance and finance team costs. No recent County issuances were located; most Orange County deals use CMFA or CSCDA (for example Valencia Garden in Orange, CMFA $18,499,022).
affordability_requirement: At least 20% of units for very low income households, or 10% very low plus 30% at 60% AMI, for the longer of 15 years or the life of the bonds (about 30 years); County loans may be added for deeper affordability.
next_deadline: Apply after site control and a lender commitment: PFAC approves the financing concept and team, the Board holds the TEFRA hearing and adopts the inducement resolution, then the County applies to CDLAC; bonds must close within 90 days of the CDLAC award. Call the CEO public finance contact before preparing an application.
layering_notes: The County keeps a conduit program on paper (Attachment H to the 2026 Supportive Housing NOFA, opened) but the pipeline shows cities and developers using CMFA and CSCDA instead; expect PFAC review to add six to eight weeks versus a JPA issuer. Bonds alone do not trigger state prevailing wage; County loans in the same deal do. Confirm current issuer fees with the CEO, as none are published.

program_name: Permanent Local Housing Allocation (PLHA), Orange County Urban County entitlement
administering_agency: OC Housing and Community Development (HCD entitlement grantee for the Urban County)
typical_award_size: HCD 2024-2028 Formula Allocation NOFA: Orange County CY 2024 $892,973, CY 2025 $956,505, five-year estimate $5,581,081. The County's PLHA Five-Year Plan (2020) directs 88.55% of each year's allocation to homeless activities under PLHA 301(a)(6): 45.55% to the Buena Park and Placentia navigation centers through a North SPA collaborative treasured by the City of La Habra, 32.79% to the Yale Transitional Center in Santa Ana for the unincorporated area, 3.54% to the Laguna Beach Alternative Sleeping Location and 6.67% to Dana Point outreach and rapid rehousing; the remaining 11.45% is for rental housing development under 301(a)(1).
affordability_requirement: PLHA statute: rental development for households at or below 80% AMI (120% workforce allowed) with 55-year covenants; the County plan's development share has not been offered through a developer NOFA.
next_deadline: HCD formula allocations arrive annually; no County PLHA NOFA to developers exists. Ask OCHCD whether the plan was amended for the state's 2024 requirement that 40% of new PLHA fund owner-occupied workforce housing, and whether the 11.45% development share is folded into the Supportive Housing NOFA.
layering_notes: Not a capital source in practice: under $1,000,000 a year and almost all of it pays for shelter and navigation center operations. Anaheim, Santa Ana, Irvine and other entitlement cities receive their own PLHA (Pass 3). Plan PDF and community development page opened on housing.oc.gov; amounts from the HCD 2024-2028 PLHA NOFA.

program_name: Housing Successor Low and Moderate Income Housing Asset Fund (Orange County Housing Authority as Housing Successor to the Orange County Development Agency)
administering_agency: Orange County Housing Authority as Housing Successor, administered by OC Housing and Community Development
typical_award_size: Housing Asset Fund balance $29,240,000 at June 30, 2024 (FY 2023-24 SB 341 report). Funds are offered only through the County's Supportive Housing NOFAs: $4,000,000 added to the 2016 PSH NOFA in April 2018; 2020 NOFA awards of $2,400,000 to Clara Vista (former Tahiti Motel, Stanton, 60 PSH units, completed Dec 2023) and $453,600 each to Mountain View (Lake Forest, 71 units) and Orchard View Gardens (Buena Park, 66 units); no Housing Successor funds were in the 2023 NOFA, but they are a named source in the 2026 NOFA.
per_unit_cap: Follows the Supportive Housing NOFA limits ($137,500 per unit in unincorporated areas and participating cities).
affordability_requirement: Health and Safety Code 34176.1: households at or below 80% AMI, at least 30% of spending over five years for extremely low income households, 55-year covenants; excess surplus rules force spending when the unencumbered balance exceeds the greater of $1,000,000 or four years of deposits.
next_deadline: Request through the open 2026 Supportive Housing NOFA. The FY 2024-25 SB 341 report link on the County page returned 404 on 2026-11-06; the FY 2023-24 report was read.
layering_notes: A large idle balance (about $29,000,000) that the County must spend to avoid excess surplus findings, so it is the most flexible local money in the NOFA pool: no federal strings, 30% AMI target through the NOFA. Use it for sites outside HOME geography or where Davis-Bacon is a problem. Public funds, so state prevailing wage applies. Housing successor page and FY 2023-24 report PDF opened on housing.oc.gov.

program_name: Housing Opportunities Overlay (Zoning Code 7-9-44), Affordable Housing Permit (7-9-124.3) and density bonus (7-9-87)
administering_agency: OC Public Works, OC Development Services, Planning Division (Deysi Munoz, 714-667-8815, Deysi.munoz@ocpw.ocgov.com)
typical_award_size: The 2024 Housing Opportunities Overlay Manual allows 100% affordable rental or ownership projects, emergency shelters, multi-service centers and low-barrier navigation centers by right in commercial and industrial districts and on listed residential arterial parcels in the unincorporated area, approved through a ministerial Affordable Housing Permit. Qualified projects must be 100% affordable to low and very low income households (at or below 80% AMI) with at least 30% of units for very low income households; the County NOFA's Attachment J lists eligible sites. Density bonus (Sec. 7-9-87.1 to 87.4) follows Government Code 65915 for bonus amounts, incentives, concessions and waivers; the Mixed-Use district allows 12 feet of extra height as a bonus incentive. No county inclusionary housing ordinance or in-lieu fee.
affordability_requirement: Overlay projects: 100% affordable, 70% low income and 30% very low income, with recorded covenants; density bonus units per state law (55 years for rental).
next_deadline: Not applicable; ministerial. Unincorporated communities include Midway City, Rossmoor, North Tustin, Ladera Ranch, Rancho Mission Viejo, Silverado and El Modena. Confirm site eligibility with OC Development Services; processing fee deposit applies.
layering_notes: The overlay matters because most of the County's own land-use authority covers small pockets; the 2026 NOFA gives unincorporated overlay sites the first 60-day application window and the higher $137,500 per unit subsidy. Density bonus and by-right approval do not trigger prevailing wage. Manual PDF opened on ocds.ocpublicworks.com; zoning code mirror on Zoneomics shows section headings and overlay affordability terms.

program_name: Development fee waiver for affordable housing (no countywide program)
administering_agency: OC Public Works, OC Development Services
typical_award_size: None adopted. The County has no impact fee waiver or deferral program for affordable housing in the unincorporated area. The 2026 Supportive Housing NOFA treats city waivers of impact, school, sanitation and mitigation fees as eligible local match, and County loans may pay building permit fees as an eligible cost.
affordability_requirement: Not applicable.
next_deadline: Not applicable. Ask the host city for fee waivers to satisfy the County NOFA match requirement.
layering_notes: Negative finding. Unincorporated projects pay full County, school district and sanitation district fees; the Affordable Housing Permit carries a processing deposit. Labor Code 1720(b)(4) counts any waived fee as public funds for prevailing wage purposes.

program_name: Welfare Exemption (property tax), Orange County Assessor
administering_agency: Orange County Assessor, Claude Parrish, 500 S. Main Street, Orange; Institutional Exemptions unit 714-834-2779; main line 714-834-2727
typical_award_size: Full or partial exemption of property tax on units occupied by households at or below 80% AMI under Revenue and Taxation Code 214(g); worth roughly 1.1% or more of assessed value a year depending on the tax rate area. The Assessor posts current BOE-267 series forms (2026 BOE-267-R is online).
per_unit_cap: Statewide $20,000,000 aggregate cap on exempted assessed value for limited partnership projects that qualify only through the managing general partner test without government financing (Rev. and Tax. Code 214(g)); projects with tax credits, bonds or government loans are outside the cap.
affordability_requirement: Nonprofit or LP with eligible nonprofit managing general partner holding a BOE Organizational Clearance Certificate; units restricted by recorded regulatory agreement or occupied by households at or below 80% AMI; BOE-267 first filing and BOE-267-L, L1 or L2 supplemental affidavits annually by Feb 15 (late claims receive a reduced exemption under Rev. and Tax. Code 270).
next_deadline: 2027-02-15 (annual claim deadline for the 2027-28 roll). File the first claim on acquisition so the construction period is covered.
layering_notes: Standard in every tax credit operating budget; underwrite only the restricted units and confirm the managing GP's OCC before closing. The Assessor's institutional exemptions page describes the welfare exemption in general terms only; the exemptions unit phone comes from the Assessor's contact page (both opened). The BOE county contacts page lists the same office.

program_name: Santa Ana, Anaheim/Orange County Continuum of Care (CA-602) and HHAP
administering_agency: County of Orange, County Executive Office, Office of Care Coordination (CoC lead agency and HHAP administrative entity); Orange County CoC Board
typical_award_size: HHAP by round, County of Orange: R1 $7,486,576, R2 $3,422,435, R3 $9,582,817, R4 $7,131,233, R5 $8,346,727, R6 $8,355,062 (agreement through June 30, 2030). Orange County CoC: R1 $8,081,116, R2 $3,823,692, R3 $10,267,304, R4 $7,600,842, R5 $8,699,841, R6 $8,923,350; Anaheim, Santa Ana and Irvine each $5,947,855 in R6 for a regional R6 total of $35,100,000 awarded April 2026. State accountability site: $152,700,000 HHAP rounds 1 to 5 to the Orange County area, $36,000,000 directly to the County ($28,900,000 obligated, $15,300,000 spent by mid-2025); Encampment Resolution Funding $8,700,000 area, $3,600,000 County. HHAP-6 CoC budget: $3,976,421 permanent housing operating subsidies, $592,335 youth operating subsidies, $1,552,663 rapid rehousing, $1,222,663 interim housing operating subsidies, $330,000 youth interim, $624,635 services, $624,635 administration and HMIS. HUD CoC FY 2024 awards to CA-602 included $1,249,326 Permanent Housing Collaborative, $731,787 rapid rehousing and $528,250 Jackson Aisle TRA (partial list). 2024 PIT: 7,322 people, 4,173 unsheltered, 9,751 year-round beds.
