Homekey+: County RFI (due Nov 27, 2024) qualified Volunteers of America, National CORE, California Supportive Housing, American Family Housing and Weingart Center as development partners.
affordability_requirement: People experiencing or at risk of homelessness per HUD and state definitions; CoC permanent housing through Coordinated Entry; HHAP-6 obligation and expenditure deadlines (75% obligated and 50% spent by June 30, 2027). HHAP-5 regional plan governs HHAP-6 uses.
next_deadline: HHAP-6 budget approved by the CoC Board in 2025 with Board of Supervisors action Jan 13, 2026; HHAP-7 is open to HHAP-6 grantees per the state. The CoC runs the HUD NOFO competition each summer and the Housing Opportunities Committee meets every other month (next listed April 8, 2026 at OCHA). Homekey+ sites move through the County RFI and the Supportive Housing NOFA.
layering_notes: HHAP in Orange County pays operating subsidies for permanent and interim housing, rapid rehousing and services; it is an operating partner for PSH, not a capital lender. The region's HHAP is split five ways (County, CoC, Anaheim, Santa Ana, Irvine), so a project inside one of those cities should approach that city's share. County Homekey and Homekey+ sites (Stanton Inn, Tahiti, Casa Paloma and the RFI list) then take OCHA PBVs and MHSA/BHSA loans. Figures from the July 23, 2025 CoC Board presentation (ceo.oc.gov, opened), the Feb 11, 2026 Housing Opportunities Committee slides, HCD HHAP-6 allocations and accountability.ca.gov.

program_name: Measure W Home Together Fund: Multifamily Homelessness Solutions capital and operating subsidy
administering_agency: Alameda County Housing and Community Development Department (HCD), 224 W. Winton Avenue, Room 108, Hayward, 510-670-6417, HCDRFP@acgov.org, with Alameda County Health, Housing and Homelessness Services (H&H)
typical_award_size: Measure W is a half-cent, ten-year general sales tax (Nov 2020) held in escrow until the lawsuit ended in April 2025: $810,000,000 accrued through June 2025 plus about $170,000,000 a year through June 2031. Board framework of July 30, 2025: 80% of ongoing revenue (about $136,000,000 a year) plus $585,800,000 one-time to the Home Together Fund ($1,400,000,000 through 2031), $170,000,000 prudent reserve, 20% to an Essential County Services Fund. FY 2025-26 Home Together Fund allocation $168,900,000 (Housing $96,000,000, Shelter $30,000,000, Access $11,000,000, Prevention $8,000,000, System Foundations $21,000,000); one-time capital acquisition line $180,000,000 for 850 or more housing and shelter units. 2025 New Construction RFP (released Oct 27, 2025, due Dec 8, 2025): about $40,000,000 for capital and operating subsidies; Board awarded $50,000,000 on March 3, 2026 to 10 shovel-ready projects (Liberation Park, 500 Lake Park, 3135 San Pablo, East 12th Circle and Brighter Bancroft Senior in Oakland; Ephesian Legacy Court and People's Park Supportive in Berkeley; 1247 McKay in Alameda; Downtown Livermore, Eden Housing 130 units; Thornton Avenue in Newark, $2,950,000), more than 900 homes with 346 for people exiting homelessness. A separate acquisition and rehabilitation RFP of about $10,000,000 was planned for early 2026, and a one-time $15,000,000 Emergency Stabilization pool for distressed nonprofit owners closed Jan 12, 2026.
per_unit_cap: Capital $175,000 per studio or one-bedroom homeless unit and $200,000 per two-bedroom unit; capitalized operating subsidy reserve up to $225,000 per Coordinated Entry unit sized to a 15-year operating gap; combined per-unit maximum about $225,000 (redlined to $250,000 in the Nov 17, 2025 revision).
affordability_requirement: Assisted units restricted to extremely low income households at or below 30% AMI referred through the Home Together Coordinated Entry System, with supportive services; rents underwritten at the lesser of 50% AMI TCAC rent or 30% of 30% AMI; County regulatory agreement senior to bank documents for 59 years (55 years allowed in tax credit deals).
next_deadline: No multifamily RFP open as of Nov 2026. The acquisition and rehabilitation round (about $10,000,000) was expected in early 2026 and the Home Together 2030 plan due summer 2026 will set the next capital rounds; sign up for the HCD developer list. Awards of March 3, 2026 require construction starts within 12 months.
layering_notes: The largest new local source in the state outside Los Angeles: a dedicated $1,400,000,000 homelessness fund with a capital line and, unusually, a 15-year capitalized operating subsidy that lets PSH units pencil without PBVs. Loan terms follow Appendix B of the RFP: 3% simple interest, 59-year term, payments amortized, deferred for ELI special needs projects, or from residual receipts with the general partner allowed up to 50% as an incentive management fee. The RFP requires California prevailing wage even where state law would not. The 2026 awards were sized to make 4% and 9% deals and Homekey+ applications competitive, so the realistic ask is $175,000 to $225,000 per homeless unit as last-in money. The services side of the fund (rental subsidies, flexible housing pool, shelter rates) is run by H&H, not HCD. Sources opened: HCD Measure W page, funding opportunities page, the revised RFP PDF, the July 30, 2025 Board presentation and the Home Together FAQ.

program_name: Measure A1 Rental Housing Development Fund (Base City Allocations, Regional Pools, Innovation and Opportunity Fund)
administering_agency: Alameda County Housing and Community Development Department (Measure A1 bond program)
typical_award_size: $580,000,000 general obligation bond approved by 73% of voters in Nov 2016, fully issued by 2021. Rental Development Fund of $425,000,000: a $225,000,000 Base City Allocation (every city and the unincorporated area by housing need) and a $200,000,000 Regional Pool awarded through competitive rounds in four regions, plus the $35,000,000 Innovation and Opportunity Fund ($25,000,000 Acquisition and Opportunity, $10,000,000 Innovation) and $21,500,000 moved from homeownership to the OakDays and Edes Avenue Homekey conversions. Status at June 30, 2026: 56 rental projects and 4,271 homes committed (1,360 for people exiting homelessness), $414,900,000 of A1 capital committed to rental development, 41 projects with 3,139 homes complete, 15 with 1,132 homes under construction or in predevelopment, $486,800,000 (84%) of the bond spent. Annual Report 4 showed only $30,200,000 of rental development funds uncommitted at mid-2022. Current openings are small Innovation and Opportunity pieces: the Tax-Defaulted Property Development Loan program (up to $3,000,000) and the Emerging Developers Predevelopment Loan program ($7,000,000, awards near $500,000, due Dec 2, 2024). A 2026 Program Income plan sets aside $3,100,000 for a senior ADU program.
per_unit_cap: Set by the 2017 Rental Housing Development policies and each city's base allocation; Regional Pool awards typically ran $5,000,000 to $15,000,000 per project. Each A1 dollar leveraged about $6 to $7 of other funds.
affordability_requirement: Households at or below 60% AMI with 20% of A1-assisted units for households at or below 20% AMI; 55-year County regulatory agreement; priority populations include seniors, veterans, people with disabilities, essential workers and people leaving homelessness or incarceration.
next_deadline: Base City and Regional Pool dollars are essentially committed; remaining A1 money is program income and Innovation and Opportunity funds offered through HCD's fall affordable housing RFP and over-the-counter predevelopment loans. Confirm balances with HCD before counting on A1; the County's 2025 Housing Plan is studying a successor revenue measure.
layering_notes: A1 was the backbone of East Bay gap financing from 2018 to 2024 and is now largely spent, which is why Measure W capital matters. Loans use the standard HCD terms (3% simple, 55 to 59 years, residual receipts). Many cities still hold uncommitted base allocation balances they control locally (Pass 3), and the County reporting site lists every project by city. Bond proceeds are public funds, so state prevailing wage applies. Figures from measurea1.acgov.org (opened) and Annual Report 4 (opened); the 2017 policies PDF on achcd.org is image-only and was not readable.

program_name: HOME Consortium and Urban County CDBG affordable housing development loans (annual HCD RFP)
administering_agency: Alameda County Housing and Community Development Department, HOME Consortium lead agency and Urban County CDBG administrator; CDBG 510-670-5971, CDBG@acgov.org
typical_award_size: HCD issues one competitive affordable housing development RFP each fall combining HOME (Consortium CHDO and Urban County shares), remaining Measure A1 and other local funds; applications are due about eight weeks after release with a mandatory bidders conference. HOME Consortium: Alameda, Fremont, Hayward, Livermore, Pleasanton, San Leandro, Union City and the Urban County (all cities except Oakland and Berkeley, which are their own participating jurisdictions); the City of Alameda's FY 2026-27 draft Action Plan reports the Consortium's 2025 HOME allocation as $1,475,257, a figure to confirm with HCD. Urban County CDBG covers the unincorporated area plus Albany, Dublin, Emeryville, Newark and Piedmont, which administer their own shares; the unincorporated CDBG RFP runs December or January with applications due March or April and contracts July 1. State ESG to the County for the CoC: $402,650 (2024). Past procurements: 2023 HOME Capital RFP, 2024 CDBG NOFA (due Jan 19, 2024).
per_unit_cap: HOME maximum per-unit subsidy limits (24 CFR 92.250); County loans sized to the gap.
affordability_requirement: HOME: households at or below 80% AMI at HOME rents for 55 years under County documents (59-year regulatory agreement standard, 55 allowed for tax credit projects); CDBG: low and moderate income benefit. 15% of Consortium HOME reserved for CHDOs.
next_deadline: Fall 2026 RFP date not posted as of Nov 6, 2026; HCD's funding opportunities page says the RFP is issued each fall. Unincorporated CDBG applications are due March or April 2027 for FY 2027-28.
layering_notes: Federal money is a small share of Alameda County's stack: the Consortium's HOME is a few million dollars a year spread across eight members, so the County's own awards are typically under $1,000,000 and ride on the same fall RFP as Measure A1 and local funds. Davis-Bacon applies to HOME projects with 12 or more assisted units; County loans carry state prevailing wage. HCD also administers HOPWA housing for the Oakland area and runs AC Boost, Renew AC and the AC Housing Secure programs from the same department. The County's own FY 2026-27 Action Plan PDF (47MB Consolidated Plan link) was not opened; figures come from the HCD CDBG page, the funding opportunities page and the City of Alameda's draft plan.

program_name: Permanent Local Housing Allocation (PLHA), Alameda County Urban County entitlement
administering_agency: Alameda County Housing and Community Development Department (HCD entitlement grantee for the Urban County)
typical_award_size: HCD 2024-2028 Formula Allocation NOFA: Alameda County CY 2024 $655,510, CY 2025 $702,148, five-year estimate $4,096,938; the 2020 entitlement formula amount was $933,865. The County's PLHA Five-Year Plan and the uses of its formula funds were not located on achcd.org.
affordability_requirement: PLHA statute: rental development for households at or below 80% AMI (workforce up to 120% allowed) with 55-year covenants; 2024 NOFA requires 40% of new funds for affordable owner-occupied workforce housing unless the plan is amended.
next_deadline: HCD formula allocations arrive annually; ask Alameda County HCD how PLHA is programmed and whether it is folded into the fall development RFP. Oakland, Berkeley, Fremont, Hayward and the other entitlement cities receive their own PLHA (Pass 3).
layering_notes: Under $1,000,000 a year for the Urban County and not visible as a separate developer source; treat as a possible add-on inside the HCD RFP. State funds, so prevailing wage applies. Amounts from the HCD 2024-2028 PLHA formula NOFA (opened this pass); County plan not found.

program_name: Multifamily Housing Revenue Bonds, County of Alameda conduit issuer
administering_agency: Alameda County Housing and Community Development Department (issuer staff) with the Board of Supervisors
typical_award_size: The County issues tax-exempt multifamily housing revenue bonds on request: example, up to $24,000,000 for SAHA's 51-unit 3268 San Pablo Apartments in Oakland (inducement Oct 9, 2018, bond resolution April 23, 2019, CDLAC Resolution 19-011). Issuer fees per that regulatory agreement: an issuance fee at closing and an annual fee of the greater of 0.125% of outstanding principal or $7,500 for the qualified project period. No 2025 or 2026 County bond issuances were located; CMFA issued for Eden Housing in Dublin, RCD in Berkeley and the Housing Authority of the City of Alameda in that period.
affordability_requirement: CDLAC and Section 142(d) minimums (20% at 50% AMI or 40% at 60% AMI) under a County regulatory agreement; County-financed projects typically carry deeper restrictions.
next_deadline: Tied to CDLAC rounds: TEFRA hearing and inducement resolution by the Board before the CDLAC application, then a bond resolution before closing. Ask HCD whether it will issue; most recent East Bay deals used CMFA or CSCDA.
layering_notes: The County will act as issuer for projects it also funds, which keeps monitoring under one regulatory agreement, but it is not an active conduit shop. Bonds alone do not trigger state prevailing wage; County A1, Measure W or HOME loans in the deal do. Terms read from the April 23, 2019 Board letter and regulatory agreement (opened); confirm current fees with HCD.

program_name: Project-Based Vouchers, Housing Authority of the County of Alameda (HACA)
administering_agency: Housing Authority of the County of Alameda, 22941 Atherton Street, Hayward, 510-538-8876; developer verifications through Jennifer Cado
typical_award_size: HACA administers 7,145 vouchers (6,973 leased at July 1, 2026): 6,361 Housing Choice, 425 VASH, 289 Mainstream, 15 EHV. HACA's Administrative Plan (Chapter 17) allows project-basing up to 30% of voucher budget authority, allocated over a multi-year period through RFPs. The November 2021 RFP offered up to 160 PBVs for new construction serving seniors, homeless families and veterans and for existing Homekey projects in Albany, Hayward, Newark and the unincorporated area; selected projects were Downtown Hayward Senior, Mission Paradise (Hayward), Albany Family Apartments, Newark Towne Place Suites, Cherryland Place and Timber Senior Housing (Newark). PBV unit totals are not published.
per_unit_cap: HUD PBV caps (20% of authorized units plus 10% for homeless, veteran, supportive services and low-poverty units); rents at the lower of reasonable rent or 110% of FMR with HACA payment standards and utility allowances.
affordability_requirement: Households at or below 50% AMI at admission (75% at or below 30% AMI); HAP contracts up to 20 years with extension; HACA referral and waitlist rules per the Administrative Plan.
next_deadline: No PBV RFP open as of Nov 2026; the last was Nov 18 to Dec 3, 2021. HACA jurisdiction: Albany, Dublin, Emeryville, Fremont, Hayward, Newark, Pleasanton, San Leandro, Union City and all unincorporated areas; Oakland, Berkeley, Alameda and Livermore have their own housing authorities (Pass 3). HACA will issue verification letters for CTCAC, CDLAC and CalHFA applications on request.
layering_notes: HACA PBVs are the operating subsidy for County-funded PSH outside Oakland and Berkeley; Measure W's capitalized operating subsidy reserve is the fallback when PBVs are unavailable. A HAP contract is not a prevailing wage trigger, but Davis-Bacon applies to PBV new construction or rehab of nine or more contract units. HACA is not a Moving to Work agency. Sources opened: HACA developers page, program data at-a-glance, jurisdiction page and the County HCD bulletin announcing the 2021 RFP.

program_name: Unincorporated inclusionary zoning and ministerial approval ordinances (in development) and state density bonus
administering_agency: Alameda County Community Development Agency, Planning Department (unincorporated area)
typical_award_size: No county inclusionary ordinance, in-lieu fee or affordable housing impact fee exists today. The Planning Department received $280,000 and hired Street Level Advisors to draft an Inclusionary Zoning Ordinance and a Ministerial Approval Ordinance to meet MTC's Transit-Oriented Communities policy (Bay Fair and Castro Valley BART areas) and Housing Element Program 6.J; draft ordinances for public comment early 2027, adoption recommendations spring 2027, completion by July 1, 2027. Working concepts: rental projects averaging 80% AMI or less (units 30% to 120% AMI), ownership averaging 120% AMI or less, ministerial approval for projects of 11 or more units meeting the set-aside, alternatives of in-lieu fee, off-site units or land dedication. Density bonus follows Government Code 65915 (state law), and the County code already allows ministerial approval for ADUs under 800 square feet.
affordability_requirement: Pending; MTC TOC minimums expected (about 10% to 20% affordable depending on tier). State density bonus units: 55 years for rental.
next_deadline: Not yet adopted. Watch the Unincorporated Services Committee and Planning Commission in 2026 and 2027; draft financial feasibility analysis dated July 2026 is posted on the policies page. State density bonus is available now by right.
layering_notes: Alameda County unincorporated areas (Ashland, Cherryland, San Lorenzo, Castro Valley, Fairview, Sunol) have no local inclusionary production or fee revenue, so county-controlled affordable housing there depends on A1, Measure W and HACA. Expect an inclusionary requirement on market-rate projects entitled after mid-2027. Density bonus alone does not trigger prevailing wage. Sources opened: County affordable housing production policies page and the Jan 26, 2026 staff report.

program_name: Development fee waiver for affordable housing (no countywide program)
administering_agency: Alameda County Community Development Agency
typical_award_size: None adopted. The County's 2025 Housing Plan lists an affordable housing impact fee on commercial development as a future unincorporated revenue option and does not describe any fee waiver or deferral program.
affordability_requirement: Not applicable.
next_deadline: Not applicable. Budget full County and special district fees in unincorporated deals; permit fees are an eligible use of County loans.
layering_notes: Negative finding. Labor Code 1720(b)(4) counts waived fees as public funds for prevailing wage purposes. Housing Plan (10-Year Housing Strategy 2025-2035, approved July 2025) opened.

program_name: Welfare Exemption (property tax), Alameda County Assessor
administering_agency: Alameda County Assessor, Phong La, 1221 Oak Street, Room 145, Oakland; Other Exemptions Unit 510-272-6587, exemptions@acgov.org
typical_award_size: Full or partial exemption of property tax on units occupied by households at or below 80% AMI under Revenue and Taxation Code 214(g); worth roughly 1.1% to 1.4% of assessed value a year depending on the tax rate area (Alameda County has high voter-approved debt rates). The Assessor posts the full BOE-267 series (267, 267-L, L1, L2, L3, L4, H, R and income worksheets) and asks claimants to contact the exemptions unit before filing with the parcel number.
per_unit_cap: Statewide $20,000,000 aggregate cap on exempted assessed value for limited partnership projects that qualify only through the managing general partner test without government financing (Rev. and Tax. Code 214(g)); projects with tax credits, bonds or government loans are outside the cap.
affordability_requirement: Nonprofit or LP with eligible nonprofit managing general partner holding a BOE Organizational Clearance Certificate (and Supplemental Clearance Certificate for LP low-income housing); units restricted by recorded regulatory agreement or occupied by households at or below 80% AMI; BOE-267 first filing and annual supplemental affidavits by Feb 15 (late claims receive a reduced exemption under Rev. and Tax. Code 270).
next_deadline: 2027-02-15 (annual claim deadline for the 2027-28 roll). File the first claim on acquisition so the construction period is covered.
layering_notes: Standard in every tax credit operating budget; underwrite only the restricted units and confirm the managing GP's OCC and SCC before closing. The Assessor's exemptions page (opened) gives the unit contact and forms but no local deadline text; the BOE's Alameda income limit letter governs tenant qualification.

program_name: Oakland-Berkeley-Alameda County Continuum of Care (CA-502) and HHAP
administering_agency: Alameda County Health, Housing and Homelessness Services (CoC lead and HHAP administrator for the County and CoC allocations); City of Oakland administers its own HHAP
typical_award_size: HHAP by round, County of Alameda: R1 $8,700,000, R2 $4,000,000, R3 $11,200,000, R4 $12,100,000, R5 $13,463,754, R6 $10,783,302. CoC: R1 $9,400,000, R2 $4,500,000, R3 $12,000,000, R4 $12,900,000, R5 $14,033,347, R6 $11,516,752. City of Oakland: R5 $28,446,566, R6 about $23,000,000; regional R6 total $45,300,000 (awarded March 2, 2026). State accountability site: $210,100,000 HHAP rounds 1 to 5 in the Alameda area, $102,500,000 directly to the County ($78,100,000 obligated, $60,500,000 spent by mid-2025); Encampment Resolution Funding $30,600,000 in the area. HUD CoC program FY 2024 awards to CA-502: $16,901,825 including Shelter Plus Care TRA $9,129,290, Housing Fast Support Network $2,619,550, YHDP $1,934,338 and Linkages $1,734,446. State ESG CoC share $402,650 (2024). 2024 PIT: 9,450 people, 6,343 unsheltered, 9,963 year-round beds. HHAP uses in the County: Coordinated Entry access points, street health and outreach, HMIS, Emerging Leaders, regional interim housing (safe parking, shelters, navigation centers) and local match for Medi-Cal Housing Community Supports.
affordability_requirement: People experiencing or at risk of homelessness per HUD and state definitions; CoC permanent housing through Coordinated Entry; HHAP-6 must obligate 75% and spend 50% by June 30, 2027, and the County needs a compliant housing element for the second half of its Round 6 award.
next_deadline: HHAP-6 regional application was due Aug 29, 2025 and awarded March 2026; HHAP-7 is available to HHAP-6 grantees. The CoC's HUD NOFO competition runs each summer through EveryOne Home; letters of interest are collected by the County. Home Together 2030 (summer 2026) sets system priorities.
layering_notes: HHAP here pays for coordinated entry, outreach, interim housing and services rather than capital; Measure W now dwarfs it and is the County's capital and operating subsidy source for PSH. Oakland and Berkeley projects should look to those cities' HHAP and CoC shares (Pass 3). CoC permanent housing dollars are mostly Shelter Plus Care tenant-based assistance. Figures from the July 17, 2025 County and Oakland HHAP-6 presentation (opened), HCD HHAP allocation lists, the HUD FY 2025 CoC award report and accountability.ca.gov.

program_name: Behavioral Health Services Act (BHSA) housing interventions, Alameda County Behavioral Health Department
administering_agency: Alameda County Behavioral Health Department (ACBHD), Alameda County Health, with Housing and Homelessness Services for the flexible housing subsidy pool
typical_award_size: Integrated Plan FY 2026-29 approved by the Board of Supervisors June 16, 2026 (public hearing April 20, 2026). BHSA budget authority about $166,188,844 a year; Housing Interventions component $37,306,397 (FY 2026-27), $41,735,347 (FY 2027-28), $44,221,971 (FY 2028-29); 52% dedicated to chronically homeless people; outreach and engagement 5% to 6%. Uses: rental subsidies, operating subsidies for existing and new PSH units (about 990 people a year), flexible housing subsidy pool, landlord mitigation, tenancy sustaining services. Capital development share: 0% in all three years; the plan states the County will consider capital development projects as needed once the BHSA transition is complete.
per_unit_cap: None; no capital program planned. Statute would allow up to 25% of the housing component for capital.
affordability_requirement: Adults, older adults, youth and families with serious mental illness or substance use disorder who are chronically homeless, homeless or at risk; Housing First; ACBHD eligibility and Coordinated Entry referral for PSH units.
next_deadline: Plan in effect July 1, 2026 with annual updates each spring; no capital NOFA. Ask ACBHD and H&H about project-based operating subsidies and flexible pool commitments for PSH units; capital requests should go to Measure W Home Together Fund instead.
layering_notes: Unlike Orange and Contra Costa, Alameda chose not to put BHSA money into capital, so BHSA is an operating and services partner only: pair a BHSA operating subsidy or flex pool commitment with Measure W capital and HACA or city PBVs. State funds would trigger prevailing wage if capital were ever offered. Figures from the June 16, 2026 Board item (304 pages, opened) and the approved plan PDF and executive summary on acbhsa.org.

program_name: County boomerang funds for housing and homelessness (former redevelopment residual property tax)
administering_agency: Alameda County Board of Supervisors through Housing and Community Development and Health, Housing and Homelessness Services
typical_award_size: 2017 policy: 20% of the prior year's boomerang receipts, $5,000,000 minimum and $7,500,000 maximum a year, as a five-year commitment starting FY 2016-17 ($5,000,000 in FY 2016-17 and FY 2017-18) for housing resource centers and coordinated entry ($2,000,000 a year), anti-displacement crisis services ($3,500,000 initial) and other Home Together system costs; a one-time $9,800,000 boomerang allocation seeded Measure A1 implementation. HCD still lists boomerang funds among its development sources and recent HCD project commitments cite boomerang dollars, but no current annual amount or policy was located and the 2025 Housing Plan does not list it as a revenue source.
affordability_requirement: Follows the program funded; development uses carry County loan terms (3% simple, 55 to 59 years, at or below 80% AMI).
next_deadline: Unknown; ask HCD whether boomerang funds remain in the fall development RFP or were absorbed into Measure W planning.
layering_notes: Recorded as needs_confirmation because the only document opened is the 2017 EveryOne Home implementation deck describing the five-year commitment; the acgov HCD page that listed boomerang funds now redirects to achcd.org without that text. Public funds, so prevailing wage applies. Housing successor (LMIHAF) reporting for the former Alameda County Redevelopment Agency was not found.

program_name: San Mateo County Affordable Housing Fund (AHF) annual NOFA (Measure K, County impact fees, MHSA/BHSA, PLHA, HOME)
administering_agency: San Mateo County Department of Housing (DOH), Housing and Community Development division, 264 Harbor Blvd, Building A, Belmont; Raymond Hodges, Director; applications through OpenGov (procurement.opengov.com/portal/smcgov)
typical_award_size: AHF 14.0 (released April 20, 2026, pre-application meeting by April 30, applications due May 20, 2026): $29,347,311 offered, made up of $24,247,311 Measure K ($19,000,000 new FY 2026-27 plus $5,247,311 recaptured), $100,000 County impact fees (unincorporated projects only) and $5,000,000 MHSA/BHSA. Ten applications sought more than $70,000,000 for 810 units. Board awards Aug 25, 2026: $24,347,311 to six projects totaling 459 units: Sand Hill Rise City, Redwood City $9,389,000 (94 units); Mercy Housing 555 Kelly, Half Moon Bay $6,575,000 (40); Related 1051 Mission, South San Francisco $3,545,414 (158, plus $9,495,420 from AHF 11); MidPen 626 Walnut, San Carlos $3,000,000 (95, County-owned site); Novin 3051 Edison, North Fair Oaks $1,537,897 Measure K and impact fees (70); Habitat Ladera, Portola Valley $300,000 (2 ownership units). AHF 13.0 (NOFA June 2, 2025, due July 3, 2025): $41,146,470 to nine projects on Oct 7, 2025 from $19,000,000 new Measure K, $18,022,198 recaptured Measure K, $824,272 PLHA, $100,000 impact fees, MHSA and HHAP. Since 2013 the AHF has awarded more than $400,000,000 to 63 projects and 4,522 units (2,339 occupied, 588 under construction, 1,595 in predevelopment).
per_unit_cap: No general per-unit cap. MHSA/BHSA units capped at $200,000 per restricted unit; minimum award $100,000 per project; projects in incorporated cities that are not supportive housing are capped at 15% of total development cost in cumulative County funds; first-time homeownership projects share a $1,000,000 cap and rehabilitation projects a $2,000,000 cap per round.
affordability_requirement: Units typically 30% to 60% AMI with a 55-year County regulatory agreement from completion (57 years from recording of the deed of trust); at least 5% of low-income units (or two units) reserved with a preference for people experiencing homelessness at 30% AMI with tenant-based subsidies and referrals held open 60 days; MHSA/BHSA units for behavioral health referrals at 30% AMI with PBVs or 20% AMI without; studio and one-bedroom rents assumed at no more than 50% AMI and larger units at 60% AMI.
next_deadline: The DOH funding page lists the next Affordable Housing Development NOFA for fall 2027; AHF 14 closed in May 2026 and its awards were approved Aug 25, 2026. Recaptured funds are offered between rounds through an over-the-counter process (NOFA Appendix C). Pre-application meetings are mandatory and applications require third-party commitments of at least the lesser of $1,000,000 or $20,000 per unit.
layering_notes: The Peninsula's main gap source: about $19,000,000 of new Measure K sales tax a year plus recaptured funds, MHSA/BHSA capital, HACSM Moving to Work money and whatever HOME and PLHA the County holds, all run through one annual NOFA. Terms (Appendix D): 3% simple interest from certificate of occupancy, 55-year term, annual payments of at least 50% of residual receipts to the County (two-thirds pooled pro rata when other public soft lenders share), deferred developer fee paid only from the borrower share, DOH will not cut its rate unless the host city and state lenders do the same. Measure K and impact fees do not trigger Davis-Bacon, but the application requires a state prevailing wage determination and all projects must comply with the County Living Wage Ordinance, so budget prevailing wage. Awards are explicitly sized to make 4% and 9% tax credit, AHSC and Homekey+ applications competitive and ranked on readiness. The NOFA does not award PBVs; HACSM must issue its own commitment letter. Documents opened: AHF 14 NOFA PDF and Appendix D underwriting guidelines, the July 29, 2026 HCDC hearing deck, and Board items 25-838 and 26-679 via the Legistar API.

program_name: Winter NOFA: HOME Consortium, Urban County CDBG, ESG and PLHA (annual federal and state funds round)
administering_agency: San Mateo County Department of Housing, Housing and Community Development division, as HOME Consortium lead and Urban County CDBG grantee
typical_award_size: FY 2026-27 Winter NOFA (issued Dec 2, 2025, applications due Jan 15, 2026, HCDC hearing March 12, Board April 21, 2026) sources: CDBG $2,315,528 plus $347,644 program income and returned funds; HOME $1,485,482 plus $1,428,857 program income and returned funds; federal ESG $208,430; state ESG $165,356; PLHA $0 (held pending housing element compliance); City of East Palo Alto minor home repair $125,000; total $6,076,297. Uses: $2,000,000 HOME for new affordable housing and preservation, $717,035 HOME CHDO set-aside left unallocated for an over-the-counter award, $620,815 CDBG rehab and public facilities, $493,716 Section 108 loan repayment (Trestle Glen). The December 2025 notice estimated about $5,000,000 in total CDBG, HOME and related funds; a separate capital projects guideline listed about $3,317,010 CDBG for capital and $1,738,713 for community development based on FY 2025-26 levels.
per_unit_cap: HOME maximum per-unit subsidy limits (HUD bulletin effective Feb 13, 2024) apply to HOME-assisted units.
affordability_requirement: HOME: households at or below 80% AMI at HOME rents, 55-year County regulatory agreement (HOME units become AHF-restricted units for the balance of the 55 years when the HOME period is shorter); CDBG: low and moderate income benefit; County loan terms as in the AHF underwriting guidelines.
next_deadline: FY 2027-28 Winter NOFA to be released Dec 1, 2026 after the HCDC needs hearing on Oct 22, 2026; applications are typically due mid-January with Board approval in April. Housing capital applicants should also watch the fall AHF round.
layering_notes: Urban County: unincorporated area plus Atherton, Belmont, Brisbane, Burlingame, Colma, East Palo Alto, Foster City, Half Moon Bay, Hillsborough, Menlo Park, Millbrae, Pacifica, Portola Valley, San Bruno, San Carlos and Woodside. HOME Consortium: the Urban County plus Redwood City, San Mateo and South San Francisco (Daly City is its own entitlement, Pass 3). Federal money is small next to Measure K, so HOME usually appears as a $1,000,000 to $2,000,000 piece inside an AHF-funded project. Davis-Bacon applies to HOME projects with 12 or more assisted units and CDBG projects with eight or more; County loans also carry state prevailing wage and the County Living Wage Ordinance. Sources opened: Winter NOFA page, FY 2026-27 Action Plan sources and uses PDF, FY 2027-28 hearing notice.

program_name: Permanent Local Housing Allocation (PLHA), San Mateo County entitlement
administering_agency: San Mateo County Department of Housing (HCD entitlement grantee)
typical_award_size: 2019-2023 five-year formula estimate $7,257,300 (CY 2021 funds $2,068,889). Calendar year 2022 and 2023 funds of $1,831,715 ($1,036,938 plus $794,777) were authorized Dec 2, 2025 and awarded by HCD in July 2026 after the County's housing element came into compliance; $824,272 is committed through AHF 13 (moved from Laurel Landing to Rotary Gardens on Aug 25, 2026) and the balance is being allocated over the counter. HCD 2024-2028 Formula Allocation NOFA estimates: CY 2024 $849,022, CY 2025 $909,428, five-year $5,306,388.
affordability_requirement: County PLHA plan funds Activity 1 (rental development for extremely low to moderate income households with 55-year covenants through the AHF process) and Activity 6 (homeless services, shelter and navigation center operations and case management); 2024 HCD rule requires 40% of new funds for affordable owner-occupied workforce housing unless amended.
next_deadline: PLHA is offered through the AHF NOFA, the Winter NOFA and over-the-counter processes as HCD releases each year's funds; CY 2022 and 2023 money must be spent on HCD's deadlines, which drove the Aug 2026 reallocation. Ask DOH whether CY 2024 and 2025 funds will appear in the fall 2027 AHF round.
layering_notes: Small and lumpy because HCD withheld San Mateo's PLHA for several years over housing element compliance; the County treats it as a swap source inside AHF awards (PLHA to the project closing soonest, Measure K to the slower one). State funds trigger prevailing wage. Figures from Board items 25-1006 and 26-706 read through the Legistar API and the HCD 2024-2028 PLHA NOFA.

program_name: Housing Endowment and Regional Trust of San Mateo County (HEART) developer loans
administering_agency: HEART of San Mateo County, joint powers authority of the County and 20 cities and towns; 2905 S. El Camino Real, San Mateo; Armando Sanchez 650-204-5640
typical_award_size: HEART reports $57,000,000 invested in affordable housing development. Two products: QuickStart (up to five years, predevelopment, acquisition, construction or rehab, principal deferred to maturity) and SemiPerm (five to 15 years including extensions, interest-only or amortized on a 30-year schedule with balloon, for acquisition, predevelopment, refinancing and rehab). Rates are described as favorable and competitive and quoted on request; origination fee 2% of loans up to $2,000,000 and 1.5% above, $3,000 application fee, borrower pays lender legal and third-party costs; loan size depends on project financials and repayment source. Recent County relationships: a $2,400,000 agreement (June 16, 2026) for HEART to run the County's mobile home replacement loan program, and a $450,000 HEART loan in HEART-SV's plan to take over Visitacion Gardens in Brisbane (May 2026). Funded projects include Montara at Bay Meadows, Ocean View, Peninsula Station, Trestle Glen, Hillcrest Senior, Serenity Senior, Fair Oaks Commons, The Village at the Crossing and 2000 South Delaware.
affordability_requirement: Up to 120% AMI (workforce) with a 55-year affordability covenant on a number of units commensurate with HEART's share, deferring to other funders' covenants when sufficient; projects must be in a member jurisdiction (the County and 20 cities and towns: Atherton, Belmont, Brisbane, Burlingame, Colma, Daly City, East Palo Alto, Foster City, Half Moon Bay, Hillsborough, Menlo Park, Millbrae, Pacifica, Portola Valley, Redwood City, San Bruno, San Carlos, San Mateo, South San Francisco, Woodside and the County) with an adopted or under-review housing element.
next_deadline: Rolling; contact HEART for current rates and available funds. The 2026 Board report notes HEART is restructuring programs (first-time homebuyer loans ended Jan 28, 2026). HEART also runs an ADU design center and received state LHTF matching grants in past rounds.
layering_notes: HEART is bridge and acquisition money, not permanent gap financing: use QuickStart to tie up a site or carry predevelopment until an AHF award and tax credits close, then take out the loan. Member dues are population based and the County administers HEART, so it reads as a county-level source even though cities co-own it. Public agency funds, so assume state prevailing wage applies to construction financed with HEART loans. Term sheets (May 24, 2023) and member list opened on heartofsmc.org.

program_name: Project-Based Vouchers, Housing Authority of the County of San Mateo (HACSM, Moving to Work agency)
administering_agency: Housing Authority of the County of San Mateo, a division of the Department of Housing, 264 Harbor Blvd, Belmont, 650-802-3300; housing@smchousing.org
typical_award_size: HACSM assists about 4,600 households and project-bases 1,930 vouchers (FY 2027 MTW Plan), with 36 new PBVs planned for 493 Eastmoor Avenue in Daly City (72 units). As an MTW agency since 1998 HACSM may project-base up to 40% of budget authority (raised from 35% in FY 2021) and awards PBVs through periodic RFPs: the last offered 200 Section 8 PBVs and 35 HUD-VASH PBVs for new construction (released Dec 2022, due Dec 30, 2022, awards Jan 2023), with at least 25% of PBVs as supportive housing units, 50% on two- and three-bedroom units, and a per-project cap of about 50% of units (waivable for supportive housing). In Jan 2025 DOH told Homekey+ applicants no PBVs were available. HACSM also provides HAP contracts up to 20 years and the County Housing Voucher Program (local funds) for Homekey sites such as Casa Esperanza.
per_unit_cap: MTW cap of 40% of budget authority agency-wide; project cap about 50% of units except supportive housing; rents per HACSM payment standards and MTW rent policies.
affordability_requirement: Households at or below 50% AMI at admission with ELI targeting; supportive housing units for homeless and special needs households referred through Coordinated Entry; new construction only in the last RFP; 20-year HAP contracts with extensions.
next_deadline: No PBV RFP open as of Nov 2026 and none since Dec 2022; the AHF NOFA states applications may not assume PBVs without an existing HACSM award letter. Watch the DOH NOFAs, Bids and Proposals page and the annual MTW Plan (FY 2027 plan posted 2026) for the next solicitation. HACSM covers the entire county; no city in San Mateo County runs its own housing authority.
layering_notes: HACSM is the operating subsidy partner for every County-funded PSH deal and uses MTW flexibility to award PBVs in bulk (1,930 outstanding), but supply is tight and awards come through RFPs rather than the AHF NOFA. A HAP contract is not a prevailing wage trigger; Davis-Bacon applies to PBV new construction or rehab of nine or more contract units. HACSM also recycles MTW HAP reserves into the Affordable Housing Fund (separate record). Sources opened: 2022 RFP page and PDF, FY 2027 MTW Annual Plan, Homekey+ RFP Q&A.

program_name: HACSM Moving to Work funds for affordable housing development (through the Affordable Housing Fund)
administering_agency: Housing Authority of the County of San Mateo (MTW Activity 2011-16 and development activity) with the Department of Housing
typical_award_size: HUD has approved HACSM's use of unspent HAP reserves (MTW funds) for affordable housing development in steps: $4,000,000 originally, $8,000,000 (FY 2013), $10,000,000 (FY 2016), $25,000,000 (FY 2020), $35,000,000 (FY 2024) and $65,000,000 (FY 2025). The FY 2027 MTW Plan reports $65,000,000 of MTW funds approved for the Affordable Housing Fund, including $7,900,000 for Ridge at Ralston in Belmont and $8,600,000 for 493 Eastmoor in Daly City.
per_unit_cap: None published; awards are sized with the AHF underwriting.
affordability_requirement: Low, very low and extremely low income rental housing in San Mateo County; HACSM loans are typically zero interest with principal repaid from residual receipts under the AHF loan documents, 55-year covenants.
next_deadline: Allocated through the AHF NOFA when HACSM has reserves to contribute; next AHF round expected fall 2027. Ask DOH whether HACSM funds are in the pool before applying.
layering_notes: Unusual source: HUD lets this MTW agency lend its unspent voucher money as capital, and the County has pushed the ceiling to $65,000,000. It arrives inside an AHF award as a zero-interest residual receipts loan, which helps cash flow versus the County's 3% Measure K loan. Federal HAP money carries Davis-Bacon and Section 3; state prevailing wage applies through the County loan. Read from the FY 2027 MTW Annual Plan PDF (opened).

program_name: Tax-exempt multifamily bonds: County TEFRA approvals for CMFA, CSCDA and CEDA issuances (County not an active issuer)
administering_agency: San Mateo County Board of Supervisors with the County Attorney (TEFRA hearings); bonds issued by the California Municipal Finance Authority, California Statewide Communities Development Authority or California Enterprise Development Authority
typical_award_size: The County is a member of CMFA, CSCDA and CEDA and holds the required TEFRA hearings for projects in the unincorporated area or where it is the member jurisdiction: CMFA bonds up to $11,000,000 for Mercy Housing's 42-unit 903 Oceana Boulevard rehabilitation in Pacifica (April 7, 2026), plus CMFA (May 6, 2025), CEDA and CSCDA (June 10, 2025) hearings. CMFA shares part of its issuance fee with the County. No County-issued multifamily housing revenue bonds were found in 2025 or 2026 Board records.
affordability_requirement: CDLAC and Section 142(d) minimums (20% at 50% AMI or 40% at 60% AMI) under the JPA issuer's regulatory agreement; County loans in the same project add 55-year County restrictions.
next_deadline: Schedule the TEFRA hearing with the County Attorney's office at least seven days after newspaper notice and before the CDLAC application; the Board hears these on consent. For projects inside cities, the city holds the hearing.
layering_notes: Expect to use CMFA or CSCDA as issuer in San Mateo County; the County's role is the TEFRA approval and a small fee share, with no County credit or staff involvement. Bonds alone do not trigger state prevailing wage; AHF, HOME or HACSM money in the deal does. Board item 26-255 read through the Legistar API.

program_name: Inclusionary Affordable Housing Ordinance (2004) with 2026 rezoning amendments, County affordable housing impact fees, and state density bonus
administering_agency: San Mateo County Planning and Building Department, 455 County Center, Redwood City; impact fees deposited to the Department of Housing's Housing Trust Fund
typical_award_size: Multifamily projects of five or more units in the unincorporated area must make 20% of units affordable, typically to lower income households (a rental project of five to nine units may provide its one required unit at moderate income; ownership projects may provide half at moderate income), with in-lieu fees, off-site units, land dedication or rehabilitation of existing affordable units allowed at the County's sole discretion. Ordinance 4927 (adopted Oct 6, 2026) removes those alternatives and the moderate-income option in the new R3-MD, PC-HD and TS-MU districts rezoned April 21, 2026 in Colma, Broadmoor and the Harbor Industrial area: 20% on site at low, very low or extremely low income. Affordable housing impact fees on residential and non-residential development were adopted in 2016 from a multi-jurisdictional nexus study and fund the AHF ($100,000 offered in each of AHF 13 and 14 for unincorporated projects); a new Multi-Jurisdictional Inclusionary Housing and Non-Residential Linkage Fee Study (Strategic Economics, $619,135, Dec 2025 to June 2027, County share $51,681) will reset fee levels for the County and ten cities. Density bonus follows Government Code 65915; the County enforces state law and has no local bonus beyond it.
affordability_requirement: Inclusionary units at lower income rents or prices for the ordinance term (long-term covenants recorded at entitlement); state density bonus units 55 years for rental.
next_deadline: Not applicable; applies at entitlement. Expect revised impact fee levels after the nexus study concludes in mid-2027. Unincorporated areas include North Fair Oaks, Colma, Broadmoor, Harbor Industrial, the Midcoast and Emerald Hills.
layering_notes: North Fair Oaks and the Colma and Broadmoor rezoning areas are where County inclusionary rules bite; 100% affordable projects satisfy them automatically and take the state density bonus. In-lieu fees and impact fees are small (about $100,000 a year reaches the AHF) because unincorporated development volume is low. Density bonus alone does not trigger prevailing wage. Sources: County inclusionary ordinance page (the ordinance PDF is image-only), Board items 26-817 and 25-1053 and the Oct 6, 2026 Board presentation and Ordinance 4927 (opened).

program_name: Development fee waiver for affordable housing (no countywide program)
administering_agency: San Mateo County Planning and Building Department
typical_award_size: None adopted. The County charges affordable housing impact fees and planning and building fees on unincorporated projects; no waiver or deferral program for affordable housing was found. The AHF NOFA scores local contributions such as land, fee waivers or inclusionary contributions from host cities as leverage toward its $1,000,000 or $20,000 per unit third-party commitment threshold.
affordability_requirement: Not applicable.
next_deadline: Not applicable. Ask the host city for fee waivers; in the unincorporated area budget full County fees.
layering_notes: Negative finding. Labor Code 1720(b)(4) counts waived fees as public funds for prevailing wage purposes. Planning fees page is linked from the County inclusionary ordinance page (opened).

program_name: Welfare Exemption (property tax), San Mateo County Assessor-County Clerk-Recorder
administering_agency: San Mateo County Assessor-County Clerk-Recorder and Elections (ACRE), Mark Church, Assessor; 555 County Center, Redwood City; 650-363-4500; institutional exemptions unit via smcacre.gov contact page
typical_award_size: Full or partial exemption of property tax on units occupied by households at or below 80% AMI under Revenue and Taxation Code 214(g); worth roughly 1.1% or more of assessed value a year depending on the tax rate area. ACRE posts the full BOE-267 series (267, 267-L, L1, L2, L3, L4, H, O, R and income worksheets) and notes the annual BOE-267-A is issued by the office rather than downloaded.
per_unit_cap: Statewide $20,000,000 aggregate cap on exempted assessed value for limited partnership projects that qualify only through the managing general partner test without government financing (Rev. and Tax. Code 214(g)); projects with tax credits, bonds or government loans are outside the cap.
affordability_requirement: Nonprofit or LP with eligible nonprofit managing general partner holding a BOE Organizational Clearance Certificate (plus a Supplemental Clearance Certificate for LP low-income housing); units restricted by recorded regulatory agreement or occupied by households at or below 80% AMI; BOE-267 first filing and annual supplemental affidavits by Feb 15 (late claims receive a reduced exemption under Rev. and Tax. Code 270).
next_deadline: 2027-02-15 (annual claim deadline for the 2027-28 roll). File the first claim on acquisition so the construction period is covered.
layering_notes: Standard in every tax credit operating budget; San Mateo's high assessed values make this the largest operating subsidy most projects receive. ACRE's institutional exemptions and forms pages (opened) list forms and the OCC and SCC requirements but no local deadline text or direct phone; the BOE county contacts page gives the main number.

program_name: Daly City/San Mateo County Continuum of Care (CA-512) and HHAP
administering_agency: San Mateo County Human Services Agency, Center on Homelessness (CoC lead agency and HHAP administrative entity for the County and CoC)
typical_award_size: HHAP joint County and CoC allocations: Round 1 $3,431,246 (Feb 2020), Round 2 $1,597,106, Round 3 $4,375,129, Round 4 $4,658,201, Round 5 $5,237,946 (County $2,564,722, CoC $2,673,224), Round 6 $5,026,361 (County $2,430,522, CoC $2,595,839; accepted June 10, 2025, awarded March 2, 2026, usable through June 30, 2029), about $24,300,000 in all. State accountability site: $19,300,000 HHAP rounds 1 to 5 to the County ($13,800,000 obligated, $11,800,000 spent by mid-2025); Encampment Resolution Funding $16,000,000 in the area, $14,100,000 to the County. HHAP-6 supports operations of the 240-unit Navigation Center in Redwood City. HUD CoC program FY 2024 awards to CA-512: $817,332 (Shelter Plus Care sponsor-based $368,857, Vendome $303,133, Redwood Family House $145,342). State ESG CoC share $188,054 (2024). 2024 PIT: 2,130 people, 1,145 unsheltered, 3,454 year-round beds. Homekey: Casa Esperanza, Redwood City (former Comfort Inn, 51 PSH units, $15,978,232 Homekey plus up to $7,697,170 ARPA match, operated by Episcopal Community Services since 2025 under a 55-year ground lease with County Housing Voucher Program operating subsidies) and a Ramada conversion in South San Francisco with ECS; Homekey+ co-applicant RFP (Jan 15 to Feb 5, 2025) to pair developer teams and sites with County match for 2025 applications.
affordability_requirement: People experiencing or at risk of homelessness per HUD and state definitions; CoC permanent housing through Coordinated Entry; HHAP-6 must obligate 75% and spend 50% by June 30, 2027.
next_deadline: HHAP-7 is available to HHAP-6 grantees; the CoC runs the HUD NOFO each summer. For capital, the County route is the Homekey+ co-applicant process through the Department of Housing and the AHF NOFA's homelessness preference units; HHAP itself funds shelter and services.
layering_notes: A small CoC (about $800,000 a year in HUD renewals) and modest HHAP, so homeless capital comes from Measure K and Homekey rather than CoC money; the County uses its own Housing Voucher Program and HACSM PBVs for operating subsidy at Homekey sites. HHAP figures from the County HSA HHAP page and Board item 25-554 (opened), HCD allocation lists and accountability.ca.gov; Homekey details from Board item 25-249 and the Homekey+ RFP page.

program_name: Behavioral Health Services Act (BHSA) housing interventions and MHSA/BHSA capital through the Affordable Housing Fund
administering_agency: San Mateo County Health, Behavioral Health and Recovery Services (BHRS), with the Department of Housing administering capital awards
typical_award_size: Three-Year Integrated Plan FY 2026-27 to FY 2028-29 approved by the Board June 9, 2026 (Behavioral Health Commission hearing closed March 5, 2026). Housing Interventions expenditures $24,427,542 (FY 2026-27), $24,374,720 (FY 2027-28), $24,374,720 (FY 2028-29); capital development $6,152,822 then $6,100,000 a year (24% of the component, near the 25% cap) delivered through the DOH Affordable Housing Fund NOFAs, where the AHF 14 round carried $5,000,000 of MHSA/BHSA capital at up to $200,000 per restricted unit; the plan lists nine capital projects and a 65-unit PSH pipeline at up to $450,000 per unit. Operating subsidies $3,540,627 plus $2,182,327, bundled rental and operating subsidies about $1,160,000 to $1,460,000, rental subsidies $1,000,000; $12,900,025 a year (51%) dedicated to chronically homeless people; 64 people a year in operating-subsidized units. San Mateo joined the state Flex Pool Technical Assistance Academy.
per_unit_cap: MHSA/BHSA capital capped at $200,000 per restricted unit in the AHF NOFA; BHSA statute caps the housing intervention share at $450,000 per unit.
affordability_requirement: MHSA/BHSA units for BHRS-referred adults with serious mental illness or substance use disorder who are homeless or at risk: 30% AMI with PBVs or 20% AMI without, Housing First, on-site supportive services; 55-year County regulatory agreement through the AHF loan.
next_deadline: Apply through the AHF NOFA (next round expected fall 2027) and meet with BHRS before applying; the plan runs July 1, 2026 to June 30, 2029 with annual updates. Ask BHRS about operating subsidies and transitional rent for MHSA/BHSA units, which the AHF NOFA counts toward its homelessness preference requirement.
layering_notes: San Mateo keeps BHSA capital at the statutory maximum and routes it through the same AHF loan documents as Measure K, so a PSH sponsor can get Measure K plus about $200,000 per BHSA unit in one award with BHRS operating subsidy behind it. State funds trigger prevailing wage. Plan read from the Board attachment on Legistar (final plan PDF, opened); the smchealth.org copies returned 404.

program_name: Marin County Affordable Housing Fund (Housing Trust Fund) and the annual federal and state housing NOFA
administering_agency: Marin County Community Development Agency, Housing and Federal Grants Division, 3501 Civic Center Drive, San Rafael; affordablehousing@marincounty.gov
typical_award_size: The Affordable Housing Fund (also called the Housing Trust Fund) is capitalized by inclusionary in-lieu fees, the single-family Affordable Housing Impact Fee, commercial linkage fees, County general fund appropriations and Measure W housing dollars, and is used both as the local match for PLHA and as standalone loans and grants. Guidelines adopted Dec 12, 2023 run through 2027: awards generally $50,000 per unit, up to $100,000 per unit depending on funds, project type, location and bedrooms, as loans with terms set project by project; projects in cities need a contribution from that city. Recent actions read in Board agendas: $5,239,098 Housing Trust Fund loan to Habitat for Humanity Greater San Francisco for predevelopment and construction (April 15, 2025); $500,000 grant to capitalize a Marin Housing Authority preservation loan pool (June 10, 2025); $300,000 Housing Trust and $210,000 Measure W to the Community Land Trust Association of West Marin for 55/65 Second Street, Point Reyes Station, plus $300,000 for the Sacred Heart rectory in Olema (April 7, 2026); Housing Trust Fund loan documents for Marinwood Plaza (125 units, April 2026); $3,000,000 predevelopment loan to Marin Housing Authority for Golden Gate Village (Dec 5, 2023) restructured April 14, 2026 into a 30-year deferred, interest-free loan. The 2026-27 NOFA (open Jan 19 to Feb 19, 2026) offered about $700,000 HOME and $900,000 PLHA matched by the Affordable Housing Fund; the Board approved FY 2026-27 CDBG, HOME, Housing Trust Fund and PLHA recommendations on June 23, 2026 (Resolution 2026-060), with about $477,000 PLHA to be matched 1:1 by the Trust Fund once the state agreement is signed.
per_unit_cap: Guidelines: generally $50,000 per unit, up to $100,000 per unit in some circumstances (figures from County pages indexed by search; the pages themselves were blocked).
affordability_requirement: Priority to projects in unincorporated Marin and to households at or below 60% AMI when paired with PLHA; County loan documents carry long-term affordability covenants (County inclusionary units are restricted in perpetuity). Projects in cities require a local government contribution.
next_deadline: The 2027-28 cycle should open in January 2027 with applications due in February, a Countywide Priority Setting Committee hearing in May and Board approval in June, matching the 2026-27 schedule (open Jan 19, 2026, closed Feb 19, 2026, PSC May 19, Board June 23, 2026). Trust Fund requests outside the NOFA have gone to the Board on their own (Habitat, CLAM, Golden Gate Village).
layering_notes: marincounty.gov, marincounty.org, assets.marincounty.gov, marinhhs.org and arcc.marincounty.gov sit behind Cloudflare and refused automated access on 2026-11-06, so County program pages could not be opened; Board agendas were read on marin.granicus.com and staff reports through its MetaViewer links where available. Marin's county money is small and project-specific: the Trust Fund mostly supplies PLHA match (about $500,000 a year) and five- to six-figure gap grants, with occasional larger loans for County-priority sites (Habitat in Novato, Oak Hill workforce housing next to San Quentin, Golden Gate Village). The County also weighed joining an Affordable Housing Guarantor Financing Program for Oak Hill in April 2025. Public funds trigger state prevailing wage; HOME and CDBG in the same award add Davis-Bacon. Sources opened: Board agendas for April 15, 2025, June 10, 2025, Dec 5 and 12, 2023, April 7 and 14, 2026 and June 23, 2026 on Granicus, the April 14, 2026 Golden Gate Village loan staff report, and the Local News Matters reports of April 6 and June 24, 2026. NOFA amounts and dates come from search engine excerpts of the County NOFA page, which is why this record is needs_confirmation.

administering_agency: Marin County Community Development Agency, Housing and Federal Grants Division, with the Countywide Priority Setting Committee

program_name: Inclusionary housing, affordable housing impact fee and commercial linkage fee (Development Code Chapter 22.22) with state density bonus (Chapter 22.24)
administering_agency: Marin County Community Development Agency, Planning Division (unincorporated area); fees deposited to the Affordable Housing Fund
typical_award_size: Chapter 22.22: 20% of units or lots in new residential projects must be affordable (projects of four or fewer units round up only above 0.70 of a unit), restricted in perpetuity unless shortened to match financing; income tiers very low (30% to 50% AMI), low (50% to 80%), moderate (80% to 120%) and middle (120% to 150%); alternatives in priority order are off-site units, land dedication and an in-lieu fee set at 125% of the requirement when a waiver is granted; single-family homes over 2,000 square feet pay an Affordable Housing Impact Fee (Ordinance 3500, 2008); non-residential projects pay a jobs-housing linkage fee by floor area and use (Ordinance 3798 and Resolution 2023-102 of Sept 19, 2023; Resolution 2016-122 for residential care and skilled nursing). Fees are indexed annually to the California Construction Cost Index; the June 23, 2026 adjustment was 3.9% and the FY 2026-27 in-lieu fee is $421,886.99 per required unit per the County fee page (2023-24 fee was $399,654). Chapter 22.24 implements Government Code 65915: base 20% bonus at 10% low or 5% very low income units, one to five concessions by affordability level, unlimited waivers of standards that physically preclude the project, height increases up to three stories near major transit for 80% lower income projects; the County may offer incentives to deed-restricted projects without a bonus but is not required to give fee waivers.
affordability_requirement: Inclusionary units restricted in perpetuity (or the maximum financing allows); density bonus rental units 30 years minimum under 22.24, moderate-income for-sale units in perpetuity. Rents capped at 50%, 65% and 100% of AMI levels for very low, low and moderate tiers.
next_deadline: Applies at entitlement; fees adjust each June (next adjustment June 2027). A multi-jurisdictional Affordable Housing Impact Fee Study by Strategic Economics for the cities and towns was authorized April 15, 2025, and the County is also studying development impact fees for infrastructure (public hearing March 10, 2026).
layering_notes: Marin's unincorporated inclusionary rule is one of the strictest in the state (20% in perpetuity, in-lieu fee only after off-site and land dedication are shown infeasible), and fee receipts flow to the Affordable Housing Fund that this database records separately. Fee revenue is modest because unincorporated development is small. A 100% affordable project satisfies the chapter automatically and uses the state density bonus. Density bonus alone does not trigger prevailing wage; Labor Code 1720(b)(4) would treat any fee waiver as public funds. Sources opened: Zoneomics mirror of Development Code Article III (Chapters 22.22 and 22.24) and the June 23, 2026 fee adjustment staff report on Granicus; the County fee calculator page was blocked.

program_name: Project-Based Vouchers and public housing conversion, Marin Housing Authority (MHA)
administering_agency: Housing Authority of the County of Marin, 4020 Civic Center Drive, San Rafael, 415-491-2525; procurement on procurement.opengov.com/portal/marinhousing
typical_award_size: MHA holds 496 public housing units and 2,541 Housing Choice Vouchers (3,037 combined, FY 2027 draft PHA Plan) and serves the whole county under cooperation agreements with every city. The FY 2027 plan begins converting the roughly 300-unit senior and disabled public housing portfolio (Mill Valley, San Rafael, Novato) to project-based vouchers through a RAD and Section 18 blend, and Golden Gate Village (296 units, Marin City) is converting under RAD with Burbank Housing: Phase 1 (88 units, $76,000,000 to $85,000,000) closed on CMFA bonds up to $50,000,000 (TEFRA Oct 14, 2025), a CDLAC allocation of $41,748,341 and about $3,985,091 in annual federal credits, with construction starting February 2026; Phase 2 TEFRA for up to $160,000,000 of bonds was set for Oct 20, 2026; the full program is estimated at $266,600,000. MHA runs PBV waitlists for partner properties (Victory Village in Novato, Edgewater, Piper Court, Fireside, Toussin Senior, Vivalon Healthy Aging Campus, 1251 S. Eliseo PSH in Larkspur) but has issued no developer PBV RFP recently; 94 Emergency Housing Voucher households were told in Oct 2025 that funding ends in 2026. The County contributes $250,000 a year for MHA's resident services director and has committed more than $6,250,000 to Golden Gate Village since 2022.
per_unit_cap: HUD PBV caps (20% of authorized vouchers plus 10% for homeless, veteran and supportive services units); MHA payment standards.
affordability_requirement: Households at or below 50% AMI at admission (75% at or below 30% AMI); PBV waitlists per property; Shelter Plus Care and HOPWA administered by MHA for the CoC; HAP contracts up to 20 years.
next_deadline: No PBV solicitation open as of Nov 2026; the FY 2027 Annual Plan was out for comment May 30 to July 14, 2026 and HUD's December 2025 budget letter limits new voucher commitments. Ask MHA about PBVs for specific PSH projects; recent awards went to Homeward Bound and Vivalon buildings.
layering_notes: MHA's capacity is going into its own RAD conversions through 2029, so new PBV awards for third-party projects are scarce; Shelter Plus Care and County-funded subsidies (Binford Road temporary rental support, $744,432 contract Dec 16, 2025) fill the gap for PSH. A HAP contract is not a prevailing wage trigger; Davis-Bacon applies to PBV construction of nine or more contract units, and RAD and public housing work carry Davis-Bacon regardless. Sources opened: MHA website pages, the FY 2027 draft PHA Plan (HUD-50075-ST), the April 14, 2026 Golden Gate Village loan staff report, Board agendas on Granicus and Patch and Local News Matters coverage of the bond approvals.
