program_name: Workforce Housing Preservation Program (WHPP), eastern Placer County deed-restriction purchases
administering_agency: Placer County Executive Office, Economic Development and Housing; down payment assistance component administered by Housing Trust Placer
typical_award_size: $4,100,000 allocated since 2021 ($500,000 General Fund and TOT in 2021, $600,000 TOT in 2023, $3,000,000 TOT in April 2024 through the NTCA TOT-TBID program); 17 deed restrictions purchased for $1,852,400 (average $108,965 per property; three in FY 2025-26 for $329,600). $2,247,500 remained through FY 2025-26, with staff seeking to extend it into FY 2026-27. May 12, 2026 amendments opened the program to multifamily properties of more than four units: maximum aggregate disbursement 16% of fair market value with a $75,000 per-unit cap (single-family cap $150,000), local businesses eligible as buyers, and a termination fee that declines over time.
per_unit_cap: $75,000 per unit for multifamily properties (and 16% of fair market value aggregate); $150,000 per single-family property.
affordability_requirement: Permanent deed restriction requiring occupancy by a household with at least one member of the local workforce (employed within the Tahoe Truckee Unified School District area); no income limit. Applies to existing homes, condos, duplexes and now multifamily rental properties in eastern Placer County.
next_deadline: Applications accepted while funds last; $2,247,500 available as of May 2026, subject to NTCA extension into FY 2026-27. Multifamily eligibility is new as of May 2026, so no multifamily transaction had closed when the guidelines were amended.
layering_notes: placer.ca.gov (including DocumentCenter PDFs) sits behind Cloudflare and refused automated access on 2026-11-06; Board items were read from the County's GovDelivery agenda attachments (content.govdelivery.com/attachments/CAPLACER), the Legistar client 'placerca', state records and news coverage. The 2026 change makes WHPP a small acquisition subsidy for buying existing North Shore apartment buildings and restricting them to local workers: a four-unit building worth $2 million could draw $300,000. The restriction is workforce occupancy rather than income, so it does not combine with LIHTC or state programs that require income limits, but it can pair with Launchpad for added units and with the welfare exemption only if a nonprofit owner also records income restrictions. program_name: Welfare Exemption (property tax), Placer County Assessor
administering_agency: Placer County Assessor, Matt Maynard; (530) 889-4300; with the State Board of Equalization (Organizational Clearance Certificate)
typical_award_size: Exemption of property taxes on units restricted to lower income households under Revenue and Taxation Code 214(g): full exemption for qualifying units in LIHTC or publicly financed projects and partial exemption for the qualifying share in mixed projects. In Placer County the 1% base rate plus voter-approved debt and direct assessments applies to the exempt value.
per_unit_cap: Statewide $20 million assessed-value cap on the 214(g) exemption for non-LIHTC projects relying only on a regulatory agreement; no cap for LIHTC projects. AB 84 (2024) allows a share of units occupied by households up to 100% AMI to remain exempt.
affordability_requirement: Nonprofit owner or limited partnership with a nonprofit managing general partner holding a BOE Organizational Clearance Certificate; recorded regulatory agreement (tax credits, bonds, County Use Deed Restriction with income limits, PLHA) restricting rents to lower income households.
next_deadline: File BOE-267 (first year) or BOE-267-A (annual) with the Assessor by February 15 each year with BOE-267-L, L1, L2 and L-A supplements as applicable; late filings through December 31 receive a partial exemption. The Assessor's web pages were not reachable on November 6, 2026; call the office for filing instructions.

HHAP has been used as a small capital and operating piece in County-area PSH (for example $1,000,000 in Lodi Commons and $1,000,000 HHAP-5 for the BeWell tiny home village), but the HHAP-6 regional plan budgets $0 for capital and shifts money to sustaining operations, so developers should treat HHAP as an operating or services source for existing PSH rather than a construction source. The 2025 Regional Homeless Action Plan reports 240 PSH units built in the past five years and 200 plus in the pipeline, and a shelter inventory growing from 1,346 to 1,934 beds by the end of 2026. HUD CoC Program funds flow through the SJCoC annual competition (2024 announcement posted on sjchsa.org); Stockton, the County and the CoC file a joint HHAP action plan.

program_name: San Joaquin Regional Housing Fund (SJRHF) gap loans, SJCOG
administering_agency: San Joaquin Regional Housing Fund Inc. (501(c)(3) subsidiary of the San Joaquin Council of Governments), fund manager Harris and Associates
typical_award_size: Round 1 (June 2026) committed $11,850,000 in gap loans to four projects: Airport Way Apartments, Manteca (TPC Housing) $2,850,000; The Junction, Tracy (CRP Affordable Housing and Community Development) $3,000,000; Lodi Commons at Salas Park, Lodi (San Joaquin Housing Authority) $3,000,000; The Don Shalvey Apartments, Stockton (Visionary Home Builders) $3,000,000. Alternates: Countrywood Cottages, Escalon; Casa De Mariposa and The View at Channel, Stockton. $750,000 held in reserve. Capitalization net of administration: $4,750,000 HCD Local Housing Trust Fund grant, $5,000,000 SJCOG Measure K smart growth local match, $2,850,000 Health Net grant ($12.6 million total; $13 million plus gross including $75,000 from the San Joaquin Community Foundation). Enterprise reports the round supports 421 affordable homes.
per_unit_cap: Underwriting guidelines adopted April 23, 2026: maximum $5 million per project; per-unit maximums for FY 2026-27 of $200,000 (0 and 1 bedroom) and $210,000 (2 or more bedrooms) for new construction and $240,000 and $250,000 for acquisition-rehab, CPI-adjusted each July; loans up to 70% of total development cost.
affordability_requirement: 55-year regulatory agreement minimum; LHTF dollars prioritize extremely low and very low income units in new construction and permanent rental housing; Measure K match requires infill and smart growth locations; Health Net dollars are flexible but prioritize low-income units. Preference for sites near transit and services.
next_deadline: Round 1 closed; funding commitment letters carry a one-year term with a one-year extension option tied to tax credit outcomes. No Round 2 date is set; SJCOG is seeking new capital and the Advisory Committee meets quarterly (March 4, June 3, September 2 and December 2, 2027). An ADU pilot of about $300,000 in REAP 2.0 funds is in design. Contact Joann Martinez, SJCOG, (209) 235-0582.
layering_notes: San Joaquin County has no county housing trust fund, no county housing bond and no inclusionary ordinance; the County's own capital for multifamily is limited to HUD pass-through funds administered by the Human Services Agency Neighborhood Preservation Division (sjchsa.org), while the regional gap lender is the SJCOG-sponsored San Joaquin Regional Housing Fund and the main voucher and development partner is the Housing Authority of the County of San Joaquin (HACSJ). This is the only countywide gap lender and the first new local soft money in the county in years; awards of $2.85 million to $3 million were sized to close 4% bond and LIHTC deals already in the pipeline, and funds disburse only after all other financing is secured. Loan terms: 3% simple interest or the Freddie Mac 30-year rate, 55-year term extendable 25 years, annual payments from 50% of residual receipts shared pro rata with other public lenders, 1% origination fee, debt service coverage of 1.15 or better in year one (TCAC minimum operating expenses per Title 4 Section 10327 unless justified). Public money from the fund is treated as a public subsidy for prevailing wage. The SJRHF board is the SJCOG board (Escalon, Lathrop, Lodi, Manteca, Mountain House, Ripon, San Joaquin County, Stockton, Tracy). Source is the June 18, 2026 Advisory Committee agenda packet with the award table and underwriting summaries; guidelines are in the April 13, 2026 packet (sjcog.org/AgendaCenter/ViewFile/Agenda/_04132026-1710).

program_name: Project-Based Vouchers, Housing Authority of the County of San Joaquin (HACSJ)

per_unit_cap: Payment standards set annually by HACSJ; PBV rents capped at the lower of reasonable rent or 110% of FMR per 24 CFR 983.
affordability_requirement: HUD PBV rules: households at or below 50% AMI at admission with 75% at or below 30% AMI; 15 to 20 year HAP contracts; HACSJ is not a Moving to Work agency so the 20% program cap and PBV competitive selection rules apply (exception for projects selected through a prior competitive public process).
next_deadline: No open PBV RFP found on hacsj.org procurement as of November 7, 2026; HACSJ reports it cannot apply for additional vouchers because of funding shortfalls, so new PBVs come from existing voucher authority. Monitor hacsj.org/resources/procurement and Public Purchase.
layering_notes: San Joaquin County has no county housing trust fund, no county housing bond and no inclusionary ordinance; the County's own capital for multifamily is limited to HUD pass-through funds administered by the Human Services Agency Neighborhood Preservation Division (sjchsa.org), while the regional gap lender is the SJCOG-sponsored San Joaquin Regional Housing Fund and the main voucher and development partner is the Housing Authority of the County of San Joaquin (HACSJ). Behavioral Health Services also carries Homekey+ (Bridge to Home, $15,900,896 agreement with CVLIHC approved January 13, 2026) and Behavioral Health Bridge Housing Round 3 contracts, and is building the SJ BeWell campus with a $38.2 million BHCIP Round 2 award (March 2026). program_name: Affordable Housing Density Bonus, Development Title Chapter 9-401 (unincorporated county)
administering_agency: San Joaquin County Community Development Department
typical_award_size: State-law density bonus codified in Chapter 9-401 (2026-10 code edition): 20% base bonus for 10% low-income, 5% very low-income or senior projects; 5% for 10% moderate-income for-sale units; 20% for 10% very low-income units for veterans, transition-age youth or homeless households; 35% for qualifying student housing; sliding scale up to 50% (2.5% per 1% very low-income above 5%, 1.5% per 1% low-income above 10%); land donation bonus 15% to 35%; floor area ratio bonus in the R-H zone for infill near transit with 20% of units at or below 50% AMI; 100% lower-income projects per Government Code 65915. One to four incentives or concessions by affordability tier plus parking reductions; the County may exceed these amounts (9-401.060).
affordability_requirement: 55-year rental affordability (longer if required by financing); for-sale units sold to qualifying buyers with equity sharing; affordable units integrated with and indistinguishable from market-rate units; replacement of existing affordable units required.
next_deadline: By application; pre-application response within 90 days; streamlined ministerial approval under 9-401.120 for eligible infill projects with at least 10% of units at or below 80% AMI (60 or 90 day review, deemed approved if missed).
layering_notes: San Joaquin County has no county housing trust fund, no county housing bond and no inclusionary ordinance; the County's own capital for multifamily is limited to HUD pass-through funds administered by the Human Services Agency Neighborhood Preservation Division (sjchsa.org), while the regional gap lender is the SJCOG-sponsored San Joaquin Regional Housing Fund and the main voucher and development partner is the Housing Authority of the County of San Joaquin (HACSJ). The unincorporated county has no inclusionary ordinance and no in-lieu fee, so the density bonus and concessions are the only land-use subsidy; the 2023-2031 Housing Element (HCD submittal revised January 2025, adopted and revised June 30, 2026 to transfer RHNA to the new City of Mountain House, 8,808 to 5,113 units) sets a quantified objective of 100 lower-income units through the bonus and commits to fee deferrals for affordable subdivisions. The ministerial pathway in 9-401.120 carries state prevailing wage and skilled workforce requirements for larger projects under Government Code 65913.4, so model labor costs before electing it. Most multifamily sites in the unincorporated county (French Camp, Garden Acres, Lodi and Stockton fringe) are constrained by water and sewer service, which the Housing Element names as the largest constraint. Source is the published Development Title chapter on gocodebook.com (County code host); confirm current text with Community Development at (209) 468-3144.

program_name: Development impact fee deferral for affordable housing (Housing Element program, unincorporated county)
administering_agency: San Joaquin County Community Development Department and Public Works
typical_award_size: Typical planning and development impact fees for a multifamily unit in the unincorporated county were about $20,000 to $20,500 per unit in 2023 (County fees of roughly $9,200 to $9,650 plus County facilities $1,564, regional transportation $2,664, habitat mitigation $1,929, school $4,041 and fire $620). The 2023-2031 Housing Element commits the County to process fee deferrals for projects affordable to lower-income households and to study fee waivers or reductions for affordable projects; no fee waiver fund or standing deferral ordinance was found.
affordability_requirement: Projects affordable to lower-income households as defined in the Housing Element programs; terms set case by case.
next_deadline: Request with the entitlement application; the Housing Element says the County will implement a deferral or reduction policy within three months of finding it feasible.
layering_notes: San Joaquin County has no county housing trust fund, no county housing bond and no inclusionary ordinance; the County's own capital for multifamily is limited to HUD pass-through funds administered by the Human Services Agency Neighborhood Preservation Division (sjchsa.org), while the regional gap lender is the SJCOG-sponsored San Joaquin Regional Housing Fund and the main voucher and development partner is the Housing Authority of the County of San Joaquin (HACSJ). Impact fees in the unincorporated county are low compared with Bay Area counties, so deferral is worth less than $20,000 per unit of carry; the larger cost issue is extending water and sewer to sites. Habitat mitigation (SJMSCP) and regional transportation fees are set by other agencies and are not waived by the County. Marked needs_confirmation because the Housing Element (opened) describes the policy as a commitment to study and implement, and no adopted deferral ordinance or fee schedule page was opened this pass; confirm with Community Development.

program_name: Welfare Exemption (property tax), San Joaquin County Assessor

Source is the County's Lodi Commons FONSI and request for release of funds (November 4, 2026); the HOME-ARP plan itself (sjchsa.org Portals HOME-ARP-Plan-.pdf) was not opened, hence needs_confirmation on the total allocation.

program_name: Health Net and Health Plan of San Joaquin housing investments (Medi-Cal plan capital grants)
administering_agency: Health Net (Centene) and Health Plan of San Joaquin, in partnership with HACSJ and the San Joaquin Regional Housing Fund
typical_award_size: Health Net granted $3,000,000 to the San Joaquin Regional Housing Fund (2026, $2,850,000 net available for loans) and $2,000,000 directly to Lodi Commons; Health Plan of San Joaquin is listed as a source for Tracy Apartments Phase I. Awards have been $2 million to $3 million per commitment.
affordability_requirement: Low-income and Medi-Cal member households; Health Net funds in the regional fund are flexible but prioritize low-income units.
next_deadline: No public application; commitments negotiated with the plans and routed through the Regional Housing Fund or directly to HACSJ projects.
layering_notes: San Joaquin County has no county housing trust fund, no county housing bond and no inclusionary ordinance; the County's own capital for multifamily is limited to HUD pass-through funds administered by the Human Services Agency Neighborhood Preservation Division (sjchsa.org), while the regional gap lender is the SJCOG-sponsored San Joaquin Regional Housing Fund and the main voucher and development partner is the Housing Authority of the County of San Joaquin (HACSJ). Managed care plan money is the newest soft source in the county and has shown up in every 2026 capital stack (Lodi Commons, Tracy Apartments, the Regional Housing Fund). It is grant money and does not by itself trigger prevailing wage, but it is always paired with public funds that do. Recorded at county level because the plans are county Medi-Cal plans and the money flows through countywide vehicles; figures are from the SJCOG March 11, 2026 announcement (source), the June 18, 2026 fund packet and the Lodi Commons FONSI.

program_name: Affordable Housing Ordinance (Zoning Code Article 29): inclusionary units and Affordable Housing Impact Fee
administering_agency: City of Redwood City, Housing Services (City Manager's Office) and Community Development
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Rental projects of 20 or more units: 20% affordable (10% moderate, 5% low, 5% very low income). Ownership projects of 20 or more units: 15% moderate income. Projects of 5 to 19 units and nonresidential projects over 5,000 square feet pay the Affordable Housing Impact Fee (Resolution 15462 of 2015; nonresidential rates raised December 20, 2021 to $23.62 per square foot for office, medical office and R&D and $5.91 for hotel, retail, restaurant and services; residential small-project rate reported at about $20 to $25 per square foot, with a temporary 25% reduction for 5 to 19 unit projects that pull vertical permits by June 30, 2027). Fees fund the City's affordable housing NOFA.
affordability_requirement: Rental units restricted at least 55 years, ownership at least 30 years, recorded covenants in first position; fractional units met by an extra unit or in-lieu fee set by Council resolution; 100% affordable projects exempt from the fee.
next_deadline: Applies at entitlement; fees due before the first building permit. The 2026 San Mateo County multi-city nexus study (Strategic Economics, Redwood City is a participant) may change percentages and fees in 2027.
layering_notes: County layer: every San Mateo County city project competes for the County Affordable Housing Fund NOFA (AHF 14 closed July 15, 2026, next fall 2027), HEART bridge loans and HACSM project-based vouchers; city money is usually the first commitment that unlocks those. Redwood City is the deepest inclusionary program in the county at 20% for rental with a very low income tier, which is why most downtown projects negotiate on-site units rather than pay the fee and why the impact fee fund grows mainly from commercial projects (Elco Yards is expected to pay about $5.8 million in 2026). Alternative compliance plans (off-site, land, conversions) go to Council. The ordinance text is on the City's code host (source, Article 29, Ordinances 1130-375 of 2018, 2498 of 2021, 1130-387 of 2023 and 1130-890 of 2024); fee amounts are from the December 20, 2021 staff report on meetings.redwoodcity.org because redwoodcity.org returns 403 to automated access. Confirm the current residential fee and the 25% reduction with Housing Services at (650) 780-7000.

program_name: Affordable Housing NOFA and Preservation Program (impact fee fund loans)
administering_agency: City of Redwood City, Housing Services
typical_award_size: May 11, 2026 Council action: about $8 million to Rise City Apartments (94 units, 1304 Middlefield Road, 20% to 70% AMI, 24 PSH units including 19 for adults with intellectual and developmental disabilities, construction early 2027) and a commitment to direct about $5.8 million of expected Elco Yards impact fees to MidPen Housing's 79-unit project at 1580 Maple Street (20% to 40% AMI, 23 special needs units, City-owned land transferred by the County, construction late 2027). layering_notes: County layer: every San Mateo County city project competes for the County Affordable Housing Fund NOFA (AHF 14 closed July 15, 2026, next fall 2027), HEART bridge loans and HACSM project-based vouchers; city money is usually the first commitment that unlocks those. City loans are residual receipts loans repaid from cash flow after operating expenses, hard debt and reserves, and are sized to leverage County AHF, HACSM PBVs and 4% or 9% credits; 1580 Maple shows the City-County land plus City fee money pattern. Marked needs_confirmation because redwoodcity.org (NOFA page, Preservation Program guidelines, fee schedule) returned 403 to automated access and figures come from the May 12, 2026 Redwood City Pulse report (source) and the City's meetings portal; confirm award terms with Housing Services.

program_name: Below Market Rate (BMR) inclusionary program and in-lieu fees (SMMC 27.16.050)
administering_agency: City of San Mateo Community Development Department, Neighborhood Improvement and Housing Division
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Projects of 11 or more units: 15% of rental units for lower income households (rents at 30% of 50% to 70% AMI, 4% annual increase cap) and 15% of ownership units for moderate income (100% to 110% AMI). Projects of 5 to 10 units and fractional units pay the BMR Housing Fee (Resolution 121 of 2008; FY 2026-27 schedule: rental $171,273 for a 5-unit project up to $342,545 for 10 units, ownership $157,187 to $314,373; fractional units $34,255 per 0.1 rental unit and $31,438 per 0.1 ownership unit). In-lieu fees are otherwise not allowed. BMR Housing Fee fund balance $254,281 at June 30, 2026 with $2,560,924 programmed for housing land purchase.
affordability_requirement: 55-year restrictions; BMR units may be up to 10% smaller than market units (20% where market units exceed 2,000 square feet); density bonus projects must provide BMR units equal to at least 15% of the base density; off-site and applicant-proposed alternatives need Council findings (Guidelines Resolution 72, June 16, 2025).
next_deadline: Applies at planning application; fees indexed in the annual Comprehensive Fee Schedule each July 1. The City is a participant in the 2026 multi-city nexus study.
layering_notes: County layer: every San Mateo County city project competes for the County Affordable Housing Fund NOFA (AHF 14 closed July 15, 2026, next fall 2027), HEART bridge loans and HACSM project-based vouchers; city money is usually the first commitment that unlocks those. San Mateo's program is unit-first: no fee option above 10 units, so inclusionary units are a given in every downtown and Hillsdale project and the City's cash sources are the Commercial Linkage Fee and the small BMR fee. Source is the adopted FY 2026-27 Comprehensive Fee Schedule (pages 11.1 to 11.2); program rules from the BMR Guidelines (cityofsanmateo.org/DocumentCenter/View/99291) and the FY 2025-26 Mitigation Fee Act report (DocumentCenter/View/107918).

program_name: Affordable Housing Commercial Linkage Fee fund (SMMC Chapter 23.61)
administering_agency: City of San Mateo Community Development Department
typical_award_size: Fee on net new nonresidential construction over 5,000 square feet, adopted September 2016 (Ordinance 2016-8): office, R&D and medical office $32.76 per square foot, hotel $13.11, retail, restaurant and services $6.55 (FY 2025-26 and FY 2026-27). 25% rebate for projects that sign a Standard Wage (area standard or prevailing wage) agreement; alternative of building 8 low-income units per 100,000 square feet of office, 3 per 100,000 of hotel, 1 per 100,000 of retail. Fund activity FY 2025-26: beginning $3,551,934, fees $1,090,711, loan repayments $514,717, ending balance $5,292,314 with $1,000,000 set aside for the Bespoke project and $4,000,000 programmed for housing land purchase.
affordability_requirement: Fund must support creation or preservation of housing for lower and moderate income workers; projects carry City regulatory agreements.
next_deadline: No NOFA. The City commits linkage fee money by Council action; the FY 2025-26 report programs $4 million toward housing land purchase. Contact housing@cityofsanmateo.org, (650) 522-7220.
layering_notes: County layer: every San Mateo County city project competes for the County Affordable Housing Fund NOFA (AHF 14 closed July 15, 2026, next fall 2027), HEART bridge loans and HACSM project-based vouchers; city money is usually the first commitment that unlocks those. With about $4.3 million unprogrammed, the City can make one meaningful land or gap commitment per cycle rather than run a competitive round; developers should pair a request with the County AHF spring NOFA. The City is a CDBG entitlement (FY 2026-27 CDBG NOFA ran through the City) and joins the County HOME Consortium. Source is the FY 2025-26 Mitigation Fee Act (AB 1600) annual report; fee rates confirmed in the FY 2026-27 Comprehensive Fee Schedule and the Development Fees handout (DocumentCenter/View/98263).

program_name: Inclusionary Housing Ordinance (DCMC Chapter 17.47, Ordinance 1423) and Affordable Housing Trust Fund
administering_agency: City of Daly City Economic and Community Development, Housing and Community Development Division
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Residential developments of 5 or more units: for-sale projects provide 20% of units at moderate income; rental projects provide 10% at low income (rents at 30% of 70% AMI). On-site units required at 15 or more for-sale units and 20 or more rental units; smaller projects pay the Required In Lieu Fee and larger projects may pay an Alternative In Lieu Fee per the City's Affordable Housing Fee schedule with Council approval. Fees go to the Affordable Housing Trust Fund, which the City uses with state and HUD funds for 100% affordable projects (Daly City is a CDBG and HOME entitlement city).
affordability_requirement: 55-year restrictions; on-site units earn state density bonus, waivers and concessions under the Affordable Housing Plan; local preference ordinance (September 2026) gives Daly City residents and workers preference for 70% of affordable units.
next_deadline: Applies at entitlement; in-lieu fee amounts are set by resolution in the Housing Impact Fees and In-Lieu Fees sheet (dalycity.org/DocumentCenter/View/925, an image file that could not be read this pass). Daly City is a participant in the 2026 multi-city nexus study.
layering_notes: County layer: every San Mateo County city project competes for the County Affordable Housing Fund NOFA (AHF 14 closed July 15, 2026, next fall 2027), HEART bridge loans and HACSM project-based vouchers; city money is usually the first commitment that unlocks those. Daly City's rental requirement (10% low income) is the lightest among the eight cities covered, and the City's own money for 100% affordable deals comes from the Trust Fund, its HOME and CDBG entitlements and the housing successor fund rather than a NOFA; the County's $14 million Midway Village loan and City loans reported at about $7.7 million for the 72-unit 493 Eastmoor project (CMFA bonds up to $25 million authorized February 9, 2026, per news summaries not opened) show the pattern. Source is the ordinance PDF on dalycity.org; the fee amounts are unconfirmed, hence needs_confirmation. Contact hcd@dalycity.org, (650) 991-8068.

program_name: Daly City Housing Development Finance Agency land offerings and housing successor fund (Carter/Martin site RFQ)
administering_agency: Daly City Housing Development Finance Agency (housing successor to the former Redevelopment Agency), Economic and Community Development
typical_award_size: Request for Developer Qualifications issued August 14, 2026 for an approximately 12.5-acre Agency-owned site at Carter and Martin Streets in the Bayshore neighborhood next to the Cow Palace (APNs 005-050-240 and 005-380-020, zoned C-1, former RDA housing asset with Community Redevelopment Law affordability obligations), marketed under Surplus Land Act exemptions for 100 or more units with at least 25% lower income or 100% affordable mixed use. Housing Asset Fund (Fund 11) balance $4,461,128 at June 30, 2025 with net deposits of $298,048 in FY 2024-25.

layering_notes: County layer: every San Mateo County city project competes for the County Affordable Housing Fund NOFA (AHF 14 closed July 15, 2026, next fall 2027), HEART bridge loans and HACSM project-based vouchers; city money is usually the first commitment that unlocks those. Carter/Martin is the largest publicly owned housing site in northern San Mateo County and will need extensive site work (slopes, wetlands, soils); the Agency can contribute land value and successor funds but will look to the County AHF, HACSM PBVs and state programs for the capital stack. program_name: Commercial Linkage Fee fund (Fund 823) and Affordable Housing Trust Fund loans
administering_agency: City of South San Francisco Economic and Community Development Department, Housing Division
typical_award_size: Commercial Linkage Fee (SSFMC 8.69, adopted 2018): office and R&D $17.38 per square foot, hotel $5.80, retail, restaurant and services $2.90 (January 2025 handout). Fund 823 revenue swung from $7.5 million (FY 2022-23) to a projected $1.5 million in FY 2025-26, $19.3 million in FY 2026-27 and $8.5 million in FY 2027-28 (Genentech, Trammell Crow and Healthpeak payments); projected year-end FY 2024-25 balances were $14 million in Fund 823, $200,000 in the Affordable Housing Trust Fund (Fund 205) and $1 million in the housing successor fund (Fund 241). City loans: Rotary Gardens Phase 1, 500 Linden Avenue, up to $7,867,409 (August 11, 2026); Synergy Community Development acquisition of the Metropolitan Hotel, 220 Linden, up to $3,115,000 from Fund 823 (February 24, 2026); 1051 Mission Road (BRIDGE, 158 units, PUC site) $2,000,000 raised to $2,362,000 as the LHTF match plus up to $14.6 million committed April 22, 2026 from the first market-rate phase for Measure K and tax credit applications; 428-432 Baden (For the Future Housing, 36 units) $4,050,000; 201-219 Grand and 418 Linden (ROEM, 84 units) $3,500,000; 201 Baden (Eden, 82 units) $2,362,500 LHTF. City also holds a $28,817,500 IIG grant for 1051 Mission and $890,000 PIP.

Requests go to Council through the Housing Division (housing@ssfca.gov, (650) 829-6620).
layering_notes: County layer: every San Mateo County city project competes for the County Affordable Housing Fund NOFA (AHF 14 closed July 15, 2026, next fall 2027), HEART bridge loans and HACSM project-based vouchers; city money is usually the first commitment that unlocks those. South San Francisco has the largest city housing fund in the county after the linkage fee rebound and uses it as the first-in local loan (residual receipts) ahead of County AHF, state IIG and LHTF money; the City also waives or pays permit fees from Fund 823 for public housing work (C Street electrification, August 2026) and holds TEFRA hearings for CMFA bonds (Rotary Gardens, August 2026). City-owned sites: 1051 Mission Road (PUC site, Development Agreement amended April 24, 2026), 220 Linden and 905 Linden under negotiation in 2026. Source is the Housing Division funding page; figures from the Affordable Housing Financing Plan PDF and Council files on ci-ssf-ca.legistar.com (Legistar API client ci-ssf-ca).

program_name: Inclusionary Housing Ordinance (SSFMC Chapter 20.380) and replacement housing rules
administering_agency: City of South San Francisco Economic and Community Development Department, Housing Division
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Market-rate projects of 5 or more units: rental 15% (10% lower income, 5% very low income); homebuyer 15% (7.5% moderate, 7.5% lower income); extended to rental housing in 2018. In-lieu fee amounts are not posted on the developer page. Demolition requires one-for-one replacement, relocation assistance and right of first refusal.
affordability_requirement: County income and rent limits (2026-27 schedule posted), utility allowances deducted, regulatory agreements control; Procedures and Guidelines for Inclusionary Units updated September 2024.

layering_notes: County layer: every San Mateo County city project competes for the County Affordable Housing Fund NOFA (AHF 14 closed July 15, 2026, next fall 2027), HEART bridge loans and HACSM project-based vouchers; city money is usually the first commitment that unlocks those. The 15% rental requirement with a very low income tier plus the linkage fee is why South San Francisco's biotech corridor funds housing elsewhere in the city; 100% affordable projects are exempt and instead draw on Fund 823 loans (see separate record). Source is the Housing Requirements for Developers page.

program_name: Below Market Rate (BMR) Housing Fund NOFA 2026/27
administering_agency: City of Menlo Park Community Development Department, Housing Division

layering_notes: County layer: every San Mateo County city project competes for the County Affordable Housing Fund NOFA (AHF 14 closed July 15, 2026, next fall 2027), HEART bridge loans and HACSM project-based vouchers; city money is usually the first commitment that unlocks those. The BMR fund is capitalized by commercial in-lieu fees (office and R&D $23.26 per square foot in FY 2026-27) and residential in-lieu payments, so its size tracks Meta and life science approvals; $4 million is enough for one gap loan or a preservation deal and is typically paired with County AHF and HACSM PBVs. program_name: Below Market Rate (BMR) Housing Program: residential inclusionary and commercial in-lieu fees (MPMC 16.96)
administering_agency: City of Menlo Park Community Development Department, Housing Division
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Residential: 10 to 19 units at least 10% BMR, 20 or more units at least 15% BMR (very low, low and moderate income); 5 to 9 units provide a unit if feasible or pay a graduated in-lieu fee of 1% to 3% of sales price; for-sale projects of 10 or more may pay 3% of the sales price per market-rate unit in lieu; rental in-lieu fee set by Council resolution based on the cost of a one-bedroom unit. Each on-site BMR unit earns one additional market-rate unit up to 15% above zoned density. Commercial: buildings of 10,000 square feet or more provide BMR units or pay in-lieu fees of $23.26 per square foot (office and R&D, Group A) or $12.62 (other commercial and industrial, Group B) for July 1, 2026 to June 30, 2027, adjusted each July 1 by a five-year CPI shelter average.
affordability_requirement: BMR rents at or below 30% of the income category limit and no more than 75% of market rents; income categories from 30% to 120% AMI; one-year live or work preference; BMR housing agreement recorded before permits.
next_deadline: Applies at application; Menlo Park leads the 2026 San Mateo County multi-city nexus study (Strategic Economics) that may raise inclusionary percentages and add a residential impact fee later in 2026 or 2027.
layering_notes: County layer: every San Mateo County city project competes for the County Affordable Housing Fund NOFA (AHF 14 closed July 15, 2026, next fall 2027), HEART bridge loans and HACSM project-based vouchers; city money is usually the first commitment that unlocks those. The commercial in-lieu fee is the engine of the BMR fund (see NOFA record); office projects in the Bayfront and downtown specific plan areas often negotiate on-site or off-site BMR units instead. Source is the City's residential BMR requirements page; commercial rates from the companion commercial page and the October 21, 2025 Guidelines (Resolution 7003).

program_name: Inclusionary Housing Ordinance (Chapter 18.37) with in-lieu fees and Affordable Housing Commercial Linkage Fee
administering_agency: City of East Palo Alto Housing Division, 1960 Tate Street
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Projects of 5 or more units: rental 20% on-site (5% at 35% AMI, 10% at 50% AMI, 5% at 60% AMI) or, with Council approval, 25% off-site or an in-lieu fee of $299,200 per required unit (FY 2025-26); for-sale 20% on-site (10% median, 10% moderate) or 25% off-site or $268,800 per unit in lieu. Projects under 5 units pay a per-unit share ($59,840 to $239,360 rental). Commercial linkage fee (Resolution 118-2020, effective October 31, 2020, ENR-indexed each April 1) applies to office, R&D and medical office; retail, restaurant, service and hotel are charged $0; the City plans to update it in 2027 after the multi-city nexus study.
affordability_requirement: Ordinance 425 (November 19, 2019) and Guidelines (Resolution 142-2020); income limits follow HCD; SB 9 lot splits exempt (September 2025); in-lieu fees reset each July (FY 2025-26 adopted July 16, 2025).

layering_notes: County layer: every San Mateo County city project competes for the County Affordable Housing Fund NOFA (AHF 14 closed July 15, 2026, next fall 2027), HEART bridge loans and HACSM project-based vouchers; city money is usually the first commitment that unlocks those. East Palo Alto has the deepest rental targeting in the county (a 35% AMI tier) and uses the fees plus Measure HH and Measure JJ revenue to fund 100% affordable projects such as Colibri Commons and Light Tree; 148 inclusionary units were in the pipeline in 2024. program_name: Affordable Housing Preservation Program (over-the-counter fund)

program_name: Affordable Housing Fund NOFA (rolling, FY 2025-26 and FY 2026-27)

layering_notes: County layer: every San Mateo County city project competes for the County Affordable Housing Fund NOFA (AHF 14 closed July 15, 2026, next fall 2027), HEART bridge loans and HACSM project-based vouchers; city money is usually the first commitment that unlocks those. The Board initiated an inclusionary zoning study on May 21, 2024 (Program H-12); the Planning Commission held an Inclusionary Zoning and Warehouse Linkage Fee workshop April 23, 2025 proposing that part of industrial community benefit fees fund affordable housing; the 2025 Housing Element Annual Progress Report (April 14, 2026) lists the ordinance options as still pending, and the FY 2026-27 budget set aside $900,000 for ordinance updates including inclusionary housing.
affordability_requirement: Proposed options include on-site units, off-site units, land dedication or an in-lieu or linkage fee for residential projects over five units and warehouse projects.
eligible_project_types: future market-rate residential and industrial development (fee payer)
next_deadline: Ordinance options were due to the Board in 2025 and 2026 and have not been adopted; track TLMA Planning Commission agendas.
layering_notes: Riverside County's Housing and Workforce Solutions (HWS) department runs the Urban County HUD programs, PLHA, HHAP, Homekey+ sponsorships and project loans, while the Housing Authority of the County of Riverside (HACR, same Board sitting as Commissioners) supplies project-based vouchers, housing successor funds and land; rivcohws.org and harivco.org block automated access, so records were built from Board of Supervisors files on riversidecountyca.iqm2.com and media.rivcocob.org, RUHS Behavioral Health, the Assessor and the County Housing Element. Recorded so the gap is explicit: the unincorporated county has no inclusionary requirement, no in-lieu fee and no housing trust fund, so County capital depends on federal and state pass-through and General Fund one-offs. An adopted warehouse linkage fee would be the first dedicated local housing revenue. Source is the Board file for the 2025 Housing Element Annual Progress Report.

program_name: Tax-exempt multifamily bonds: County TEFRA approvals for CMFA, CSCDA and CalPFA issuances
administering_agency: Riverside County Housing and Workforce Solutions (public hearings) and Office of Economic Development; Board of Supervisors adopts the approving resolution

affordability_requirement: Bond regulatory agreements (20% at 50% AMI or 40% at 60% AMI) under CDLAC rules.
next_deadline: Request a TEFRA hearing through HWS at least six weeks before the CDLAC application; no County fee was stated in the Board file.

program_name: Affordable Housing Development NOFO (HOME, HOME-CHDO, HOME-ARP and PLHA combined annual round)
administering_agency: Fresno County Department of Public Works and Planning, Community Development Division (ComDev@fresnocountyca.gov, (559) 600-4292)
typical_award_size: The February 19, 2025 NOFO offered about $15,534,572 across PLHA, HOME, HOME-CHDO and HOME-ARP; all five applications were reserved: Cherry Crossing II, Sanger (64 units, Self-Help Enterprises), Reedley Elderly and Selma Elderly (Self-Help, $2,000,000 HOME-CHDO each for 11 assisted units, $181,818 per unit), Sanger Modular now Sendero Commons (UPholdings and RH Community Builders) and Park Kingsburg (Horizon ELOM, $2,000,000). The 2026-27 Action Plan reserves $5,018,870 of HOME for projects selected under the 2026 NOFO. Historic County awards were capped at $1,000,000; the 2025 NOFO raised the recommended maximum to $2,000,000 per project with justified requests above that considered.
per_unit_cap: Recommended maximum $2,000,000 gap per project (not a hard cap); HUD HOME maximum per-unit subsidy limits apply (2024: $181,488 0-bedroom to $252,994 2-bedroom and up).
affordability_requirement: HOME 20-year federal affordability (County loan terms typically 55 years; Reedley and Selma Heritage: 15-year HOME affordability on 11 units, loan repaid by March 31, 2083); PLHA 55 years with half the PLHA units at 60% AMI and half at 80% AMI; HOME-ARP qualifying populations.
next_deadline: 2025 cycle: NOFO released February 19, 2025, Round 1 applications due March 6, 2025 (timed to CTCAC 9% Round 1), reservation letters by March 12, 2025, then ongoing applications reopened March 14, 2025 while funds remained. A 2026 NOFO ran on the same calendar with awards identified before July 21, 2026. Expect the 2027 NOFO in January or February 2027 with a late February or early March deadline ahead of CTCAC 9% Round 1.
layering_notes: Fresno County splits housing work three ways: the Department of Public Works and Planning, Community Development Division (ComDev) runs the Urban County HUD programs, PLHA and the annual Affordable Housing Development NOFO; the County Administrative Office's new Office of Housing and Homelessness (OHH, created November 18, 2025) administers HHAP, the Continuum of Care and Transitional Rent and is absorbing housing programs from Behavioral Health and ComDev (Phase 2 approved November 3, 2026); and the Department of Behavioral Health co-applies for Homekey+ and NPLH and funds BHSA housing. Fresno Housing (the joint City and County Housing Authorities) is the dominant developer and voucher source. The City of Fresno and Clovis are separate entitlements with their own programs (Pass 3). fresnocountyca.gov and fresnohousing.org open normally; Board records are on fresnocounty.legistar.com and the Legistar web API client 'fresnocounty'. This is the County's only standing capital program and it is explicitly sized as gap money for 9% tax credit deals: 0% or 3% simple interest at the applicant's election, repayment deferred to maturity or as residual receipts (recent deals 50/50 split), non-recourse, subordinate to senior debt, loan term at least through the affordability period, and HOME may be converted to a grant by Board action. Eligible locations are the Urban County only: Fowler, Kerman, Kingsburg, Mendota, Orange Cove, Reedley, Sanger, Selma and unincorporated areas including County islands inside Fresno and Clovis; projects inside the cities of Fresno and Clovis are ineligible. Davis-Bacon applies at 12 or more HOME-assisted units and state prevailing wage applies to PLHA. Reservation letters are written to support CTCAC applications; final agreements require NEPA, subsidy layering review and Board approval and typically land 8 to 12 months after reservation. Source is the NOFO page with the 2025 NOFO PDF and reservation letters; the Reedley and Selma Heritage agreements are at fresnocounty.legistar.com (files 26-0593 and 26-0069, June 30, 2026).

Capital development $6,098,789 to $6,118,094 a year (24.8% of the component in year one, under the 25% cap), permanent rental subsidies $7,092,044 plus bundled rental and operating $2,526,608, interim rental subsidies $1,207,577 and bundled $2,250,773, outreach $1,709,758, participant assistance $373,266, Housing Flex Pool start-up $400,000 a year, flex pool share rising from 50% to 80%. Parkway Drive, Fresno; Fresno Housing conversion of a shelter to 42 units, 41 PSH for chronically homeless) conditional $6,300,000 capital plus $287,000 a year operating subsidy for 30 years ($8,610,000) and on-site services valued at $424,872 a year, contingent on 2026 Round 2 9% tax credits (resolution June 30, 2026).

program_name: Inclusionary Housing Ordinance (Chapter 21.03 Affordable Housing Regulations) and in-lieu fee
administering_agency: San Benito County Resource Management Agency, Planning and Building (sbcplan@sanbenitocountyca.gov, (831) 637-5313)
typical_award_size: Requirement rather than a subsidy: 15% of units affordable on site (for-sale and rental) or 20% off site under Sections 21.03.006 and 21.03.007; developments of 1 to 5 units exempt, 6 to 10 units pay the in-lieu fee automatically, 11 or more units build on or off site and pay the fee on fractions below 0.7 unit. In-lieu fee adopted December 13, 2022 (Ordinance 1052, Resolution 2022-149): $30 per square foot for for-sale homes based on the 15% requirement (Vernazza Wolfe affordability gap study). Before 2022 developers paid a negotiated $4,500 per unit through development agreements (Sunnyside Estates). Example compliance: Lands of Lee subdivision affordable housing plan approved September 15, 2026 under Resolution 2024-146 (about 30 affordable units, 21% of the project).
affordability_requirement: Very low (50% AMI), low (80% AMI) and moderate (120% AMI) income units per Section 21.03.003; off-site rental projects of 24 or more lots carry an updated income breakdown (Ordinance 1059, September 12, 2023); affordable housing plans are approved by the Planning Commission and Board (Housing Advisory Committee dissolved 2023).
eligible_project_types: market-rate subdivisions and multifamily projects of 6 or more units in unincorporated San Benito County
off-site affordable rental projects built to satisfy another developer's obligation
land donation or subsidy to nonprofit developers as alternative compliance (Section 21.03.008(F))
next_deadline: Applies with each land use entitlement. The Board's Housing Policy Reform Ad Hoc Committee (formed February 11, 2025) has reviewed Chapter 21.03 but no 2025 or 2026 amendment was found in Board agendas; in-lieu payments qualify only where sites are on septic or wells, zoned for large lots, or more than 10 miles from an incorporated city.
layering_notes: San Benito County is a small non-entitlement county with no housing department: the Resource Management Agency (Planning and Building, Abraham Prado, (831) 637-5313) administers the inclusionary ordinance, in-lieu fees, density bonus and TEFRA hearings; the Health and Human Services Agency (Community Services and Workforce Development) runs HHAP, the shelter and the Migrant Center; Behavioral Health holds BHSA; and the Housing Authority of the County of Santa Cruz administers vouchers and PBVs for Hollister and San Juan Bautista. The County has no HOME or CDBG entitlement, no housing trust fund NOFA and no County loan program; Hollister runs its own PLHA and CDBG programs (Pass 3). sanbenitocountyca.gov and the amlegal code library block automated access, so records were built from Board of Supervisors packets on cosb.granicus.com (attachments on d2kbkoa27fdvtw.cloudfront.net), HCD allocation tables and hacosantacruz.org. For an affordable developer the ordinance matters in two ways: market-rate projects in the Hollister fringe (Santana Ranch, Lands of Lee, builder's remedy filings) must deliver or fund affordable units, and Section 21.03.008(F) lets them satisfy the obligation by donating land or subsidizing a nonprofit rental project, which is the County's only recurring local capital source. In-lieu fees go to an affordable housing fund (see separate record). Source is the December 13, 2022 Board packet adopting the amendments and fee; current code text is on codelibrary.amlegal.com (blocked to automated access).

program_name: Affordable Housing Impact Fee (AHIF): exemption for deed-restricted affordable units and fee fund
administering_agency: Santa Cruz County Community Development and Infrastructure, Planning Division, Housing Section
typical_award_size: Current rates (2026 Affordable Housing Guidelines, Chapter V): market-rate rental units $2 per habitable square foot (ADUs of 750 square feet or less exempt); ownership projects of fewer than seven units $2 to $15 per square foot scaled by unit size and project size (5 or more homes $15 per square foot at all sizes); non-residential $3 per net new square foot ($1 for agricultural barns). eligible_project_types: density bonus and mixed-income rental projects (waiver available)

layering_notes: Ventura County's housing money runs through the County Executive Office, Community Development (CEO-CD, 800 S. Victoria Avenue, Ventura, (805) 654-2681), which administers the Urban County CDBG and HOME programs, the HOME Consortium, PLHA, General Fund housing NOFAs and Homekey sponsorships; the Resource Management Agency Planning Division handles density bonus, RHD zoning and streamlining; the Health Care Agency Behavioral Health holds BHSA; the Ventura County Continuum of Care (CA-611) sits in the CEO; and the Area Housing Authority of the County of Ventura (AHACV) supplies vouchers outside Oxnard, Ventura, Port Hueneme and Santa Paula, which have their own housing authorities. HOME is a $1 million soft loan on a CHDO or tax credit deal, usually paired with County PLHA, General Fund NOFA money and an HTFVC loan. Davis-Bacon applies at 12 or more HOME units. program_name: Housing Trust Fund Ventura County revolving loan fund and residual receipts loan program (County-capitalized)
administering_agency: Housing Trust Fund Ventura County (nonprofit CDFI, Camarillo; Linda Braunschweiger, CEO)
typical_award_size: Revolving Loan Fund: below-market loans of $250,000 to $5,000,000 for acquisition, predevelopment, gap and construction, generally 1 to 5 years, for projects with 30 to 55 year affordability; $53,795,034 approved or funded since 2013 producing 2,255 affordable homes; $18,425,566 of state LHTF matching funds leveraged 2020-2024 plus a $4,406,179 final-round LHTF award. County capital: $300,000 General Fund (2020), $1,500,000 ARPA (2022) and PLHA Activity 3 grants. New Residual Receipts Loan Program (about $4.6 million from a REAP 2.0 grant): 15 to 18 year residual receipts loans for new affordable rental housing at 0% to 80% AMI meeting infill criteria, in development by June 30, 2031; first round applications June 2 to July 2, 2026. Recent loans: Santa Clara Apartments, Ventura (Ventura Housing) $2,000,000 residual receipts, 18 years (2026); Gateway Grove, Santa Paula (Many Mansions, 21 studios at 30% AMI) $500,000 predevelopment (2026); Lockwood III, Oxnard $500,000 (February 4, 2026); Cypress Gardens Phase II, Oxnard (Peoples Self-Help) $1,500,000 (December 16, 2025); Fillmore Terrace II $1,000,000 (September 26, 2025); Aspire Apartments, Oxnard (Many Mansions) $750,000 (April 30, 2025).
affordability_requirement: Lower income (80% AMI and below) with priority for extremely low income, veterans, transition age youth, homeless households and farmworkers; residual receipts loans require 0% to 80% AMI units and long-term covenants.
eligible_project_types: acquisition and conversion of market-rate or non-residential property
self-help and affordable ownership (case by case)
next_deadline: Revolving Loan Fund: contact HTFVC to discuss the pipeline; invitations to apply follow. Residual Receipts Loan Program: the first round closed July 2, 2026; watch for a 2027 round timed to CTCAC applications.
layering_notes: Ventura County's housing money runs through the County Executive Office, Community Development (CEO-CD, 800 S. Victoria Avenue, Ventura, (805) 654-2681), which administers the Urban County CDBG and HOME programs, the HOME Consortium, PLHA, General Fund housing NOFAs and Homekey sponsorships; the Resource Management Agency Planning Division handles density bonus, RHD zoning and streamlining; the Health Care Agency Behavioral Health holds BHSA; the Ventura County Continuum of Care (CA-611) sits in the CEO; and the Area Housing Authority of the County of Ventura (AHACV) supplies vouchers outside Oxnard, Ventura, Port Hueneme and Santa Paula, which have their own housing authorities. Source is the HTFVC funding programs page; loan list from the July 23, 2026 loan summary.

program_name: Density bonus (Non-Coastal Zoning Ordinance Article 16) and Residential High Density zone ministerial approvals with affordability requirement
administering_agency: Ventura County Resource Management Agency, Planning Division (plan.counter@venturacounty.gov, (805) 654-2488)
typical_award_size: State density bonus and incentives implemented in NCZO Article 16 (Housing Element program HE-M update completed) and Coastal Zoning Ordinance Section 8175-6. Residential High Density (RHD) zone: seven parcels (four in El Rio/Del Norte, two in Santa Susana, one in the Thousand Oaks area) allow 20 to 22 units per acre by ministerial RHD Zoning Clearance with no hearing; standards updated September 16, 2025 (program HE-H). Each RHD project must choose 20% lower income, 10% very low income, 5% extremely low income, or 30% lower income through alternative compliance (land donation, acquisition assistance to an affordable developer in a same-or-higher resource area, or an equivalent action). Piru expansion area projects must keep 10.5% of units affordable to low income households.
affordability_requirement: Government Code 65915 thresholds for the bonus; RHD affordability options as listed with recorded affordable housing agreements.
eligible_project_types: density bonus projects in residential zones
next_deadline: Requested with the zoning clearance or permit application; RHD Zoning Clearance checklist on the RMA RHD page.

program_name: Inclusionary housing program and housing impact mitigation fee (studied, postponed June 9, 2026)
administering_agency: Ventura County Resource Management Agency, Planning Division
typical_award_size: Housing Element program HE-K study by Economic and Planning Systems (funded by REAP 2.0 through the Ventura Council of Governments, September 2025) modeled a 5% moderate-income requirement on for-sale projects and 5% low-income on rentals, and a commercial linkage fee of about $4 per square foot on projects generating more than 30 employees (estimated $1.2 million over seven years). affordability_requirement: Not adopted.
eligible_project_types: none (no requirement or fee in effect in unincorporated Ventura County)
next_deadline: No action expected before the 7th cycle Housing Element (2029-2031). Cities with inclusionary programs: Oxnard, Ventura, Moorpark, Thousand Oaks, Santa Paula, Port Hueneme.

program_name: Streamlined ministerial approvals for affordable, supportive and farmworker housing (SB 35, AB 2162, AB 1783, SB 330) and Prohousing Designation
administering_agency: Ventura County Resource Management Agency, Planning Division
typical_award_size: Because the County has not met its above-moderate RHNA progress, qualifying multifamily projects with the required affordability are approved ministerially under SB 35 using the County's Streamlined Multifamily Zoning Clearance application; supportive housing is by right where multifamily is allowed (AB 2162); farmworker housing on agricultural land qualifies under AB 1783 and the County's Agricultural Worker Housing regulations (Somis Ranch farmworker complex, AMCAL). The County applied for the state Prohousing Designation in 2026 (public comment through May 29, 2026; Board resolution April 28, 2026), which adds points in state funding programs, and is completing a countywide Farmworker Housing Study and Action Plan (approved September 22, 2026).
affordability_requirement: SB 35: 10% or 50% affordable depending on RHNA shortfall category; AB 2162 supportive housing thresholds; AB 1783 farmworker housing requirements.
eligible_project_types: 100% affordable and mixed-income multifamily on eligible sites
next_deadline: Submit the Streamlined Multifamily Zoning Clearance application with objective standards compliance; SB 330 preliminary applications lock in standards.

program_name: Homeless Housing, Assistance and Prevention (HHAP) Rounds 5 to 7, Madera County allocation within the Fresno Madera CoC CA-514
administering_agency: Madera County (Behavioral Health Services and Social Services, as the County applicant) with the Fresno Madera Continuum of Care
typical_award_size: HHAP-6 County of Madera allocation $610,483.23 (awards announced March 2, 2026 as part of the nearly $20.7 million Fresno-Madera regional award with Fresno County $4,301,909.86, City of Fresno $10,491,196.56 and CoC $5,246,520.28); HHAP-7 preliminary allocation $787,530.13. Rounds 1 to 5 brought $6.8 million to the Madera area of which $2.4 million went directly to Madera County ($2.3 million obligated, $1.4 million spent per the state accountability dashboard).
affordability_requirement: Homeless and at-risk households; 10% youth set-aside; shared Regionally Coordinated Homelessness Action Plan with Fresno County, the City of Fresno and the CoC.
next_deadline: No local NOFA; the County programs its share directly and the CoC programs the regional share. HHAP-7 allocations are preliminary for FY 2026-27.
layering_notes: Madera County is a small non-entitlement county: the Community and Economic Development Department (planning, state CDBG and HOME applications) and Behavioral Health Services (BHSA, bridge housing) are the only County housing actors, the Housing Authority of the City of Madera (HACM) is the PHA for the county, and the Fresno Madera Continuum of Care (CA-514, led by Fresno County) handles HHAP and CoC funds. There is no County housing trust fund, NOFA, inclusionary ordinance or impact fee waiver program. The City of Madera is a separate CDBG and HOME entitlement with its own PLHA plan (Pass 3). maderacounty.com blocks automated access (403 on pages and documents), the PrimeGov and IQM2 portals returned no 2026 meetings, and Board agendas were read from PDFs mirrored on maderacountywater.com; other sources were HCD allocation tables, maderaha.org, zoneomics (County Code Title 18), CEQAnet and press coverage. At about $600,000 to $800,000 a year HHAP covers Madera's shelter and outreach system and is not a capital source; the regional CoC allocation is administered by Fresno County's Office of Housing and Homelessness. Source is HCD's HHAP-6 allocation table; round 1 to 5 totals from the state accountability dashboard.

Confirmation needed: BHSA housing dollars, exemption status and any PSH capital plans. Madera's pattern is motel-based bridge housing and contracted beds rather than capital; a developer would be looking at an operating or master-lease contract. Source is the County MHSA/BHSA page (blocked to automated access); the bridge housing and BHCIP details come from the Madera Tribune (July 9, 2023) and Board meeting summaries.

administering_agency: Mendocino County Planning and Building Services (Julia Krog, Director, (707) 234-6650)

affordability_requirement: Government Code 65915 thresholds with recorded restrictions; equity-sharing payments on for-sale bonus units go to the County Affordable Housing Trust Fund.
eligible_project_types: multifamily and mixed-income housing in residential and mixed-use zones
motel conversions (Golden Rule approved with a water concession)
next_deadline: Requested with the land use application; expect new Housing Element programs and possible incentive changes in 2027.

program_name: Monterey County Housing Trust Fund (MCHTF) loans for affordable rental development
administering_agency: Monterey County Housing and Community Development Department
typical_award_size: Established May 17, 2022 (Resolution 22-100) to replace redevelopment set-aside; by April 2023 the County had committed $10,033,984 of local cash, land assets and PLHA to capitalize it, including about $420,000 of PLHA delegated by Carmel-by-the-Sea, Greenfield and Soledad plus about $289,000 a year from those cities' later allocations. Loans: Greenfield Commons (EAH Housing, 100 units, Greenfield) $1,929,046 ($1,028,833 trust fund plus $900,213 PLHA) approved March 2023 and increased by $550,000 trust fund plus $9,982 PLHA on December 22, 2025 for cost overruns; Lightfighter Village (EAH and Veterans Transition Center, 71 units, Marina) $500,115. Loan origination fee corrected to 0.5%. The County applied to the state Local Housing Trust Fund matching program in 2022 (unsuccessful) and 2023 (up to $5 million match on $3,544,645 eligible local funds); a 2024 Board referral explored using 1220 Natividad Road to recapitalize the fund.
per_unit_cap: Not published; awards of $500,000 to $2.5 million per project (about $5,000 to $25,000 per unit).
affordability_requirement: Lower income rental housing with 55-year County regulatory agreements; LHTF rules (3% simple maximum, predevelopment, acquisition, construction and permanent loans) when matched by state funds.
next_deadline: No standing NOFA; awards have gone by Board resolution to projects identified in the County's LHTF application. Contact HCD housing staff about trust fund and PLHA availability for 2027 tax credit applications; the pending inclusionary fee restructuring is intended to feed this fund.
layering_notes: Monterey County's Housing and Community Development Department (HCD, Craig Spencer, Director; Darby Marshall, Housing Program Manager) runs the Inclusionary Housing Ordinance, the Monterey County Housing Trust Fund, PLHA, the Urban County CDBG and HOME programs and County land dispositions; the County Administrative Office Homelessness Strategies and Initiatives Division (CAO-HSI) runs HHAP and the SHARE Center; the Health Department Behavioral Health Bureau holds BHSA; the Coalition of Homeless Services Providers leads the CoC (CA-506, shared with San Benito); and the Housing Authority of the County of Monterey (HACM) and its Development Corporation supply vouchers and develop housing. The trust fund is the County's gap lender of record but is thinly capitalized (two projects to date); its future depends on inclusionary in-lieu fee revenue and PLHA delegations from small cities. program_name: Inclusionary Housing Ordinance (Chapter 18.40), in-lieu fees and the 2026 fee-based restructuring proposal
administering_agency: Monterey County Housing and Community Development Department; Housing Advisory Committee
typical_award_size: Current ordinance (first adopted 1980, revised 2003): 20% of units in residential projects affordable, analyzed by Keyser Marston as 6% very low, 6% low and 8% moderate income plus a 5% Workforce I component, with in-lieu fees for fractional units and small projects; in-lieu fees collected at building permit 2021-2025 are tabulated in the September 2026 workshop packet. The 2026 KMA In-Lieu Fee Analysis found maximum supportable fees of $73.90 to $305.60 per square foot of saleable area by product type. Staff recommended (Housing Advisory Committee workshops September 2 and 11, 2026) converting to an entirely fee-based program for projects under 250 units, charging 33 to 35 percent of the maximum fee on habitable square footage above the first 1,500 square feet, exempting all multifamily (duplex to fourplex and ADUs under 1,200 square feet), encouraging land donation for 20% affordable units on projects of 250 or more units, indexing the fee annually and allowing fee revenue to be spent countywide.
affordability_requirement: Very low (50% AMI), low (80% AMI), moderate (120% AMI) and Workforce I (to 150% AMI) for-sale and rental units with long-term resale and rent restrictions; inclusionary units are calculated on base plus density bonus units.
eligible_project_types: market-rate subdivisions and multifamily in unincorporated Monterey County
nonprofit projects receiving in-lieu fee revenue or donated land
next_deadline: Board action on the restructured ordinance and new fee schedule expected late 2026 or 2027 after Housing Advisory Committee recommendations; LeSar and KMA remain under contract (Amendment 10, April 2026) to complete the fee studies. Until adoption the 2003 ordinance and existing in-lieu fees apply.
layering_notes: Monterey County's Housing and Community Development Department (HCD, Craig Spencer, Director; Darby Marshall, Housing Program Manager) runs the Inclusionary Housing Ordinance, the Monterey County Housing Trust Fund, PLHA, the Urban County CDBG and HOME programs and County land dispositions; the County Administrative Office Homelessness Strategies and Initiatives Division (CAO-HSI) runs HHAP and the SHARE Center; the Health Department Behavioral Health Bureau holds BHSA; the Coalition of Homeless Services Providers leads the CoC (CA-506, shared with San Benito); and the Housing Authority of the County of Monterey (HACM) and its Development Corporation supply vouchers and develop housing. Salinas, Monterey, Seaside and other entitlement cities run their own programs (Pass 3). countyofmonterey.gov blocks automated access (pages and documents), so records were built from the Legistar web API client 'monterey' and its Granicus attachments, hamonterey.org, chsp.org, zoneomics and HCD tables. The County concluded the inclusionary mandate produces few units (about five per project) and wants a reliable fee stream for the Housing Trust Fund, land acquisition and leverage of state programs; a fee-based ordinance would make market-rate permits the County's main local revenue source for affordable housing. Source is the September 11, 2026 Housing Advisory Committee workshop item (Legistar file 26-799) with the staff report and KMA analysis attached.

program_name: County land for affordable housing: 855 East Laurel Drive, Salinas (Eden Housing) and SHARE Center reconfiguration
administering_agency: Monterey County Housing and Community Development Department and County Administrative Office, Homelessness Strategies and Initiatives
typical_award_size: 855 East Laurel Drive (County-owned, declared exempt surplus August 31, 2022; Eden Housing selected with the City of Salinas through an RFQ September 2022; ENA February 17, 2023): 132-unit 100% affordable rental project (53 low, 48 very low, 29 extremely low income, 2 manager units) in two phases (78 and 54 units) approved by the Board on February 28, 2025 with a Lease Disposition and Development Agreement (ground lease); groundbreaking targeted for late 2026 subject to local funding then tax credits. The adjoining SHARE Center (845 East Laurel Drive, 128-bed navigation center) is being reconfigured with twelve non-congregate family cabins and a 30-bed recuperative care area using a Central California Alliance for Health Housing Fund award of $3,222,262 and Health Department match for a $6,444,524 budget (October 30, 2026, Resolution 26-194).
affordability_requirement: 100% affordable at extremely low to low income under the LDDA and state funding regulatory agreements; recuperative care beds limited to Medi-Cal members.
eligible_project_types: 100% affordable rental on County ground lease
interim housing and recuperative care capital (Medi-Cal plan funding)
next_deadline: Eden Housing is assembling local funding (County trust fund and PLHA, City of Salinas) before CTCAC applications; no other County sites are currently offered. Developers should watch Surplus Land Act notices and Board referrals on County property (1220 Natividad Road was referred for trust fund capitalization in 2024).
layering_notes: Monterey County's Housing and Community Development Department (HCD, Craig Spencer, Director; Darby Marshall, Housing Program Manager) runs the Inclusionary Housing Ordinance, the Monterey County Housing Trust Fund, PLHA, the Urban County CDBG and HOME programs and County land dispositions; the County Administrative Office Homelessness Strategies and Initiatives Division (CAO-HSI) runs HHAP and the SHARE Center; the Health Department Behavioral Health Bureau holds BHSA; the Coalition of Homeless Services Providers leads the CoC (CA-506, shared with San Benito); and the Housing Authority of the County of Monterey (HACM) and its Development Corporation supply vouchers and develop housing. Salinas, Monterey, Seaside and other entitlement cities run their own programs (Pass 3). countyofmonterey.gov blocks automated access (pages and documents), so records were built from the Legistar web API client 'monterey' and its Granicus attachments, hamonterey.org, chsp.org, zoneomics and HCD tables. East Laurel Drive is the model for County participation: land by ground lease plus trust fund and PLHA loans, with the City of Salinas as co-sponsor; the Alliance Housing Fund award shows Medi-Cal plan capital is available for interim and recuperative housing in the county. Source is the February 28, 2025 Board approval item (Legistar file RES 25-041); SHARE Center details from file RES 26-194.

program_name: Behavioral Health Services Act Integrated Plan FY 2026-29: housing interventions and capital development
administering_agency: Monterey County Health Department, Behavioral Health Bureau
typical_award_size: Three-Year Integrated Plan and budget approved by the Board in June 2026 (Legistar file 26-552): Housing Interventions expenditures $9,025,327 (FY 2026-27), $9,296,089 (FY 2027-28) and $9,574,972 (FY 2028-29); capital development projects $1,130,582 rising to $1,199,435 a year (12.5% of the component); permanent rental subsidies $915,771 a year and interim rental subsidies $305,257 a year plus operating subsidies and a housing flex pool; 51.9% of housing funds dedicated to chronically homeless people; about 1,345 adults and 61 youth served a year.
per_unit_cap: Not published; BHSA capital limited to 25% of the component (County planned 12.5%).
affordability_requirement: BHSA eligible adults and youth with serious mental illness or substance use disorder; at least half of housing funds for chronically homeless people.
eligible_project_types: permanent supportive housing capital (about $1.1 million a year)
operating subsidies and flex pool units
next_deadline: No NOFA; the Behavioral Health Bureau programs capital and subsidies through contracts. The June 2026 Board item also reported 22 prevention providers losing MHSA PEI funding under the BHSA restructuring.

The HACM Development Corporation develops and co-owns housing (Haciendas 1-4 and Tynan Village in Salinas, Rippling River in Carmel Valley with a 2006 County HOME and CDBG loan of $1,262,500, Benito Farm Labor Center in Soledad, Oak Park in Paso Robles) and in May 2026 reaffirmed Milestone Housing Group as development partner for its Greenfield sites (Resolution 3160).

affordability_requirement: PBV households at or below 50% AMI (75% extremely low income); farm labor housing for agricultural workers.
eligible_project_types: new construction and rehabilitation LIHTC projects countywide
HACM joint ventures and RAD conversions
next_deadline: No open PBV RFP on hamonterey.org as of November 2026; contact the Director of Development about PBV commitments or a joint venture. HACM is not a Moving to Work agency.

program_name: Density bonus and incentives (Chapter 21.65) and Sixth Cycle Housing Element implementation (by-right approvals, objective design standards)
administering_agency: Monterey County Housing and Community Development Department, Planning Services
typical_award_size: Chapter 21.65 (Ordinance 5177, 2011) implements state density bonus law up to a 35% bonus (5% very low income units earn 20%, rising by 2.5 points per additional percent) with incentives, parking reductions, child care and land donation bonuses; Section 21.65.110 states the bonus does not satisfy the Inclusionary Housing Ordinance and inclusionary units are computed on base plus bonus units. The Sixth Cycle (2023-2031) Housing Element Update and implementation package went to the Board on October 23, 2026 (ORD 26-021) after the Planning Commission on October 7, 2026, adding Chapter 18.20 objective design standards, a coastal by-right approval chapter (20.59), rezoning of housing sites and amendments to Titles 18, 20 and 21; HCD had found the third submittal (April 2026) still needing revisions.
affordability_requirement: Government Code 65915 thresholds with recorded qualifying unit agreements (Section 21.65.120); inclusionary obligations remain.
eligible_project_types: multifamily and mixed-income housing in unincorporated zones
projects on Housing Element rezoned sites (by-right where 20% affordable)
next_deadline: Requested with the land use application; confirm Housing Element adoption and HCD certification status (late 2026) because HHAP second disbursements and state program eligibility depend on it.

program_name: County TEFRA approvals for CSCDA and other conduit issuers
administering_agency: Monterey County Board of Supervisors (Housing and Community Development or sponsoring department)

program_name: Western Nevada County Regional Housing Trust Fund (WNCRHTF) gap loans
administering_agency: Nevada County Housing and Community Services Department (with City of Grass Valley and Nevada City)
typical_award_size: Formed July 14, 2020 (Resolutions 20-315, 20-316, 20-317) by the County, Grass Valley and Nevada City, capitalized with PLHA, a state Local Housing Trust Fund (LHTF) matching grant awarded February 3, 2021, HHSA Intergovernmental Transfer funds, ARPA and a $1 million General Fund commitment repurposed as match in 2025. Awards to date: Cashin's Field (51 units, Nevada City, Resolution 21-116 loan, completed January 2023); Lone Oak Senior Apartments II (31 units, Penn Valley, Pacific West Communities) $1,024,775 under RFP 3 (Resolution 23-227, May 23, 2023) plus $1,281,373 (Resolution 25-167, May 13, 2025) for a $2,306,128 loan approved May 19, 2026 (Resolution 26-196); Habitat for Humanity Ventana Sierra (owner-occupied, May 2023 RFP).
per_unit_cap: Not published. Lone Oak II works out to about $74,000 per unit; Cashin's Field loan amount not stated on the trust fund page.
affordability_requirement: Low income rental or owner-occupied housing; the Lone Oak II loan is an unsecured deferred loan repaid from residual receipts with affordability tied to the TCAC regulatory agreement. LHTF rules (lower income, 55-year rental covenants, 3% simple maximum) apply to the state-matched share.
next_deadline: No open RFP. Resolution 24-121 lets HCS pre-select LHTF projects by RFP and publish preliminary awards on the trust fund page when a new LHTF round opens. The June 16, 2026 PLHA plan amendment states LHTF match is no longer available, so PLHA Rounds 4 and 5 will fund projects directly rather than through the trust fund. Check nevadacountyca.gov/3926 for any new RFP.
layering_notes: Nevada County's Housing and Community Services Department (HCS, Tyler Barrington, Director, 950 Maidu Ave, Nevada City, 530-265-1645, Housing@nevadacountyca.gov) sits inside the Health and Human Services Agency and administers the Western Nevada County Regional Housing Trust Fund, PLHA (as delegated applicant for Grass Valley and Nevada City), state HOME and CDBG awards, the MORE mobile home program and the new Down Payment Assistance Program; the Behavioral Health and Homelessness Department (Cari Yardley, Director) holds Homekey+, BHSA and the Truckee Navigation Center; HHAP is administered by the Homeless Resource Council of the Sierras as the CoC CA-531 lead; and the Regional Housing Authority (Sutter, Nevada, Yuba, Colusa and Lake counties, Yuba City) supplies vouchers. Grass Valley, Nevada City and Truckee run their own programs (Pass 3). The County has no inclusionary ordinance, no housing impact fee and no affordable housing fee waiver program; the only land use incentive is the state density bonus ordinance. nevadacountyca.gov opens directly and the Legistar web API client 'nevco' exposes staff reports and attachments at legistar.granicus.com/nevco/attachments/. The trust fund is the County's only local gap source and has been used as the TCAC local contribution that moved Lone Oak II from unfunded to a December 2025 4% award. Expect small amounts ($1 million to $2.3 million) and a Board resolution for each loan. Pair with state HOME (Lone Oak II received $11,041,628) and CMFA or CSCDA conduit bonds. Future awards are likely to come as direct PLHA loans scored jointly with the two cities instead of trust fund loans.

program_name: Permanent Local Housing Allocation (PLHA) regional program (County, Grass Valley and Nevada City)
administering_agency: Nevada County Housing and Community Services Department
typical_award_size: $3,074,180 in PLHA for 2020 through 2024 across the County, Grass Valley and Nevada City; Rounds 1 to 3 funded affordable housing development (Lone Oak II and Habitat Ventana Sierra through the trust fund), owner-occupied construction and homeless services; Rounds 4 and 5 total $808,089 and will be awarded directly under the plan amended June 16, 2026 (Resolution 26-317). Per HCD's 2024-2028 formula NOFA the County's own annual allocation is $207,009 (2024) and $238,910 (2025) and Nevada City's is $53,734 and $57,661; Grass Valley's is delegated to the County under the MOU extended August 11, 2026.
per_unit_cap: Not published. Rental awards must be low-interest deferred loans secured by a deed of trust with a 55-year regulatory agreement (resolution certification 9).
affordability_requirement: PLHA guidelines: households at or below 60% AMI for rental development, with 55-year covenants; owner-occupied units deed-restricted per Guidelines 302(c)(6).
next_deadline: No NOFA published as of November 8, 2026. Staff report (August 11, 2026) says the County will score proposals for Rounds 4 and 5 jointly with the two cities once the MOU extension is executed by both city councils.

next_deadline: Depends on HCD's next state HOME rental NOFA; the County applies on behalf of a specific developer and project. Contact HCS before HCD releases the NOFA.
