program_name: Homekey+ permanent supportive housing (County with AMI Housing)
administering_agency: Nevada County Behavioral Health and Homelessness Department with Advocates for Mentally Ill Housing (AMI Housing); funds from California HCD
typical_award_size: Two HCD Homekey+ awards to the County of Nevada and AMI Housing: Stagecoach Motel, Grass Valley (acquisition and rehabilitation, 17 units, 16 assisted, 10 veteran) $5,866,160 awarded November 13, 2025 ($4,742,960 capital, $823,200 operating, $300,000 veteran operating); Nevada County Permanent Supportive Housing Expansion Project (single-family scattered site, 24 units) $5,231,453 awarded December 16, 2025 ($4,641,430 capital, $590,023 operating). Board authorized applications up to $8,000,000 (Resolutions 25-165, 25-476, 26-410) and released $595,000 from Fund 1589 to buy 135 East Empire Street for PSH (December 1, 2025).

program_name: Behavioral Health Services Act (BHSA) Housing Interventions, 2026-2029 Integrated Plan
administering_agency: Nevada County Behavioral Health Department
typical_award_size: Three-year BHSA plan (FY 2026/27 to 2028/29, approved June 2, 2026, Resolution 26-231) budgets $27,502,891 in BHSA spending, with the required 30% for housing interventions (about $2.75 million a year) and half of that for chronic homelessness. The County will use housing funds for rental subsidies and operating costs of its PSH units and for outreach (HOME Team, Commons Resource Center, 865 people a year); it will NOT use BHSA for capital development (0% of the allowed 25%) or for CalAIM-covered tenancy services. BHSA-funded PSH beds grew from 20 (2019) to 94 (2026) plus 24 Homekey+ units coming.
per_unit_cap: Not applicable; no capital or per-unit awards.
affordability_requirement: BHSA-eligible adults with serious mental illness or substance use disorder experiencing or at risk of homelessness; BHSA is the funding source of last resort for PSH.
eligible_project_types: permanent supportive housing operating and rental subsidies
next_deadline: Integrated Plan runs through FY 2028/29 with annual updates; contact Nevada County Behavioral Health (530-265-1437) about operating subsidies for PSH units.

program_name: Urban County Action Plan NOFA: HOME and CDBG affordable housing development loans
administering_agency: San Luis Obispo County Department of Social Services, Homeless Services Division
typical_award_size: 2027 Action Plan NOFA (issued September 28, 2026, applications due October 30, 2026): HOME estimated $690,900 available for projects (allocation $767,667), CDBG $1,418,895 across the Urban County (County share $368,732 for projects; cities $30,236 to $371,200 each). 2026 Action Plan (approved April 7, 2026) put $499,969 of HOME into one affordable rental project and CDBG into rehab, shelters and a recuperative care facility. Recent HOME and Title 29 layered projects: Rolling Hills III (Templeton, 28 units, Peoples' Self-Help Housing), Cambria Pines (33 units, $373,418 HOME/PLHA/Title 29 in 2025), Monterey Family Apartments (50 units), Balay Ko on Monterey (56 senior units) and Arroyo Terrace (63 units), the last three by HASLO's nonprofit.
per_unit_cap: HUD HOME maximum per-unit subsidy; County scores cost effectiveness (maximum per unit subsidy, 10 points) and number of new grant-supported units (10 points). More than 12 HOME-assisted units triggers Davis-Bacon.
affordability_requirement: HOME: 90% of households at or below 60% AMI, 20% of units at 50% AMI in projects of five or more HOME units; affordability 20 years for new construction (longer under County agreements); 25% HOME match and 15% CHDO set-aside. CDBG: 51% low and moderate income.
next_deadline: 2027 Action Plan applications closed October 30, 2026; draft housing recommendations hearing February 2027; Board of Supervisors approval April 2027; FY 2027/28 awards begin July 1, 2027. The 2028 Action Plan NOFA is expected in September 2027.
layering_notes: San Luis Obispo County's Department of Social Services Homeless Services Division (HSD, Devin Drake, Director; George Solis, Principal Administrative Manager; HSDgrants@co.slo.ca.us) runs one combined annual Action Plan NOFA each fall for CDBG, HOME, ESG, HHAP, PLHA, Title 29 and County General Fund Support on the Neighborly portal, and is the Continuum of Care collaborative applicant and administrative entity (CA-614). Scoring (100 points) weights scope and expertise (40), funding readiness (15), cost effectiveness and unit count (20), entitlement readiness (10), site standards, vulnerable population targeting and alignment with the Countywide Plan to Address Homelessness (15). HOME awards are small ($400,000 to $900,000) and are typically layered with Title 29, PLHA, SB 1090 and Housing Trust Fund loans under TCAC. Apply through Neighborly; attend the October information session.

program_name: SHRA Multifamily Lending Program (City of Sacramento gap financing: HOME, Housing Trust Fund, Mixed Income Housing fund, PLHA)
administering_agency: Sacramento Housing and Redevelopment Agency (SHRA) on behalf of the City of Sacramento and the Housing Authority of the City of Sacramento
typical_award_size: Gap loans sized to the gap after all other sources, no stated per-project cap. City funds posted June 1, 2026: HOME $5,000,000, Housing Trust Fund/Workforce Housing $1,000,000, Mixed Income Housing/Workforce Housing $2,500,000, PLHA $680,000 (about $9.2M). Applicants request gap funds without naming a source. January 2026 City pre-applications: Hotel Berry (Jamboree, preservation, $5.1M) invited; Florin Family Apartments (CCH, $5.1M) and Q Street Apartments (Community HousingWorks, $2.0M) invited; requests of $6.5M to $12M (Mercy 2601 5th Street, Danco 6779 Q Street, TWG 1220 H Street, Dos Rios) declined for insufficient funds. Projects must have 12 or more units.
per_unit_cap: No published cap; subsidy per restricted unit cannot exceed HUD Section 234 limits for the Sacramento area; HOME units capped by 24 CFR 92.250. Annual SHRA monitoring fee charged per assisted unit.
affordability_requirement: 55-year regulatory agreement (HOME units per federal rules). SHRA minimum: at least 15% of units at or below 50% AMI and 5% at or below 30% AMI based on feasibility; regulated share at least proportional to SHRA share of total development cost; restricted rents at least 10% below market. Housing Trust Fund and Mixed Income fund money is limited to workforce households (up to 80% AMI, jobs-housing nexus). Priorities: preservation at risk, then new construction and nonresidential conversion (PSH and homeless housing, veterans, workforce 30% to 60% AMI, other), then rehab of regulated stock, then market-rate to affordable conversion.
next_deadline: Two rounds a year aligned to CTCAC 9% rounds. 2026: pre-applications Jan 2 and July 1 (Builder's Patch), full applications March 2 and Sept 1, Council approvals June 16, 2026 and Jan 19, 2027. SHRA was not accepting pre-applications as of 2026-11-08; the 2027 schedule and a new funds-available notice are expected on the SHRA multifamily page at least 30 days before the next pre-application deadline, likely early January 2027. Phone (916) 440-1393.
layering_notes: This is the City-side pool parallel to the County SHRA record (Pass 2); a project uses one or the other based on location, both run on the same schedule and policies (2026 City Multifamily Lending and Mortgage Revenue Bond Policies, amended July 29, 2026). Terms: up to 3% simple interest or the AFR, term up to 40 years from conversion or 55 years when senior public lenders require, 1.10x to 1.20x combined DSCR, payments deferred during construction and deferred developer fee repayment, residual receipts allowed; nonprofit managing general partner required; developer fee limited to $25,000/$15,000/$12,000 per unit tiers for non-tax-credit deals and deferred maximum fee for LIHTC deals. Federal HOME (12 or more units) and CDBG (8 or more units) trigger Davis-Bacon; SHRA treats state prevailing wage as applying unless the below-market loan exemption (40% of units at 80% AMI for 20 years) fits. Stack with the City Zero-Dollar Rate impact fee reduction, Housing Impact Fee exemption at 40 du/acre, SacSewer fee waivers (County record) and Housing Authority of the City of Sacramento bonds. SHRA does not expect a project-based voucher RFP in 2026. SB 802 moves SHRA into the Sacramento Area Housing and Homelessness Agency by Jan 1, 2028, so confirm the lender entity on 2027 and later commitments.

program_name: City of Sacramento Housing Trust Fund (commercial linkage fee, City Code Chapter 18.56 Article IV)
administering_agency: City of Sacramento Community Development Department, Planning Division (fee assessment); SHRA (fund administration and lending)
typical_award_size: Fee source for SHRA City gap loans. Nonresidential rates effective July 1, 2024 through June 30, 2026: office $3.33, hotel $3.18, commercial $2.68, manufacturing $2.08, warehouse $0.91 per square foot, adjusted annually by the San Francisco construction cost index (the FY 2026-27 notice was not posted as of 2026-11-08). 2024 fund: $411,805 fees collected, $140,000 spent, $4.85M ending balance of which $807,861 uncommitted; $1.0M posted as available June 1, 2026.
per_unit_cap: None published; SHRA policies apply (HUD Section 234 limit per restricted unit).
affordability_requirement: Fund is restricted to housing for workforce households up to 80% AMI (very low and low income wage earners) under the 1989 jobs-housing nexus; 55-year SHRA regulatory agreement.
next_deadline: Deployed through the SHRA two-round schedule (next pre-application likely early January 2027). Fee is paid at building permit on nonresidential projects; contact Ryan Dodge, (916) 808-8044, rdodge@cityofsacramento.org for fee questions.
layering_notes: Adopted 1989 (Chapter 17.708), moved into the Development Impact Fee chapter 18.56 on Feb 14, 2017; Council raised the fee 81.3% in 2004 (phased) and allows changes by resolution. Small and lumpy: about $0.4M to $0.6M a year in fees, so it is the smallest of the four City pools and is usually blended into a single SHRA loan with HOME and Mixed Income money. Parallel County Housing Trust Fund covers the unincorporated area (County rates $3.26 office to $1.08 warehouse since March 28, 2025). Annual report posted each May by SHRA.

program_name: Mixed Income Housing Ordinance and Housing Impact Fee (City Code Chapter 17.712)
administering_agency: City of Sacramento Community Development Department, Planning Division (fee); SHRA (Mixed Income Housing fund and 100-acre housing strategies)
typical_award_size: Requirement and fee, not a subsidy. Housing Impact Fee effective July 1, 2026 through June 30, 2027: $3.58 per square foot for single-unit, duplex and multi-unit dwellings below 20 and 40 dwelling units per net acre respectively; $0.00 for single-unit or duplex at 20 du/acre or more, multi-unit at 40 du/acre or more, and nonresidential-to-residential conversions; $1.55 per square foot in the Housing Incentive Zone. Fee revenue (about $1.7M in 2024, $4.2M lent to projects that year) goes to the SHRA-administered Mixed Income Housing fund; $2.5M posted available June 1, 2026. Projects over 100 gross acres must adopt a Council-approved mixed income housing strategy.
affordability_requirement: Exempt from the fee: developments with 10% regulated low-income units (80% AMI), room additions, second units, owner-builder single homes, mobilehome parks, projects with pre-ordinance development agreements or pre-November 2015 entitlements. No mandatory inclusionary requirement citywide.
next_deadline: Fee assessed at building permit, adjusted every July 1. The Housing Element Program H1 review ended Dec 9, 2025 when Council voted to make no changes, so the current structure holds through at least 2027. Contact Greta Soos, (916) 808-2027.
layering_notes: Most 4% and 9% multifamily deals in Sacramento pay nothing: at 40 du/acre or more the rate is $0, and any project with 10% low-income units is exempt, so the fee mainly hits single-family subdivisions and low-density apartments. The fund it feeds is the largest City gap pool after HOME ($2.5M June 2026). Compare the County Affordable Housing Ordinance ($3.91 per square foot with on-site credit) for unincorporated sites. A 2023 to 2025 study considered mandatory inclusionary and higher fees; Council declined, so no inclusionary units are required citywide.

program_name: Reduced Residential Development Impact Fees for Affordable Dwelling Units (Zero-Dollar Rate Program)
administering_agency: City of Sacramento Community Development Department, Planning Division (Form CDD-0410); affordability confirmed by SHRA or CADA
typical_award_size: Reduction of City-controlled development impact fees to a $0 rate for deed-restricted affordable units, capped at $10,000 per qualifying unit, funded by a $3 million annual General Fund/Measure U appropriation (reauthorized July 2025). Eligible fees: park development impact fee (Ch. 18.56 Art. II), sewer, combined sewer, water system and storm drainage development fees (Ch. 13), and the 65th Street, Central City, Jacinto Creek, North Natomas, Railyards, River District and Willowcreek area fees. School fees and SAFCA fees are not City-controlled and still apply.
per_unit_cap: $10,000 per qualifying affordable dwelling unit; mixed-income projects receive a proportional reduction.
affordability_requirement: Rental: occupied by low or moderate income households (80% or 120% AMI per H&S 50093) at affordable rent (H&S 50053), restricted at least 30 years by a recorded regulatory agreement with the City, SHRA or another public agency. For-sale: low income (80% AMI) at an affordable price, 30 years.
next_deadline: First come, first served against each fiscal year's $3M; LIHTC and Homekey projects may reserve funds when awarded. Apply with Form CDD-0410 before permit issuance; contact planning@cityofsacramento.org early. Program resolutions 2018-0428, 2019-0185 and 2024-0233 (June 25, 2024).
layering_notes: Worth roughly $5,000 to $10,000 per unit depending on area fees; stackable with the SacSewer impact fee waiver (County record) which covers the regional sanitation fee the City program does not touch, and with the Housing Impact Fee $0 rate. Because Labor Code 1720(b)(4) treats waived fees as public funds, a fee reduction can by itself trigger state prevailing wage for a project that is otherwise exempt; most LIHTC projects already pay prevailing wage. The 2018 version waived fees without a cap; the 2024 modification added the $10,000 cap and the $3M budget, so large projects should not assume full waivers. Deferral of remaining impact fees to final inspection is available separately (CDD-0330).

program_name: City of Sacramento Development Impact Fee Deferral Program
administering_agency: City of Sacramento Community Development Department, Building Division (Form CDD-0330)
typical_award_size: Deferral, not waiver: City impact fees may be paid at final inspection instead of permit issuance, useful for phased or multi-building projects. No cost figure published. Fee estimates available for a low-cost application. The Statewide Community Infrastructure Program (CSCDA SCIP) is also accepted for financing eligible City impact fees.
affordability_requirement: None; open to all residential projects.
next_deadline: Apply with CDD-0330 before permit issuance; fees due at final inspection.
layering_notes: Carries impact fees through construction so they can be paid from permanent loan proceeds; pair with the Zero-Dollar Rate reduction on the affordable units and SCIP bond financing of remaining fees. The County runs a separate deferral program for unincorporated projects (County record).

program_name: Density bonus (City Code Chapter 17.704) and ministerial infill housing permits (Chapter 17.860 and SB 35/SB 423)
administering_agency: City of Sacramento Community Development Department, Planning Division
typical_award_size: State density bonus law as implemented in Chapter 17.704 (no local enhancement beyond state minimums identified): e.g., 5% very low income units earns a 20% bonus plus one concession and unlimited waivers; up to 50% bonus and the 100% affordable 80% bonus per Government Code 65915. City ministerial permit (CDD-0428, adopted Aug 27, 2020) covers 2 to 200 unit residential or mixed-use infill projects meeting objective standards, no affordability or prevailing wage requirement, no CEQA, 60 to 90 day review; the state SB 35 permit (CDD-0427) requires 10% lower-income units at 11 or more units. Density bonus requests can be processed ministerially with either permit.
affordability_requirement: Per state law for the bonus; none for the City ministerial permit.
next_deadline: Rolling at entitlement. Parking: none required within a quarter mile of light rail, 50% reduction within a half mile.
layering_notes: Sacramento is the state's first Prohousing jurisdiction (renewed Dec 23, 2025 with the top score) and already has high base densities, so the bonus is mostly used for height, parking and setback waivers rather than unit count. Combining the City ministerial permit with a density bonus avoids hearings and CEQA for 100% affordable infill without the SB 35 prevailing wage trigger. Missing Middle zoning (2024) allows multi-unit on former single-family lots citywide.

program_name: Multifamily Mortgage Revenue Bonds, Housing Authority of the City of Sacramento (SHRA conduit issuance)
administering_agency: Sacramento Housing and Redevelopment Agency for the Housing Authority of the City of Sacramento
typical_award_size: Tax-exempt and taxable conduit bonds for rental projects of 12 or more units in the City; no minimum or maximum issue size (cost-effectiveness usually sets a floor). Applications for bonds without an SHRA loan are accepted year round; bond-plus-loan requests follow the SHRA pre-application schedule. Private placements require accredited or qualified institutional buyers in $250,000 denominations with investor letters.
affordability_requirement: Federal minimum 20% at 50% AMI or 30% at 60% AMI plus 10% at 50% AMI (H&S 34312.3); CDLAC and CTCAC rules govern; SHRA adds its 15% at 50% AMI and 5% at 30% AMI policy when an SHRA loan is included; non-competitive CTCAC deals averaging above 60% AMI must average at or below 59% AMI. Refundings that extend maturity require at least 10% of units at 50% or 60% AMI for 15 more years.
next_deadline: Bond-only applications any time; bond-with-loan applications on the SHRA schedule (next pre-application likely early January 2027). SHRA Commission then City Council approval, then CDLAC allocation.
layering_notes: SHRA prefers to be the issuer for City projects and pairs bonds with its gap loan; CSCDA or CMFA remain alternatives if timing does not fit. Bond policy requires the nonprofit owner to have material day-to-day involvement for projects claiming the welfare exemption, matching BOE scrutiny of managing general partners (see County Assessor record). Policies: 2026 City Multifamily Lending and Mortgage Revenue Bond Policies (Section 9).

program_name: Prohousing Designation (state scoring preference for City of Sacramento projects)
administering_agency: City of Sacramento Community Development Department (designation held by the City; HCD administers the program)
typical_award_size: Not a direct subsidy. Projects in a Prohousing jurisdiction receive priority processing or bonus points in state programs including AHSC, Infill Infrastructure Grant, TCC, TIRCP and related transportation programs, and the City may apply to the Prohousing Incentive Program for added funds. Sacramento was the first designated city (Feb 10, 2022) and renewed Dec 23, 2025 with 108 points, the highest score in the state as of June 2026.
affordability_requirement: None at the project level; benefit flows to any eligible affordable project in the City.
next_deadline: Designation runs on HCD's renewal cycle; next renewal due around 2029. Contact Angel Anguiano, (916) 808-5519.
layering_notes: Relevant to layering: AHSC and IIG applications for City sites score Prohousing points that unincorporated-county and most other Sacramento-area cities (Elk Grove, Rancho Cordova, Citrus Heights, Folsom were not confirmed as designated this pass) do not get. Check HCD's designated-jurisdictions tracker before assuming points for a non-City site.

program_name: City of Elk Grove Affordable Housing Fund and Affordable Housing Impact Fee (Municipal Code Chapters 16.88 and 16.89)
administering_agency: City of Elk Grove Housing and Public Services Division (fund and RFPs); Finance Department (fee collection)
typical_award_size: Fee-funded local gap loan fund. Current (2025) fees per the 2026 EPS nexus study: $6,396 per single or two-unit dwelling and $3,837 per multi-unit dwelling; nonresidential $1.05 commercial/retail, $3.11 hotel, $1.19 manufacturing, $1.28 warehouse and $0.00 office per square foot, indexed annually. Staff recommended (Sept 23, 2026 hearing) converting to per square foot: $3.59 single-unit, $3.29 owner-occupied multi-unit, $1.46 renter-occupied multi-unit, plus commercial $2.15 shopping center, $2.29 office, $0.39 industrial, $1,146.75 per hotel room and other categories (maximums supportable were $47.80, $43.80 and $19.50 per square foot). The City releases an RFP when the fund balance can support a project (generally about $5 million); the City reports $84 million lent to sixteen projects since inception (developer page, not opened this pass).
per_unit_cap: None published; set in each RFP and loan agreement.
affordability_requirement: Fund restricted to housing for low and very low income households (HCD limits); 2026 update would also allow a local preference for City-based workers where fair housing law permits. Density bonus affordable units are exempt from the residential fee (Zoning Code 23.50.080).
next_deadline: No open RFP found as of 2026-11-08; watch elkgrove.gov/affordable-housing/developers and the City's purchasing RFP page. Outcome of the September 23, 2026 fee update hearing (ordinance amending 16.88 and 16.89 and a fee resolution) was not confirmed; contact Joshua Tovar, Management Analyst II, jtovar@elkgrove.gov, or the Housing and Public Services Division, (916) 683-7111.
layering_notes: Elk Grove is an impact-fee jurisdiction (like the City and County of Sacramento) with no inclusionary option, so market-rate rental projects pay the fee rather than build units; the 2026 renter-occupied rate was deliberately set low ($1.46 per square foot recommended) because the nexus study found multifamily infeasible at higher fees. Elk Grove is outside the SHRA lending area (SHRA finances in other cities only under cooperation agreements), so this fund, state sources and Elk Grove's own PLHA are the local layer. Past RFPs tied fund loans to City-owned sites (Sheldon Farms North and Old Town, 2023). elkgrove.gov and codepublishing.com return 403 to automated access; facts here come from the City's Sept 23, 2026 public hearing notice and the June 2026 EPS nexus study PDFs on elkgrove.gov.

program_name: Density bonus and developer incentives (Elk Grove Municipal Code Chapter 23.50) and streamlined housing approvals (Chapter 23.17)
administering_agency: City of Elk Grove Development Services, Planning Division
typical_award_size: State density bonus law implemented in Chapter 23.50 (eligibility at 10% lower income, 5% very low income, senior, 10% moderate for-sale, special needs, 100% affordable), one bonus with concessions per Government Code 65915; Section 23.50.080 (Ord. 12-2022) exempts affordable units built under the chapter from the Chapter 16.88 affordable housing fee. Chapter 23.17 provides ministerial streamlined approvals for infill affordable projects, affordable housing in commercial zones, mixed-income projects along commercial corridors, middle-class housing, adaptive reuse, faith and higher-education land, and urban subdivisions (titles confirmed; detailed standards not read this pass).
affordability_requirement: Per state law; fee exemption applies only to the deed-restricted affordable units.
next_deadline: Rolling at entitlement.
layering_notes: No local enhancement beyond state minimums identified. The fee exemption in 23.50.080 is the useful local layer: a density bonus project avoids the per-unit affordable housing fee on its affordable units, and the 2026 fee update proposed keeping the renter multi-unit fee low. Elk Grove adopted its Chapter 23.17 streamlining menu in response to the 2021-2029 Housing Element.

program_name: Elk Grove Permanent Local Housing Allocation (PLHA) and CDBG entitlement funds for affordable housing
administering_agency: City of Elk Grove Housing and Public Services Division
typical_award_size: Not verified this pass. Elk Grove is believed to receive its own CDBG entitlement and a PLHA formula allocation (a December 2024 Council resolution referencing the 2024 PLHA NOFA appeared in search results) and is not in the Sacramento County HOME Consortium (members per the Citrus Heights 2024 Action Plan: County, City of Sacramento, Citrus Heights, Rancho Cordova). Amounts and multifamily eligibility unknown.
affordability_requirement: PLHA: per the City's HCD-approved five-year plan; CDBG: HUD rules.
next_deadline: unknown, verify with agency
layering_notes: Recorded so the Elk Grove layer is complete; the City's housing pages (elkgrove.gov/affordable-housing) return 403 to automated access and the Council resolution PDFs moved off the old elkgrovecity.org paths. Confirm with Housing and Public Services, (916) 683-7111, whether PLHA is pooled with Affordable Housing Fund RFPs.

program_name: Rancho Cordova Housing Trust Development Impact Fee (Municipal Code Chapter 16.89) and city affordable housing gap financing
administering_agency: City of Rancho Cordova Housing Division (Community Development)
typical_award_size: Not verified this pass. Rancho Cordova levies a housing trust development impact fee on nonresidential development (Chapter 16.89, confirmed by title in search results and by Sacramento County's Housing Trust Fund page listing Rancho Cordova among five cities with similar fees). Current rates, fund balance and loan terms unknown. The City's PLHA plan directs 100% of its PLHA allocation to gap financing for new affordable and permanent supportive housing (search snippet, document not opened).
affordability_requirement: Unknown; expected low and very low income per nexus.
next_deadline: unknown, verify with agency
layering_notes: cityofranchocordova.org and codepublishing.com return 403 to automated access and the City's Legistar instance has no public API, so this record is a placeholder. Rancho Cordova is in the Sacramento County HOME Consortium (SHRA-administered) and is a CDBG entitlement city that runs an annual CDBG NOFA (a 2026 CDBG NOFA workshop was listed on the City's housing page per search results). Recent City-supported deals include Mather Veterans Village Phase 4 and The Liora (ministerial design review 2026). Confirm fee schedule, fund balance and any NOFA with the Housing Division via the City's main line (916) 851-8700.

program_name: Affordable Housing Plan requirement for new growth areas (Housing Element policy, south of Highway 50)
administering_agency: City of Rancho Cordova Planning Department and Housing Division
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Per the May 6, 2026 Keyser Marston survey prepared for Sacramento County, Rancho Cordova has no formal inclusionary ordinance but its Housing Element requires new residential projects in newly developing areas (generally south of Highway 50, mostly high-resource areas) to include an Affordable Housing Plan showing how the project contributes to affordable housing production; compliance options are on-site units, land dedication, rehabilitation of existing affordable units, or in-lieu fees negotiated through development agreements for master plans and specific plans.
affordability_requirement: Set project by project in development agreements; no fixed percentage.
next_deadline: Applies at specific plan or development agreement approval.
layering_notes: For affordable developers the practical effect is land: master plan developers (Rio del Oro, Suncreek, Arboretum, Westborough, etc.) often satisfy the plan by dedicating sites or paying negotiated fees, which creates site opportunities and sometimes developer contributions for 9% and 4% deals. Source is a county consultant memo; the City's Housing Element text was not opened because the City site blocks automated access.

program_name: Housing incentives and density bonus (Rancho Cordova Municipal Code Chapter 23.710)
administering_agency: City of Rancho Cordova Planning Department
typical_award_size: State density bonus law implemented in Chapter 23.710 (Ord. 17-2021): one density bonus with concessions for 10% lower income, 5% very low income, special needs housing, senior housing, 10% moderate for-sale, 10% foster youth/disabled veteran/homeless units (55-year restriction), or 100% affordable projects; parking capped at 1.0 space for studios and one-bedrooms, 1.5 for two and three bedrooms, 2.5 for four or more; waivers of standards that would preclude the bonus.
affordability_requirement: Per state law.
next_deadline: Rolling at entitlement.
layering_notes: No local enhancement beyond state minimums identified; the chapter's special-needs category mirrors state law. Rancho Cordova approved The Liora affordable project through ministerial major design review in 2026, so objective-standards ministerial review is available for qualifying affordable projects.

program_name: Citrus Heights Affordable Housing Fee on commercial development (Resolution 2022-048) and City Housing Trust Fund
administering_agency: City of Citrus Heights Housing and Grants Division (fund); Building Division (fee collection)
typical_award_size: Fee source, not a subsidy program with published terms. Per the July 9, 2026 development impact fee sheet: office (including medical and assisted living) $1.95, hotel $2.35, commercial and retail $1.77, industrial (flex and R&D) $1.67 per square foot on new commercial construction of 5,000 square feet or more or added commercial square footage; residential is exempt. Rates were raised in June 2022 to the regional average after no update since 1992. Revenue goes to the City Housing Trust Fund administered by the Housing and Grants Division; fund balance and any lending terms not published.
affordability_requirement: Unknown; linkage fee funds are for very low income housing per the original 1992 ordinance title (Nonresidential Construction Fees for Funding Very Low Income Housing).
next_deadline: No NOFA found; projects should approach the Housing and Grants Division directly, (916) 727-4830, housing@citrusheights.net.
layering_notes: Citrus Heights has no inclusionary ordinance and no residential affordable housing fee, and no city fee waiver program for affordable units was found; the fee sheet also lists multimodal ($1,591 per multifamily unit), park, Measure A transportation, drainage, sewer, school and fire fees that apply to apartments. The trust fund is small because the city is built out with little new commercial construction; the realistic city layer is the CDBG, HOME Consortium and PLHA record below plus SHRA bonds under a cooperation agreement.

program_name: Citrus Heights CDBG entitlement, Sacramento County HOME Consortium share, and Permanent Local Housing Allocation (PLHA)
administering_agency: City of Citrus Heights Housing and Grants Division (CDBG and PLHA); SHRA administers the HOME Consortium
typical_award_size: CDBG: about $600,000 a year in entitlement funds plus about $50,000 program income (2024 Action Plan), used mostly for public improvements, public services (15% cap, competitive round each summer) and a housing rehabilitation revolving loan fund. HOME: the City is a member of the Sacramento County HOME Consortium with the County, City of Sacramento and Rancho Cordova; its consortium share funded $3,580,000 to the 47-unit Sunrise Pointe permanent supportive housing project (approved 2018, completed August 2023). PLHA: $1,876,554 five-year allocation from HCD, partly for the Sayonara Drive redevelopment project and a navigator program.
affordability_requirement: Per federal and PLHA rules; HOME at or below 60% AMI with 20% of HOME units at 50% AMI.
next_deadline: CDBG public service applications are due in early August each year (2027 round announced); capital and housing allocations are negotiated through the Annual Action Plan (public hearing each October for the following calendar year). Multifamily HOME requests go through SHRA's two-round schedule with a Citrus Heights consortium set-aside, confirm with SHRA (916) 440-1393.
layering_notes: The HOME Consortium share is the only meaningful city-level capital source: Citrus Heights directed its share to Sunrise Pointe via SHRA rather than running its own NOFA. CDBG is largely spent on infrastructure and services. Federal funds trigger Davis-Bacon (HOME at 12 or more units, CDBG at 8 or more) and NEPA. Sayonara Drive is a City-led acquisition and redevelopment site that may seek a development partner.

program_name: Affordable housing incentives and density bonus (Citrus Heights Zoning Code Chapter 106.32)
administering_agency: City of Citrus Heights Planning Division
typical_award_size: State density bonus law implemented in Chapter 106.32 (Ord. 2019-004, 2022-007): eligibility at 10% lower income, 5% very low income, senior housing, 10% moderate for-sale, 10% foster youth/disabled veteran/homeless, 20% low-income student housing, or land donation of at least one acre; bonus table follows Government Code 65915; minimum project size five units; bonus and incentives for projects with child care facilities; density bonus agreement recorded.
affordability_requirement: Per state law; moderate income bonuses only for for-sale units.
next_deadline: Rolling at entitlement; Council determines the bonus.
layering_notes: No local enhancement beyond state minimums identified. Citrus Heights is built out, so bonus use is on infill and commercial corridor sites (Sunrise Boulevard, Auburn Boulevard) and the Sunrise Tomorrow Specific Plan area at Sunrise Mall, where a 2026 public-private agreement started redevelopment; housing phases there are a future opportunity.

program_name: Folsom Affordable Housing Loan (AHL) Program (Folsom Housing Fund 238 and Housing Trust Fund 221)
administering_agency: City of Folsom Community Development Department, Housing Services (loan consultant TDA, Inc.)
typical_award_size: Gap loans from the City's inclusionary in-lieu fee fund and commercial housing trust fund. Unaudited cash available for projects at June 30, 2025: $23.9 million (Fund 238 $22.8M, Fund 221 $0.9M, legacy funds $0.2M). Track record: 11 loans since 2005 totaling over $36 million supporting 1,095 units (e.g., a $2.7M conditional loan for 52 units in 2020). Guidelines adopted by Resolution 11427 on August 26, 2025 standardize terms and allow the City to issue NOFAs.
per_unit_cap: None published; sized by the City's consultant review of the pro forma against TCAC underwriting.
affordability_requirement: Minimum 55-year income, rent and affordability restrictions recorded senior to foreclosable liens; serves extremely low, very low and low income households; priority to sites outside concentrations of existing regulated housing and to Housing Element goals (seniors, large families, special needs). Fund 238 must spend at least 50% on construction or major rehab of multifamily rentals affordable to low and very low income households (Sacramento Housing Alliance settlement).
next_deadline: No NOFA issued as of 2026-11-08; the 2025 guidelines contemplate strategic NOFAs when resources are available, and staff planned a Council policy discussion on priorities for the housing funds. Requests may still be submitted ahead of tax credit rounds; contact Housing Services via the Community Development Department (Pam Johns, Director), (916) 461-6000.
layering_notes: The largest city-controlled pool in Sacramento County outside the City of Sacramento (about $23M) with few competing applicants, because Folsom's rental projects are scarce and the Folsom Plan Area south of Highway 50 generates most in-lieu revenue. Loans are repaid from 50% of residual cash flow after allowed expenses; operating and replacement reserves required for the 55-year term; underwriting and compliance aligned to TCAC and LIHTC rules. Folsom is outside the SHRA lending area (cooperation agreement needed), so this fund plus state sources is the local layer; a Folsom Plan Area MOU committing to 890 deed-restricted affordable units (2024 General Plan amendments, not opened this pass) creates sites. Chapter 17.104.070 also allows fee waivers or deferrals and density bonuses for inclusionary units. folsom.ca.us returns 403 to automated access; the staff report and resolution were read from the City's public agenda host.

program_name: Folsom Inclusionary Housing Ordinance (Municipal Code Chapter 17.104) and in-lieu fee (Ordinance 1359, Resolution 11510)
administering_agency: City of Folsom Community Development Department, Housing Services
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. For-sale residential projects of 10 or more units (and rental projects of 10 or more units receiving City assistance) must make 10% of units affordable: 3% very low income and 7% low income; market-rate rental apartments are exempt. In-lieu fee effective February 12, 2026 (replacing 1% of the lowest sales price): $3.00 per square foot for single-family for-sale units and $2.50 per square foot for multifamily for-sale units of 1,500 square feet or less, paid at building permit into the Folsom Housing Fund (Fund 238); at least 50% of fee revenue must go to lower-income rental development. Prior-year collections exceeded $3.8M, mostly from the Folsom Plan Area. Alternatives: land dedication, off-site units, acquisition-rehab or conversion of market-rate units, inclusionary credits, combinations.
affordability_requirement: Rental inclusionary units restricted at least 30 years (or longer if state law requires); for-sale units resale-restricted; projects of nine or fewer market-rate units exempt.
next_deadline: Applies at entitlement; fee per unit in effect at permit issuance. Council adopted Ordinance 1359 on January 13, 2026 (first reading December 9, 2025) and set fees by Resolution 11510 the same night; next review expected with the Housing Element cycle. Developers paying fees only need a letter of intent, not a full inclusionary housing plan.
layering_notes: Nearly all Folsom Plan Area builders pay the fee, which is why Fund 238 holds about $22.8M and funds the AHL Program (record above). Rental multifamily was kept exempt in 2026 despite AB 1505 authority, so apartment developers owe no inclusionary units or fee. Developers who provide more than 10% can bank and sell inclusionary housing credits for five years (17.104.070). The ordinance text was read from the City Council's January 13, 2026 agenda packet on the City's public agenda host and the zoneomics code mirror.

program_name: Folsom Housing Trust Fund commercial development fee (Municipal Code Chapter 3.90, Fund 221)
administering_agency: City of Folsom Community Development Department (fee) and Housing Services (fund)
typical_award_size: Commercial linkage fee of $2.08 per square foot on new commercial development (established 2002), deposited in the Housing Trust Fund (Fund 221) and used mainly to fill financing gaps in affordable rental projects through the AHL Program. Fund 221 balance was $918,311 at June 30, 2025.
affordability_requirement: Fund supports affordable housing development; AHL Program 55-year restrictions apply to loans.
next_deadline: Deployed through the AHL Program (no NOFA as of 2026-11-08). Fee paid at building permit.
layering_notes: Minor source compared with Fund 238; Folsom's rate ($2.08) is below the City of Sacramento ($2.68 commercial) and above the County ($2.17). Chapter 3.90 text itself was not opened (codepublishing.com and folsom.ca.us return 403); the rate and balance come from the August 26, 2025 staff report on the City's public agenda host.

program_name: Density bonus and other developer incentives (Folsom Municipal Code Chapter 17.102)
administering_agency: City of Folsom Community Development Department, Planning Services
typical_award_size: State density bonus law implemented in Chapter 17.102 (Ord. 1145, 2011) for very low, low, moderate and senior households, with additional incentives or concessions per Government Code 65915(i), an added bonus for child care facilities, and resale and occupancy restrictions on moderate income units. Multifamily objective design standards were adopted in late 2025 to enable ministerial review.
affordability_requirement: Per state law (affordable rent defined as 30% of 50% or 80% AMI).
next_deadline: Rolling at entitlement.
layering_notes: No local enhancement beyond state minimums identified; the chapter predates recent state amendments and defers to Government Code 65915 where they conflict. The 2024 General Plan and Folsom Plan Area amendments added capacity for about 6,046 units in targeted multifamily areas, which is where bonus requests will land. Inclusionary projects may also request fee waivers or deferrals under 17.104.070 and Chapter 16.60.

program_name: Folsom legacy housing funds: Oaks at Willow Springs inclusionary fund (Fund 274) and former redevelopment bond proceeds (Fund 280)
administering_agency: City of Folsom Community Development Department, Housing Services
typical_award_size: Largely spent. Fund 274 held $25,672 at June 30, 2025 from a 2006 $3.1M inclusionary payment ($2.7M went to the Granite City Apartments site on Sibley Street). Fund 280 held $149,695 of pre-2011 redevelopment bond proceeds that SB 107 (2015) let the City use for housing; over $9.6 million was invested in multiple affordable projects after redevelopment dissolved in 2012.
affordability_requirement: Low and very low income housing per the original sources.
next_deadline: No new rounds; residual balances may be folded into an AHL Program loan.
layering_notes: Recorded as negative information: Folsom's redevelopment successor housing money is essentially exhausted, so the City's capacity now rests on the in-lieu fee fund. Figures from the August 26, 2025 Housing Fund update staff report.

program_name: Inclusionary Housing Ordinance (City Code Chapter 6.27, Ordinance 1180, adopted December 2024) and Workforce Housing Fund in-lieu fees
administering_agency: City of South Lake Tahoe Development Services Department, Planning Division and Housing Division (fund held by the Finance Director); 1052 Tata Lane, 530-542-7417
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. New residential construction, redevelopment of 50% or more of a building with dwellings, or condo conversion must provide inclusionary units or pay an in-lieu fee scaled to unit size (habitable square feet): 2,000 sq ft or less exempt; 2,001 to 2,500 sq ft 5% of units or $5.29 per sq ft; 2,501 to 3,000 sq ft 6% or $5.84 per sq ft; 3,001 to 5,000 sq ft 9% or $16.77 per sq ft; over 5,000 sq ft 17% or $17.65 per sq ft. Fees are paid before building permit issuance (by phase for phased projects) into the Workforce Housing Fund for housing affordable to low and moderate income households. Fund balance and collections to date are not published; the 2027-2035 draft Housing Element commits the City to post requirements, fee amounts and annual collections by mid-2027 and to publish a five-year in-lieu fee report under AB 2663.
affordability_requirement: Inclusionary units deed restricted for rent or sale to lower income households (80% AMI or below, El Dorado County), priced at no more than 30% of gross income including utilities, dispersed on site, comparable in exterior quality and bedroom mix, built concurrently with market-rate units. No affordability term is stated in the chapter text that was read.
eligible_project_types: single-family and condominium projects over 2,000 sq ft per unit (compliance)
deed-restricted units at or below 120% AMI (exempt)
long-term multifamily rental projects of two or more units (exempt)
next_deadline: Applies at building permit; fee schedule in effect at permit issuance. Annual monitoring review each June under draft Program 2-10 with amendments within six months if warranted; first AB 2663 reporting for calendar 2026 due in 2027. Verify any fee indexing with the Planning Division before permit.
layering_notes: This is the only locally generated housing fund in South Lake Tahoe. Multifamily rental projects are exempt from both the unit requirement and the fee, so apartment developers owe nothing; the fund is fed by large single-family and condo construction, which is the dominant product in the Basin. Spending the Workforce Housing Fund is at Council discretion with no NOFA or guidelines published; pair requests with the City's HOME program income, PLHA formula and Prohousing Incentive Program dollars (see the City direct financing record) and with the County Affordable Housing Trust Fund, County PLHA and County HOME/CDBG records, which also have no standing NOFA. The ordinance grew out of Housing Element Program 2-11 (2022 to 2027 cycle) and the January 2023 Analysis of Local Funding Sources, which modeled TOT and transfer tax increases, a vacancy tax, a commercial linkage fee and an in-lieu fee against a $3.35 million annual local funding need; Council proceeded only with the inclusionary fee. No vacation rental (Measure T) or TOT revenue is earmarked for housing, and Measure T itself was struck down by the El Dorado County Superior Court in March 2025 and replaced by VHR Ordinance 2025-1200 (effective July 17, 2025) and a 2026 ordinance. Blocked hosts: codepublishing.com (the City's code host) returned 403 and the City Agenda Center search errored; the chapter was read on the gocodebook code mirror, and the adoption date and background come from the City's August 2026 public review draft 2027-2035 Housing Element (cityofslt.gov DocumentCenter View 24379).

program_name: City direct gap and predevelopment financing for affordable housing (HOME program income, Housing Successor and Redevelopment Agency program income, PLHA formula funds, Prohousing Incentive Program funds, general fund, residential units of use) and state application sponsorship
administering_agency: City of South Lake Tahoe Development Services Department, Housing Division (Housing Manager, mmanuel@cityofslt.gov, 530-542-7417); City Council approves each commitment
typical_award_size: Deal-by-deal Council commitments, no NOFA or written guidelines. Track record: over $2.5 million of HOME program income, Redevelopment Agency program income and general fund to Sugar Pine Village (248 units, Related California and Saint Joseph Community Land Trust on state surplus land; Phase 1A 68 units opened fall 2024, Phase 2A 60 units fall 2025, Phase 1B 60 units summer 2026, Phase 2B seeking financing), plus City-sponsored AHSC ($17,359,470), MHP ($19.6 million), IIG, LGMG, HOME and PLHA awards; a $564,073 predevelopment loan plus $500,000 of Prohousing Incentive Program funds to Novin Development for the 75-unit 3900 and 3908 Lake Tahoe Boulevard project (SB 35 approval 2025, AHSC pending); about $1,791,669 CDBG-CV and $120,000 PIP for rehabilitation of three Homekey properties (72 supportive units) with Tahoe Coalition for the Homeless; 21 multifamily residential units of use donated to Lake Tahoe Community College's 100-bed dorm (about $315,000 market value); three Al Tahoe lots donated to Saint Joseph Community Land Trust. City awards 2020 to 2025 included PLHA formula about $880,000 total, PLHA competitive $15 million over three awards, HOME $6,538,240 and PIP Round 2 $620,000. Legacy RDA Low and Moderate Income Housing Fund loans (AB 987 database) total $16.46 million HOME, $2.15 million RDA and $1.18 million CDBG across 296 units in eight projects.
affordability_requirement: Follows the state source layered in: Sugar Pine Village and 3900 Lake Tahoe Boulevard are 55-year deed restrictions at 30% to 80% AMI; TRPA deed restriction also required when bonus units are used. HOME program income follows HOME rules.
next_deadline: No NOFA. Approach the Housing Division ahead of the AHSC, MHP and PLHA competitive rounds; the City committed to apply for at least one state or federal grant per year (Housing Element Program 2-1). Phase 2B of Sugar Pine Village still lacked a local match as of the August 2026 draft Housing Element. Final 2027-2035 Housing Element adoption was scheduled for a September 8, 2026 Council hearing; confirm the adopted program list.
layering_notes: South Lake Tahoe is a non-entitlement city that has out-raised most small cities by sponsoring state applications (PLHA competitive, AHSC, HOME, IIG, LGMG) for a nonprofit or private developer, so the City's own cash is small but its sponsorship is the key to the state layer. Gap order used on Sugar Pine Village: LIHTC and bonds, AHSC and MHP, IIG and LGMG, HOME and PLHA, City program income last. County layers available in the Tahoe Basin: El Dorado County PLHA formula and County HOME/CDBG participation requests, County Affordable Housing Trust Fund (no development NOFA), County PHA project-based vouchers, CMFA TEFRA approvals, welfare exemption, BHSA housing funds; the County Traffic Impact Fee offset (Policy B-14) does not apply inside the city because the City levies its own fees. TRPA layer: bonus units and the allocation exemption are required for any deed-restricted project (see the TRPA record), and TRPA application fees are waived for affordable projects. Residential allocations are scarce (33 market-rate per year citywide, one third reserved for multifamily), which is why deed-restricted projects using bonus units are the only route to scale. Workforce Housing Fund in-lieu fees (inclusionary record) are a separate, newer pool. No local housing trust fund, no city NOFA, no local tax-exempt issuer. Source is the City's August 2026 public review draft 2027-2035 Housing Element on the City DocumentCenter; the City's CivicPlus pages opened directly but council packets were not reachable (Granicus and Legistar hosts not found).

program_name: City permit fee waiver for nonprofit and public agency affordable housing (City Code Section 6.55.090), lot consolidation fee waiver for deed-restricted units (Housing Element Program 1-7) and Sugar Pine Village inspection fee reduction
administering_agency: City of South Lake Tahoe Development Services Department (Planning and Building Divisions); waivers approved by the City Council at a public hearing
typical_award_size: Case by case. Nonprofits and public agencies developing affordable housing may request waiver of City permit fees, granted by Council resolution (about 45 days from request to approval, run concurrently with permit review). The City also reduced building inspection fees for Sugar Pine Village because HCD inspects the modular units. Program 1-7 commits the City to waive the lot line adjustment fee when the resulting project includes deed-restricted affordable units. City planning fees are modest relative to TRPA fees; City multifamily impact charges are mainly utility connection fees set by South Tahoe Public Utility District (not waived; $7,500 deposit and 10% of capacity fees at plan review). No waiver of TRPA water quality ($1.86 per sq ft) or excess coverage mitigation fees ($8.50 per sq ft), though TRPA application fees are waived for affordable, moderate and achievable bonus-unit projects and the mobility mitigation fee may be waived.
affordability_requirement: Affordable housing project sponsored by a nonprofit or public agency; deed restriction consistent with TRPA affordable, moderate or achievable definitions when bonus units are used. No specific AMI threshold published for the City waiver.
next_deadline: Request with the entitlement or building permit application; Council hearing required. Verify current practice with the Housing Division (530-542-7417) because the code text could not be opened.
layering_notes: Fee relief is small in dollar terms; the real cost drivers in the Basin are TRPA mitigation fees, land coverage purchases and development rights, which the TRPA bonus unit program (separate record) addresses. Combine with the TRPA application fee exemption and with the Phase 2 Housing Amendments height, coverage and density relief. Private for-profit developers are not eligible for the 6.55.090 waiver unless partnered with a nonprofit or public agency. The County Traffic Impact Fee offset (Board Policy B-14) is not available inside the city. The City's code host (codepublishing.com) returned 403 and the gocodebook mirror had no Chapter 6.55 page, so Section 6.55.090 was not read directly; the description is taken from the fees and exactions analysis in the City's August 2026 public review draft 2027-2035 Housing Element (pages 4-203 to 4-206) and from Program 1-7 of the adopted 2022-2027 Housing Element.

program_name: TRPA Residential Bonus Unit Program (TRPA Code Chapter 52), allocation exemption (Chapter 50.5.1) and Phase 2 Housing Amendments as applied in South Lake Tahoe Town Centers (Tourist Core, Tahoe Valley and Midtown Area Plans)
administering_agency: Tahoe Regional Planning Agency (TRPA), with City of South Lake Tahoe Planning Division as lead reviewer inside Area Plan boundaries; City holds a voting seat on the TRPA Governing Board
typical_award_size: Regulatory, not cash, but it substitutes for development rights that otherwise must be bought. Deed-restricted affordable (80% AMI), moderate (120% AMI) or achievable (TRPA-set percentage tied to median home price) units receive residential bonus units at no cost in place of a residential unit of use (potential unit plus allocation), are exempt from the City's annual allocation (33 market-rate allocations per year citywide, one third reserved for multifamily), and are exempt from TRPA application fees. About 946 of the 1,124 bonus units set aside in 2018 remained as of the 2026 draft Housing Element, all reserved for deed-restricted housing and prioritized for Centers and multifamily zones. Phase 2 Housing Amendments (TRPA Governing Board, December 2023; MAP settlement July 2024) remove the maximum density cap for 100% deed-restricted projects in Town Centers, allow heights up to 65 feet in Centers (step-back, shade and scenic findings above 56 feet), allow 100% deed-restricted projects outside Centers to transfer in coverage up to 70% of high-capability land if runoff is treated by a public stormwater system, and allow use of the TRPA basin-wide parking study to reduce parking. Affordable projects using these tools have reached 61 to 67 units per acre in the city (Sugar Pine Village, 3900 Lake Tahoe Boulevard).
per_unit_cap: One bonus unit per deed-restricted unit; no dollar cap. Market value of a multifamily residential unit of use is about $15,000 (the City valued 21 units given to Lake Tahoe Community College at about $315,000).
affordability_requirement: Permanent TRPA deed restriction recorded as a permit condition: occupancy limited to affordable, moderate or achievable households (or local employees for achievable units), no second-home or vacation rental use, annual compliance report to TRPA (penalties up to $5,000 per day), real estate disclosure on transfer; project within one half mile of transit. Height, coverage and density incentives under Phase 2 require 100% deed-restricted units plus stormwater and transportation contributions.
eligible_project_types: motel or hotel conversion to residential
acquisition-rehab (coverage and density relief for 100% deed-restricted)
next_deadline: Bonus units assigned at TRPA permit (about 120 days of TRPA review, or City-only review for qualifying projects inside the TCAP and TVAP). Watch: TRPA Phase 3 (Cultivating Community, Conserving the Basin) EIS scoping closed March 16, 2026 with further code changes pending; City Midtown Area Plan (MTAP) adoption was pending a September 2026 hearing; TRPA 2025-2026 income limits and achievable percentages are updated each July.
layering_notes: Flag for every South Lake Tahoe deal: the Tahoe Basin is dual-jurisdiction. The City cannot grant a state density bonus law bonus or concessions that exceed TRPA standards; TRPA gives full density relief only to 100% deed-restricted projects and gives no comparable benefit or mandatory concessions to mixed-income projects that set aside a share of units, which the draft 2027-2035 Housing Element names as a continuing constraint (Program 2-8 asks TRPA to allow state density bonus compliance). Land coverage (Bailey system, 30% base outside Area Plans, 70% inside TCAP and TVAP), scenic and height limits and the allocation system govern feasibility more than zoning. Projects using bonus units must carry a TRPA deed restriction in addition to TCAC, HCD or City covenants; coordinate the three so income limits (TRPA uses county AMI for a family of three) and terms do not conflict. The TRPA application fee waiver stacks with the City Section 6.55.090 waiver (separate record). County layers (PLHA, Trust Fund, PBVs, welfare exemption) apply as in the rest of El Dorado County. Source pages at trpa.gov opened directly; City-specific figures (946 bonus units remaining, 61 to 67 du per acre, 65-foot height, MTAP status) come from the City's August 2026 draft Housing Element on the City DocumentCenter.

program_name: Affordable Housing Density Bonus, Placerville City Code Title 10 Chapter 12 (Sections 10-12-1 to 10-12-13; 2015 text, state-law update ZC 24-05 pending under ROI 2024-01)
administering_agency: City of Placerville Development Services Department, Planning Division, 3101 Center Street, (530) 642-5252, pv.planning@gmail.com
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. The local chapter still reflects the 2015 version of Government Code 65915: bonus up to 35% for 5% very low, 10% lower or 10% moderate (for-sale) units, 20% for senior housing, land donation bonus up to 35% combined; one to three incentives (reduced lot size, setbacks, lot coverage, height, parking, mixed-use zoning, other cost-reducing regulatory relief) and by-right parking ratios of 1 space (0 to 1 bedroom), 2 (2 to 3 bedrooms) and 2.5 (4 or more). Where the chapter conflicts with state law, state law controls (10-12-1), so the current 80% bonus for 100% affordable projects, unlimited bonus near major transit and up to five concessions apply by operation of state law. The 2025 Annual Progress Report (March 2026) reports the full density bonus ordinance update was deferred to 2026 because of evolving state law.
affordability_requirement: Per state law: income-restricted units for very low (50% AMI), lower (80% AMI) or moderate (120% AMI, for-sale) households with a recorded density bonus housing agreement (10-12-12); rental affordability term per Government Code 65915 (55 years).
next_deadline: Request with the entitlement application (optional pre-application conference). Watch for the Planning Commission and City Council hearings on text amendment ZC 24-05 (density bonus update), dates still TBD on the City's project list; adoption targeted in 2026.
layering_notes: No local enhancement beyond state law. Placerville has no local housing trust fund, no inclusionary ordinance or in-lieu fee, no commercial linkage fee, no city NOFA and no redevelopment successor housing funds; the City's affordable housing tools are this chapter, the Housing Opportunity Overlay by-right sites, fee deferral under SB 937, SCIP impact fee financing and sponsorship of state CDBG, HOME and PLHA applications (separate records). Stack with the El Dorado County density bonus and the County PLHA, Trust Fund, HOME/CDBG, PBV and welfare exemption records; the County Traffic Impact Fee offset (Policy B-14) does not apply inside the city, which levies its own traffic impact mitigation fee. Chapter text read from the City's own zoning ordinance PDF; the City page links the amlegal code library, which was not opened.

program_name: Housing Opportunity Overlay Zone (HO, Title 10 Chapter 5 Section 24, Zone Change 2016-01) by-right affordable sites and Housing Element Programs A-3 and A-5
administering_agency: City of Placerville Development Services Department, Planning Division
typical_award_size: Regulatory. Sites in the HO overlay (and the R-5 Very High Density Multi-Family zone) allow owner-occupied or multifamily housing by right at a minimum 20 and maximum 24 units per acre with compliance with local design standards and no discretionary action (Government Code 65583.2 sites). The overlay covers about 17 acres with three additional sites proposed for 2026. Two of the four original HO parcels produced Mallard Apartments (72 units, 30% to 60% AMI, 55 years) and Middletown Apartments (82 units, 30% to 60% AMI, 55 years), both by Pacific Southwest Community Development Corporation and under construction in 2025 (82 Middletown permits issued in 2025). Objective design standards (LEAP $65,000 and SB 2 $160,000 funded) were still being completed as of March 2025.
affordability_requirement: By-right status is tied to lower income housing need under state law; projects on HO sites have been 100% affordable at 30% to 60% AMI with 55-year covenants. No local inclusionary percentage.
eligible_project_types: mixed-income multifamily on HO or R-5 sites
next_deadline: Ministerial site plan review on HO or R-5 sites at any time. Three additional HO sites were proposed for 2026 rezoning; confirm status and the objective design standards with Planning.
layering_notes: The HO overlay is where Placerville's deal flow has actually occurred; both recent projects paired by-right siting with City-sponsored CDBG and CPLHA loans, IIG and MHP (see the City state-funding record). The 2025 APR reports 244 lower income units of site capacity against a 90-unit lower income RHNA, so no-net-loss is not a constraint. Combine with the state density bonus (Chapter 12) and SB 35 or AB 2011 streamlining. Source is the City's 2021-2029 Housing Element policy document (Programs A-3 and A-5); the 2016 draft HO ordinance was also read on the City's EvoGov agenda host. No local trust fund or NOFA exists in Placerville.

program_name: Development impact fee deferral for affordable projects (SB 937 implementation, Housing Element Program C-5), ADU impact fee reductions, and Statewide Community Infrastructure Program (SCIP) impact fee financing (Program C-7)
administering_agency: City of Placerville Development Services Department (Planning and Building Divisions) and Finance; SCIP bonds issued by California Statewide Communities Development Authority (CSCDA)
typical_award_size: Timing relief, not a reduction, for multifamily: the City reports it implemented fee deferrals under SB 937 in 2025 so impact fees on qualifying affordable projects are collected at certificate of occupancy rather than permit issuance. Housing Element Program C-5 also offers deferment to completion or occupancy, payment over 12 months or longer after completion, or fee reductions where the applicant documents lower facility demand. Impact fee reductions (water, sewer, traffic impact mitigation, park fees) have been implemented only for ADUs and JADUs consistent with state law. SCIP lets a developer finance City impact fees and public improvements through tax-exempt CSCDA bonds repaid by a special assessment on the parcel; the City intends to offer it for all projects, especially housing, but no development had used SCIP as of the 2023 and 2025 progress reports. No general fee waiver for affordable housing exists.
affordability_requirement: SB 937 deferral applies to projects meeting the statute's affordability definitions (generally 100% affordable or qualifying mixed-income projects); Program C-5 options are for affordable housing providers. SCIP has no affordability requirement.
next_deadline: Request deferral at building permit; SCIP participation requires a City resolution and CSCDA application ahead of permit issuance. Confirm the current fee schedule and deferral form with the Building Division.
layering_notes: Placerville levies its own traffic impact mitigation, park and utility fees, so the El Dorado County Traffic Impact Fee offset (Board Policy B-14) does not apply to city projects; deferral is the only local fee tool. SCIP assessment financing of impact fees is senior to other liens and must be cleared with TCAC and permanent lenders. Pair with the HO overlay by-right sites and City-sponsored CDBG, PLHA and HOME loans (separate records). Sources read: the March 24, 2026 City Council staff report accepting the 2025 Housing Element Annual Progress Report (SB 937 deferral statement), the City's Housing Resources page describing SCIP (updated March 4, 2025) and Programs C-5 and C-7 of the 2021-2029 Housing Element.

program_name: City-sponsored state CDBG, Competitive PLHA and HOME loans for affordable multifamily (non-entitlement city; Housing Element Program C-4) and partnership with Housing El Dorado
administering_agency: City of Placerville Development Services Department (applicant and lender of record for state CDBG and PLHA competitive funds) with El Dorado County Housing Authority (HHSA) and Housing El Dorado
typical_award_size: Pass-through loans sized to each state award, no local cash. Mallard Apartments (Mallard Lane and MacIntosh, 72 units): City CDBG loan $756,000 for acquisition, Competitive PLHA (CPLHA) loan $756,000 for architecture and engineering, IIG $1,105,000 for frontage and offsite work, MHP $11,000,000. Middletown Apartments (Cold Springs Road and Middletown Road, 82 units): CDBG loan $861,000 for acquisition, CPLHA loan $861,000, IIG $2,158,000, MHP $13,000,000. The 2025 progress report adds a $400,000 PLHA loan secured for Mallard/Middletown. Program C-4 commits the City to meet annually with nonprofit developers, apply or co-apply for state and federal funds (CDBG, HOME, PLHA, Section 202 and 811, CalHome), and to establish priority processing and fee deferrals for extremely low income projects.
per_unit_cap: None; limited by the state program caps (state CDBG and PLHA competitive NOFAs).
affordability_requirement: Follows the state source: Mallard and Middletown are 100% affordable at 30% to 60% AMI for 55 years; CDBG and PLHA require at least 55-year covenants for rental new construction.
next_deadline: Tied to HCD state CDBG and PLHA competitive NOFAs (typically fall or late winter per the Housing Element) and HUD rounds in late spring. Contact Planning at least one cycle ahead so the City can adopt the required resolutions; no city NOFA exists.
layering_notes: Placerville competes in the same non-entitlement state CDBG, HOME and competitive PLHA pools as El Dorado County, so coordinate with the County's Affordable Housing Unit (Housing@edcgov.us) to avoid both jurisdictions applying for the same project; the County's own records cover County HOME/CDBG participation requests, County PLHA formula funds and the County Trust Fund (no development NOFA). County PHA project-based vouchers and the welfare exemption apply inside the city. Gap order used on the two Placerville projects: 4% LIHTC and bonds (CMFA TEFRA via the County), MHP, IIG, City CDBG and CPLHA loans. The City has no local trust fund, inclusionary fee, linkage fee or RDA successor housing funds; a first-time homebuyer program and workforce housing study (Program C-8, CDBG planning grant by spring 2025) were not advanced as of the 2025 progress report. Source is the City's 2023 Housing Element Annual Progress Report tables (October 8, 2024 Council packet); the 2025 APR staff report of March 24, 2026 was also read.

program_name: Affordable Housing Ordinance (Davis Municipal Code Article 18.05, Ordinance 2646) and Rental Housing Inclusionary Guidelines (Resolution 25-002, in-lieu fee)
administering_agency: City of Davis Social Services and Housing Department, Affordable Housing Manager Iris Grace and Director Dana Bailey; Community Development Department for entitlements
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Rental projects of 20 or more units must provide 15% affordable units, half low income and half very low income (ordinance adopted July 2023). Resolution 25-002 (adopted January 7, 2025, 4 to 1) set the in-lieu fee for non-discretionary rental projects at $250,000 per required affordable unit and $125,000 for a fractional unit when the whole units are built on site. Staff had proposed $608,000 per unit (cost of the most recent all-affordable project) and the Council rejected $369,000. The fee is indexed annually by the construction cost index with a one-time payment or a multi-year option at a 10-year net present value. Ownership projects have separate land dedication and in-lieu options approved case by case.
affordability_requirement: 15% of rental units (7.5% low income at 80% AMI and 7.5% very low income at 50% AMI) with long-term covenants; alternatives (in-lieu fee, land dedication, Project Individualized Plan) must deliver equivalent affordability value and discretionary projects need Council approval of the alternative.
next_deadline: None (ordinance). Council on December 16, 2025 directed staff to amend the land dedication option as soon as possible; an amendment requiring land dedicators to also provide funding was introduced in March 2026 per local coverage. A broader revision of the ownership inclusionary rules is in progress. Verify current text with the Affordable Housing Manager, (530) 757-5602.
layering_notes: The ordinance is the engine behind Davis's two main local tools: in-lieu fees and negotiated contributions flow to the City Housing Trust Fund, and land dedication produces fully improved affordable sites (see the Housing Trust Fund and land dedication records). For a 100% affordable developer this means partnering with a market-rate applicant on a dedicated site, or seeking Housing Trust Fund gap money. Staff's October 21, 2025 informational report found production lagging RHNA and proposed a mandatory financial review when a developer claims infeasibility; Councilmembers asked staff to look at 10% extremely low income in place of part of the 15% requirement. Section 40.27.110 of the zoning code ties Article 18.05 to state density bonus law. Stack with county records: no Yolo County housing trust fund or county NOFA exists; Yolo County Housing project-based vouchers and the state CDBG and HOME competitions are the county-level layers. Access: cityofdavis.org (Akamai) returns 403 to scripts and to WebFetch; the Council minutes on documents.cityofdavis.org open and were used. The Resolution 25-002 text (showpublisheddocument/20364) and the October 21, 2025 staff report could not be opened.

program_name: City of Davis Housing Trust Fund (in-lieu fees and negotiated developer contributions, Article 18.05)
administering_agency: City of Davis Social Services and Housing Department (Housing Trust Fund administered by the Affordable Housing Manager; Social Services Commission reviews affordable housing plans)
typical_award_size: Project-specific gap contributions sized by Council; no published NOFA or guidelines found. Revenue is in-lieu fees under Resolution 25-002 ($250,000 per unit) plus negotiated contributions from peripheral Measure J/R/D projects: Village Farms Exhibit E (approved December 16, 2025, revised January 13, 2026) commits $6,000,000 to the Housing Trust Fund ($2 million with dedication of the first land site, $1 million at the first building permit, $3 million before any Phase 3 building permit); Willowgrove's plan reportedly adds $1.8 million. Earlier years the fund was small (the 2023 single-family in-lieu fee was about $82,000 per unit) and the City has historically funded projects such as Paul's Place and Creekside from it. Current balance not published in any document opened this pass.
affordability_requirement: Low and very low income units with long-term covenants; Council direction prioritizes very low and extremely low income and deed-restricted ownership.
next_deadline: No NOFA. Contributions arrive with Village Farms and Willowgrove milestones only if voters approved the projects (Village Farms was placed on the June 2026 ballot and Willowgrove on the November 2026 ballot); verify election outcomes and timing with the Affordable Housing Manager, (530) 757-5602.
layering_notes: The only local soft money in Davis. Sized to projects on the dedicated land sites first (the Village Farms plan says the money should support affordable housing on the dedication sites but may be used elsewhere consistent with the plan). Layer as the last gap after 9% or 4% credits, HCD MHP or AHSC, Yolo County Housing project-based vouchers and the Davis CDBG and HOME allocations; City money is public funds and triggers prevailing wage. Councilmembers raised formalizing the fund into a structured trust (April 2026). Davis has no RDA successor housing fund. Blocked: cityofdavis.org pages and the Village Farms Exhibit E staff reports (403); facts are from the December 16, 2025 and January 13, 2026 Council minutes on documents.cityofdavis.org, which did open.

program_name: Affordable housing land dedication sites under Article 18.05 (Village Farms 16-acre dedication, Project Individualized Plan Exhibit E)
administering_agency: City of Davis Community Development Department and Social Services and Housing Department (Council subcommittee negotiates development agreements)
typical_award_size: Land, not cash. Village Farms Davis (Development Agreement Exhibit E, approved December 16, 2025 and revised January 13, 2026) dedicates 16 acres to the City for 280 low and very low income units on fully improved sites (no more than 4 parcels, none under 2.5 acres), to be developed with a qualified affordable housing developer selected by the City, with the City to endeavor to add 80 moderate income units. Baseline features now require construction to commence on 100 affordable units before Phase 3 and no permits beyond the first 150 until that starts; the City holds an option after 150 units. Together with the $6 million Housing Trust Fund payment the package is valued by the applicant at over $6 million plus land.
affordability_requirement: 280 low and very low income units (plus up to 80 moderate) on dedicated land; affordability covenants set in the City's developer agreement.
next_deadline: City selection of the affordable developer for the Village Farms sites has not been scheduled; it depends on voter approval of the project (June 2026 Measure J/R/D vote) and on the first land dedication. Watch Council agendas and the Social Services Commission.
layering_notes: This is how 100% affordable developers get sites in Davis: the inclusionary ordinance's land dedication option plus Housing Trust Fund money, then compete for 9% credits, MHP, AHSC or HCD Super NOFA money. Vice Mayor Vaitla's December 2025 direction to amend the land dedication option (so dedicators also provide resources) led to a March 2026 ordinance introduction, so later projects should carry cash with the land. Earlier dedications (Cannery, Chiles Ranch, Bretton Woods) produced sites now built or in pipeline. Davis has no city-owned surplus land program beyond these dedications. Pair with Yolo County Housing PBVs and the CoC HHAP money for supportive units.

program_name: Density bonus (Davis Municipal Code Section 40.27.110, deviations under Article 18.05 and state density bonus law)
administering_agency: City of Davis Community Development Department, Planning Division
typical_award_size: Regulatory. Section 40.27.110 (Ordinance 2322, 2008) allows deviations from zoning standards in accordance with the density bonuses and incentives provided for affordable housing by Article 18.05 and state density bonus law (Government Code 65915). Davis has no local enhancement beyond the state schedule; Article 18.05 alternatives (in-lieu fee, land dedication) are the local layer.
affordability_requirement: State density bonus law thresholds (5% very low, 10% low, 100% affordable up to 80% bonus and unlimited near transit) or Article 18.05 inclusionary units.
next_deadline: None; applied with the entitlement application. Davis is updating its General Plan (2025 to 2027), which may fold density bonus text into a zoning rewrite.
layering_notes: Standard state law implementation; Davis downtown zones (Article 40.13) are form-based and the 2021-2029 Housing Element rezoned sites to meet RHNA, so the bonus matters most on R-3 and R-HD infill sites. Davis is not Prohousing designated. No fee waiver program for affordable units exists at the City level; development impact fees are set by Council annually. The code mirror (zoneomics) was used because qcode.us is blocked; confirm against the official code.

program_name: CDBG and HOME entitlement allocations (2025-2029 Consolidated Plan, Resolution 25-061) and PLHA formula allocation
administering_agency: City of Davis Social Services and Housing Department, Housing and Grants Management (Director Dana Bailey)
typical_award_size: Davis is a CDBG entitlement city and a HOME participating jurisdiction. Council adopted the 2025-2029 Consolidated Plan and the Program Year One (2025) Annual Action Plan on April 15, 2025 (Resolution 25-061). Local coverage puts year one CDBG plus HOME at about $1.06 million; HOME has historically funded first-time homebuyer loans and rental project gap loans, CDBG funds public services, facilities and the Pathways to Employment and homelessness programs. HCD's 2024-2028 PLHA NOFA lists Davis at about $1.33 million over five years; staff told Council on February 18, 2025 that PLHA would be used for homeownership opportunities.
per_unit_cap: HOME per-unit subsidy limits apply (HUD 221(d)(3) limits for Yolo County).
affordability_requirement: CDBG at or below 80% AMI; HOME at or below 80% AMI with at least 90% of rental assistance at 60% AMI and 20% of units at 50% AMI in projects with 5 or more HOME units.
next_deadline: Program Year 2026-27 Action Plan process runs winter to spring 2027 (public hearing typically April). Confirm amounts and the HOME set-aside with the Grants Management office, (530) 757-5602.
layering_notes: Federal money is the only recurring Davis source for rental projects, but the annual HOME amount is small (hundreds of thousands) and competes with homebuyer uses; combine with Housing Trust Fund gap money and state credits. HOME triggers federal Davis-Bacon only at 12 or more HOME-assisted units; state prevailing wage applies when City funds are added. Davis also receives HHAP through the Davis, Woodland/Yolo County CoC (see county record) for supportive housing operations. Yolo County's own CDBG and HOME (state non-entitlement) cover only unincorporated areas, so there is no overlap. Blocked: the Grants Management page and the Consolidated Plan PDF on cityofdavis.org (403); the April 15, 2025 minutes on documents.cityofdavis.org were opened and record the adoption.

program_name: Affordable Housing Ordinance (Woodland Municipal Code Chapter 15.16, Ordinance 1662 of 2020) inclusionary requirements and in-lieu fee
administering_agency: City of Woodland Community Development Department (Housing Analyst Franklin Cui, (530) 661-2019) with the Community Services Department
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy.
