Citywide outside the Spring Lake Specific Plan: for-sale and multifamily rental projects of 30 or fewer units are exempt; 31 to 80 units provide 5% low income units; 81 or more units provide 10% low income, reduced to 5% if the project is built at 95% or more of maximum allowed density; in Downtown, Corridor Mixed Use and Neighborhood Commercial areas projects of at least 10 units built at maximum density (and at least 10 units per acre) owe 5% for-sale units. Very low income requirements were dropped in the April 2020 amendments. Alternatives: land dedication valued at the in-lieu fee times required units, or in-lieu fees per an adopted fee schedule (reviewed annually) or, if none is adopted, as negotiated in the inclusionary housing agreement and paid before building permits. Example: Ashley and Main (168 units, 2020) paid $469,413. Fees go to the Affordable Housing Fund (Fund 1327); up to 10% of annual income may fund administration.
affordability_requirement: Low income (80% AMI) rental units must be permanently affordable; for-sale affordable units 10 years minimum reset at each resale with a $1,000 silent second and equity share; rents calculated at 50% AMI for very low and 80% AMI for low income units.
next_deadline: None (ordinance). The 2020 temporary relief provisions were set to expire in April 2022 unless dwelling unit goals were met; the Housing Element (Program A.27) committed to a LEAP-funded study of a standardized square-foot in-lieu fee, including nonresidential. Confirm whether a fee schedule has been adopted with the Housing Analyst.
layering_notes: Woodland's inclusionary program feeds the only local soft money in the city (Fund 1327, see the in-lieu fund record). Thresholds are generous to market-rate builders (exempt to 30 units, 5% at 31 to 80), so most revenue has come from Spring Lake development agreements and large projects. Spring Lake has its own stricter rules (separate record). Rental inclusionary units must accept Section 8 vouchers (Yolo County Housing PBVs can layer). Chapter 15.16 also now contains the City's state density bonus procedures. No county inclusionary applies inside city limits (Yolo County Chapter 8-8 is unincorporated only). ecode360 hosts the official Woodland code and opened directly.

program_name: Affordable Housing In-Lieu Fees Fund (Fund 1327) and Spring Lake off-site fee revenues: City gap loans to affordable projects
administering_agency: City of Woodland Community Development Department, Housing (Deputy Director Erika Bumgardner; Housing Analyst Franklin Cui, (530) 661-2019)
typical_award_size: Case-by-case residual receipts loans. Most recent: $1,500,000 to Yolo County Housing for Tupelo Family Apartments (73 units, 72 restricted, 30% to 80% AMI, Yolano-Donnelly Choice Neighborhoods early project), approved July 15, 2025 as a 55-year residual receipts loan at 3% simple interest with a 55-year regulatory agreement; about $20,833 per affordable unit, which staff compared with Mutual Housing at Spring Lake Phase I ($38,462 per unit) and Vista Del Robles Phase II ($41,667 per unit). Earlier the City lent $2,410,000 of in-lieu and Spring Lake off-site fees to Mutual Housing's farmworker phases (100 units) and granted $1.48 million plus free City land for the 61-unit East Beamer Way supportive housing campus. Fund balance not stated; staff noted that in-lieu receipts over the prior four years were enough to replace $500,000 of ARP funds.
per_unit_cap: None published; recent awards $20,833 to $41,667 per unit.
affordability_requirement: Extremely low, very low and low income rental units with 55-year covenants; Council priority for projects leveraging tax credits, AHSC and other state funds.
next_deadline: No NOFA; developers request funding through Housing staff ahead of state or TCAC applications. Tupelo received a $27,999,100 AHSC award in December 2025 and will pursue tax credits in 2026 or 2027; staff planned a fall 2025 ARP spending plan update. Contact the Housing Analyst before an application round.
layering_notes: Woodland's pattern is a City commitment letter sized to make the AHSC or TCAC application competitive, with Yolo County Housing or Mutual Housing as developer and Sutter Health or Alta California Regional Center philanthropic layers (Tupelo also has $1.5 million from Sutter and $2.3 million from Alta). Loans are residual receipts and subordinate, so they fit under 4% bond deals. Fund revenue is lumpy (large projects and Spring Lake development agreements); confirm the balance before relying on it. Layer order: AHSC or MHP, 4% or 9% credits, Yolo County Housing PBVs, City Fund 1327, CDBG for off-site infrastructure. Agenda packets are on CivicClerk (woodlandca.api.civicclerk.com file streams open; the portal itself is a JavaScript app).

program_name: Spring Lake Specific Plan Affordable Housing Plan: inclusionary requirements, Off-Site Affordable Housing Fee and 25% density bonus
administering_agency: City of Woodland Community Development Department (Spring Lake Specific Plan area)
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Multifamily projects in Spring Lake must make at least 20% of units affordable to and occupied by very low income households plus 10% low income, or alternatively 25% very low income, with a 25% density bonus for complying projects. For-sale projects owe 10% low income units (exempt under 10 units), with land dedication or, only at City initiative for projects under 50 units, an in-lieu fee equal to the appraised affordability gap per unit plus administration. All single-family market-rate units pay an Off-Site Affordable Housing Fee of $1,100 per unit (Council may reset it, not above $1,300), collected before final map approval and spent anywhere in the City on qualifying affordable units; up to 10% may fund administration.
affordability_requirement: Multifamily: 20% very low plus 10% low, or 25% very low income, permanently affordable; for-sale 10% low income for the longest feasible period.
next_deadline: None (specific plan requirement). The Housing Element (Program A.24) proposes amending the Spring Lake Specific Plan to clarify affordability provisions; several Spring Lake single-family projects have paid in-lieu fees under development agreements.
layering_notes: Spring Lake is where most of Woodland's affordable pipeline sits: Mutual Housing at Spring Lake (farmworker, 100 units), a 4.6-acre multifamily site dedicated in 2019 to a nonprofit in place of $900,000 of fees (112 lower income senior units required), and R-20 and R-25 sites intended for 25% very low income projects. A 100% affordable developer can acquire a Spring Lake R-20 or R-25 site and satisfy a market-rate builder's obligation, then draw on Fund 1327 and the off-site fee revenues as gap money. The Plan still names the Redevelopment Agency as fund recipient; the City is housing successor. Chapter 15.16 applies in Spring Lake only where the Specific Plan is silent.

program_name: Density bonus ordinance (Woodland Code Sec. 25-21-25, now implemented in Chapter 15.16) with fee waiver and fee deferral incentives
administering_agency: City of Woodland Community Development Department, Planning Division
typical_award_size: Regulatory incentive. Projects of 5 or more units qualify with 10% lower income, 5% very low income, senior housing or 10% moderate income condominiums; base bonus 20% rising 1.5% per 1% of lower income units (2.5% per 1% very low) to a 35% cap under the posted ordinance, and Chapter 15.16 now grants bonuses, concessions, waivers and parking ratios as a matter of right per current Government Code 65915 (up to 50% and unlimited near transit). Listed local incentives include use of local affordable housing funds, waiver or reduction of City building permit, plan check and inspection fees, and waiver or deferral of City impact fees until certificate of occupancy.
affordability_requirement: State density bonus law thresholds (5% very low, 10% low, 10% moderate for-sale, senior or special needs) with covenants of 55 years for rental.
next_deadline: None; request with the planned development, design review or other entitlement application. The Housing Element (Program A.10) commits to keep the ordinance current with state law and to publish a one-page fact sheet.
layering_notes: The fee waiver and impact fee deferral incentives are the city's only fee relief for affordable units and are granted project by project with the density bonus agreement (see the fee deferral record). The 2021 Housing Element found the posted ordinance out of date with Government Code 65915; the ecode360 Chapter 15.16 density bonus section (Ordinance 1662, 2020) is the operative text. Woodland's realistic densities already run near maximums (Spring Lake 101-unit project at 80% of RM density), so the bonus matters most on CMU corridor sites such as Tupelo's CMU-A parcel. City fee waivers are public subsidy and can trigger prevailing wage; impact fee deferrals alone generally do not.

program_name: Development Impact Fee Deferral Program (MPFP fee deferral for multifamily, December 2008 ordinance) and case-by-case deferrals for affordable projects
administering_agency: City of Woodland Community Development Department and Administrative Services (Finance)
typical_award_size: Deferral, not waiver. The December 2008 ordinance, extended through June 30, 2022, lets multifamily and nonresidential projects defer seven Major Projects Financing Plan (MPFP) impact fees (General City, Library, Police, Water, Roads, Administration, Storm Drain) for up to 24 months or until certificate of occupancy. Separately, the Council has approved interest-free deferral of a portion of impact fees for affordable housing projects to just before certificate of occupancy, and small units under 1,450 square feet pay the multifamily MPFP rate. Dollar value depends on the fee schedule (MPFP fees are several tens of thousands of dollars per multifamily unit in the Housing Element fee tables).
affordability_requirement: Case-by-case for affordable housing projects; the general multifamily deferral had no affordability test.
next_deadline: Unknown, verify with agency. The general program's June 30, 2022 sunset may have been extended; the 2021 Housing Element (Program A.16) commits the City to continue offering fee deferrals and reduced MPFP fees for infill and multifamily housing. Confirm status and the current MPFP schedule with Community Development, (530) 661-5820.
layering_notes: Deferral improves construction-period cash flow but is not a subsidy; combine with the density bonus fee waiver incentive and Fund 1327 loans. Woodland has no fee waiver fund and no Prohousing designation. Spring Lake has its own financing plan with payback and fee reduction mechanics tied to building unit allocations. Facts are from the HCD-hosted 2021-2029 Housing Element (Appendix D); the City's fee pages were not checked for a current ordinance.

program_name: CDBG entitlement program (2025-2029 Consolidated Plan, annual Action Plan NOFA) and PLHA formula allocation
administering_agency: City of Woodland Community Development Department, Housing (Housing Analyst Franklin Cui, (530) 661-2019, franklin.cui@cityofwoodland.gov)
typical_award_size: FY 2025/26 CDBG allocation $473,643 (FY 2024/25 $475,086; FY 2026/27 estimated $443,278), about $2.4 million over the 2025-2029 Consolidated Plan adopted July 15, 2025. Allocation pattern: 65% public infrastructure (ADA Accessibility Project $307,868 in FY 25/26 and $299,622 in FY 26/27), 15% public services capped (about $55,000 to $66,000 to food, shelter and fair housing), 20% administration. The five-year plan budgets only $100,000 for the Improve Housing Access and Quality goal, so direct CDBG support to rental development is minimal; past awards funded shelters, supportive housing services and fair housing. HCD's 2024-2028 PLHA NOFA lists Woodland at about $1.09 million over five years. Woodland is not a HOME participating jurisdiction and applies to the state HOME competition (used for first-time homebuyer loans; the interest list is closed).
affordability_requirement: CDBG at or below 80% AMI or low and moderate income area benefit; state HOME at or below 80% AMI.
next_deadline: FY 2027/28 NOFA expected mid February 2027 with applications due about mid March (the FY 2026/27 cycle: NOFA February 18, 2026, applications due March 18, 2026, Council hearing July 21, 2026). Program year starts July 1.
layering_notes: Treat Woodland CDBG as a source for off-site infrastructure or ADA work adjacent to an affordable project rather than construction gap; the housing goal is $100,000 over five years. State HOME and PLHA are the city's other formula sources but have gone to homebuyer assistance; ask Housing staff whether PLHA could be redirected to a rental project. Yolo County's CDBG and HOME cover only unincorporated areas. Pair with Fund 1327 loans and Yolo County Housing PBVs. The CDBG page and DocumentCenter PDFs on cityofwoodland.gov open directly; some scanned PDFs (one-pager, SB 341 report) have no text layer.

program_name: Woodland Housing Successor Agency (former Redevelopment Agency) Low and Moderate Income Housing Asset Fund (SB 341 reporting)
administering_agency: City of Woodland as Housing Successor to the former Woodland Redevelopment Agency (Community Services and Community Development Departments)
typical_award_size: Unknown. The City posts an FY 2021/22 Senate Bill 341 report for the Woodland Housing Successor Agency on its Housing page, confirming the City holds housing successor assets (loans, covenants and any residual Low and Moderate Income Housing Asset Fund balance) from the former Redevelopment Agency, which once received Spring Lake off-site fees. No current fund balance, excess surplus calculation or deployment plan was found in documents opened this pass; recent City gap loans have been drawn from in-lieu Fund 1327, not successor funds, suggesting the LMIHAF is small or encumbered.
affordability_requirement: Health and Safety Code 34176.1 targets: at least 30% of LMIHAF expenditures for rental housing at or below 30% AMI, remainder at or below 60% AMI, with 55-year covenants.
next_deadline: Unknown, verify with agency. Ask Housing staff for the latest SB 341 annual report (due with the Housing Element Annual Progress Report by April 1 each year) and any excess surplus.
layering_notes: Useful negative information: Woodland's post-RDA housing money is the inclusionary Fund 1327, not a successor fund. Any LMIHAF loan repayments or land sale proceeds would be an additional city-controlled layer with extremely low income targeting. The posted SB 341 report (DocumentCenter 9562) is a scanned PDF with no text layer and could not be read by script; the Housing page listing it was opened.

program_name: Inclusionary Housing Ordinance (West Sacramento Municipal Code Chapter 15.40, Ordinance 14-4) with Housing Trust Fund Program in-lieu alternative and Urban Infill Area incentive
administering_agency: City of West Sacramento Economic Development and Housing Department, Housing Division (Housing Manager Raul Huerta, (916) 617-4555)
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Residential projects of 5 or more units citywide (adopted April 2014, replacing the redevelopment-area Chapter 15.10): rental projects set aside 10% of units (5% very low income, 5% low income); for-sale projects 10% low income, with rental units substitutable. Units on site, dispersed, at least 90% of the smallest market unit size, concurrent with each 25% of market units. Alternatives at Council discretion: payment into the Housing Trust Fund Program at the amount set in the Book of City Imposts Section VIII-N (a regional comparison in late 2025 listed West Sacramento's in-lieu fee at about $7,699 per dwelling unit, assessed per market-rate unit), acquisition and rehabilitation of market units, off-site construction, or preservation of at-risk units. Projects in the priority Urban Infill Area earn a discount on the in-lieu fee based on adjusted density (dwelling unit equivalents for structured parking, public open space and ground floor commercial). Incentives include reduced parking, priority processing, standards waivers and technical assistance; financial incentives only to the extent City programs exist.
affordability_requirement: Rental: 5% very low (50% AMI) and 5% low income (80% AMI) for 55 years; for-sale: 10% low income with a 45-year goal and recapture on early release.
next_deadline: None (ordinance). The Housing Element (Program HE-PR-1.2) commits to refining Chapter 15.40 to target lower incomes and reduce the burden on market-rate housing; six affordable housing agreements were approved 2018 to 2020. Confirm the current Book of City Imposts fee with the Housing Division.
layering_notes: The in-lieu alternative is the main revenue source for the City's Housing Trust Fund (Fund 261-9385), which funds gap loans (separate record). Because the per-unit fee is low relative to Davis ($250,000) and Folsom, most subdivisions in Southport pay the fee rather than build, so West Sacramento's affordable production comes from City-assisted 100% affordable projects in the Bridge District and Washington (West Gateway Place I and II, Landmark Lofts, the Grand Gateway 114-unit project). Overconcentration cap: no more than 40% of a project's units may be inclusionary. No county inclusionary applies inside the city. ecode360 hosts the official West Sacramento code and opened directly; cityofwestsacramento.org (Akamai) returns 403 to scripts and WebFetch, and the Book of City Imposts could not be opened.

program_name: West Sacramento Housing Trust Fund (Fund 261-9385) gap financing loans, HOME program income and City land contributions
administering_agency: City of West Sacramento Economic Development and Housing Department, Housing Division (Housing Manager Raul Huerta; Community Investment Principal Planner David Tilley, (916) 617-4661)
typical_award_size: Project-sized gap loans from Chapter 15.40 in-lieu receipts, used for gap financing to projects with affordable units, infrastructure supporting affordable housing and predevelopment. Most recent example (developer fact sheet, not a City document): The Bridge at West Gateway / West Gateway Place II (60 units, 20% to 60% AMI, six PSH units at 20% AMI, opened June 2025) received $5,194,626 from the City Housing Trust Fund, $2,000,000 of City HOME program income and City land valued at $3,344,500 alongside $11.17 million HCD MHP and $24.76 million California Housing Accelerator. Earlier: $1,191,428 of CDBG program income for West Gateway Place Phase 1 infrastructure and $2.6 million AHSC. Fund balance not published in documents opened this pass.
per_unit_cap: None published; West Gateway Place II implies roughly $87,000 per unit of trust fund money plus land.
affordability_requirement: Very low and low income rental units with 55-year covenants; Housing Element priority for extremely low income and large family units in the Bridge District, Washington and Grand Gateway areas.
next_deadline: No NOFA; the City negotiates commitments with its development partners (Jamboree with the West Sacramento Housing Development Corporation, Mercy Housing, New Hope CDC) ahead of state rounds. Ask the Housing Division for the current Fund 261 balance and the Grand Gateway affordable site schedule.
layering_notes: West Sacramento is the most active city funder in Yolo County: City land plus trust fund plus HOME program income have repeatedly made 100% affordable Bridge District projects competitive for MHP, Accelerator and AHSC (MOSA won $43 million AHSC in December 2025). The structure is a subordinate residual receipts loan plus ground lease or land conveyance. Layer order: AHSC or MHP, 4% bonds and credits (CMFA or CSCDA conduit with City TEFRA), Yolo County Housing PBVs, City trust fund, PLHA, CDBG for infrastructure. Successor agency land and EIFD financing are separate records. Blocked: cityofwestsacramento.org Housing Division pages, the Housing Policies and Studies page and the SB 341 report (403); the Legistar API only holds 2019 to 2022 matters and the Granicus feed is empty; the City now posts agendas on its own site. Facts are from the HCD-hosted 2021-2029 Housing Element plus the Jamboree fact sheet.

program_name: Affordable Housing, Density Bonuses and Incentives (West Sacramento Municipal Code Chapter 17.23, Ordinance 19-1)
administering_agency: City of West Sacramento Community Development Department, Planning Division
typical_award_size: Regulatory. Chapter 17.23 applies in all zones allowing residential use and grants qualifying developments and qualifying land transfers the density bonus, incentives and concessions specified in Government Code 65915 by reference (no local enhancement, no local cap). Requests are processed with the entitlement and approved if state criteria are met; a continued availability agreement is required before approval. Section 17.23.070 restates Housing Accountability Act limits on denying projects with at least 20% low income units. The 2019 zoning code update raised minimum and maximum densities in medium, high density and mixed-use zones (about 2,025 acres), so the Housing Element targets only about 5 density bonus units for the cycle.
affordability_requirement: State density bonus law thresholds (5% very low, 10% low, 10% moderate for-sale, senior, 100% affordable) with covenants per Government Code 65915(c).
next_deadline: None; request in writing to the Planning Division with the project application. The City reviews the chapter in its biannual zoning code update.
layering_notes: West Sacramento's leverage is zoning (high base densities in the Bridge District, Washington and Pioneer Bluff specific plan areas, mixed-use and waterfront zones) rather than the bonus itself. SB 35 and now SB 423 streamlining accepted for 10% or more affordable projects. Chapter 15.40 incentives (parking reductions, priority processing, standards waivers) can be combined. The code mirror (zoneomics) matches ecode360's section list; confirm against the official code.

program_name: Permanent Local Housing Allocation (PLHA) formula funds, Resolution 25-15 five-year plan
administering_agency: City of West Sacramento Economic Development and Housing Department, Housing Division (Housing Manager Raul Huerta)
typical_award_size: Council adopted Resolution 25-15 on February 19, 2025 (5 to 0) authorizing the PLHA application and a five-year plan for $763,253 of 2021, 2022 and 2023 formula allocations: 55% ($419,789) for the affordable housing component of the Grand Gateway Master Plan, specifically a proposed 114-unit affordable project serving households at 30%, 50%, 60% and up to 80% AMI; 40% ($305,301) for owner-occupied rehabilitation grants up to $30,000 through existing nonprofit contracts; 5% administration. HCD's 2024-2028 PLHA NOFA lists West Sacramento at about $1.04 million over the next five years. The City filed a CEQA notice of exemption for the plan on February 19, 2025.
affordability_requirement: Rental component at or below 80% AMI with deeper targeting (30% to 60% AMI) at the Grand Gateway site; owner rehabilitation for low income owners in qualifying neighborhoods.
next_deadline: The Grand Gateway affordable project has no published developer selection or construction date; later PLHA years (2024 onward) need a plan amendment. Verify with the Housing Division.
layering_notes: Small but useful: about $420,000 earmarked to one City-sponsored project in the Grand Gateway District (City-owned land, see successor agency record). Any developer of that site should expect PLHA plus Housing Trust Fund plus land, then compete for MHP or AHSC. State funds trigger prevailing wage. Yolo County's own PLHA is unincorporated only. Source is the state CEQA notice of exemption filed by the City; the resolution and staff report on cityofwestsacramento.org returned 403, and dollar figures are from local press coverage of the February 19, 2025 meeting.

program_name: Redevelopment Successor Agency housing assets, Enhanced Infrastructure Financing District and City-owned land (Grand Gateway Master Plan area, Bridge District, Washington Specific Plan)
administering_agency: City of West Sacramento as Housing Successor and Redevelopment Successor Agency (Economic Development and Housing Department; Yolo Countywide Successor Agency Oversight Board)
typical_award_size: Land and tax increment tools rather than a cash fund. With the loss of redevelopment the City repealed Chapter 15.10 and formed an Enhanced Infrastructure Financing District with 14 project areas that, with Measure G sales tax, funds infrastructure for infill, high-density, transit-oriented housing in the riverfront districts (Community Investment Program HE-PR-1.4). The City owns the Grand Gateway Master Plan area (former West Capitol Avenue redevelopment parcels; the Oversight Board approved sale of three Successor Agency parcels at 485 Lighthouse Drive and 2400 and 2600 West Capitol Avenue to the City for $1,310,000 in 2024) where a 114-unit affordable project is planned, and has contributed land to West Gateway Place I and II in the Bridge District. Housing successor Low and Moderate Income Housing Asset Fund balance and SB 341 reports were not accessible this pass.
affordability_requirement: LMIHAF uses follow Health and Safety Code 34176.1 (30% of spending at or below 30% AMI, remainder at or below 60% AMI, 55-year covenants); City land deals carry negotiated covenants.
next_deadline: Unknown, verify with agency. Watch for a developer solicitation for the Grand Gateway affordable site and for the annual SB 341 housing successor report (due by April 1 with the APR).
layering_notes: West Sacramento is the only Yolo County city with an active successor agency land program and an EIFD; the brief's note that it has active successor programs is confirmed in the Housing Element but current LMIHAF numbers could not be read. Developers should ask the Housing Division about (1) City-owned sites in Grand Gateway, Washington and Bridge District, (2) EIFD or Measure G infrastructure contributions that reduce off-site costs, and (3) any LMIHAF balance for extremely low income units. Layer with the Housing Trust Fund, PLHA and state AHSC (the 2016 to 2021 cycle brought $4.13 million AHSC infrastructure plus $2.6 million for West Gateway Place). Blocked: cityofwestsacramento.org and yolocounty.gov (403); the Oversight Board facts come from search snippets of Yolo County documents, so confirm.

program_name: CDBG entitlement program (2026-2030 Consolidated Plan) and HOME program income
administering_agency: City of West Sacramento Economic Development and Housing Department, Housing Division
typical_award_size: West Sacramento became a CDBG entitlement city in FY 2016/17 and receives about $546,000 a year (the City's March 2026 notice anticipated an amount similar to the prior year's $546,333). The draft 2026-2030 Consolidated Plan and FY 2026-27 Annual Action Plan were out for comment March 6 to April 7, 2026. Housing uses have been infrastructure for affordable projects ($1,191,428 of CDBG program income for West Gateway Place Phase 1), fair housing services, homeless coordinator staffing, first-time homebuyer help and owner rehabilitation. The City is not a HOME participating jurisdiction but holds HOME program income from earlier state HOME awards ($2,000,000 went into West Gateway Place II). State LHTF applications ($1,000,000) were not awarded.
affordability_requirement: CDBG at or below 80% AMI or area benefit; HOME program income at or below 80% AMI with HOME rent limits.
next_deadline: FY 2027-28 Action Plan comment period expected March to April 2027; subrecipient applications typically open in winter. Confirm with the Housing Division.
layering_notes: Use for off-site infrastructure and public improvements around a Bridge District or Washington project rather than vertical construction; HOME program income is the more flexible pot and has gone straight into City-sponsored projects. Yolo County's state CDBG and HOME cover only unincorporated areas. Facts come from the HCD-hosted Housing Element and search snippets of the City's 2026 notices; the CDBG page and Consolidated Plan PDFs on cityofwestsacramento.org returned 403.

program_name: West Sacramento Housing Development Corporation (City-affiliated nonprofit co-developer and property owner)
administering_agency: West Sacramento Housing Development Corporation (501(c)(3), EIN 94-3184534, 2950 Beacon Boulevard) working with the City Housing Division
typical_award_size: Partnership capacity rather than a funding program. The Housing Element names the West Sacramento Housing Development Corporation (WSHDC) alongside Yolo County Housing as the City's standing nonprofit partners for pursuing state and federal funds (Programs HE-PR-1.6 and 1.9). WSHDC co-developed West Gateway Place (77 units, 2017, $29.8 million) and West Gateway Place II / The Bridge at West Gateway (60 units, 2025) with Jamboree Housing on City-contributed land, and owns scattered rental properties managed by a third-party manager.
affordability_requirement: Projects to date serve 20% to 60% AMI families with permanent supportive units; terms set by the City and state funding.
next_deadline: None; WSHDC has no NOFA. Approach through the City Housing Division when proposing a joint venture on City or successor agency land.
layering_notes: For an outside developer WSHDC is the local partner that unlocks City land, Housing Trust Fund and HOME program income commitments and local-nonprofit scoring; Jamboree has been its repeat co-developer. Mercy Housing (Esperanza Crossing, CMFA bonds) and New Hope CDC (9% award for a West Sacramento project) have also worked in the city without WSHDC. Pair with Yolo County Housing PBVs and the welfare exemption (county records). WSHDC has no website; corporate facts are from nonprofit registries and the Jamboree fact sheet.

program_name: Santa Rosa Housing Trust annual Notice of Funding Availability (Housing Authority affordable housing loans: local Housing Trust, CDBG, PLHA and Prohousing Incentive Program funds)
administering_agency: Housing Authority of the City of Santa Rosa, Housing and Community Services Department (Santa Rosa Housing Trust)
typical_award_size: FY 2026-27 NOFA (issued May 1, 2026, due June 5, 2026): about $3.6 million, made up of about $1,399,000 local Housing Trust funds, $1,056,071 CDBG and $1,187,500 state Prohousing Incentive Program (PIP) funds; two applications received for $4 million and 93 units; August 24, 2026 awards: $2,000,000 to Ponderosa Village Phase II (CRDC and Danco, 30 units, 250 Roseland Ave) and $1,642,571 to Caritas Homes Phase II (360 Seventh St). FY 2025-26 NOFA: about $3.5 million (about $2,210,500 local, $1,082,310 CDBG); awards Sept 2025: $489,228 Zane-Wolff Veterans Village rehab, $1,238,310 Apple Valley Scattered Sites rehab, $2,000,000 Ridley Family Apartments (50 units). FY 2024-25: about $3.1 million for 170 units. Local Housing Trust revenue is one half of the City's real property transfer tax allocation ($2.275 million total in FY 2026-27, split equally with Homeless Services) plus housing impact fees and commercial linkage fees (about $1.44 million collected in 2025). Application fee $2,203.
per_unit_cap: No published per-unit cap; awards sized by gap and scored on a 100-point system (affordability 20, developer experience 15, special needs 12, readiness 10, leveraging 10, TCAC/CDLAC competitiveness 10, bedrooms 8, services 7, other 5, amenities 3). Requests have run $0.5 million to $2 million per project.
affordability_requirement: Units restricted to extremely low, very low and low income households up to 60% AMI (unless another source restricts further) for 55 years from initial occupancy under a recorded Regulatory Agreement. Standard loan: 3% simple interest, principal and interest deferred 55 years, residual receipts split 75% to the Authority and 25% to the developer.
next_deadline: FY 2026-27 round closed June 5, 2026 and was awarded August 24, 2026. Next NOFA expected about May 2027 with an early June 2027 deadline, after a Housing Authority priorities study session in April 2027. Projects must start construction within 12 months of award or funds are rescinded. Contact housingtrust@srcity.org, Rebecca Lane (707) 543-3300.
layering_notes: This is the primary local gap source inside Santa Rosa city limits and is separate from the County CFH, County HOME/CDBG (Santa Rosa is its own CDBG entitlement and is not in the Urban County) and County PLHA records. Santa Rosa is also a HOME participating jurisdiction and has run a continuous HOME NOFA in the past (2020); HOME TBRA guidelines were revised September 2026. The City's own PLHA 2024-2028 allocation (separate record) and the $1.25 million PIP grant (accepted April 7, 2026, must be spent by June 30, 2028) are folded into this NOFA, so a single application reaches all City sources; applicants cannot pick the source. Typical stack: City NOFA loan plus RED Housing Fund (county record) plus County CFH or PBVs, then 4% or 9% LIHTC. The FY 2026-27 round had a five-point preference for rehabilitation and a five-point deduction for applicants that previously declined or failed to close an award. Prevailing wage: the NOFA requires compliance with California prevailing wage and, for federal funds, Davis-Bacon. Note the City's Capital Facilities Fee pilot waiver (separate record) is not available to units receiving City or Housing Authority loan funds, so developers must choose between the fee waiver and NOFA funds. Access notes: srcity.org returns 403 to scripts; records were read from the Legistar web API (client santa-rosa) and legistar.granicus.com attachments, and the ca-santarosa.civicplus.com mirror for some pages.

program_name: Santa Rosa Inclusionary Housing Ordinance, City Code Chapter 21-02 (Housing Allocation Plan): on-site allocated units, housing impact fee and commercial linkage fee
administering_agency: City of Santa Rosa Planning and Economic Development Department (compliance) and Housing Authority (affordability agreements and fee proceeds)
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. For-rent projects: 8% of units for low income or 5% for very low income households; for-sale: 10% moderate income; Downtown multifamily: 4% low or 3% very low (rental) and 5% moderate (for-sale). Projects of six or fewer units pay the housing impact fee. Any project may instead pay the housing impact fee set by Council resolution, indexed to CPI each July (rate not opened this pass; the fee is paid before final inspection for rentals). Commercial linkage fee applies to new commercial development, due at building permit. Collections in 2025: $1,436,870 ($1,257,641 housing impact fees and $179,229 commercial linkage fees), down from $1.52 million in 2024. In 2025, permits were issued for 23 on-site allocated units (20 very low, 2 low, 1 moderate) out of 661 qualifying units.
affordability_requirement: Allocated units restricted 55 years by recorded affordability agreement with the Housing Authority; deed-restricted affordable projects (units restricted 55 years under agreement with the City), homeless shelters, SROs and ADUs are exempt. Fee revenue must fund housing within City limits for lower and moderate income households with 55-year agreements; Downtown fees are reserved two years for Downtown projects.
next_deadline: Applies at entitlement; fee rate in effect at payment. Council reviewed the 2025 General Plan and Inclusionary Housing Annual Review on March 17, 2026; the next annual review is expected in March 2027. HAP last substantively amended by Ordinance 2019-015 (Ordinance 3998 of October 22, 2019).
layering_notes: Fee proceeds feed the Santa Rosa Housing Trust NOFA (record above), so market-rate pipeline volume drives local loan capacity. Developers providing on-site units get one incentive or concession under Chapter 20-31 and may count the same units toward a state density bonus (bonus units are excluded from the base when computing the inclusionary share). Alternatives (off-site units in the same quadrant, land dedication, conversion of market-rate units, preservation of at-risk units, inclusionary credits usable for 10 years) require Director approval; off-site units cannot receive City or Housing Authority subsidy. The County's separate Affordable Housing Program fee applies only in unincorporated areas. Read on the ecode360 mirror of the Santa Rosa City Code because qcode.us and srcity.org block scripts; collection data from the 2025 Annual Review (Legistar matter 26-0150).

program_name: Santa Rosa development fee deferral for affordable housing units, City Code Chapter 21-01 (Section 21-01.020)
administering_agency: City of Santa Rosa Planning and Economic Development Department; agreements approved by City Council
typical_award_size: Deferral, not a waiver: Government Code 66000(b) development impact fees on affordable units under contract with the City may be deferred up to two years from the date otherwise due, secured by a deed of trust, with the balance (at the rate in effect when originally due) payable on sale, transfer or placement of permanent financing. Separately, all City development impact fees are due at final inspection rather than permit issuance (Section 21-01.030), which is itself a cash-flow benefit, and water and sewer demand fees may use a Board of Public Utilities payment plan.
affordability_requirement: Only units under an affordability contract with the City or Housing Authority qualify.
next_deadline: Application must be filed with Planning and Economic Development at least 120 days before fees are due; each deferral agreement needs Council approval. No standing deadline.
layering_notes: Stacks with the Capital Facilities Fee pilot waiver (separate record) for remaining fees such as park and utility fees, and with the Housing Trust NOFA. The County's Multi-Family Development Fee Deferral Program (county record) applies only to unincorporated projects. Deferral agreements are not assignable without City Attorney consent, which matters when a LIHTC partnership takes title after entitlement. Read from the ecode360 mirror; the Housing Element implementation ordinance introduced December 2025 (PLN25-0397) amended Titles 20 and 21 but the redline was not reviewed for changes to this chapter.

program_name: Santa Rosa Affordable Housing Capital Facilities Fee Pilot Program (Resolution RES-2024-175) and 50% permit fee reduction for 100% deed-restricted projects
administering_agency: City of Santa Rosa Planning and Economic Development Department with Housing and Community Services (deed restrictions through the Housing Authority)
typical_award_size: Capital Facilities Fee (Chapter 21-04) set at $0 for new units deed-restricted through the Housing Authority at very low (0-50% AMI, including acutely and extremely low), low (50-80% AMI) and moderate (80-120% AMI) income levels, for building permits issued during the three-year pilot (adopted late 2024, runs until about late 2027 or adoption of a new CFF nexus study, whichever is first). The City's 2026 Prohousing renewal application also cites a 50 percent reduction in permit fees for projects in which 100 percent of units are deed-restricted affordable, and streamlined design review. The CFF for a multifamily unit is several thousand dollars, so the waiver is worth roughly $100,000 to $500,000 on a typical project (confirm with the current fee schedule).
per_unit_cap: Per-unit waiver equal to the applicable CFF for each restricted unit; no dollar cap published.
affordability_requirement: Units must be deed-restricted through the Housing Authority at the AMI categories above. Units receiving locally sourced financial assistance from the City or Housing Authority loan programs are NOT eligible for the CFF waiver.
eligible_project_types: conversion of temporary housing units approved under Section 20-16.030 to permanent units
next_deadline: Applies to building permits for vertical construction issued during the pilot period (three years from the late 2024 effective date of RES-2024-175, roughly through fall 2027, unless a new nexus study ends it sooner). Permit fee reduction has no stated sunset.
layering_notes: Key conflict: a project cannot take both the CFF waiver and a Santa Rosa Housing Trust NOFA loan, so model both paths; for a 100% affordable LIHTC deal the NOFA loan is usually larger than the CFF waiver, but the waiver has no competition and no application cycle. The waiver stacks with the Chapter 21-01 deferral of other impact fees, state density bonus and the County welfare exemption (county record). The County's 2025-2026 traffic and parks fee waiver (county record) applies only in unincorporated Sonoma County. Read from the resolution text included in the City's draft 2026 Prohousing Designation renewal application (Legistar matter 26-0547, Council hearing August 4, 2026); the City's designation expires January 1, 2027 and renewal is pending with HCD.

program_name: Santa Rosa Density Bonus and Other Developer Incentives, Zoning Code Chapter 20-31 (state density bonus plus local Supplemental Density Bonus up to 100%)
administering_agency: City of Santa Rosa Planning and Economic Development Department; Density Bonus Housing Agreements through the Housing Authority
typical_award_size: Regulatory, not cash. State density bonus up to 50% with incentives and concessions; 100% affordable rental projects (very low and low income, up to 20% moderate) get a 100% density bonus. Local enhancements: (1) an Additional Density Bonus of up to 100% above maximum density for projects that reach the 50% base bonus and add very low income units (5% additional VLI units earns 20%, up to 10% VLI earns 38.75%) or moderate income units; (2) a Supplemental Density Bonus through a Minor Conditional Use Permit using Eligibility Points, at least 60% earned by on-site affordable units and up to 40% by community benefits (public open space, park or capital facilities fee contributions, landmark rehabilitation, family-sized affordable units), with three total incentives or concessions; (3) incentives for specialized housing (10% of units for special needs at very low income rents, 55 years) and child care facilities.
affordability_requirement: Affordable units restricted 55 years under a recorded Density Bonus Housing Agreement; inclusionary units may count toward both Chapter 21-02 and the density bonus.
next_deadline: Density bonus application filed with the first entitlement application and processed concurrently; Supplemental Density Bonus requires a Minor CUP. Chapter last amended by Ordinance 2023-006 (June 6, 2023); further Title 20 amendments to implement the 2023-2031 Housing Element were introduced December 2025 (PLN25-0397).
layering_notes: Santa Rosa's supplemental bonus goes beyond state law and beyond the County's Chapter 26 density bonus program (county record), which is useful on infill sites near the two SMART stations and Downtown where the Downtown Station Area Specific Plan already allows high densities. A single affordability agreement can cover inclusionary and density bonus units. Pairing a 100% density bonus with the CFF pilot waiver and the Housing Trust NOFA is the standard local stack. Read from the ecode360 mirror of the Santa Rosa City Code.

program_name: Permanent Local Housing Allocation (PLHA), City of Santa Rosa formula allocation and 2024-2028 PLHA Plan
administering_agency: City of Santa Rosa Housing and Community Services Department; loans awarded by the Housing Authority through its NOFA
typical_award_size: Five-year 2024-2028 formula allocation of up to $3,046,056 ($487,369 for 2024 and $522,044 for 2025 applied for after an October 13, 2026 public hearing); up to 5% ($152,303) for administration. The prior 2019-2023 allocation of $4,012,612 was committed to four projects totaling 196 units. Funds are loaned at 3% simple interest, deferred, repaid from surplus cash, secured by deed of trust and regulatory agreement.
per_unit_cap: None published; sized within the annual NOFA.
affordability_requirement: Priority for multifamily rental housing affordable to households at or below 60% AMI (predevelopment, development, acquisition, rehabilitation and preservation); PLHA statute allows up to 120% AMI for some activities. Preference for the most units at the deepest affordability.
next_deadline: PLHA dollars are released through the Housing Authority's annual NOFA (next expected May 2027). HCD standard agreement for the 2024 and 2025 allocations was pending after the October 13, 2026 Council action; later years require annual HCD applications.
layering_notes: Santa Rosa is a direct PLHA entitlement recipient, so its allocation is separate from the County PLHA record (which covers the unincorporated area and non-entitlement cities such as Sonoma and Rohnert Park). Petaluma also receives its own PLHA (see Petaluma record). Because PLHA, CDBG, PIP, HOME and local Housing Trust money all flow through the same NOFA, one application reaches all City sources. Read from the Council staff report and Exhibit A PLHA Plan on the City's Legistar agenda host (matter 26-0770).

program_name: Santa Rosa tax-exempt multifamily housing revenue bonds (City Council conduit issuance under the City Bond Policy and Term Sheet)
administering_agency: City of Santa Rosa Housing and Community Services Department (Housing Authority) and City Council as issuer
typical_award_size: Conduit tax-exempt multifamily housing revenue bonds issued by the City Council on request for housing, mobilehome park purchases and similar public-purpose projects; amounts set per project within CDLAC allocation. Issuer fees and policy terms are in the City's Bond Policy and Bond Policy Term Sheet (DocumentCenter 21065 and 21066), which could not be opened this pass because srcity.org returns 403 to scripts.
affordability_requirement: Governed by CDLAC and Section 142(d) requirements (20% at 50% AMI or 40% at 60% AMI minimum) plus any City policy overlays in the term sheet (not confirmed).
next_deadline: Request to Council timed to CDLAC application rounds; confirm issuer fee schedule and TEFRA hearing lead time with Housing and Community Services, (707) 543-3300.
layering_notes: Alternative to CSCDA, CMFA or CalHFA conduit issuance for 4% LIHTC deals in Santa Rosa; using the City as issuer can simplify coordination with Housing Authority loans and regulatory agreements. The Developer Information page (opened on the City's civicplus mirror) confirms the program exists and lists local funds (real property transfer tax and housing impact fees), CDBG, HOME and HCD funds used by the Housing Authority. Confirm current issuer fees and whether the City still issues or defers to JPAs.

program_name: Petaluma Inclusionary Housing Program (Implementing Zoning Ordinance Section 3.040, Ordinance 2663 N.C.S.) and Housing In-Lieu Fee (Resolution 2018-142 N.C.S.)
administering_agency: City of Petaluma Community Development Department, Housing Division
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Residential projects of five or more units, including residential components of mixed-use projects, must provide 15% of units on site as affordable (rental and ownership alike). Alternatives require City Council approval as alternative compliance: land donation, an in-lieu payment to the City Housing Fund equal to a 20% inclusionary requirement, or other methods. In-lieu fee for fractional units under 0.5 or approved alternative compliance: $10.12 per square foot (2024 Development Impact and Capacity Fees booklet, effective July 1, 2024), collected at close of escrow for for-sale homes and at final inspection or certificate of occupancy for multifamily. Projects deemed complete before January 1, 2019 use the prior rules.
affordability_requirement: Affordability restrictions of at least 45 years for ownership units and 55 years for rental units; the 2023-2031 Housing Element targets 1,000 inclusionary units (400 very low, 400 low, 200 moderate) over eight years.
next_deadline: Applies at entitlement. Housing Element Program 11 called for a 2024 review of thresholds, in-lieu options and fee structure and a fee recalculation at least every four years; no 2025 or 2026 ordinance or resolution amending the program was found (cityofpetaluma.org blocks scripts, so recent council actions could not be checked). Fee schedule for FY 2025-26 and FY 2026-27 could not be opened.
layering_notes: Because the 2018 ordinance removed the by-right in-lieu option, most market-rate projects now build units on site and in-lieu revenue to the Housing Fund has slowed; the Housing Element reports the In-Lieu Fund at $3,323,128 on July 1, 2022 (see Petaluma Housing Fund record). Petaluma's 15% rental requirement is higher than Santa Rosa's 8% low income rule and lower than the City of Sonoma's 25%. The County's Affordable Housing Program fee (county record) applies only in unincorporated areas. Fee data read from the City's 2024 fee booklet and schedule hosted on the City's ProudCity storage; ordinance text itself was not opened because petaluma.municipal.codes and cityofpetaluma.org return 403.

program_name: Petaluma Commercial Development Housing Linkage Fee (Ordinance 2171 N.C.S. of 2004, as amended 2011)
administering_agency: City of Petaluma Community Development Department, Housing Division; collected by Building at permit
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Fee on new or expanded nonresidential square footage, effective July 1, 2024: commercial $3.47, retail $6.00 and industrial $3.57 per square foot of building space (July 2022 rates were $3.36, $5.81 and $3.46), due before building permit issuance, escalated annually by the ENR Construction Cost Index 20-city average. Exempt: public facilities, public and private schools, churches. Fund balance $2,158,717 as of July 1, 2022 (Housing Element).
affordability_requirement: Proceeds fund housing affordable to households between 80% and 100% AMI under the 2004 ordinance; Housing Element Program 12 directs the City to consider widening the target to extremely low, very low and low income households and to add an automatic CPI adjustment.
eligible_project_types: funds workforce rental and ownership housing
next_deadline: Fee rate in effect at building permit; FY 2025-26 and FY 2026-27 schedules could not be opened. Program 12 set 2024 for a nexus study review and end of 2024 to consider revising the AMI target; outcome not confirmed.
layering_notes: The linkage fund is one of three revenue sources for Petaluma's Local Housing Trust Fund (see Housing Fund record) and is the only local source aimed at 80-100% AMI workforce units, which makes it a possible match for moderate-income or mixed-income deals that cannot use LIHTC. Petaluma's rates are far higher than Rohnert Park's 2008 linkage fee ($0.69 to $1.19 per square foot) and the County's Workforce Housing fee applies only in unincorporated areas. Read from the City's 2024 Development Impact Fee Schedule on City ProudCity storage.

program_name: Petaluma Housing Fund and Local Housing Trust Fund (Inclusionary In-Lieu Fund, Commercial Linkage Fund, PLHA formula allocation and HCD Local Housing Trust Fund match)
administering_agency: City of Petaluma Community Development Department, Housing Division
typical_award_size: No fixed award size and no NOFA; the City negotiates gap loans and grants project by project. Balances reported in the certified 2023-2031 Housing Element: In-Lieu Fund $3,323,128 and Commercial Linkage Fee fund $2,158,717 as of July 1, 2022; PLHA about $250,000 per year with a $470,905 balance from 2019-2020 program years; HOME program income of $900,000 and $1.1 million of in-lieu funds went to MidPen's 43-unit project at 414 Petaluma Blvd North; the City also received a $1,100,000 HCD Local Housing Trust Fund award in 2022 (HCD award list, not a City page). CDBG entitlement about $330,000 per year (FY 2022-23), mostly for public services and rehab, not new construction.
affordability_requirement: In-lieu and PLHA funds target lower income households (PLHA priority at or below 60% AMI); linkage funds target 80-100% AMI under current ordinance. Terms set in each loan agreement; expect 55-year regulatory agreements consistent with inclusionary rental rules.
next_deadline: No NOFA cycle; approach the Housing Division before a TCAC or CDLAC round. Housing Element Program 13 committed the City to explore new revenue (TOT, short-term rental fees, vacant home tax, employer fee) and to pursue options by 2025, and to consider joining the Renewal Enterprise District JPA; status not confirmed. PLHA allocations require HCD applications each cycle.
layering_notes: Petaluma is a CDBG entitlement city and its own PLHA recipient, so it is outside the County's Urban County CDBG and County PLHA records; it is not a HOME participating jurisdiction (uses state HOME and program income). Local funds are small relative to Santa Rosa, so the usual stack is City gap loan plus County CFH plus RED Housing Fund (county records; Petaluma was exploring RED membership) plus LIHTC. Housing Element Program 14 lists expedited review, a dedicated project manager, trust fund participation, density bonus beyond state law and waived, reduced or deferred impact fees as incentives (see density bonus record). Current fund balances were not available because cityofpetaluma.org and its housing reports page return 403 to scripts; the certified Housing Element was read from the City's planpetaluma.squarespace.com site.

program_name: Petaluma density bonus and affordable housing incentive package (Housing Element 2023-2031 Programs 14 and 15; Implementing Zoning Ordinance density bonus chapter)
administering_agency: City of Petaluma Community Development Department, Planning and Housing Divisions
typical_award_size: Regulatory. The City applies state density bonus law (Government Code 65915) through its Implementing Zoning Ordinance, which the Housing Element says must be updated for AB 1763 and later changes. Program 14 committed the City to adopt by December 2023 an incentive package for affordable projects: expedited review, a dedicated project manager, financial participation from the Local Housing Trust Fund, density bonus beyond state law, waived, reduced or deferred impact fees for affordable units (scaled by affordability), and streamlined review for 100% affordable projects. Whether the package and any local bonus or fee waiver were adopted could not be confirmed.
affordability_requirement: State density bonus thresholds (5% very low, 10% low, 10% moderate for-sale, 100% affordable for the 80% bonus); local enhancements, if adopted, would set their own thresholds.
next_deadline: Unknown, verify with agency. Confirm with Petaluma Planning whether the December 2023 incentive package, a local density bonus and affordable housing fee waivers were adopted, and the status of the Workforce/Missing Middle program (Program 15).
layering_notes: Only the certified Housing Element could be opened; the Implementing Zoning Ordinance (gocodebook and petaluma.municipal.codes return 403) and cityofpetaluma.org housing pages were blocked. Petaluma has been Prohousing designated, which the Housing Element notes was based in part on fee reductions and the trust fund. If fee waivers exist they would stack with the Housing Fund and state density bonus; the County fee waiver and deferral programs (county records) do not apply inside Petaluma.

program_name: Rohnert Park Inclusionary Housing Ordinance, Municipal Code Section 17.08.010 (re-adopted by Ordinance 991, January 27, 2026): for-sale inclusionary units, Housing In-Lieu Fee and Rental Affordable Housing Fee
administering_agency: City of Rohnert Park Development Services Department (Planning and Building)
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. For-sale projects over 50 units: 15% of units affordable, half low income (80% AMI) and half moderate income (120% AMI), with 99-year resale restrictions; for-sale projects of 50 units or fewer may instead pay the Affordable Housing In-Lieu Fee of $15,891.95 per unit (Development Impact Fees handout revised July 16, 2026). All new rental projects pay the Rental Affordable Housing Fee of $4.11 per square foot at building permit (first adopted at $3.23 per square foot; adjusted each July 1 by the ENR-CCI San Francisco index); market-rate rental projects have no on-site unit requirement since the 2019 amendment. Fee revenue goes to a segregated affordable housing account used for acquisition, construction and rehabilitation of affordable housing, subsidies, and assistance to other entities, with an annual public report. Developers providing all required units at median, low or very low income get an extra 5% density bonus; alternatives (land donation, transferable inclusionary credits, off-site units, second units for up to half the requirement) need Council approval.
affordability_requirement: For-sale inclusionary units: 99-year minimum agreements; rental projects pay the fee instead. Exemptions include projects with vested rights, fire or disaster rebuilds of the same size, and projects whose development agreement sets alternative affordable housing terms.
next_deadline: Fees adjust every July 1 (ENR-CCI); planning and building application fees are being restudied for a July 1, 2027 update. Ordinance 991 (comprehensive Title 17 update) was adopted January 27, 2026. Large specific plan areas (University District, Southeast Specific Plan, SOMO Village, Downtown) are governed by development agreements that set their own affordable housing terms (University District and SESP at 15%; downtown CenterCal project exempted from the rental fee in exchange for pursuing 15 affordable units).
layering_notes: The Rental Affordable Housing Fee is Rohnert Park's main local housing revenue source since the 2011 loss of redevelopment; proceeds (budget Fund 4220) plus in-lieu fees fund gap assistance negotiated case by case (see Rohnert Park affordable housing funds record). A 100% affordable rental project would owe the $4.11 per square foot fee unless waived through a development agreement or the Section 17.08.010(I) adjustment process, so request a waiver early. Rohnert Park's for-sale requirement is lower than City of Sonoma's 25% and Petaluma's 15% (which also covers rentals). Ordinance text read from the zoneomics mirror of Title 17; fee amounts from the City's Development Impact Fees handout on rpcity.ca.gov (the former rpcity.org pages redirect and return 404).

program_name: Rohnert Park Affordable Housing Linkage Fee (Municipal Code Chapter 3.36)
administering_agency: City of Rohnert Park Development Services Department
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Nonresidential projects (new buildings, added square footage, remodels or changes of use that increase employment density) pay a linkage fee based on classification: commercial $0.69, retail $1.19 and industrial $0.71 per square foot, rates effective July 1, 2008 and apparently never updated (Development Impact Fees handout revised July 16, 2026). Fund 4225 (Affordable Linkage Fee) held $13,430 at June 30, 2023 after $285,000 of expenditures.
affordability_requirement: Proceeds support affordable housing for very low, low and moderate income households under the inclusionary ordinance's use-of-fees rules.
next_deadline: Fee in effect at building permit; no scheduled update found. A 2024 Generation Housing action plan recommended impact fee reform in Rohnert Park; no council action confirmed.
layering_notes: Revenue is minor compared with the Rental Affordable Housing Fee and in-lieu fee, so it adds little gap capacity; it is listed for completeness. Petaluma and Santa Rosa linkage fees are several times higher. Read from the City's Development Impact Fees handout (rpcity.ca.gov DocumentCenter); the Chapter 3.36 code text was not opened (municipal code hosts block scripts).

program_name: Rohnert Park Density Bonus (Municipal Code Section 17.08.020) and affordable housing concessions under Section 17.08.010(E)
administering_agency: City of Rohnert Park Development Services Department, Planning Division
typical_award_size: Regulatory. Section 17.08.020 adopts state density bonus law (Government Code 65915 et seq.) by reference with no local increase beyond the state schedule; it sets application contents (project summary table, base and bonus unit counts, replacement housing compliance, parking) and ministerial processing without separate Planning Commission action. Section 17.08.010(E) lets the City Council grant for-sale projects exceeding the inclusionary requirement, and rental projects that include affordable units, additional concessions: an extra density bonus or incentives of equal financial value, waiver of City standards, direct financial assistance (loan or grant) from trust funds, and deferral of all City fees on market-rate units until certificate of occupancy. Projects making all inclusionary units affordable at median, low or very low income get an additional 5% density bonus.
affordability_requirement: State thresholds (5% very low, 10% low, 10% moderate for-sale, 100% affordable) for the state bonus; Council discretion for the local concessions, tied to on-site affordable units.
next_deadline: Submitted with the entitlement application; Council concessions requested through the project approval or a development agreement. Housing Element Program HO-3.B (City Density Bonus Program) and HO-2.E (Workforce Housing Overlay, to be presented by January 2026 and adopted by December 2026 if directed) may add local bonuses; status not confirmed.
layering_notes: Rohnert Park relies on development agreements and specific plans rather than a formal local bonus, so negotiate fee deferral, rental fee relief and gap funding together. The Workforce Housing Overlay would be the first local density tool beyond state law; check Planning for its status. The County's density bonus chapter applies only in unincorporated areas. Read from the zoneomics mirror of Title 17 (Ordinance 991, January 27, 2026 version).

program_name: Rohnert Park affordable housing funds (Rental Affordable Housing Fee and Housing In-Lieu Fee account, Housing Fund) and Essential Housing Bond Financing Program (Housing Element Programs HO-3.F and bond program)
administering_agency: City of Rohnert Park Development Services Department and City Manager's office; City Council approves assistance
typical_award_size: No NOFA; the City provides gap loans or grants and land through development agreements and Council action, drawing on the segregated affordable housing fee account (budget Funds 4220 Affordable Housing Rental Fee and 4225 Affordable Linkage Fee) and the Housing Fund named in the 2023-2031 Housing Element as a funding source for Programs HO-1.B and HO-3.F (affordable housing on underutilized City sites, including extremely low income units). The Housing Element's Essential Housing Bond Financing Program commits the City to authorize CSCDA or another JPA to issue an estimated $191.3 million in governmental-purpose bonds for acquisition-conversion of market-rate apartments and new deed-restricted housing, forgoing about $337,346 in property tax and targeting at least 222 units (99 very low, 57 low, 66 moderate). Current fund balances and any adopted lending guidelines were not found; the City's budget and Housing Successor (LMIHAF) reports could not be located online.
affordability_requirement: Fee revenue must serve very low, low and moderate income households (Section 17.08.010(J)); bond program units for very low to moderate income; City-site projects target extremely low income units.
next_deadline: Unknown, verify with agency. Contact Development Services (707-588-2231, Planning@rpcity.org). The Housing Element set July 2023 for joining a JPA for the bond program and January 2026 for the Workforce Housing Overlay; a Council and Planning Commission joint meeting on housing was held February 5, 2026.
layering_notes: Rohnert Park was Prohousing designated August 4, 2023 (42 points), which gives projects in the city AHSC and IIG scoring preferences. Local money is thin, so the practical stack is County CFH, County PLHA (Rohnert Park is a non-entitlement city within the County PLHA), RED Housing Fund and County PBVs (county records) plus LIHTC, with the City contributing fee deferrals, land (Program HO-3.F) or a modest gap loan. Rohnert Park's former Community Development Commission was a redevelopment agency, so a Housing Successor LMIHAF may exist; no annual report was found (flag for follow-up). The CivicPlus agenda search on rpcity.ca.gov returned no results for affordable housing and the old rpcity.org pages 404, so recent council actions could not be verified. Source is the adopted 2023-2031 Housing Element on the City's DocumentCenter.

program_name: City of Sonoma Inclusionary Housing requirement and in-lieu fee, Development Code Chapter 19.44 (Sections 19.44.020 and 19.44.030, Ordinance 06-2021)
administering_agency: City of Sonoma Planning Department
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Projects of five or more parcels or units must make at least 25% of units affordable: rental projects 5% extremely low, 10% very low and 10% low income (sequenced ELI, VLI, LI, then middle income); ownership projects 5% low, 10% moderate and 10% middle income. Projects of four or fewer units pay an in-lieu fee per Section 19.44.030; fractions below 0.5 may be paid as a fee. In-lieu fees are paid before building permit into the City's housing trust fund. Fee amount is set by Council resolution (amount not opened); Housing Element Program 1 called for a nexus-supported in-lieu fee by December 2023 and a July 2024 amendment requiring perpetual affordability. Units of 850 square feet or less, ADUs and additions under 850 square feet are exempt. Affordability is in perpetuity under Section 19.44.060.
affordability_requirement: Rental: 25% of units split 5% ELI, 10% VLI, 10% LI; ownership: 25% split 5% LI, 10% moderate, 10% middle income; restricted in perpetuity by recorded affordability agreement; affordable units must average at least 75% of market-rate unit floor area with the same bedroom count.
next_deadline: Applies at entitlement. Housing Element Program 1 schedules a review of the inclusionary provisions and Development Code amendments by 2026; Program 15 Development Code amendments were noticed under CEQA in January 2026. Check with Planning (707) 938-3681 for the current in-lieu fee resolution.
layering_notes: At 25% with deep targeting, this is the strictest inclusionary rule among the Sonoma County priority cities, and the City says it has produced about 293 inclusionary and density bonus rental units inside 40 market-rate projects (about six units a year). Because the required ELI and VLI units can also qualify a project for a state density bonus (Chapter 19.44 counts inclusionary units when calculating the bonus), most market-rate rental projects in Sonoma pair the two. In-lieu revenue feeds the Affordable Housing Trust Fund (separate record). Growth management (Chapter 19.94 Housing Allocation Process) exempts affordable and density bonus units from the annual allocation. Code read from the zoneomics mirror (codepublishing.com returns 403); the City's Housing Policies page confirms the 25% rule.

program_name: City of Sonoma Affordable Housing Trust Fund (established May 2019, funded by 1% of Transient Occupancy Tax and inclusionary in-lieu fees)
administering_agency: City of Sonoma City Manager's office and Planning Department; grants approved by City Council
typical_award_size: Small, case-by-case grants and loans approved by Council. Most recent award: $250,000 grant approved June 18, 2025 (agreement authorized July 16, 2025) to Burbank Housing toward acquisition and 55-year preservation of 18 units at Setzer Senior Apartments (8 units, 673 First St West) and Maysonnave Apartments (10 units, 270 First St East), leveraged with a $4.5 million BAHFA Housing Preservation Loan Pilot loan and San Francisco Housing Accelerator Fund financing; closed fall 2025. Revenue: Council approved on June 10, 2019 the final 1% of the Measure S TOT increase (TOT now 13%) effective September 1, 2019 to address affordable housing, estimated at the time at about $350,000 to $400,000 per year, plus in-lieu fees under Section 19.44.030. Press accounts put the balance at roughly $1.4 million to $1.9 million in 2025-2026; no City balance figure was opened.
affordability_requirement: Grant terms set per project; the 2025 preservation deal requires affordability for at least 55 years with rents averaging 30% of 80% AMI and tenants protected on modest income increases. The fund is earmarked for very low, low and moderate income housing (Section 19.44.030).
next_deadline: No NOFA. Requests go to City Council; the Council's 2026 priorities include creating a funding plan and policy for use of the Housing Trust Fund, so an allocation policy may be adopted in 2026-2027 (verify with the City Manager's office, (707) 938-3681).
layering_notes: Sonoma is a non-entitlement city inside the County's Urban County and County PLHA area, so projects in the city should combine this fund with County CFH, County HOME and CDBG, County PLHA, RED Housing Fund and County PBVs (county records); the 2025 Burbank deal shows the pattern with BAHFA regional preservation money. Housing Element Program 7 commits the City to pursue a Prohousing Designation and to request RED JPA membership in 2024 (status not confirmed). The City also runs an ADU fee waiver program (housing strategies page) and lists Policy H-4.6 fee waivers for affordable housing, but no multifamily fee waiver ordinance was found. Council staff reports on the civicweb portal could not be reached by meeting date; the City's press release and TOT page were used as sources.

program_name: City of Sonoma Density Bonus and incentives, Development Code Sections 19.44.040 through 19.44.080 (Housing Element Program 19)
administering_agency: City of Sonoma Planning Department and Planning Commission (reductions in standards); City Council for other incentives
typical_award_size: Regulatory. Adopts state density bonus law (Government Code 65915 through 65918) by reference; bonus percentage calculated under 65915(f), inclusionary units count toward the bonus, one bonus per project, Planning Commission may waive or modify standards to fit bonus units, incentives include reduced standards, mixed-use zoning, other cost-reducing incentives and state parking ratios. No local bonus beyond state law, though Housing Element Program 19 contemplates streamlined processing and a density bonus or incentives for projects not otherwise eligible under state law, and reduced parking for affordable and special needs housing (Program 18). Density bonus and inclusionary units are exempt from the Chapter 19.94 growth management allocation.
affordability_requirement: State thresholds; affordable units restricted in perpetuity under Section 19.44.060 (2016 amendments raised the term from 30 to 55 years and 2021-2023 amendments made it perpetual).
next_deadline: Density bonus request filed with the first entitlement application; Housing Element Program 19 schedules an update of Chapter 19.44 to current state law (Program 15 code amendments noticed January 2026).
layering_notes: Past projects using the bonus include Firehouse Village and Maysonnave Apartments. In a city with low base densities and an urban growth boundary, the state bonus plus the 25% inclusionary rule is the main production tool; pair with the Affordable Housing Trust Fund and County sources. Read from the zoneomics mirror of the Sonoma Development Code (codepublishing.com and sonoma.municipal.codes return 403).

program_name: City of Sonoma Affordable Housing Fees for Nonresidential Development (Resolution 12-2020) and planned residential affordable housing impact fee (Housing Element 2023-2031 Program 8)
administering_agency: City of Sonoma Planning Department
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Resolution 12-2020 established Affordable Housing Fees for Nonresidential Development (commercial linkage); the rate schedule was not opened. Housing Element Program 8 directs the City to adopt by December 2023 a per-square-foot impact fee on single-family homes and 2 to 4 unit projects (now below the five-unit inclusionary threshold) and by December 2025 to expand the commercial linkage fee after nexus studies so it covers extremely low, very low, low and moderate income workforce housing. The City's housing strategies page still states the City does not require housing impact fees for projects below five units or for commercial projects without housing, so adoption of the residential fee is unconfirmed.
affordability_requirement: Fee proceeds to the housing trust fund for very low, low and moderate income housing.
next_deadline: Unknown, verify with agency. Confirm whether the residential impact fee (due December 2023) and the expanded nonresidential fee (due December 2025) were adopted and at what rates; the City's 2026 Fee Study and Master Fee Schedule Update is underway and may carry them.
layering_notes: Any new fee revenue would flow to the Affordable Housing Trust Fund (separate record) and expand the City's gap capacity, which is now mostly TOT-based. The County's Affordable Housing Program fees (county record) do not apply inside the city. Source is the adopted Housing Element on the City's ProudCity storage; Resolution 12-2020 and council fee resolutions could not be opened on the civicweb portal.

program_name: Fairfield Housing Trust Fund and Low/Moderate Income Housing (Housing Successor) funds, developer NOFA (August 2024 round)
administering_agency: City of Fairfield Housing Services Department (Fairfield Housing Authority as Housing Successor), 1000 Webster Street, Fairfield, 707-428-7392
typical_award_size: Gap loans from the City's Housing Trust Fund and former redevelopment Low/Mod funds. The August 2024 NOFA (Council goal HS 3.1, estimated $2,100,000) drew four proposals; Council approved financing for two. The March 2026 Council Goals report shows Danco approved for $1,500,000 with a Homekey+ application for a combined $23,500,000. A 2024 City press release (not opened, fairfield.ca.gov returns 403) described the round as about $1,000,000 of Local Housing Trust Fund money plus CDBG, applications due September 24, 2024. Closing of the 1600 Woolner site generated $1,121,000 in Low/Mod funds; the City also obtained a $700,000 state HOME grant and applied for an $800,000 MORE grant. Disposition of Successor Agency properties (Sem Yeto school site, Highway 12 parcel) is meant to replenish Low/Mod funds; an LOI for Sem Yeto was under review in December 2025. Council has also approved project-based voucher and housing trust fund financing for a multifamily preservation deal (Dec 2025 report).
per_unit_cap: None published. Danco approval equals $1,500,000 for one project.
affordability_requirement: Extremely low to moderate income households; Housing Element Action 3.1 requires long-term covenants (45 to 55 years) on City-assisted units.
next_deadline: No NOFA open as of November 2026. The City issues NOFAs when funds accumulate (last August 2024). Housing Element Action 3.2 commits to a NOFA a year before any tax credit compliance period ends for at-risk projects. Contact Housing Services before the next TCAC round.
layering_notes: Fairfield is the only Solano city with a working local trust fund plus Low/Mod successor money, so it is the first local gap source after the Solano County Housing Trust Fund (county record; the County put $4,500,000 ARPA through Fairfield for an EAH project in 2022 and proposed $400,000 for EAH's Tabor Commons in Aug 2026). Stack order for a Fairfield 9% deal: TCAC credits, City trust fund or Low/Mod loan, County SCHTF, Fairfield Housing Authority PBVs, fee deferral (separate record). Housing Element Action 1.1 says the Trust Fund is fed by a Housing Trust Fund fee and the City will study increasing it, dedicating excess property transfer tax, and a housing bond. Low/Mod funds carry Health and Safety Code 34176.1 spending rules (80% to 30% AMI and below once excess surplus triggers). Fairfield submitted a Prohousing Designation application in 2024 and was resubmitting for more points in 2025 (designation not confirmed), which would add scoring preference in state programs. Public funds trigger prevailing wage. fairfield.ca.gov and its showpublisheddocument PDFs return 403 to scripts and WebFetch; the City's ClearPoint Council Goals reports on transparency.fairfield.ca.gov were the opened record.

program_name: Fairfield Inclusionary Housing Policy and in-lieu fee (nexus study complete, ordinance in revision; Housing Element Action 1.2; Council goal HS 1.1)
administering_agency: City of Fairfield Housing Services Department and Community Development Department
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Not yet adopted. Council budgeted $120,000 for the nexus study (vendor under contract FY23-24) and $100,000 for policy development (FY24-FY27). Progress: Council study session October 2024, developer meeting January 2025, draft market and feasibility studies and draft ordinance completed early 2025, draft ordinance study session planned May 13, 2025. March 2026 status: study completed, revisions underway based on developer feedback. Fee levels and set-aside percentages are not public.
affordability_requirement: Not set. Housing Element objective is an inclusionary program with an in-lieu fee option whose revenue flows to the Housing Trust Fund.
next_deadline: Unknown. Watch Fairfield City Council agendas for the revised draft ordinance in 2026-2027; Housing Element timeframe was adoption by end of 2025.
layering_notes: Currently Fairfield's only existing production requirement is the Below Market Rate Program in the Housing Element resource list: 10% of detached homes in Residential Medium zones sold to moderate-income buyers with 45-year resale controls. An adopted inclusionary fee would capitalize the Housing Trust Fund (record above) and change underwriting for mixed-income rentals. Vallejo is adopting its ordinance (Chapter 16.216) in November 2026; Vacaville and Suisun City have only study programs. City pages 403; status read from the City's Council Goals performance reports.

program_name: Fairfield affordable housing Fee Deferral Program (Municipal Code Chapter 5, Article I), Fee Credit Bank and Train Station Specific Plan fee reduction
administering_agency: City of Fairfield Community Development Department (Director approves deferrals and fee credits)
typical_award_size: Deferral, not waiver: affordable projects defer certain building and development fees to certificate of occupancy or permanent financing. Fee Credit Bank: credits from demolished buildings (water and sewer connection fees, not school or Solano County public facilities fees) can be applied to affordable projects. Train Station Specific Plan area: 25% reduction in development fees for multifamily units above 24 units per acre. ADUs under 750 square feet exempt from park, Cordelia open space, sewer connection and County public facilities fees; all ADUs exempt from a long list of City fees. No published dollar value of deferrals.
affordability_requirement: Deferral: multifamily must be at least 50% moderate-income and 25% low-income units, 55-year rental covenant (45 years ownership). Fee credits: low- and moderate-income units with a covenant of up to 55 years.
