next_deadline: Apply to the Community Development Department with the building permit; no cycle. The City was updating its AB 1600 traffic and Northeast (TSSP) fees in 2022-2023; confirm current fee schedule.
layering_notes: Deferral improves construction-period cash flow but fees are still paid, so budget them. Fee credits are a real reduction when a demolition site has banked credits; ask the Director for the current bank balance. Solano County public facilities fees cannot be deferred or credited by the City (County record: no County waiver program). A fee credit or reduction is public funds under Labor Code 1720(c) if above de minimis, hence unclear. Source is the HCD-posted October 2022 review draft of the 2023-2031 Housing Element (adopted February 7, 2023, certified April 10, 2023 per the City's housing element site, not opened); Chapter 5 of the Municipal Code itself is on a blocked code host.

program_name: Fairfield Density Bonus (Zoning Code Section 25.38, Ordinance 2021-02)
administering_agency: City of Fairfield Community Development Department, Planning Division
typical_award_size: State Density Bonus Law as implemented locally: 5+ unit projects with 5% very low, 10% lower, 10% moderate (for-sale), senior or other qualifying categories get bonus units, incentives and concessions, waivers and parking ratios per Government Code 65915; childcare facility adds bonus or concession. Density bonus application fee set by Council resolution. Applications processed concurrently with the project entitlement and decided by the same review authority (Section 25.41).
affordability_requirement: Government Code 65915 set-asides; 55-year rental covenants.
next_deadline: Not applicable; file with the planning entitlement.
layering_notes: No local enhancement beyond state law; the ordinance states Section 65915 supersedes any conflicting local text. Fairfield also offers priority processing for affordable projects (Housing Element Action 2.4) and lot consolidation incentives in the Heart of Fairfield and Train Station plan areas. Read on the zoneomics code mirror because the City's code host returns 403. Pair with the Fee Deferral Program and Trust Fund records.

program_name: Fairfield CDBG and HOME, multifamily rehabilitation NOFAs and PLHA formula allocation
administering_agency: City of Fairfield Housing Services Department (HUD CDBG entitlement; state HOME and CalHome grantee; HCD PLHA formula recipient)
typical_award_size: CDBG multifamily rehabilitation NOFAs: about $475,000 CDBG offered in 2024 (due September 24, 2024) and about $400,000 offered July 22, 2026 (due September 4, 2026, rehab complete by June 30, 2027, minimum score 75) per City news releases found in search but not opened. FY 2026-27 Annual Action Plan reportedly budgets $115,120 for multifamily rehabilitation. State HOME grant of $700,000 obtained (2024-2025) and $800,000 MORE grant applied for. PLHA formula: Fairfield CY 2024 $274,392, CY 2025 $293,914, five-year 2024-2028 estimate $1,714,950 (HCD NOFA); Housing Element dedicates 20% of PLHA to homeownership, and three PLHA down payment loans closed in FY 2025-26.
per_unit_cap: HOME per-unit subsidy limits (24 CFR 92.250) for HOME-funded units.
affordability_requirement: CDBG rehab: at least 51% of units at or below 80% AMI. HOME: 20% at 50% AMI, balance at 60% AMI, 55-year HCD covenant. PLHA: per the City's five-year plan (not opened).
next_deadline: CDBG rehab NOFA closed September 4, 2026; expect the next round summer 2027 with the FY 2027-28 Action Plan (public comment typically April to May). Contact Miesha Garnett, mgarnett@fairfield.ca.gov.
layering_notes: Small money. CDBG rounds are rehab-only (no new construction or acquisition) and sized at $400,000 to $475,000. Fairfield is not a HOME participating jurisdiction and competes for state HOME through HCD, so HOME for a Fairfield project needs the City as applicant. PLHA at about $280,000 a year is partly committed to down payment assistance. Davis-Bacon applies to CDBG rehab of 8+ units and HOME 12+ units. Items marked as reported came from fairfield.ca.gov search snippets; the site returns 403 to scripts and WebFetch, so dollar figures should be confirmed with Housing Services. The opened source is the City's March 2026 Council Goals report, which records the CDBG NOFA step, the HOME and MORE grants and the PLHA loans.

program_name: Fairfield Housing Authority Project-Based Vouchers
administering_agency: Fairfield Housing Authority (City of Fairfield Housing Services Department), 707-428-7392
typical_award_size: HCV-only agency (about 750 vouchers to issue per the March 2026 Council Goals report; 894 vouchers administered at the start of 2024 per the 2024 Administrative Plan found in search). The FY 2026-27 PHA Annual Plan approved by Council April 7, 2026 reportedly adds 50 project-based vouchers to a program with over $10,000,000 in annual HAP. Existing PBV sites include Laurel Gardens. Council approved PBV plus housing trust fund financing for a multifamily preservation project in late 2025.
per_unit_cap: HAP contract rent capped at the lower of reasonable rent or 110% of FMR; FY 2026 payment standard not increased.
affordability_requirement: Households at or below 50% AMI at admission (75% at 30% AMI); PBV units capped at 25% of a building unless serving elderly, disabled or supportive-services households.
next_deadline: No PBV RFP located. HUD's 2026 budget guidance asked PHAs to pause new PBV commitments, so confirm with the Housing Authority whether the 50 additional PBVs in the FY 2026-27 plan are being awarded. HCV waitlist opened March 4 to 6, 2026.
layering_notes: PBVs are the operating subsidy that makes 30% AMI units pencil in Fairfield deals (Fair Haven Commons, Parkside Flats, Tabor Commons). Fairfield's PHA covers only the city; Suisun City, Vacaville, Vallejo and Solano County each have their own (separate records). PBVs alone do not trigger state prevailing wage; Davis-Bacon applies to PBV new construction or rehab of 9+ contract units. The PHA plan and press items were not opened (fairfield.ca.gov 403; aggregator summaries only); the opened source is the City's Council Goals report, which gives the voucher count and the PBV financing approval.

program_name: Vacaville Affordable Housing, Density Bonuses and Incentives (Land Use and Development Code Chapter 14.09.210; Ordinance 1972 of February 22, 2022, amended by Ordinance 1996 of July 23, 2024)
administering_agency: City of Vacaville Community Development Department, Planning Division
typical_award_size: Mirrors Government Code 65915: 5+ unit projects with 5% very low, 10% low, 10% moderate (for-sale), senior, foster youth/veteran/homeless, student, or 100% affordable (80% bonus, no density cap within one half mile of a major transit stop or in a very low vehicle travel area) qualify; one to five incentives by tier; 100% affordable projects near transit get up to three extra stories or 33 feet; childcare facility bonus. Housing Element Program HE-1 says the City will grant bonuses above the state minimum for more affordable units, but the code text tracks state law.
affordability_requirement: Government Code 65915 set-asides; 55-year rental covenants.
next_deadline: Not applicable; file with the planning application.
layering_notes: No local enhancement found in the code text; the Housing Element quantified objective is 300 lower-income units through density bonus. Vacaville's Housing Element also raised the Residential High zone from 24 to 30 units per acre (Program HE-18) and allows reduced parking (HE-19). Vacaville has no housing trust fund, inclusionary ordinance or fee waiver (separate negative record), so the density bonus and PBVs are the main city tools. Read on the zoneomics code mirror; cityofvacaville.gov returns 403 to scripts and WebFetch.

program_name: Vacaville local affordable housing fund, inclusionary ordinance and fee waiver (none adopted; Housing Element Programs HE-5, HE-14 and HE-16 study items)
administering_agency: City of Vacaville Housing and Community Services Department, 40 Eldridge Avenue Suite 2, Vacaville, 707-449-5675
typical_award_size: Negative finding. Vacaville has no housing trust fund, inclusionary requirement, in-lieu fee or affordable housing fee waiver. The 2023-2031 Housing Element (adopted June 27, 2023; HCD found it in compliance) commits only to study them: Program HE-5(b) evaluates a housing trust fund, commercial linkage fee, sales or transient occupancy tax increase, or general obligation bond; HE-16 was to decide on an inclusionary ordinance by December 2023; HE-14 was to consider a lower impact fee structure or waivers for affordable and infill projects by December 2025 (impact fee nexus study adopted June 28, 2022). HE-5(e) says the City will pursue HOME entitlement status. The 2022 Housing Strategy is the policy basis.
affordability_requirement: Not applicable.
next_deadline: No program exists. Ask Housing and Community Services whether Council acted on HE-16 (inclusionary decision) or HE-14 (fee reductions) in 2024-2026; the City's pages that would show this returned 403.
layering_notes: Budget full City impact fees in Vacaville (a 2022 fee update differentiates single-family fees by size but has no affordable discount). Local gap money for a Vacaville deal is therefore the County SCHTF (county record: $200,000 proposed for Habitat's Harmony Village, Vacaville, Aug 2026), City PLHA and CDBG (separate record), and Vacaville Housing Authority PBVs (separate record). Pony Express Senior Apartments used CMFA bonds ($27,726,315). Source is the HCD-posted October 2022 review draft; the adopted June 2023 element and HCD letter are on cityofvacaville.gov (403).

program_name: Vacaville Housing Authority Project-Based Vouchers (Moving to Work agency)
administering_agency: Vacaville Housing Authority, City of Vacaville Housing and Community Services Department, 40 Eldridge Avenue Suite 2, 707-449-5675
typical_award_size: The Housing Element reports 1,365 Housing Choice Vouchers allocated to the Vacaville Housing Authority, including 50 Family Unification, 41 VASH, 101 Mainstream and 31 Emergency Housing Vouchers; the Authority is a Moving to Work agency and also administers the Solano County Housing Authority under contract. A December 2024 PBV RFP (results posted on the City's PBV page, not opened) awarded 85 PBVs to CSH Elan Apartments (California Supportive Housing); an earlier plan reported 48 PBVs awarded to two projects. PBV waitlists have opened for Orchard Maples, Hillside Senior, The Willows, Lincoln Corner and Pony Express Senior Apartments. The City's April 14, 2026 budget update reportedly shows the Vacaville Housing Authority at about $20,700,000 and the Solano County Housing Authority at $4,450,000.
per_unit_cap: HAP contract rent capped at the lower of reasonable rent or 110% of FMR; MTW agency may adopt alternative payment standards.
affordability_requirement: Households at or below 50% AMI at admission (75% at 30% AMI); PBV share limits per HUD rules with MTW flexibility.
next_deadline: No open RFP found as of November 2026; the last round was December 2024. Ask Housing and Community Services about the next PBV solicitation and whether HUD's 2026 pause on new PBV commitments applies.
layering_notes: The largest voucher pool in Solano County and the reason supportive housing deals (Elan, 85 PBVs) can carry 30% AMI rents in Vacaville. Stacks with TCAC, CMFA bonds, County SCHTF and City PLHA. PBVs alone do not trigger state prevailing wage; Davis-Bacon applies to PBV new construction or rehab of 9+ contract units. cityofvacaville.gov (housing pages, PBV results, PHA plans) returns 403 to scripts and WebFetch and the archive mirror rate-limited; voucher counts were read from the HCD-posted Housing Element and the Elan award from a search snippet of the City's PBV page.

program_name: Vacaville CDBG entitlement, Section 108 loan application and PLHA formula allocation
administering_agency: City of Vacaville Housing and Community Services Department (HUD CDBG entitlement; HCD PLHA formula recipient)
typical_award_size: CDBG entitlement of roughly $550,000 a year (April 2026 budget slide, not opened). On July 22, 2025 Council considered the 2025-2030 Consolidated Plan, the 2025-26 Annual Action Plan and a HUD Section 108 loan guarantee application (public notice found in search, not opened). Vacaville is not a HOME participating jurisdiction. PLHA formula (HCD 2024-2028 NOFA): CY 2024 $168,814, CY 2025 $180,825, five-year estimate $1,055,088; the City's five-year PLHA plan is posted on cityofvacaville.gov (not opened). The City's PLHA page says funds support developing and preserving rental housing, affordable homeownership, program administration and homelessness.
per_unit_cap: HOME limits do not apply; PLHA per the City plan.
affordability_requirement: CDBG: 51% of units at or below 80% AMI. PLHA: at or below 60% AMI for rental assistance unless the plan targets higher; 55-year covenant for rental development.
next_deadline: CDBG applications run with the Annual Action Plan each winter for a July 1 program year; PLHA allocations arrive annually from HCD. Confirm whether the Section 108 application was approved and what it funds.
layering_notes: A Section 108 guarantee, if approved, would be Vacaville's first sizable city-controlled capital source (up to five times the annual CDBG grant). Otherwise CDBG and PLHA together are under $750,000 a year. Vacaville's $250,000 federal community project grant (2024-2026) went to Habitat's Harmony Village. CDBG carries Davis-Bacon on 8+ units; PLHA is state money and triggers prevailing wage. The opened source is HCD's PLHA formula NOFA; all City pages returned 403.

program_name: Vallejo Inclusionary Housing Ordinance (Municipal Code Chapter 16.216, Affordable Housing Requirements; Housing Element Program B 2.1.1)
administering_agency: City of Vallejo Planning and Development Services Department, Long Range Planning (Hector Rojas, 707-553-7283)
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Introduced October 27, 2026; Council directed the Planning Commission version: applies to residential projects of 10 or more units; rental projects provide 4% affordable (2% very low, 2% low); ownership projects of 10 to 100 units 7% (4% low, 3% moderate), over 100 units 10% (6% low, 4% moderate). Staff had proposed a 20-unit threshold with 5% rental (1% VLI, 4% LI). In-lieu fee may be paid for some or all units, set by a later Council resolution and deposited in a separate City affordable housing fund; fractional units under 0.50 may be paid as fee. Alternatives: off-site units in the same census tract, rental units in ownership projects. EPS feasibility (March 13, 2026) found a subsidy gap of about $369,000 per very low-income apartment and $471,614 per low-income single-family unit, which are the equivalent in-lieu fee ceilings. Effective 90 days after final passage. Exemptions: disaster rebuilds, ADUs, residential care facilities, applications complete before the effective date.
affordability_requirement: Rental units at 30% of HCD income limits less utilities (2026 Solano three-person limits: VLI $61,850, LI $98,950, MOD $134,550); 55-year minimum covenants for rental and ownership units; Affordable Housing Plan and recorded Affordable Housing Agreement required; one-for-one replacement of demolished deed-restricted units.
next_deadline: Second reading and adoption scheduled November 10, 2026; in-lieu fee resolution to follow before the effective date (about February 2027). Planning Commission asked for annual reports and a new feasibility study about two years after enactment. A Commercial Linkage Fee ordinance is to be drafted after adoption.
layering_notes: Vallejo's RHNA is 2,900 units with 1,446 lower and moderate units still unmet after 2025. This is the first inclusionary ordinance in Solano County; its in-lieu fund will be a new, small local gap source alongside the Housing Successor LMIHAF (separate record). Developers of 10+ unit rentals should model 4% affordable units or the fee once set. Underwriting in Vallejo is weak (EPS found rental yields of 4.7% to 5.0% against a 5.5% threshold), so the fee is expected to be modest. Staff report and draft ordinance opened on the City's inclusionary project page.

program_name: Vallejo Housing Successor Low and Moderate Income Housing Asset Fund (LMIHAF), Housing Authority of the City of Vallejo
administering_agency: Housing Authority of the City of Vallejo acting as Housing Successor; City of Vallejo Housing and Community Development Department, 200 Georgia Street, 707-648-4507 (Alicia Jones, Housing Director)
typical_award_size: FY 2023-24 report (dated December 5, 2024): deposits $376,807, expenditures $2,404,145 (of which $2,403,420 for extremely low-income housing development), ending balance $605,550, LMIHAF loans and grants receivable $15,773,272, no real property held. FY 2022-23: deposits $1,747,828, no expenditures, ending balance $3,534,099, receivables $13,199,965. $182,210 of a 2015-16 $500,000 excess surplus transfer to HOME match remains encumbered. Four properties in the Long-Range Property Management Plan are used for affordable housing. FY 2024-25 report (due December 2025) not located.
affordability_requirement: Health and Safety Code 34176.1: at least 30% of expenditures for households at or below 30% AMI and no more than 20% for 60% to 80% AMI over each five-year period; 55-year rental covenants; excess surplus rules.
next_deadline: No NOFA; the Housing Authority board (City Council) commits funds project by project and reviews the annual report each December. Ask the HCD Department what the $2,400,000 FY 2023-24 commitment funded and what remains after the FY 2024-25 report.
layering_notes: After the FY 2023-24 spend-down the fund holds about $600,000 in cash and relies on loan repayments from a $15,800,000 portfolio of legacy redevelopment loans, so it is a small, lumpy source. Pair with Vallejo HOME and CDBG (separate record), Vallejo Housing Authority PBVs, CMFA bonds (county record: $75,750,000 Step Up Housing and $32,131,176 Sacramento Street Apartments issues) and TCAC. Former redevelopment funds are public funds and trigger prevailing wage. The Dissolution Law housing obligations (Buchongo settlement, 425 units) are fully met. Report opened from the Vallejo Housing Authority news page.

program_name: Vallejo CDBG and HOME entitlement funds (FY 2025-2030 Consolidated Plan, FY 2026-27 Annual Action Plan)
administering_agency: City of Vallejo Housing and Community Development Department (HUD CDBG entitlement and HOME participating jurisdiction), 200 Georgia Street, 707-553-7204 (Chari Francisco)
typical_award_size: FY 2026-27: CDBG allocation $1,049,400 plus $380,000 prior-year resources; HOME $420,114.54 (the draft plan's resource table also shows $1,554,400 CDBG and $1,049,400 HOME, an internal inconsistency). Activities: program administration, HOME TBRA, first-time homebuyer assistance, microenterprise, housing rehabilitation loans and grants, social services, permanent supportive housing (Broadway Village and Blue Oak Landing), Homeless Navigation Center, street and sidewalk repairs, housing counseling. CDBG program menu includes Affordable Rental Housing Development. HOME-ARP allocation $2,213,960 (2022). The Broadway Project, a 47-unit PSH conversion at 2441 Broadway, received a $12,000,000 Homekey grant, $3,500,000 Solano County ARPA and about $643,000 in City opioid settlement funds, and opened in late 2025.
affordability_requirement: CDBG: 51% of units at or below 80% AMI. HOME: 20% of HOME units at 50% AMI, balance at 60% AMI (rental), 55-year City covenant on larger awards.
next_deadline: Consolidated Plan adopted July 8, 2025 (FY 2025-26 through 2029-30). The FY 2026-27 plan had a needs hearing February 5, 2026 and public hearing April 23, 2026, with Council action June 23, 2026. Expect the FY 2027-28 application cycle to open in late 2026 through the HCD Commission; contact the department by January 2027.
layering_notes: Vallejo is the only HOME participating jurisdiction in Solano County, so it is the one city where HOME development loans are a city decision. Recent HOME money has gone to TBRA, homebuyer and rehab programs rather than multifamily; a developer must ask for a HOME or CDBG set-aside during the Action Plan process. Stack with the Housing Successor LMIHAF, Vallejo Housing Authority PBVs, CMFA bonds and TCAC. Davis-Bacon applies to CDBG 8+ units and HOME 12+ units; state prevailing wage applies to any City loan. Draft Action Plan opened from the City's Housing News page.

program_name: Vallejo Housing Authority Project-Based Vouchers (December 2024 RFP, up to 200 PBVs)
administering_agency: Housing Authority of the City of Vallejo (HACV), City of Vallejo Housing and Community Development Department, 200 Georgia Street, 707-648-4507; PBV contact Rosanna Roldan 707-648-4373
typical_award_size: RFP issued December 10, 2024 (proposals due January 2, 2025) for up to 200 project-based vouchers for existing, substantial rehabilitation and new construction units within the city, with awards to more than one respondent; a prior RFP closed July 8, 2024 and two RFPs ran in 2019. Existing PBV sites listed: Avian Glen Apartments (25 family units) and Blue Oak Landing (74 special needs units); October 2025 PBV interest lists opened for Sereno Village, Avian Glen and the Vallejo Housing Collaborative. Public comments on the 2024 Administrative Plan were heard December 10, 2024.
per_unit_cap: HAP contract rent capped at the lower of reasonable rent or 110% of FMR.
affordability_requirement: Households at or below 50% AMI at admission (75% at 30% AMI); PBV units capped at 25% of a building unless serving elderly, disabled or supportive-services households; project preferences for homeless referrals.
next_deadline: No RFP open as of November 2026; the Authority has run rounds roughly annually (2019, mid 2024, December 2024). Watch the HACV news page and PlanetBids portal 42510 for the next PBV RFP; HUD's 2026 guidance to pause new PBV commitments may delay it.
layering_notes: The 2024 round offered up to 200 PBVs, the largest project-basing opportunity in the county and the key operating subsidy for the Step Up Housing and Sacramento Street Apartments conversions financed with CMFA bonds (county record). The Authority was understaffed in 2024-2025, so allow time for HAP contract execution. PBVs alone do not trigger state prevailing wage; Davis-Bacon applies to PBV new construction or rehab of 9+ contract units. Opened the HACV Recent News page, which carries the RFP notices and PBV site list.

program_name: Vallejo Affordable Housing Incentives and density bonus (Municipal Code Chapter 16.214)
administering_agency: City of Vallejo Planning and Development Services Department, Planning Division
typical_award_size: State Density Bonus Law applied: 5+ unit projects providing 20% lower income or 10% very low income units (and other 65915 categories) receive a 5% to 35% bonus (more under current state law), concessions and incentives, land donation and childcare bonuses, and SB 35 streamlining procedures (16.214.14). Section 16.214.07 states the City is not required to provide financial incentives, land, fee waivers or dedication waivers but may at its discretion; 16.214.08 notes financial incentives may trigger prevailing wage. Recorded Affordable Housing Agreement required (16.214.09).
affordability_requirement: Government Code 65915 set-asides; recorded Affordable Housing Agreement with 55-year rental covenants.
next_deadline: Not applicable; file with the planning entitlement.
layering_notes: No local enhancement; the chapter text still cites the older 5% to 35% range, and the City defers to Government Code 65915 as amended. Once Chapter 16.216 (inclusionary) takes effect in 2027, inclusionary units can count toward density bonus set-asides per state law; confirm with Planning how the two chapters interact. Vallejo adopted its 2023-2031 Housing Element December 30, 2024 (certified the next day); no Prohousing Designation for Vallejo was found on HCD's lists. Read on the zoneomics code mirror.

program_name: Vallejo PLHA formula allocation and pending Commercial Linkage Fee
administering_agency: City of Vallejo Housing and Community Development Department (PLHA); Planning and Development Services (linkage fee)
typical_award_size: PLHA formula (HCD 2024-2028 NOFA): Vallejo CY 2024 $354,734, CY 2025 $379,973, five-year estimate $2,217,088; 2021 award was $505,369. How the City programs PLHA was not found on its pages. Commercial Linkage Fee: a draft ordinance is to be prepared after the inclusionary ordinance is adopted (late 2026 or 2027), based on the EPS work; no fee level yet.
affordability_requirement: PLHA: at or below 60% AMI for rental assistance unless the five-year plan targets higher; 55-year covenant for rental development. Linkage fee: not yet set.
next_deadline: PLHA allocations arrive annually from HCD; ask the HCD Department for the City's five-year PLHA plan and whether any share is reserved for multifamily gap loans. Linkage fee draft expected after November 10, 2026 adoption of Chapter 16.216.
layering_notes: About $360,000 to $380,000 a year, the largest city PLHA share in the county. Combined with the inclusionary in-lieu fund and LMIHAF it gives Vallejo three small local pots that could be pooled into a NOFA; none has been. State funds trigger prevailing wage. The opened source is HCD's PLHA formula NOFA; the City's PLHA plan was not located on cityofvallejo.net.

program_name: Suisun City Housing Authority Project-Based Vouchers (2023 RFP, up to 96 PBVs) and Almond Gardens Apartments
administering_agency: Suisun City Housing Authority (City Council plus two tenant commissioners), 701 Civic Center Boulevard; Jason Goltiao, Housing Program Manager, 707-421-7332, jgoltiao@suisun.com
typical_award_size: October 4, 2023 RFP (proposals due October 25, 2023) offered up to 64 project-based vouchers plus 32 for exception categories (seniors, persons with disabilities receiving services), 96 total; a project may receive the greater of 25 units or 25% of units (100% for exception projects); contract rents capped at 110% of FMR or an approved exception payment standard; 100-point scoring. The vouchers went to Almond Gardens Apartments (707-815 Almond Street, Harbor Park LLC): 97 new units (96 restricted at 30% to 50% AMI) replacing a condemned 51 to 52 unit complex, total cost about $66,126,000, estimated HUD PBV funding about $3,274,484 a year, CDLAC allocation of $30,276,660 in tax-exempt bonds through CMFA plus $2,917,820 annual federal and $5,994,579 state credits (December 11, 2024). NEPA FONSI June 26, 2025, release of funds about July 15, 2025; construction June 2025 to January 2027.
per_unit_cap: HAP contract rent capped at 110% of FMR or exception payment standard.
affordability_requirement: Households at or below 50% AMI at admission (75% at 30% AMI); Almond Gardens units at 30% and 50% AMI with 55-year regulatory agreement.
next_deadline: The 2023 PBV allocation is fully committed to Almond Gardens. A new 5-Year PHA Plan (July 1, 2025 to June 30, 2030) was heard March 18, 2025. Ask the Housing Program Manager whether any PBVs remain or a new RFP is planned; HCV waitlist is closed.
layering_notes: Suisun City's housing authority is small (HCV only) and its PBV capacity is tied up in one deal, so a second Suisun project would need Fairfield, Vacaville or Solano County Housing Authority vouchers (separate records), which do not cover Suisun City. Almond Gardens shows the Suisun stack: CMFA bonds, 4% and state credits, PBVs, City land and impact fee waiver (separate record). PBVs alone do not trigger state prevailing wage; Davis-Bacon applies to PBV new construction of 9+ contract units. suisun.com returns 403 to scripts; the Housing Authority page was opened with WebFetch and the CTCAC staff report (treasurer.ca.gov) supplied the financing figures.

program_name: Suisun City land contribution and impact fee waiver for affordable housing (Almond Gardens; Successor Agency and Housing Authority property)
administering_agency: City of Suisun City, Suisun City Housing Authority and Successor Agency to the Redevelopment Agency (Bret Prebula, City Manager and Executive Director, 707-421-7300)
typical_award_size: Case by case, no ordinance. The CTCAC staff report for Almond Gardens (CA-24-602) lists Suisun City land and an impact fee waiver among permanent sources alongside Citibank bonds, deferred developer fee and tax credit equity; the table shows amounts of $350,000 and about $1,557,898 next to those lines but the mapping could not be confirmed from the text extraction. The Housing Authority signed a disposition and development agreement with Harbor Park LLC in 2021 for the former Almond Gardens site. The Housing Authority also owns 707 Main Street and the Successor Agency owns 701, 711, 713 and 717 Main Street; on May 26, 2026 the Council, Successor Agency and Housing Authority considered purchase and sale agreements for these parcels (and two City parcels between Main and Kellogg Streets) to CF Suisun 1 LLC and CF Suisun 2 LLC.
affordability_requirement: Negotiated; Almond Gardens is 100% affordable at 30% to 50% AMI for 55 years.
next_deadline: No program or deadline. Any waiver or land write-down requires Council or Housing Authority action; Housing Element Program 1.B promises impact fee deferrals and density bonuses for mixed-use and residential projects in the Downtown Waterfront Specific Plan area.
layering_notes: Suisun City has no trust fund, inclusionary fee or LMIHAF report found online, so land and fee concessions are its only local contribution. The Main Street sales to California Forever entities (CF Suisun LLCs) may generate Successor Agency or Housing Authority proceeds; ask the City whether housing asset proceeds will be re-deployed. A fee waiver on a 97-unit project is public funds under Labor Code 1720(c), hence prevailing wage true (the project is also bond and credit financed). Source is the CTCAC report; the Housing Authority DDA and the May 26, 2026 staff reports were not opened (suisun.com 403; Granicus agenda PDF opened but attachments not).

program_name: Suisun City Residential Density Bonus and Density Incentives (Municipal Code Chapter 18.47, Ordinance 743 of March 21, 2017)
administering_agency: City of Suisun City Development Services Department, Planning Division, 707-421-7335
typical_award_size: Applies to multifamily, live-work and mixed-use projects of five or more units; implements Government Code 65915 to 65918 set-asides and bonuses; 15% to 35% additional bonus for land donation (18.47.065); childcare facility bonus or concession (18.47.070); parking ratios on request (18.47.080). Section 18.47.075 lets the Planning Commission or Council grant a bonus greater than the chapter requires for qualifying projects.
affordability_requirement: Government Code 65915 set-asides; 55-year rental covenants; density bonus agreement.
next_deadline: Not applicable; file with the planning application.
layering_notes: The 2017 chapter predates AB 1287 and other state changes; state law governs where the chapter is less generous, but 18.47.075 is a useful local hook for asking for more than the state formula. Housing Element Program 1.B adds priority processing, fee deferrals and density and intensity bonuses for residential and mixed-use projects in the Downtown Waterfront Specific Plan area, and Program 3.A promotes the density bonus and fee deferrals for special-needs housing. Read on the zoneomics code mirror; the City's code host returns 403.

program_name: Suisun City local housing fund, inclusionary ordinance and PLHA (no trust fund or inclusionary; Housing Element Programs 1.B, 1.C, 1.E; PLHA formula share)
administering_agency: City of Suisun City Development Services Department and Suisun City Housing Authority
typical_award_size: Negative finding for local funds. The 2023-2031 Housing Element (adopted March 21, 2023, modified May 16, 2023, HCD certified May 2023) has no trust fund, in-lieu fee or fee waiver program; Program 1.E was to decide on an inclusionary ordinance within two years of adoption (by spring 2025) and adopt one within a year if appropriate; Program 1.C commits the City to apply for state HOME, CDBG, MHP and CalHFA funds for nonprofit developers; Program 1.F explores mortgage revenue bonds and MCCs with other Solano jurisdictions. Suisun City is not a CDBG or HOME entitlement (state programs). PLHA formula (HCD 2024-2028 NOFA): CY 2024 $80,369, CY 2025 $86,957, five-year estimate $502,306.
affordability_requirement: PLHA: at or below 60% AMI unless the plan targets higher; state HOME and CDBG rules when the City applies as grantee.
next_deadline: PLHA allocations arrive annually from HCD; the City's PLHA plan and any inclusionary decision were not found (suisun.com 403). Ask Development Services whether Council acted on Program 1.E and how PLHA is programmed.
layering_notes: A Suisun City project must bring its own subsidy: state HOME or CDBG with the City as applicant, CMFA bonds and TCAC (Almond Gardens model), County SCHTF (county record), and the City's land or fee concessions (separate record). About $85,000 a year of PLHA is too small for gap loans unless pooled. Source is the HCD-posted October 2022 review draft; the adopted element PDF on suisun.com returned 403.

program_name: Napa Affordable Housing Impact Fee Fund (Affordable Housing Trust Fund) development loans, rolling NOFA
administering_agency: City of Napa Housing Division (Housing Manager Stephanie Gaul, 707-257-9628)
typical_award_size: Gap loans sized by the joint City and County Multi Family Transaction Underwriting Guidelines (Jan 21, 2020). Minimum award $100,000, no set maximum. Fund balance at June 30, 2025 was $8.7 million unaudited, of which $5 million was formally reserved for specific projects; FY 2024-25 fee collections were about $1.7 million. Track record: $2.2 million general fund plus trust fund money each to Heritage House (90 units, 40 PSH) and Valley Lodge (54 units PSH) in 2022; four projects held reservations from the impact fee and TOT funds at the time of the 2023 Prohousing application. Application fee 1% of the loan request, minimum $10,000 ($5,000 cashier's check at pre-application, $5,000 at award).
per_unit_cap: No fixed per unit cap. Joint underwriting guidelines limit developer fee for small projects ($25,000 per unit for units 1-10, $15,000 for units 11-30, $12,000 above 30) and size the loan by gap analysis.
affordability_requirement: Units must serve households at or below 80% AMI (rents at 30% of 30%, 50% or 60% AMI by tier). 55-year regulatory agreement for rental, 45 years for ownership, recorded under NMC Chapter 15.94. Mixed income projects are funded only for the proportional share of affordable units. Units must count toward the City RHNA (new construction, adaptive reuse, or qualifying rehab); transitional housing and shelters not eligible. Scoring gives 15 points for at least 20% PSH units and 10 points for 100% affordable.
next_deadline: Rolling, first come first served through the Neighborly portal (portal.neighborlysoftware.com/NAPACA/Participant). The 2023 NOFA accepted applications until June 30, 2024 or until funds were allocated; the City states funds are released at least once every two years by NOFA. No 2025 or 2026 NOFA document was found on cityofnapa.org as of 2026-11-08; contact the Housing Division before preparing an application.
layering_notes: The largest city controlled pool in Napa County and the normal local gap layer for 4% and 9% deals inside Napa city limits (Heritage House, Valley Lodge, Jamboree Silverado Trail PSH). Terms mirror the Napa County Affordable Housing Fund record: 3.0% simple interest, 55-year term, 50/50 residual receipts split, subordinate to senior debt, 90% maximum senior LTV, $100 per unit monitoring fee. Stack order: CTCAC credits and CMFA or CalHFA conduit bonds first, then HCD programs (MHP, AHSC, NPLH, Homekey), then City impact fee loan, then City 1% TOT loan for moderate income or missing middle units, with HACN project based vouchers for PSH units. County Affordable Housing Fund money is usually not available for sites inside the city (County preference for unincorporated projects) but the two agencies share underwriting guidelines and have co-funded projects. City loans are public funds, so state prevailing wage applies. Sources opened: 2023 NOFA (source_url), FY 2024-25 CAPER for fund balances, Prohousing Designation matrix, 2023 Housing Element APR.

program_name: Napa 1% Transient Occupancy Tax for Affordable and Workforce Housing Fund (Measure F, November 2018)
administering_agency: City of Napa Housing Division
typical_award_size: Special tax of 1% on hotel and short term rental stays (TOT raised from 12% to 13%), effective January 1, 2019, dedicated solely to affordable and workforce housing projects, programs and services in the City of Napa. FY 2024-25 revenue about $2.8 million; fund balance at June 30, 2025 about $10.2 million unaudited, of which $4 million was formally reserved for specific projects. Measure F campaign estimate was $2.1 million a year. Awards are low or no interest deferred loans under the same rolling NOFA as the impact fee fund.
per_unit_cap: No fixed per unit cap. No separately adopted underwriting guidelines for the TOT fund; the City applies the joint City and County guidelines by analogy.
affordability_requirement: Households at or below 120% AMI. Under the NOFA the TOT fund is targeted primarily to the missing middle (81% to 120% AMI, rents at 30% of 110% AMI) and applications serving that band receive automatic full leverage points. 55-year rental and 45-year ownership regulatory agreements.
next_deadline: Rolling through the Neighborly portal under the combined Affordable Housing and TOT NOFA; City commits to a NOFA at least every two years. No 2025 or 2026 NOFA document found online as of 2026-11-08; confirm availability with the Housing Division (707-257-9628).
layering_notes: The only sizable local source in Napa County for moderate income and workforce rental or ownership units, which state programs rarely fund. Pairs with the impact fee loan (80% AMI units) in a mixed income project: impact fee dollars on the low income units, TOT dollars on the 81% to 120% AMI units. The County (Measure I) and the other four cities adopted parallel 1% TOT measures in 2018; each is a separate fund with its own geography, so a Napa city project cannot draw on the County or St. Helena funds. Sources opened: FY 2024-25 CAPER (source_url, fund balance and revenue), 2023 NOFA, Measure F argument in favor, HCD Prohousing designation release (Napa designated 2024) and Prohousing matrix.

program_name: Napa Affordable Housing Impact Fee (NMC Chapter 15.94, Ordinance O2018-011) and alternative equivalent proposals
administering_agency: City of Napa Community Development Department (Chief Building Official) and Housing Division
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Fee per gross square foot set by implementing resolution; schedule effective January 1, 2017 (phased in from May 2016): multifamily $4.05, single family and condominium $4.75, office and retail $3.55, hotel $6.00, industrial $3.50 per square foot. Collections ran $0.4 million to $3.6 million a year in FY 2014-15 through FY 2018-19 and about $1.7 million in FY 2024-25. An impact fee nexus study was underway in 2023 (Housing Element Program H2-2.7, fee schedule update due by 2028), so expect a higher schedule.
per_unit_cap: Not applicable. Fee exempt units: affordable units restricted to extremely low, very low or low income households under a recorded affordable housing agreement, any dwelling unit of 500 square feet or less (O2018-011), and any affordable housing project in which 15% or more of units are affordable.
affordability_requirement: Exemption requires rents at 30% of 60% AMI (low), 30% of 50% AMI (very low) or 30% of 30% AMI (extremely low) with a 55-year rental or 45-year ownership affordable housing agreement under 15.94.080. Market rate units, including units for median and moderate income households, pay the fee.
next_deadline: Fee due before building permit issuance, or deferred under a recorded secured building agreement (Government Code 66007) to final inspection or certificate of occupancy; the City routinely defers fees for affordable projects to occupancy. Developers may propose an alternative equivalent proposal (on or off site affordable units, land dedication, conversion of market rate units, preservation) with City Council approval under 15.94.070. Petitions for adjustment or waiver under 15.94.100 must be filed within 30 days of the fee determination.
layering_notes: Napa replaced its 1999 inclusionary ordinance with this fee in 2012, so market rate apartments owe no on site affordable units and 100% affordable projects (15% or more affordable) pay nothing. The fee stream capitalizes the Affordable Housing Impact Fee Fund record above. Compare the County fee under County Code 18.107 (Pass 2 record), which was overhauled on October 21, 2025 and phases in from January 16, 2026; the City schedule still dates from 2017 until the nexus study update is adopted. A fee exemption is not a City expenditure, but the City's loans are, so prevailing wage turns on the loan not the exemption. Code text read on the ecode360 mirror (source_url) and the 2018 ordinance PDF; the 2017 rate sheet is at cityofnapa.org/DocumentCenter/View/102.

program_name: Napa Density Bonus (NMC 17.52.130) with Supplemental Density Bonus up to 100%, and :AH Affordable Housing Overlay District incentives (NMC Chapter 17.36)
administering_agency: City of Napa Community Development Department, Planning Division
typical_award_size: Requirement and entitlement incentive, not a direct subsidy. State density bonus law implemented through 17.52.130 (O2010-3, O2011-2). Local enhancement: a Supplemental Density Bonus allows the decision making body to grant bonuses, incentives or concessions above the state maximum up to a total of 100% for projects that exceed the state affordability tables or provide amenities and public benefits (underground parking, superior design, common space). Small project bonus lets duplexes and triplexes exceed pod density if the extra units are very low or lower income (30-year restriction). :AH overlay sites (over 2.5 acres, under 10% slope, within one half mile of transit or services) must deliver 10% very low plus 10% low income units in RM, MU or MP districts and receive priority processing, fee deferral to occupancy for all affordable units, access to local affordable housing funds, Housing Authority marketing and density flexibility under 17.52.140.
affordability_requirement: State density bonus thresholds (5% very low, 10% lower income, 10% moderate for sale, senior, etc.) with 55-year restrictions; supplemental bonus requires affordability above the state tables or public benefits. :AH overlay requires 20% affordable (10% very low and 10% low) or an approved alternative equivalent proposal.
next_deadline: Applies at entitlement; large project density bonus decisions are made by the City Council. The 2023-2031 Housing Element (adopted October 17, 2023, certified December 5, 2023) found 17.52.130 out of date with AB 682, AB 1551, AB 2334, AB 571 and SB 290 and committed to update it (Program H2-2.1) in the comprehensive zoning ordinance update that was underway in 2024-2025; check the current code before relying on local terms.
layering_notes: Napa is one of the few California cities with a codified local bonus above the state maximum (to 100% total), which matters for small infill sites downtown and along the four General Plan corridor focus areas. AB 2334 (unlimited density and three extra stories for 100% affordable projects in Napa County, a very low vehicle travel area) applies by state law even before the local text is updated. :AH overlay sites in the Housing Element site inventory (including City owned sites under Program H2.F) carry the fee deferral and local fund incentives, which pair with the impact fee and TOT loans above. Density bonus alone does not trigger prevailing wage; City funds do. Code text read on the Zoneomics mirror (source_url for 17.52; chapter_18 for 17.36); the Housing Element PDF and 2023 APR were opened on cityofnapa.org.

program_name: Napa fee deferral and reduced building permit fees for affordable and workforce housing (Housing Element Programs H2-2.8 and H2-1.1)
administering_agency: City of Napa Community Development Department (Building Division) and Housing Division
typical_award_size: Documented practice of deferring impact fees to occupancy for any qualifying affordable project (Prohousing matrix item 3C; Housing Element constraint analysis). Housing Element Program H2-2.8 commits to fees deferred, reduced or waived plus fast tracking for 100% affordable projects by 2025 (reported as not initiated in the 2023 APR). Napa Valley Register coverage of a 2021 council vote (3-2) reports a 50% reduction in building permit, plan check and inspection fees for housing at or below 120% AMI and for ADUs of 500 square feet or less; that fee resolution was not located on cityofnapa.org this pass.
per_unit_cap: Not applicable; percentage reduction of permit fees, no dollar cap published.
affordability_requirement: Affordable and workforce housing at or below 120% AMI per the reported 2021 action; impact fee deferral applies to affordable units as defined in NMC 15.94 (80% AMI or below).
next_deadline: Applied at permit issuance on request. Confirm the current master fee schedule discount and the status of the H2-2.8 fast track program with the Building Division (NapaON permit portal) before underwriting; Housing Element fee realignment is due by 2028.
layering_notes: Fee relief is modest relative to the impact fee and TOT loans but is routinely combined with them. Napa Valley Unified School District and Napa Sanitation District fees are outside the City's control. Waived or reduced fees can count as public funds under Labor Code 1720(b)(4), so confirm with counsel. The Prohousing matrix (source_url) and the Housing Element were opened; the 50% figure comes from news coverage and is marked needs_confirmation.

program_name: Napa CDBG entitlement program (Community Development Improvements category) and state HOME and CalHome program income
administering_agency: City of Napa Housing Division (CDBG Advisory Committee recommends, City Council approves)
typical_award_size: About $600,000 of CDBG a year (FY 2026-27 estimate about $600,000, HUD amount pending). After the 15% public service cap and 20% administration cap, the remainder (roughly $390,000) funds physical improvements, housing rehabilitation, property acquisition and nonprofit capital improvements with no category cap. Requests typically total twice the money available. FY 2024-25 rehab loans and grants totaled $135,650 for 10 households. The City is not a HOME participating jurisdiction; it recycles program income from past state HOME and CalHome grants into deferred homebuyer loans.
per_unit_cap: No published per unit cap; awards are small, historically well under $300,000 per project.
affordability_requirement: Must meet a CDBG national objective (principally low and moderate income benefit, 80% AMI or below) and a Consolidated Plan 2025-2030 priority: housing rehabilitation, emergency shelter services, nonprofit capital improvements, fair housing, outreach for Latino residents, services for youth aging out of foster care, infill sidewalks in low income block groups.
next_deadline: Annual application cycle each winter for the Annual Action Plan adopted in spring (the 2026-2027 draft Annual Action Plan is posted); next cycle for FY 2027-28 applications expected about January 2027. Contact the Housing Division at 707-257-9543.
layering_notes: Napa is the only CDBG entitlement jurisdiction in Napa County (the County and other cities are state non-entitlement, see Pass 2 HOME and CDBG record), but the dollars are small and mostly committed to rehab and services, so CDBG is a predevelopment or site improvement layer rather than a construction gap source. Federal Davis-Bacon applies to CDBG assisted construction of 8 or more units and state prevailing wage applies to public funds. CDBG-DR and CDBG-MIT contract reporting also runs through this office. Source page and the FY 2024-25 CAPER and 2025-2030 Consolidated Plan were opened.

program_name: Napa Land Banking Program and City sponsored affordable housing sites (Jefferson/Trower, The Crescent at Old Sonoma Road, Harvest Middle School Program H2-3.3)
administering_agency: City of Napa Housing Division and Housing Authority of the City of Napa
typical_award_size: City acquires or controls land for affordable development and selects developers by RFP. Current pipeline: about 3 acres at 3875 Jefferson Street (bought 2023; Jefferson/Trower, 19 affordable ownership units on a community land trust model, developer selected in 2025, development phase from early 2026); The Crescent, 77 deed restricted units on the former County HHSA campus on Old Sonoma Road (first 40 units for low and moderate income households, financing targeted to close January 2026 with construction in 2026; AHSC application was not funded). Housing Element Program H2-3.3 offers the Harvest Middle School owner an RFP, fee deferral or waiver, fast tracking and financial assistance for at least 53 low income units restricted 55 years.
per_unit_cap: Not applicable; land contribution plus City loans sized by gap.
affordability_requirement: Deed restrictions of 55 years (rental) or 45 years (ownership) for City assisted units; Crescent first phase targets low and moderate income; Jefferson/Trower targets low and moderate income first time buyers.
next_deadline: Developer RFPs issued as sites become available (Jefferson site RFP released 2024). Next watch item: Crescent construction start in 2026 and future phases seeking state grants; Harvest Middle School negotiations. Monitor the City Council agenda (Legistar client napa) for RFP notices.
layering_notes: City land plus impact fee and TOT loans is the model Napa uses to make 100% affordable projects pencil; the Crescent is a joint City and County effort on a County campus, so both the County Affordable Housing Fund and City funds are in the stack. A City land contribution and City loans are public funds, so prevailing wage applies. Source: Council Focus Areas FY 2025-2027 page (opened); the 2023 Housing Element APR and Housing Element Program H2-2.6 were also opened.

program_name: Napa Successor Agency housing funds: 20% Low and Moderate Income Housing Fund (Fund 229) and Local Housing Fund (Fund 230)
administering_agency: Housing Authority of the City of Napa as housing successor to the Napa Community Redevelopment Agency; City Housing Division staff
typical_award_size: Residual redevelopment housing assets (Low and Moderate Income Housing Asset Fund under Health and Safety Code 34176) administered by the Housing Authority, plus a Local Housing Fund. The Prohousing matrix (item 4H) states the City created the Low/Mod Fund from residual redevelopment funds and uses it for affordable housing. Current balances were not found online this pass; the AB 987 database of RDA assisted units is posted at cityofnapa.org/DocumentCenter/View/101.
affordability_requirement: Health and Safety Code 34176.1 rules for housing successors: funds for households at or below 80% AMI with at least 30% of expenditures for 30% AMI households over each five year period, 55-year rental covenants.
next_deadline: No separate NOFA; deployed through the Housing Authority Board (the City Council plus two resident commissioners) with the rolling impact fee and TOT NOFA. Confirm balances with the Housing Division (707-257-9543) and the latest SB 341 housing successor annual report.
layering_notes: Likely small relative to the impact fee ($8.7 million) and TOT ($10.2 million) funds but adds flexibility for loan repayments and land. The funds are described in the City's FY 2017-18 and 2018-19 adopted budget (source_url, Successor Agency and Housing Authority sections) and the Prohousing matrix; the current biennial budget PDF was not opened this pass, so balances are unconfirmed. State prevailing wage applies to housing successor funds.

program_name: Napa Permanent Local Housing Allocation (PLHA) formula share and Junior Unit Initiative Program (ADU and JADU forgivable loans)
administering_agency: City of Napa Housing Division (also delegated administrator of PLHA for American Canyon, Calistoga, St. Helena and Yountville)
typical_award_size: Napa's PLHA formula allocation is programmed 80% to Junior and Accessory Dwelling Unit creation, 15% to homeless services and 5% to administration. The Junior Unit Initiative provides forgivable financing up to $50,000 to create a JADU or conversion ADU, an additional $25,000 interest free deferred loan for conversion ADUs, up to $5,000 for ADA improvements, and design and engineering grants. Owner must occupy one unit and rent the other to a low income tenant under a recorded regulatory agreement.
per_unit_cap: $50,000 forgivable plus $25,000 deferred per ADU, plus $5,000 ADA grant.
affordability_requirement: Rental unit affordable to a household at or below 80% AMI; owner occupancy of the other unit; regulatory agreement term per program guidelines (10 years in the delegated city plans).
next_deadline: Rolling while PLHA and program funds last; 2026 program flyer posted. Not a multifamily source.
layering_notes: Recorded because PLHA is the only state formula money the City controls directly and because the City runs the same ADU program for the other four Napa jurisdictions under delegation agreements (November 15, 2022 Council action), which is why no city in the county has a PLHA multifamily set aside. For multifamily deals this is a negative finding: PLHA in Napa County goes to ADUs and rehab, not construction gaps. See the Pass 2 County PLHA record and the County Affordable ADU Forgivable Loan record for the parallel county program. Sources opened: PLHA page (source_url) and the Junior Unit Initiative page.

program_name: American Canyon Inclusionary Housing Requirements (ACMC Chapter 19.28, repealed and replaced by Ordinance 2026-04)
administering_agency: City of American Canyon Community Development Department (Brent Cooper, Director)
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Rental projects of five or more units: 5% very low, 5% low and 5% moderate income units (15% total), rental only, 55-year covenants. Ownership projects of five or more units: 10% of units affordable to lower income households (rental or ownership), 55 years. Fractions of 0.3 or more round up. Alternatives with findings of infeasibility: off site units, land dedication, acquisition and rehab of existing rentals (affordability extended 55 years), deeper affordability with fewer units, and as a last resort payment of the Affordable Housing Nexus Fee in lieu, deposited in the City housing fund for very low and low income housing. Inclusionary credits may be transferred to another project with Council approval.
affordability_requirement: Lower income means 80% AMI or below for Napa County; moderate up to 120% AMI. New residential development deed restricted to lower income households and tax exempt nonresidential development are exempt from the chapter.
eligible_project_types: market-rate rental projects of 5 or more units (compliance)
for-sale subdivisions of 5 or more units (compliance)
next_deadline: Applies at entitlement with a recorded housing agreement. Ordinance 2026-04 was introduced September 1, 2026 and adopted September 15, 2026 (effective 30 days later) after Planning Commission hearings on April 23, June 25 and July 30, 2026. Crawford Way (100 townhomes, 2026 construction) is subject to the chapter.
layering_notes: American Canyon is the only Napa County city that still requires on site inclusionary units in market rate rental projects (Napa converted to a fee in 2012; Calistoga allows a moderate income option; St. Helena requires 20%). The 15% rental requirement, 5% at very low, can be paired with the state density bonus (5% very low earns the base bonus) and with HACN project based vouchers. City assistance under 19.28.060 includes density increases, reduced parking, reduced setbacks and waived, reduced or deferred planning, plan check, building permit and impact fees when on site units are infeasible. 100% affordable projects are exempt from the chapter and from the nexus fee. Code text read on the City's own law library (source_url) and in Ordinance 2026-04.

program_name: American Canyon Affordable Housing Nexus Fee (ACMC 19.28.090) and Affordable Housing In-Lieu Fee Fund (Fund 340)
administering_agency: City of American Canyon Community Development Department and Finance Department
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. 2026 fee per gross square foot (Resolution 2025-94, adopted December 2, 2025, effective January 31, 2026, CPI adjusted each year, capped at 2% under Resolution 2016-15): single family and townhouse $3.64, stacked flats and apartments $4.22, ADU $0.00, office, hotel, retail and other nonresidential $0.93, warehouse and industrial $0.60. Fund 340 unaudited balance at June 30, 2023 was $400,075 after FY 2022-23 collections of $217,698 and a $70,492 transfer for the 189 Theresa demolition; the FY 2024-25 AB 1600 report was accepted December 16, 2025 but could not be opened this pass.
affordability_requirement: ADUs and affordable housing (deed restricted to lower income households) are exempt. Fee revenue is restricted to housing affordable to very low and low income households.
next_deadline: Paid at building permit issuance. Next CPI adjustment resolution expected on a December 2026 Council consent agenda for January 2027 effectiveness.
layering_notes: The fund is small and the City spends it on services (landlord tenant assistance, Section 8 support, farmworker housing contribution, maintenance of City owned housing, rent stabilization administration) rather than development loans, so there is no American Canyon trust fund NOFA to layer; a developer asking for a City contribution should request a Council action on a case by case basis. Exemption of affordable projects means 100% affordable deals pay no City housing fee. Fee resolution read on the City's Legistar download host (source_url); code sections and the AB 1600 FY 2022-23 report (americancanyon.gov PDF, retrieved via WebFetch because the site blocks scripts) were also opened. Fee revenue sits on top of the Pass 2 County fee structure only for unincorporated parcels; inside city limits only the City fee applies.

program_name: American Canyon Density Bonus Ordinance (ACMC Chapter 19.27, repealed and replaced by Ordinance 2026-04)
administering_agency: City of American Canyon Community Development Department, Planning Division
typical_award_size: Requirement and entitlement incentive, not a subsidy. Restates Government Code 65915 as of 2026: base bonuses up to 50%, the 65915(v) additional bonus for projects that first reach 50%, 80% bonus (or unlimited density plus three stories or 33 feet within one half mile of a major transit stop) for 100% affordable projects, one to five concessions by affordability tier (four for 16% very low or 45% moderate for sale), land donation bonus of 15% up to a combined 35%, child care facility bonus, and parking maximums with zero parking for qualifying transit adjacent or 100% affordable projects. Equity sharing required on for sale moderate income units. The chapter states it does not require direct financial incentives or fee waivers.
affordability_requirement: State thresholds: 10% lower income, 5% very low, 10% moderate for sale, senior, student, or special needs units with 55-year restrictions.
next_deadline: Applies at entitlement; Ordinance 2026-04 adopted September 15, 2026 and effective 30 days later. The 2025 Housing Element APR (Planning Commission February 26, 2026, Council March 17, 2026) reports Crawford Way used a 15% state bonus (87 to 100 units).
layering_notes: No local enhancement beyond state law, so American Canyon offers nothing more than Government Code 65915; the chapter is recorded to show that the City's density bonus and inclusionary rules were brought current in 2026. Inclusionary units count toward the bonus thresholds. The City has no local housing trust fund NOFA, no HOME or CDBG entitlement (it is in the state non-entitlement pool, see Pass 2 record), and its PLHA share is programmed to ADUs through the City of Napa, so the local layer for an American Canyon deal is the state density bonus, HACN project based vouchers, CMFA bonds and state programs. Sun Square (30 units, 100% affordable revision pending) and Domaine (291 market rate units) are the active multifamily projects. Ordinance text read on the City law library (source_url) and the Planning Commission staff reports on the City's agenda host.

program_name: American Canyon Permanent Local Housing Allocation share (administered by the City of Napa) for ADU and JADU forgivable loans
administering_agency: City of Napa Housing Division as delegated administrator for the City of American Canyon
typical_award_size: 95% of American Canyon's 2019-2023 PLHA formula allocation funds a Junior ADU and ADU loan program modeled on Napa's Junior Unit Initiative (forgivable loans and technical assistance to homeowners), 5% administration. Projected 4 households a year, 20 over five years. Allocation size is a small non-entitlement formula share (low six figures over five years).
per_unit_cap: Modeled on Napa's $50,000 forgivable plus $25,000 deferred per unit.
affordability_requirement: ADU or primary unit rented to a household at or below 80% AMI under a recorded regulatory agreement.
next_deadline: Rolling through the City of Napa Housing Division while funds last; the 2022 five year plan covers the 2019-2023 allocations and the 2024-2028 PLHA cycle requires a new plan.
layering_notes: Negative finding for multifamily: American Canyon's only state formula housing money is committed to ADUs and no multifamily set aside exists. The 2025 APR shows 17 affordable ADU permits since 2023 against a 16 unit goal, so the program is working as intended. Source is the City of Napa posted PLHA plan for American Canyon (source_url); americancanyon.gov pages return 403 to scripts and the Housing Resources page could not be opened, so confirm current status with the City of Napa Housing Division (707-257-9543).

program_name: St. Helena Affordable Housing Trust Fund (Fund 751, SHMC 17.30.050) development loans and project commitments
administering_agency: City of St. Helena Community Development Department and Administrative Services Director (fund administrator); City Council approves commitments
typical_award_size: Fund 751 beginning balance July 1, 2025 of $2,404,218, projected $2,448,125 at June 30, 2026 and $2,492,032 at June 30, 2027 before new commitments; recurring revenue is small (about $60,000 to $65,000 a year of housing impact and in-lieu fees plus interest, with a $583,991 spike in FY 2023-24). Track record: about $2,450,000 committed to Turley Flats (8 units, $700,000 incl. deferred fees), Brenkle Court (8 units) and 963 Pope Street (5 units) through 2021, and the Housing Element states the City has funded every developer request since 2015. Press reports (not confirmed on the City site) describe a $1.4 million loan to Our Town St. Helena for the Christine Apartments and a March 2026 commitment of $2.2 million ($1.5 million early, $700,000 later) to the 40 unit Fountain Street project by Our Town St. Helena and Burbank Housing (about $27 million total cost, land donated).
per_unit_cap: None published; recent commitments equal roughly $55,000 to $90,000 per unit.
affordability_requirement: Fund must be used solely to increase and improve housing affordable to moderate, low and very low income households, with priority for extremely low income households and the western part of the city (Programs H-DD and H-MM). Rental affordability agreements recorded; the City targets 55-year terms on assisted rental projects.
next_deadline: No NOFA; developers request funds directly and the City Council acts by resolution (typically one to two actions a year). Remaining uncommitted balance after the Fountain Street pledge should be confirmed with Community Development (707-968-2740, Director Leza Mikhail). The biennial review of fees and inclusionary requirements under 17.30.050(B) is due in 2026.
layering_notes: Small but reliable: St. Helena has funded every request since 2015 and pairs trust fund loans with reduced or deferred City fees (Program H-CC) and Measure E money (separate record). Stack order for a St. Helena deal: CTCAC credits, HCD programs, County Affordable Housing Fund (the County funded Turley Flats $798,000 and 963 Pope $200,000, see Pass 2 record), then City trust fund and Measure E, with HACN project based vouchers. City loans are public funds, so prevailing wage applies. Figures from the adopted FY 2025-26 and 2026-27 budget (source_url, Fund 751 worksheet); the 2023-2031 Housing Element draft on hcd.ca.gov and the code mirror were also opened. The City AgendaCenter search returned no results to scripts, so 2026 council actions rest on press coverage and are marked as such.

program_name: St. Helena Measure E 1% Transient Occupancy Tax for affordable and workforce housing (Fund 752)
administering_agency: City of St. Helena Administrative Services and Community Development Departments; City Council
typical_award_size: Special tax of 1% on hotel stays (TOT 12% to 13%) effective January 1, 2019, restricted to programs and services for affordable and workforce housing. Revenue about $300,000 to $315,000 a year (FY 2024-25 estimate $287,718 including interest; FY 2025-26 budget $322,504; FY 2026-27 $328,684). Fund balance $636,312 at July 1, 2025, projected $858,816 at June 30, 2026 and $1,187,500 at June 30, 2027 (includes a $160,000 long term receivable for an affordable housing loan). Only $100,000 of Planning and Building services is budgeted against it in FY 2026-27, so most of the balance is available for projects.
affordability_requirement: Households earning up to 120% AMI (rental and for sale), per the fund description; the City prioritizes extremely low and very low income units in its Housing Element programs.
next_deadline: No NOFA; City Council allocates by resolution. Press coverage indicates Measure E money is part of the two fund total (about $1.5 million) the Council pledged to Fountain Street in March 2026; confirm the uncommitted balance with the City.
layering_notes: Measure E is the City's only source for moderate income (81% to 120% AMI) units, which neither the trust fund's nexus based dollars nor state programs cover well; use it on workforce units in a mixed income project while the trust fund covers lower income units. Parallel to Napa's Measure F, Calistoga's Measure D and the County's Measure I, each a separate fund with its own geography. Figures from the adopted FY 2025-26 and 2026-27 budget (source_url, Fund 752 worksheet); the Housing Element estimate of $280,000 a year was also read.

program_name: St. Helena Affordable Housing Program: 20% inclusionary requirement, housing in-lieu fee and nonresidential Housing Impact Fee (SHMC Chapter 17.30, Ordinance 23-4)
administering_agency: City of St. Helena Community Development Department
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Inclusionary: at least 20% of all new dwelling units in any residential project (no project size threshold; new units under 850 square feet and ADUs are excluded) must be affordable units of the same tenure, built concurrently. Rental projects with four or more affordable units split them by RHNA need (as of March 2022: 55% very low, 31% low, 14% moderate); three or fewer units are assigned one each to very low, low then moderate. Ownership projects: half the affordable units at or below 100% AMI (or 80% AMI, which earns an extra 5% density bonus beyond state law) and half at moderate income, 45-year resale restrictions renewed at each resale. In-lieu fee (per square foot of net new floor area, set by Council resolution) is available by right only to projects of four or fewer units; larger projects need a Council infeasibility finding that density bonus concessions cannot cure. Housing impact fee on nonresidential development and conversions per the master fee schedule (wineries, nonprofits, schools, public uses and small day care exempt); the Council considered a 2024 proposal to raise the hotel fee to about $41,797 per room and commercial to $14 per square foot (press report, adoption not confirmed).
affordability_requirement: Rental affordable units restricted by recorded agreement (very low, low and moderate by RHNA ratio); ownership units 45 years. The Council may forgive part of a rental project's obligation for undue hardship where the project contributes significantly to affordable housing.
next_deadline: Applies at the first discretionary or ministerial approval through an inclusionary housing plan and recorded affordable housing agreement before building permit. Code is current through Ordinance 26-4 (May 12, 2026). Biennial review of fees and requirements due 2026. Current master fee schedule amounts were not located online; confirm with Community Development (707-968-2740).
layering_notes: The strictest inclusionary rule in Napa County (20% with no threshold) means almost every market rate project in St. Helena produces deed restricted units or fee revenue for the trust fund record above. 100% affordable projects satisfy the requirement by definition and pay no in-lieu fee; nonresidential impact fees and in-lieu fees capitalize Fund 751. Chapter 17.29 (Density Bonus) implements state law and is cross referenced for concessions. Code text read on the Zoneomics mirror of the City zoning code (source_url); cityofsthelena.gov pages opened but the agenda search returned nothing to scripts, and codepublishing and gocodebook mirrors return 403.

program_name: St. Helena reduced, deferred or waived fees for affordable housing (Housing Element Program H-CC) and Density Bonus Chapter 17.29
administering_agency: City of St. Helena Community Development Department; City Council
typical_award_size: The City reduces, defers or waives application and impact fees for affordable developments case by case; through January 1, 2022 it had reduced, deferred or waived fees for 21 affordable units (Turley Flats, Brenkle Court, 963 Pope Street), in part by lending trust fund money to cover deferred fees. The 2023-2031 Housing Element sets a goal of fee relief for 30 extremely low or very low income units and commits to adopt eligibility criteria and higher incentives for extremely low and very low income units. Chapter 17.29 implements the state density bonus (one to three concessions at 10%, 17% and 24% lower income, etc.) with the 5% local bonus add on for ownership projects under 17.30.030(G).
per_unit_cap: Not applicable; fee relief sized per project.
affordability_requirement: Affordable housing developments, with priority for extremely low and very low income units; deed restrictions required under the City affordable housing agreement.
next_deadline: Request with the entitlement application; Council approves fee relief with the funding commitment. Housing Element program timelines run through 2031.
layering_notes: Fee relief is routinely bundled with trust fund and Measure E commitments, so a St. Helena request should ask for all three at once. St. Helena's PLHA share (95% rehab loans up to $60,000 through the City of Napa) and its Housing Services Agreement with HACN (Section 8, regulatory monitoring, loan servicing) round out the local layer; there is no HOME or CDBG entitlement. Waived or reduced fees can count as public funds under Labor Code 1720(b)(4). Source: 2023-2031 Housing Element HCD review draft on hcd.ca.gov (source_url; the City adopted the element in 2023 and the final version was not located on the City site); the City budget and code mirror were also opened.

program_name: Calistoga Affordable Housing Fund (CMC 17.08.050), capitalized by the Housing Linkage Fee (17.08.040) and inclusionary in-lieu fees
administering_agency: City of Calistoga Planning and Building Department (Senior Planner Andrew Amelung) and Administrative Services; City Council
typical_award_size: Special purpose fund for construction, acquisition, rehabilitation and subsidy of very low, low and moderate income housing. Balance about $2.1 million per the 2023-2031 Housing Element; the FY 2024-25 AB 1600 report shows $247,238 in the linkage fee account at June 30, 2025 to be lent to a future project once enough accumulates (the in-lieu fee account balance is shown only in an image table). Linkage fee (Resolution 2014-110, CPI adjusted): retail and restaurant $4.11, office $2.85, industrial $2.09 per square foot and $1,897.17 per guest room for tourist accommodation; inclusionary in-lieu fee $12,000 per unit (Housing Element figure). Uses to date: $650,000 for the 611 Washington site (2015), $472,000 (2017) and $500,000 (2018) for housing sites, several million dollars of in-lieu fees that funded the 30 unit Calistoga Senior Apartments (2017), and a reported $2 million impact fee loan for the 78 unit Lincoln Avenue Apartments (For the Future Housing), backfilled by future fees and Measure D.
affordability_requirement: Very low, low and moderate income households (up to 120% AMI); 55-year affordability agreements under 17.08.020. Council reviews fund programs and distribution annually.
next_deadline: No NOFA; City Council acts on developer requests and reviews the fund with the annual budget (FY 2026-27 budget adopted June 2026). The Housing Advisory Committee (meets monthly) previews housing proposals; two new housing project applications were under conceptual review in June 2026.
layering_notes: Calistoga's fund is the second largest city pool in the county after Napa's and is paired with Measure D TOT money (separate record) and County Affordable Housing Fund loans. Hotel and resort development drives linkage fee revenue, so the fund grows with the visitor economy; the per guest room linkage fee is Calistoga's hotel related housing mitigation (no separate hotel housing fee exists). Stack: CTCAC, HCD, County fund, then City fund and Measure D, HACN project based vouchers for lower income units. City loans are public funds (prevailing wage). Sources opened: FY 2024-25 AB 1600 report on the City's CivicWeb agenda host (source_url), CMC Chapter 17.08 on ecode360, the 2023-2031 Housing Element on hcd.ca.gov. calistogaca.gov pages and PDFs return 403 to scripts; CivicWeb (calistoga.civicweb.net/filepro/documents) is the working route to staff reports.

program_name: Calistoga Inclusionary Housing Requirements (CMC 17.08.020, Ordinances 709, 733 and 780)
administering_agency: City of Calistoga Planning and Building Department
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Applies to subdivisions of five or more parcels or condominiums and rental projects of five or more units. Ownership projects of 5 to 19 units pay the in-lieu fee ($12,000 per unit per the Housing Element, set by resolution) for every unit. Ownership projects of 20 or more units and rental projects of five or more units provide either 20% of units affordable to moderate income households (120% AMI) or 10% affordable to low income households (80% AMI), restricted 55 years; projects with 10 or more inclusionary units must make 10% of them three bedroom. Alternatives with a Commission or Council infeasibility finding: in-lieu fee, land dedication, off site units, or equivalent methods; the Council may waive or reduce the obligation for economic hardship and may assist developers with subsidies or design flexibility (17.08.020(H)).
affordability_requirement: 20% moderate or 10% low income, 55-year recorded affordable housing agreement; ADUs do not count toward the requirement; off site units do not count toward a receiving site's density bonus.
eligible_project_types: market-rate rental projects of 5 or more units (compliance)
next_deadline: Applies at the first approval through an affordable housing plan; agreement recorded with the final map or before building permit. Ordinance 780 (adopted December 9, 2025 as the Housing Element implementation package) amended 17.08.010 to add special needs groups and set a citywide minimum density of 50% of the maximum (17.03.110).
layering_notes: The 20% moderate option is the loosest inclusionary standard in the county and lets market rate rental projects avoid low income units entirely; a developer wanting state density bonus concessions must instead hit the 65915 thresholds, and inclusionary units count toward the bonus. 100% affordable projects satisfy the requirement and generate no fee. In-lieu revenue flows to the Affordable Housing Fund record above. Code text read on ecode360 (source_url); the December 9, 2025 second reading staff report and ordinance were opened on the City's CivicWeb host.

program_name: Calistoga Affordable Housing Incentives and Density Bonus (CMC 17.08.030) with Missing Middle Housing Combining District (2026)
administering_agency: City of Calistoga Planning and Building Department; Planning Commission and City Council
typical_award_size: Entitlement incentive, not a direct subsidy. 17.08.030 implements Government Code 65915 and adds local enhancements: the City may grant an additional density bonus beyond state law, and the Council may grant financial incentives or concessions that produce identifiable cost reductions, including City subsidies for infrastructure improvements or development fees and City sponsorship of mortgage bond financing. The Planning Commission may waive lot size, setback, coverage and height standards; incentives involving City funds, public land, mixed use zoning or Public Works modifications go to the Council. Example: Calistoga Senior Apartments (30 units, 23 very low) approved in 2016 with a 58% bonus; Lincoln Avenue Apartments also used a bonus. In 2026 the Council initiated General Plan, zoning map and code amendments for a Missing Middle Housing Combining District (Opticos Design proposal received October 2026) to allow small multiplex and workforce housing near downtown.
affordability_requirement: State density bonus thresholds; inclusionary units under 17.08.020 count toward qualification; recorded agreement guaranteeing the targeted units for the period set by the Council consistent with state law.
next_deadline: Filed with the development application; Planning Commission hearing concurrent with entitlements, Council hearing where City funds or land are involved. Missing Middle Housing ordinance work (RFP for outreach and CEQA in mid 2026, recommended proposal October 2026) should produce code amendments in 2027; check the CivicWeb staff report folder for hearing dates.
layering_notes: Calistoga's code expressly authorizes fee subsidies and bond sponsorship as density bonus concessions, which is the hook for asking the Council to pay impact or connection fees from the Affordable Housing Fund or Measure D. AB 2334 unlimited density for 100% affordable projects applies in Napa County. Pair with the inclusionary record (units count toward the bonus) and the funds records.
