Density bonus alone does not trigger prevailing wage; City funded fee subsidies do. Code text read on ecode360 (source_url); the May 2026 Missing Middle resolution staff report and the October 2026 Opticos proposal were opened on the City's CivicWeb host (documents 114701 and 118222).

program_name: Calistoga Measure D 1% Transient Occupancy Tax for affordable and workforce housing (Resolution 2018-072, effective January 1, 2019)
administering_agency: City of Calistoga Administrative Services Department; City Council allocates
typical_award_size: Special tax of 1% on hotel stays (TOT 12% to 13%) held in a separate account and restricted to affordable and workforce housing programs and services, including land acquisition and donation, building acquisition, rehabilitation and demolition, housing construction, mobile home preservation, housing subsidies and preservation of expiring subsidies. Campaign estimate about $512,325 a year; an annual Government Code 50075.3 report is required. Uses: backfill of deferred fees for the Lincoln Avenue Apartments (78 units) and the proposed ADU Fee Assistance Program (annual transfer subject to appropriation). Council members questioned slow disbursement in 2024, so unspent balance is likely several million dollars; the balance was not found in a text document this pass.
affordability_requirement: Affordable and workforce housing; the City applies it to households up to 120% AMI for development and, for the ADU program, rentals at or below 160% AMI with a 10-year deed restriction.
next_deadline: No NOFA; allocated by City Council with the annual budget (FY 2026-27 budget adopted June 2026) and by resolution for specific projects. Confirm the fund balance with Administrative Services (707-942-2807).
layering_notes: Measure D is Calistoga's most flexible housing money (no nexus limits) and the natural source for moderate income units, fee backfill and land purchase (Council FY 2025-26 priorities include developing the City owned Earl and Eddy parcels). Combine with the Affordable Housing Fund for lower income units and the County fund. Parallel measures exist in Napa (F), St. Helena (E) and the County (I), each separate. Sources opened: October 6, 2026 ADU Fee Assistance staff report on CivicWeb (source_url, cites Resolution 2018-072 and the Measure D use restriction) and the Measure D City Attorney impartial analysis PDF (retrieved from calistogaca.gov via WebFetch because the site blocks scripts).

program_name: Calistoga ADU Fee Assistance Program (Measure D funded connection and impact fee grants) and ADU fee waivers
administering_agency: City of Calistoga Planning and Building Department and Public Works
typical_award_size: Proposed by resolution at the October 6, 2026 City Council meeting (Housing Element Action A1.2-2): the City would pay, as a Measure D funded grant, water and sewer connection and capacity charges (about $28,500 per ADU) and development impact fees for ADUs over 750 square feet (total fees up to about $43,500) for the first three ADUs with complete building permit applications each calendar year, first come first served, subject to annual appropriation. Existing policy already waives impact fees for ADUs under 750 square feet and utility connection fees for ADUs not built with the primary home. Alternatives discussed: five ADUs a year, tiered connection fee relief (75% for 5-year, 50% for 10-year, 25% for 15-year, 0% for 20-year deed restrictions), monitoring by HACN under the FY 2026-28 intergovernmental agreement.
affordability_requirement: 10-year recorded deed restriction requiring the ADU to be rented at rents affordable to households at or below 160% AMI, no rentals under 30 days; violations trigger repayment with 10% interest and a lien. Council was asked whether to tighten to 120% AMI.
next_deadline: First three complete ADU permit applications each calendar year once adopted; confirm whether the Council adopted the resolution on October 6, 2026 and whether the Chapter 17.37 ADU ordinance amendments (under HCD review in fall 2026) have taken effect. ADU Forgivable Loan outreach with Napa County Housing and Community Services was planned for 2026.
layering_notes: Single unit program recorded because it shows how Calistoga deploys Measure D and because the same connection fee burden (about $28,500 per unit) hits small multifamily projects, which can request similar relief as a density bonus financial concession under 17.08.030. Layers with the County Affordable ADU Forgivable Loan ($105,000 maximum, 5-year restriction) and Calistoga's PLHA share (60% ADU loans, 35% rehab through the City of Napa). Fee grants are public funds; prevailing wage exposure for a homeowner ADU is a question for counsel. Source: October 6, 2026 staff report on the City's CivicWeb host (source_url); the May 18, 2026 Housing Advisory Committee report and April 2026 ADU ordinance review were also opened.

program_name: San Rafael Affordable Housing Trust Fund (Affordable Housing In-Lieu Fee Fund 243), Resolution 14760 guidelines, periodic NOFA and rolling acquisition process
administering_agency: City of San Rafael Community and Economic Development Department, Housing Division (Alexis Captanian, Housing Manager, (415) 485-3383, housing@sanrafael.gov)
typical_award_size: Small gap fund capitalized by residential in-lieu fees and commercial linkage fees. Balance was $2,034,226 in July 2023 and about $1,000,000 unencumbered on August 15, 2024. 2023 NOFA offered $1,400,000 and awarded $1,450,000 across three projects (BRIDGE Housing rehabilitation of 125 units at Nova Albion and Las Gallinas $1,000,000; Eden Housing 3301 Kerner Blvd 40-unit PSH adaptive reuse $250,000 on top of $2,101,663 prior awards; Canal Alliance Marin Villa Estates renovation $200,000). The June 2025 round awarded $600,000 across three projects (an acquisition, a rehabilitation and new construction) and was issued jointly with Marin County. Rolling acquisition process approved September 3, 2024: up to $250,000 per year total, unawarded amounts do not roll over. Awards are grants or loans at Council discretion.
per_unit_cap: No fixed cap; guidelines score per-unit subsidy for reasonableness. Rolling acquisition requests are limited by the $250,000 annual pool.
affordability_requirement: Rental units income and rent restricted for not less than 55 years. 100% affordable rental or ownership projects serving seniors, families and special needs, including formerly homeless households. Scoring favors transit proximity (within a quarter mile), units for larger families (Resolution 15438) and very low income service.
application_cycle: rolling (acquisitions, up to $250,000 a year); NOFA issued only when the balance supports it, aligned with the County January cycle
next_deadline: No City NOFA planned for 2026 (City statement on its funding page). Acquisition requests accepted any time after a pre-application meeting with staff. Watch the County NOFA in January 2027 for the next joint round.
layering_notes: San Rafael is the only Marin city with a recurring NOFA practice, but the pool is thin: in-lieu revenue has fallen because most projects now use State Density Bonus with on-site units instead of paying the fee (Oct 5, 2026 staff report). Typical use is last-mile gap money of $200,000 to $1,000,000 that unlocks the Marin County Affordable Housing Fund (County guidelines require a city contribution for projects inside city limits) and County PLHA (2023 example: $250,000 City plus $250,000 County Trust Fund plus $250,000 PLHA for 3301 Kerner). CDBG and HOME for San Rafael flow through the Marin Urban County; the City received $508,032 in CDBG in 2026 and the 2026-27 County cycle offered $1,500,000 CDBG, $700,000 HOME and $900,000 PLHA. Pair with CMFA bonds and 4% credits; LIHTC deals in the City pipeline include 88 Vivian (124 units) and 1100 Los Gamos (192 units, Community Development Partners). City funds are public funds, so assume Labor Code 1720 prevailing wage unless the award is structured as an exempt grant. Resolution 14760 itself (Jan 21, 2020) was not opened; terms come from the Sept 3, 2024 staff report, the July 2023 NOFA award report, the April 2024 Marin Villa amendment and the 2025 Annual Progress Report, all opened. marincounty.gov remained Cloudflare-blocked this pass; County programs are referenced from the Marin County records in this database.

program_name: Affordable Housing Requirement (inclusionary), SRMC 14.16.030(B), Ordinance 1990 and Resolution 14890 guidelines, in-lieu fee set by Resolution 15179
administering_agency: City of San Rafael Community and Economic Development Department, Planning and Housing Divisions
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. In-lieu fee per required affordable unit: $396,702 for July 1, 2026 to June 30, 2027 ($389,032 in FY 2025-26, $368,274 in FY 2024-25, $362,817 in FY 2023-24), indexed annually to the California Construction Cost Index under Resolution 15179 (Dec 19, 2022). Fees are paid before building permit issuance and deposited to the Affordable Housing Trust Fund.
affordability_requirement: Primary requirement: projects of 2 to 15 units provide 10% of base units (excluding density bonus units) for low income households; projects of 15 or more units provide 5% low income. Secondary requirement for projects over 15 units: an additional 5% low income or 10% moderate income on site, or an in-lieu fee equal to 5% of base units, or off-site units within a half mile with an experienced affordable developer, or land donation appraised at or above the fee. Affordability in perpetuity, reducible to not less than 40 years on a Council finding of financial infeasibility. Fractional units below 0.5 pay the fee; 0.5 and above round up. Exempt: single-family homes, ADUs and JADUs, projects with pre-ordinance development agreements.
next_deadline: Fee resets every July 1; FY 2027-28 figure will post after the index update. Resolution 14890 requires a program review every 3 to 5 years, so watch for amendments alongside the 2027 Housing Element mid-cycle work.
layering_notes: Low on-site percentages (5% to 10%) make San Rafael one of the lighter inclusionary regimes in Marin, compared with Novato's 20% and Mill Valley's 15% (25% before 2026) and the County's 20%. Developers of 100% affordable projects satisfy the requirement automatically and the City counts inclusionary units with density bonus units when they overlap, which is why in-lieu receipts have dropped (Oct 2026 staff report). The Northgate Town Square redevelopment (Merlone Geier, up to 1,422 units, entitled Dec 2, 2024, demolition began fall 2025) is the largest pipeline source of inclusionary units or fee revenue; the City pages opened state that it includes affordable housing but do not quantify the count, so confirm the development agreement terms in the Laserfiche project documents before relying on them. Fee revenue funds the Trust Fund record above. Ordinance 1990, Resolutions 14890 and 14891 were opened as PDFs on the City fees page; Resolution 15179 is on the City's Laserfiche public records portal, which refused connections this pass.

program_name: Commercial linkage fee for nonresidential development, SRMC 14.16.030(D) and (E), Ordinance 1990, rates updated December 2023
administering_agency: City of San Rafael Community and Economic Development Department
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Rates effective July 1, 2024: office or research and development $13.33 per square foot; retail, restaurant or personal service $10.00 per square foot; hotel or motel $5.00 per square foot. Applies to new nonresidential construction of 5,000 square feet or more, additions and residential-to-commercial conversions. Underlying nexus in Table 14.16.030-3: office 0.03 affordable units per 1,000 square feet, retail 0.0225, manufacturing 0.01625, warehouse 0.00875, hotel 0.0075, with 20% of employee housing need assigned to the project. Receipts go to the segregated housing in-lieu fee fund.
affordability_requirement: Fee may be satisfied instead by on-site or off-site units or land dedication at Planning Commission or Council discretion; mixed-use projects whose residential component meets the nonresidential requirement are exempt from the fee.
next_deadline: Rates are not indexed by the ordinance text read; the City says fees are subject to change and the last update was December 2023 (effective July 1, 2024). Confirm before application.
layering_notes: One of only two active commercial linkage fees among the three Marin priority cities (Novato's code mirror shows no linkage fee and Mill Valley committed only to study one by 2025 under Housing Element Program 12); Marin County's Chapter 22.22 linkage fee applies in unincorporated areas only. Low commercial construction volume means this is a minor revenue line for the Trust Fund. Ordinance 1990 PDF opened on the City fees page.

program_name: San Rafael Density Bonus and Height Bonus program, SRMC 14.16.030(C) and 14.16.190, Resolution 14891 (Tables 3 and 4), Downtown Precise Plan Chapter 7.3 bonus
administering_agency: City of San Rafael Community and Economic Development Department, Planning Division
typical_award_size: Requirement framework, not a cash subsidy. Resolution 14891 (Feb 16, 2021) implements Government Code 65915 by Council resolution so tables update without a code amendment: Table 3 scales bonuses from 20% at 5% very low or 10% lower income up to 50% at 15% very low or 24% lower income, 35% at 40% moderate ownership, 20% for senior housing, land donation, supportive housing and student housing categories, and 80% or unlimited density with a three-story height increase for 100% affordable projects within a half mile of a major transit stop. Table 4 lists concessions including a 20% reduction in yard setback, lot coverage or landscape requirements each counted as one concession, mixed-use allowances and parking at state maximums. Section H allows an affordable housing applicant to request a planning fee waiver under Resolution 11025. A separate height bonus (14.16.190) and the Downtown Precise Plan Chapter 7.3 bonus add floors for affordable units downtown; the City's October 2026 Prohousing self-assessment states its program exceeds statutory requirements by 12 percent.
affordability_requirement: Per Government Code 65915 thresholds; 55-year affordability for very low and low rental units that earn the bonus. 100% affordable projects may include up to 20% moderate income units and one manager unit.
next_deadline: Resolution 14891 anticipated amendment once the Downtown Precise Plan bonus was finalized; the City is also drafting Objective Design Standards (Housing Element Program 25) and parking standard revisions (Program 43) through 2027 as Prohousing commitments.
layering_notes: Most San Rafael rental projects now use this path rather than paying the in-lieu fee (City staff, Oct 5, 2026), which reduces Trust Fund revenue but speeds entitlements; recent examples include 1515 Fourth Street, 4040 Civic Center Drive, 930 Irwin and 1100 Los Gamos (190 affordable units, seven stories). The City also reports no traffic mitigation fee on affordable units (see fee waiver record). Stack with the County Trust Fund and PLHA, which do not depend on the bonus. Resolution 14891 PDF opened from the City fees page; the Downtown Precise Plan Chapter 7.3 text was not opened this pass.

program_name: Prohousing Designation application (Resolution of October 5, 2026) and Prohousing Incentive Pilot eligibility
administering_agency: City of San Rafael Community and Economic Development Department (Greg Minor, (415) 680-4707, greg.minor@sanrafael.gov)

Designation gives City-sponsored projects scoring priority in AHSC, IIG, TCC, SCCP, LPP, TIRCP and STPG and lets the City apply to HCD's Prohousing Incentive Pilot (PIP); the staff report notes the smallest award in the most recent PIP round was $315,762.38 and that no Marin jurisdiction held the designation as of August 10, 2026. Draft application posted for public review October 9 to November 8, 2026, then submitted to HCD, which has 60 days to decide; designation lasts three years.
affordability_requirement: Not applicable. The City commits to implement Housing Element Programs 19 (City-owned lots), 20 (North San Rafael Precise Plan), 25 (Objective Design Standards), 36 (fee reductions for affordable housing) and 43 (parking standards) to keep its score.

layering_notes: If approved, San Rafael becomes the only Prohousing jurisdiction in Marin, which matters for AHSC and IIG scoring on transit-adjacent sites like Northgate and Downtown. program_name: Novato Affordable Housing Requirements (inclusionary), Novato Municipal Code Division 19.24 (Ordinances 1576, 1676 and 1718), with in-lieu fees to the City housing fund
administering_agency: City of Novato Community Development Department, 922 Machin Avenue, Novato, (415) 899-8989
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. In-lieu fee amounts are set by Council resolution (not published on the code mirror); fees are paid before building permit issuance into a separate City fund earmarked for very low, low and moderate income housing (19.24.040). Council approval of an in-lieu payment is discretionary for projects of 7 or more units and by right for 3 to 6 unit projects and for fractions below 0.70.
affordability_requirement: Sliding scale by project size: 3 to 10 units 10%, then one percentage point per unit from 11 units (11%) to 20 or more units (20%). Rental projects: half of the required units at 50% AMI rents and half at 60% AMI rents (very low and low income). Ownership: half low income (65% AMI pricing) and half moderate income (90% AMI pricing). Fractions of 0.70 or more round up. Deed restrictions through a recorded Inclusionary Housing Agreement; one-for-one replacement of demolished deed-restricted units. Exempt: ADUs and JADUs, residential care facilities for the elderly, single or two-unit projects with homes of 3,000 square feet or less, and AHO overlay projects that meet the overlay's 20% requirement.
next_deadline: Ordinance 1718 (Sept 10, 2024) was the latest amendment read. Confirm the current in-lieu fee resolution and any Housing Element Program 3.F (Evaluate and Adjust Impact Fees) follow-up with the Planning Division.
layering_notes: Novato's 20% at 20-plus units with a 50/50 very low and low split is the strictest rental inclusionary standard among the three Marin priority cities and matches the County's 20% in unincorporated Marin; State Density Bonus units are excluded from the base count. Because in-lieu payment needs Council approval above six units, fund revenue is small and lumpy; a 2019 Planning Commission record cited a housing fund balance of about $1,200,000 (search snippet, not opened). Habitat for Humanity's 80-unit Redwood Boulevard project shows how the City layers: about $1,000,000 in City fee reductions and waivers approved March 2025 on top of $1,000,000 allocated in 2023 from the City's Affordable Housing Fund, with a $5,239,098 Marin County Housing Trust Fund loan (April 15, 2025, see County record). novato.gov and novato.org returned 403 to every request this pass (HTML pages, showpublisheddocument PDFs and the news module); Novato has no Legistar API client and no Granicus or IQM2 host was found, so City pages, the 2023-2031 Housing Element, the 2025 Annual Progress Report and Council staff reports could not be opened. program_name: Novato Density Bonus (Division 19.25) with Local Senior Density Bonus and the Affordable Housing Opportunity (AHO) Overlay District (Section 19.16.070)
administering_agency: City of Novato Community Development Department, 922 Machin Avenue, Novato, (415) 899-8989

program_name: Mill Valley Affordable Housing Trust Fund (MVMC 20.80.070, Ordinance 1295, Resolution 20-26 Administrative Guidelines, Resolution 24-60 Local Housing Trust Fund match)
administering_agency: City of Mill Valley Planning and Building Department (Danielle Staude, dstaude@cityofmillvalley.org), with Housing Advisory Committee priorities and City Council approval of every award
typical_award_size: Funded by the 1% affordable housing impact fee on residential permits at or above the construction valuation threshold ($142,000 since May 1, 2024) plus inclusionary in-lieu payments and donations; collections were $345,000 by Feb 2020, roughly $300,000 a year per the Housing Element and about $600,000 a year per the 2024 Annual Progress Report, with about $1,000,000 unencumbered in 2024. Resolution 24-60 (Sept 5, 2024) committed $1,000,000 of Trust Fund match for an HCD Local Housing Trust Fund application ($1,200,000 requested; HCD's Round 5 applicant list shows the City with a self-score of 60) so that $2,400,000 total would be available: $1,000,000 ($500,000 grant plus $500,000 match) for Bayfront Terrace at 1 Hamilton Drive and $1,400,000 for other projects to be solicited. Loans at simple interest of no more than 3% as construction or deferred-payment permanent financing; up to 5% administration. Ongoing uses: Marin Housing Authority BMR administration, Home Match contract (up to $30,000 a year), Bayfront Terrace predevelopment, and the Lease to Locals pilot ($3,500 to $14,000 per converted rental, running through 2027).
per_unit_cap: None published; LHTF-matched funds must put at least 30% toward extremely low income (30% AMI) units and no more than 20% toward 80% AMI units, with the remainder at or below 60% AMI.
affordability_requirement: Low income households per Chapter 20.80 covenants; LHTF-matched awards target 60% AMI and below with a 30% extremely low income set-aside. Projects must be inside Mill Valley, scored on feasibility, funding needed, unit count and location outside the very high fire severity zone. Council approves each award at a public hearing. The City adopted HCD's Uniform Multifamily Regulations for underwriting.
application_cycle: rolling (Council awards); a solicitation for the remaining $1,400,000 was promised if the state grant is received
next_deadline: unknown, verify with agency. The City said it would announce a solicitation in early 2025 contingent on the HCD LHTF award; no award or solicitation was found on the City site as of November 2026, and the 2028 Mitigation Fee Act five-year review and impact fee extension decision are the next fixed milestones.
layering_notes: Mill Valley's fund is unusually well capitalized for a 14,000-person city because the 1% fee hits every large remodel; it is the only Marin priority city with a committed state LHTF match strategy. Money has gone almost entirely to the City's own site (Bayfront Terrace, EAH Housing, 45 units) and to tenure programs, so a third-party developer should expect the $1,400,000 remainder and future fee receipts (about $600,000 a year) as the ceiling. Layer under the Marin County Affordable Housing Fund (the County awarded 1 Hamilton $500,000 in 2022 and $1,000,000 total by 2024 per County documents cited in search results, not opened), County HOME ($360,000 to the Eden Housing Mill Valley rental project in FY 2026-27, see County record) and PLHA; CDBG and HOME flow through the Marin Urban County. City loans are public funds for prevailing wage. Trust Fund page, Resolutions 20-26 and 24-60, 2024 APR, Housing Element and HCD's LHTF applicant list all opened. marincounty.gov remained Cloudflare-blocked this pass; County programs are referenced from the Marin County records in this database.

program_name: Mill Valley Affordable Housing Requirements: inclusionary units and affordable housing impact fee, MVMC Chapter 20.80 (Ordinance 1295 of 2017, inclusionary update adopted 2026 under Housing Element Programs 7 and 11)
administering_agency: City of Mill Valley Planning and Building Department
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Impact fee: 1% of construction valuation on single-family and small multifamily residential work at or above the valuation threshold ($100,000 in 2018, $105,000 in 2020, $130,000 in 2023, $142,000 from May 1, 2024, indexed to the California Construction Cost Index), paid at building permit into the Affordable Housing Trust Fund; collection was extended five years by Council resolution on March 20, 2023. The 2026 update lowered the inclusionary requirement from 25% to 15%, exempted 2 to 6 unit projects from building affordable units and waived their impact fee when units stay under 850 square feet (one bedroom), 1,000 (two bedrooms) or 1,200 (three bedrooms), and eliminated micro-unit caps. Fractional units of 0.50 or more may be met by an in-lieu payment calculated by applying the fraction to the impact fee formula.
affordability_requirement: Projects of 7 to 9 units: 15% affordable with at least one unit for moderate income households. Projects of 10 or more units: 15% affordable, at least half of the affordable units for low income households and the rest moderate income. Rental affordable units restricted in perpetuity or the maximum term allowed by law (20.80.060). Exempt: ADUs, micro units, projects below the valuation threshold, projects vested before November 1, 2018. Off-site units, land dedication or acquisition-rehabilitation alternatives at the City's sole discretion; Chapter 20.80.080 allows reducing moderate income unit counts when units are instead restricted to very low or low income.
next_deadline: Threshold adjusts each calendar year. Housing Element Program 11 requires a further look at inclusionary ratios at the 2028 RHNA mid-point; Program 12 calls for considering a commercial linkage fee and single-family impact fee changes with other Marin jurisdictions.
layering_notes: The 2026 drop from 25% to 15% (half low, half moderate) brings Mill Valley below Novato (20%) and the County (20%) and closer to San Rafael's 5% to 10%; combined with the Housing Overlay Districts (17 to 40 units per acre) it is meant to make 7-plus unit infill feasible on commercial corridors. The impact fee is the engine of the Trust Fund record above; no commercial linkage fee exists yet. The 2026 ordinance PDF (Attachment 1, as adopted per the City zoning updates page), the Zoneomics mirror of Chapter 20.80, the 2024 APR and the Housing Element were opened; the City's eCode360 host was not needed.

program_name: Mill Valley development fee waivers for affordable housing (MVMC 5.32 as amended October 3, 2022, Housing Element Programs 14 and 23) and lot merger fee waiver in the Opportunity Site Housing Overlay
administering_agency: City of Mill Valley Planning and Building Department; City Council resolution for waivers
typical_award_size: 100% waiver of City application processing fees for projects managed and operated by affordable housing organizations when at least 10% of units serve very low income households (Housing Element Program 14 text) or extremely low income households (Program 23 and 2024 APR wording), adopted by ordinance and resolution in October 2022. Lot merger fees are waived for projects using the Opportunity Site Housing Overlay (Ordinance establishing the overlays, 2024). Affordable projects are also exempt from the Chapter 20.80 impact fee. Dollar value depends on the City fee schedule; a handout on incentives was a 2024 work plan item.
affordability_requirement: At least 10% of units for very low or extremely low income households and operation by an affordable housing organization; the City also may consider a fee waiver program for ADUs under Program 30.
next_deadline: Request at application. Confirm the exact MVMC 5.32 threshold (very low versus extremely low) with Planning before underwriting; the two City documents read describe it differently.
layering_notes: A processing-fee waiver is worth tens of thousands of dollars on a Mill Valley project, not a gap closer, but it counts as public funds under Labor Code 1720(b)(4). Stack with the Trust Fund, the housing overlays and State Density Bonus. Mill Valley's title 5 code text was not opened (eCode360 not attempted); terms come from the certified 2023-2031 Housing Element Chapter 4 (opened), the 2024 Annual Progress Report (opened) and the overlay ordinance (opened). marincounty.gov remained Cloudflare-blocked this pass; County programs are referenced from the Marin County records in this database.

program_name: Mill Valley Density Bonus (MVMC Chapter 20.81) and Housing Overlay Zoning Districts (Small Lot, Office Conversion and Opportunity Site overlays, 2024 ordinance)
administering_agency: City of Mill Valley Planning and Building Department
typical_award_size: Requirement framework, not a cash subsidy. Chapter 20.81 applies Government Code 65915 by reference (bonus, incentives, waivers, parking ratios; senior projects get no concessions unless state law requires). The 2024 Housing Overlay Districts, applied on top of base zoning to Housing Element sites, allow 17 to 40 units per acre (20 to 40 in the Opportunity Site overlay), 40-foot height, one parking space for units of 1,000 square feet or less, waived lot merger fees, and let projects also use State Density Bonus to modify standards; projects reserving 20% of units for lower income households get streamlined review. Affordable units in overlay projects follow Chapter 20.80 deed restriction rules. Bayfront Terrace (45 units) was rezoned to RM-B and approved as a 100% affordable project using density bonus incentives but not the density increase.
affordability_requirement: State thresholds for Chapter 20.81; overlay projects must meet Chapter 20.80 inclusionary (15% since 2026) or provide 20% lower income units for the streamlined path. Density bonus affordability covenants recorded before building permit (20.81.050).
next_deadline: None. The 2026 inclusionary ordinance also updated the Opportunity Site overlay to the 15% standard and removed micro-unit restrictions; parking standards were updated November 3, 2025.
layering_notes: Mill Valley's overlays are the practical density path because base multifamily zoning is scarce; combine overlay density with the State bonus, the 15% inclusionary rule and the Trust Fund. No local bonus exceeds state law. Overlay ordinance (DocumentCenter 7829) and the Zoneomics mirror of Chapter 20.81 were opened; the City's eCode360 host was not attempted.

program_name: City-owned land for affordable housing: Bayfront Terrace at 1 Hamilton Drive (EAH Housing, 45 units, Lease, Development and Loan Agreement) under Housing Element Program 10
administering_agency: City of Mill Valley (City Manager and Planning and Building Department) with EAH Housing as developer
typical_award_size: Land plus local loan. The City declared the northern 1.60 acres of 1 Hamilton Drive exempt surplus land (Sept 20, 2021), selected EAH Housing through an RFQ and ENA, approved the project, EIR and a Lease, Development and Loan Agreement with a 99-year ground lease on February 5, 2024, and reapproved it with a 0.15-acre smaller footprint on January 12 and 20, 2026 to use a 2025 CEQA statutory exemption. City money committed: $1,000,000 from the Affordable Housing Trust Fund ($500,000 City match plus $500,000 requested HCD LHTF grant) toward the extremely low income units, after Trust Fund payment of predevelopment and environmental costs. Marin County Trust Fund awards of $500,000 (2022) and a reported $1,000,000 total appear in County documents cited in search results (not opened).
affordability_requirement: 44 restricted units plus one manager unit: 9 at or below 50% AMI, 9 at or below 60% AMI, 26 at or below 80% AMI, with at least 40% of units at or below 60% AMI and half of those at or below 50% AMI (Surplus Land Act), all subject to a TCAC regulatory agreement.
next_deadline: EAH is assembling tax credit and other financing; leasing interest sign-ups were anticipated for early 2026 and construction timing depends on credit awards. No other City-owned site is in process.
layering_notes: Mill Valley's first affordable development in about three decades and the model for how the City layers: surplus land under a 99-year lease, Trust Fund match, County Trust Fund, HOME through the Marin Urban County, and 4% or 9% credits with CMFA bonds. For a third-party developer the record shows that City resources are already concentrated here through at least 2027. Hamilton Drive project page, Jan 12, 2026 Council agenda and staff report (270 pages, Granicus) and Resolution 24-60 opened. marincounty.gov remained Cloudflare-blocked this pass; County programs are referenced from the Marin County records in this database.

program_name: Concord Inclusionary Housing Ordinance (Concord Development Code Chapter 18.185.040, Ord. 24-1) and in-lieu fee (Fees and Charges Schedule, Res. 26-6042.1)
administering_agency: City of Concord Housing and Community Services Division (Sophia Huckabay, Housing Manager, 925-671-3387) with the Planning Division
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Projects of 5 or more units: ownership projects 15% inclusionary (7.5% low, 7.5% moderate); rental projects 6% inclusionary (1% very low, 1% low, 4% moderate), with a fixed rotation order for each inclusionary unit. In-lieu fee effective July 1, 2026 (adjusted annually by a construction cost index): $20.13 per gross square foot of market-rate development for ownership projects and $15.10 per gross square foot for rental projects of 10 or more units; fractional-unit fee $256,497 x fractional unit (ownership) and $174,160 x fractional unit (rental). Rental projects may pay the fee for the whole obligation; ownership projects may pay only for fractional units or for 5 to 9 unit projects. In the five years before the 2023 Housing Element the City collected only about $170,000 in in-lieu fees.
affordability_requirement: Rental inclusionary units restricted 55 years and ownership units 45 years under a recorded Affordable Housing Agreement; density bonus units meeting the table income levels count toward the inclusionary requirement; projects of 1 to 4 units, replacement of units lost to natural disaster, and office-to-residential conversions of buildings commercial for at least 5 years are exempt.
eligible_project_types: market-rate rental and ownership projects of 5 or more units (compliance)
off-site acquisition-rehab (2 rehabilitated units per required unit)
next_deadline: Applies at entitlement; fee rate in effect at building permit. Fee schedule last adopted April 28, 2026 (Res. 26-6042.1) effective July 1, 2026; the schedule is readopted each spring. Housing Element Program 12.4 called for a fee update by July 2024, which produced the March 14, 2024 fee basis now indexed annually.
layering_notes: Low rental percentage (6%) and a relatively low rental in-lieu fee ($15.10 per square foot) mean most Concord apartment projects either build a handful of moderate-income units or pay the fee; this is why the City's inclusionary fund is small relative to Walnut Creek's. In-lieu revenue goes to a restricted fund alongside the Concord Housing Fund (see the Concord Affordable Housing Fund record). Chapter 18.185.040(G) also lets the City grant development incentives, including deferral of development fees until first occupancy (approved by the City Manager) and expedited processing, when an affordable housing agreement is signed. County Chapter 822-4 inclusionary ordinance does not apply inside Concord. codepublishing.com (the City's code host) returns 403 to automated access; chapter text was read on the zoneomics mirror (https://www.zoneomics.com/code/concord-CA/chapter_4) and the City's 2024 Inclusionary Housing Ordinance Summary Sheet (https://www.cityofconcord.org/DocumentCenter/View/13659). Fee amounts were read from the adopted July 1, 2026 fee schedule (source_url).

program_name: Concord Affordable Housing Fund and Concord Housing Fund (Housing Successor Low and Moderate Income Housing Asset Fund, SB 341 report FY 2024/25)
administering_agency: City of Concord Housing and Community Services Division (Housing Successor to the former Concord Redevelopment Agency)
typical_award_size: Housing Successor fund at June 30, 2025: available cash $3,063,558; FY 2024/25 deposits $1,020,949 (including a $615,049 Pavilion loan repayment and $222,705 in loan payoffs); FY 2024/25 expenditures $596,214 (mostly $334,957 in first-time homebuyer loans; no multifamily loan issued); housing loans receivable $33.9 million. The 2023 Housing Element reported a combined Housing Trust Fund balance of about $6.2 million including inclusionary in-lieu fees. Track record: Spring 2018 NOFA offered $14 million of City Affordable Housing Funds and awarded $7.8 million to Resources for Community Development for the 62-unit Rick Judd Commons at 1313-1321 Galindo Street (opened 2025). The Housing Element committed to another NOFA by December 2025 for the remaining funds, including acquisition-rehab of existing affordable complexes; as of November 2026 the City's Affordable Housing Toolkit states there is currently no affordable housing development funding available and invites acquisition-rehab proposals to the Housing Manager.
per_unit_cap: None published; 2018 awards ran about $126,000 per unit.
affordability_requirement: Housing Successor funds must follow Health and Safety Code 34176.1: at least 30% to rental housing for households at or below 30% AMI, no more than 20% for 60% to 80% AMI, balance at or below 60% AMI; the City's five-year extremely-low-income test (July 2020 to June 2025) showed 0% spent on ELI rental housing, so the next multifamily award is likely to be steered to ELI units. City-funded projects carry long-term regulatory agreements (Rick Judd Commons is 55 years).
next_deadline: No NOFA open as of 2026-11-08; the Housing Element's December 2025 NOFA target was not met. Watch Council Housing and Economic Development Committee agendas (stream2.ci.concord.ca.us OnBase agenda portal) for a NOFA tied to the next TCAC rounds; contact Sophia Huckabay, Housing Manager, 925-671-3387.
layering_notes: Concord's own fund is modest (about $3 million liquid in the successor fund plus in-lieu balances) and is best used as the local match that unlocks County HOME, CDBG-Housing and Measure X awards (county records: Contra Costa County Affordable Housing Program, Measure X Housing Fund). Lakeside Recapitalization (RCD, Concord) received $2 million County HOME in May 2026 without City funds, showing County money can lead. The City's Resources for Housing Developers page points developers first to County Measure X and HCD. Gap order for a Concord deal: 4% credits and bonds, County HOME or Measure X, then a City successor-fund loan sized to the ELI set-aside, plus fee deferral under CDC 18.185.040(G). The OnBase agenda portal is JavaScript-only, so 2025 and 2026 council items could not be scanned for a NOFA; status taken from the Toolkit page (https://www.cityofconcord.org/1174/Affordable-Housing-Toolkit) and the SB 341 report (source_url).

program_name: Concord Affordable Housing Incentive Program (CDC 18.185.060), Density Bonus Program (CDC 18.185.050) and Transit Station Overlay density increase
administering_agency: City of Concord Community Development Department, Planning Division (zoning@cityofconcord.org, 925-671-3152)
typical_award_size: Regulatory incentive, not a cash subsidy. Local alternative to state density bonus law for projects with at least 40% affordable units on parcels of 10,000 square feet or more in RM, RH, CO, NC, CMX, DMX and DP districts: RM density rises from 32 to about 45 units per acre (1 unit per 970 square feet, a 40% bonus), RH from 100 to about 145 units per acre (45% bonus), NC from 24 to about 33 units per acre plus FAR increases; reduced parking and other standard modifications; bonuses under 18.185.060 are not additive with 18.185.050. Separately, the Transit Station Overlay District grants a 25% density and floor area increase (Housing Element program to make it by right with objective standards). State-law density bonuses (Gov. Code 65915) are processed by the Community Development Department under 18.185.050; written findings are required to deny; an affordable housing agreement is recorded before building permit.
affordability_requirement: 18.185.060 rental eligibility: at least 20% of units at very low income plus another 20% at low or very low income (40% total); for-sale: 20% at low or very low plus 20% at up to 100% AMI. 18.185.050 follows state density bonus thresholds.
next_deadline: Applies at entitlement; no deadline. Concord completed its AFFH rezoning (at least 1,000 lower-income units of capacity in higher-resource areas) in March 2026 and allows multifamily by right in commercial and mixed-use districts when objective design standards are met.
layering_notes: The 40% affordability threshold for the local incentive program is high, so most mixed-income projects use state density bonus law instead; 100% affordable projects (which qualify for an 80% state bonus or unlimited density near transit) get the most value from the local program's FAR and parking relief in downtown districts. No City fee waiver program exists; fee deferral to first occupancy is available under 18.185.040(G) by affordable housing agreement. Pair with the County's conduit bond issuer and HACCC project-based vouchers (county records). codepublishing.com returned 403; chapter text read on the zoneomics mirror (source_url) and confirmed against the City's Affordable Housing Toolkit page.

program_name: Concord CDBG entitlement and Contra Costa Consortium three-year NOFA (FY 2027/28 to 2029/30)
administering_agency: City of Concord Housing and Community Services Division (Sophia Huckabay, sophia.huckabay@cityofconcord.org) within the Contra Costa HOME Consortium
typical_award_size: Concord is a CDBG entitlement city; its FY 2026/27 HUD entitlement was estimated at $967,306 in the City's public notice (figure from a search snippet of the notice, not an opened City page). Concord's HOME share is pooled in the County-administered Contra Costa HOME Consortium (Antioch, Concord, Pittsburg, Walnut Creek and the Urban County). The Consortium released the FY 2027/28 RFP and NOFA on October 15, 2026 (City Data Services) for CDBG and ESG, covering a three-year cycle FY 2027/28 through 2029/30; one joint application serves all five jurisdictions. Concord historically uses CDBG for public services, homeowner rehabilitation, fair housing and public facilities, with housing development funded from the City's own funds.
affordability_requirement: CDBG national objective (low and moderate income benefit, 80% AMI); HOME requests go through the County (55-year County regulatory agreement).
application_cycle: annual NOFA (three-year cycle; applications due December 7, 2026)
next_deadline: Applications due Monday, December 7, 2026 at 5:00 PM via City Data Services; Concord Council adopts the FY 2027/28 Action Plan in April or May 2027 for a July 1, 2027 program year.
layering_notes: For multifamily development, treat Concord CDBG as minor (fair housing and rehab set-asides) and apply to the County for HOME and Measure X through the same Consortium application (county record: Contra Costa County Affordable Housing Program: HOME and CDBG-Housing). Davis-Bacon applies to CDBG-assisted projects of 8 or more units and HOME projects of 12 or more. The Consortium NOFA dates and Concord contact were read on the City of Antioch's Community Grants page (source_url), which lists all Consortium contacts; Concord's own CDBG page could not be located on cityofconcord.org (several guessed URLs 404) and the FY 2026/27 Action Plan PDF was not opened, hence needs_confirmation for the Concord dollar figure.

program_name: Concord Naval Weapons Station Reuse Project affordable housing requirement (Concord Reuse Project Area Plan, 2012; 2026 Navy EDC Term Sheet; Brookfield master developer)
administering_agency: City of Concord Economic Development and Base Reuse Division, acting as Local Reuse Authority (1950 Parkside Drive MS/56, 925-671-3001)
typical_award_size: Requirement and future land pipeline, not a current subsidy. The Area Plan and Reuse Plan call for about 12,000 housing units on roughly 2,300 to 2,400 acres, of which 25% (about 3,000 units) must be affordable to low and very low income households, including 125 supportive housing units, 195 units for people experiencing homelessness and 20 self-help units. The Council approved the Navy financial Term Sheet and revised Brookfield Term Sheet on May 26, 2026 (reported Navy price $628 million over 30 years); the Navy executed the Economic Development Conveyance Term Sheet in September 2026; SB 328 (2026) was signed; Brookfield is now preparing the Specific Plan with community engagement starting early 2027.
affordability_requirement: 25% of all units affordable to low and very low income households per the Area Plan; specific income tiers, phasing and affordable-site delivery mechanics will be set in the Specific Plan and Disposition and Development Agreement.
application_cycle: closed/inactive (future pipeline; Specific Plan expected 2027 or later)
next_deadline: No affordable developer solicitation yet. Brookfield-led Specific Plan work starts winter 2026-27; first phase entitlements likely 2028 or later. Monitor concordreuseproject.org news flashes and the semiannual CRP Program Report.
layering_notes: The largest single affordable pipeline in central Contra Costa (about 3,000 deed-restricted units over three decades), delivered through Brookfield's affordable-site dedications to nonprofit partners rather than City cash; Brookfield also has a project labor agreement with the Contra Costa Building Trades, so prevailing or union wages should be assumed on the affordable sites. Nonprofit developers should position for receiver-site selection and plan to layer County Measure X and HOME, HACCC project-based vouchers and 4% credits on each phase. The 25% figure and homeless and supportive sub-allocations were read in the City's certified Housing Element Programs Document (source_url); the term sheet milestone was read on the Concord Community Reuse Project site (http://www.concordreuseproject.org/m/newsflash/home/detail/95).

program_name: Concord surplus and underutilized public land for affordable housing (Concord Town Center II at 1765 Galindo Street, Downtown Parcels at Laguna and Mount Diablo Streets, Housing Element surplus land program)
administering_agency: City of Concord Housing and Community Services Division and Planning Division (surplus land inventory, Housing Element sites program)
typical_award_size: Land contribution rather than cash. City-owned surplus sites declared May 24, 2022: Concord Town Center II, 1765 Galindo Street, 3.1 vacant acres zoned DMX, Housing Element site for 309 lower-income units and an MTC Priority Site; the City issued an RFP in January 2025 and as of November 2025 is negotiating with a selected developer for sale and entitlement. Concord Downtown Parcels 1 (Mount Diablo Street, 3.2 acres, 304 lower-income units) and 2 (Oak Street, 1.1 acres, 106 lower-income units) are surplus DMX sites with an MTC technical assistance grant studying street vacations. BART's Monument Boulevard property (8.2 acres, 782 mixed-income units) is in BART's 2029-2033 solicitation window. The City committed that surplus land used for housing will provide at least 25% of units affordable to lower-income households and to notify a developer list before any disposal.
affordability_requirement: Minimum 25% lower-income units on City surplus land (Surplus Land Act and Housing Element program); the Galindo and Downtown sites are inventoried for lower-income RHNA capacity, so deeper affordability is expected in dispositions.
next_deadline: Town Center II negotiations under way as of November 2025; Downtown Parcels RFP timing depends on the street-vacation study. Join the City's housing interested-parties list (FormCenter link on the Housing and Community Services page) for Surplus Land Act notices.
layering_notes: City land write-downs are the main way Concord adds local value to a deal given its small housing fund; a land contribution plus a City successor-fund loan, County HOME or Measure X and a HACCC PBV allocation is the realistic stack. Public land dispositions trigger Surplus Land Act procedures and, with any City financial participation, prevailing wage under Labor Code 1720. Inventory read from the City's publicly owned and surplus sites list (source_url), linked from the Affordable Housing Toolkit page.

program_name: Richmond Inclusionary Housing and Affordable Housing Linkage Fee Ordinance (Richmond Municipal Code Article 15.04.603, readopted 2020) and in-lieu fee
administering_agency: City of Richmond Community Development Department, Housing Division (Jesus Morales, Housing Manager, 510-620-6649) and Planning Division
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Applies to residential and mixed-use projects of 10 or more units. Compliance options: for-sale projects 7% of units at low income or 10% at moderate income; rental projects 9% at very low income or 10% at low income. The in-lieu fee is per square foot and geographically tiered, $0 to $12 per square foot (rental projects south of I-580 and on the Point San Pablo peninsula pay $12 per square foot; market-rate projects north of I-580 are exempt from on-site units and the fee after a 2020 feasibility study); for-sale projects south of I-580 and on Point San Pablo must build units and may not pay the fee. A non-residential affordable housing linkage fee was authorized in the same 2020 update. Collections: $803,055 in-lieu fees in calendar 2020 and $677,194 in 2021. Other alternatives: 10% very low income rental units in a for-sale project, off-site construction, or land dedication yielding at least 10% more units than required.
affordability_requirement: 45-year affordability for for-sale inclusionary units and 55 years for rental units under a recorded Inclusionary Housing Agreement; incentives include the Article 15.04.602 density bonus, clustering of units where a funding source requires it, and smaller or different unit types if at least 5% more affordable units result.
eligible_project_types: market-rate rental and for-sale projects of 10 or more units (compliance)
off-site construction and land dedication alternatives
next_deadline: Applies at entitlement; fee due per the Inclusionary Housing Agreement. Housing Element Program 2.A called for reassessment of the ordinance and linkage fee by first quarter 2024 and any amendments by third quarter 2025, with annual performance reports; confirm with the Housing Division whether amendments were adopted.
layering_notes: Richmond's 2020 rewrite deliberately lowered requirements north of I-580 (Hilltop, North Richmond edge) to make market-rate housing feasible, so most inclusionary units and fees come from the south side (Marina Bay, downtown, Point San Pablo). Fees and linkage revenue fund the City Affordable Housing Fund (separate record). Richmond's Rent Program (Measure L, 2016) caps rent increases on pre-1995 multifamily and sets just-cause rules, which affects underwriting of acquisition-rehab deals. The County's Chapter 822-4 inclusionary ordinance does not apply inside Richmond. ci.richmond.ca.us pages for the ordinance redirect to a login page and the Municode host is blocked, so terms were read from the City's adopted 2023-2031 Housing Element (Resolution 7-23, source_url, Appendix C and Appendix G); the $12 per square foot tier was corroborated in the City of Antioch's January 2026 countywide in-lieu fee comparison (Attachment G to the March 10, 2026 Antioch council packet).

program_name: Richmond Affordable Housing Fund (RMC 15.04.603.130; inclusionary in-lieu and linkage fee revenue)
administering_agency: City of Richmond Community Development Department, Housing Division
typical_award_size: Dedicated local fund receiving all in-lieu fees, linkage fees and related revenue under Article 15.04.603. Known deposits: $803,055 (2020) and $677,194 (2021) in in-lieu fees; the only reported expenditures in 2020-2021 were $69,165 for legal services on the ordinance amendments, so the fund has been accumulating. Eligible uses: land acquisition, predevelopment, rehabilitation with added affordability restrictions, new construction, administration and compliance monitoring. No published NOFA, loan guidelines or current balance were found; the Housing Element requires the balance and expenditures to be reported in each Annual Progress Report.
affordability_requirement: Extremely low, very low, lower and moderate income households and special needs populations; long-term affordability covenants expected to match the inclusionary terms (55 years rental).
application_cycle: rolling (no published NOFA; request through the Housing Division)
next_deadline: Unknown, verify with agency. Ask the Housing Division for the current fund balance (reported in the City's Housing Element Annual Progress Report each spring) and whether Council has set award guidelines.
layering_notes: Small but growing local source (likely several million dollars by 2026) with no competing formal process, so an early developer request to the Housing Division and Council can secure it as predevelopment or gap money alongside County HOME and Measure X (county records), HACCC project-based vouchers and the County conduit bond program. Richmond's recent large deals relied on State and County money (Trinity Plaza received $2.5 million County CDBG and $1.5 million HOME in May 2026; the Civic Center Homekey conversion carries a City loan increased to $10.3 million in February 2026 from other City sources). Fund mechanics were read from the adopted Housing Element (source_url) because City ordinance pages redirect to a login and Municode is blocked.

program_name: Richmond Low and Moderate Income Housing Assets Fund (Housing Successor to the Richmond Community Redevelopment Agency; Housing Element Program 2.C)
administering_agency: City of Richmond as Successor Agency to the Richmond Community Redevelopment Agency, Housing and Community Development (HCD) Division, 450 Civic Center Plaza
typical_award_size: Housing successor assets (real property, bond proceeds, loan and rent payments) used for affordable housing. Track record: funded development of Miraflores Senior Housing (80 units, completed June 2018, leased by August 2019, with 79 Richmond Housing Authority project-based vouchers) and about $1.1 million toward the RAD renovation of Friendship Manor and other former public housing. No current balance or SB 341 report was found online; the City is required to publish one annually.
affordability_requirement: Health and Safety Code 34176.1 targeting: at least 30% of expenditures for rental housing at or below 30% AMI, no more than 20% for 60% to 80% AMI, balance at or below 60% AMI; 55-year covenants on successor-funded rental housing.
next_deadline: Unknown, verify with agency. Request the latest SB 341 Housing Successor annual report from the Housing Division; Housing Element Program 2.C commits the City to seek new sources (including social impact bonds) for low-mod housing assets on an ongoing basis.
layering_notes: Richmond's former redevelopment areas (Iron Triangle, Harbour, Hilltop, Nevin) left land assets that the City can contribute to deals; Nevin Plaza Phase II (EAH, 76 units) and the Hacienda Apartments rehabilitation (150 units, CDBG-assisted) are current examples of City-assisted projects. Successor funds stack with HOME, Measure X and the County conduit bond program (county records) and with HACCC project-based vouchers, which now administer the former Richmond Housing Authority voucher program. The Successor Agency web page (https://www.ci.richmond.ca.us/97/Successor-Agency-To-Redevelopment) was opened but is dated (2015-2016 Oversight Board materials); program details were read from the adopted Housing Element (source_url).

program_name: Richmond Affordable Housing Density Bonus (RMC Article 15.04.602) and Housing Element Program 3.D
administering_agency: City of Richmond Community Development Department, Planning Division
typical_award_size: Regulatory incentive, not a cash subsidy. Article 15.04.602 implements state density bonus law; the Housing Element acknowledges the article lagged recent state amendments (AB 2345 and later) and commits the City to apply current state law directly and to update the ordinance (target fourth quarter 2025). Richmond also eliminated parking minimums near transit under AB 2097 (Program 1.L), offers expedited review for housing (Program 1.E), objective design standards in the form-based code (Program 3.C), and inclusionary incentives such as unit clustering and smaller unit types. No local bonus above state law.
affordability_requirement: State density bonus law thresholds (Gov. Code 65915); density bonus units with qualifying affordability count toward Richmond's inclusionary requirement.
next_deadline: Applies at entitlement; ordinance conformance update was targeted for fourth quarter 2025, verify adoption with the Planning Division.
layering_notes: No local housing trust fund NOFA, fee waiver program or local density bonus enhancement exists beyond state law in Richmond; the City's development impact fees are being converted to per square foot (Program 2.B, by 2027) which helps smaller units. Stack state density bonus with County conduit bonds, HOME and Measure X (county records) and the City's Affordable Housing Fund. Source is the adopted Housing Element (source_url); the City's Housing Element Progress page (https://www.ci.richmond.ca.us/4836/Housing-Element-Progress) shows 1,016 units entitled and 326 permitted through December 2024, 65% of entitled units at or below 80% AMI.

program_name: Richmond CDBG and HOME entitlement funds (Housing Division) and Richmond Housing Authority project-based voucher legacy
administering_agency: City of Richmond Community Development Department, Housing Division (Jesus Morales, Housing Manager, 510-620-6649); Richmond Housing Authority (Antoinette Terrell, Executive Director, 510-621-1300)
typical_award_size: Richmond is a HUD entitlement jurisdiction outside the Contra Costa HOME Consortium (HUD announced $1,092,323 CDBG for Richmond in 2015; current amounts were not found on an opened City page). The Housing Element lists CDBG as a City resource and cites the CDBG-assisted rehabilitation of the 150-unit Hacienda Apartments (vacant since 2015). The Richmond Housing Authority transferred its Housing Choice Voucher program (about 1,700 vouchers including project-based vouchers) to the Housing Authority of the County of Contra Costa and now owns Nevin Plaza and Nystrom Village under RAD; Miraflores received 79 RHA project-based vouchers before the transfer.
affordability_requirement: CDBG national objective (80% AMI); HOME rents and 20-year or longer HOME affordability periods; HACCC PBV requirements for voucher-assisted units.
next_deadline: Unknown, verify with agency. Richmond adopts its own Annual Action Plan each spring (PY July 1); ask the Housing Division for the FY 2027/28 application schedule.
layering_notes: Because Richmond is not in the County HOME Consortium, Richmond projects cannot apply for County HOME; they rely on Richmond's own CDBG and HOME, County Measure X and CDBG-Housing (the County awarded Trinity Plaza $2.5 million CDBG and $1.5 million HOME in May 2026, which indicates County CDBG-Housing and HOME do reach Richmond sites; confirm eligibility with County DCD), the Richmond/Contra Costa CoC (CA-505, county record) and HACCC PBVs. The Housing Element's statement that the City is part of the Contra Costa CDBG Urban County conflicts with Richmond's entitlement status and should be confirmed. The Housing Division page (https://www.ci.richmond.ca.us/98/Housing-Division) was opened but lists only staff contacts; no Action Plan or NOFA document could be located on ci.richmond.ca.us (several pages 404 or redirect to login), hence needs_confirmation. Source is the adopted Housing Element (source_url).

program_name: Antioch Inclusionary Housing Ordinance (proposed AMC Title 9, Chapter 5, Article 43) and Inclusionary Housing Trust Fund (not adopted; continued into the General Plan Update on March 10, 2026)
administering_agency: City of Antioch Community Development Department, Planning Division (Zoe Merideth, Planning Manager, 925-779-6159)
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy, and not in effect. Proposed terms: all residential projects of 5 or more units citywide; 15% of units affordable (10% very low income, 5% low income) in perpetuity; in-lieu fee $202,500 per required unit not built (PlaceWorks financing-gap method: $440,000 Antioch development cost per unit times a 46.02% countywide gap), adjusted each July 1 by CPI and due at building permit; an Inclusionary Housing Trust Fund with administrative guidelines (new construction, preservation, acquisition-rehab, ADUs, predevelopment loans, land purchase, homebuyer assistance) and an annual compliance monitoring fee. The Planning Commission recommended adoption 4-0 on February 4, 2026 (Resolution 2026-02, asking for Antioch resident priority, union preference and ELI priority). On March 10, 2026 the City Council voted 4-1 to continue the IHO into the broader General Plan Update instead of adopting it.
affordability_requirement: Proposed: 15% of units at very low (10%) and low (5%) income, affordable in perpetuity, with units at least 90% of market-rate unit size and the same bedroom mix.
eligible_project_types: market-rate residential projects of 5 or more units (compliance, if adopted)
application_cycle: closed/inactive (not adopted; folded into the General Plan Update)
next_deadline: No adoption date. Track the Antioch General Plan Update (antioch.generalplan.org) for the inclusionary and trust fund components; a review every two years after adoption was proposed and would set the first in-lieu fee review.
layering_notes: Antioch currently has no inclusionary requirement, no in-lieu fee and no local housing trust fund, so market-rate developers face no affordable obligation and affordable developers have no City trust fund to apply to; the only City money is Housing Successor and PLHA (separate record). If adopted later, the $202,500 per unit fee would be the highest flat fee in the county (Pleasant Hill charges $271,350; Concord $15.10 to $20.13 per square foot; Walnut Creek $26.04 per square foot; San Ramon $15.16 per square foot for small projects). The County's Chapter 822-4 ordinance does not apply inside Antioch. antiochca.gov returns 403 to automated access; the ca-antioch.civicplus.com mirror serves the same pages, and the full March 10, 2026 council packet (399 pages, including Attachment G countywide fee comparison) was read at source_url.

program_name: Antioch Community Grants: CDBG, Housing Successor (LMIHAF) and PLHA funds (FY 2027/28 to 2029/30 cycle via the Contra Costa Consortium NOFA)
administering_agency: City of Antioch Community Services Department, Housing and Homelessness Division (housing@antiochca.gov, cdbg@antiochca.gov, 925-779-7082, 4703 Lone Tree Way)
typical_award_size: Antioch anticipates about $850,000 CDBG, $350,000 PLHA and $500,000 Housing Successor funds per year for the FY 2027-2030 cycle (about 30 programs funded annually; the City notes that funding for affordable housing development is limited and directs developers to County HOME). 2025-2030 Consolidated Plan anticipated resources: CDBG $911,040 annual allocation plus $272,888 program income and $1,174,496 prior-year resources in year 1 (prior-year includes $1,257,347 returned by Hope Solutions after a project did not proceed); PLHA $509,164 year 1 and $1,416,898 remainder; Housing Successor $600,000 year 1 and $1,750,000 remainder, of which $350,000 per year funds homeless shelter, services and prevention. Five-year goals include PLHA $150,000 for 10 new rental units, CDBG $850,000 for 65 homeless housing units, CDBG $1,367,157 plus PLHA $609,164 for 50 owner rehabs, and Housing Successor and PLHA loans for ADUs (25 ADUs). Antioch's HOME share is administered by the County through the HOME Consortium.
per_unit_cap: None published; the 2025-30 plan assumes about $15,000 per unit for new rental units and about $13,000 per homeless housing unit.
affordability_requirement: CDBG 80% AMI national objective; Housing Successor funds follow Health and Safety Code 34176.1 (at least 30% to rental housing at or below 30% AMI); PLHA eligible activities for households at or below 60% AMI for rental; City priority on 30% and 50% AMI households.
next_deadline: Applications due Monday, December 7, 2026 at 5:00 PM through City Data Services (one joint application for Antioch, Concord, Pittsburg, Walnut Creek and the County); the Antioch CDBG Grant Committee (two councilmembers) hears presentations February to March 2027; Council adopts the FY 2027/28 Action Plan April to May 2027; funds effective July 1, 2027.
layering_notes: Antioch's local layer is thin (about $500,000 per year of Housing Successor money, much of it committed to homeless services) and there is no inclusionary trust fund, so Antioch deals depend on County HOME, CDBG-Housing and Measure X (county records), HACCC project-based vouchers, the County conduit bond program and State programs; the $2 million Housing Successor goal for 30 permanent supportive housing units in the prior Consolidated Plan went unspent after the Hope Solutions project fell through, so staff are motivated to place successor funds in a viable PSH or ELI project. Housing Successor compliance reporting (AB 987 and SB 341) is posted at https://ca-antioch.civicplus.com/1005/Housing-Successor-Reporting-Compliance. antiochca.gov returns 403; the civicplus mirror (source_url) and the 2026-27 Action Plan PDF (https://ca-antioch.civicplus.com/DocumentCenter/View/5073/2026-27-Antioch-Action-Plan) were read this pass.

program_name: Antioch Housing Element incentives for lower-income housing (Programs 2.1.6, 2.1.7 and 4.1.3: fee support, land write-downs, expedited processing, density bonus ordinance)
administering_agency: City of Antioch Community Development Department, Planning Division, with CDBG and Housing Programs staff
typical_award_size: Regulatory and discretionary incentives, not a funded program. The certified 2023-2031 Housing Element (HCD certification October 12, 2023) commits the City to encourage extremely low income housing through targeted developer outreach, financial or in-kind technical assistance, fee support, land write-downs and expedited or priority processing, and to offer incentives supplementing state density bonus law (quantified objective: 175 ELI units); to meet at least three nonprofit developers annually and support funding applications; and to keep the density bonus ordinance consistent with state law (Program 4.1.3). Rezoning under the Housing Element raises many sites to 35 units per acre, and the Commercial Infill Housing (CIH) Overlay allows housing on commercial sites. No adopted fee waiver schedule exists; the proposed inclusionary ordinance expressly excluded fee waivers.
affordability_requirement: Case by case; state density bonus thresholds apply; City incentives target extremely low, very low and low income and special needs housing.
next_deadline: Applies at entitlement; no deadline. Housing Element program review occurs with each Annual Progress Report (April).
layering_notes: Antioch has no local fee waiver ordinance, housing trust fund or in-lieu fund, so these Housing Element commitments are the only local incentives beyond state density bonus law; developers should negotiate fee deferrals, land contributions from the City's surplus list (largest parcel about 5 acres, per the Consolidated Plan) and Housing Successor or PLHA gap loans as part of entitlement. Density bonus and incentives stack with County HOME, Measure X and HACCC PBVs (county records). Programs read from the certified Housing Element Goals, Policies and Programs chapter on the civicplus mirror (source_url) because antiochca.gov returns 403.

program_name: Walnut Creek Inclusionary Housing Ordinance (Zoning Code Article 9, Sections 10-2.3.903 et seq., amended November 2017) and housing in-lieu fee
administering_agency: City of Walnut Creek Housing Division (Housing Programs), Community and Economic Development Department
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Applies to all residential development of one or more units except ADUs and disaster replacement units. New ownership projects: 10% moderate, or 7% low, or 6% very low income units, or pay the in-lieu fee (ownership projects of any size may pay the fee). New rental projects: 10% low or 6% very low income units, or pay the fee (rental units restored after AB 1505). Condominium conversions: 15% low or 11% very low. Fractions of 0.7 or more round up; partial fee payment allowed pro rata; blended income levels allowed. In-lieu fee reset to $18.00 per square foot effective January 1, 2018 with annual construction-price-index adjustments ($19.27 in 2021; about $26.04 per square foot in 2026 per the City of Antioch's January 2026 countywide comparison). Walnut Creek Transit Village alone paid over $4 million in in-lieu fees and is expected to generate $6 to 7 million for the City's Housing Trust Fund.
affordability_requirement: Rental inclusionary units affordable 55 years and ownership units 45 years; units dispersed on site with the same bedroom mix and comparable quality; one-for-one replacement of demolished low-income units built within 30 years.
eligible_project_types: off-site construction and land dedication alternatives
next_deadline: Applies at entitlement; fee indexed each January. Housing Element Program H-2.D (6th cycle) continues the ordinance and contemplates an updated nexus study; confirm the current per square foot fee with the Housing Division (brynen@walnutcreekca.gov).
layering_notes: Walnut Creek's fee-first ordinance is the engine of its Local Housing Trust Fund (separate record): most downtown and BART-area apartment projects pay the per square foot fee rather than build 6% very low income units, which is why the City can fund 42 to 97 unit affordable projects itself. The County's Chapter 822-4 ordinance does not apply inside the city. walnutcreekca.gov (including showpublisheddocument PDFs) returns 403 to automated access; ordinance terms were read from the City's 2023-2031 Housing Element hosted by HCD (source_url, Chapter 3 Section 3.3.7 and Chapter 6) and the 2026 fee level from the Antioch comparison table.

program_name: Walnut Creek Commercial Linkage Fee (Zoning Code Part IV, Chapter 13, Fee on Commercial Development for Affordable Housing; 2005, amended November 2017)
administering_agency: City of Walnut Creek Housing Division, Community and Economic Development Department
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. $5.00 per square foot on new commercial development, deposited to the Local Housing Trust Fund. The November 2017 update eliminated the first 1,000 square foot exemption and extended the fee to additional use classifications including skilled nursing facilities and hospitals (effective January 2018). Together with housing in-lieu fees the City projected about $16 million in the Local Housing Trust Fund over the 2025-2029 Consolidated Plan period (including an anticipated State Local Housing Trust Fund matching grant).
affordability_requirement: Not applicable to the payer; proceeds fund extremely low to moderate income housing.
next_deadline: Applies at building permit; Housing Element Program H-2.E calls for a periodic nexus study update (last EPS nexus study 2015-2016) before any rate change.
layering_notes: Low rate ($5 per square foot) relative to the housing in-lieu fee, but the downtown office and medical base (John Muir Medical Center area) keeps it producing. Revenue is pooled with inclusionary fees in the Local Housing Trust Fund that funds the City's Affordable Housing Subsidy RFP (separate record). Read from the HCD-hosted Housing Element (source_url) because the City's commercial linkage fee page returned 403.

program_name: Walnut Creek Local Housing Trust Fund and Affordable Housing Subsidy Request for Proposals (annual developer RFP; FY26 round October to December 2025)
administering_agency: City of Walnut Creek Housing Division (Housing Programs), Community and Economic Development Department; contact brynen@walnutcreekca.gov
typical_award_size: The City maintains a Local Housing Trust Fund fed by housing in-lieu fees and commercial linkage fees and projects about $16 million available over the 2025-2029 Consolidated Plan period, with $4.14 million in general and local funds also programmed for housing and community services. Track record: $5 million to St. Paul's Commons (44 units, 2019) plus a $366,642 City fee waiver; $400,000 plus later gap funding to Riviera Family Apartments; $5,150,000 to Habitat for Humanity's 42-unit Las Juntas ownership project; acquisition, predevelopment and development funding for the 95 to 97 unit Civic Crossing at 699 Ygnacio Valley Road (TCAC application CA-24-649 shows $10.5 million of City funds); $300,000 per year budgeted for first-time homebuyer loans. The City's developer page (not opened, 403) describes an FY26 Affordable Housing Subsidy RFP open October 14 to December 19, 2025, Council review March to April 2026 and award notification May 2026; Council retains sole discretion to fund one, several or no projects.
per_unit_cap: None published; past awards ran about $110,000 to $120,000 per unit.
affordability_requirement: Projects must be within Walnut Creek city limits and consistent with the Housing Element; 55-year City regulatory agreements on rental projects; priority to extremely low, very low and low income and special needs households; all other funding sources must be identified before disbursement.
next_deadline: FY26 round closed December 19, 2025 with awards expected May 2026 (outcome not confirmed). Expect the FY27 RFP in fall 2026 or early 2027; confirm with the Housing Division since the City website blocks automated access.
layering_notes: The strongest city-level gap source in Contra Costa outside the County itself: Walnut Creek routinely commits $5 million to $10 million per project, equal to or above County HOME awards, and pairs it with fee waivers and expedited processing. Stack order for a Walnut Creek deal: City subsidy RFP award and fee waiver first (secures local commitment for TCAC tie-breaker), then County HOME or Measure X (county records; Civic Crossing also received $6.8 million County funds), then 4% credits and County or CMFA conduit bonds. The City is also pursuing a Prohousing Designation (program page exists but was not opened) which adds points in State NOFAs. The City is the Housing Successor for its former redevelopment agency but reported minimal boomerang funds. Because walnutcreekca.gov and its PDFs returned 403 (RFP document and developer page not opened), the fund description is taken from the City's 2025-2029 Consolidated Plan strategic plan posted by Contra Costa County (source_url) and the HCD-hosted Housing Element; RFP dates come from search snippets of the City page and need confirmation.

program_name: Walnut Creek CDBG entitlement, Community Services Grant and Homeless Services Fund (Contra Costa Consortium three-year cycle)
administering_agency: City of Walnut Creek Housing Division (Housing and Community Service Grants); contact brynen@walnutcreekca.gov
typical_award_size: Walnut Creek is a CDBG entitlement city in the Contra Costa HOME Consortium. The 2025-2029 Consolidated Plan estimates $2.12 million in federal resources over five years (PY 2025-26 CDBG entitlement estimated around $350,000 to $400,000) plus $4.14 million in general and local funds through the Community Services Grant and Homeless Services Fund; the five-year goal table programs CDBG of $100,000 to $500,000 per goal with $500,000 of local funds per year for several goals and $2.5 million for affordable housing (AH-1). Historically the City sets aside part of CDBG for the Home Rehabilitation Loan and Emergency Grant Program. Awards are competitive on the Consortium's two- and three-year cycle; the FY 2027/28 to 2029/30 NOFA was released October 15, 2026.
affordability_requirement: CDBG 80% AMI national objective; Walnut Creek has nine low and moderate income block groups (census tracts 3390.01, 3400.01, 3511.01 to 3511.05) prioritized for area-benefit activities.
application_cycle: annual NOFA (three-year cycle; applications due December 7, 2026)
next_deadline: Consortium applications due December 7, 2026 at 5:00 PM via City Data Services; Walnut Creek Council adopts its PY 2027-28 Annual Action Plan in May 2027 (the PY 2026-27 plan hearing was May 5, 2026).
layering_notes: Walnut Creek's CDBG is small (under $500,000 a year) and mostly funds services and rehab; for development, the City's Local Housing Trust Fund RFP (separate record) and County HOME or Measure X (county records) carry the weight, with HOME requests filed through the same Consortium application the County administers. Davis-Bacon applies to CDBG-assisted projects of 8 or more units. Consolidated Plan read from the County-hosted copy (source_url); Consortium NOFA dates and the Walnut Creek contact were read on the City of Antioch's Community Grants page (https://ca-antioch.civicplus.com/993/Community-Grants) because walnutcreekca.gov returns 403.

program_name: San Ramon Inclusionary Housing Ordinance (Ordinance 520, adopted October 24, 2023; San Ramon Municipal Code Sections C4-175 to C4-183) and Affordable Housing Fund (C4-180)
administering_agency: City of San Ramon Community Development Department, Planning Services Division (Lauren Barr, Director; Planning@sanramon.ca.gov, 925-973-2560)
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Applies to all residential projects of 2 or more units (ADUs excluded). Projects of 2 to 9 units (for-sale or rental) may pay an affordable housing fee equal to 25% of total new livable square footage times the per square foot rate in the City Fee Resolution (about $15.16 per square foot per the City of Antioch's January 2026 countywide comparison). For-sale projects of 10 or more units (single-family and multifamily) must build 15% affordable units allocated 20% very low, 30% low and 50% moderate income (must-build added in 2023). Rental projects of 10 or more units must provide 15% affordable units, half very low and half low income. Alternatives (C4-179): voluntary rental units in a for-sale project, off-site construction within San Ramon, preservation of at-risk units with 55-year extensions, land dedication (fully improved with impact fees paid) or combinations. Fees go to the Affordable Housing Fund with an annual report to Council on balance and commitments; the balance was $4.28 million as of March 3, 2022.
affordability_requirement: 55-year affordability (raised from 30 years in 2023) for rental and for-sale units, renewed for 55 years on each resale; resale price capped at purchase price grown by AMI; City first right of refusal on affordable ownership units.
eligible_project_types: market-rate rental and for-sale projects of 2 or more units (compliance)
next_deadline: Applies at first approval with an Affordable Housing Plan; Affordable Housing Agreement before final map or building permit. Housing Element Program 8 scheduled a 2024 review of the inclusionary and commercial linkage fee structure; the Council heard a FY 2026-27 Master Fee Schedule and nexus study update in March 2026, so confirm the current per square foot rate with Planning Services.
