layering_notes: San Ramon's 15% rental requirement with half the units at very low income is the deepest in the county among the priority cities and, combined with Bishop Ranch's build-out, produces receiver-site deals: the Canopy (BR 8) Affordable Site Development Agreement introduced January 13, 2026 (Ordinance 536, adopted January 27, 2026) has Sunset Development dedicating a rough-graded site with impact fees paid to Eden Housing for 161 affordable units that absorb the inclusionary obligations of 255 Canopy single-family homes (raised from 15% to 22.5%) and the CityWalk apartments, plus $3,000 per market-rate unit (about $765,000) paid into the Affordable Housing Fund. Dougherty Valley affordable units (Highlands Point, Muirlands, Seville, Valencia, Cornerstone at Gale Ranch and others, about 1,886 affordable units citywide) are governed by Contra Costa County affordability agreements under the Dougherty Valley Settlement Agreement and the County's Chapter 822-4, not this ordinance, and several 20-year moderate-income agreements expire in 2026. Ordinance text read at source_url; the Canopy staff report was read on the City's IQM2 agenda host (https://sanramonca.iqm2.com/Citizens/Detail_LegiFile.aspx?ID=4882).

program_name: San Ramon Affordable Housing Commercial Linkage Fee (Inclusionary Housing and Commercial Linkage Ordinance, April 2019) and Affordable Housing Fund
administering_agency: City of San Ramon Community Development Department, Planning Services Division
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. A per square foot fee on net new gross floor area of all new commercial construction, including the commercial portion of mixed-use projects, regardless of zoning; exempt: projects adding 5,000 square feet or less, schools and places of public assembly, public facilities, and like-for-like replacement of buildings destroyed by calamity. Developers may instead build affordable units on an appropriate site, dedicate land or provide other housing resources. Mixed-use developments that meet the inclusionary policy are exempt from in-lieu fees. Fees are deposited into the City's Affordable Housing Fund ($4.28 million as of March 3, 2022, before Canopy and other recent payments). The per square foot rate is set in the Master Fee Schedule and was not found on an opened page.
affordability_requirement: Not applicable to the payer; the fund supports very low (including extremely low), low and moderate income rental and ownership housing in San Ramon.
next_deadline: Applies at building permit. Housing Element Program 8 called for a 2024 review of the linkage fee structure to reflect affordable construction costs; the Council considered updated nexus fee studies with the FY 2026-27 Master Fee Schedule in March 2026 (confirm adopted rate).
layering_notes: Bishop Ranch and the City Center office base make this the City's steady fund source; the Affordable Housing Fund has no published NOFA and is deployed by Council through development agreements and project-specific commitments (the City adopted Priority Access System guidelines for City-funded projects), so developers should request Affordable Housing Fund support directly in entitlement negotiations. Stack with County HOME and Measure X (San Ramon is in the Urban County for HOME and CDBG, county records), HACCC project-based vouchers and the City's fee waiver policy (separate record). Read from the HCD-hosted 2023-2031 Housing Element draft (source_url, Sections 11.3.1.4, 11.4.7.1 and Program 8); the adopted element (Resolution 2023-017) is linked from https://www.sanramon.ca.gov/news/what_s_new/adopted_2023_2031_housing_element.

program_name: San Ramon Affordable Rental Housing Fee Waiver Policy (adopted October 11, 2022) for 100% affordable rental projects
administering_agency: City of San Ramon Community Development Department, Planning and Building Divisions
typical_award_size: Waiver of development impact fees and a capped waiver of City service fees for rental projects in which all units are affordable to households at or below 80% AMI. Impact fee waiver options: City Traffic Impact Fee, School Age Child Care Fee, Park and Recreation Facility Impact Fee, Private Sector Art and Beautification Fee, Open Space Development Impact Fee, Specific Plan Recovery Fees, General Plan Recovery Fee, Zoning Ordinance Recovery Fee and the Tri-Valley Transportation Development Fee (already waived for affordable units). City service fee waivers (building plan check and inspection, planning plan check, engineering plan check and inspection) capped at 25%. City example: a typical 100-unit affordable project receives about $24,000 per unit in impact fee waivers and $5,865 per unit in service fee waivers, over $2.5 million total. The City counts waived fees as local match for State funding applications; value calculated at building permit.
per_unit_cap: About $24,000 per unit impact fees plus about $5,865 per unit service fees (City example); actual amount depends on unit mix and fees in effect at permit.
affordability_requirement: 100% of units (except managers' units) affordable to households at or below 80% AMI under a recorded affordable housing or density bonus agreement; San Ramon's 2026 rent table caps 80% AMI rents at $2,376 (1 person) to $3,938 (6 persons).
next_deadline: Applies at building permit issuance; no application deadline. The Canopy (BR 8) Eden Housing project (161 units, 2026 entitlements) and Eden's 2453 Camino Ramon project are the first users; confirm the policy remains in the FY 2026-27 Master Fee Schedule.
layering_notes: The only formal fee waiver program among the five priority cities and worth roughly $3 million on a 100-unit deal; combined with Bishop Ranch land dedications it makes San Ramon unusually feasible for 100% affordable 4% credit deals despite high land costs. Waivers are public funds for Labor Code 1720 purposes (prevailing wage) and are reported as local match to TCAC and HCD. Layer with County HOME and Measure X, HACCC PBVs and County conduit bonds (county records); the County has no comparable fee waiver program (county record: development fee waiver for affordable housing, discretionary only). Policy terms read from the HCD-hosted Housing Element (source_url) and confirmed in the January 13, 2026 Canopy staff report on the City's IQM2 host.

program_name: San Ramon Density Bonus Ordinance (Zoning Ordinance Division D4, Chapter VIII, Sections D4-76 to D4-80) and Priority Access System for City-funded housing
administering_agency: City of San Ramon Community Development Department, Planning Services Division
typical_award_size: Regulatory incentive, not a cash subsidy. Chapter VIII implements Government Code 65915 by reference: any changes to state density bonus law supersede local text; waivers of development standards are granted unless specified findings are made; parking may be modified or covered-parking requirements waived for affordable units; a density bonus housing agreement is recorded before final map or building permit; a processing fee set by resolution applies. No local bonus beyond state law. Separately, the City's Priority Access Guidelines give San Ramon residents and workers priority in City-funded affordable projects, and the Housing Element targets 200 very low or extremely low, 200 low and 400 moderate income inclusionary units over 2023-2031 against a RHNA of 5,111 units.
affordability_requirement: State density bonus law thresholds (Gov. Code 65915); density bonus units are excluded from the inclusionary unit count under C4-177, so they stack on top of the 15% inclusionary requirement.
next_deadline: Applies at entitlement; no deadline.
layering_notes: San Ramon has no city-run NOFA, no RDA successor housing fund (the City never had a redevelopment agency) and its Affordable Housing Fund is deployed by Council through development agreements rather than competitive rounds; local tools are the inclusionary receiver-site model, the fee waiver policy and state density bonus. Most existing affordable stock in Dougherty Valley sits under Contra Costa County affordability agreements (county records: Inclusionary Housing Ordinance Ch. 822-4 and Residential Density Bonus Ch. 822-2) rather than City agreements. Zoning text read on the zoneomics mirror (source_url); the City's code host (qcode) is blocked.

program_name: Roseville Local Housing Trust Fund (LHTF) gap loans, including Prohousing Incentive Program (PIP) program income NOFA (Resolution 26-404, November 4, 2026)
administering_agency: City of Roseville Economic Development Department, Housing Division (316 Vernon Street, Suite 150; 916-774-5270; housing@roseville.ca.gov)
typical_award_size: Project-by-project gap loans from the City's Local Housing Trust Fund, which receives in-lieu fees, affordable purchase loan payoffs and state grant program income. Most recent round: a NOFA released August 31, 2026 offered $1,000,000 of PIP program income (from a $1,050,000 developer loan payoff on the City's 2023 PIP Round 1 award of $1,610,000) for predevelopment of lower-income rental housing; two applications were received (Eden Housing, 505 Royer, 58 senior units; Mercy Housing, Pleasant Grove Apartments Phase II, 49 units) and staff recommended reserving the full $1,000,000 for Pleasant Grove Phase II on November 4, 2026. Earlier LHTF and in-lieu commitments include $4.36M reserved for Junction Crossing (80 units, St. Anton) and, per the City's pipeline report, $6,000,000 for Pleasant Grove Apartments (pipeline PDF returned 502 this pass). The 2021 Housing Element commits the City to re-apply for state LHTF matching funds as rounds open.
per_unit_cap: None published. The PIP award of $1,000,000 for 49 units is about $20,400 per unit.
affordability_requirement: Set by loan documents and an Affordable Rental Housing Agreement; PIP money is limited to lower-income (at or below 80% AMI) rental housing, and the 2026 NOFA targeted 30% to 60% AMI projects with preference for units for persons with disabilities and supportive services. Projects in high opportunity areas or areas at risk of displacement are prioritized (Housing Element Programs 9, 10 and 12).
application_cycle: annual NOFA (as program income is received)
next_deadline: No open NOFA as of 2026-11-08; the August 31, 2026 PIP NOFA closed and funds were reserved November 4, 2026. Loan documents for Pleasant Grove Phase II return to Council at a future meeting; construction expected 2027. Watch for the next LHTF or PIP program-income NOFA from the Housing Division.
layering_notes: This is the city layer that stacks under 9% or 4% LIHTC and tax-exempt bonds (county TEFRA via CalPFA, CMFA or CSCDA; the County is not an issuer). Roseville's LHTF is separate from Placer County's in-lieu fee gap loans (Hope Way, Destination at Placer One) and from Housing Trust Placer; a Roseville project can seek all three plus Roseville Housing Authority project-based vouchers. Gap order: LIHTC and bonds first, then City LHTF or PIP reservation, then County or Housing Trust Placer money. Roseville's municipal website (roseville.ca.us, now roseville.ca.gov) opens, but the pipeline PDF and script-rendered agenda pages do not; staff reports were read from the City's CivicClerk API file streams (rosevilleca.api.civicclerk.com).

program_name: Roseville 10% Affordable Housing Goal in Specific Plan Areas (General Plan Policy LU5.5, Housing Element Programs 6 and 9) with Affordable Housing Regulatory Agreements and case-by-case in-lieu fees
administering_agency: City of Roseville Housing Division (compliance) and Development Services Department, Planning Division (specific plans)
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Every specific plan area must designate 10% of total units as affordable (General Plan goal since 1989: 20% of the affordable units at middle income up to 100% AMI, 40% low income up to 80% AMI, 40% very low income up to 50% AMI), allocated to specific medium and high density parcels and secured by Development Agreements and Affordable Housing Regulatory Agreements recorded before building permits or final small-lot maps. Since 1989 the policy has produced 5,167 affordable units (1,357 very low rental, 2,271 low rental, 427 middle rental, 325 moderate rental, plus 787 purchase units), about 140 per year. The City has no formal in-lieu fee ordinance; in-lieu fees are negotiated case by case ($1,036,410 collected 2013 to 2021). A 2025 Housing Tools Inclusionary Housing Policy Analysis recommended standard fee levels, for example $150,000 per required affordable for-sale unit in projects under 20 units, applied in the East Street Subdivision amendment approved November 4, 2026.
affordability_requirement: Rental units restricted by Affordable Rental Housing Agreements (about 2,700 units under agreement in the 2021 to 2029 period); density bonus (Chapter 19.28) may be assigned by the Regulatory Agreement as part of the subsidy. Sierra Vista Specific Plan: 10% of 8,679 units (about 868) allocated to MDR and HDR parcels, with transfers and credits between parcels allowed by Housing Division approval.
eligible_project_types: affordable parcels dedicated inside specific plans
next_deadline: Applies at specific plan and Development Agreement approval; the in-lieu fee option is considered case by case at agreement amendment. The 2021 Housing Element also directs work on a commercial linkage fee (nexus study November 2021, draft ordinance posted, not adopted as of this pass).
layering_notes: The reason Roseville has a steady supply of affordable parcels and developers: specific plan landowners (Sierra Vista, West Roseville, Amoruso Ranch, Villages West and others) carry a 10% obligation and typically deliver dedicated HDR parcels or partner with USA Properties, Mercy Housing, St. Anton, Eden Housing and others. Hope Way and the County in-lieu fee program (County Code Chapter 15.65) apply only in unincorporated Placer; inside Roseville this goal and the Regulatory Agreements govern. In-lieu fees collected flow to the Local Housing Trust Fund (record above). Density bonus units are excluded from the 10% base. Verified from the adopted 2021 Housing Element PDF, the Sierra Vista Specific Plan Affordable Housing chapter and the November 4, 2026 Council packet.

program_name: Roseville development impact fee deferral for affordable multifamily (Municipal Code Section 4.04.040, Ordinance 6830; Sierra Vista Apartments deferral, Resolution 26-336)
administering_agency: City of Roseville Economic Development Department (Gina McColl, 916-774-5452) with the Finance Department
typical_award_size: Deferral, not waiver: city-controlled impact fees are deferred from building permit to final or certificate of occupancy, with interest at the City's pooled rate (ten-year average about 2.23%) and an administrative processing fee per permit. Deferrals of $100,000 or more need Council approval. Example approved September 16, 2026: about $2,987,339 deferred for the 192-unit Sierra Vista Apartments (Greek Orthodox Housing Corporation, parcel JM-30, 4950 Upland Drive), covering fire construction tax, sewer and water connection, drainage, SVSP traffic mitigation, citywide and neighborhood parks, bike trail, public benefit and solid waste fees (about $373,000 per building). For a 100% affordable project (three or more units, all units low, very low or extremely low income, Affordable Housing Agreement under Section 19.28.110, objective design standards, secured promissory note) payment may be pushed up to one year after the first certificate of occupancy. The City's policy is not to waive fees; CSCDA SCIP fee financing is also offered.
per_unit_cap: None; about $15,600 per unit deferred in the Sierra Vista example.
affordability_requirement: Standard deferral is open to any multifamily project on request; the extended one-year post-occupancy deferral requires 100% of units (except managers) affordable to low, very low or extremely low income households under a recorded Affordable Housing Agreement.
next_deadline: Request through the Economic Development Department when fee estimates are prepared; a Council hearing under Government Code 53083 is required for deferrals of $100,000 or more.
layering_notes: Timing relief only; fees are still paid in full with interest, so it does not reduce basis but eases construction-period cash needs. Placer County Capital Facilities fees and traffic fees are not city-controlled and are not deferred; age-restricted projects get reduced traffic and County capital facilities rates. Roseville also made a $571,850 CDBG loan (September 4, 2024) to the same Sierra Vista sponsor for land purchase, showing how CDBG, fee deferral, the Regulatory Agreement and LIHTC stack on one project. Read from the September 16, 2026 City Council agenda packet via the CivicClerk API file stream.

program_name: Roseville Housing Successor Low and Moderate Income Housing Asset Fund (SB 341 reports; Housing Element Program 12)
administering_agency: City of Roseville acting as Housing Successor to the former Redevelopment Agency; Housing Division
typical_award_size: Small gap loans and Homeless Prevention and Rapid Rehousing grants. Fund balance $2,379,350 at June 30, 2025 (FY2024-25 deposits $1,032,069, including $737,249 from the 20% share of City loan payoffs; FY2024-25 expenditures $434,196 with $0 for development). Past development loans: $5,760,000 to Mercy Housing for 623 Vernon Street (58 units, 2016 to 2018), $600,000 deferred loan to Junction Crossing (80 units, approved October 20, 2021), $500,000 to Hampstead's Prospera at Fiddyment workforce housing (104 units, approved April 3, 2024). HPRR spending is capped at $250,000 per year; on September 2, 2026 Council budgeted $1,250,000 from the fund for FY2026-27 together with $1,374,763 of PLHA.
per_unit_cap: None stated; past loans ranged from about $4,800 to $99,000 per unit.
affordability_requirement: Health and Safety Code 34176.1 targeting: development money must serve households at or below 80% AMI, with at least 30% spent on 30% AMI households and no more than 20% on 60% to 80% AMI; 55-year covenants used; no senior-only restriction issue (0% of assisted units senior-restricted in the last 10 years).
next_deadline: No NOFA; developers approach the Housing Division. Revenue is only loan repayments (projected through 2036), so expect commitments of a few hundred thousand dollars per project. The FY2025-26 SB 341 report is due by December 31, 2026.
layering_notes: Roseville is the only Placer jurisdiction with a Housing Successor fund actively lending (Lincoln has a Redevelopment Successor Agency but no housing fund activity was found; Rocklin's Low/Mod Housing Fund is described under its Affordable Housing Incentive Program). Stacks with LHTF and PIP money (record above), PLHA, county in-lieu fee loans and LIHTC. Excess surplus test: the balance must stay under the greater of $1,000,000 or four years of deposits, which pushes the City to commit funds. Read from the FY2024-25 SB 341 Report of Required Information posted on the Affordable Housing Funds page.

program_name: Roseville CDBG entitlement and HOME funds (annual Action Plan) and Permanent Local Housing Allocation (PLHA) Plan adopted September 2, 2026
administering_agency: City of Roseville Housing Division (Dani Calli, Housing Analyst, 916-774-5277, dcalli@roseville.ca.gov)
typical_award_size: Roseville is a HUD entitlement city; the 2026-27 CDBG award was expected at roughly $700,000 with about $730,000 of prior-year carryover and about $50,000 program income (2026 Action Plan hearing May 6, 2026; 2025-26 CAPER public comment August 29 to September 16, 2026). CDBG is mostly used for owner rehabilitation loans (deferred loans up to $100,000, $5,000 grants for elderly and disabled owners), accessibility work (over $1 million earmarked in 2026 for Sierra Gardens accessibility upgrades) and public services, but it has funded affordable housing land acquisition: a $571,850 CDBG loan to Greek Orthodox Housing Corporation on September 4, 2024 for parcel JM-30 (192-unit Sierra Vista Apartments). HOME funds (state-administered) support first-time homebuyer and rehabilitation programs. PLHA: Roseville's formula allocation under HCD's July 2026 NOFA (about $285 million statewide, five-year term) is programmed in the City's PLHA Plan (Resolution 26-327) for Homeless Prevention and Rapid Rehousing, not development; $1,374,763 of PLHA was budgeted for HPRR in FY2026-27.
per_unit_cap: None; the CDBG acquisition loan example is about $3,000 per unit.
affordability_requirement: CDBG national objective (low and moderate income benefit; 2026 Sacramento PMSA limits: 1 person $73,600, 4 persons $105,100); HOME and PLHA income rules per program.
next_deadline: 2026 round: applications were due February 2, 2026, with the hearing May 6, 2026. Expect the 2027 CDBG and HPRR NOFA in December 2026 or January 2027 with applications due about early February 2027 and Council action in May 2027; confirm with the Housing Division.
layering_notes: Roseville runs its own CDBG and PLHA; Placer County's PLHA allocation (county record, needs_confirmation) covers the unincorporated area and non-entitlement cities such as Auburn, while Lincoln became its own CDBG entitlement in 2026 and Rocklin receives its own PLHA formula share. CDBG land loans trigger federal cross-cutting rules (Davis-Bacon for 8 or more units, environmental review, Section 3). PLHA is currently committed to HPRR, so do not count on PLHA for development in Roseville. The CDBG page, PLHA notice and the September 2, 2026 agenda were opened; the PLHA Plan PDF link itself was not fetched.

program_name: Roseville Housing Authority (RHA) Project-Based Vouchers and Housing Choice Vouchers (jurisdiction includes Rocklin)
administering_agency: Roseville Housing Authority, a department of the City of Roseville (Housing Division, 916-774-5270, housing@roseville.ca.gov)
typical_award_size: Rental subsidy, not capital. RHA (established October 2, 1974) administers tenant-based Housing Choice Vouchers for roughly 850 households (about 1,600 individuals) at or below 50% AMI in Roseville and Rocklin, plus VASH and Mainstream vouchers. It project-bases vouchers in new affordable developments (the City's news release on The Crawford, 265 units by USA Properties, cites eight RHA project-based vouchers) and runs a Project Based Voucher waiting list (waitlistcheck.com CA1217-4334). Payment standards effective October 1, 2026 and utility allowances effective June 1, 2026 are posted for Roseville (95661, 95678, 95747) and Rocklin.
per_unit_cap: Per-unit PBV contract rents at or below RHA payment standards; the count of PBVs per project is negotiated with RHA (HUD caps apply).
affordability_requirement: HCV income limits: 50% AMI at admission (2026: 1 person $46,000, 4 persons $65,700), with 75% of new admissions at or below 30% AMI; PBV units must meet HUD HQS and the Housing Element directs RHA to expand use in high opportunity areas.
next_deadline: PBV commitments are requested from RHA during predevelopment; RHA reports quarterly to Council (next quarterly status update early 2027). Contact RHA before TCAC or CDLAC applications to secure a PBV commitment letter.
layering_notes: Roseville and Rocklin projects have two voucher sources: RHA (city) and Placer County Housing Authority (county record, PBVs and special-purpose vouchers); Rocklin is covered by both. PBVs raise achievable rents on 30% AMI units and support bond or 4% deals. Not a public works trigger by itself. Verified on the RHA page opened this pass.

program_name: Roseville Residential Density Bonus (Zoning Ordinance Chapter 19.28) and Prohousing Designation renewal (Resolution 25-346, November 5, 2025)
administering_agency: City of Roseville Development Services Department, Planning Division (Lauren Hocker, Senior Planner, 916-774-5272)
typical_award_size: Regulatory incentive, not a subsidy. Chapter 19.28 mirrors Government Code 65915: bonuses of 20% to 50% for very low, lower and moderate income set-asides, 80% (or no limit near major transit) for 100% affordable projects, 20% for senior, foster youth, disabled veteran and homeless housing, 35% for student housing, land donation and child care bonuses, up to four incentives, parking caps (0.5 space per unit for qualifying projects near transit, none for 100% lower-income rental near transit or qualifying senior projects). Applications require a pro forma, an appraisal of the bonus value and a sources and uses statement showing the financing gap. Roseville was among the first ten Prohousing-designated jurisdictions (2022); the designation expired at the end of 2025 and Council authorized renewal on November 5, 2025 (application published for 30-day review through September 29, 2025). The City reports over $1 million in grants attributable to the designation and received $1,610,000 of PIP Round 1 funds in 2023.
affordability_requirement: State density bonus thresholds (5% very low, 10% lower, 10% moderate for-sale, or 100% affordable); Affordable Housing Agreement recorded for 55 years (rental) under Section 19.28.110.
next_deadline: Processed with entitlements; no deadline. HCD action on the Prohousing renewal application was pending at the time of the November 2025 hearing; confirm current designation status with Planning before claiming Prohousing points in MHP, AHSC or IIG applications.
layering_notes: No local enhancements beyond state law other than the explicit pro forma and appraisal submittal requirements. Density bonus units do not count toward the 10% specific plan goal, and the Regulatory Agreement can assign bonus units as part of the City's subsidy. Prohousing status gives bonus points on state NOFAs for projects located in Roseville (not available in Rocklin, Lincoln or Auburn, none of which held the designation as of this pass). Chapter text read on the zoneomics code mirror; Roseville's own code host (ecode360) returns partial PDFs only.

program_name: City-owned land for affordable housing: 505 Royer Street and 300 Taylor Street sale to Eden Housing (Resolution 26-331, September 16, 2026)
administering_agency: City of Roseville Economic Development Department (Gina McColl, 916-774-5452) with the Housing Division
typical_award_size: Land sale at appraised value rather than a grant: two parcels totaling 1.17 acres in the Downtown Specific Plan (former Placer County courthouse site, demolished 2021, declared surplus October 23, 2019) sold to Eden Housing for $580,000 after a May 2025 RFP (Eden was the sole respondent) for a 58-unit senior affordable project at 30% to 60% AMI. A prior 2022 contract with Bridge Housing for a similar project was terminated in September 2024 for lack of financing. Escrow closes no later than January 31, 2027; construction estimated January 2030. Eden also applied for the City's 2026 PIP NOFA for this site but was not selected.
per_unit_cap: About $10,000 per unit in land cost.
affordability_requirement: Senior affordable housing for lower-income households (30% to 60% AMI) per Eden's proposal; regulatory agreement terms to be set with City financing.
next_deadline: No open city land offering as of 2026-11-08. The City also tracks vacant parcels obligated for affordable housing under specific plan agreements (list posted on the Housing Division page); watch for Surplus Land Act notices for future sites.
layering_notes: Shows Roseville's practice of running Surplus Land Act and RFP processes for infill sites and pairing them with LHTF or PIP loans and CDBG. The Eden project will still need County gap money (Placer County in-lieu fee loans or Housing Trust Placer), RHA or PCHA PBVs and LIHTC. Read from the September 16, 2026 agenda packet via the CivicClerk API.

program_name: Rocklin Affordable Housing Incentive Program (AHIP): Low/Mod Housing Fund residual receipts loans (Resolution 2024-039, repealed and replaced September 9, 2025)
administering_agency: City of Rocklin City Manager's Office, Housing Division (Housing@rocklin.ca.us; 3970 Rocklin Road, 916-625-5000)
typical_award_size: Residual receipts loan of up to $40,000 for each very low and extremely low income unit constructed, funded from the City's Low/Mod Housing Fund. Approved subsidies as of September 2025 (contingent on full project financing): CHW Pacific Street Apartments, 109 affordable units, $2.6 million; USA Properties The Steven, 179 affordable age-restricted units, $2.23 million. AHIP was adopted January 23, 2024 and restated September 9, 2025 to align its fee deferral component with SB 937; the loan and fee reduction terms were unchanged.
per_unit_cap: $40,000 per very low or extremely low income unit.
affordability_requirement: Loans attach to units restricted to very low (50% AMI) and extremely low (30% AMI) income households; the fee reduction companion applies at 60% AMI or lower; qualified affordable housing developments per the AHIP resolution.
next_deadline: No NOFA; developers request a commitment from the Housing Division during entitlement so the City estimate can be included in LIHTC applications. Confirm the remaining Low/Mod Housing Fund balance with staff; the two approved commitments total $4.83 million.
layering_notes: Rocklin's only direct gap source; it stacks with the 40% impact fee reduction and SB 937 fee deferral (next record), the new inclusionary in-lieu fee trust fund, Placer County in-lieu fee loans and Housing Trust Placer, and PBVs from either Roseville Housing Authority or Placer County Housing Authority (both cover Rocklin). Rocklin is in the Roseville, Rocklin and Placer County Continuum of Care (CA-515). The City's websites (rocklin.ca.us legacy and rocklin.ca.gov CivicPlus) return 403 to scripts; staff reports were read from the City's Legistar packet files on d2kbkoa27fdvtw.cloudfront.net and the fee deferral form from the DocumentCenter.

program_name: Rocklin impact fee reduction of 40% for affordable units (Ordinance 1159, January 10, 2023) and SB 937 fee deferral program (Resolution adopted August 26, 2025)
administering_agency: City of Rocklin City Manager's Office, Housing Division (Housing@rocklin.ca.us) and Community Development Department
typical_award_size: 40% reduction of City development impact fees for deed-restricted units at 60% AMI or lower, calculated unit by unit (adopted by Ordinance 1159 with the rate set by resolution the same night). Fee deferral: City park development, traffic, community and recreation center, construction tax, park improvement, public facilities and trails impact fees deferred from building permit to final inspection or certificate of occupancy, secured by a promissory note and deed of trust that may be subordinated to construction financing; since the August 26, 2025 SB 937 policy, deferral to final inspection applies to all designated residential projects without interest, and the AHIP deferral is aligned with it. Staff reported in September 2025 that no reductions or deferrals had yet been processed but estimates had been issued to developers for their financing packages.
per_unit_cap: No cap; 40% of city impact fees on each qualifying unit.
affordability_requirement: Fee reduction: units deed-restricted at 60% AMI or lower. AHIP fee deferral eligibility: at least 10% of units at affordable rents for very low income households or at least 49% of units affordable to low income households; fees become payable with interest penalties if the promised units are not delivered by certificate of occupancy.
next_deadline: Apply to Housing@rocklin.ca.us with a preliminary title report before building permit issuance; reductions must be requested before signing a deferral agreement. Municipal Code chapters on impact fees were slated for SB 937 clean-up at a future Council meeting (not confirmed adopted as of this pass).
layering_notes: A real cost reduction (not just timing), unlike Roseville, which defers but does not waive. Combine with the $40,000 per unit Low/Mod loan (record above). Placer County Capital Facilities fees and school fees are outside the City program. Verified from the September 9, 2025 Council staff report and the City's fee deferral application form (rocklin.ca.gov/DocumentCenter/View/457).

program_name: Rocklin Inclusionary Housing Requirements (Municipal Code Chapter 17.95, Ordinance 1195, November 11, 2025) and in-lieu fee into the Inclusionary Housing Trust Fund
administering_agency: City of Rocklin Community Development Department, Planning Division, with the City Manager's Office Housing Division
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Housing development projects of 10 or more units must provide 15% of units for low income households, or 10% for very low income, or 5% for extremely low income (rental projects provide rental units; fractional units round up). Exempt: projects complete or with SB 330 preliminary applications before the effective date, projects with at least 50% affordable units, historic landmark portions and statutory development agreement projects. Alternatives: off-site construction, acquisition and rehabilitation of market-rate units, or an in-lieu fee once set by Council resolution, paid before building permit into a separate Inclusionary Housing Trust Fund. Council held a January 13, 2026 hearing on a proposed interim fee of $10 per square foot (opposed by the California Apartment Association) and, per the City's June 9, 2026 Council recap found in search results but not opened, approved an in-lieu fee of $2.75 per square foot with further ordinance updates still in progress. Paying the fee does not qualify a project for a state density bonus.
per_unit_cap: Not applicable (fee reported at $2.75 per square foot, unconfirmed).
affordability_requirement: Rental inclusionary units restricted 55 years, for-sale units 45 years, by recorded inclusionary housing agreement approved by Council with the entitlements; units dispersed and comparable to market-rate units; the City tenant preference policy applies.
eligible_project_types: market-rate multifamily and subdivisions of 10 or more units (compliance)
next_deadline: Applies to applications deemed complete after the ordinance took effect (December 2025). The $2.75 per square foot fee and the trust fund guidelines should be confirmed with Planning; a broader fee study (consultant RFP issued 2024) and ordinance amendments were pending in mid-2026.
layering_notes: New in 2025, so the Inclusionary Housing Trust Fund has little or no balance yet; over time it will feed the AHIP Low/Mod loans. A 100% affordable project is exempt and instead benefits from the ordinance by competing for the fee revenue. Compare Placer County Chapter 15.65 (10% inclusionary, unincorporated area). The ordinance text was verified on the zoneomics mirror of the Rocklin code; the fee resolution and June 9, 2026 staff report could not be opened (rocklin.ca.gov 403, Legistar API returns 500 for client rocklin), hence needs_confirmation.

program_name: Rocklin Density Increase Incentive Program (Municipal Code Chapter 17.96, Ordinance 977) and Housing Element Program 10 Residential Minimum Density Overlay rezones (August 26, 2025)
administering_agency: City of Rocklin Community Development Department, Planning Division (Arwen Wacht, Planning Manager; Nathan Anderson, Principal Planner)
typical_award_size: Regulatory incentive, not a subsidy. Chapter 17.96 (2011) incorporates Government Code 65915 by reference for projects of five or more units in any residential zone: bonus amounts and concessions as specified in state law, applications processed with entitlements and approved if state criteria are met, affordability secured for 30 years or longer if required by financing. Separately, on August 26, 2025 Council approved General Plan amendments, a CEQA addendum and an ordinance applying the Residential Minimum Density Overlay (Chapter 17.53) to alternative RHNA sites to cure the shortfall HCD identified in its April 8, 2025 letter, including sites in the Rocklin West annexation.
affordability_requirement: State density bonus thresholds; 30-year minimum affordability covenant in the local chapter (state law now requires 55 years for rental units, which controls).
next_deadline: Processed with entitlements. Confirm the final adoption date of the alternative sites rezone ordinance (introduced August 26, 2025) and the current RHNA site list with Planning.
layering_notes: No local enhancements beyond state law; Rocklin's incentives sit in AHIP (fee reduction, Low/Mod loans) rather than the density bonus chapter. The minimum density overlay sites are the practical pipeline of by-right multifamily land for 2021 to 2029 RHNA units. Chapter text read on the zoneomics mirror; the August 26, 2025 staff report cover was read from the Legistar packet on d2kbkoa27fdvtw.cloudfront.net.

program_name: Lincoln CDBG entitlement program (first-time entitlement, 2026-2030 Consolidated Plan and 2026 Annual Action Plan)
administering_agency: City of Lincoln City Manager's Office (Nita Wracker; publiccomments@lincolnca.gov, 916-434-2427; 600 Sixth Street)
typical_award_size: Lincoln became a HUD CDBG entitlement city in 2026 with a first-year allocation of $272,325. The 2026-30 Consolidated Plan (public hearing May 12, 2026, submitted to HUD June 3, 2026) prioritizes community services and administration; it states the City has not yet set standards for subrecipients and will look for opportunities to support affordable housing with entitlement funds but does not program CDBG for housing development in year one. Stakeholders asked for local gap financing, PBV support and tax credit competitiveness funds, which the City said it will continue to evaluate.
per_unit_cap: None; the annual allocation is about $272,000 in total.
affordability_requirement: CDBG national objectives (low and moderate income benefit); no housing development set-aside adopted.
next_deadline: The 2027 Annual Action Plan process is expected in spring 2027 (30-day comment and Council hearing, likely April to May 2027); confirm the application window with the City Manager's Office.
layering_notes: Lincoln has no local housing trust fund, inclusionary ordinance, in-lieu fee or city NOFA; CDBG is its only city-controlled housing-related money and it is small. Development gap funding for Lincoln projects comes from Placer County (in-lieu fee gap loans, PLHA, Housing Trust Placer) and PCHA project-based vouchers. Lincoln has a Redevelopment Successor Agency (meets with Council) but no Low and Moderate Income Housing Asset Fund activity was found in 2026 agendas. lincolnca.gov pages open; the Consolidated Plan PDF was read from the City's govstack media host.

program_name: Lincoln 2021-2029 Housing Element Actions 2.6 and 2.7: project-by-project incentives (deferred development fees, reduced parking, expedited review) for affordable housing in Villages 1, 5 and 7
administering_agency: City of Lincoln Community Development Department, Planning Division (916-434-3370; 600 6th Street)
typical_award_size: Negotiated, not codified. The Housing Element (adopted January 2023 per the City's 2025 Annual Progress Report, 2021 to 2029 cycle, RHNA 5,120 units) commits the City to offer incentives on a project-by-project basis for lower-income housing in Village 1, Village 5 and Village 7, including deferred development fees, reduced parking requirements, expedited application review and technical assistance (Action 2.7), and to provide financial or in-kind assistance and incentives beyond the density bonus for extremely low income housing (Action 2.6). Action 2.9 commits only to explore a local inclusionary program; none has been adopted. No dollar amounts, fee schedules or fund are attached.
affordability_requirement: Lower-income (at or below 80% AMI) and extremely low income housing as described in the Housing Element; terms set case by case in a development agreement.
eligible_project_types: mixed-income multifamily in Village specific plans
next_deadline: Negotiate with Planning at the specific plan or tentative map stage. The 2025 Housing Element Annual Progress Report went to Council on March 10, 2026; the 2026 APR is due to HCD by April 1, 2027.
layering_notes: Lincoln's village specific plans (Lincoln Crossing, Village 7 and others) carry no fixed inclusionary percentage, unlike Roseville's 10% goal, so affordability in Lincoln depends on developer-by-developer agreements plus County and state money. The Consolidated Plan notes two-story height limits and two spaces per unit parking standards as constraints the City may relax for affordable projects. The Housing Element PDF itself could not be located on the redesigned lincolnca.gov site (housing element and general plan URLs returned 404); the actions were read from the City's 2026-30 Consolidated Plan, hence needs_confirmation.

program_name: Lincoln density bonus (state Government Code 65915 applied directly; Housing Element Action 2.3 reported implemented, no stand-alone zoning chapter located)
administering_agency: City of Lincoln Community Development Department, Planning Division
typical_award_size: Regulatory incentive, not a subsidy. The Consolidated Plan lists Housing Element Action 2.3 (amend the Zoning Ordinance to allow and promote density bonuses) as implemented, but the Lincoln Zoning Ordinance (Title 18) as mirrored on zoneomics contains no density bonus chapter in Divisions I through XI (R-3 multiple residential, PD planned development, parking in-lieu fee and ADU Chapter 18.37, repealed and re-enacted September 23, 2025 by Ordinance 1099B, are present). Projects therefore rely on state density bonus law directly: 20% to 50% bonuses, 80% for 100% affordable projects, up to four concessions, parking caps.
affordability_requirement: State thresholds (5% very low, 10% lower, 10% moderate for-sale, 100% affordable); 55-year covenants for rental units under state law.
next_deadline: Processed with entitlements; no deadline. Confirm with Planning whether a density bonus section was added to Title 18 or the PD district after 2023.
layering_notes: No local enhancements and no local trust fund, fee waiver ordinance, inclusionary fund or city NOFA exist in Lincoln beyond the negotiated incentives in the Housing Element (record above) and CDBG. Lincoln's ADU chapter (18.37) was updated in 2025 for state compliance. The zoning code was read on the zoneomics mirror because the City does not host its code in fetchable form; needs_confirmation because the Housing Element and any post-2023 code amendment were not opened.

program_name: Auburn Density Bonus ordinance (Municipal Code Sections 159.330 to 159.342, ministerial density bonus permit)
administering_agency: City of Auburn Planning and Public Works Department (1225 Lincoln Way, Auburn)
typical_award_size: Regulatory incentive, not a subsidy. Implements Government Code 65915 to 65918 through a ministerial density bonus permit processed with other entitlements: bonuses per state tables for very low, lower and moderate income units, 20% for senior, foster youth, disabled veteran and homeless housing, 80% for 100% affordable projects (no density limit within one half mile of a major transit stop), incentives and concessions by threshold with a three-story or 33-foot height increase when four concessions apply near transit, unlimited waivers of standards that physically preclude the project, land donation bonus, parking ratios per state law, and a recorded density bonus housing agreement. The Director must determine completeness and the eligible bonus within 30 days. Filing fee set by Council resolution.
affordability_requirement: State thresholds; affordable units governed by Section 159.340 (affordable rent and housing cost per Health and Safety Code 50053 and 50052.5) with 55-year rental covenants.
next_deadline: Processed with entitlements; no deadline.
layering_notes: Auburn (population about 14,000) has no local housing trust fund, inclusionary ordinance, in-lieu fee fund, housing successor fund or city NOFA; this chapter and the negotiated fee reductions in the Housing Element (next record) are the City's only tools. The Housing Element credits past density bonuses (one project received a 400% bonus with apartments in an R-1 zone and a 50% parking reduction) and Placer County land donation and Housing Trust Placer money for a 79-unit project. Gap funding for Auburn projects comes from Placer County in-lieu fee loans, County PLHA, Housing Trust Placer and PCHA PBVs. Chapter read on the zoneomics mirror (Auburn's code publisher is blocked); auburn.ca.gov DocumentCenter PDFs open directly.

program_name: Auburn 2021-2029 Housing Element Program A and Program I: case-by-case fee reductions or deferrals, alternative development standards and state CDBG and HOME applications for affordable housing (adopted May 24, 2021)
administering_agency: City of Auburn Planning and Public Works Department, with participating nonprofit and for-profit housing providers
typical_award_size: Negotiated, not codified. Program A commits the City to consider fee reductions or deferrals sized to the financial need of each affordable development, to negotiate alternative standards (parking, street improvements, density, lot coverage), to apply for state-administered CDBG, HOME and other funds on behalf of affordable developers or support their applications, and to meet at least twice in the planning period with housing providers; Program I adds land write-downs, expedited processing, identification of impact fee reductions and incentives beyond the density bonus for extremely low income housing, with priority in high resource areas and the Baltimore Ravine Specific Plan. Track record: 2010 and 2014 state HOME grants for owner rehabilitation and first-time buyers (completed November 2017); the City did not apply for 2018 HOME funds due to staff turnover and no new award was found. No dollar amounts or fee schedule exist.
affordability_requirement: Extremely low, very low, low and moderate income housing as defined in the Housing Element; terms set per project.
next_deadline: Request during entitlement; Council action is needed for any fee reduction. Auburn is a non-entitlement city, so state CDBG and HOME NOFAs (HCD) are the vehicles, with the City as applicant or supporter; check HCD NOFA calendars and the City's annual NOFA review.
layering_notes: Because Auburn is non-entitlement, Placer County's PLHA and the County's in-lieu fee gap loans (county records) are the nearest local money; the County's Priority Applicant Policy (effective July 1, 2026) would apply to County-funded units. Fee deferral for residential projects is now mandated statewide by SB 937 (to final inspection), so the Housing Element's deferral promise mainly adds the possibility of a reduction. Verified from the adopted 2021 Housing Element PDF on auburn.ca.gov; no 2024 or 2025 Annual Progress Report could be located (CivicPlus Agenda Center and search pages are script-rendered).

program_name: Measure U Affordable Housing Bond: New Construction Notice of Funding Availability (NC NOFA), Resolutions 90419, 90552, 90894 and 91377 C.M.S.
administering_agency: City of Oakland Housing and Community Development Department (HCD), Housing Development Division, 250 Frank H. Ogawa Plaza, Suite 5313; Fay Darmawi, Deputy Director, fdarmawi@oaklandca.gov, (510) 238-3714
typical_award_size: Measure U (Nov 2022, $850,000,000 bond, $350,000,000 for affordable housing in three tranches). Tranches 1 and 2 committed $248,000,000 to 32 projects (New Construction 15 projects, 1,172 units, $167,035,412; R2H2/Homekey 6 projects, $31,564,588; ACAH 11 projects, $37,000,000; 5% admin $12,400,000), leveraging about $5 outside per $1 City. 2024 NC NOFA: 24 applications requesting $424,000,000; January 2025 awards $80,500,000 to 5 projects (583 units); November 2025 pipeline awards $63,500,000; 13 unfunded pipeline applications (919 units, $246,000,000 requested) remain. Tranche 3: $50,000,000 appropriated in the FY 2026-27 midcycle budget and authorized by Resolution 91377 C.M.S. (October 2026), about $35,000,000 of it for the NC NOFA. Typical City loans run roughly $8,000,000 to $20,000,000 per project, 55-year residual receipts.
per_unit_cap: No fixed cap published; awards sized by gap underwriting, cost per unit and leverage. Oakland Housing Authority has indicated up to $8,000,000 in operating, predevelopment or capital assistance for NC NOFA and R2H2 projects with PSH or deeply affordable units (OHA Board action pending).
affordability_requirement: At least 20% of units targeted to homeless exits or extremely low income (0-30% AMI) households with supportive services plan; 55-year regulatory agreement; scoring favors public land, ministerial approvals, readiness for tax credits, emerging developer joint ventures, displacement-risk neighborhoods.
application_cycle: biennial (pipeline NOFA with supplemental awards as funds arrive)
next_deadline: Next NC NOFA planned for late 2026 or early 2027 after state HDFC rules settle; awards timed to the spring 2027 tax credit round. Existing pipeline applicants may be advanced ahead of a full round. Confirm release date with HCD (NOFA mailing list).
layering_notes: Oakland is the largest city funder in the county (42% of Alameda County affordable permits 2024-25). Stacks with Alameda County Measure A1 Oakland base allocation and Measure W Home Together New Construction RFP (five Oakland projects won Measure W in March 2026: Liberation Park, 500 Lake Park, 3135 San Pablo, East 12th Circle, Brighter Bancroft), county PBVs via OHA, and state HDFC/TCAC. City commitment is intended as the first local layer so projects can show match for county and state rounds. Measure U loans carry Oakland local hire, First Source and prevailing wage requirements; a Project Labor Agreement debate for Measure U projects occurred in 2024. Measure KK (2016, $100,000,000 housing) is fully committed and reported with Measure U. Non-bond sources commingled in the same NOFA: Affordable Housing Impact Fee Fund 1872, Jobs/Housing Impact Fee Fund 1871, boomerang Fund 1870, LMIHAF 2830, HOME 2109, PLHA 2145, excess redevelopment bond funds. oaklandca.gov returns 403 to scripts; all material read from Oakland Legistar attachments and the City's OpenCities prelive host.

program_name: Acquisition and Conversion to Affordable Housing (ACAH) Program and Housing Accelerator Fund partnership (rolling ACAH NOFA, Resolutions 90308 and 90118 C.M.S.)
administering_agency: City of Oakland HCD, Housing Preservation Services, with the San Francisco Housing Accelerator Fund (HAF) as program administrator; applications go to HAF
typical_award_size: Since 2017 ACAH has awarded $59,800,000 to preserve 339 units, with set-aside pools for community land trusts and cooperatives. Current structure (June 2024): $10,000,000 unsecured City loan to HAF pooled with private capital (HAF targets 2.5 to 1 leverage, $25,000,000) for short-term bridge acquisition loans, plus $20,000,000 to $30,000,000 of Measure U committed for City take-out permanent loans that revolve the pool. Rolling ACAH NOFA of $22,000,000 released December 2025. 2025 preserved 48 units (1432 12th Avenue co-op with St. Mary's Center, 1534 29th Avenue with Bay Area Community Land Trust).
per_unit_cap: None published; bridge loans sized to acquisition price, permanent take-out sized to residual receipts capacity.
affordability_requirement: 55-year regulatory agreement; all units rented to households averaging 80% AMI and below; priority to naturally occurring affordable housing in displacement-risk neighborhoods, CLTs and co-ops.
eligible_project_types: small sites (single family to mid-size apartments)
next_deadline: Rolling; the December 2025 $22,000,000 NOFA remains open through HAF until funds are committed. Confirm balance with HAF or Oakland HCD.
layering_notes: Oakland's preservation layer. Comparable to Berkeley's Small Sites Program but much larger. Pairs with Measure W acquisition-rehab RFP planned by the County (about $10,000,000) and county boomerang funds. Rehab scopes over bridge period are modest; larger rehabs can later use 4% credits and bonds. Measure U is the primary capital source so City labor standards apply. Source documents are the October 2026 HCD funding authorization report (Legistar) and the 2025 HCD Annual Impact Report (OpenCities prelive host); the ACAH NOFA itself sits on the 403-blocked oaklandca.gov site.

program_name: Rapid Response Homeless Housing (R2H2) and local Homekey program (Resolutions 89977 and 90419 C.M.S.)
administering_agency: City of Oakland HCD, Homeless Housing Development unit
typical_award_size: Program capitalized in 2023 with boomerang Fund 1870 and LMIHAF: $10,400,000 capital plus $19,600,000 operating subsidy; $21,000,000 Measure U Tranche 2 capital added September 2024 for $31,400,000 total capital. Four awards to date (Mandela House, Friendly Manor, Covenant House, the Holland), leveraging over $87,000,000 outside funds (about $4 to $1). About $7,000,000 of Measure U Tranche 2 remained available for new applications as of September 2026; Tranche 3 may add more. City also co-applies for state Homekey+: 2025 awards $7,100,000 The Maya (23 units), $33,000,000 Mark Twain Homes (109 units), $6,500,000 34th and San Pablo (15 PSH units).
affordability_requirement: Permanent supportive housing or permanent transitional housing for people experiencing homelessness; quick-build, ready to house residents within 12 months of award and fully operational within 15 months; Housing First.
next_deadline: Rolling RFP since November 2023; apply any time while capital remains. Confirm remaining balance with HCD.
layering_notes: Oakland analog to state Homekey; projects typically combine R2H2 capital with Homekey+, county Measure W Housing dollars, HHAP and county BHSA. Operating subsidy is the binding constraint; the Prohousing Incentive Program award ($2,390,000 in 2023, up to $1,600,000 requested in Round 4, 2026) is dedicated to capitalized service reserves for R2H2 and NC NOFA PSH units. OHA may add project-based vouchers or operating subsidy.

program_name: Affordable Housing Impact Fee, OMC Chapter 15.72 (2025 amendments, Ordinance 13853 C.M.S.), with exemption for affordable housing projects and Fund 1872
administering_agency: City of Oakland Planning and Building Department (collection, impactfees@oaklandca.gov) and HCD (expenditure through NOFAs)
typical_award_size: Requirement on market-rate housing and a funding source for affordable housing. July 15, 2025 amendments converted the fee from per unit to per square foot (AB 602): multifamily Zone 1 $36.17 per sq ft (was $29,658 per unit), Zone 2 $29.18 (was $23,929), Zone 3 $19.73 but set at 0% through FY 2027-28; townhome $14.98 / $10.97 / $5.99 (Zone 3 at 0%); single family $12.66 / $9.08 / $4.40 (Zone 3 at 0%). Annual Marshall and Swift inflation adjustment each July 1. Exempt: 100% affordable projects, projects providing the on-site or off-site affordable units specified in 15.72.100-110, ADUs, 2 to 4 unit projects, single-family homes under 1,750 sq ft, SB 684 projects, and the first four smallest units in larger projects. All impact fee payments deferred to certificate of occupancy for 100% affordable and density bonus projects (SB 937 alignment). FY 2024-25 AHIF fund: start $18,162,106, end $10,737,051, $6,577,455 spent, $5,893,752 committed, $4,843,299 being committed to NOFA pipeline projects.
per_unit_cap: Not applicable (exemption). Mixed-income option: provide on-site affordable units at the percentages in 15.72.100 to zero out the fee.
affordability_requirement: Exemption requires 100% affordable (manager units excepted) or the on-site mix in 15.72.100 (chosen to align with state density bonus thresholds); fee revenue funds 100% affordable developments for extremely low to moderate income households through the NC NOFA.
next_deadline: Fee due at building permit (installments) or deferred to certificate of occupancy for affordable and density bonus projects; rates adjust each July 1. Zone 3 zero rate expires June 30, 2028 unless extended.
layering_notes: Oakland has no general permit or impact fee waiver program; the AHIF exemption plus SB 937 deferral of transportation and capital improvement fees is the relevant relief. Affordable projects still pay the Transportation Impact Fee (Ch. 15.74) but are exempt from the Capital Improvements Impact Fee. AHIF revenue (Fund 1872) is one of the non-bond sources commingled with Measure U in the NC NOFA, so this record both reduces developer cost and feeds the Oakland NOFA record. No county impact fee exists for comparison. Fee rate schedule read in the July 2025 Master Fee Schedule exhibit on Legistar; the annual report FY 2024-25 (November 2025) supplied balances.

program_name: Jobs/Housing Impact Fee (commercial linkage fee), OMC Chapter 15.68, Fund 1871
administering_agency: City of Oakland Planning and Building Department (collection) and HCD (expenditure)
typical_award_size: Linkage fee on office and warehouse projects over 25,000 sq ft: $7.87 per sq ft for permits applied July 1, 2024 to June 30, 2025 ($8.05 in FY 2023-24), inflation adjusted; paid 25% at permit, 50% at certificate of occupancy, 25% eighteen months later. The 2025 amendments extended the fee to additional nonresidential categories. FY 2024-25 JHIF fund: start $13,964,433, end $12,546,460, $12,060,074 committed to affordable developments, $486,386 being committed to pipeline projects.
affordability_requirement: Revenue restricted to acquisition, new construction, substantial rehabilitation and preservation of affordable housing, awarded through HCD NOFAs.
next_deadline: Fee collected continuously; funds flow to the NC NOFA pipeline (next round late 2026 or early 2027).
layering_notes: Oakland is one of only two priority cities in the county with a commercial linkage fee (Fremont also has one). Revenue is modest relative to Measure U but is flexible local money with no bond restrictions, which HCD uses for early predevelopment commitments. Developers do not apply to this fund directly; it is part of the NOFA sources table.

program_name: Density Bonus and Incentive Procedure, Oakland Planning Code Chapter 17.107 (Ordinance 13684 C.M.S., 2022), and S-13 Affordable Housing Combining Zone
administering_agency: City of Oakland Planning and Building Department, Bureau of Planning
typical_award_size: Requirement and entitlement, not a subsidy. Implements Government Code 65915 with the state tables (20% to 50% bonus for 10% to 24% low income; 20% to 50% for 5% to 15% very low; 80% bonus for 100% affordable projects). Local additions: 100% affordable projects within one-half mile of a major transit stop may waive all density maximums and receive up to three additional stories or 33 feet; condominium conversions with 33% moderate or 15% lower income units get a 25% unit bonus or equivalent incentive; incentive counts of one, two, three or four follow state tiers; parking ratio reductions per 65915(p) and no parking required for qualifying transit-adjacent 100% affordable projects; incentives expressly exclude fee waivers and City land.
affordability_requirement: State thresholds (10% low, 5% very low, 10% moderate for sale, 100% affordable with up to 20% moderate); 55-year restriction for rental.
next_deadline: Submitted concurrently with the planning application; no deadline.
layering_notes: Oakland does not offer a local bonus above state law except the transit-adjacent height add for 100% affordable projects. Fee relief comes separately through the AHIF on-site exemption (Ch. 15.72), which was deliberately keyed to density bonus thresholds so a mixed-income project can satisfy both with one affordability mix. Code read on the zoneomics mirror because the City's codepublishing site blocks scripts.

program_name: Prohousing Designation (renewed 2025, Resolution 90836 C.M.S.) and Prohousing Incentive Pilot Program grants
administering_agency: City of Oakland HCD, Housing Policy Unit
typical_award_size: Oakland was the first Bay Area jurisdiction designated Prohousing (December 2022); renewal for a 3-year term authorized September 16, 2025. Prohousing Incentive Program awards: $2,390,000 (Round 1, 2023) dedicated to capitalized service reserves for deeply affordable housing; Rounds 2 and 3 unsuccessful ($1,390,000 requests); Round 4 application for up to $1,600,000 authorized March 2026 for capitalized service reserves for PSH units in R2H2 or NC NOFA projects.
per_unit_cap: None; grants are sub-awarded to projects by HCD as grants or loans.
affordability_requirement: Capitalized service reserves for permanent supportive housing and deeply affordable units identified through City NOFAs.
application_cycle: annual NOFA (state PIP rounds, when issued)
next_deadline: Round 4 results pending as of March 2026; next state PIP round unknown, verify with HCD.
layering_notes: Developers benefit indirectly: Oakland projects receive Prohousing scoring points in AHSC, IIG, TCC and other state programs, and PIP dollars are routed to service reserves that make PSH projects feasible. Hayward and San Leandro also hold or expect Prohousing status. No county equivalent.

program_name: Low and Moderate Income Housing Asset Fund (LMIHAF, Fund 2830), boomerang Affordable Housing Trust Fund (Fund 1870) and HOME program income authorizations (Resolution 90894 C.M.S., 2025)
administering_agency: City of Oakland HCD (housing successor to the Oakland Redevelopment Agency) and Community Development Division (HOME entitlement)
typical_award_size: Program income from residual receipts and payoffs: LMIHAF collected $5,634,227 (FY 2021-22), $5,820,444 (FY 2022-23), $2,132,775 (FY 2023-24) and $2,309,139 (FY 2024-25); HOME program income reallocated through the budget. October 2025 resolution authorized HCD to commit accumulated and future LMIHAF and HOME program income to NOFA pipeline projects without returning to Council, alongside an additional $40,000,000 of Measure U Tranche 2 and just under $30,000,000 from other sources. Boomerang Fund 1870 (former RDA residual property tax) seeded the R2H2 program and remains an eligible NOFA source for predevelopment, acquisition, new construction, operating subsidies and homeless prevention.
per_unit_cap: HOME per-unit subsidy limits apply to HOME-assisted units.
affordability_requirement: LMIHAF: housing successor rules (Health and Safety Code 34176.1), majority to 60% AMI and below; HOME: 80% AMI and below with HOME rents; boomerang: locally restricted to affordable housing and homelessness.
next_deadline: No separate application; funds are awarded within the NC NOFA, R2H2 RFP, ACAH and Rehab NOFA processes.
layering_notes: Oakland is a HOME participating jurisdiction and CDBG entitlement city in its own right (not in the Alameda County HOME Consortium), so its HOME dollars are separate from the County's consortium RFP recorded at county level. County boomerang funds (county record) and City boomerang Fund 1870 are distinct pots from the same RDA dissolution. These sources are the most flexible local money for predevelopment and operating subsidy where Measure U bond proceeds cannot be used.

program_name: Rehabilitation of Existing Affordable Housing NOFA (Rehab NOFA, planned 2027) and Health and Safety Rehabilitation Loan Program (Resolutions 86126, 86366, 89605 C.M.S.)
administering_agency: City of Oakland HCD, Asset Management Services unit
typical_award_size: Rehab NOFA: last issued FY 2019-20; $7,000,000 of Measure U Tranche 2 earmarked in 2024 and a competitive round planned for 2027 using already authorized Tranche 2 funds plus Tranche 3. Health and Safety Loan Program: over-the-counter emergency loans to owners of City-subsidized multifamily housing, generally up to $250,000 per project, 0% interest, 55-year term; balance fully committed ($250,000 Christian Church Homes, $100,000 Coliseum Connections) and a $2,000,000 recapitalization was recommended in October 2026.
per_unit_cap: Health and Safety loans generally limited to $250,000 per project.
affordability_requirement: Existing City-regulated affordable portfolio properties; affordability restrictions extended or maintained for 55 years.
application_cycle: biennial (Rehab NOFA irregular; Health and Safety loans rolling when funded)
next_deadline: Rehab NOFA expected 2027; Health and Safety Program accepting requests once the $2,000,000 recapitalization is funded. Verify with HCD Asset Management.
layering_notes: Covers Oakland's aging City-funded portfolio, the same need Berkeley addressed with its 2024 HTF rehab RFP. Larger recapitalizations pair with 4% credits and tax-exempt bonds (City of Oakland or CMFA conduit). Not a source for third-party acquisition; see ACAH.

program_name: Berkeley Housing Trust Fund (HTF) development, acquisition and predevelopment loans (BMC 21.28; 2021 HTF Guidelines; 2024 HTF RFP)
administering_agency: City of Berkeley Health, Housing and Community Services Department, Housing and Community Services Division, 2180 Milvia Street; housingdevelopment@berkeleyca.gov, (510) 981-5400
typical_award_size: Single application pools Measure O bond, inclusionary in-lieu and Affordable Housing Mitigation Fee revenue, Measure U1 general funds, HOME, PLHA and state pass-throughs. Current reservations: new construction $26,500,000 BUSD educator housing (110 units, Measure O), $11,996,669 1740 San Pablo (54 units), $11,996,669 St Paul Terrace (50), $14,531,301 Ephesian Legacy Court (80), $14,359,593 People's Park supportive housing (119), North Berkeley BART Lot B $11,563,636 plus EBALDC $5,926,364 plus Insight PSH $9,010,000 ($21,500,000 reserved); renovation $500,000 to $8,500,000. 2024 rehab RFP: about $5,800,000 available (including $1,200,000 HOME), $11,500,000 requested, awards $2,990,000 Adeline Street Apartments and $2,868,571 Ashby Lofts (June 2025). Standard terms: 55 years at 3% simple interest, annual payments from residual receipts; predevelopment loans 5 years at 3%. Fees: 1% origination, $600 subordination or assumption, $3,000 modification, $130 per hour project management.
per_unit_cap: City subsidy normally capped at 40% of total development cost (Guidelines IV.C.1, waivable); HOME per-unit limits apply to HOME-assisted units.
affordability_requirement: At least 60% of units restricted to households at or below 30% and 60% AMI (BUSD educator housing up to 120% AMI by waiver); 55-year minimum regulatory agreement; portion of units to Section 8 and Shelter Plus Care voucher holders; Berkeley housing preference policy applies to lottery units.
next_deadline: Predevelopment requests may be submitted any time; development funds released by RFP when Council allocates money (last new construction RFP 2019-2021 Measure O rounds, rehab RFP November 2024). No development RFP open as of 2026-11-08; Ashby BART East Lot developer selection underway (October 2026). Funding reservations expire after 24 months and were extended to January 2028 for SHiPP, Ephesian and NBB in late 2025.
layering_notes: Berkeley's HTF is the second largest city pool in the county and the gateway to Measure O, U1 and in-lieu revenue. Reservations above show how the City layers Measure O (capital only), AHMF or in-lieu fees and U1 (operating reserves and predevelopment, which Measure O cannot fund). Stacks with Alameda County Measure A1 Berkeley base allocation and regional pool, Measure W (Ephesian Legacy Court and People's Park won Measure W in March 2026), Berkeley Housing Authority project-based vouchers, and state LHTF match (City applied for NBB projects). HTF Guidelines require state prevailing wage on all City-funded construction and a First Source hiring agreement (BMC 13.26). FY 2026 budget deficit left no U1 available for unfunded rehab requests, so near-term capacity depends on in-lieu fee collections (about $9,000,000 a year average).

program_name: Small Sites Program (SSP) NOFA 2025, $3,800,000 (HTF subset, created 2018)
administering_agency: City of Berkeley Health, Housing and Community Services Department, Housing and Community Services Division, 2180 Milvia Street; housingdevelopment@berkeleyca.gov, (510) 981-5400
typical_award_size: $2,500,000 NOFA released August 18, 2025 and increased to $3,800,000; applications accepted on a rolling basis from August 25, 2025 and reviewed in order received (first three applications or twice the available funding). Three projects funded since 2018 under four NOFAs, including Bay Area Community Land Trust at 2627 California Street ($3,599,948 with U1 general funds) and Northern California Land Trust sites. No dedicated funding source; Council allocates by budget.
per_unit_cap: Program guidelines score projects by subsidy per unit; no hard cap published (prior awards roughly $300,000 to $420,000 per unit including rehab).
affordability_requirement: Acquisition and rehabilitation of rent-controlled or vacant multifamily buildings with up to 25 units, converted to 55-year regulatory agreements; LIHTC projects are not eligible; cooperatives subject to additional requirements (Exhibit H).
next_deadline: Open until the $3,800,000 is committed; questions encouraged by August 3, 2026 per the November 2026 NOFA update; acquisition must close within 36 months of award. Check the HTF page weekly for status.
layering_notes: Berkeley's analog to Oakland ACAH at much smaller scale. Pairs with the Bay Area Community Land Trust and Northern California Land Trust pipelines, county Measure A1 acquisition funds and private CDFI bridge debt. Over-the-counter approval by the City Manager, no Council action, so timing is fast relative to the HTF RFP. SSP projects follow HTF loan terms (55 years, 3% simple, residual receipts) and the City prevailing wage requirement.

program_name: Measure O Affordable Housing General Obligation Bond (November 2018, $135,000,000)
administering_agency: City of Berkeley HHCS with the Measure O Bond Oversight Committee and Housing Advisory Commission
typical_award_size: Voter-approved $135,000,000 GO bond for development, rehabilitation and preservation of affordable housing for extremely low through middle income households. First issuance about $30,000,000 (2019-20) funded Berkeley Way ($23,500,000 reservation less operating reserve) and 1601 Oxford ($6,000,000) and a 2019 HTF RFP of about $14,500,000. Later issuances fund the current HTF reservations: BUSD educator housing $26,500,000, 1740 San Pablo $11,996,669, North Berkeley BART projects $21,500,000 (with AHMF and HTF), Supportive Housing in People's Park and Ephesian Legacy Court (with AHMF and U1). Measure O cannot fund predevelopment or capitalized operating reserves, which the City covers with U1 or fee revenue.
per_unit_cap: None published; awards made through HTF RFPs.
affordability_requirement: HTF Guidelines (60% of units at or below 30% to 60% AMI) with Council-approved exceptions up to 120% AMI for BUSD educator housing; 55-year restrictions.
application_cycle: closed/inactive (remaining authorization reserved to named projects; new rounds only if reservations lapse)
next_deadline: No open Measure O round; most remaining proceeds are reserved for NBB, SHiPP, Ephesian and BUSD projects with reservations extended to January 2028. Verify unreserved balance with HHCS or the Measure O Bond Oversight Committee.
layering_notes: Measure O is Berkeley's counterpart to Oakland Measure U and County Measure A1; it is permanent capital only, so projects pair it with AHMF or in-lieu funds and U1 for predevelopment and reserves, Berkeley Housing Authority PBVs for operating support, and Measure A1 or Measure W for the balance. Oversight by the Measure O committee acts in place of the HAC for bond-funded RFPs. The 2019 Council report and the November 2025 HAC packet were the documents opened; a current bond balance statement was not found on berkeleyca.gov.

program_name: Inclusionary Housing Ordinance, BMC Chapter 23.328, and Affordable Housing In-Lieu Fee (Resolution 71,674-N.S.; successor to the Affordable Housing Mitigation Fee, BMC 22.20.065)
administering_agency: City of Berkeley Planning and Development Department (compliance plans) and HHCS (BMR program and HTF)
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Projects over 5,000 sq ft of residential unit floor area must provide 20% of units as BMR (rental: half at 50% AMI, half low income, with Section 8 and Shelter Plus Care set-asides; ownership: all at 80% AMI) or pay an in-lieu fee of $62.83 per sq ft of residential unit floor area effective July 1, 2025 (up from $56.25; biennial California Construction Cost Index adjustment, next July 1, 2027), or a prorated mix. Full-fee payers deduct 5,000 sq ft (2,500 for single family); density bonus projects pay on the base project area. Fee due before certificate of occupancy. Revenue to the HTF: AHMF collections $3,112,000 (FY 2021), $16,208,000 (FY 2022), $14,224,000 (FY 2023), $10,716,000 (FY 2024), $831,000 (FY 2025); FY 2025 pipeline of 22 projects, 2,482 units, 214 BMR units and $22,600,000 projected fees. BMR portfolio 605 units in 61 properties.
affordability_requirement: 20% BMR for life of project (rental half at 50% AMI, half at 80% AMI; ownership at 80% AMI); projects with building permit or preliminary application before April 1, 2023 remain under the AHMF ordinance.
next_deadline: Applies at entitlement (preliminary Affordable Housing Compliance Plan) and building permit (final AHCP); fee indexed July 1, 2027.
layering_notes: This fee is Berkeley's primary dedicated affordable housing revenue (about $9,000,000 a year average) and funds the HTF record above, so BMR unit production and fee collections move inversely. Revenue is lagging while the IHO pipeline moves from AHMF to IHO entitlements, which matters for near-term HTF capacity. Developers using the state density bonus must still meet the 20% inclusionary requirement; 23.330.070 ties qualifying bonus units to 23.328 standards. Compare Oakland's per-square-foot AHIF ($19.73 to $36.17) and Fremont's $44 per sq ft for-sale in-lieu fee.

program_name: Density Bonus, BMC Chapter 23.330 (Ordinance 7787-NS, 2021; 7853-NS, 2023)
administering_agency: City of Berkeley Planning and Development Department, Zoning Officer and Zoning Adjustments Board
typical_award_size: Requirement and entitlement, not a subsidy. Incorporates Government Code 65915 and 65917.2 by reference with administrative regulations; incentives and concessions counted per dimensional or quantitative standard; City bears the burden of proof to deny; waivers negotiated through Use Permit and Design Review; regulatory agreement required before certificate of occupancy; qualifying units must meet Chapter 23.328 standards.
affordability_requirement: State thresholds; bonus units count toward the base for the 20% inclusionary requirement only as provided in 23.328.
next_deadline: Concurrent with the housing development permit application; no deadline.
layering_notes: No local enhancement beyond state law; Berkeley's leverage for affordable projects is instead the Southside and transit-corridor rezonings and the Housing Element Program upzonings. Inclusionary in-lieu fee applies to the base project only, which modestly favors bonus projects. Code read on the zoneomics mirror because berkeley.municipal.codes is script-blocked.

program_name: Measure U1 general fund allocation to the Housing Trust Fund (2016 rental housing business license tax increase) and CHDO operating support
administering_agency: City of Berkeley HHCS; allocation set by City Council in the biennial budget
typical_award_size: Measure U1 raised the business license tax on rental property owners (2016) with the stated intent of funding affordable housing and homelessness programs; Council allocates a share to the HTF each budget. Recent U1 uses: California Street Apartments $3,599,948 (BALCT, with HTF), University Homes Homekey $8,500,000, 2321-2323 10th Street $3,324,225, MLK House $2,000,988, Ephesian Legacy Court (with Measure O and AHMF), capitalized operating reserves and predevelopment loans that Measure O cannot fund, and CHDO operating grants of up to $30,000 per organization per year FY 2026 to FY 2030 (with HOME). The HAC recommendation in 2025 to add U1 to the rehab RFP was withdrawn because the FY 2026 budget projected a deficit with limited U1 available.
affordability_requirement: Follows HTF Guidelines when loaned through the HTF (60% of units at or below 30% to 60% AMI); flexible general fund otherwise.
next_deadline: Dependent on the FY 2027-28 biennial budget; no set-aside guaranteed. Verify with HHCS.
layering_notes: U1 is the only Berkeley source usable for operating reserves and predevelopment, which makes it the critical complement to Measure O and county capital for PSH deals (Berkeley Way needed up to $14,000,000 in operating reserve until BHA project-based vouchers reduced it). Competes with homelessness services for the same general fund. Documented in the 2021 HTF Guidelines, the June 2025 RFP reservations report and the November 2025 HAC packet.

program_name: Fremont Affordable Housing Fund NOFA (Affordable Housing In-Lieu Fee Fund 196, Low and Moderate Income Housing Asset Fund 111, commercial linkage fees)
administering_agency: City of Fremont Community Development Department, Housing Division, 39550 Liberty Street; housing@fremont.gov, (510) 494-4500
typical_award_size: Periodic NOFAs: November 2021 round awarded $14,000,000 to MidPen (Osgood, with up to $11,500,000 more), $6,000,000 to TPC/Maracor (Osgood South) and $7,600,000 to RCD (3900 Thornton, with up to $9,700,000 more). August 2023 NOFA (about $30,000,000 estimated, $35,000,000 available) awarded $34,850,000 on March 19, 2024: $12,850,000 USA Properties Centerville Station Phase 1 (150 units; $8,850,000 Fund 196 plus $4,000,000 Fund 111), $12,000,000 TPC/Maracor Warm Springs (240 units, $50,000 per unit; $9,500,000 redirected to acquisition in March 2025), $10,000,000 Community Development Partners 39340 Fremont Blvd (96 units, $104,000 per unit). Loans are 55 years at 3% simple interest, capital and predevelopment only (no operating subsidy or services). City contributed $30,700,000 of restricted funds to the 560 units opened in 2025 and funded four of the six developments (918 units) breaking ground in fall 2026.
per_unit_cap: No formal cap; staff benchmark recent City subsidy at about $110,000 per unit and favored requests of $50,000 to $104,000 per unit.
affordability_requirement: Households at or below 80% AMI with a target mix including extremely low (under 30% AMI), very low (under 50% AMI) and low income units; all-electric construction; site control required at application; 55-year regulatory agreement.
application_cycle: biennial (NOFA issued roughly every two years as fund balance allows)
next_deadline: No NOFA open as of 2026-11-08; prior rounds were 2021 and August 2023 (due October 31, 2023). Next round expected when Fund 196 rebuilds; verify with the Housing Division.
layering_notes: Second largest city pool in the county after Oakland and Berkeley, funded almost entirely by developer fees (for-sale in-lieu fee, rental AHO fee, commercial linkage) plus LMIHAF program income. Awards are timed so projects can apply to CDLAC/TCAC (Warm Springs waited for enhanced credits in a Small DDA).
