Stacks with Alameda County Measure A1 Fremont base allocation and regional pool, Measure W, and HACA project-based vouchers (Fremont is in the HACA jurisdiction and the County HOME Consortium). fremont.gov returns 403 to scripts, so the NOFA page could not be opened; terms were read from the March 19, 2024 and March 18, 2025 Council staff reports on the City's IQM2 agenda host and City GovDelivery bulletins.

program_name: Fremont Affordable Housing Ordinance, FMC Chapter 18.155 (2021 update, effective 2022) with in-lieu fees and live/work preference (2022)
administering_agency: City of Fremont Community Development Department, Housing Division and Planning Division
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. October 12, 2021 update: for-sale projects 15% inclusionary (5% moderate, 10% low) or in-lieu fee phased to $44 per sq ft by January 2024 (stacked flat rates unchanged); rental projects 10% low income or an alternative of 7.5% low plus 7.5% very low (15%); hybrid option of on-site moderate units plus partial fee; mixed for-sale and rental projects may satisfy the obligation with affordable rental units. Rental in-lieu fee and the separate commercial linkage (jobs-housing) fee remained unchanged. Fee revenue goes to Fund 196 and funds the Affordable Housing Fund NOFA. New affordable housing processing fees for BMP resales, refinances and loan modifications were adopted January 2026.
affordability_requirement: For-sale 15% (5% moderate, 10% low); rental 10% low or 15% split low and very low; long-term affordability agreements with the City.
next_deadline: Applies at entitlement; fee set by the Master Fee Schedule (updated January 5, 2026). Verify current per-square-foot amounts with the Housing Division.
layering_notes: Fremont is the only priority city in the county besides Oakland with both a residential inclusionary fee and a commercial linkage fee, which is why Fund 196 could support $34,850,000 of awards in 2024. The ordinance text (FMC 18.155) on fremont.gov and the code publisher are script-blocked; summary read from the City's 2021 GovDelivery notice and the November 2025 Master Fee Schedule staff report on IQM2. 2021 fee increase phasing and any 2024 to 2026 indexing should be confirmed.

program_name: State Density Bonus Law implementation in Fremont (no local bonus chapter; Lopes Road determination, November 2025)
administering_agency: City of Fremont Community Development Department, Planning Division
typical_award_size: Requirement and entitlement, not a subsidy. Fremont applies Government Code 65915 directly; all three 2024 NOFA awardees used concessions or waivers to reduce ground-floor commercial, open space or setbacks in TC-P, WSI-8 and Downtown zones, and AB 2097 removed parking minimums near transit. In November 2025 the Council upheld staff and Planning Commission denial of a concession to reduce the 50 unit per acre minimum density for a 127-townhome project at Lopes Road near Warm Springs BART, consistent with an HCD technical assistance letter. Commercial density bonus (Gov Code 65915.7) is available but unused.
affordability_requirement: State thresholds (10% low, 5% very low, 10% moderate for sale, 100% affordable).
next_deadline: Concurrent with the entitlement application.
layering_notes: No local enhancement; the City's incentives for affordable projects are fee based. Fremont adopted a development impact fee deferral and a 50% impact fee reduction for affordable housing projects under FMC 18.290 (2021 and later actions) according to City notices, but the fremont.gov pages describing them were blocked (403) this pass and the zoneomics 18.290 text defines affordable housing (up to 120% AMI) without stating the reduction; treat the fee reduction as needs_confirmation. Fremont also adopted a Streamlined Affordable Housing overlay through Housing Element Program implementation ordinances in 2025 (PLN2025-00065 and PLN2025-00074) that were not opened.

program_name: Development impact fee reduction and deferral for affordable housing projects, FMC Chapter 18.290
administering_agency: City of Fremont Community Development Department, Building and Housing Divisions
typical_award_size: City communications state that the June 2021 impact fee update added a 50% reduction of development impact fees for affordable housing projects and that a separate fee deferral program lets affordable developers pay impact fees later in the process. Chapter 18.290 defines affordable housing as units restricted to households at or below 120% AMI and provides for exemptions, exclusions, exceptions (18.290.110) and adjustments or waivers (18.290.240). Fremont's AB 1600 fees are capital facilities, fire facilities, traffic impact, parkland and park facilities fees (2025 Impact Fee Report).
affordability_requirement: Deed-restricted units at or below 120% AMI per 18.290 definition; confirm whether the 50% reduction requires 100% affordable projects.
next_deadline: Applies at building permit; verify current terms with the Building Division.
layering_notes: Could not open fremont.gov fee pages (403) or the implementing fee resolution; the 18.290 text was read on the zoneomics mirror and the fee list from the December 9, 2025 Impact Fee Report item on IQM2. Fee relief plus Fund 196 loans and SB 937 deferral make Fremont competitive with Oakland on soft cost; Alameda County has no countywide fee waiver (county record). Confirm the reduction percentage, eligible AMI level and whether school and water district fees (FUSD, ACWD, USD) are outside City control.

program_name: Fremont CDBG entitlement and HOME Consortium allocations (FY 2025/26 to 2029/30 Consolidated Plan)
administering_agency: City of Fremont Human Services Department (CDBG and ESG) and Housing Division; HOME through the Alameda County HOME Consortium
typical_award_size: Fremont is a CDBG and ESG entitlement city (annual action plan adopted July 8, 2025 with the FY 2025/26 to 2029/30 Consolidated Plan) and a member of the Alameda County HOME Consortium since 1992, receiving a formula share of the Consortium's HOME allocation each year. Dollar amounts for FY 2025/26 were not read this pass.
affordability_requirement: CDBG: low and moderate income benefit (80% AMI); HOME: 80% AMI with HOME rents, 15 to 20 year federal affordability plus City regulatory agreement.
application_cycle: annual NOFA (Consolidated Plan action plan cycle, spring)
next_deadline: FY 2026/27 Annual Action Plan hearing expected spring 2026 to July 2026; HOME Consortium cooperation agreement renews for FY 2027-2029. Verify with Human Services.
layering_notes: Small relative to Fund 196 but useful for acquisition and rehab. The County's HOME Consortium RFP (county record) is the vehicle for larger HOME development loans; the County proposed centralizing HOME administration for FY 2027-2029, which may change how Fremont's share is awarded. Source is the July 8, 2025 Council agenda on IQM2 listing the Consolidated Plan hearing; the staff report itself was not opened.

program_name: Hayward Affordable Housing Ordinance (HMC Chapter 10, Article 17; Ordinance 17-20, amended April 11, 2023), in-lieu fees (Resolution 17-167 as amended 2023) and Affordable Housing Trust Fund
administering_agency: City of Hayward Development Services Department, Housing Division, 777 B Street, Hayward; housing@hayward-ca.gov, (510) 583-4454
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Applies to all projects of two or more net new units: on-site units, in-lieu fee, off-site units or alternatives. In-lieu fees (10 or more units, per sq ft of habitable space, 2023 schedule): high-density condominiums 35 units per acre or more $19.35; lower-density ownership under 35 units per acre $26.00; all other dwelling types including rental $23.46; plus 10% if paid at occupancy; projects of 2 to 9 units pay 50% to 89% of the calculated fee. Fees fund the Affordable Housing Trust Fund, used solely to increase and preserve housing for extremely low to moderate income households (land acquisition and development subsidies). Collections 2020 to mid-2026 total $8,926,851: $3,599,171 (2020), $2,193,532 (2021), $2,013,770 (2022), $199,507 (2023), $489,948 (2024), $378,237 (2025), $52,687 (2026 YTD).
affordability_requirement: On-site compliance percentages set in 10-17.205 (historically 10% of units for ownership and rental); local tenant preference policy in 10-17.805; 55-year rental affordability.
next_deadline: Applies at entitlement; fee per the annual Master Fee Schedule (FY 2027 schedule adopted June 2026). Verify current indexed amounts with the Housing Division.
layering_notes: Hayward's trust fund is small and shrinking because most recent developments provided on-site units rather than paying fees (City's December 2024 competitiveness analysis), so the City lacks local match for state applications. The AHO text on municode is script-blocked; requirements were read from the City's affordable housing page, Resolution 17-167 and the 2023 in-lieu fee resolution on Hayward Legistar. Compare Fremont ($44 per sq ft for-sale) and Berkeley ($62.83).

program_name: Hayward Affordable Housing NOFA (local housing funds with Alameda County Measure A1 base allocation; last round 2018)
administering_agency: City of Hayward Development Services Department, Housing Division, 777 B Street, Hayward; housing@hayward-ca.gov, (510) 583-4454
typical_award_size: 2018 NOFA: about $7,000,000 in local housing funds plus recommendations for Hayward's Measure A1 base allocation ($18,200,000 available at the time) and local match to position projects for the A1 regional pool. Maximum City loan 10% of total residential development cost of the affordable units; HOME per-unit limits for HOME-assisted units ($144,050 studio to $285,149 four bedroom in 2018); 24-month commitment with one-year extension. CDBG available for predevelopment or acquisition by request. No NOFA has been issued since; the City reports only one City-supported project remaining in the pipeline and limited general fund for housing.
per_unit_cap: City loan capped at 10% of the affordable units' total development cost (2018 terms).
affordability_requirement: Rental and supportive housing for lower income households; Measure A1 policies require at least 20% of units at 20% AMI for A1-funded projects; scoring favors special needs, homeless, larger units and deeper targeting.
next_deadline: No open NOFA as of 2026-11-08. The December 2024 Housing Policy and Resource Committee report floated an annual general fund allocation for a regular NOFA but no funding was identified. Watch the Doing Business with Hayward page and the Housing Division mailing list.
layering_notes: Hayward's role is mainly as pass-through for its Measure A1 base allocation (county record) and HOME Consortium share; local dollars are limited to the Affordable Housing Trust Fund balance and CDBG. Developers should expect to rely on Measure A1, Measure W, HACA project-based vouchers and state sources with the City providing land (surplus sites), entitlements under the Streamlined Affordable Housing Overlay, and its Prohousing designation points. NOFA page and 2018 program description were opened on hayward-ca.gov.

program_name: Streamlined Affordable Housing Overlay District, HMC Section 10-1.2650 (Ordinance 24-04, April 2, 2024)
administering_agency: City of Hayward Development Services Department, Planning Division
typical_award_size: Entitlement streamlining, not a subsidy. Ministerial site plan and tentative map approval for housing on sites carried over from prior housing element cycles and listed in the 6th Cycle Housing Element lower-income inventory, provided the project meets the Housing Element minimum density assumptions and at least 20% of units are deed restricted for extremely low, very low or low income households for 55 years (rental) or 45 years (ownership); site must not meet Gov Code 65913.4(a)(6) exclusion criteria; objective standards and standard conditions apply.
affordability_requirement: At least 20% of units at low income or below, 55-year rental or 45-year ownership restriction.
next_deadline: Ministerial application any time; approval lapses per 10-1.2690.
layering_notes: Hayward has no local density bonus chapter; state density bonus requests are processed with site plan review (recent approvals include townhome projects with 10% to 11% affordable units). The overlay lowers entitlement risk on the inventory sites and pairs with state SB 35/SB 423 streamlining. Fee relief for affordable projects is not offered by the City. Code read on the zoneomics mirror because municode is blocked.

program_name: HOME Investment Partnerships funds through the Alameda County HOME Consortium and CDBG entitlement (Cooperation Agreement FY 2027-2029)
administering_agency: City of Hayward Development Services Department, Housing Division; Alameda County HCD as Consortium lead
typical_award_size: Hayward has received over $15,000,000 in HOME funds since 1991 as a Consortium member (annual formula share), used for Glenn Berry, Sara Conner Court, Huntwood Commons, Tennyson Gardens, Leidig Court, Cypress Glen, Weinreb Place, Alta Mira and Mission Paradise, plus Project Independence tenant-based rental assistance ($500,000 renewed July 2026). Hayward is also a CDBG entitlement city; CDBG has funded predevelopment and acquisition. The County proposes to centralize HOME administration, compliance and allocation during the FY 2027-2029 term, with Consortium members reviewing future allocations.
affordability_requirement: 100% of HOME funds to households at or below 80% AMI with HOME rent limits; federal affordability period plus City regulatory agreement.
application_cycle: annual NOFA (Consortium allocation each program year)
next_deadline: FY 2027 allocation set spring 2026; future allocations may be awarded through the County's HOME Consortium RFP (county record) under the centralized model. Verify with the Housing Division.
layering_notes: Small annual amounts (several hundred thousand dollars) but the only recurring development money Hayward controls. Pairs with the County HOME Consortium RFP, Measure A1 and HACA PBVs. Hayward's December 2024 analysis identified weak local match, GHG scoring and a thin rent differential as reasons three of five recent projects struggled to win state funds, and cited an expected Prohousing designation as a strength.

program_name: San Leandro Affordable Housing Development RFP (released February 28, 2025, continuous): HOME, Prohousing Incentive Program and PLHA funds
administering_agency: City of San Leandro Community Development Department, Housing Services Division, 835 East 14th Street; housing@sanleandro.org, (510) 577-6006
typical_award_size: Open-ended RFP for affordable housing development loans from the City's HOME Consortium share, Prohousing Incentive Program award and PLHA allocation; amounts available on request to the Housing Division. HOME available as of April 2026: $201,134 FY 2027 ($190,548 program) plus $593,119 prior-year funds (FY 2024 $225,238 due 6/30/2027, FY 2025 $179,013, FY 2026 $188,868); $783,667 committed to Eden Housing for rehabilitation of The Surf (46 units, 15320 Tropic Court). PLHA also funds a BACS shallow rental subsidy program. City contributions to the Lewelling interim housing project (HCEB, opened 2025) were $65,000 predevelopment and $309,500 acquisition from the AHTF.
per_unit_cap: HOME per-unit subsidy limits for HOME-assisted units; otherwise sized to gap.
affordability_requirement: Regulatory agreement typically 55 years; PLHA-funded projects must follow Housing First; HOME units at or below 80% AMI; priority to people experiencing or at risk of homelessness.
next_deadline: Continuous until funds are committed; HOME FY 2024 funds must be spent by June 30, 2027. Contact Housing Services before applying.
layering_notes: San Leandro's local money is thin (AHTF balance $336,166 at June 30, 2025), so the RFP mainly packages federal and state pass-throughs. Realistic stack: County Measure A1 San Leandro base allocation and regional pool, Measure W, HACA project-based vouchers, AHSC (City co-applied with Pacific West Communities in Rounds 9 and 10 for a BART-area project), and CMFA or County conduit bonds. The City expects the County to centralize HOME administration for FY 2027-2029. RFP read on the City's DocumentCenter; some sanleandro.org pages returned 403 after repeated requests.

program_name: Inclusionary Housing Ordinance, San Leandro Zoning Code Chapter 6.04 (Ordinance 2004-023, amended 2020-002), in-lieu fee and Affordable Housing Trust Fund (6.04.156)
administering_agency: City of San Leandro Community Development Department, Housing Services Division, 835 East 14th Street; housing@sanleandro.org, (510) 577-6006
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. At least 15% of units in residential developments must be inclusionary units for moderate, low or very low income households (density bonus units excluded from the base); for-sale projects of 2 to 6 units may pay an in-lieu fee equal to (median San Leandro sales price minus affordable ownership cost) times a fractional unit of 0.30 to 0.90; larger projects may combine fees with off-site alternatives only with approval. Exempt: for-sale projects and condo conversions under 2 units and rental projects under 4 units. Fees, condo conversion fees and loan repayments go to the Affordable Housing Trust Fund. FY 2025 AHTF revenue $24,682 (no in-lieu fees), balance $336,166 at June 30, 2025 (FY 2024 restated to $311,484 after audit). Recent BMR production: Centro Callan (10 BMR rental units), Poppy Lane (3 BMR homes).
affordability_requirement: 15% of units for moderate, low or very low income households; rental inclusionary units subject to recorded covenants administered under the BMR Procedural Manual (SLMC 19.172.030).
next_deadline: Applies at map or planning approval; the 2023-2031 Housing Element commits to an economic feasibility study and ordinance amendments during the cycle (not yet scheduled).
layering_notes: The AHTF is too small to fund projects on its own; it has covered predevelopment grants and a site acquisition contribution. The ordinance predates AB 1505 and still exempts small rental projects; developers of rental projects with 4 or more units owe 15% on-site, which is above Hayward's and Fremont's rental percentages and a cost consideration for mixed-income deals. Ordinance text read on the zoneomics mirror (qcode is blocked); fund figures from the FY 2025 AHTF report adopted by Resolution 2025-163 (December 15, 2025).

program_name: Residential Density Bonus, San Leandro Zoning Code Chapter 6.08, and inclusionary incentives (6.04.136)
administering_agency: City of San Leandro Community Development Department, Planning Division
typical_award_size: Requirement and entitlement, not a subsidy. Chapter 6.08 grants the bonus, incentives and concessions exactly as specified in Government Code 65915, processed concurrently with other entitlements and approved if the applicant complies with state law; continued availability of bonus units secured by agreement. Section 6.04.136 allows additional flexibility in density, lot size, yards and parking to accommodate required inclusionary units, but density bonus affordable units are in addition to the inclusionary requirement. Condominium conversions get the 65915.5 bonus (5.32.136).
affordability_requirement: State thresholds; inclusionary 15% must still be met on the base project.
next_deadline: Concurrent with the entitlement application.
layering_notes: No local enhancement beyond state law. San Leandro's affordable housing tools beyond density bonus are the inclusionary ordinance, the small AHTF, the HOME/PIP/PLHA RFP and the 2025 park fee exemption; there is no fee waiver for building permits and no local trust fund NOFA with meaningful capital. Code read on the zoneomics mirror.

program_name: Park Facilities Development Impact Fee exemption and 50% reduction for affordable units (Administrative Code Section 8.8.121, Council item 25-347, July 2025)
administering_agency: City of San Leandro Community Development Department and Recreation and Parks
typical_award_size: Park impact fees restructured in July 2025 from per-unit-type ($18,074 per multifamily unit in FY 2024-25) to unit-size tiers: under 550 sq ft $6,052; 550 to 750 sq ft $7,565; 751 to 1,150 sq ft $11,600; 1,151 to 1,650 sq ft $16,140; 1,651 to 1,950 sq ft $20,679; over 1,950 sq ft $25,723 (land acquisition plus improvement components, CPI and ENR indexed). New Section 8.8.121: a residential development is exempt from the park fee if 100% of units (excluding manager units) are affordable and the applicant is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit or controlled by one; any other affordable unit pays 50% of the otherwise applicable rate. ADU fees eliminated by companion resolution.
per_unit_cap: Not applicable (exemption or 50% reduction per affordable unit).
affordability_requirement: Affordable unit per Health and Safety Code 50093 with affordable rent (50053) or affordable housing cost (50052.5) under a recorded restrictive covenant; full exemption requires 100% affordable nonprofit ownership.
next_deadline: Applies at building permit; fees index annually. Confirm adoption of the final ordinance and resolution (introduced July 1, 2025) with the City Clerk.
layering_notes: The only development fee relief among the five priority cities that is written into local code for 100% affordable nonprofit projects (Oakland's AHIF exemption is comparable in effect). Saves roughly $6,000 to $12,000 per small unit. Other City fees (building permit, sewer connection) are not waived; school and EBMUD fees are outside City control. The document read was the draft resolution attached to the July 1, 2025 Council item on Legistar.

program_name: HOME Investment Partnerships Program through the Alameda County HOME Consortium (Cooperative Agreement FY 2027-2029, Council item 26-152) and PLHA
administering_agency: City of San Leandro Community Development Department, Housing Services Division, 835 East 14th Street; housing@sanleandro.org, (510) 577-6006
typical_award_size: San Leandro is too small for a direct HUD HOME allocation and has been a Consortium member since 1992. FY 2027 HOME allocation $201,134 ($190,548 program, $10,586 admin); prior-year balances $593,119; combined $783,667 committed March 2026 to Eden Housing for rehabilitation of The Surf (46 affordable units). Past HOME projects: Estabrook Place (51 senior units), Marea Alta (115 family units). PLHA formula funds support a BACS homelessness prevention shallow subsidy program (18 months, FY 2025-26 to 2026-27) and are offered for development through the City RFP.
affordability_requirement: HOME: 80% AMI and HOME rents; PLHA: per state PLHA plan, Housing First for services.
application_cycle: annual NOFA (HOME program year; projects selected through the City's Multifamily Affordable Housing Rehabilitation and Preservation selection process)
next_deadline: FY 2028 allocation expected spring 2027; HOME FY 2024 funds must be expended by June 30, 2027. The County may centralize HOME awards under the FY 2027-2029 agreement.
layering_notes: Duplicates the county HOME Consortium record in mechanism but the City controls its own formula share and selects the project. Recent use is rehabilitation of existing affordable stock rather than new construction. Pairs with the County HOME RFP, Measure A1 and 4% credit recapitalizations.

program_name: Stockton Affordable Housing NOFA (annual Housing NOFA; HOME, HOME-ARP, PLHA, LMIHF, NSP, CDBG, HHAP and PIP loan pool)
administering_agency: City of Stockton Economic Development Department, Housing Division (underwriting consultant TDA Consulting Inc.)
typical_award_size: 2025 Housing NOFA released October 30, 2025, closed December 18, 2025: 8 proposals requesting $28.2 million for 522 units; $11,979,838 available after de-obligating $1,614,000 of HOME and LMIHF from Sierra Vista III. Awards: Fairview Terrace (Mutual Housing California, 76 senior units) $2,800,000 gap loan approved March 31, 2026 (Resolution 2026-03-31-1601) on top of $7,037,865 HOME awarded November 19, 2024; Don Shalvey Apartments (Visionary Home Builders, 108 family units, TDC $84.0 million) $5,000,000 and Danny Drive (DCDC, 66 senior units, TDC $39.7 million) $4,179,838 recommended April 2026 after Council deferred them on March 31. 2024 NOFA (January 29, 2024) offered about $16.1 million and funded Fairview Terrace $7,037,865 HOME, Kentfield Apartments rehab $1,126,893 PLHA and LMIHF, Casa de Mariposa $747,055, plus two HHAP projects. Typical award $0.7 million to $7 million per project.
per_unit_cap: No published cap; 2025 applications ranged from about $27,000 to about $294,000 of City funds per unit. HOME subsidy limits apply when HOME is the source.
affordability_requirement: 55-year regulatory agreement and loan term at 3% simple interest, repaid from residual receipts proportionate to the City share of permanent financing; projects served 30% to 80% AMI (families) and 30% to 60% AMI (seniors). HOME-funded units carry the HOME affordability period inside the 55-year term. Article XXXIV authority: voters allow Council to approve up to 500 assisted units per year.
next_deadline: Next Housing NOFA expected about October 2026 under the Council-approved process (Motion 2025-11-04-1601: release, two-week question window, due date at least 45 days after release, pass/fail review, three-rater scoring, matrix to Council two weeks before award). No 2026 NOFA posted on the housing page as of 2026-11-08; confirm with hhep@stocktonca.gov, (209) 937-8538.
layering_notes: Stockton is the only city in San Joaquin County running a competitive gap-loan NOFA, and it is the main local soft source after the SJCOG San Joaquin Regional Housing Fund (county record). Pool is HUD and state pass-through plus housing successor LMIHF, so awards must fit each source's rules and deadlines; the City requires the full stack to be committed before executing loan documents and de-obligates allocations older than three years that cannot start within three years (Sierra Vista III lost $1.6 million in 2026). Scoring: developer capacity 30, proforma 30, populations served 15, design 15, leverage 10; an AI score was averaged with three human raters in 2025. Stacks with HACSJ project-based vouchers, County HOME (Urban County does not cover Stockton), BHSA and managed care plan grants (county records), the City PFF exemption and the 100% density bonus (records below). 2026 awards included HOME-ARP and PIP as eligible sources. Source documents read through the Stockton Legistar API and Granicus attachments; stocktonca.gov Economic Development pages have moved to /business/economic_development/housing_index.php.

program_name: CDBG, HOME and ESG entitlements, City of Stockton (2026-27 Annual Action Plan, CDBG/ESG NOFA and Real Property Acquisition NOFA)
administering_agency: City of Stockton Housing, Homelessness, Events and Parking Department (formerly Economic Development Department Housing Division)
typical_award_size: 2026-27 allocations: CDBG $3,229,216 plus about $350,000 program income, HOME $1,382,561, ESG $284,821. HOME budget: $1,324,906 HOME Housing Loans for multifamily rehab or new construction, $207,384 CHDO set-aside, $150,000 program delivery, $138,256 admin. CDBG largely to public infrastructure ($4,914,998 with carryover) and public services; 2026-27 CDBG/ESG public service NOFA awarded $498,509 CDBG and $262,528 ESG to nonprofits. 2024 Real Property Acquisition NOFA offered about $4,551,524 of CDBG and PIP for nonprofit site acquisition (5 applications, $10.0 million requested; awards included $1,500,000 to Parents by Choice for transitional youth housing at 523 E. Main and up to $800,000 CDBG to STAND for scattered-site acquisition).
per_unit_cap: HOME per-unit subsidy limits (24 CFR 92.250); no local cap.
affordability_requirement: HOME rents and incomes (at or below 60% AMI for rental, 15% CHDO set-aside), CDBG national objective, ESG homeless eligibility. HOME preference policy (2024, in 2025-2029 Consolidated Plan) favors projects serving targeted populations named in the Consolidated Plan.
next_deadline: HOME and other housing capital are awarded through the annual Housing NOFA (see NOFA record). CDBG/ESG public service NOFA runs each winter for awards in April (2026-27 awards approved April 2026). Substantial Amendments to the 2025-2029 Consolidated Plan and 2026-27 AAP were out for comment October 9 to November 10, 2026 with a Council hearing November 10, 2026. 2027-28 AAP draft expected spring 2027.
layering_notes: Stockton is its own HUD entitlement and HOME participating jurisdiction, so it is outside the San Joaquin Urban County CDBG/HOME program (county record) and County HOME cannot be used inside Stockton city limits. HOME match is currently 100% waived by HUD. HOME money is the backbone of the City Housing NOFA and has been combined with PLHA, LMIHF, HHAP and PIP in every recent award. CDBG has been used for land acquisition NOFAs for nonprofits, which is unusual in the region. HACSJ has secured City NOFA funds for its DCDC projects (Danny Drive, Sierra Vista). Draft 2026-27 AAP read from the Stockton Legistar attachment; the City housing page lists the same plans.

program_name: Low and Moderate Income Housing Fund (LMIHF), Successor Agency to the Stockton Redevelopment Agency (housing successor)
administering_agency: City of Stockton as Housing Successor; administered by the Housing Division through the Housing NOFA
typical_award_size: Fund balance not published in the 2026 NOFA documents; the Housing Source Funds Description lists LMIHF as a NOFA source for acquisition, new construction and conversion or rehabilitation for households up to 120% AMI. Recent uses: part of $1,614,000 HOME and LMIHF allocated to Sierra Vista III in 2019 and 2020 (de-obligated March 2026 and returned to the NOFA pool); part of $1,126,893 PLHA and LMIHF to Kentfield Apartments rehab (2024).
affordability_requirement: Housing successor rules (Health and Safety Code 34176.1): 55-year rental covenants, income targeting by statute with at least 30% of expenditures for extremely low income households over each five-year period; City NOFA applies a 55-year regulatory agreement.
next_deadline: Deployed only through the Housing NOFA (next expected about October 2026); no standalone LMIHF application. Check the annual housing successor report filed with the City's HCD Annual Progress Report for the current balance.
layering_notes: Stockton is one of the few San Joaquin County cities with legacy redevelopment housing money; Tracy, Manteca and Lodi records show none in active use. LMIHF is the most flexible source in the Stockton pool (local money, up to 120% AMI, no federal cross-cutting rules) and is usually paired with HOME to cover costs HOME cannot. Treat as a small, lumpy source: the only recent LMIHF commitments were under $1.7 million each. Combine with HACSJ PBVs and SJRHF gap loans (county records). Fund description opened from the Stockton Legistar attachment for the April 2026 award item; the Successor Agency meets concurrently with Council.

program_name: City-Wide Affordable Housing Development Public Facilities Fee (PFF) Exemption Program (with Greater Downtown Residential PFF Exemption; Resolutions 2015-11-17-1602, 2018-02-06-0504, 2018-11-06-1402, 2020-12-15-1105)
administering_agency: City of Stockton Economic Development Department (fee programs) with Community Development Department Permit Center
typical_award_size: Full exemption from seven Public Facilities Fee categories (city office space, libraries, fire stations, parkland, community recreation centers, police stations, street improvements) for qualifying new affordable housing anywhere in city limits; the same categories are exempt for all new residential development in the Greater Downtown area. Dollar value depends on the current PFF schedule (not published on the program page); the program was cited by HCD as a basis for Stockton's 2023 Prohousing Designation. Other PFFs (water, wastewater, air quality, habitat, school fees) and the SJMSCP habitat fee still apply.
per_unit_cap: Not applicable (fee exemption per unit equals the exempted PFF categories).
affordability_requirement: Qualifying affordable housing development as defined in the authorizing resolutions (deed-restricted units); confirm the affordability threshold and covenant term with the Economic Development Department before relying on it.
next_deadline: Programs sunset when the City completes its Master Infrastructure Plans and PFF Nexus Study and adopts new fees; Resolution 2020-12-15-1105 extended them, and the related Stockton Economic Stimulus Plan (SESP) fee reduction is being phased out over five years from 2025. Apply before building permit issuance through the Economic Development Department.
layering_notes: Most valuable local incentive in Stockton after the NOFA; the exemption reduces per-unit soft costs by the PFF categories listed and the downtown exemption applies to market-rate units too, which helps mixed-income deals. A non-residential short-term PFF deferral program (through December 31, 2027) and the non-residential 5 or 10 year deferral do not apply to housing. Stacks with the Chapter 16.40 density bonus and the Housing NOFA; fee exemptions count as public assistance for Labor Code 1720 analysis, so confirm prevailing wage exposure with counsel. Read from the City Business Assistance page (financial_assistance.php); authorizing resolutions are linked there.

program_name: Affordable Housing Incentives and Density Bonus Provisions, Stockton Municipal Code Chapter 16.40 (State bonus to 50%, Tier-1 to 75%, Tier-2 to 100%; Ord. 2020-12-01-1502, 2022-07-12-1601-02, 2025-06-03-1601)
administering_agency: City of Stockton Community Development Department, Planning Division
typical_award_size: Requirement and entitlement incentive, not a subsidy. State Density Bonus up to 50%; Tier-1 supplemental bonus 50% to 75% with 30 eligibility points; Tier-2 76% to 100% with 50 points. Points: one per additional percent of very low or low income units, LEED 15 to 30, CALGreen Tier I up to 20, 10% on-site renewable 15, adaptive reuse of historic buildings 20, plus other community benefits. Projects not qualifying for state concessions get three local concessions: setback reduction up to 25%, parking reductions of 25% to 100% scaled to the share of lower income units, lot coverage or FAR increases of 5% to 20%, lot coverage up to 25%, height plus 12 feet or 10%.
affordability_requirement: State law thresholds (5% very low, 10% low, 100% affordable, senior, moderate for-sale) for the base bonus; supplemental tiers require additional affordable units or community benefits scored under 16.40.050; density bonus housing agreement recorded per 16.40.070.
next_deadline: Applies at entitlement. Title 16 was amended June 3, 2025 and again in 2025-2026 (Chapter 16.20, 16.80.310, 16.244.010) to implement the 2023-2031 Housing Element; check the current code before design.
layering_notes: Stockton's 100% bonus exceeds state law and was one of HCD's stated reasons for the Prohousing Designation. Pair with the PFF exemption and the Housing NOFA; the Housing Element also allows duplexes by right in single-family zones. Parking can go to zero for projects with 75% or more lower income units, which matters for downtown and transit sites. Read from the zoneomics code mirror of Title 16 Division 3 because the City's code publisher blocks scripts.

program_name: Prohousing Designation and Prohousing Incentive Pilot (PIP) funds, City of Stockton (2023 designation, 2026 renewal application, PIP Rounds 1 to 4)
administering_agency: City of Stockton Housing, Homelessness, Events and Parking Department with HCD
typical_award_size: Stockton received $2.37 million in PIP funds after its 2023 designation (one of 22 jurisdictions then designated) and applied by March 31, 2026 for PIP Round 4 ($1,000,000 base plus up to $500,000 bonus, $1.5 million total, no match). PIP funds are placed in the Housing NOFA for predevelopment, construction, acquisition, rehabilitation or capitalized operating subsidies for households up to 120% AMI, and PIP was part of the $4.55 million 2024 property acquisition NOFA. The 2026 renewal application is out for public comment November 2 to December 8, 2026 (Council hearing December 8, 2026, 1:00 PM) and would keep the City eligible for PIP and HHAP preferences through 2029.
affordability_requirement: PIP: affordable to extremely low through moderate income households, or workforce housing up to 120% AMI (150% in high-cost areas); City NOFA covenants apply.
next_deadline: PIP money reaches developers only through the City Housing NOFA (next expected about October 2026). Prohousing renewal hearing December 8, 2026; PIP Round 4 award decision pending from HCD.
layering_notes: Designation also gives Stockton projects scoring preference in state competitive programs (AHSC, IIG, MHP, HHAP), which helps the local stack indirectly. Stockton Measure M (Strong Communities sales tax) funds libraries and recreation, not housing, and Measure W funds public safety; neither is a housing source despite appearing in the brief. Read from the City housing page, which also lists the 2025-2029 Consolidated Plan and 2026-27 AAP documents.

program_name: Density Bonus, Tracy Municipal Code Title 10 Chapter 10.08 Article 36.5 (Sections 10.08.4650 to 10.08.4695; Ordinance 1378 adopted January 20, 2026)
administering_agency: City of Tracy Community and Economic Development Department, Planning Division
typical_award_size: Requirement and entitlement incentive, not a subsidy. Ordinance 1378 repealed the 2008 article (Ord. 1113) and re-enacted Article 36.5 to match current state law: bonus of 5% to 35% (higher for 100% affordable projects under Government Code 65915), one or more concessions or incentives, parking caps, land donation and child care bonuses, and a recorded density bonus housing agreement (10.08.4686).
affordability_requirement: State thresholds: 10% very low, 20% low (code text uses 70% AMI for low), 50% senior, 20% moderate condominium units; 100% affordable projects under state law.
next_deadline: Applies at entitlement. Adopted as part of the Housing Element implementation package introduced December 2025 and adopted January 20, 2026; no further hearing scheduled.
layering_notes: Tracy's bonus is the state minimum with no local enhancement, unlike Stockton's 100% tier. The 2023-2031 Housing Element (adopted July 1, 2025, HCD compliance letter August 11, 2025, RHNA 8,830) relies on rezoning rather than local subsidy. Tracy's Residential Growth Management Ordinance governs allotments for market-rate units; confirm whether affordable projects are exempt. Read from the zoneomics mirror of Title 10 because cityoftracy.org returns 403 to scripts and its Municipal Code host blocks automated access.

program_name: Tracy Affordable Housing Ordinance, in-lieu fee and Affordable Housing Fund (status unconfirmed)
administering_agency: City of Tracy Community and Economic Development Department
typical_award_size: Not confirmed this pass. The current Title 10 Chapter 10.08 code mirror contains only the Article 36.5 density bonus; no inclusionary article, in-lieu fee or affordable housing fund section appears, and Article 33 is absent from the chapter sequence. Search snippets show a June 1, 2021 Council goal to evaluate an inclusionary and in-lieu fee program and a housing trust fund, which suggests any earlier ordinance was repealed or never funded. No Tracy Affordable Housing Fund NOFA was found.
affordability_requirement: Unknown; none in current code mirror.
application_cycle: closed/inactive (no active local inclusionary requirement or fund identified)
next_deadline: Verify with Planning (209) 831-6400 whether an Affordable Housing Fund balance exists from past in-lieu payments and whether the 2023-2031 Housing Element programs commit to a new inclusionary or linkage fee study; the Housing Element PDF (about 12 MB) could not be opened this pass.
layering_notes: Tracy appears to have no local gap money for multifamily: no trust fund, no in-lieu fee receipts identified, no RDA housing successor fund in current agendas, and HUD money flows through the San Joaquin Urban County (county record). The realistic local layer is land use (density bonus, Housing Element rezoning sites) plus the regional sources: SJRHF gap loans, HACSJ PBVs, County HOME and HOME-ARP, BHSA and managed care plan grants (Health Plan of San Joaquin gave Tracy $595,000 and $1.2 million for its shelter). Blocked: cityoftracy.org (Akamai 403 to scripts; HTML pages under 10 MB readable only through the WebFetch tool), tracyca.prod.govaccess.org (connection refused), Tracy PrimeGov agenda portal not reached. Source is the City's Housing Element Update page, which was opened and documents the July 1, 2025 adoption.

program_name: CDBG and HOME in Tracy (San Joaquin Urban County share, City FY 2026-27 CDBG/HOME application) and City use of PLHA and HHAP
administering_agency: City of Tracy Economic Development (CDBG/HOME) and Homeless Services Division; funds pass through San Joaquin County Neighborhood Preservation Division
typical_award_size: Tracy's FY 2026-27 Urban County CDBG entitlement request is $521,683 (county record). The City posted a FY 2026-27 CDBG and HOME Notice of Funding Availability (contact Alexandra Pineda, cdbg.home@cityoftracy.org, (209) 831-6491) but the notice could not be opened this pass. City uses of flexible funds have gone to the Temporary Emergency Housing Facility shelter: $331,794 CDBG recommended for shelter operations (January 30, 2026), $18,650 County CDBG for furnishings (March 3, 2026), a $786,574 PLHA application for shelter operations (February 20, 2026), HHAP Round 4 $436,246 and a Round 5 application (December 19, 2025), plus $7.17 million County ARPA and a $3 million HUD EDI grant for shelter site work.
per_unit_cap: HOME subsidy limits (24 CFR 92.250) when County HOME is used.
affordability_requirement: HUD CDBG national objective and HOME rent and income limits; County Urban County rules apply.
next_deadline: County Urban County NOFA for FY 2027-28 expected about October to December 2026 (county record); Tracy's own CDBG/HOME application window for FY 2026-27 has closed. Confirm the City's next cycle with cdbg.home@cityoftracy.org.
layering_notes: Tracy does not control HOME: HOME rental awards are made by the County (for example Lodi Commons and STAND), so a Tracy multifamily deal applies to the County HOME NOFA with a City support letter, and Tracy's CDBG share is small and has been committed to the shelter. PLHA and HHAP have been used for shelter operations rather than capital. Layer County HOME, SJRHF, HACSJ PBVs and BHSA (county records) with the Tracy density bonus. The City news article announcing the CDBG/HOME application returned 404 and the govaccess PDF host refused connections; facts above were read from the City's homelessness actions page (opened) and the county record.

program_name: Density Bonus and Other Incentives, Manteca Municipal Code Chapter 17.72 (Ord. 1501, 2011) and Draft Zoning Code Update (public review October 22 to November 21, 2026)
administering_agency: City of Manteca Development Services Department, Planning Division
typical_award_size: Requirement and entitlement incentive, not a subsidy. One density bonus with concessions per Government Code 65915 for 10% lower income, 5% very low income, senior or 10% moderate for-sale units; parking caps of 1 space (0-1 bedroom), 2 (2-3 bedrooms), 2.5 (4 or more bedrooms); waivers of standards that physically preclude the project; density bonus agreement required; pro forma review consultant paid by applicant unless nonprofit. The Draft Zoning Code Update (implementing the 2043 General Plan and 6th Cycle Housing Element) rewrites 17.72 and the 17.200 density bonus definitions and makes Council the approval authority.
affordability_requirement: State density bonus thresholds; continued affordability per Government Code 65915 (55 years rental) under the agreement required by 17.72.030.
next_deadline: Applies at entitlement. Draft Zoning Code Update comment period closed November 21, 2026; Planning Commission hearing noticed, Council adoption expected late 2026 or early 2027.
layering_notes: Manteca's 2011 chapter has not kept pace with state law (no 50% or 100% bonus tiers, old parking ratios), so state law controls in practice; the pending Zoning Code Update should fix this. Section 17.72.030.G still references a Chapter 17.32 Affordable Housing Requirements that no longer exists in the code (see next record). Manteca has no local trust fund, in-lieu fund or NOFA, so the land-use incentive plus County and regional sources (Urban County CDBG and HOME, SJRHF, HACSJ PBVs, BHSA) are the whole local layer. Read from the zoneomics mirror of Title 17 (ecode360 blocks scripts); the City's Title 17 page confirms the update schedule.

program_name: Manteca Affordable Housing Requirements (former Chapter 17.32) and proposed affordable housing fee (no active inclusionary ordinance, in-lieu fund or housing trust fund)
administering_agency: City of Manteca Development Services Department
typical_award_size: Not an active program. Current Title 17 has no Chapter 17.32; the chapter is only referenced in 17.72.030.G, indicating the inclusionary requirement was repealed. Local press reported a City nexus study supporting a maximum $16.86 per square foot affordable housing fee and Council discussion of adopting a fee, but no ordinance or fee resolution was found on manteca.gov or in the Draft Zoning Code Update. No Manteca Housing Trust Fund, in-lieu fee fund or housing successor LMIHAF appears in City pages.
affordability_requirement: None in effect.
next_deadline: Verify with Planning (209) 456-8540 whether an affordable housing impact or linkage fee is scheduled for Council action with the Zoning Code Update, and whether any in-lieu balance remains from the former Chapter 17.32.
layering_notes: Manteca receives CDBG through the San Joaquin Urban County ($420,911 FY 2026-27 request, county record) and HOME through the County NOFA; the City is a member of the SJCOG San Joaquin Regional Housing Fund. Expect no City gap money; County HOME, SJRHF, HACSJ PBVs and BHSA plus the density bonus are the stack. Blocked this pass: manteca.prod-as.govaccess.org (6th Cycle Housing Element PDF, connection refused), manteca.gov site search and Agenda Center (JavaScript only); the adopted General Plan PDF on manteca.gov lists the Housing Element under separate cover. Source is the Title 17 code mirror chapter that carries the dangling 17.32 reference.

program_name: Manteca 6th Cycle Housing Element implementation and Urban County CDBG/HOME (no city-run housing NOFA)
administering_agency: City of Manteca Development Services Department; San Joaquin County Human Services Agency Neighborhood Preservation Division for CDBG and HOME
typical_award_size: Manteca's FY 2026-27 Urban County CDBG request is $420,911; HOME for Manteca projects comes from the County HOME NOFA (about $973,290 countywide entitlement). The City itself publishes no housing NOFA, trust fund or fee waiver program; its housing work in 2025-2026 is the Zoning Code Update implementing the 2043 General Plan (adopted 2023) and the 6th Cycle Housing Element (RHNA 4,822 units, about 3,270 at or below 120% AMI per press coverage of the draft).
per_unit_cap: HOME subsidy limits apply to County HOME awards.
affordability_requirement: HUD CDBG national objective and HOME rent and income limits for County-funded projects; Housing Element programs may offer density bonus and streamlined review only.
next_deadline: County Urban County NOFA for FY 2027-28 expected about October to December 2026 (county record). Confirm Manteca Housing Element programs (fee deferral, surplus land, incentives) with Planning once the Housing Element PDF is reachable.
layering_notes: Documented so the gap is explicit: Manteca is the county's fastest growing city but has no local affordable housing capital. Developers should apply to the County HOME NOFA, SJRHF gap loans, HACSJ PBVs and BHSA (county records) and use the Chapter 17.72 density bonus. The Title 17 page (opened) confirms the Zoning Code Update implements the 6th Cycle Housing Element; the Housing Element document itself is hosted on the blocked govaccess server.

program_name: CDBG entitlement, City of Lodi (2026-27 Annual Action Plan and annual CDBG application cycle)
administering_agency: City of Lodi Community Development Department, Neighborhood Services Division (CDBG administration consultant Michael Baker International)
typical_award_size: 2026-27 CDBG award $665,263 (2025-26 $655,037; 2024-25 $675,615): capital projects $434,263 including Public Works $235,000, DCDC/HACSJ Salas Park (Lodi Commons) $115,000 and $84,263 unassigned; CBO services $98,000 (15% cap); admin $133,000 including fair housing. 2026-27 cycle anticipated about $310,000 for capital and infrastructure applications. City guideline: 40% of the award net of admin to community-based organizations. No program income.
per_unit_cap: None; HOME limits do not apply because Lodi has no HOME allocation.
affordability_requirement: HUD CDBG national objective (low and moderate income benefit); Consolidated Plan 2024-2028 goal to preserve and increase affordable housing through rehabilitation, land acquisition or partnerships with housing developers.
eligible_project_types: site acquisition and infrastructure for affordable housing
application_cycle: annual NOFA (applications December to late January)
next_deadline: 2026-27 applications ran December 8, 2025 to January 27, 2026; the 2027-28 cycle should open about December 2026 with applications due late January 2027 and funds available July 1, 2027. 2025-26 CAPER hearing was September 2, 2026. Contact NeighborhoodServices@lodi.gov.
layering_notes: Lodi is a CDBG entitlement city but not a HOME participating jurisdiction; HOME for Lodi projects comes from the San Joaquin Urban County NOFA (Lodi Commons received $230,024 plus $500,000 program income in 2026-27 and $2 million HOME-ARP, county records). City CDBG contributions to housing are small infrastructure or predevelopment pieces ($115,000 to Salas Park in 2026-27), so treat CDBG as a sub-$250,000 layer. Lodi joined the SJCOG San Joaquin Regional Housing Fund by resolution on July 17, 2024 and gets HHAP Round 4 ($652,126) and Round 5 subrecipient funds for shelter and transitional housing. Read from the City CDBG page and the 2026-27 Annual Action Plan PDF.

program_name: Residential Density Bonus, Lodi Municipal Code Section 17.36.050 (Development Code; Housing Element Program 1.1 update pending)
administering_agency: City of Lodi Community Development Department, Planning Division
typical_award_size: Requirement and entitlement incentive, not a subsidy. Bonus of 20% to 35% for 10% low income or 5% very low income units, 5% to 35% for 10% moderate income common interest units, 20% for senior projects, additional child care bonus; maximum 35% in the code text, with the code deferring to state law where it conflicts. At least one incentive for qualifying projects of five or more units.
affordability_requirement: State density bonus thresholds; affordability covenants per Government Code 65915 (55 years rental).
next_deadline: Applies at entitlement. Housing Element Program 1.1 commits the City to update 17.36.050 to the current state tier framework (up to 50% and 100% bonuses); the 2025 Development Code amendments (Ordinances 2030 and 2034) addressed other sections, so the density bonus update is still pending as of 2026-11-08.
layering_notes: Lodi has no inclusionary ordinance (Housing Element confirms) and no local in-lieu fee, so the density bonus is the only land-use subsidy. Because the code defers to state law, developers can claim the full state bonus despite the outdated 35% text. Pair with County HOME, SJRHF, HACSJ PBVs and the City surplus land program (next record). Read from the zoneomics mirror of Title 17 Article 3 because municode blocks scripts.

program_name: City-owned sites for affordable housing (Housing Element Program 1.16 Surplus Land Act; Salas Park right-of-way with HACSJ; 130 West Century Boulevard)
administering_agency: City of Lodi Community Development Department and City Council
typical_award_size: Land contribution, not cash. Salas Park former right-of-way (about 3 acres rezoned to High Density Residential by Ordinance 2026, August 2024): City agreement with the Housing Authority of the County of San Joaquin for up to 110 affordable units, first phase Lodi Commons (DCDC Senior Housing at Salas Park, 54 senior units plus manager) funded with County HOME, HOME-ARP, HHAP, Congressional Community Project funds and $115,000 City CDBG. 130 West Century Boulevard (about 2.5 acres, Housing Element capacity 53 lower income units) under Council discussion January 27, 2026 with no decision. Program 1.16 targets 101 lower income units on four City sites, with RFP or sale by 2026, ENA 2026, entitlements 2027-2028, permits 2029.
affordability_requirement: Lower income units counted toward RHNA; Surplus Land Act priority to affordable housing developers (25% affordable minimum under Government Code 54233 when sold for housing).
next_deadline: Housing Element Program 1.16 calls for an action plan to sell or RFP City-owned land for affordable housing by 2026 and incentives for affordable housing on City sites by 2026; watch Council agendas for a Surplus Land Act declaration on 130 West Century Boulevard and the remaining Salas Park phase (56 units).
layering_notes: Lodi's only material local contribution to multifamily deals is land; the City budget has no housing fund and no RDA housing successor fund appears in the Housing Element or in Council items since 2024. The HACSJ partnership shows the working model: City land plus County HOME and HOME-ARP, HHAP, HACSJ PBVs and tax credits (county records). A developer other than HACSJ would need a Surplus Land Act process. Read from the City 2026-27 Annual Action Plan PDF (Salas Park partnership) and the Legistar staff reports for the January 27, 2026 Century Boulevard item.

program_name: Lodi Housing Element 2023-2031 incentive programs (Program 1.6 fee waivers, reductions or deferrals for infill at 20 or more units per acre; Program 1.12 incentives for special needs housing; Program 1.5 funding applications)
administering_agency: City of Lodi Community Development Department
typical_award_size: Not yet adopted as a standing program. Program 1.6 commits the City to adopt by 2025 one or more incentives for infill housing at 20 or more units per acre: parking credits, fee waivers, reductions or deferrals when financially feasible, priority processing. Program 1.12 commits to incentives (reduced standards, fee waivers or financial assistance) for housing for persons with disabilities by 2026. Program 1.5 sets a goal of the City securing $1 million in state or federal housing funds by 2028 and $2 million by 2031. Housing Element impact fee estimate: about $18,948 development impact fees plus $11,468 building fees per single-family home; multifamily fees lower per unit.
affordability_requirement: Program 1.6 objective: incentivize 100 extremely low, 200 very low and 200 low income units on infill parcels; Program 1.12 objective 40 special needs units.
eligible_project_types: new construction (infill, 20 or more units per acre)
next_deadline: No adopting resolution found through 2026-11-08; the Housing Element deadline for Program 1.6 (2025) has passed, so ask Planning (209) 333-6711 whether a fee deferral or waiver policy is before Council. Lodi is also adding Chapter 15.69 (Agricultural Mitigation Fee) and 15.70 (Parkland Dedication and In-Lieu) in October 2026, which add costs rather than relief.
layering_notes: Lodi has no housing trust fund, inclusionary ordinance, in-lieu fee or housing successor fund; HOME comes only through the County. Until Program 1.6 is adopted, the only fee relief is state law (ADU fee exemptions, SB 937 fee timing). Expect County HOME plus SJRHF, HACSJ PBVs and BHSA (county records) to carry gap financing, with City CDBG for off-site infrastructure. Programs read from the adopted 2023-2031 Housing Element PDF on lodi.gov (HCD certified April 11, 2024).

program_name: Affordable Housing Development RFP No. 26-004A (Inclusionary Housing Fund, HOME, HOME-ARP and Housing Successor Agency loans)
administering_agency: City of Santa Ana Community Development Agency, Housing Division, 20 Civic Center Plaza M-26, (714) 667-2250; bid contact Jacques Lam, JLam@santa-ana.org; solicitation on PlanetBids portal 20137
typical_award_size: Open RFP issued May 1, 2026 with $17,507,926 available: Inclusionary Housing Funds $2,628,194, HOME $11,533,196, HOME-ARP $715,622 (permanent supportive housing only), Housing Successor Agency Funds $2,630,914, plus Housing Authority project-based vouchers and Housing Successor land. Available funds are republished each quarter in the Housing Division Quarterly Report and added to the RFP by addendum. Recent City awards: Crossroads at Washington $4,600,000 plus 15 PBVs (86 units), WISEPlace $5,200,000 plus 25 PBVs (48 units), Estrella Springs $1,600,000 plus 89 PBVs (89 units), Wellington $920,000 (9 ownership units, approved July 1, 2025), Richard Lehn Intergenerational Housing $2,021,319 HHAP plus 8 PBVs (11 units).
per_unit_cap: None fixed for local funds; HOME subsidy is limited to the HUD maximum per-unit subsidy limits and the City's Affordable Housing Funds Policies and Procedures (amended Aug 18, 2020) cap by-right applications at the HUD per-unit limits.
affordability_requirement: At least 55-year covenants; Inclusionary and Housing Successor funds serve moderate (120% AMI), low, very low and extremely low income households and may fund mixed-income and mixed-use projects; HOME units at High and Low HOME rents with 20% of HOME-assisted units at 50% AMI in projects of five or more HOME units; HOME-ARP units are permanent supportive housing only. Priority points for substantial rehabilitation and adaptive reuse (motel and office conversions), homeownership, and by-right or shovel-ready projects.
application_cycle: rolling (quarterly deadlines under a one-year open RFP)
next_deadline: Quarterly proposal deadlines: January 11, 2027 and May 3, 2027 at 4:00 p.m. (July 1 and October 1, 2026 rounds have passed); question deadlines November 30, 2026 and April 5, 2027. The City's stated objective is to issue one affordable housing RFP per year and finance at least one multifamily project per year.
layering_notes: Santa Ana is the deepest city pool in Orange County: about $17,500,000 in one RFP, mostly HOME, with loans at 3% simple interest, 55-year term, repaid from 50% of residual receipts, TCAC developer fee limits and a Review Panel scoring process under the 2020 Affordable Housing Funds Policies and Procedures (opened). City-funded projects must comply with the Community Workforce Agreement (30% of craft hours from Santa Ana and Orange County ZIP codes, union hiring halls) and state prevailing wage; Davis-Bacon applies to HOME projects of 12 or more assisted units. Stack with County 2026 Supportive Housing NOFA loans and OCHA or SAHA PBVs, OCHFT gap loans (WISEPlace took $2,500,000 OCHFT MHSA plus $1,500,000 County ARPA) and 4% or 9% credits. The County NOFA pays $95,000 to $105,000 per unit inside Santa Ana, so the City loan is normally the larger local layer. RFP PDF, RFP page, policies PDF and FY 2025-26 Q4 quarterly report opened on santa-ana.gov and its Google Cloud document store.

program_name: Affordable Housing Opportunity and Creation Ordinance (Municipal Code Chapter 41, Article XVIII.I, Secs. 41-1900 to 41-1909; Ordinance NS-3019) and in-lieu fee to the Inclusionary Housing Fund
administering_agency: City of Santa Ana Planning and Building Agency (inclusionary housing plans) and Community Development Agency Housing Division (Inclusionary Housing Fund)
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Applies to projects of five or more units (lowered from 20 by NS-3019, adopted April 19, 2022) that receive a discretionary density or land use increase. Rental projects: 15% low income, or 10% very low, or 5% extremely low, or a 10% mix (5% low, 3% very low, 2% extremely low). For-sale projects: 5% moderate income. In-lieu fee per habitable square foot on a tiered schedule of $6.00, $9.00, $12.00 and $15.00 by project size, with the $15.00 rate for 20 or more units reducible to $10.00 or $5.00 when the developer commits to local hire (30% of hours) and skilled and trained workforce percentages. The earlier NS-2994 amendment had cut the fee from $15 to $5 per square foot before the 2022 rewrite. Inclusionary Housing Fund receipts since inception: $31,147,483 (FY 2009-2020 $10,800,251; FY 20/21 $3,709,875; FY 21/22 $6,933,320; FY 22/23 $0; FY 23/24 $834,000; FY 24/25 $0; FY 25/26 $1,685,995 from the 408-unit Lowe Enterprises project at 2828 N. Main St.). Fund expenditures to date $20,558,250 for 224 units plus The Link interim shelter ($7,893,866); commitments $1,357,021. Only 35 on-site inclusionary units (25 ownership, 10 rental) have been built since 2011, so the ordinance functions mainly as a fee.
affordability_requirement: On-site units restricted 55 years; fund may be spent on moderate, low, very low and extremely low income rental and ownership housing, shelter and down payment assistance. Sec. 41-1904.1 incentives for on-site production: up to 25% setback reduction, up to 20 feet of added height, and a local density bonus of 1.5% for each 1% of for-sale units above 5% moderate income, up to 35%.
eligible_project_types: market-rate rental and for-sale projects of 5 or more units (compliance)
next_deadline: Applies at entitlement; fee due before building permit. Fee schedule may be changed only by a five-vote Council supermajority (Sec. 41-1904(c)). The Housing Element programs commit the City to periodic review of the threshold and fee.
layering_notes: This fee stream feeds the Inclusionary Housing Fund that is offered through the City's annual Affordable Housing Development RFP (record above), which is the only Orange County city in-lieu fund with a regular competitive outlet. Orange County has no county inclusionary ordinance, so this is a city-only requirement. Market-rate developers often use the ordinance's local density bonus with the state bonus; the Housing Element notes the 2022 rewrite was meant to recover fee revenue lost after NS-2994 cut the rate to $5. Ordinance page, NS-3019 PDF and the zoneomics code mirror for Article XVIII.I opened; fund figures from the FY 2025-26 Q4 Housing Division Quarterly Report (opened).

program_name: Low and Moderate Income Housing Asset Fund (Housing Authority of the City of Santa Ana as Housing Successor to the Santa Ana Community Redevelopment Agency)
administering_agency: Housing Authority of the City of Santa Ana as Housing Successor, staffed by the Community Development Agency Housing Division
typical_award_size: LMIHAF ending balance $4,134,871 at June 30, 2025 (FY 2024-25 SB 341 report); $305,772 deposited and $0 spent on development that year. $2,630,914 of Housing Successor funds are in RFP 26-004A. Past commitments: $6,195,000 in 2016 for 69 units and $13,222,740 in 2017 for 118 units. The Housing Successor also ground-leases former RDA sites for 65 to 99 years: 1126 and 1146 Washington (Crossroads at Washington, 86 units, completed October 2024), 801-809 E. Santa Ana Blvd (FX Residences, 16 to 17 PSH units, completed April 2025), 826 N. Lacy (two Habitat homes, 2023). The City and Housing Successor loan portfolio totals $155,432,612 in 344 loans (325 deferred or residual receipts).
per_unit_cap: Subject to the HUD per-unit limits adopted in the City's Affordable Housing Funds Policies for by-right requests; otherwise sized by gap analysis.
affordability_requirement: Low and moderate income (up to 120% AMI) under Health and Safety Code 34176.1; at least 30% of expenditures over each five-year period must serve households at or below 30% AMI (extremely low income test reported for July 2020 to June 2025); senior housing limited to 50% of assisted units over 10 years.
application_cycle: rolling (offered through the annual Affordable Housing Development RFP)
next_deadline: Next RFP quarterly deadline January 11, 2027; land assets are offered when the Housing Authority issues site-specific RFPs.
layering_notes: Small compared with the County's $29,000,000 LMIHAF but flexible: no federal strings, can serve moderate income and mixed-use, and the Housing Authority's land is the real asset (Crossroads and FX Residences were built on 65- and 99-year ground leases). Pair with HOME in the same RFP, SAHA PBVs, County MHSA/BHSA capital and OCHFT. Public funds trigger state prevailing wage and the City's Community Workforce Agreement. FY 2024-25 Housing Successor Annual Report PDF and the Successor Agency page opened on santa-ana.gov.

program_name: HOME Investment Partnerships, CDBG and ESG entitlement (FY 2025-2029 Consolidated Plan)
administering_agency: City of Santa Ana Community Development Agency, Housing Division (HOME Participating Jurisdiction since 1994)
typical_award_size: Five-year Consolidated Plan FY 2025-2029 anticipates $41,700,000: CDBG $30,123,118, HOME $9,093,495, ESG $2,504,870. HOME development funds are deployed as loans through the Affordable Housing Development RFP ($11,533,196 of HOME and $715,622 of HOME-ARP available in RFP 26-004A), with 15% of each annual HOME allocation reserved for certified CHDOs. CDBG funds public services, infrastructure, the Residential Rehabilitation Program (grants up to $25,000, closed in Q4 FY 2025-26 when funds ran out) and shelter; HOME also funds the My First Home mortgage assistance program.
per_unit_cap: HOME: HUD maximum per-unit subsidy limits; affordability period 5, 10 or 15 years for rental assistance under $25,000, $25,000 to $50,000, and over $50,000 per unit (20 years for new construction), but the City records 55-year covenants on its loans.
affordability_requirement: HOME rental units at or below 80% AMI at High and Low HOME rents, 20% of HOME-assisted units at 50% AMI in projects of five or more HOME units; CDBG national objective benefit to low and moderate income persons.
next_deadline: Annual Action Plan adopted each spring for the July 1 program year; developer requests go through the Affordable Housing Development RFP quarterly deadlines (next January 11, 2027). Public service and CDBG applications are solicited in the winter before the Action Plan.
layering_notes: Santa Ana's HOME grant (about $1,800,000 a year) is larger than the County Urban County HOME grant ($1,244,583) and the City lends most of it to multifamily deals rather than TBRA, which is why HOME is the largest line in the RFP. Davis-Bacon applies at 12 or more HOME-assisted units; HOME brings NEPA, Section 3 and a HUD subsidy layering review. HOME-ARP is limited to permanent supportive housing. Santa Ana is outside the County Urban County program, so County HOME is not available inside the city. Consolidated Plan page, CDBG page, HOME page and Grants page opened on santa-ana.gov; RFP PDF supplies the HOME terms.

program_name: Project-Based Vouchers, Housing Authority of the City of Santa Ana (SAHA)
administering_agency: Housing Authority of the City of Santa Ana (Community Development Agency), waiting list hotline (714) 667-2284
typical_award_size: PBVs are committed to City-financed projects through the Affordable Housing Development RFP: Estrella Springs 89 PBVs (89 PSH units, former Budget Inn), WISEPlace on Broadway 25 PBVs (15 set aside for domestic violence survivors), Crossroads at Washington 15 PBVs (43 PSH units of 86), Richard Lehn Intergenerational Housing 8 PBVs (11 units, under construction), plus earlier commitments at Casa Querencia (57 units), Heroes' Landing (75), The Orchard (72) and FX Residences (17). PBV waiting lists for Crossroads at Washington and Andalucia closed April 30, 2026. SAHA received 25 Foster Youth to Independence vouchers in August 2025. Total HCV count not confirmed from an opened document.
affordability_requirement: PBV households at or below 50% AMI at admission (30% of adjusted income toward rent); PSH units generally 30% AMI with Coordinated Entry referrals; HAP contracts up to 20 years.
application_cycle: rolling (requested with or without capital in the Affordable Housing Development RFP)
next_deadline: Request PBVs in the RFP quarterly rounds (next January 11, 2027); SAHA's FY 2026 Annual Plan draft (Feb 17, 2026) was opened but lists no fixed PBV allotment.
layering_notes: Santa Ana is one of four PHAs in Orange County (with OCHA, Anaheim and Garden Grove) and has been the most active in project-basing: 89 PBVs at Estrella Springs is the largest single PBV award in the county. A HAP contract is not itself a prevailing wage trigger but Davis-Bacon applies to new construction or rehab of nine or more PBV units and PBVs bring a HUD subsidy layering review. Combine with City HOME or Housing Successor loans, County MHSA/BHSA capital and OCHFT. The City also receives its own HHAP allocation (Richard Lehn used $2,021,319 HHAP), so the operating stack for PSH can be entirely city-controlled. PSH properties page, Housing Authority page, PBV waiting list notices and the 2025 Affordable Housing Awards release opened on santa-ana.gov.

program_name: Density Bonus for Affordable Housing (Municipal Code Chapter 41, Article XVI.I, Secs. 41-1600 to 41-1607) and Density Bonus Agreements
administering_agency: City of Santa Ana Planning and Building Agency, Planning Division, (714) 667-2700
typical_award_size: Requirement and entitlement, not a subsidy. The local article grants a 25% density bonus plus one additional development incentive under a recorded Density Bonus Agreement, with waivers or modifications of development standards decided under Sec. 41-1607; state law (Government Code 65915) now governs bonus amounts up to 50% or more, up to five incentives or concessions and unlimited waivers, and the City applies the state schedule. The FY 2025-26 Q4 Housing Division report lists the Density Bonus Agreements executed to date, including 415 and 547 rental units restricted under two agreements and smaller sets of 92, 19, 11 and 2 very low income units.
affordability_requirement: State law thresholds: 5% very low, 10% low, 10% moderate for-sale, or 100% affordable; local code covenants of 30 years when an additional incentive is granted (state law requires 55 years for rental); a monitoring fee set by resolution applies.
next_deadline: Applies at project application; agreements recorded before building permit.
layering_notes: Santa Ana projects routinely combine the state density bonus with the AHOCO local bonus and the Transit Zoning Code (SD-84) and Metro East overlays; the Housing Element credits the City with 5,130 permits from 2021 to 2024, 152% of its very low, low and moderate RHNA progress through 2025. No fee waiver or impact fee deferral ordinance for affordable housing was found; the County NOFA treats city fee waivers as match but Santa Ana offers none. Density bonus alone does not trigger prevailing wage. Code text read on the zoneomics mirror; the Q4 quarterly report lists agreements.

program_name: Prohousing Designation (HCD Prohousing Designation Program)
administering_agency: City of Santa Ana Planning and Building Agency; designation issued by HCD
typical_award_size: Not a direct subsidy. Santa Ana appears on HCD's list of Prohousing Designated Jurisdictions, which gives projects inside the city bonus points or priority processing in AHSC, Infill Infrastructure Grant, Transformative Climate Communities, SCCP, LPP, TIRCP and STPG, and makes the City eligible for the Prohousing Incentive Program (PIP).
affordability_requirement: Follows the state program applied for (AHSC and IIG serve lower income projects at or below 80% AMI).
next_deadline: Designation is good for four years from award and must be renewed; PIP rounds are announced by HCD. Confirm the designation date with the Planning Division.
layering_notes: The only Prohousing city among the five Orange County priority cities (Anaheim, Irvine, Huntington Beach and Garden Grove are not on the list opened 2026-11-08), so AHSC and IIG applications in Santa Ana carry the designation points. The City's own HHAP allocation, SAHA PBVs and the RFP loans make a full local stack for AHSC-sized projects. HCD designated jurisdictions page opened.

program_name: Permanent Local Housing Allocation (PLHA), City of Santa Ana entitlement
administering_agency: City of Santa Ana Community Development Agency, Housing Division
typical_award_size: Amount not published on the City site. The 2021-2029 Housing Element lists PLHA alongside Inclusionary and HOME as a funding source for the City's rental production, acquisition-rehabilitation and homeownership programs, and the City's own HHAP allocation is budgeted separately. The Housing Division Quarterly Report (FY 2025-26 Q4) does not list PLHA among available development funds, which suggests the allocation is committed to homeless services and homeownership rather than offered to developers.
affordability_requirement: Per PLHA statute: rental production at or below 60% AMI, assistance to persons experiencing homelessness, affordable ownership and workforce housing.
next_deadline: unknown, verify with agency; confirm the five-year PLHA plan allocation and whether any PLHA is set aside for development.
layering_notes: Santa Ana is an HCD PLHA entitlement separate from the County Urban County allocation (County CY 2025 $956,505), and its share is likely larger than the County's, but no City page or report with the figure could be opened this pass; santa-ana.gov site search returned no PLHA page. Treat as a possible add-on to the Housing Division RFP rather than a stand-alone source. Housing Element PDF (September 2022 certified element) opened and is the source for the program description.

program_name: Anaheim Local Housing Trust Fund (A-LHTF), Ordinance No. 6588; Program Guidelines and Funding Allocation Plan (adopted May 29, 2025, revised June 9, 2026)
administering_agency: City of Anaheim Housing and Community Development Department, with transfers to the Anaheim Housing Authority by cooperation agreement; 201 S. Anaheim Blvd., Suite 201
typical_award_size: Initial Funding Allocation Plan of $16,000,000: Build More Homes Initiative $5,000,000 (includes $1,000,000 from a federal grant restricted to housing production), First-Time Homebuyer programs $5,000,000 ($50,000 downpayment loans), Housing Stability Program $1,000,000, administration $500,000 (3.12%), reserve $4,500,000. Build More Homes funds pay for site acquisition, site preparation (environmental, demolition, relocation) and gap financing, structured as loans at 4% simple interest repaid from a residual receipts split; A-LHTF money may not exceed 50% of total City investment in a project. Eligible deposits include General Fund, federal PRO Housing grant, state Local Housing Trust Fund matching grants, REAP 2.0 (gap financing for infill with at least 65% residential floor area in mixed-use), Development Agreement community benefit payments, philanthropy and in-lieu fees paid under the City's Affordable Housing Ordinance.
per_unit_cap: None published; sized by financial analysis and capped at 50% of City investment per project.
affordability_requirement: Affordability follows the leveraged source (LIHTC, HOME, PLHA); where none applies the City sets project-specific requirements, generally 55-year covenants. Target beneficiaries: workforce households, households experiencing homelessness, active older adults 55 and over, special needs (transition-age youth, persons with disabilities, persons with AIDS). Shelters, transitional housing and group homes are ineligible.
application_cycle: rolling (project-by-project Council actions; annual Funding Allocation Plan in the City budget)
next_deadline: No NOFA. Each expenditure requires a separate Council action; the Funding Allocation Plan is updated in the annual budget cycle (next spring 2027). Approach Housing and Community Development with a site or gap request.
layering_notes: Anaheim's answer to losing $15,000,000 to $17,000,000 a year of redevelopment set-aside: the trust consolidates HOME (FY 2024 $1,314,088), PLHA (about $3,000,000 a year), REAP 2.0 and General Fund into one locally controlled pool, with City gap financing averaging about $6,000,000 per recent project (Finamore Place, Miraflores) before land. The 50% leverage rule means A-LHTF is a secondary layer behind HOME, PLHA, County MHSA/BHSA loans, OCHFT and Anaheim Housing Authority PBVs. The Guidelines are also the City's vehicle for state LHTF matching grants, so expect future rounds to be tied to HCD LHTF deadlines. Public funds trigger state prevailing wage; REAP 2.0 funds carry infill and reporting rules. Guidelines PDF opened via anaheim.gov DocumentCenter (anaheim.net links return 403).

program_name: HOME, PLHA and CDBG entitlement funds used as affordable housing gap financing (Build More Homes Initiative)
administering_agency: City of Anaheim Housing and Community Development Department (HUD Programs division) and Anaheim Housing Authority
typical_award_size: HOME allocation FY 2024 $1,314,087.60 (down from $2,240,380 in FY 2010); PLHA about $3,000,000 a year since 2019; together about $4,600,000 a year of recurring production money, though a large share of HOME is committed to tenant-based rental assistance. City cash gap financing has averaged $6,000,000 per project on the last two developments (Finamore Place, 101 family units, completed February 2022; Miraflores, 85 PSH family units, 2024, with a 60-year ground lease, a $3,000,000 HOME loan and 8 vouchers). Center of Hope (72 PSH units, 2023) received a $2,000,000 City construction loan and 50 vouchers. Anaheim also administers CDBG, ESG and HOPWA for the region.
per_unit_cap: HOME: HUD maximum per-unit subsidy limits.
affordability_requirement: HOME rents and 80% AMI limits with 20% of HOME units at 50% AMI; PLHA rental production at or below 60% AMI; City deals have typically been 100% affordable family, senior or supportive housing with 55-year covenants.
application_cycle: rolling (project-specific RFPs and negotiated agreements; no standing developer NOFA)
next_deadline: Annual Action Plan adopted each spring; developer solicitations are issued per site (recent Housing Authority RFPs covered 212 S. Beach Blvd and State College at Lincoln). Verify the FY 2026-27 HOME and PLHA figures with the department; the City documents page lists only the FY 2022-23 Action Plan.
layering_notes: Anaheim does not run a competitive NOFA; it assembles sites (Beach Boulevard corridor, former motels) and selects developers by RFP, then layers HOME, PLHA, A-LHTF and Housing Authority PBVs. The City is an HHAP direct recipient and a HOPWA grantee for Orange County, so operating subsidies for PSH can come from the same department. Stack order seen in practice: City land lease plus HOME or PLHA loan, Housing Authority PBVs, County MHSA/BHSA or OCHFT loan, 4% credits with CMFA or CSCDA bonds. Davis-Bacon on HOME projects of 12 or more assisted units; state prevailing wage on all City funds.
