Figures from the June 2026 A-LHTF Guidelines PDF (opened); Housing and Community Development documents page and 2026 affordable housing fact sheet opened; Action Plan PDFs and CivicAlerts pages returned 403.

program_name: Low and Moderate Income Housing Asset Fund (Anaheim Housing Authority as Housing Successor to the Anaheim Redevelopment Agency)
administering_agency: Anaheim Housing Authority as Housing Successor, administered by Housing and Community Development
typical_award_size: Balance not confirmed this pass: the Housing Successor page describes the LMIHAF and annual SB 341 reporting but the report PDFs (for example the FY 2020-21 report, DocumentCenter 70278) returned 403. The Authority holds former Agency housing assets, loans and land; a January 2026 Authority agenda report (per search snippet, not opened) said the Authority owned one vacant building at 883 S. Anaheim Blvd pending long-term housing plans. Before dissolution the Agency's housing set-aside was $15,000,000 to $17,000,000 a year.
affordability_requirement: Health and Safety Code 34176.1: low and moderate income households (up to 120% AMI), at least 30% of five-year expenditures for households at or below 30% AMI, senior cap of 50% over 10 years.
next_deadline: unknown, verify with agency; request the latest Housing Successor Annual Report and LMIHAF balance from Housing and Community Development.
layering_notes: Anaheim's former Agency was one of the largest in Orange County, so LMIHAF repayments and land (Beach Boulevard, Center City) remain a meaningful site source even if cash is thin; the A-LHTF Guidelines say Trust funds may be transferred to the Housing Authority to combine with other sources for site acquisition. Treat as land and residual receipts rather than a cash NOFA. Public funds trigger state prevailing wage. Housing Successor Agency page opened on anaheim.gov; report PDFs blocked.

program_name: Project-Based Vouchers, Anaheim Housing Authority
administering_agency: Anaheim Housing Authority, 201 S. Anaheim Blvd., Suite 201, (714) 765-4320; Housing and Community Development Department
typical_award_size: About $144,000,000 a year in Section 8 rent assistance to about 6,500 households (2026 fact sheet). PBVs are committed to City-assisted projects: Southeast Corner of Beach and Lincoln (208 S. Beach Blvd) 37 senior units (some HOPWA) and 9 transition-age youth units, waiting list referrals opening November 5, 2026; Center of Hope 50 vouchers (72 PSH units, 2023); Miraflores 8 vouchers (85 units, 2024). The City counts 4,156 affordable apartments in 50 communities (45 fully affordable), 2,851 family, 1,113 senior and 332 special needs units.
affordability_requirement: PBV admission at or below 50% AMI (30% of adjusted income toward rent); City PSH projects target 30% AMI with Coordinated Entry referrals; HAP contracts up to 20 years.
application_cycle: rolling (committed through the City's project-specific development agreements)
next_deadline: No open PBV solicitation; request vouchers when responding to a Housing Authority site RFP or negotiating a City loan. Beach and Lincoln waiting list opens November 5, 2026.
layering_notes: Anaheim Housing Authority is a separate PHA from OCHA, so projects inside Anaheim can get PBVs from either; the City's own vouchers are the standard operating layer on City land deals, and HOPWA units can be project-based through the same office. Davis-Bacon applies to new construction or rehab of nine or more PBV units; HAP contracts bring a HUD subsidy layering review. Housing Authority page and 2026 affordable housing fact sheet (DocumentCenter 54022) opened on anaheim.gov; Public Documents page (1947) returned 403.

program_name: Affordable Housing chapter: density bonus, by-right review of Housing Element sites, replacement housing and affordable parking ratios (Anaheim Municipal Code Chapter 18.52, Ord. 6627, August 11, 2026)
administering_agency: City of Anaheim Planning and Building Department, Planning Services Division
typical_award_size: Requirement and entitlement, not a subsidy. Sec. 18.52.020 adopts Government Code 65915 density bonuses and incentives by reference; sites in the Sixth Cycle Housing Element candidate inventory for low and very low income units are reviewed by right (no discretionary hearing) when at least 20% of units are restricted to lower income households. Sec. 18.52.030 implements Housing Crisis Act replacement housing with exemptions for 100% lower income projects. Sec. 18.52.100 sets reduced parking ratios for affordable projects, which the Platinum Triangle Mixed Use Overlay (Chapter 18.20) cross-references for its residential parking.
affordability_requirement: State density bonus thresholds (5% very low, 10% low, 10% moderate for-sale, 100% affordable) with 55-year rental covenants; by-right review requires 20% lower income units on inventory sites.
next_deadline: Applies at project application; code last amended August 11, 2026.
layering_notes: Anaheim has no inclusionary ordinance of general application and no affordable housing fee waiver ordinance was located; the A-LHTF Guidelines mention in-lieu fees under an Affordable Housing Ordinance but that ordinance text could not be opened (anaheim.gov code pages blocked), so verify whether a citywide inclusionary requirement exists. The Platinum Triangle and Beach Boulevard specific plans offer density, not money. Density bonus and by-right approval do not trigger prevailing wage. Chapter 18.52 and Chapter 18.20 read on the zoneomics mirror.

program_name: City-owned and Housing Authority-owned site solicitations for affordable housing (Beach Boulevard corridor and Center City developer RFPs)
administering_agency: Anaheim Housing Authority and Housing and Community Development Department, Real Property and Housing Development staff
typical_award_size: Land contributions under long-term ground leases plus City gap loans rather than a cash NOFA: Miraflores (85 units) on a 60-year City ground lease with a $3,000,000 HOME loan; Southeast Corner of Beach and Lincoln (46 affordable senior and transition-age youth units) on former Housing Authority land with 46 PBVs; earlier RFPs for 212 S. Beach Blvd (Silvermoon) and State College at Lincoln (about 0.51 acre) sought developers for lower income and special needs housing. The A-LHTF Build More Homes Initiative funds site acquisition for future solicitations.
affordability_requirement: Project-specific: City solicitations have required 100% affordable or supportive housing with 55-year covenants and local resident preference.
next_deadline: unknown, verify with agency; no open RFP was located this pass. Watch Housing Authority agendas for Beach Boulevard parcels (Anaheim Lodge demolition site, 39 Commons remainder).
layering_notes: The most valuable Anaheim resource is land, not cash: the Housing Authority assembled Beach Boulevard motel sites and the City leases them at nominal rent, which replaces a $5,000,000 to $10,000,000 land cost in a 4% deal. Pair with Housing Authority PBVs, HOME or PLHA loans, A-LHTF gap money and County MHSA/BHSA. The RFP pages and Authority agendas could not be opened (anaheim.gov CivicAlerts and DocumentCenter returned 403; Granicus archive lists meetings but not staff reports), so details are from the A-LHTF Guidelines, the Housing Authority page and the 2026 fact sheet.

program_name: Inclusionary Housing Ordinance, Affordable Housing Implementation Procedure (Irvine Zoning Ordinance Chapter 2-3, Secs. 2-3-1 to 2-3-11; Ord. 04-15, 24-13, 25-16)
administering_agency: City of Irvine Community Development Department, Planning Services and Housing staff
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Residential projects must provide 15% of units as affordable: 5% extremely low or very low income, 5% low income, 5% moderate income (ownership units for very low or low earn 2:1 credit; extremely low units 1.6:1; three- and four-bedroom units 1.4:1 and 1.6:1). Projects with at least 10% very low or extremely low units satisfy the combined 10% lower income requirement. Alternatives (menu option) are allowed only when on-site units are infeasible or in the City's interest: converting market units for 55 years, extending expiring covenants 55 years, in-lieu fees set by Council resolution, transferring units to a nonprofit, buying affordable housing credits (Sec. 2-3-6), alternative housing (SROs, special needs, shelters at 1:1), or dedicating land or resources of at least equal value. Projects up to 100% affordable may be approved in any planning area and can only be denied under Government Code 65589.5(d). Community preference policy in Sec. 2-3-11.
affordability_requirement: Covenants of at least 55 years at the income level provided; bedroom mix must match the market units and affordable units must be dispersed; affordable housing plans and annual compliance reports required; revocation of entitlements for noncompliance.
next_deadline: Applies at entitlement; in-lieu fee amount determined at building permit under the current Council resolution (fee study drafted August 3, 2023; current schedule not confirmed). Chapter last amended June 24, 2025 (Ord. 25-16).
layering_notes: Irvine's 15% requirement is the highest of the five Orange County priority cities and is the engine behind the Irvine Company planning area affordable sites that nonprofits (Jamboree, C&C, Related, ICLT) build with 4% and 9% credits; a nonprofit taking an inclusionary site typically gets the land at low cost plus City or Irvine Community Land Trust support, then layers County MHSA/BHSA, OCHFT and OCHA PBVs. Sec. 2-3-7 states the City has no obligation to provide financial incentives, so there is no guaranteed city subsidy. cityofirvine.gov returned 403 to all fetch methods this pass; the ordinance was read on the zoneomics mirror.

program_name: Affordable Housing In-Lieu Fee Fund (Irvine Zoning Ordinance Sec. 2-3-5.B.3.c; fee set by City Council resolution)
administering_agency: City of Irvine Community Development Department
typical_award_size: In-lieu fees are deposited in the City's affordable housing fund and used for projects serving low, very low and extremely low income households and Housing Element needs; the fee is set by Council resolution and determined at building permit (a legacy $17,000 per unit rate applied only to Irvine Business Complex projects filed before 2007). An Affordable Housing Requirement and In-Lieu Fee Update draft study was posted August 3, 2023 (per the City page title captured in search results), but the adopted schedule and the current fund balance could not be read because cityofirvine.gov blocked access. The City's FY 2023-25 budget reported a four-acre land conveyance to the Irvine Community Land Trust as part of its 100% affordable housing support.
affordability_requirement: Fund uses limited to low, very low and extremely low income households and Housing Element implementation; recipients record 55-year covenants under Chapter 2-3.
eligible_project_types: land for Irvine Community Land Trust projects
next_deadline: unknown, verify with agency; no NOFA located. Ask Community Development for the current in-lieu fee resolution, fund balance and whether a developer round is planned.
layering_notes: Because most Irvine builders provide units on-site or through credits, the in-lieu fund is smaller than Santa Ana's; its visible use is land and loans to Irvine Community Land Trust projects (Salerno, Parc Derian, Doria, Alegre, Sage Park) which then take LIHTC, HOME, OCHFT and County MHSA money. Public funds trigger state prevailing wage. Code section read on zoneomics; City pages (node 81916 and affordable housing pages) returned 403.

program_name: Irvine Community Land Trust (ICLT) land and development partnerships
administering_agency: Irvine Community Land Trust, 501(c)(3) created by the City of Irvine in 2006, 503 Nightmist, Irvine 92618; Board chaired by Ryan Aeh (2026)
typical_award_size: ICLT acquires or receives land (including City conveyances such as the four-acre site reported in the City's FY 2023-25 budget) and ground leases it to development partners so that units stay affordable permanently. Portfolio: Alegre Apartments, Doria Apartments, Parc Derian Apartments, Salerno Apartments (501 Nightmist) and Sage Park (affordable ownership); it reports hundreds of affordable units in Irvine and, since its 2017 mission expansion, elsewhere in Orange County. ICLT finances projects with LIHTC, HOME, Orange County Housing Finance Trust loans, FHLB AHP and HUD programs; dollar values of land contributions are not published.
affordability_requirement: Permanent affordability through recorded ground lease covenants; rental projects have served extremely low to low income households and Sage Park serves moderate income buyers.
next_deadline: No solicitation open; contact ICLT through its partnerships page. Note the September 2026 governance dispute: ICLT directors wrote to the City Council on September 23, 2026 defending Resolution 26-803 (consultant contract, 5 to 1 vote), which could affect City-ICLT land conveyances.
layering_notes: ICLT is how Irvine converts inclusionary land dedications and City-owned parcels into 100% affordable projects without a city loan program; a developer partnering with ICLT gets site control at nominal ground rent and then stacks 4% or 9% credits, County MHSA/BHSA capital, OCHFT (Cypress Village Irvine took $3,500,000 in the 2024 OCHFT round) and OCHA PBVs. ICLT is a nonprofit, not a public agency, so its land alone does not trigger prevailing wage, but City land conveyed through it may. ICLT home, about, history, process, partnerships and properties pages and the September 23, 2026 letter opened on irvineclt.org.

program_name: Affordable Housing Credits Program (Irvine Zoning Ordinance Sec. 2-3-6)
administering_agency: City of Irvine Community Development Department (credits database and three-party credits agreements)
typical_award_size: Market mechanism, not a subsidy. Projects that build more affordable units than the 15% requirement earn transferable credits in three income categories (extremely low or very low, low, moderate) that they may sell to market-rate projects or mixed projects with a shortfall; credits become available after building permits are issued for the excess units and a completion bond or certificate of occupancy is in place. A three-party credits agreement (buyer, seller, City) must be executed before the buyer's building permits; sale prices are not disclosed to the City.
affordability_requirement: Credits track the income level of the excess units; the receiving project satisfies its required affordable component at that level.
next_deadline: Agreement before building permit; City maintains the credits database on request.
layering_notes: For a 100% affordable developer this is a revenue source unique among the five Orange County priority cities: excess units can be monetized to market-rate builders in the same or other planning areas, effectively a private in-lieu payment. Confirm with the City how many credits are outstanding and the recent trading range. Read on the zoneomics mirror because cityofirvine.gov returned 403.

program_name: Residential Density Bonus Standards (Irvine Zoning Ordinance Sec. 2-3-10)
administering_agency: City of Irvine Community Development Department, Planning Services
typical_award_size: Requirement and entitlement, not a subsidy. Implements Government Code 65915 to 65918 by reference: density bonuses, incentives and concessions, waivers and parking ratios per state law, documented in a density bonus housing agreement recorded as a condition of the discretionary approval; development standards may be modified under Sec. 2-3-10.C for projects providing the Chapter 2-3 affordable units.
affordability_requirement: State thresholds (5% very low, 10% low, 10% moderate for-sale, 100% affordable); 55-year rental covenants.
next_deadline: Applies at project application.
layering_notes: Irvine has no local housing trust fund NOFA, no fee waiver ordinance for affordable units and no city-run developer NOFA; the local tools are the 15% inclusionary requirement, in-lieu fund, credits program, Irvine Community Land Trust and this density bonus section. Irvine receives its own CDBG, HOME, PLHA and HHAP allocations (HHAP Round 6 $5,947,855 per the County record) but those pages could not be opened this pass. program_name: Affordable Housing (Inclusionary Housing) Ordinance, Huntington Beach Zoning and Subdivision Ordinance Sec. 230.26, and in-lieu fee
administering_agency: City of Huntington Beach Community Development Department, Housing Division (Charles Kovac, Housing Manager, charles.kovac@surfcity-hb.org; Gregory Hoang, Senior Housing Analyst, 714-536-5473)
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. New residential projects of three or more units (including conversions) must restrict at least 10% of units: rental units at the lower income level (or very low or extremely low at the developer's choice), ownership units at moderate income, with fractional units rounded up or paid as fee. In-lieu fees may be paid by ownership projects of any size and rental projects of 100 units or fewer, per a fee schedule set by Council resolution and indexed annually to Orange County new home prices; fees are paid before building permit (pro rata for phased projects) and deposited in the Affordable Housing Trust Fund. Land dedication is allowed at Council discretion. Projects that exceed the requirement on-site are eligible for reduced City fees (the 2025 Annual Progress Report cites over $1,000,000 of development impact fee exemptions for a 78-unit project with 8 ELI, 32 VL and 37 low units). A 6-1 Council vote amended the ordinance and the fee formula to make payment more flexible (date not confirmed).
affordability_requirement: Affordability term at least 55 years for rental and 45 years for ownership; affordable rental units built by a separate affordable developer on a parcel within an ownership project may not request City financial assistance; at least 40% of such units must have two or more bedrooms; interior standards equal to LIHTC minimums.
eligible_project_types: market-rate rental and for-sale projects of 3 or more units (compliance)
next_deadline: Applies at entitlement; fee per the current Council resolution at building permit. Council must review the Trust Fund and fee within 180 days after each fiscal year end (by late December).
layering_notes: A low 3-unit threshold but a fee-out for all ownership and all rental projects up to 100 units, so in practice most Huntington Beach projects pay the fee; the Trust Fund (next record) is the resulting local source. The ordinance's fee-reduction incentive is the only affordable housing fee relief found among the five cities. Housing Element status matters here: HCD's March 6, 2026 letter found the 2021-2029 element cannot be certified until the Program 2A and 2B rezonings (Affordable Housing Overlay) are complete, and the state litigation over the element continues, which exposes projects to builder's remedy and limits state funding points. Code read on the zoneomics mirror; Legistar attachments (HCD letter, 2025 APR) opened via the Legistar web API.

program_name: Affordable Housing Trust Fund (Sec. 230.26.E and F) and City inclusionary loans
administering_agency: City of Huntington Beach Community Development Department, Housing Division; Huntington Beach Housing Authority

Current balance and annual receipts were not published in an opened document. Example of use: the City holds an Inclusionary Housing promissory note on Pelican Harbor Apartments that was amended (First Amendment to City Inclusionary Housing Promissory Note) with a HOME note amendment and CMFA bond TEFRA approval on October 21, 2025 (Resolution 2025-65) to allow the project's refinancing; Five Points Senior Villas covenants were extended by amendment in August 2025.
affordability_requirement: Fund projects must have at least 50% of units affordable to very low and low income households with at least 20% very low income, under a recorded affordable housing agreement with 55-year covenants; Council may add permitted uses by resolution with the annual fee schedule.
next_deadline: unknown, verify with agency; no NOFA. Council reviews the fund annually within 180 days of fiscal year end. Request the fund balance from the Housing Division.
layering_notes: Small and reactive: Huntington Beach uses the Trust Fund and HOME CHDO reserve for project-specific loans and covenant extensions rather than rounds. Combine with the City's CDBG and HOME, County 2026 Supportive Housing NOFA loans ($95,000 to $105,000 per unit inside Huntington Beach), OCHA PBVs (Oasis Huntington Beach took 62) and OCHFT. The Huntington Beach Housing Authority is also the housing successor; its LMIHAF balance was not opened this pass. Public funds trigger state prevailing wage. Code text on zoneomics; Legistar matter 25-856 attachments list opened (the inclusionary note PDF itself is an image scan with no text).

program_name: Affordable Housing Density Bonus (Zoning and Subdivision Ordinance Sec. 230.14) and Affordable Housing Overlay (Beach and Edinger Corridors Specific Plan)
administering_agency: City of Huntington Beach Community Development Department, Planning Division
typical_award_size: Requirement and entitlement, not a subsidy. Sec. 230.14 implements Government Code 65915: 20% base bonus for 10% lower income units rising 1.5% per additional 1% to 35%, 5% base bonus for 10% moderate income for-sale units rising 1% per 1% to 35%, one to three incentives or concessions by affordability tier, land donation option under 65915(h). The Beach and Edinger Corridors Specific Plan Affordable Housing Overlay provides non-discretionary review for qualifying affordable projects, and the HBHA Pathways RFQ sought 100% affordable supportive housing at 60% AMI or less with by-right processing for projects with at least 20% affordable units.
affordability_requirement: State thresholds; 55-year rental covenants; in-lieu fees under Sec. 230.26 are calculated on units before the density bonus.
next_deadline: Applies at project application. Housing Element Program 2B (expand the Affordable Housing Overlay) is the rezoning HCD requires before certification; Resolution 2026-25 to adopt the element was heard June 2 and June 8, 2026.
layering_notes: Huntington Beach's local code mirrors the pre-2020 state schedule (35% cap), but state law controls and allows larger bonuses; the practical constraint is political and legal (Measure U voter control, State v. City of Huntington Beach over the Housing Element). Until the element is certified, projects may use builder's remedy and the City cannot earn Prohousing points. No local fee waiver ordinance beyond the Sec. 230.26 fee-reduction incentive. Density bonus does not trigger prevailing wage. Code read on zoneomics; HCD March 6, 2026 letter and Legistar matter list opened.

program_name: Residential Density Bonus and Affordable Housing Regulatory Agreements (Garden Grove Municipal Code Chapter 9.60, Secs. 9.60.040 and 9.60.050; Housing Element Program 10)
administering_agency: City of Garden Grove Community and Economic Development Department, Planning Services Division
typical_award_size: Requirement and entitlement, not a subsidy. Chapter 9.60 implements the State Density Bonus Law, Housing Accountability Act, Housing Crisis Act and No Net Loss law: density bonus, incentives, concessions, waivers and parking ratios per Government Code 65915 and 65915.5 as amended, processed concurrently with the land use application; ministerial review for qualifying housing development projects; replacement of protected units; regulatory agreement required for every affordable unit (Sec. 9.60.050) including a rule that voucher holders pay the affordable rent, not FMR. The 2021-2029 Housing Element reports surveyed projects averaging 183% of base density through bonuses and commits the City to the updated ordinance by 2025 (Program 10) and to study an inclusionary ordinance (Program 11).
affordability_requirement: State thresholds (5% very low, 10% low, 10% moderate for-sale, 100% affordable) with 55-year rental covenants in the City regulatory agreement.
next_deadline: Applies at project application. Program 11 inclusionary study was due within the Housing Element cycle; no inclusionary ordinance or in-lieu fee exists as of this pass.
layering_notes: Garden Grove has no inclusionary ordinance, in-lieu fee, local housing trust fund or affordable housing fee waiver; density bonus plus Housing Element Program 4 (technical and financial assistance for 10 affordable units a year, expedited processing, land write-downs from General Fund, HOME, LMIHAF and PLHA) is the full local toolkit beyond the Housing Successor land and GGHA vouchers. Garden Grove is not a Prohousing designated city. Density bonus does not trigger prevailing wage. Chapter 9.60 read on the zoneomics mirror; 2021-2029 Housing Element PDF opened on ggcity.org.

program_name: Inclusionary Housing Program (Municipal Code Chapter 17.36, Ordinance 1252)
administering_agency: City of Hollister Community Development Department, Planning Division and Housing Division (housing@hollister.ca.gov, (831) 636-4360 x1254)
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. All for-sale and rental residential projects of 10 or more units must provide 15% of base units (before any density bonus) as on-site inclusionary units: at least 6% very low income, at least 5% very low or low income, and at least 4% very low, low or moderate income (Section 17.36.050). Fractions of 0.25 or more round up. No in-lieu fee option exists; the only alternatives (Section 17.36.060) are affordable rental units inside a for-sale project or acquisition and rehabilitation of existing market-rate units (rehab value at least 25% of pre-rehab value, physical needs assessment, on a residentially zoned site). Council approved the ordinance June 18, 2024 (second reading August 2024 per Housing Element Policy Action H4.1); goal of 150 inclusionary units during 2023-2031.
affordability_requirement: Inclusionary units sold or rented only to very low (50% AMI), low (80% AMI) or moderate (120% AMI) households per San Benito County HCD limits (2025 AMI $140,200 for a family of four); units must average at least 85% of the square footage of market units with the same bedroom count, match bedroom mix, finishes and exterior design, and be dispersed on site; buyers and renters screened through an open public process by the City or a third-party administrator; for-sale units carry resale controls and rental units carry recorded affordability covenants.
eligible_project_types: market-rate for-sale subdivisions and condominium projects of 10 or more units (compliance)
market-rate rental projects of 10 or more units (compliance)
acquisition-rehab of existing units as alternative compliance
next_deadline: Applies at entitlement; inclusionary units must be permitted and occupied in proportion to market-rate units in each phase (Section 17.36.050 F). Exempt: ADUs, projects under 10 units, vesting tentative maps and development agreements in effect at the June 2024 effective date, and complete applications filed before that date. Council may set administration and monitoring fees by resolution (Section 17.36.080).
layering_notes: Hollister's program is stricter than the San Benito County Chapter 21.03 ordinance (15% on site or 20% off site, with a $30 per square foot in-lieu fee) because it allows no fee payment and requires on-site units for both rental and for-sale projects; as a result the City has no inclusionary in-lieu fund to redeploy as gap financing. Inclusionary units may be used to qualify for a density bonus under Chapter 17.34 (Section 17.36.050 C), so a 15% inclusionary project can stack the state bonus and concessions. The City's Below Market Rate Housing Program (affordable_housing.php) administers waitlists for inclusionary units; all waitlists were closed as of this pass. Hollister's prior Housing Developer Resources page (opened) states the City previously had no inclusionary ordinance; the code text was read on the zoneomics mirror because library.municode.com blocks automated access. Pairs with the Housing Authority of the County of Santa Cruz PBVs and the CMFA conduit bonds recorded at the county level (Baler Place, 340 Bridgevale Road, is a Hollister project).

program_name: Hollister Housing Trust Fund ($300,000 initial deposit, Housing Element Policy Action H5.12 and 2026 stipulated judgment with HCD and the Attorney General)
administering_agency: City of Hollister Planning and Housing Divisions (program procedures subject to HCD approval)
typical_award_size: Initial capitalization of $300,000 from the City general fund, required by the March 26, 2026 stipulated judgment (People of the State of California and HCD v. City of Hollister) and carried into the adopted 2023-2031 Housing Element as Policy Action H5.12. The fund must support housing for extremely low, very low and low income households, including migrant housing, emergency shelters, supportive housing, single-room occupancy and transitional housing. Award form (grant or loan), per-project limits and the application procedure are to be set in a program document approved by HCD. Any money remaining five years after deposit transfers to the State Building Homes and Jobs Trust Fund unless HCD agrees otherwise.
affordability_requirement: Extremely low, very low and low income households (at or below 80% AMI); affordability terms to be set in the HCD-approved procedures.
next_deadline: Not yet open. Council adopted the Housing Element April 20, 2026 (Planning Commission Resolution 2026-03, March 26, 2026); the element was still pending HCD certification when the City's Housing Element page was opened this pass. The judgment requires the City to submit the draft trust fund program to HCD and deposit the $300,000 within 30 days after HCD finds the element in substantial compliance. The 2025 Annual Progress Report lists H5.12 as continuous with no trust fund activity yet. Contact housing@hollister.ca.gov to be notified when procedures are published.
layering_notes: This will be the only city-controlled capital source for affordable development in Hollister; there is no inclusionary in-lieu fund (Chapter 17.36 requires on-site units) and the former redevelopment agency's housing assets are limited to a Housing Division loan and resale monitoring portfolio (Successor Agency page opened). At $300,000 it is predevelopment-scale money; realistic use is a predevelopment loan or local match that strengthens a TCAC, HCD or AHSC application, layered under county sources (San Benito County PLHA, HHAP, CMFA conduit bonds) and Housing Authority of the County of Santa Cruz PBVs. The five-year sunset creates pressure to commit funds quickly, which favors shovel-ready sponsors. H5.12 also commits the City to annual developer meetings, one-on-one technical assistance and support letters. Marked needs_confirmation because the fund did not exist as of this pass; the judgment text (oag.ca.gov Exhibit B) and the adopted Housing Element PDF were both opened.

program_name: Density Bonus Ordinance (Municipal Code Chapter 17.34, Ordinance 1230 of 2023 as amended by Ordinance 1267 of 2025)
administering_agency: City of Hollister Community Development Department, Planning Division
typical_award_size: Implements Government Code 65915 to 65918 for housing developments of five or more units: bonuses from 20% (5% very low or 10% lower income) up to 50%, 80% for 100% affordable projects (up to 20% moderate), no density maximum for 100% affordable projects within one-half mile of a major transit stop with a height waiver of up to three stories or 33 feet, 15% base bonus plus increments for land donation (Table 17.34-4), 20% senior bonus, 35% student housing bonus, child care facility bonus (17.34.080), one to four incentives or concessions (17.34.060), reduced parking, density bonus housing agreement and deed restrictions (17.34.120 to 17.34.150). Section 17.34 B allows the City to grant a greater bonus than state law requires but no local enhancement schedule is codified.
affordability_requirement: State density bonus law thresholds: very low (50% AMI), lower (80% AMI) and moderate income for-sale units (120% AMI); rental affordability covenants of 55 years; equity sharing on for-sale units.
eligible_project_types: mixed-use with five or more residential units
next_deadline: Submitted with the planning entitlement (17.34.100). Housing Element Policy Action H3.6 states the ordinance update was adopted October 2025 (Ordinance 1267, Zoning Ordinance Overhaul Phase 2) with annual review; goal of two density bonus projects per year. The 2025 Annual Progress Report shows 2 applications requesting a bonus (23 units) and 0 projects permitted with a bonus.
layering_notes: Mirrors state law with no extra local bonus, so it is comparable to the San Benito County Chapter 21.03 Section 13 density bonus. Inclusionary units required under Chapter 17.36 count toward the bonus thresholds (17.36.050 C), and bonus units are excluded from the inclusionary base, so a 15% inclusionary project of 10 or more units in Hollister can claim at least a 20% to 27.5% bonus plus concessions at no extra affordability cost. Housing Element Policy Action H3.3 commits to continuing lower sewer, water connection and traffic impact fees for multifamily and to adopting a permit fee reduction or waiver program for affordable and special needs housing by August 2026 (2025 APR status: not yet started); Phase 3 zoning procedure amendments and Housing Element implementation rezonings (ZOA 2026-1) were heard April 20, 2026. Code text read on the zoneomics mirror; municode blocks automated access.

program_name: Permit fee waiver program for affordable and special needs housing and reduced multifamily impact fees (Housing Element Policy Action H3.3)
administering_agency: City of Hollister Planning, Building and Finance Divisions and Engineering Department
typical_award_size: Existing: lower sewer and water connection fees and traffic impact fees for multifamily development (per-unit basis; the City is considering a square-foot basis). Committed: a reduction or waiver of permit processing fees for affordable and other special needs housing projects, to be established by August 2026 following the user fee study now underway; the Housing Element also calls for waiving permit fees for ADUs under certain sizes or deed restricted as affordable to lower income households, and the sites strategy table contemplates reducing development fees for key sites. Amounts not yet set.
affordability_requirement: Affordable and special needs housing projects as defined in the program procedures to be adopted; ADU waivers tied to size or lower income deed restriction.
next_deadline: Housing Element timeframe: establish the fee waiver program by August 2026 with annual fee assessments; the 2025 Annual Progress Report (filed 2026) lists H3.3 as 'Not Yet Started'. Confirm status with the Planning Division (Community Development Permit Center appointment system) before underwriting any waiver.
layering_notes: Hollister has no codified fee waiver today, unlike San Benito County Section 21.03.012, which can reimburse impact fee waivers for 100% affordable projects from county in-lieu fees. Because Hollister collects no inclusionary in-lieu fees, any waiver will be a general fund cost, which is why the City is tying it to the user fee study. Density bonus concessions under Chapter 17.34 remain the only guaranteed path to fee or standard relief until the program is adopted. Recorded as negative information per schema rule 4 and so the August 2026 commitment can be tracked.

program_name: Permanent Local Housing Allocation (PLHA) entitlement formula grant and state CDBG, CalHome and HOME grants administered by the City Housing Division
administering_agency: City of Hollister Community Development Department, Housing Division (339 Fifth Street, housing@hollister.ca.gov, (831) 636-4360 x1254)
typical_award_size: PLHA: Hollister is a PLHA entitlement jurisdiction with an estimated $1,081,498 over the five-year cycle; awards $180,249 (2019), $280,173 (2020), $290,339 (2021), $147,123 (2022) and $110,381 (2023); the Housing Element reports $750,761 awarded for 2020-2022. The City's five-year plan directs PLHA to homeless services (Emmaus House and the H.O.M.E. Resource Center), not to development. State CDBG: 2017 awards totaled $2,279,116 (parks, senior services, food bank, administration) and 2020 awards were $229,032 (Meals on Wheels) plus $151,177 CDBG-CV. CalHome: application filed under the 2023 Homeownership Super NOFA for first-time homebuyer and rehabilitation assistance. HOME: the City has not applied in the past five years. LEAP planning grant $150,000.
affordability_requirement: PLHA and CDBG serve households at or below 80% AMI (PLHA may serve up to 120% for some activities); CalHome serves low and very low income owners.
eligible_project_types: homeless services and rapid rehousing (current PLHA plan)
next_deadline: Unknown, verify with agency. HCD PLHA formula allocations are drawn annually under the City's 2019-2023 five-year plan; a new five-year plan is due for the 2024-2028 allocations. State CDBG and CalHome applications follow HCD NOFAs (the 2025 state CDBG NOFA was described in the county record). Housing Element Policy Action H4.3 commits the City to apply for at least one grant per year.
layering_notes: Negative finding for multifamily sponsors: none of Hollister's current city-controlled grant money is programmed for rental development. PLHA goes to homeless services, CDBG has gone to parks and public services, and HOME has not been pursued. The Successor Agency to the Hollister Redevelopment Agency holds no residual housing fund beyond a loan and resale-restriction portfolio that the Housing Division monitors (a former RDA downtown site produced 22 condos including 4 affordable units). Developers should instead look to the pending $300,000 Housing Trust Fund (record above), San Benito County PLHA and HHAP, CMFA conduit bonds with County TEFRA approval, and Housing Authority of the County of Santa Cruz PBVs, with TCAC and HCD programs carrying the capital stack. The Grant Programs page (files.hollister.ca.gov) and Housing Element Appendix D were opened; the PLHA five-year plan link on the page was not retrievable.

program_name: Inclusionary Housing Ordinance (Zoning Code Chapter 11-09) and affordable housing in-lieu fee account
administering_agency: City of San Juan Bautista Planning Department (contract planning staff; City Hall 311 Second Street)
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Residential projects of six or more units (the Housing Element describes the rental threshold as five or more) must reserve one affordable unit for every five market-rate units (about 16.7% of base units, calculated before any density bonus) for very low or low income households, for sale or as rentals (Section 11-09-400); fractions may be met with a partial in-lieu fee. In-lieu payment of the whole obligation is allowed only at the City Council's discretion after a Planning Commission recommendation (11-09-500); the per-unit fee formula (11-09-505) is the San Benito County median home sales price for the prior fourth quarter minus the maximum affordable three-bedroom sales price, divided across all project units and paid at building permit. Fees go to a separate interest-bearing account used solely to provide housing opportunities for very low and low income households anywhere in the City (11-09-510). Off-site and joint-venture off-site rental compliance allowed on an infeasibility showing (11-09-600).
affordability_requirement: Very low (50% AMI) and low (80% AMI) households by San Benito County HUD limits; for-sale and rental reserved units deed restricted for at least 55 years; rental units may not convert to condominiums during the restriction; reserved units must match the design and bedroom and square footage proportions of market units.
eligible_project_types: market-rate subdivisions and multifamily projects of six or more units (compliance)
off-site affordable rental projects satisfying another developer's obligation
next_deadline: Applies at entitlement; reserved units built before or with market units and in proportion by phase. The 2023-2031 Housing Element (certified by HCD) adds a program to update the inclusionary provisions and notes that most buildable lots fall under the six-unit threshold, so no project has yet triggered the requirement; fee reductions or waivers have been negotiated in development agreements.
layering_notes: The in-lieu account has no reported balance (the ordinance was adopted in 2007 and the Housing Element says the City has no staff or financial resources for a stand-alone housing program), so it is not a realistic gap source. The one-in-five requirement is roughly comparable to San Benito County's 15% on-site standard but with deeper targeting (very low and low only, no moderate). Mixed-use infill in the downtown and gateway districts is the City's moderate-income strategy; exclusively residential new construction on commercial-only Mixed Use parcels is allowed only when 100% affordable, which pairs well with a 100% affordable density bonus project. Layer with San Benito County PLHA (the City passes its own PLHA allocation to the County for homeless services under an MOU), County HHAP and state programs; Housing Authority of the County of Santa Cruz PBVs cover San Benito County. Code text read on the zoneomics mirror.

program_name: State density bonus implementation and city housing finance capacity (2023-2031 Housing Element programs on density bonus, PLHA and CDBG)
administering_agency: City of San Juan Bautista Planning Department and City Manager's office
typical_award_size: No local enhancement. The Housing Element states the City offers the state density bonus (described as up to 35%, now up to 50% or more under current Government Code 65915) with required concessions, reduced parking and modified standards, and that no project has ever requested a density bonus; a program commits the City to amend the Zoning Code to match current density bonus law (target December 2024). The zoneomics mirror of Title 11 lists no density bonus chapter, so the City applies state law directly. Financial resources: the City holds a PLHA five-year plan ($455,999 for 2019-2023) but passes its allocation to San Benito County for homeless services under an MOU; it has no CDBG, HOME or redevelopment funds, and the Housing Element says the City must partner with nonprofits and the County for any development program.
affordability_requirement: State density bonus law thresholds (5% very low, 10% lower, 10% moderate for-sale, senior, 100% affordable); inclusionary units under Chapter 11-09 are counted before bonus units.
eligible_project_types: mixed-use residential in the Mixed Use district
next_deadline: Unknown, verify with agency. Confirm whether the density bonus code amendment has been adopted; the City's Housing Element page states the 2023-2031 element is adopted and certified but the adopted PDF link could not be resolved this pass (the September 2023 HCD review draft hosted on the City site was read instead).
layering_notes: Explicit negative finding: San Juan Bautista has no local housing trust fund, no fee waiver program, no city NOFA and no city-controlled development funds beyond the dormant Chapter 11-09 in-lieu account. Development capacity is also constrained by water and sewer (a sewer force main to Hollister is a City project) and by the 15 units per acre mixed-use cap except for senior and affordable projects. The only city-level tools are the inclusionary ordinance (record above), state density bonus and SB 35 streamlining; capital must come from San Benito County (PLHA, HHAP, CMFA conduit bonds), Housing Authority of the County of Santa Cruz PBVs and state programs. Marked needs_confirmation because the certified Housing Element text and any adopted density bonus amendment were not opened; the draft element and the City's Housing Element pages were.

program_name: Santa Cruz Affordable Housing Trust Fund (AHTF), Resolution NS-26,410, guidelines revised September 10, 2024
administering_agency: City of Santa Cruz Community Development Department, Housing and Community Development Division (affordablehousing@santacruzca.gov, (831) 420-5150)
typical_award_size: Construction and deferred-payment permanent loans at simple interest of no more than 3% per year, plus gifts, grants, loan guarantees and credit enhancement. Revenue: Chapter 24.16.030 inclusionary in-lieu fees, the City's PLHA formula allocation (HCD estimate about $1.5 million over five years, deposited directly to the AHTF) and donations. Pipeline list dated September 2024 of 100% affordable rental projects eligible after the first-phase funding review: 136 River Street (For the Future Housing) $1,800,000 loan commitment, predevelopment; 119 Lincoln Street (Eden Housing with For the Future Housing) ground lease plus $5,555,000 loan commitment, predevelopment. Income targets: 30% of funds for extremely low income, up to 70% for lower income, maximum 20% for moderate income, 15% contingency; administrative costs capped at 5%. Fund balance is not published; the 2026 AB 2663 in-lieu fee report (opened) lists fee descriptions but no balance.
per_unit_cap: None published; underwritten by sources and uses and subsidy layering review (Attachment I), with at least 10% equity after completion and promissory-note predevelopment loans limited to 15% of estimated project cost.
affordability_requirement: Rental housing for low (80% AMI) and very low (50% AMI) income households; for-sale housing for moderate, low and very low income; priority first to projects guaranteeing perpetual affordability and second to at least 55 years with recapture; extra points for lowest rents, highest share of affordable units, committed other sources, leverage of tax credits and state and federal programs, and sponsor track record.
eligible_project_types: conversion of market-rate units to affordable
next_deadline: No NOFA; requests are reviewed on a rolling basis through a first-phase funding review that places eligible 100% affordable rental projects on the AHTF pipeline list, followed by Council approval of loan commitments. Contact the Housing Division before submitting; the pipeline list was last updated September 2024.
layering_notes: The City's primary local gap source and the usual local match for TCAC, HCD and AHSC applications (the Downtown Library and Affordable Housing Project secured $33.5M AHSC, $55.1M of tax credits and $55.6M of CDLAC bond authority). Separate from the County of Santa Cruz Housing Funds NOFA (LMIHAF, County PLHA and County AHIF), which covers unincorporated projects only, and from the County's Chapter 17.10 Measure J program; city projects stack AHTF with Housing Authority of the County of Santa Cruz PBVs, City HOME and CDBG (record below) and Prohousing scoring bonuses. In-lieu fee revenue depends on how many Measure O projects pay fees rather than build units, so balances fluctuate; the City also takes land dedications (Anton Pacific dedicated land for the Pacific Station expansion). cityofsantacruz.com now redirects to santacruzca.gov, which returns 403 to scripted fetches; the AHTF page, guidelines PDF, pipeline list and in-lieu report were opened through the WebFetch tool.

program_name: Measure O Inclusionary Housing Program (Municipal Code Chapter 24.16 Part 1, Ordinance 2021-04) and inclusionary in-lieu fee
administering_agency: City of Santa Cruz Housing and Community Development Division, with tenant and buyer eligibility intake by the Housing Authority of the County of Santa Cruz (2160 41st Avenue, Capitola)
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Voter-approved Measure O requires residential projects to provide a share of units affordable to very low, low or moderate income households under Chapter 24.16 Part 1 as revised by Ordinance 2021-04 (effective April 13, 2021); units may be built as rental or for-sale and carry long-term or permanent deed restrictions. Before the 2021 revision the ordinance required 15% of new rental units at or below 80% AMI; the City's June 2018 Keyser Marston feasibility analysis tested 15%, 25% and 35% alternatives and Downtown versus non-Downtown subareas under AB 1505, and the revised percentage (reported as 20%) was not confirmed from code text this pass. In-lieu fees under Section 24.16.030(6) are calculated project by project on the affordability gap between market and inclusionary rents (2018 sample: $168,478 gap per unit, $25,271 per market-rate unit or $34.86 per square foot at 15%), are usually paid before building permit issuance and are deposited to the Affordable Housing Trust Fund for new low income units with long-term restrictions or preservation. No refunds or interfund transfers occurred 2021-2025 (2026 AB 2663 report). Measure O rents and incomes are set annually by resolution (2025 schedule effective July 1, 2025, Resolution NS-16,452 series; eight implementing resolutions listed through NS-29,463).
affordability_requirement: Very low, low and moderate income households per the City resolution governing each unit; Measure O rentals restricted to very low and low income tenants or Housing Choice Voucher holders with annual income recertification; eligibility letters issued by the Housing Authority expire after three months; $250 processing fee paid by the seller or landlord.
next_deadline: Applies at entitlement; in-lieu fee due at building permit. Annual rent and income schedules take effect July 1. Confirm the current inclusionary percentage and any Downtown subarea rate with the Housing Division (affordablehousing@santacruzca.gov) because the code publisher (codepublishing.com) and the Measure O resolution PDFs (scanned images) could not be read this pass.
layering_notes: Primary feeder of the AHTF (record above). Compared with the County's Measure J (15% of for-sale projects of seven or more units, rental projects pay the Affordable Housing Impact Fee), the City program applies to rental projects, so market-rate apartment developers downtown face either on-site units or a gap-based fee; recent mixed-income downtown projects show the pattern (175 condos with 20 affordable at Front Street Riverfront, 276 market-rate with 37 affordable at 530 Front Street, 233 market-rate with 35 affordable at 130 Center Street). Inclusionary units can qualify for the state density bonus under Chapter 24.16 Part 3. The 2022 ballot Measure O (library and housing site) outcome was not addressed on any City page opened; the Downtown Library and Affordable Housing Project on City Lot 4 is under construction with 124 units (all but one manager unit affordable), so the project proceeded. Sources opened: Measure O program page, Resolutions and Ordinances page, FAQ page, For Rent Units page, KMA 2018 analysis PDF and the 2026 in-lieu fee report PDF, all via WebFetch because santacruzca.gov blocks scripted fetches.

administering_agency: City of Santa Cruz Community Development Department, Planning Division and Housing Division

Santa Cruz also created Flexible Density Units in four commercial zones (auxiliary units allowed up to the full floor area ratio regardless of density) and the My House My Home senior ADU program, both cited in the 2023 Prohousing application. program_name: Prohousing Designation (awarded August 4, 2023; renewal application 2026, Resolution NS-30,681) and Downtown Library and Affordable Housing Project on City Lot 4
administering_agency: City of Santa Cruz Economic Development and Housing (Housing Division) with the Planning Division
typical_award_size: Not a direct subsidy. The designation (57 points, 7th highest of 47 jurisdictions as of April 2024) gives City projects scoring preference or priority processing in AHSC, Infill Infrastructure Grant, Transformative Climate Communities and other state programs and made the City eligible for Prohousing Incentive Program Round 2 ($9.5 million statewide pool). Example: the Downtown Library and Affordable Housing Project on City-owned Lot 4 (Cathcart, Cedar and Lincoln Streets) received a $33.5M AHSC award, a $55.1M TCAC tax credit award and $55.6M of CDLAC bond authority for 124 units (all affordable except one manager unit) above a new library funded by Measure S, with child care, 240 parking spaces and a $250,000 Economic Development Trust Fund contribution for the farmers market. The 2023 designation expires January 1, 2027; the City applied for renewal in 2026.
affordability_requirement: Not applicable to the designation; the Lot 4 housing is 100% affordable (income levels not stated on the project page; Eden Housing manages the interest list for studio to three-bedroom units).
next_deadline: Renewal decision by HCD pending; current designation valid through January 1, 2027. Lot 4 housing framing was underway on levels 4 through 8 as of the latest project update, with completion dates not stated.
layering_notes: Prohousing points are additive to the AHTF and HOME layers and have been decisive for Santa Cruz downtown projects competing in AHSC. The City disposes of its own land for 100% affordable projects (Lot 4, Pacific Station North 125 units and Pacific Station South 70 units with Santa Cruz Community Health and Dientes, 119 Lincoln Street ground lease) and accepts land dedications from market-rate developers under Measure O (Anton Pacific). Santa Cruz County does not hold a Prohousing designation in the records compiled; Watsonville, Capitola and Scotts Valley pages opened this pass do not mention one. The Prohousing page, the May 2024 Economic Development journal article and the Downtown Library project page were opened; the 2026 resolution PDF returned 403 to scripted access.

program_name: CDBG and HOME entitlement grants (HUD Consolidated Plan 2025-2030, Annual Action Plan PY 2026-2027)
administering_agency: City of Santa Cruz Community Development Department, Housing and Community Development Division (housing@santacruzca.gov)
typical_award_size: PY 2026 (July 2026 to June 2027): $497,393 CDBG and $237,080.42 HOME from HUD, both lower than PY 2025; CDBG total available $512,553 with about $15,000 program income; HOME total available $793,841 including about $100,000 program income and $456,761 of prior-year funds for reprogramming. The City describes typical levels as about $600,000 CDBG and about $400,000 HOME per year. CDBG funds community programs (public services capped at 15%), infrastructure and facility improvements and delivery costs for two housing programs; HOME funds acquisition, homebuyer assistance, homeowner rehabilitation and rental development, with repaid rehabilitation and homebuyer loans automatically reprogrammed to affordable housing. Santa Cruz receives no ESG.
per_unit_cap: HUD HOME maximum per-unit subsidy limits apply; none set locally.
affordability_requirement: CDBG benefits households at or below 80% AMI; HOME rental units at or below 60% AMI (High HOME rents) with HUD affordability periods of 5 to 20 years depending on subsidy; Section 3 applies to construction and rehabilitation.
next_deadline: PY 2027-2028 application period open as of this pass; the cycle normally opens in October with applications due mid-December, proposals advertised in November, public review and Council approval February through May, and the Action Plan submitted to HUD by May 15. Applications: online CDBG form, HOME application (DOCX) and CDBG supplemental budget; CBDO certification available. Email housing@santacruzca.gov to join the HUD notification list.
layering_notes: Small but predictable; HOME is the realistic development piece (under $800,000 available in PY 2026) and is typically paired with an AHTF loan and PBVs from the Housing Authority of the County of Santa Cruz. Federal Davis-Bacon applies to HOME projects of 12 or more assisted units and CDBG projects of 8 or more units. The County administers state HOME and CDBG for the unincorporated area, Watsonville (CDBG entitlement separately), Capitola and Scotts Valley, so Santa Cruz is the only Santa Cruz County city with its own HOME entitlement. Documents opened via WebFetch: HUD Consolidated Plan Documents page and the PY 2026-2027 Annual Action Plan PDF.

program_name: Affordable Housing Ordinance (Municipal Code Chapter 14-46, Ordinance 1480-25 effective October 9, 2025) with in-lieu and commercial fees
administering_agency: City of Watsonville Community Development Department, Housing Division (275 Main Street, Suite 400, (831) 768-3080)
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Projects of 7 to 50 units: for-sale 15% (5% above moderate, 5% median, 5% moderate), rental 20% (5% low, 5% median, 10% very low or Housing Choice Voucher and other subsidy recipients). Projects over 50 units: 20% for both tenures (for-sale 10% above moderate, 5% moderate, 5% median). In-lieu fees are required from projects of six or fewer units or lots, from new commercial and industrial development over 1,000 square feet (a commercial linkage fee) and from condominium conversions; fee amounts are set by Council resolution and indexed annually at 50% of the Santa Cruz-Watsonville House Price Index increase, paid at building permit or final map (14-46.070). Income categories use the Watsonville median household income, defined as 70% of the Santa Cruz County median. Federal, state or City-assisted affordable projects meeting the percentages satisfy the chapter in full (14-46.040(c)). Projects with 50% or more affordable units receive priority processing (14-46.080). Release fees for de-restricting units are paid into the affordable housing fund.
affordability_requirement: Rental units 55 years, ownership units 45 years, deed restricted; very low means the lower of 80% of Watsonville median or 50% of county AMI, low up to 100% of Watsonville median or 50% to 80% county AMI, median up to 120% of Watsonville median or 80% county AMI, moderate up to 150% of Watsonville median, above moderate up to 170%; preference for households living or working in Watsonville at least one year; minimum unit sizes and amenity standards in 14-46.060; affordable units built concurrently with market units.
eligible_project_types: market-rate rental and for-sale projects of seven or more units (compliance)
small residential projects and commercial or industrial development (fee payers)
next_deadline: Applies at entitlement; affordable housing agreement approved by Council and recorded before final map or construction. Ordinances 1480-25 and 1481-25 (density bonus) took effect October 9, 2025 and removed the prior exemption for unsubsidized rental projects, so all rental projects of seven or more units now owe 20%. Current in-lieu fee resolution amounts were not located; request the fee schedule from the Housing Division.
layering_notes: The deepest city inclusionary requirement in Santa Cruz County (20% of rental units with half at very low income or voucher holders) and the only city program with a commercial linkage component; it exceeds the County's Measure J (for-sale only) and Capitola's and Scotts Valley's 15% standards. Because 100% affordable projects satisfy the chapter automatically and get priority processing, tax credit developers face no added inclusionary cost, while mixed-income developers can satisfy the very low tier with Housing Authority of the County of Santa Cruz PBV units. Fees flow to the City's Affordable Housing fund (record below). The 2025 code text was read on the zoneomics mirror because codepublishing.com and gocodebook.com returned 403; the City's Affordable Housing page (watsonville.gov/172) was also opened.

program_name: Inclusionary Housing in-lieu fee Affordable Housing fund, HOME program income and Successor Agency housing assets
administering_agency: City of Watsonville Community Development Department, Housing Division, and the City as Successor Agency to the Watsonville Redevelopment Agency
typical_award_size: The 2025-2029 Consolidated Plan states that in-lieu fees from Chapter 14-46 go to the City's Affordable Housing fund and are reinvested in development, acquisition, rehabilitation and preservation of affordable units as gap financing, alongside HOME, CDBG, CalHome and PLHA; the City holds over $1,850,000 of HOME program income available for future HOME-eligible activities (no active state HOME grant; last award $1,546,000 in 2011) and has 280 inclusionary ownership units in its portfolio. The Successor Agency holds vacant former redevelopment properties that the Consolidated Plan identifies for additional affordable housing. No fund balance for the in-lieu account, loan terms or application procedure is published; news reports have cited a balance of about $1.6 million but that figure was not confirmed from a City document.
affordability_requirement: Affordable to households at or below the Chapter 14-46 income categories (70% of county AMI basis) or HOME limits (80% AMI, 60% AMI for HOME rental units) with recorded affordability covenants of 45 to 55 years.
eligible_project_types: first-time homebuyer and owner rehabilitation loans
next_deadline: Unknown, verify with agency. No NOFA is published; developers negotiate assistance project by project with the Housing Division ((831) 768-3080). Confirm the in-lieu fund balance, the HOME program income balance and the status of Successor Agency property dispositions.
layering_notes: Watsonville's local gap sources are modest and discretionary; the HOME program income (over $1.85 million per the 2025-2029 Consolidated Plan) is the largest identifiable pool and carries federal HOME rules and Davis-Bacon for 12 or more units. Stack with the County of Santa Cruz state HOME tenant-based assistance (which covers Watsonville), Housing Authority of the County of Santa Cruz PBVs, HHAP through the Watsonville/Santa Cruz CoC, and City CDBG (record below). Unlike Santa Cruz city there is no adopted trust fund guideline document. Marked needs_confirmation because no fund balance or program guideline could be opened; the 2025-2029 Consolidated Plan and 2020-2024 Consolidated Plan PDFs on watsonville.gov were read.

program_name: Density Bonus Ordinance (Municipal Code Chapter 14-47, Ordinance 1481-25 effective October 9, 2025) with impact fee deferral concession
administering_agency: City of Watsonville Community Development Department, Planning Division (Director approves ministerial projects; Council approves discretionary projects)
typical_award_size: Adopts Government Code 65915 by reference for all housing developments; bonus calculated under 65915(f) for very low, lower, moderate for-sale, senior, foster youth, student and 100% affordable projects, with land donation, child care and condominium conversion bonuses. Local concession menu (14-47.120) adds deferral of development impact fees (park, fire, sanitary sewer, storm drain and traffic fees) until immediately before occupancy, plus other cost-reducing incentives proposed by the applicant or City. Parking capped at 1 space for 0 to 1 bedroom, 1.5 for 2 to 3 bedrooms and 2.5 for 4 or more bedrooms, tandem and uncovered allowed. Density bonus units do not count toward Chapter 14-46 inclusionary units.
affordability_requirement: Rental target units 55 years at affordable rent as defined in Chapter 14-46; for-sale target units 45 years with equity sharing under 65915(c)(2); occupancy as principal residence; density bonus housing agreement recorded.
next_deadline: Submitted with the first project approval as a density bonus housing plan; projects with 30 or more affordable bonus units must identify a monitoring funding mechanism. Processing and monitoring fees are set by Council resolution.
layering_notes: The fee deferral concession is the only codified fee relief in Watsonville (no waiver program); 100% affordable projects can also use Chapter 14-46 priority processing. Watsonville's bonus mirrors state law with no local enhancement, unlike the County's enhanced bonus in Chapter 17.12.065. Watsonville was certified for its 2023-2031 Housing Element and offers Downtown Watsonville Specific Plan densities; the Specific Plan (Chapter 14-47 of Part 26 on some mirrors) was not opened. Code read on the zoneomics mirror; codepublishing and gocodebook returned 403.

program_name: CDBG entitlement grant (2025-2029 Consolidated Plan, Annual Action Plans FY 2025-2026 and FY 2026-2027)
administering_agency: City of Watsonville Community Development Department, Housing Division ((831) 768-3080)
typical_award_size: PY 2025-2026 allocation $634,804 plus $48,897 of prior-year funds and about $20,000 of program income; PY 2026-2027 anticipated about $634,000 plus $100,000 of unspent prior-year funds and about $100,000 of program income from rehabilitation loan repayments.
