The 2025-2029 Consolidated Plan, the FY 2025-2026 and FY 2026-2027 Action Plans and the City Housing page (watsonville.gov/165) were opened.

program_name: Affordable (Inclusionary) Housing Ordinance (Municipal Code Chapter 18.02, Ordinance 1062 of 2023) and in-lieu fee
administering_agency: City of Capitola Community and Economic Development Department ((831) 475-7300), with buyer intake by the Housing Authority of the County of Santa Cruz
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Projects creating seven or more for-sale units, residential parcels, mobile home parcels or converted condominiums must restrict 15% of units for sale to moderate, low or very low income households; rental projects are exempt from the inclusionary requirement but pay the Affordable Housing Impact Fee (record below). Alternatives (18.02.050): in-lieu fees at the rate in the Council fee schedule ($10 per square foot per the City's 2021 EPS fee feasibility analysis), payable with deferral allowed if the Council finds it aids feasibility; off-site units; land dedication yielding at least 10% more affordable units than otherwise required. In-lieu fees are deposited to the City's housing trust fund for construction of new low and very low income units. Adopted November 2004, amended 2013, 2021 and by Ordinance 1062 (introduced August 24, 2023) to update definitions, mobile home sales procedures and eligibility. The City may require more than 15% only when it provides a grant, subsidy, loan, fee waiver or other fiscal benefit.
affordability_requirement: Buyers at or below 120% of Santa Cruz County AMI with assets no more than 1.5 times the income limit (excluding up to $500,000 in retirement plans); affordable price set at 35% of gross income including a 10% down payment; resale restrictions with equity sharing and release payments to the trust fund; condominium conversions of five or more units mitigate through on-site units or in-lieu fees.
eligible_project_types: for-sale subdivisions and condominium projects of seven or more units (compliance)
next_deadline: Applies at entitlement; in-lieu fee per the schedule in effect at payment. Inventory to date: eight inclusionary condos at Capitola Beach Villas (2008), four other inclusionary homes, seven affordable lots at Turner Lane and 12 new units added citywide in 2025 (69 in the 6th cycle). Housing Element Program 2.8 commits the City to an economic analysis of the inclusionary ordinance during the planning period.
layering_notes: Lighter than the County's Measure J only in scope (same 15%, same seven-unit threshold, for-sale only) and much lighter than Watsonville. Rental developers owe the $25 per square foot Affordable Housing Impact Fee instead, so a 100% affordable rental project in Capitola should seek the impact fee exemption or deferral at entitlement. The ordinance text was read from the Council's Ordinance 1062 packet attachment on the City's public agenda host (mccmeetingspublic) because codepublishing.com returned 403 and the City's own chapter PDF link is dead; the City's Affordable Housing page and 2023-2031 Housing Element (certified August 30, 2024) were also opened.

program_name: Capitola Affordable Housing Trust Fund (established November 2004) and Affordable Housing Impact Fee ($25 per square foot, adopted 2021)
administering_agency: City of Capitola Community and Economic Development Department ((831) 475-7300)
typical_award_size: Trust fund balance about $144,000 (2023-2031 Housing Element, certified August 2024); revenue to date has come only from inclusionary in-lieu fees, with donations allowed. Uses: matching funds for state and federal sources, acquisition of units for affordable resale, and gap assistance; no loan guidelines, per-project limit or NOFA are adopted. Affordable Housing Impact Fee: $25 per square foot on new market-rate residential development, including multifamily rental, adopted in 2021 after a nexus study (the earlier schedule was $6 per square foot on rental projects, $10 per square foot in-lieu on for-sale projects and $2.50 per square foot on additions); exemptions or waivers for deed-restricted affordable units are not stated on the pages opened. PLHA: state estimate of $630,557 for Capitola over the 2020-2024 cycle, application pending at the time the Housing Element was written. Capitola imposes no park, transportation, administration or childcare exactions; school fees ($4.08 per square foot) and Central Fire District fees ($0.53 per square foot) apply.
affordability_requirement: Trust fund monies are directed to new low and very low income units (Section 18.02.050) and to affordable units for moderate income and below; the impact fee is used exclusively to facilitate affordable housing development.
eligible_project_types: acquisition of units for affordable resale
local match for state and federal awards
next_deadline: No application cycle; requests are negotiated with the Community and Economic Development Director and approved by Council. The 52-unit 100% affordable development at 1098 38th Avenue (building permit application filed, 2025 Annual Progress Report) is the first candidate for City assistance; confirm whether the impact fee is waived or deferred for that project.
layering_notes: Capitola's fund is too small (about $144,000) to serve as gap financing; its value is as a local match or fee offset in a TCAC or HCD application, with capital from the County's Chapter 17.10 AHIF fund being unavailable inside city limits. The $25 per square foot impact fee is a significant cost on market-rate rental projects (the County charges $2 per habitable square foot on rentals), so mixed-income sponsors should model it; the fee feasibility analysis (EPS, 2021) warned rental development was marginal even before the increase. Density increases are available under the mixed-use AHO successor provisions for 20% lower income units (record below). Sources opened: 2023-2031 Housing Element PDF (DocumentCenter 1797), 2021 fee feasibility analysis (DocumentCenter 699) and the March 23, 2026 Annual Progress Report memo.

program_name: Density Bonus Ordinance (Municipal Code Chapter 18.03, 2009, amended by the 2024-2025 Housing Element implementation ordinance) and mixed-use density increase for 20% lower income units
administering_agency: City of Capitola Community and Economic Development Department, Planning Division
typical_award_size: Chapter 18.03 (adopted 2009) was rewritten by the Council ordinance amending Title 17, Chapter 18.03 and the zoning map to implement the 2023-2031 Housing Element (certified August 30, 2024), establishing density bonus procedures consistent with current Government Code 65915 (up to 50% bonus, 80% or unlimited for 100% affordable projects, 55-year covenants, replacement units) and including specific incentives for child care facilities in affordable projects. The Housing Element also allows density increase requests on mixed-use sites in exchange for 20% of units for lower income households (or a smaller share at extremely low and very low income), with an in-lieu fee option where on-site units are infeasible. The 2025 Annual Progress Report shows zero density bonus applications and zero projects permitted with a bonus; the obsolete Affordable Housing Overlay (-AH) from the 5th cycle is being retired.
affordability_requirement: State density bonus law thresholds (very low 50% AMI, lower 80% AMI, moderate for-sale 120% AMI, senior, 100% affordable) with 55-year rental covenants; mixed-use density increase requires 20% lower income units.
eligible_project_types: mixed-use on commercial corridors (41st Avenue, Capitola Mall area)
next_deadline: Requested with the planning application. Multifamily zoning and Capitola Mall code updates consumed 18 Council and Planning Commission meetings in 2025; the mall site is the City's largest housing opportunity. Verify the adopted date of the Chapter 18.03 amendment with Planning (the public review draft was dated August 26, 2024).
layering_notes: State-law mirror with no local bonus enhancement, like Watsonville and unlike the County's Chapter 17.12.065 enhanced bonus. Because rental projects are exempt from the inclusionary ordinance, a developer can combine the 20% lower income mixed-use density increase or the state bonus with the Chapter 18.02 fee structure and seek relief from the $25 per square foot impact fee as a concession. Capitola has no fee waiver program, no city NOFA and no city-controlled development funds beyond the small trust fund; Capitola projects rely on the County's state HOME tenant assistance (which covers Capitola), Housing Authority PBVs, HHAP and state capital. The amending ordinance was read from the Council agenda attachment on the City's public agenda host; codepublishing.com returned 403 and the zoneomics mirror covers only Title 17.

program_name: Inclusionary Housing (Below Market Rate) Ordinance (Municipal Code Section 14.01.030, Affordable Housing Committee) and affordable housing in-lieu fee fund
administering_agency: City of Scotts Valley Planning Department (planningdepartment@scottsvalley.gov, 1 Civic Center Drive) with the Council's Affordable Housing Committee setting project terms
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Within the former redevelopment project area boundary (unchanged since 1990), residential developments of seven or more units (for sale or rental) must set aside 15% of units for very low, low and moderate income households on site, or off site in limited cases; developments of six or fewer units pay an in-lieu fee; projects of seven or more units with average lot sizes over one acre may pay the fee with Council approval. The in-lieu fee equals the median sales price of a home in the project minus the City-determined affordable price. The two-member Affordable Housing Committee recommends unit counts, sizes and affordability levels for each project, subject to Council confirmation. The ordinance has produced 84 affordable rental and 50 affordable ownership units; in-lieu fees from small projects have subsidized smaller rental projects (the City loaned funds to Emerald Hill Apartments, 46 units with MidPen Housing, including impact fee offsets). Exempt: subsidized projects deed restricted through state or federal programs, single homes on existing lots, additions, ADUs and hardship cases. Housing Element Program H-1.8: comprehensive study by July 2026 and a citywide amendment with income-tier standards by January 2027.
affordability_requirement: Very low, low and moderate income households as set per project by the Affordable Housing Committee; inclusionary units carry restricted equity accrual, resale price and rental price limits; subsidized affordable projects meeting the standard are exempt.
eligible_project_types: market-rate for-sale and rental projects of seven or more units within the RDA boundary (compliance)
small projects of six or fewer units (fee payers)
next_deadline: Applies at entitlement; the Affordable Housing Committee meets as special meetings noticed 24 hours ahead. Watch for the July 2026 inclusionary study and the January 2027 citywide ordinance amendment (Program H-1.8), which may change the boundary, percentage and in-lieu formula.
layering_notes: The in-lieu fee fund is the City's only local housing money; no balance, guidelines or NOFA are published, so treat it as a small negotiated gap or fee-offset source, as with Emerald Hill. The 15% standard matches Capitola and the County's Measure J but applies to rentals as well; it is lighter than Watsonville's 20%. 100% affordable projects are exempt and instead use Chapter 17.41 ministerial approval and the Chapter 17.62 state density bonus (records below); the 4444 Scotts Valley Drive project is the first 100% affordable project under the 6th cycle element. Regional sources: County state HOME tenant assistance (covers Scotts Valley), Housing Authority PBVs, Housing Trust Silicon Valley loans (Beverly Gardens, 25 units, $3,277,500 acquisition loan), HHAP. The 2023-2031 Housing Element PDF (certified April 2, 2024), the City Housing page (scottsvalley.gov/220) and the Affordable Housing Committee page were opened; the municode text of Section 14.01.030 was not (blocked host).

program_name: Density Bonus Ordinance (Municipal Code Chapter 17.62, Ordinance 16.142 adopted December 4, 2024)
administering_agency: City of Scotts Valley Planning Department
typical_award_size: Chapter 17.62 was replaced in its entirety on December 4, 2024 to implement State Density Bonus Law (Government Code 65915 to 65918) and the 2023-2031 Housing Element: concurrent request with the first permit application, summary density table, eligibility under 65915(b)(1) and additional bonuses under 65915(v)(1), incentives and concessions (65915(k)), waivers (65915(e)), reduced parking (65915(p)), land donation bonuses, replacement housing documentation, regulatory agreements (17.62.060) and affordable unit design standards (17.62.050). No local bonus beyond state law is codified; the chapter states that state law definitions and limits control.
affordability_requirement: State density bonus law thresholds with 55-year rental covenants recorded in a regulatory agreement; affordable units comparable in design and construction to market units.
next_deadline: Submitted with the first permit application; the Maximum Allowable Density Worksheet is available from the Community Development Department for sites without a units-per-acre standard. The City is filing a 2026 technical update to the Housing Element sites inventory (projects at 4444 Scotts Valley Drive, 75 Mount Hermon Road and 4575 Scotts Valley Drive).
layering_notes: Mirrors state law, like Watsonville and Capitola; the County's enhanced bonus does not apply inside Scotts Valley. Pairs with the inclusionary exemption for subsidized projects and the Chapter 17.41 ministerial path for 20% or 100% affordable projects (record below); the City Housing page also lists SB 35 procedures and an AB 1332 pre-approved ADU program. Scotts Valley offers no fee waiver program; the Housing Element lists permitting fee waivers only as a possible case-by-case action for special needs housing. Code text read on the zoneomics mirror.

program_name: Housing Element Opportunity Site Combining District (Municipal Code Chapter 17.41, Ordinance 16.142.1 adopted June 18, 2025): ministerial approval and standards relief for affordable projects
administering_agency: City of Scotts Valley Planning Department
typical_award_size: Not a subsidy. Streamlined permitting on Housing Element opportunity sites: multifamily projects with 20% or more of units affordable to lower income households receive the Chapter 17.41 A permitting path (ministerial or reduced review), other projects follow Subsection B; 100% affordable projects (all units deed restricted at least 55 years, rentals at or below 80% AMI, ownership at or below 120% AMI, residential at least 85% of mixed-use floor area) may obtain deviations from development standards needed to make the project feasible. Mixed-use sites in the district require residential uses below 70% of gross floor area unless the project qualifies as affordable. The chapter was adopted December 4, 2024 (Ordinance 16.142) and rewritten June 18, 2025 to carry out Housing Element Programs H-1.1 and H-1.2 (rezoning of at least 8.7 acres to R-VH-2 and 32.2 acres to R-VHM, by-right development).
affordability_requirement: At least 20% lower income units for the affordable permitting path; 100% affordable (rental 80% AMI, ownership 120% AMI, 55 years) for standards deviations.
eligible_project_types: new construction on Housing Element opportunity sites
mixed-use with at least 85% residential floor area
next_deadline: Available now for sites mapped in the combining district; Program H-1.1 required the rezonings within the Housing Element timeline and Program H-1.2 maintains by-right approval for lower income sites. Confirm site eligibility with the Planning Department.
layering_notes: Scotts Valley's main local incentive for tax credit projects, substituting for the absence of a trust fund or fee waiver; it stacks with the Chapter 17.62 state density bonus and the inclusionary exemption for subsidized projects, and with Housing Authority PBVs and state capital. The 4444 Scotts Valley Drive 100% affordable project (first under the 6th cycle element, using state density bonus and SB 35) is the template. Code text read on the zoneomics mirror; the HCD certification letter (April 2, 2024) and the City Housing Element page were also opened.

program_name: Gap Financing Program, rolling Request for Proposals with Notice of Funding Availability addenda (new construction and preservation)
administering_agency: City of San Jose Housing Department, Residential Development, Production and Preservation
typical_award_size: Construction-permanent and acquisition loans from the Low and Moderate Income Housing Asset Fund, Inclusionary Fee Fund, Measure E Real Property Transfer Tax Fund and impact fee funds. The April 14, 2025 joint New Construction/Preservation RFP was backed by a $50 million commitment; the June 2025 Round 1 NOFA addendum has produced three awards so far. 2025 awards: $48.3 million for Berryessa TOD and Gateway Tower (415 units); Gateway Tower $38.44 million total ($174,727 per unit on 220 units, later revised to $25.56 million after CalHFA MIP and state credits); 1510 North 1st Street hotel conversion $5.7 million (58 units, October 2026); Capitol Station $8.4 million LMIHAF. Since January 2023 the City has provided $222.7 million to 16 developments producing 1,639 units.
per_unit_cap: No published cap. Recent per-unit City subsidy ranged from about $100,000 (1510 North 1st, with project-based vouchers) to $174,727 (Gateway Tower before state awards).
affordability_requirement: City affordability covenant of at least 55 years, senior to any deed of trust. Rolling RFP prioritizes construction-ready developments, extremely low and very low income units, permanent supportive housing with County vouchers, and preservation of at-risk units. Preservation NOFA target is $5 million average per year (Housing Element Program R-2).
application_cycle: rolling (NOFA addenda to a rolling RFP, roughly annual)
next_deadline: Second NOFA addendum to the rolling RFP was planned for Q2 2026 and waitlisted applications refreshed; confirm the current addendum and submission window with the Housing Department (Banu San, Deputy Director, 408-975-4489). The RFP document is hosted on Biddingo and requires registration.
layering_notes: The primary local gap lender in the county alongside County Measure A (now fully committed, see county record). Staff align awards with County OSH funds and Santa Clara County Housing Authority project-based vouchers ($47.4 million County funds and 298 PBVs leveraged in 2025). Typical stack: 4 percent credits and bonds (City can be issuer under Policy 1-16 or CMFA/CSCDA), CalHFA MIP, AHSC, County SHDF, then City gap loan. The City's August 2026 alternative financing frameworks (see separate record) let staff combine gap financing with inclusionary projects and master-lease structures. Measure E dollars for new development were sharply reduced in the FY 2025-26 budget, so LMIHAF program income ($22.5 million deposited in FY 2024-25) and inclusionary in-lieu fees are the main recurring sources. sanjoseca.gov returns 403 to automated access; all documents were read from the Legistar attachment host.

program_name: Measure E Real Property Transfer Tax (Municipal Code Chapter 4.59) and Council Policy 1-18 Section 22 spending allocations
administering_agency: City of San Jose Housing Department and City Manager's Budget Office; Real Property Transfer Tax Fund
typical_award_size: Transfer tax on sales above $2.3 million (threshold indexed from $2 million as of July 1, 2025): 0.75 percent from $2 million to $5 million, 1.0 percent from $5 million to $10 million, 1.5 percent above $10 million. About $225 million collected July 2020 through mid 2023. FY 2025-26 revenue estimate $55.0 million, FY 2026-27 $60.0 million. Original policy (April 2022) directed 40 percent to extremely low income housing, 30 percent low income, 5 percent moderate income, 10 percent homelessness prevention, 15 percent homeless support. The June 10, 2025 revision allows up to 90 percent of revenue after 5 percent administration for homeless sheltering and interim housing, with only the remainder for new or preserved affordable housing; the FY 2025-26 plan puts $0 of new revenue into affordable housing development. Prior-year Measure E reserves are still being drawn for development, for example $14 million for the Gateway Tower land acquisition (September 2025).
affordability_requirement: When used for development: new or preserved rental housing for extremely low (30 percent AMI) and low income households under City regulatory agreements; previously set by AMI category in Policy 1-18 Section 22.
application_cycle: rolling (appropriated through the annual budget and project-specific Council actions)
next_deadline: No standalone Measure E NOFA. Future allocations for affordable housing depend on the FY 2026-27 budget (June 2026) and later budgets; shifts between 15 and 90 percent for shelter can be made without the 60-day notice and two-thirds vote. Verify remaining Measure E reserve balances with the Housing Department.
layering_notes: Measure E was the City's largest discretionary housing source from 2020 to 2024 and funded many Gap Financing Program awards. Expect limited new Measure E development money through at least FY 2026-27 because the General Fund shortfall shifted $39.2 million (rising to $42.8 million) of homelessness costs into this fund. Developers should underwrite LMIHAF and inclusionary fee funds first and treat Measure E as upside. A Measure E transfer tax refund pilot for qualifying nonprofit purchases (Section 4.59.230) ran July 2021 through June 30, 2024 with one application; it is now expired. Documents read via Legistar attachments because sanjoseca.gov is blocked.

program_name: Low and Moderate Income Housing Asset Fund (LMIHAF), Housing Successor to the San Jose Redevelopment Agency
administering_agency: City of San Jose Housing Department as Housing Successor
typical_award_size: Ending balance June 30, 2025: $95,884,306. Deposits in FY 2024-25: $22,478,762 (loan repayments and interest). FY 2024-25 expenditures $24.1 million, of which $12.5 million housing development (mostly extremely low income units) and $11.4 million monitoring and administration. Gross value of Housing Successor assets $721 million (loan portfolio and land). Recent LMIHAF commitments: $17.97 million construction-permanent plus $2.17 million acquisition for Gateway Tower, $8.4 million Capitol Station, $5.7 million 1510 North 1st Street.
per_unit_cap: None published; sized through the Gap Financing Program underwriting.
affordability_requirement: Dissolution Law targets: at least 30 percent of expenditures for rental housing at or below 30 percent AMI and no more than 20 percent for 60 to 80 percent AMI, measured over five-year periods; City covenants of 55 years or longer.
application_cycle: rolling (through the Gap Financing Program rolling RFP)
next_deadline: Funds are awarded through the rolling RFP and NOFA addenda described in the Gap Financing Program record; next addendum expected 2026. Annual Housing Successor report is presented each March with the Housing Element APR.
layering_notes: The largest and most stable local pool in the county at about $96 million, replenished by about $20 million per year of loan repayments as older RDA loans mature. Draws require a Council appropriation from the Housing Project Reserve. Stacks with County Measure A, SCCHA project-based vouchers, 4 percent credits and CalHFA MIP. Program income rules make it less flexible than inclusionary fee funds for moderate income units. sanjoseca.gov blocked; the Housing Successor Annual Report was read as an attachment to the March 2026 APR Council item.

program_name: Inclusionary Housing Ordinance, Municipal Code Chapter 5.08, in-lieu fees and Surplus Credits Exchange (2026 amendments)
administering_agency: City of San Jose Housing Department
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Applies to residential developments of 10 or more units (threshold lowered from 20 in 2021). On-site rental options after the January 27, 2026 amendments: 5 percent at 60 percent AMI, 5 percent at 80 percent AMI and 5 percent at 110 percent AMI (15 percent total); the former 10 percent at 30 percent AMI alternative was removed. For-sale: 15 percent at 120 percent AMI with the price cap raised to 120 percent AMI. Off-site rental: 30 percent (10 percent each at 60, 80 and 100 percent AMI); off-site for-sale 25 percent at 110 percent AMI. In-lieu fee is set per square foot in the annual Schedule of Fees; about $50 million in in-lieu fees collected from 15 fee-only projects since March 2021 ($38.2 million fee-only plus $12.4 million mixed compliance). Fees flow to the Inclusionary Fee Fund, which is a Gap Financing Program source ($4.3 million committed to Gateway Tower in 2025). Pipeline: 73 projects, 12,900 units, 1,900 affordable.
affordability_requirement: Inclusionary rental units restricted for 55 years (reduced from 99 years in 2026 to match TCAC and state density bonus terms). 100 percent affordable developments at or below 100 percent AMI now comply by recording an abbreviated City covenant that mirrors their TCAC, HCD or CDLAC regulatory agreements instead of a full Inclusionary Housing Agreement.
next_deadline: Ordinance adopted January 27, 2026 and effective in 2026. The Surplus Credits Exchange (Section 5.08.540) will get a 12-month performance review; check the Housing Department for exchange rules and current in-lieu fee rates (set each June in the Schedule of Fees and Charges).
layering_notes: For affordable developers the key uses are: (1) the Inclusionary Fee Fund as a gap source, (2) the 2026 Surplus Credits Exchange, where a 100 percent affordable or mixed-income project that exceeds its requirement can sell credits (room-count equivalency) to market-rate projects, a potential new equity-like revenue stream, and (3) streamlined compliance for 100 percent affordable projects. Alternative Financing Model 1 (August 2026) pairs Gap Financing loans with deeper inclusionary set-asides (for example 10 percent at 50 percent AMI) in tower and wrap projects. Market-rate projects in the Multifamily Housing Incentive Program pay a $0 in-lieu fee if they provide 5 percent at up to 110 percent AMI on site, which reduces fee revenue to the fund. State density bonus can be layered on inclusionary units. sanjoseca.gov blocked; memo and ordinance read from Legistar.

program_name: Affordable Housing Impact Fee (Chapter 17.14, suspended 2021) and Commercial Linkage Fee (Chapter 5.11)
administering_agency: City of San Jose Housing Department
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. AHIF: $17.00 per livable square foot on market-rate rental projects at adoption (2014), escalating 2.4 percent a year to $20.08 when suspended for projects first approved on or after June 29, 2021 (Resolution 80149). Cumulative AHIF revenue and interest $25.6 million; fund balance $11.4 million at June 30, 2025, all to be committed through the Gap Financing Program. CLF (Ordinance 30475, September 22, 2020): FY 2025-26 rates are $17.86 per square foot for office at or above 100,000 square feet downtown and nearby (lower tiers for smaller office), hotel $5.95, industrial over 100,000 square feet $3.57, warehouse $5.95, residential care $7.15, with reduced rates outside downtown. Cumulative CLF revenue $6.1 million, to be allocated through the Gap Financing Program.
affordability_requirement: Fee revenue funds housing for extremely low, very low, low and moderate income households under City regulatory agreements (55 years or longer).
application_cycle: closed/inactive (AHIF suspended for new projects; CLF continues to accrue and is deployed through the Gap Financing Program)
next_deadline: No direct application; the funds are awarded through the Gap Financing Program rolling RFP. Next Mitigation Fee Act annual report due to Council in late 2026.
layering_notes: Both funds are small relative to LMIHAF and are blended into Gap Financing awards. The CLF was adopted at well below the Keyser Marston nexus maximum and office construction has been weak, so expect only a few million dollars a year. The AHIF was replaced by extending the Inclusionary Housing Ordinance to rental projects of 10 or more units. Compare with Mountain View and Sunnyvale, whose commercial linkage fees have generated far larger balances. sanjoseca.gov blocked; the FY 2024-25 annual report memo was read from Legistar.

program_name: Multifamily Housing Incentive Program (MHIP), construction tax reductions and inclusionary in-lieu fee waiver (Municipal Code Sections 4.46.039.13 and 4.47.098)
administering_agency: City of San Jose Housing Department with Planning, Building and Code Enforcement, Public Works and Finance
typical_award_size: Phase I (projects that apply by February 28, 2027 and pull building permits by that date, capacity expanded from 1,800 to 3,600 units on January 27, 2026): 50 percent reduction of the Building and Structure Construction Tax (1.54 percent to 0.77 percent of valuation), 50 percent reduction of the Commercial, Residential and Mobile Home Park Construction Tax (2.42 percent to 1.21 percent), reduced inclusionary requirement of 5 percent of units at 100 percent AMI (or up to 110 percent AMI) and a $0 inclusionary in-lieu fee. Phase II (after capacity or March 2027): 25 percent Building and Structure tax reduction (to 1.16 percent) plus the inclusionary benefits. Approved waivers range from $4.07 million (498 West San Carlos, 278 units) to $6.93 million (3896 Stevens Creek Phase 1, 311 units, September 2026). Five projects with 1,444 units started construction under the program by January 2026.
per_unit_cap: Roughly $14,000 to $22,000 per unit in waived taxes and fees in approved projects.
affordability_requirement: Market-rate high-density projects (50 or more units per acre in growth areas) providing at least 5 percent of units affordable at up to 100 or 110 percent AMI; recorded affordability restriction required. Financial infeasibility finding under Municipal Code Section 14.10.310 and the 2025 Cost of Residential Development Study.
eligible_project_types: high-density market rate with on-site workforce units
application_cycle: rolling (first come first served with tiered readiness prioritization)
next_deadline: Phase I application deadline February 28, 2027; building permit must be obtained by February 28, 2027 for the 50 percent reductions. Each waiver requires a Council public hearing under Government Code 53083.
layering_notes: Not a subsidy for 100 percent affordable projects, which generally are exempt from these construction taxes anyway, but it is the City's main production incentive for mixed-income market-rate towers and wraps and it shapes the inclusionary pipeline (lower on-site percentages, zero in-lieu fee revenue). Alternative Financing Model 3 (August 2026) pairs MHIP incentives with master-lease financing so that a public or nonprofit master lessee can take down units at 80 to 110 percent AMI. Developers combining MHIP with state density bonus should confirm the 5 percent at 100 percent AMI units count toward density bonus moderate income thresholds. sanjoseca.gov blocked; staff memo read from Legistar.

program_name: Multifamily Housing Revenue Bonds, City Council Policy 1-16 (City as conduit issuer)
administering_agency: City of San Jose Housing Department and Finance Department
typical_award_size: City-issued tax-exempt multifamily housing revenue bonds and notes for 4 percent LIHTC projects, for example Berryessa TOD (March 2026), 525 North Capitol (June 2025) and La Moraga refunding (July 2025). Policy 1-16 was amended April 28, 2026 to streamline readiness requirements, financing team selection, private placements and alternative structures, and to prioritize developments leveraging substantial non-City subsidy, preservation of at-risk units and permanent supportive housing. City fees and procedures are moving to an administrative procedures document.
per_unit_cap: Limited by CDLAC allocation and project debt capacity, not by City policy.
affordability_requirement: Federal 20 percent at 50 percent AMI or 40 percent at 60 percent AMI minimum under Section 142(d), plus City regulatory agreement; City prioritizes deeper affordability and PSH.
next_deadline: Applications track CDLAC allocation rounds (typically three per year); submit the City inducement request at least one Council cycle before the CDLAC deadline. Check the revised administrative procedures with the Housing Department.
layering_notes: San Jose is one of the few cities in the county that issues its own bonds rather than relying solely on CMFA or CSCDA, which avoids JPA issuer fees but adds City fees and Council timing. Alternative Financing Model 2 (August 2026) contemplates private activity bonds with master-lease financing for projects without 4 percent credits. County TEFRA approvals cover unincorporated projects only. sanjoseca.gov blocked; memo read from Legistar.

program_name: Alternative financing frameworks for affordable housing (Gap Financing plus IHO, PAB plus master-lease, production incentives plus master-lease)
administering_agency: City of San Jose Housing Department
typical_award_size: Council resolution of September 1, 2026 authorizing the Housing Director to implement four mixed-financing models: (1) Gap Financing Program loans in exchange for deeper inclusionary set-asides (example: 10 percent of units at 50 percent AMI instead of 5 percent at 60 and 5 percent at 80); (2) private activity bonds combined with master-lease financing; (3) production incentive programs (MHIP) combined with master-lease financing; (4) master-lease financing combined with the Inclusionary Housing Ordinance. Target rents 40 to 110 percent AMI. No new dollars; uses existing Gap Financing, bond and incentive tools.
affordability_requirement: Varies by model; 40 percent AMI up to 110 percent AMI with recorded restrictions; Model 1 limited to tower and wrap projects already paying prevailing wage.
next_deadline: Housing Director may implement without further Council action subject to funding approvals; individual loan or master-lease commitments still return to Council. No deadline.
layering_notes: Relevant to developers of mixed-income towers (prevailing wage already assumed) and to nonprofit or public master lessees. Models borrow from the Bay Area Housing Finance Authority and CalHFA middle-income work; they will compete with the Multifamily Housing Incentive Program pipeline for the same market-rate projects. Prohousing: San Jose applied for HCD Prohousing Designation in June 2023 (memo read); current designation status was not confirmed this pass, verify on HCD's designated jurisdictions list. sanjoseca.gov blocked; memo read from Legistar.

program_name: HUD entitlement grants (CDBG, HOME, ESG, HOPWA), FY 2026-2027 Annual Action Plan
administering_agency: City of San Jose Housing Department
typical_award_size: FY 2026-27 entitlement estimate $13,743,769: CDBG $7,445,057, HOME $2,484,924, ESG $658,211, HOPWA $1,869,366, HOPWA-PSH $1,286,211. Total available with prior-year balances and program income $36,340,762, including HOME $23.16 million (prior-year balance $18.99 million) available for affordable housing development. HOME funds are typically committed to Gap Financing Program developments as loans.
per_unit_cap: HOME per-unit subsidy limits (HUD 221(d)(3) based) apply.

program_name: Below Market Rate Housing Program, City Code Chapter 36 Article XIV Division 2 (moving to Chapter 46), 2026 amendments and in-lieu fee schedule
administering_agency: City of Mountain View Housing Department
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Projects of 7 or more units: 15 percent BMR for rental and non-townhome ownership, 25 percent for rowhouse and townhouse projects; projects under 7 units pay fractional in-lieu fees with a new graduated reduction for 1 to 6 units. Rental BMR units at over 50 to 80 percent AMI with a 65 percent AMI weighted average; ownership at over 80 to 120 percent AMI (100 percent weighted average) plus a further 10 percent of townhome units at 120 to 150 percent AMI. Affordable in perpetuity; rents may rise at most 3 percent a year. In-lieu fees (now only a valuation yardstick for alternative compliance, since Council removed fee payment as a compliance option): rental $118 per net new habitable square foot in 2025 falling to $98 in FY 2026-27; townhome $153 to $118; other ownership $67 to $91; escalated by the California Construction Cost Index. Alternative compliance (land dedication, off-site units, or acquisition and preservation of existing housing) requires Council approval and a $32,000 cost-recovery fee.
affordability_requirement: Rental 65 percent AMI weighted average (range over 50 to 80 percent AMI); ownership 100 percent AMI weighted average; perpetual affordability; 15 percent of BMR units (or one unit) to be accessible under the 2026 amendments.
next_deadline: First reading of the Phase 2 ordinance was May 12, 2026 after the March 4, 2026 EPC hearing; updated in-lieu amounts take effect with the FY 2026-27 Master Fee Schedule. Confirm adoption and effective date with the Housing Department.
layering_notes: BMR in-lieu fees historically funded the City's NOFA (for example $10 million to 1012 Linda Vista in 2023 and $6.3 million to Lot 12), so removing fee compliance will shrink the BMR Housing Fund over time; the City seeded the Affordable Housing Initiative Fund with $1 million from this fund in January 2026. The new acquisition and preservation compliance path lets a market-rate developer buy and deed-restrict existing units, a potential partnership for nonprofit preservation buyers. Precise plan areas (North Bayshore, East Whisman) carry their own affordability and land dedication requirements (North Bayshore six land dedication sites, Middlefield Park two sites); those plans were not opened this pass. State density bonus is available on top of BMR units. mountainview.gov returns 403 to automated access; Council reports were read from the Legistar attachment host.

program_name: Affordable Housing Ordinance (Ordinance 297, 2018; amended 2022), Municipal Code Title XII Chapter 1, residential in-lieu fee and non-residential affordable housing impact fee (Resolution 8852)
administering_agency: City of Milpitas Office of Housing (Planning and Neighborhood Services Department)
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. New residential projects of 10 or more units must provide 15 percent of units as affordable on site; alternative compliance (including in-lieu fees) requires Council approval. Fee schedule under Resolution 8852, indexed annually: residential in-lieu fee $49.13 per square foot (July 2025 to June 2026) and $51.20 (July 2026 to June 2027) for all ownership and rental types; non-residential impact fee $10.59 per square foot commercial (office, retail, hotel) rising to $11.04, and $5.29 industrial (R&D, manufacturing, warehouse) rising to $5.51. Housing Element Program 17 targets 1,160 inclusionary units over the cycle and calls for defining very low, low and moderate income shares and extra credit for extremely low income units by the end of 2025.
affordability_requirement: 15 percent of units affordable; income mix to be defined by the pending 2025 AHO amendment (current practice follows the ordinance and administrative guidelines under development). Preference program for McKinney-Vento families, current and former Milpitas residents and Milpitas workers.
next_deadline: AHO amendment defining income tiers was due by end of 2025 and a full review by 2027 under the Housing Element; confirm status with the Office of Housing (408-586-3222, housing@milpitas.gov). Fee rates step up July 1, 2027 by index.
layering_notes: In-lieu and impact fee revenue goes to the City's affordable housing fund administered with the Milpitas Housing Authority; no NOFA process was found and the fund balance was not published on the pages opened. Most Milpitas affordable projects (for example Mosaic Court, $42.3 million County Measure A; 355 Sango Court) are financed by County Measure A, SCCHA and state sources rather than City cash. Fee deferrals are offered for projects with on-site affordable units (Housing Element constraints chapter). milpitas.gov opened directly; the Legistar API has no Milpitas client, and Milpitas agendas are on CivicClerk.

program_name: Housing Opportunity Districts (HOD), Neighborhood Commercial Mixed-Use and Town Center zoning incentives (Resolution 9404, adopted April 15, 2025)
administering_agency: City of Milpitas Planning Division
typical_award_size: Zoning incentive, not a cash subsidy. LEAP-funded rezoning effective June 6, 2025 that raises allowable residential density to 60 units per acre in NCMU zones and 65 units per acre in Town Center zones, lowers minimum commercial FAR to 0.10 or 0.20, cuts residential parking to 1 space per unit and commercial to 1 per 300 square feet, reduces open space standards, and exempts 100 percent affordable projects in NCMU and Town Center areas from non-residential requirements. Implements Housing Element Program 15 (Housing Opportunity Zones) with a goal of at least 200 affordable units in these districts; Program 15 also contemplated a supplemental density bonus beyond state law, reduced impact fees and ministerial approval.
affordability_requirement: Affordable units per the AHO (15 percent) or 100 percent affordable projects, which receive the non-residential exemption; state density bonus can be layered.
next_deadline: In effect since June 6, 2025. The financial incentive and supplemental density bonus elements of Program 15 were not confirmed as adopted; check with Planning.
layering_notes: The HOD is Milpitas's main local tool beyond state density bonus. The City's 2008 Density Bonus Ordinance defers to state law where inconsistent and was slated for update by end of 2024 (Programs 16 and 21); the update ordinance was not located this pass. Impact fees remain high (about $48,500 per unit in the Metro Specific Plan area including the Transit Area Development Impact Fee, about $29,064 elsewhere, mostly park in-lieu), so fee deferral or waiver for 100 percent affordable projects (Program 20 explores this for specific plan areas) matters more here than in neighboring cities. milpitas.gov opened directly.

program_name: Milpitas Housing Authority fund (former redevelopment housing successor, LMIHAF) and Below Market Rate programs
administering_agency: City of Milpitas Office of Housing and Milpitas Housing Authority
typical_award_size: The Milpitas Housing Authority (housing successor to the Milpitas Redevelopment Agency) holds the Low and Moderate Income Housing Asset Fund and is listed as the funding source for Housing Element Programs 16 (affordable housing development: site acquisition and predevelopment assistance, deferred, reduced or waived fees), 19 (BMR homeownership program administered by Housekeys) and 7 (tenant assistance), and may supplement CDBG for capital projects. Fund balances were not in the documents opened; the FY 2022-23 and later Housing Successor Annual Reports are posted on milpitas.gov DocumentCenter and CivicClerk (links found but PDFs not readable this pass). Program 16 also directed staff to evaluate an affordable housing bond or EIFD by end of 2025.
affordability_requirement: Dissolution Law income targets for LMIHAF; City agreements for assisted units.
next_deadline: No NOFA found. Contact the Office of Housing (408-586-3222) for the current LMIHAF balance and the status of the bond or EIFD evaluation.
layering_notes: Needs confirmation: the Housing Authority Annual Report PDF (DocumentCenter/View/6324 for FY 2022-23) and the April 2025 Council APR item on CivicClerk were not readable by script, so balances are unverified. Expect a modest fund; Milpitas projects rely on County Measure A (Mosaic Court, Sango Court), SCCHA vouchers, Housing Trust Silicon Valley and state programs. Expedited review is offered for projects with more than 20 percent lower income units (Program 16). milpitas.gov opened directly; CivicClerk agenda links returned empty pages.

program_name: Community Development Block Grant, FY 2026-27 Annual Action Plan (2025-2030 Consolidated Plan)
administering_agency: City of Milpitas Office of Housing
typical_award_size: FY 2026-27 CDBG entitlement $538,212 plus about $8,000 program income, $294,688 carryover program income and $116,072 prior-year unused entitlement; roughly $561,000 for capital and housing rehabilitation activities (including Rebuilding Together Silicon Valley critical home repairs), $136,000 public services, with the remainder for other activities and administration. No HOME entitlement (Milpitas is in the County HOME Consortium). Council may supplement CDBG with the Housing Authority Fund.
affordability_requirement: CDBG low and moderate income benefit; housing rehabilitation for lower income owners.
next_deadline: Public hearing on the FY 2026-27 plan was June 16, 2026; FY 2027-28 applications are typically reviewed by Council in February with adoption in May or June 2027.
layering_notes: Too small to matter for multifamily gap financing; Milpitas developers use the County HOME Consortium and County Measure A or SHDF (see county records) and SCCHA vouchers. milpitas.gov opened directly.

program_name: Density Bonus Ordinance (2008) update and affordable housing fee deferrals and waivers, Housing Element 2023-2031 Programs 16, 20 and 21
administering_agency: City of Milpitas Planning Division and Office of Housing
typical_award_size: The Housing Element states the City provides fee deferrals for projects with on-site affordable units and commits to: update the 2008 Density Bonus Ordinance to current state law and clarify waivers and concessions (by end of 2024); explore fee deferrals, reductions or waivers for 100 percent affordable projects in the Metro and Gateway-Main Street specific plan areas (Program 20); develop incentives such as extra density bonuses and expedited processing for large family units, extremely low income units and supportive housing (Programs 22 and 23); and facilitate missing middle housing (Program 24). No adopted fee waiver ordinance or updated density bonus chapter was located this pass.
affordability_requirement: On-site affordable units per the AHO or 100 percent affordable projects, depending on the incentive.
eligible_project_types: 100 percent affordable in specific plan areas
next_deadline: Confirm with Planning whether the density bonus ordinance update (Program 21) and specific plan fee relief (Program 20) were adopted in 2025 or 2026; none appeared on the pages opened.
layering_notes: Recorded so the gap is explicit: Milpitas has no local housing trust fund NOFA, no adopted fee waiver program for affordable housing beyond case-by-case deferrals, and relies on state density bonus law (its local ordinance defers to state law where inconsistent). The HOD rezoning is the only adopted local enhancement. milpitas.gov opened directly; municode code pages are blocked to scripts.

program_name: City of San Diego Affordable Housing Fund (Housing Trust Fund and Inclusionary Housing Fund, SDMC Chapter 9, Article 8, Division 5) and SDHC Affordable Housing and Permanent Supportive Housing NOFA (FY27 NOFA-27-01)
administering_agency: San Diego Housing Commission (SDHC), Real Estate Division, 1122 Broadway, Suite 300, San Diego 92101; NOFA contact Morgan Patterson, morganp@sdhc.org; NOFAs posted on the SDHC PlanetBids vendor portal
typical_award_size: FY 2027 Annual Plan: about $42.5 million available July 1, 2026 to June 30, 2027 ($5.4M new fees and loan repayments plus $37.1M fund balances, of which $22.4M is already committed to projects and prior NOFAs). Rental Housing Production allocation $30.39M: $11.09M prior Board commitments, $9.8M FY26 NOFA earmark, $0.5M FY24 NOFA earmark, and a $9.0M FY27 NOFA ($6.5M Inclusionary Housing Fund plus $2.5M Housing Trust Fund linkage fees). FY27 production goal 183 units closing plus 348 units in development. FY 2025: $18.08M committed, each AHF dollar leveraged about $9; two closings (Kindred 125 units, Rose Creek 59 units) took $3.85M. Recent per project awards $1.0M to $2.85M (The Iris at San Ysidro, 99 units, $2.3M).
per_unit_cap: None published; SDHC underwrites to gap. Code caps: no more than 25 percent of a loan or grant to a single development in some HTF categories (SDMC 98.0504), 60 percent of HTF to very low income, no more than 10 percent to median income.
affordability_requirement: Minimum 55 years. HTF: at least 60 percent of funds for very low income (up to 50 percent AMI), no more than 20 percent for low income, no more than 10 percent for median income. IHF: priority to new construction of units for very low and low income households; rents at or below 30 percent of income, generally at least 10 percent below market.
next_deadline: FY27 NOFA-27-01 draft guidelines public comment closed October 29, 2026 (stakeholder meeting October 22, 2026); final guidelines and release expected after SDHC Board approval, likely late 2026 or early 2027. Register on the SDHC PlanetBids portal to receive the release. FY28 Annual Plan comment period typically February to March.
layering_notes: Largest city-controlled gap source in the county. Stacks under 4 percent and 9 percent LIHTC, SDHC bonds (separate record), SDHC project-based vouchers through the same NOFA, and County HCDS NOFA 2026-03 money only where a project sits in the City but County IHTF rarely funds City of San Diego sites. The City's Bridge to Home LMIHAF and PLHA NOFA (separate record) is run by the Economic Development Department, not SDHC, and projects commonly take both. HOME funds awarded to the City are administered by SDHC and folded into the same NOFA. AHF also funds ADU construction loans up to $250,000 at 3 percent for low income homeowners (7 year affordability) and homeless programs. FY27 plan and FY25 annual report read on sdhc.org.

program_name: Bridge to Home Program NOFA (Low and Moderate Income Housing Asset Fund, PLHA and CDBG gap loans), Round 8 (2026)
administering_agency: City of San Diego Economic Development Department, Community Development Division, 1200 Third Ave., 14th Floor, San Diego 92101; Kristian Castro, KCastro@sandiego.gov, (619) 236-6700
typical_award_size: Round 8 (opened August 31, 2026, due October 19, 2026) offered $15 million: $10M LMIHAF for new construction of rental housing at 30 to 60 percent AMI and $5M PLHA restricted to units at or below 30 percent AMI for households experiencing or at risk of homelessness. Round 7 (February 3 to April 6, 2026) offered $16.5M and recommended three projects (430 homes). Round 6 (July 2025) about $16.65M for three projects (391 homes). Round 5 (2025) used $18.38M CDBG for acquisition (Mercado Apartments $15.275M for 222 units; Navajo Family $3.1M for 44 units). Seven rounds have recommended about $141.4M; typical awards $3.0M to $6.65M per project. LMIHAF cash balance $100.5M at June 30, 2025 (SB 341 report), FY25 deposits $8.19M and expenditures $13.37M.
per_unit_cap: No fixed cap. The City scores lower funding per unit higher and may set a per project or per unit cap in a given round. Monitoring fee $157.50 per affordable unit per year.
affordability_requirement: 55 year covenants. LMIHAF: all assisted units at or below 80 percent AMI with at least 30 percent of units at or below 30 percent AMI and no more than 20 percent between 60 and 80 percent AMI (Health and Safety Code 34176.1). PLHA share only for 30 percent AMI units.
application_cycle: annual NOFA (one to two rounds per year; Round 8 closed October 19, 2026)
next_deadline: Round 8 closed October 19, 2026; funding recommendations expected at the Economic Development and Intergovernmental Relations Committee in December 2026 and Council OPAs in early 2027. Round 9 not yet announced; developers must pre-qualify through the rolling RFQ at least two weeks before a NOFA deadline.
layering_notes: Two-step process: developer RFQ pre-qualification (Pre-Qualified Developer List updated October 7, 2026; small and emerging developers may partner), then NOFA. NOFA requires state prevailing wage on the whole project and 55 year covenants recorded senior to foreclosable liens. Pairs with SDHC AHF NOFA and SDHC bonds (separate records); the City prioritizes transit priority areas and Communities of Concern. The Affordable Housing Master Plan (2023 update) governs use of former redevelopment housing assets; since 2012, $233M has gone to over 4,000 units. Successor Agency surplus sites are offered by RFP (808 West Cedar RFP closed December 8, 2025; none open as of December 2025). County HCDS NOFAs normally exclude City of San Diego projects, so this and the SDHC AHF are the local layers. Prohousing: City designation (November 2022) lapsed January 2026 and renewal is pending (separate record).

program_name: Inclusionary Affordable Housing Regulations and Inclusionary In Lieu Fee (SDMC Chapter 14, Article 2, Division 13; O-21167 as amended through O-22109)
administering_agency: San Diego Housing Commission (administration, monitoring and Inclusionary Housing Fund; Genevieve Hernandez, genevieveh@sdhc.org, (619) 578-7588) and City Development Services Department (DS-530 checklist, fee collection)
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Developments of 10 or more units: at least 10 percent of total units rented to very low or low income households at rents not exceeding 30 percent of 60 percent of AMI (phased in from July 1, 2020; now fully effective). For-sale alternatives: 10 percent at 100 percent AMI or 15 percent at 120 percent AMI. In lieu fee $25.00 per square foot of net building area of market rate units (July 1, 2024 and after; $12.73 for projects deemed complete before July 1, 2020). Other compliance: off-site units, rehabilitation or conversion of existing units or SRO or hotel rooms to 55 year affordable units, land donation. North City Future Urbanizing Area requires 20 percent. Condominium conversions of 20 or more units: 10 percent at 100 percent AMI. IHF fee revenue FY25 $17.76M (255 percent above budget); FY27 projected new IHF revenue $4.04M.
affordability_requirement: Rental inclusionary units restricted at least 55 years; on-site affordable units count toward state density bonus; developments restricted at or below 80 percent AMI by agreement are exempt.
eligible_project_types: market-rate rental and mixed-use projects of 10 or more units (compliance)
next_deadline: Applies at permit; fee rate in effect at building permit issuance. Division 13 was amended June 15, 2026 by O-22109 (effective July 15, 2026, not yet effective in the Coastal Overlay Zone); Information Bulletin 532 revised August 2026.
layering_notes: Fees feed the Inclusionary Housing Fund, the larger of the two Affordable Housing Fund accounts (about $30.7M projected balance entering FY27) and the main source of the SDHC NOFA (record above). Projects that pay the fee are not eligible for the Affordable Housing Expedite Program; projects providing on-site units get expedite processing and may stack state density bonus and Complete Communities Housing Solutions FAR bonuses. Compare Chula Vista (10 percent at 20 or more units), Carlsbad (15 percent at 7 or more units) and Oceanside (15 percent at 3 or more units); the unincorporated County ordinance is a separate county record. Code PDF read on docs.sandiego.gov and the SDHC inclusionary page.

program_name: Housing Impact Fee (commercial linkage fee) funding the San Diego Housing Trust Fund (SDMC Chapter 9, Article 8, Division 6)
administering_agency: City of San Diego Facilities Financing (calculation) and Development Services Department (collection); San Diego Housing Commission administers the resulting Housing Trust Fund
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Charged per square foot on new office, hotel, research and development, retail and other commercial development; the 2014 compromise ordinance (adopted November 10, 2014) phased rates to $2.12 per square foot for office, $1.28 for hotel and retail, and $0.80 for research and development, with exemptions for manufacturing, warehouse and certain Enterprise Zone uses and an option to dedicate land in lieu of the fee. Revenue: FY25 collections $1.78M (39 percent above budget); FY27 projected $1.36M in new HTF revenue; projected HTF balance $6.38M entering FY27.
affordability_requirement: Fee revenue must serve very low, low and median income households (at least 60 percent of HTF to very low income).
next_deadline: Paid at building permit. SDHC adopts the Affordable Housing Fund Annual Plan each spring; FY27 plan allocated $2.5M of HTF to the FY27 NOFA and $150,000 to transitional housing grants.
layering_notes: The HTF has been a declining share of SDHC's local money; the Inclusionary Housing Fund is now about five times larger. HTF money is the most flexible local source (loans, grants, indirect assistance) and is used for the SDHC NOFA, homeless housing grants and administration. No comparable city linkage fee exists in Chula Vista, Oceanside, Escondido or Carlsbad (Carlsbad's trust fund collects housing impact fees under a different code section). Code PDF read on docs.sandiego.gov; the current fee amount should be confirmed with Facilities Financing because the code table shows the 2014 phase-in schedule.

program_name: SDHC Multifamily Housing Revenue Bond Program (Housing Authority of the City of San Diego conduit bonds, Policy 300.301)
administering_agency: San Diego Housing Commission, Real Estate Division, Multifamily Housing Bond Program, 1122 Broadway, Suite 300, San Diego 92101; Colin Miller, (619) 578-7429, colinm@sdhc.org; MultifamilyBondProgram@sdhc.org
typical_award_size: Conduit tax-exempt private activity bonds sized to project debt; no City or SDHC liability. Application: Bond Inducement Application (DocuSign), $3,000 application fee and $10,000 deposit (refunded at closing, when issuer and ongoing administrative fees apply), plus notarized Developer Disclosure Statement. Issuances since 1982; program policy enacted 1989.
affordability_requirement: At least 20 percent of units at or below 50 percent AMI or 40 percent at or below 60 percent AMI; 55 year affordability; 95 percent of proceeds to capital costs.
next_deadline: Rolling; inducement must precede the CDLAC application rounds (CDLAC calendar sets the practical deadlines). Housing Authority (City Council) approval required for issuance.
layering_notes: SDHC is the issuer of choice inside the City; CMFA and CSCDA issuances are also used with City TEFRA approval (County TEFRA practice is a separate county record). Pairs with 4 percent LIHTC and the SDHC AHF NOFA and Bridge to Home loans. Chula Vista's Housing Authority now acts as issuer in most cases within that city (separate record); Oceanside has issued only occasionally (last 2016); Escondido and Carlsbad rely on JPAs.

program_name: Complete Communities Housing Solutions (SDMC Chapter 14, Article 3, Division 10): FAR bonus, Development Impact Fee waiver and Neighborhood Enhancement Fee
administering_agency: City of San Diego Development Services Department and City Planning Department; SDHC reviews affordable unit compliance
typical_award_size: Optional incentive program in Transit Priority Areas replacing density limits with floor area ratio tiers (FAR allowance web map). Required: on-site deed restricted units (program page: 15 percent of base units at 50 percent AMI, or 10 percent at 60 percent AMI plus 15 percent at 120 percent AMI, per the FAR tier) and replacement of naturally affordable units. Section 143.1010(f): waiver of Development Impact Fees for all covenant restricted affordable units, all units of 500 square feet or less, and covenant restricted three bedroom units at or below 150 percent AMI, when the project reaches at least 120 percent of base maximum density (Housing Action Package 2.0, O-2024-41, 2023). Neighborhood Enhancement Fee $9.00 per square foot of lot area (or build a public promenade), waived for developments meeting the 50 percent AMI affordability tier. Permitting: 1,917 homes in 2024 and 3,372 homes 2021 to 2024.
affordability_requirement: Deed restricted on-site units for very low, low and moderate income households (up to 120 percent AMI) for 55 years; right to return and priority preference (75 percent of affordable units) for Communities of Concern residents.
next_deadline: Ministerial review; January 10, 2024 executive order requires departmental review within 30 days. The 2026 Land Development Code update (adopted mid 2026) adjusted FAR bonuses and DIF provisions; verify current 143.1010 text before relying on the waiver.
layering_notes: Can be combined with the inclusionary requirement (the required units satisfy both) but not with the state density bonus on the same project in most cases; developers choose Complete Communities or the Affordable Housing Density Bonus (separate record). DIF waiver is a City fee waiver and may be treated as public funds for Labor Code 1720 purposes; confirm with DIR. Expedite Program and Affordable Housing Permit Now apply to qualifying projects. Code PDF read on docs.sandiego.gov; program page on sandiego.gov/complete-communities.

program_name: Affordable Housing Density Bonus Regulations (SDMC Chapter 14, Article 3, Division 7) and ADU Home Density Bonus Program
administering_agency: San Diego Housing Commission (density bonus affordable unit review; Genevieve Hernandez, (619) 578-7588) and City Development Services Department
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Local enhancements adopted March 6, 2018 (Housing SD): 10 percent density bonus for projects within the permitted building footprint, incentives or waivers available without requesting a bonus, 100 percent density bonus for micro-units within the footprint, and bonuses for sites with existing or recently expired rent restricted units. State bonuses up to 50 percent (80 percent or unlimited for 100 percent affordable) apply. ADU Home Density Bonus: one bonus ADU for each deed restricted affordable ADU (unlimited in TPAs, adjusted by O-21989 in 2025). Permitting: 2,619 homes under the density bonus in 2024 (8,726 in 2021 to 2024); 653 ADUs under the ADU bonus in 2024 (892 in 2021 to 2024, 41 percent affordable). SDHC charges land use application fees (adjusted November 1, 2025).
affordability_requirement: Government Code 65915 tiers (5 percent very low, 10 percent low, 10 percent moderate for-sale, senior, 100 percent affordable); 55 years for rental units; ADU bonus units restricted 15 years at moderate or low income.
next_deadline: Applies at entitlement; density bonus and ADU bonus regulations were amended in 2025 (O-21989) and the 2026 Land Development Code update; coastal zone versions lag Coastal Commission certification.
layering_notes: Developers choose between this and Complete Communities Housing Solutions (separate record). 100 percent affordable projects also get the Affordable Housing Expedite Program and Permit Now processing (separate record) and may use the Division 10 DIF waiver only if they elect Complete Communities. SDHC reviews affordability agreements for all programs and records them. Chula Vista, Oceanside, Escondido and Carlsbad ordinances simply conform to state law without these local enhancements. Read on sdhc.org (density bonus and ADU pages) and the City's 2025 Annual Report on Homes.

program_name: Affordable, In-Fill Housing and Sustainable Buildings Expedite Program (Information Bulletin 538, Council Policy 600-27, SDMC 143.0915) and Affordable Housing Permit Now (Executive Order 2023-1)
administering_agency: City of San Diego Development Services Department, Expedite Team (DSD-ExpediteProgram@sandiego.gov) and Ministerial Project Managers (DSDMinisterialPM@sandiego.gov)
typical_award_size: Expedite program fees are waived for 100 percent affordable projects (otherwise fees per IB-503, capped at 40 percent of staff hourly billings). Discretionary review cycles cut to about half of standard (20 business day first review, 10 day subsequent reviews, completeness check in 5 days); ministerial expedite goal 25 percent faster. Permit Now: first review of 100 percent affordable and shelter building and engineering permits within 30 business days, dedicated project managers, collaborative review meetings; 26 projects completed by July 2026 and 3,094 homes permitted 2023 to 2024. Expedite program 2018 to 2024: 435 projects, 3,490 homes. Section 143.0920 allows deviations through a Process Two Neighborhood Development Permit.
affordability_requirement: Eligibility: 10 or more units with at least 10 percent at or below 60 percent AMI (rental) or 100 percent AMI (for-sale, or 15 percent at 120 percent AMI); SDHC-funded projects with 15 percent at 120 percent AMI; projects restricted at or below 80 percent AMI by public agreement; infill projects in Transit Priority Areas with all units at or below 150 percent AMI; Promise Zone projects. Projects paying the inclusionary fee are not eligible.
next_deadline: Rolling; request eligibility confirmation by email before submittal. IB 538 dated March 2023; Permit Now 3-year progress report issued March 2026.
layering_notes: Processing benefit rather than cash, but the fee waiver and timeline savings matter for TCAC readiness deadlines. Stack with the SDHC AHF NOFA, Bridge to Home and Complete Communities. Mandatory Initial Review is required for discretionary expedite projects. No comparable formal expedite program was found for Chula Vista, Oceanside or Carlsbad; Escondido offers pre-application consultation and expedited review under Housing Element Program 2.8.

program_name: City of San Diego CDBG entitlement NOFA (FY2028 RFQ and RFP cycle) and HOME entitlement administered through SDHC
administering_agency: City of San Diego Economic Development Department, Community Development Division, 1200 Third Ave., Suite 1400, MS 56D, San Diego 92101; CDBG@sandiego.gov, (619) 236-6700; HOME administered by SDHC
typical_award_size: FY2027 CDBG competitive categories: public services about $1.29M, community and economic development about $2.72M, nonprofit facility improvement $2.0M (March 2026 funding decision memos). Capital funds for affordable housing acquisition are deployed through Bridge to Home rounds (Round 5 used $18.38M CDBG for two acquisitions). City HOME: in FY2026, 113 of 709 affordable rental units built were HOME funded; HOME is combined with Affordable Housing Fund money in the SDHC NOFA.
per_unit_cap: HOME per-unit subsidy limits apply to HOME units; CDBG category caps set annually.
affordability_requirement: CDBG national objective (low and moderate income benefit); HOME units at or below 60 percent AMI rents for 15 to 20 years or longer under the SDHC NOFA (55 years).
next_deadline: FY2028 CDBG RFQ released October 5, 2026, RFQ responses due November 6, 2026 (5 pm), RFP to qualified organizations December 7, 2026, mandatory workshop December 8, proposals due January 15, 2027 (5 pm), CPAB scores March 5, 2027, Council action April to June 2027 with the FY2028 Annual Action Plan.
layering_notes: Developers rarely apply to the CDBG public services round; the relevant path is Bridge to Home (CDBG acquisition) and the SDHC NOFA (HOME). Federal cross-cutting rules (Davis-Bacon, NEPA, Section 3) attach. The County's Urban County CDBG and HOME Consortium (county records) do not cover the City of San Diego, which is its own entitlement and participating jurisdiction. FY2026 CAPER and FY2027 Annual Action Plan are posted on the CDBG page.

program_name: State Prohousing Designation, City of San Diego (2022 designation and 2025 renewal application)
administering_agency: City of San Diego City Planning Department, Prohousing@sandiego.gov
typical_award_size: Not a direct subsidy. Prohousing status gives bonus points or set-asides in state AHSC, IIG, MHP and PLHA competitive rounds and eligibility for Prohousing Incentive Program grants. The City was designated in November 2022; the designation was valid until January 2026 and the City circulated a draft renewal application in November 2025. HCD's designated jurisdictions list as of August 10, 2026 shows Chula Vista and San Diego County but not the City of San Diego, so renewal appears still pending.
affordability_requirement: Not applicable.
next_deadline: unknown, verify with agency; check HCD's Prohousing Designation Application Tracker for the City's renewal status before claiming points in a 2027 state application.
layering_notes: Matters for layering state funds onto SDHC and Bridge to Home awards: without the designation, City projects lose Prohousing points in AHSC and MHP scoring that Chula Vista and unincorporated County projects receive. Read the City Planning Prohousing page and HCD's designated list this pass; the renewal decision itself could not be confirmed.

program_name: Chula Vista Housing Authority housing successor loans (Low and Moderate Income Housing Asset Fund) and Local Housing Trust Fund gap financing; 2025-2026 affordable housing NOFA
administering_agency: City of Chula Vista Housing and Homeless Services Department (Housing Manager Brian Warwick) acting for the Chula Vista Housing Authority as Housing Successor to the former Redevelopment Agency
typical_award_size: Residual receipts style gap loans of $3M to $4M per project. June 16, 2026: Housing Authority Resolution 2026-006 and Council Resolution 2026-130 approved up to $4,000,000 (recommended as $3,000,000 Low-Mod plus $975,000 Local Housing Trust Fund) to Wakeland Housing for the 68-unit Park Hill UMC project at 545 East Naples Street, conditioned on reducing density to 62 units; Bayview Family Apartments was the alternate. June 10, 2025: up to $4.0M Low-Mod loan to Community HousingWorks for 201 Third Avenue (HA Resolution 2025-004); March 2025: $3.0M Low-Mod for the Palomar Motel permanent supportive housing conversion with Homekey+. The 2024-2025 NOFA offered about $4,000,000 for new multifamily construction (applications due January 15, 2026). Local Housing Trust Fund seeded in 2024 with a $500,000 City match (Resolution 2024-102) and a $500,000 HCD LHTF matching grant (Resolution 2024-163, awarded January 2026). FY 2026-27 Low-Mod administration and homeless prevention appropriation $800,000.
per_unit_cap: None published; awards have run about $44,000 to $59,000 per unit.
affordability_requirement: 55 year covenants; LMIHAF rules (Health and Safety Code 34176.1: 80 percent AMI maximum, 30 percent of funds to 30 percent AMI units); LHTF units for lower income households.
application_cycle: annual NOFA (as funds accumulate; 2025-2026 round due January 15, 2026)
next_deadline: Next NOFA not announced; the Housing and Homelessness Advisory Commission received an affordable housing projects update on October 28, 2026. Contact the Housing and Homeless Services Department for the next round.
layering_notes: Chula Vista's only city gap source beyond fee waivers. Stacks with Chula Vista Housing Authority conduit bonds (separate record), County HCDS NOFA 2026-03 (Chula Vista projects are eligible for County IHTF and HOME Consortium funds because the City is in the Urban County for HOME), HACSD project-based vouchers and 4 percent LIHTC. Housing Element (2021) noted the Balanced Communities in-lieu fund held only about $1.1M in 2020 and was inadequate for gap financing; the new Housing Inclusionary Fund (CVMC 19.91.070) will add in-lieu fees. Palomar Motel used Homekey+. chulavistaca.gov blocks automated access (403); agendas, minutes and item summaries were read on the City's eSCRIBE agenda portal, but staff report PDFs (filestream.ashx) return 403, so loan terms come from the agenda item text.

program_name: Inclusionary Housing Ordinance, CVMC Chapter 19.91 (Ordinance 3572, 2024; threshold amended to 20 units by Ordinance 3581, November 2024) and Housing In-Lieu Fee / Housing Inclusionary Fund
administering_agency: City of Chula Vista Housing and Homeless Services Department and Development Services Department
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Residential and mixed-use projects of 20 or more units (applications deemed complete on or after July 1, 2024) must restrict 10 percent of units, split as evenly as possible between moderate income and low income households, for rental or for-sale product; density bonus units are excluded from the base. In-lieu fee for fractional units or in place of on-site units set by Council resolution on a square footage basis with different rates for for-sale and rental product (Master Fee Schedule Chapter 16, Resolution 2024-100, May 21, 2024, based on the RSG Inclusionary Policy and In-Lieu Fee Study); paid before the first building permit into the Housing Inclusionary Fund. Alternatives: off-site units within one mile or in TCAC high or moderate resource areas, land dedication, conversion of market rate units, preservation of at-risk units, transferable credits (10 year life), and incentive credits (for example 3.5 rental units of credit per very low income unit provided in place of a moderate unit). Replaced the 1981 Balanced Communities Policy (10 percent of 50 or more units).
affordability_requirement: 55 years rental (45 years ownership); moderate income (up to 120 percent AMI) and low income (up to 80 percent AMI) units; Chapter 19.94 marketing and lottery rules give preference to displaced Chula Vista residents and local residents and workers.
eligible_project_types: market-rate rental and for-sale projects of 20 or more units (compliance)
next_deadline: Applies at entitlement; the Council on May 21, 2024 voted 5-0 to set the threshold at 20 units (first reading) and adopted the Chapter 19.91 threshold amendment on November 12, 2024. Code is current through Ordinance 3617 (February 2026). Check the Master Fee Schedule Chapter 16 for the current per square foot in-lieu rate.
layering_notes: Projects of 20 to 24 units routinely pay fees, so the Housing Inclusionary Fund will grow slowly; Otay Ranch village developers (for example Village 8 East, Affordable Housing Agreement approved November 4, 2025) satisfy the requirement with dedicated affordable sites that then seek City Low-Mod loans and bonds (separate records). Inclusionary units may count toward the state density bonus (19.91.060). Ordinance text read on the zoneomics code mirror (chulavista.municipal.codes returns 403); Council actions read on the eSCRIBE agenda portal.

program_name: Parkland Acquisition and Development fee exemption for affordable units (Ordinance 3573 amending CVMC 17.10, 2024) and project fee waivers and deferrals for affordable housing
administering_agency: City of Chula Vista Development Services Department and Housing and Homeless Services Department; waivers by City Council resolution
typical_award_size: Ordinance 3573 (second reading May 28, 2024) exempts affordable units from Parkland Acquisition and Development (PAD) fees. Council also waives parkland dedication and in-lieu requirements case by case: Resolution 2026-087 (May 19, 2026) for the 96-unit Sol Vista (Enclave Montecito) affordable rental project in Otay Ranch Village 2 and Resolution 2024-060 (April 9, 2024) for the 100 percent affordable Chula Vista Seniors project at 178 Third Avenue. The Housing Element (Program 4.5) describes Council waivers or deferrals of development impact fees for projects with affordable units and a development fee deferral program for infill rental housing west of I-805. PAD fees in Chula Vista run tens of thousands of dollars per unit, so the exemption is a material subsidy.
affordability_requirement: Deed restricted affordable units; 100 percent affordable projects have received full parkland waivers.
next_deadline: Exemption applies at permit; discretionary waivers go to Council with the project's financing approvals. Confirm the current CVMC 17.10 text and whether other DIFs (transportation, public facilities) can be deferred for a specific project.
layering_notes: Fee relief is the second city layer after Low-Mod and LHTF loans (separate record). Waived City fees may be public funds under Labor Code 1720, so projects usually assume prevailing wage once they also take City or bond financing. County HCDS impact fee waivers (county records) do not apply inside the city. Read on the City's eSCRIBE agenda portal (May 19, 2026 and May 2024 agendas); chulavistaca.gov is blocked to scripts.

program_name: Chula Vista Housing Authority tax-exempt multifamily housing revenue bonds (conduit issuer; 2024 bond policies)
administering_agency: Chula Vista Housing Authority (City Council acting as Authority), staffed by the Housing and Homeless Services Department
typical_award_size: Conduit private activity bonds sized to project debt. Enclave Montecito / Sol Vista (96 units, Otay Ranch Village 2): inducement up to $25 million (HA Resolution 2025-006, August 5, 2025), TEFRA hearing and bond issuance approval April 21, 2026 with an issuance amount not to exceed $14,000,000; TEFRA for the Otay Ranch II project May 19, 2026. Resolution 2024-103 (May 21, 2024) updated the Authority's conduit bond policies so the City is the issuer in most instances rather than JPAs; Master Fee Schedule Chapter 19 sets Housing Authority application, issuance and monitoring fees.
affordability_requirement: Federal 20 percent at 50 percent AMI or 40 percent at 60 percent AMI minimum; City regulatory agreements typically mirror the inclusionary and Low-Mod covenants (55 years).
next_deadline: Rolling; inducement needed before CDLAC application rounds. Contact the Housing and Homeless Services Department for the bond policy and fee schedule.
layering_notes: Replaces CMFA or CSCDA issuance for most Chula Vista deals, which keeps issuer fees local; the County TEFRA practice (county record) is not needed when the City issues. Pairs with 4 percent LIHTC, City Low-Mod and LHTF loans and parkland fee waivers (separate records). Read on the City's eSCRIBE agenda portal; bond policy PDF not downloadable (403).

program_name: Affordable Housing Incentives / Density Bonus, CVMC Chapter 19.90 (Ordinance 3572, 2024)
administering_agency: City of Chula Vista Development Services Department with Housing and Homeless Services Department
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Chapter 19.90 adopts Government Code 65915 by reference: bonus, incentives, concessions, waivers and parking reductions as set in state law; no local enhancement beyond state minimums. Requires a recorded density bonus agreement senior to monetary liens, concurrent construction and on-site dispersal of affordable units (separate structure allowed where needed for LIHTC), and an administrative fee for agreement processing (19.90.080).
affordability_requirement: State tiers; occupancy, rent and term per Government Code 65915 (55 years rental).
next_deadline: Applies at entitlement; pre-application conference encouraged. Density bonus units are exempt from the inclusionary requirement and are not counted in its base.
layering_notes: Inclusionary units can count toward both the inclusionary and density bonus requirements (19.91.060). Otay Ranch village SPA plans carry their own affordable housing plans.
