Chula Vista is on HCD's Prohousing list (as of August 10, 2026) and received a Prohousing Incentive Program grant (Resolution 2025-179, November 4, 2025), which adds points for state applications on Chula Vista sites. Ordinance text read on the zoneomics code mirror.

program_name: Chula Vista CDBG and HOME entitlement, PLHA Cycle 2 allocation and Prohousing Incentive Program grant
administering_agency: City of Chula Vista Housing and Homeless Services Department (HUD grants), Carlos Rodriguez, Management Analyst (PLHA)
typical_award_size: FY 2026-27 HUD allocations appropriated June 16, 2026 (Resolution 2026-118): $2,501,482.59 CDBG and $1,200,730.78 HOME, plus ESG; Annual Action Plan adopted May 19, 2026 (Resolution 2026-089). PLHA: Council on October 6, 2026 adopted the PLHA CY2024-2028 302(c)(4) Plan and accepted Cycle 2 funds (Resolutions 2026-211 and 2026-212), directing them to Chula Vista Village at Otay shelter operations, as it did with earlier PLHA (Resolution 2025-084, June 2025). Prohousing Incentive Program grant application authorized November 4, 2025 (Resolution 2025-179). Chula Vista is on HCD's Prohousing Designation list as of August 10, 2026.
affordability_requirement: CDBG and HOME income rules; HOME development awards are made through the City's affordable housing NOFA or by Council action.
next_deadline: FY 2027-28 Annual Action Plan public review period is expected March to April 2027 (Housing and Homelessness Advisory Commission reviews in spring); PLHA and PIP uses set by Council resolution.
layering_notes: HOME has been the main federal layer in City NOFAs along with Low-Mod and LHTF (separate record); PLHA in Chula Vista is committed to shelter operations, not capital, so do not count on it for development. The City is a separate CDBG and HOME entitlement, outside the County Urban County and HOME Consortium (county records). Read on the City's eSCRIBE agenda portal.

program_name: Inclusionary Housing Ordinance, Oceanside City Code Chapter 14C (Ordinance 24-OR0004-1, 2024) and Inclusionary Housing In-Lieu Fee
administering_agency: City of Oceanside Housing and Neighborhood Services Department (Housing Division) and Development Services Department (Planning)
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Applies to residential projects of three or more units (rental projects included since the September 9, 2020 Phase 1 amendment). Ordinance 24-OR0004-1 (approved by Council February 10, 2024) raised the set-aside for low and moderate income households from 10 percent to 15 percent, raised the applicability threshold and added requirements for reserved units within multifamily projects; it was folded into Local Coastal Program amendment LCPA23-00002, which Coastal Commission staff recommended certifying with modifications at the February 2026 hearing (acutely low income definition, 15 percent of base units). In-lieu fee calculated per square foot under a 2022 nexus study (Development Impact Fee schedule effective July 1, 2025 lists a per development, per unit and per square foot structure, adjusted annually); deferral of the in-lieu fee allowed on the same terms as impact fee deferral. Fees must be used exclusively for low and moderate income housing in the City; the Housing Element reports $360,000 of in-lieu fees used for homebuyer assistance and in-lieu fees as a source for preservation (Program 19). A further Chapter 14C revision was noticed for a Community Development Commission hearing on May 6, 2026.
affordability_requirement: 15 percent of base units for low and moderate income households (rental units for low income); 55 year terms under the 2024 ordinance; density bonus units excluded.
eligible_project_types: market-rate rental and for-sale projects of 3 or more units (compliance)
next_deadline: Applies at entitlement; coastal zone projects remain under the previously certified 10 percent rule until the Coastal Commission certifies LCPA23-00002 (hearing February 5, 2026, outcome not confirmed). Confirm the current in-lieu fee rate on the City's FY 2025-26 impact fee schedule and whether the May 6, 2026 revisions were adopted.
layering_notes: In-lieu fee revenue is Oceanside's only recurring local housing fund; the Housing Element lists inclusionary fees with HOME, Housing Asset Funds, project-based vouchers and PLHA as sources for the Affordable Housing Strategy NOFAs (separate record). Compare Carlsbad (15 percent at 7 or more units) and the unincorporated County ordinance (county record). ci.oceanside.ca.us returns 403 and the oceanside.prod-as.govaccess.org document hosts time out, and the Legistar web API has no Oceanside client, so the ordinance text was read in the California Coastal Commission's February 2026 staff report (Exhibit 2 contains the strikeout ordinance) and the City's 2021-2029 Housing Element on hcd.ca.gov. The City's Legistar calendar (oceanside.legistar.com) opens for current agendas only.

program_name: Oceanside Affordable Housing Strategy RFP/NOFA (Housing Element Program 4): HOME, Housing Successor Agency asset funds, inclusionary in-lieu fees, PLHA and project-based vouchers
administering_agency: City of Oceanside Housing and Neighborhood Services Department, Housing Division, and the Housing Successor Agency to the Oceanside Community Development Commission; recommendations through the Housing Commission
typical_award_size: Amounts vary by round; no standing allocation. The Council on September 9, 2020 directed an RFP/NOFA implementing the Affordable Housing Strategy with priority to homelessness and extremely low income housing (temporary shelters, bridge housing, vouchers, permanent supportive housing). Funding sources named: HOME entitlement (City is a HOME participating jurisdiction), remaining Housing Asset Funds (former redevelopment), inclusionary in-lieu fees, project-based vouchers from the Oceanside Housing Authority (Housing Choice Voucher program) and PLHA (PLHA earmarked for emergency shelter operations). Program 19 (preservation) and Program 15 (acquisition and rehabilitation) use CDBG, HOME and in-lieu fees. The Housing Element set an objective of 634 extremely low income units and 1,268 lower income units for 2021-2029 and a 2024-2025 reassessment of incentives.
per_unit_cap: HOME per-unit subsidy limits apply to HOME units; no City cap published.
affordability_requirement: Lower income and extremely low income households; 55 years for HOME and in-lieu assisted rental units.
next_deadline: unknown, verify with agency; no open NOFA found. The November 10, 2026 City Council agenda had no housing funding item. Contact the Housing Division for the FY 2026-27 Annual Action Plan HOME development set-aside and any Housing Commission funding recommendations.
layering_notes: Oceanside projects also compete in the County HCDS NOFA 2026-03 only for IHTF (the City is its own HOME participating jurisdiction and CDBG entitlement, outside the County consortium), and can use HACSD or Oceanside Housing Authority project-based vouchers. The City last issued its own multifamily revenue bonds in 2016 (Villa Storia, 38 units; Program 1) and otherwise relies on CMFA or CSCDA. Fee deferrals for affordable units are offered on the same terms as impact fee deferrals. Program text read in the 2021-2029 Housing Element (October 2022 revision, HCD-hosted); the certified September 2023 re-adoption and current Annual Action Plan could not be opened because City document hosts block or time out.

program_name: Oceanside Density Bonus Ordinance (Zoning Ordinance, Housing Element Program 2) and development impact fee deferral for affordable units
administering_agency: City of Oceanside Development Services Department, Planning Division
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. The Housing Element committed to amend the density bonus ordinance within one year of adoption to conform to AB 1763, SB 1227 and AB 2345 (up to 50 percent bonus; 80 percent or unlimited for 100 percent affordable projects); Coastal Commission staff describe the City's 2024 inclusionary amendments as paired with a density bonus for projects reserving at least 15 percent of base units for very low income, 24 percent for lower income or 44 percent for moderate income households. The City's density bonus application notes that inclusionary income tiers may not be modified or combined with bonus units. Impact fee deferral is available to residential projects and extends to the inclusionary in-lieu fee.
affordability_requirement: Government Code 65915 tiers; 55 year rental affordability.
next_deadline: Applies at entitlement. Confirm the current Zoning Ordinance density bonus article and any 2026 amendments with Planning; City code hosts were not reachable this pass.
layering_notes: No local enhancements beyond state law were found; the practical local tools are the inclusionary in-lieu fund and the Affordable Housing Strategy NOFA (separate records). Smart and Sustainable Corridors Plan (Program 9) adds capacity along transit corridors. Read in the 2021-2029 Housing Element (HCD-hosted) and the Coastal Commission February 2026 staff report.

program_name: Oceanside Housing Revenue Bonds (Multi-Family), Housing Element Program 1
administering_agency: City of Oceanside Housing and Neighborhood Services Department, Housing Division (City as conduit issuer)
typical_award_size: Conduit tax-exempt private activity bonds issued by the City when appropriate; last used in 2016 for Villa Storia (38 units) with a CDLAC award. The City commits to issue bonds in conjunction with other financing as needed.
affordability_requirement: Federal 20 percent at 50 percent AMI or 40 percent at 60 percent AMI minimum; City regulatory agreement terms set per project.
next_deadline: unknown, verify with agency; no issuance policy or fee schedule was located. Most recent Oceanside deals have used JPA issuers with City TEFRA approval.
layering_notes: Low volume issuer; expect to use CMFA or CSCDA with a City TEFRA hearing instead, as the County does (county record). Pairs with 4 percent LIHTC and the Affordable Housing Strategy sources (separate record). Read in the 2021-2029 Housing Element (HCD-hosted); City pages blocked.

program_name: Escondido HOME and CDBG entitlement: HOME affordable housing development awards (Resolution 2026-50, Valley Creek Senior Apartments) and HOME acquisition-rehabilitation RFP
administering_agency: City of Escondido Development Services Department, Housing and Neighborhood Services Division, 201 North Broadway, Escondido 92025; Danielle Lopez, Housing and Neighborhood Services Manager, (760) 839-4841
typical_award_size: FY 2025-26 HUD allocation $1,931,930 ($1,341,561 CDBG, $590,369 HOME); FY 2026-27 announced April 10, 2026: $1,394,624 CDBG and $563,047.23 HOME ($1,957,671 total, no ESG); HOME expected about $2.9M over the 2025-2029 Consolidated Plan. April 8, 2026: Council adopted Resolution 2026-50 allocating $3,000,000 in HOME ($583,938.80 expiring 2018 funds plus $2.4M unspent 2019-2023 funds) to National CORE and San Diego Community Housing Corporation for Valley Creek Senior Apartments, a 136-unit 100 percent affordable senior project with 14 units for homeless or at-risk veterans on a 1.88-acre County-owned site at East Valley Parkway and Fig Street, piggybacking on the County's RFP with the County as lead agency. Council also considered a City RFP option of $8.5M for an affordable project. The FY 2025-26 CAPER reports a HOME RFP being prepared for acquisition, rehabilitation and preservation of units for households under 80 percent AMI. HOME also funds the Rental Subsidy Program ($388,000 amendment, $500 per month) and the HELP homebuyer program.
per_unit_cap: HOME per-unit subsidy limits apply; City committed about $22,000 per unit on Valley Creek.
affordability_requirement: HOME rents and incomes (low income, 60 percent AMI for most units) for the HOME affordability period; the Valley Creek award is paired with County and tax credit covenants of 55 years.
application_cycle: annual NOFA (HOME development funds released periodically by RFP)
next_deadline: HOME acquisition-rehab RFP expected FY 2026-27 (date not published); CDBG RFP 26-11 for FY 2026-27 public services and facilities closed in spring 2026; FY 2027-28 CDBG and HOME hearings expected February and June 2027 per the City's cycle.
layering_notes: Escondido is a CDBG entitlement and HOME participating jurisdiction outside the County HOME Consortium, but the Valley Creek deal shows the City will layer its HOME onto County HCDS NOFA awards (county records) on County-owned land. No local trust fund, inclusionary fund or linkage fee exists; the other local layers are recycled redevelopment funds (separate record), density bonus and fee deferral (separate record). Read the April 8, 2026 staff report on the City's agenda host (mccmeetingspublic) and the Housing and Neighborhood Services, CDBG and HOME pages and the FY 2025-26 CAPER on escondido.gov.

program_name: Escondido Successor Housing Agency (Resolution 2012-16) recycled redevelopment housing funds and affordable housing development assistance (Housing Element Program 2.8)
administering_agency: City of Escondido Housing and Neighborhood Services Division acting for the Successor Housing Agency to the former Community Development Commission; City Council sits as the Successor Agency
typical_award_size: Case by case gap loans from recycled Low and Moderate Income Housing Asset Fund money and loan repayments; no NOFA. Recent uses: Valley Senior Village (completed 2023, 50 units, 24 homeless and 25 units at 30 to 60 percent AMI) used recycled RDA funds; 10 affordable homeownership units at 245 East El Norte Parkway (2024). Housing Element Program 2.8 lists Recycled RDA Funds with LIHTC, CalCHA bonds, CalHFA, CalHome, PLHA and HOME as sources the City will pursue, and commits to pre-application consultation, expedited review and City-owned sites (Program 1.4; one City-owned site under review). SB 341 annual reports are posted under Policy and Regulatory Documents on escondido.gov (page not reachable this pass).
affordability_requirement: LMIHAF rules (80 percent AMI maximum, 30 percent of expenditures to 30 percent AMI units over five year periods); 55 year covenants typical.
next_deadline: unknown, verify with agency; no competitive round. Approach the Housing and Neighborhood Services Division before County HCDS or TCAC deadlines; Council approves loans individually.
layering_notes: Small pool (balance not confirmed; SB 341 report link on the City page was broken). Stacks with City HOME (separate record), County HCDS NOFA 2026-03 (Escondido projects are eligible for County IHTF), HACSD project-based vouchers and state density bonus. Escondido has no inclusionary ordinance (Program 2.9 feasibility study triggered by the 2023 APR) and no housing trust fund. Read the Housing and Neighborhood Services page on escondido.gov, the 2023 Annual Progress Report staff report and the draft 2021-2029 Housing Element on escondido.gov.

program_name: Density Bonus and Residential Incentives Ordinance (Escondido Zoning Code Article 67, Sections 33-1410 to 33-1421) and Development Fee Deferral Policy
administering_agency: City of Escondido Development Services Department, Planning Division
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Article 67 grants state law density bonuses (up to 50 percent; 80 percent or unlimited for 100 percent affordable projects) and incentives and concessions to projects of five or more units (three or more in some areas), including student housing and child care provisions, in-lieu incentives of equivalent land value, land donation bonuses and a sliding scale (one percent bonus per one percent increase above the 10 percent very low income minimum); amended in 2020, 2021 and 2022 for AB 2345. Agreement processing and administrative fee apply (33-1421). The 2012 Development Fee Deferral Policy lets residential projects of five or more units defer development fees to occupancy (up to one year from permit). Density transfer programs exist in the Downtown and East Valley Specific Plan areas (Resolution 2019-69; Ordinance 2023-10).
affordability_requirement: Government Code 65915 tiers; affordability tenure per 33-1418 (55 years rental).
next_deadline: Applies at entitlement; density bonus request form on escondido.gov. A zoning ordinance update with lot consolidation incentives was planned for 2025; confirm current Article 67 text with Planning.
layering_notes: State conforming with no local fee waiver: a 2024 staff report noted neither state law nor the Municipal Code requires the City to give direct financial assistance to density bonus projects. The fee deferral is the only fee relief. Escondido is not on HCD's Prohousing list (as of August 10, 2026). Pair with City HOME and recycled RDA funds (separate records) and County HCDS NOFA. Article text read on the zoneomics code mirror; Housing Element and APR read on escondido.gov.

program_name: Essential Middle Income Rental Housing Program (California Community Housing Agency JPA membership, January 13, 2021; Housing Element Program 2.3)
administering_agency: City of Escondido Housing and Neighborhood Services Division with the California Community Housing Agency (CalCHA)
typical_award_size: Not a direct subsidy. As a CalCHA member, the City allows CalCHA to acquire existing market rate apartment communities with governmental purpose bonds; CalCHA's property tax exemption converts the complexes to rent restricted units for low, median and moderate income households up to 120 percent AMI with rents capped at 35 percent of the applicable AMI and annual increases capped at 4 percent; no displacement of existing tenants. Program 2.3 commits the City to identify properties for acquisition; no Escondido acquisition was confirmed this pass.
affordability_requirement: Low, median and moderate income households (up to 120 percent AMI); rent caps at 35 percent of AMI tier; terms per CalCHA regulatory agreement.
next_deadline: unknown, verify with agency; CalCHA transactions depend on bond market conditions and City host approval of each acquisition.
layering_notes: Middle income JPA structure, not stackable with LIHTC. Useful only for workforce housing acquisitions; the City forgoes its share of property tax. The welfare exemption for nonprofit LIHTC owners (county record) remains the tax tool for deed restricted projects. Read in the draft 2021-2029 Housing Element on escondido.gov; program status not confirmed.

program_name: Carlsbad Housing Trust Fund gap loans (Inclusionary Housing in-lieu fees, housing credit purchases and housing impact fees; CMC 21.85.110 and 21.85.120)
administering_agency: City of Carlsbad Housing and Homeless Services Department (Mandy Mills, Director); recommendations by the Housing Commission, approvals by City Council
typical_award_size: Residual receipts gap loans typically $500,000 to $4.25M per project. June 9, 2026: Council Resolutions 2026-107 and 2026-108 authorized sale of the City-owned 945 Chestnut Avenue (Chestnut Apartments) to The Chestnut Apartments, LP (Kingdom Development) through a carryback loan at appraised value plus a Housing Trust Fund loan not to exceed $850,000 for rehabilitation gap financing (Housing Commission Resolution 2026-004, May 14, 2026). Earlier: $4.25M residual receipts loan to Affirmed Housing (Windsor Pointe, about $8.3M total City assistance) and a 2025 $500,000 recommendation for West Oaks. Fund balance about $12.4M at October 30, 2020 (Housing Element); the FY 2025-26 Housing Trust Fund Annual Report was accepted by the Housing Commission October 8, 2026 (Resolution 2026-006). Fund sources: in-lieu fees ($4,515 per market rate unit as of 2020, fee study pending), sale of affordable housing credits, housing impact fees, loan interest and fund interest. The fund has helped produce about 2,300 affordable homes and leverages City money up to five times.
per_unit_cap: None published; sized by pro forma review.
affordability_requirement: 55 year affordability for lower income households (up to 80 percent AMI; rents no more than 90 percent of the lower income limit rent per 21.85.040). Trust fund dollars may not be used to satisfy a project's own inclusionary requirement, only to exceed it.
next_deadline: No NOFA; requests go to the Housing Commission (meets second Thursday) then Council. Next regular Housing Commission meetings follow the 2027 schedule adopted in late 2026; the FY 2025-26 Housing Trust Fund Annual Report went to Council after October 8, 2026.
layering_notes: Carlsbad's trust fund is the best capitalized city fund in North County relative to deal flow, but Council has been selective (Chestnut, Windsor Pointe, West Oaks). Stacks with County HCDS NOFA 2026-03 IHTF and HOME Consortium funds (Carlsbad is in the County HOME Consortium and received County HOME for Vista Las Flores), HACSD or Carlsbad Housing Agency project-based vouchers, CMFA or CSCDA bonds and LIHTC. The CDBG-funded Housing Reserve Fund (separate record) can add acquisition money. carlsbadca.gov and its govaccess document host return 403 or time out; agendas were read on the City's Laserfiche WebLink (records.carlsbadca.gov) and the Housing Element on hcd.ca.gov. The annual report figures should be pulled from the October 2026 Housing Commission packet.

program_name: Inclusionary Housing Ordinance, Carlsbad Municipal Code Chapter 21.85 (Ordinance NS-535 as amended through CS-474, 2024), in-lieu fees and inclusionary housing credits
administering_agency: City of Carlsbad Housing and Homeless Services Department and Community Development Department (Planning)
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Residential developments of seven or more units must build and restrict at least 15 percent of total approved units (including density bonus units) for lower income households; off-site combined projects are allowed with Council approval and the percentage is computed on total units (market units divided by 0.85). Projects of fewer than seven units pay an in-lieu fee per market rate unit equal to 15 percent of the subsidy needed to make a typical new attached unit affordable to a lower income household ($4,515 as of 2020; schedule set by Council resolution; fee study authorized). Alternatives: off-site units, land dedication, contribution to special needs housing, purchase of surplus affordable housing credits from Villa Loma and other combined projects, and inclusionary credit schedules for units serving lower tiers. Offsets (21.85.100): the City may grant density increases, standards modifications, fee waivers and subsidies at its discretion. Rental inclusionary units required since 2017 (CS-324) after the 2010 Palmer suspension. The ordinance has produced 1,708 affordable units.
affordability_requirement: Lower income households (up to 80 percent AMI); rental units restricted 55 years with rents no more than 90 percent of the lower income limit; for-sale units resale restricted.
eligible_project_types: market-rate rental and for-sale projects of 7 or more units (compliance)
next_deadline: Applies at entitlement through an Affordable Housing Agreement (21.85.140) before final map or building permit; in-lieu fee per Council resolution schedule, assessed on market rate units at building permit.
layering_notes: Fees and credit sales fund the Housing Trust Fund (separate record). Density bonus units count in the 15 percent base, which makes Carlsbad's requirement stricter than the state density bonus tiers; the inclusionary units themselves qualify the project for state density bonus incentives (CMC 21.86, separate record). Master and specific plans must carry inclusionary provisions (21.85.035). Code read on the zoneomics mirror; Housing Element Program 2.1 on hcd.ca.gov.

program_name: Carlsbad Density Bonus Ordinance, Carlsbad Municipal Code Chapter 21.86 (Ordinance CS-382, 2020; CS-426, 2022)
administering_agency: City of Carlsbad Community Development Department, Planning Division
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Implements Government Code 65915 (bonus, incentives, concessions, waivers, parking ratios) with a density bonus plan submittal, staff review fee set by Council resolution, Local Coastal Program consistency findings and an affordable housing or senior housing agreement. Section 21.86.060 states nothing requires direct financial incentives (subsidies, public land, fee waivers or dedication waivers); the City may grant them at its sole discretion.
affordability_requirement: Government Code 65915 tiers; 55 year rental affordability; applicant may accept a smaller bonus but not reduce required affordable percentages.
next_deadline: Applies at entitlement; coastal zone projects need Coastal Development Permit consistency.
layering_notes: No local enhancement; Carlsbad's binding tool is the 15 percent inclusionary requirement (separate record), with the density bonus layered on top (inclusionary units qualify for state incentives). Housing Element Program 1.1 rezoned sites to R-35 and R-40 for RHNA. Carlsbad is not on HCD's Prohousing list (as of August 10, 2026). Code read on the zoneomics mirror.

program_name: Carlsbad Housing Reserve Fund (CDBG set-aside for affordable housing acquisition) and CDBG entitlement; Section 108 and County HOME Consortium access
administering_agency: City of Carlsbad Housing and Homeless Services Department; CDBG Advisory Committee recommends allocations
typical_award_size: The City reserves part of its annual CDBG entitlement (about $535,000 in FY 2025-26 per the Annual Action Plan; figure not confirmed on a City page) in a Housing Reserve Fund that accumulates for acquisition or development of affordable units; once a property is identified the reserve is reallocated to that project. Carlsbad used a $1.2M CDBG Section 108 loan in the 1990s for the Villa Loma site and may pursue Section 108 again. Carlsbad is in the San Diego Urban County HOME Consortium, so HOME development funds come through the County HCDS NOFA (over $675,000 awarded to Vista Las Flores rehabilitation).
per_unit_cap: CDBG and HOME per-unit rules apply.
affordability_requirement: CDBG low and moderate income benefit (80 percent AMI); HOME rents and terms for County-awarded HOME.
application_cycle: annual NOFA (CDBG action plan each spring; reserve deployed by Council action)
next_deadline: FY 2027-28 CDBG application period expected winter 2026-27 with the CDBG Advisory Committee; Council adopts the Annual Action Plan in spring 2027. Confirm the current Housing Reserve Fund balance with the Housing and Homeless Services Department.
layering_notes: Minor source next to the Housing Trust Fund (separate record) but useful for site acquisition because CDBG can buy land. HOME must be sought from County HCDS NOFA 2026-03 (county record), which also offers IHTF and PLHA for Carlsbad sites. Read in the 2021-2029 Housing Element on hcd.ca.gov; carlsbadca.gov pages blocked (403).

program_name: Inclusionary Housing Requirements (Municipal Code Chapter 17.138, Ord. 1719, 2022) and Commercial Linkage Fee (Chapter 4.60)
administering_agency: City of San Luis Obispo Community Development Department, Housing Programs
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Rental projects: 6% of units affordable (3% very low, 3% low). For-sale projects: 10% of units (5% low, 5% moderate). In-lieu fee calculated on new habitable square footage at a rate set by Council resolution in the comprehensive fee schedule; the City's inclusionary page (not opened this pass, slocity.org blocks automated access) reports about $26.73 per sq ft for-sale and $21.42 per sq ft rental, with commercial linkage fees of about $6.42 per sq ft (office, service, hotel, retail) and $5.35 per sq ft (industrial, institutional). All in-lieu and linkage fees go to the City Affordable Housing Fund. By 2020 the program had produced more than 850 affordable units and $10.45 million in in-lieu funds committed to 464 units.
affordability_requirement: Inclusionary units deed restricted 55 years rental, 45 years ownership, at City Affordable Housing Standards. Fractional units may be met by paying a fractional in-lieu fee. Exempt: ADUs and JADUs, 100% affordable projects, projects using a density bonus, downtown flexible density units (Chapter 17.141), additions and remodels that add no units.
next_deadline: Not applicable; requirement applies at entitlement and in-lieu fee is paid before building permit issuance (phased projects pay proportionally).
layering_notes: Core local requirement for any market-rate multifamily deal in the City of SLO. 100% affordable projects and density bonus projects are exempt, so an LIHTC deal normally pays nothing and instead competes for the in-lieu revenue through the Affordable Housing Fund (separate record). Ordinance replaced the 1999 program in 2022 after a nexus study; the City notes Chapter 17.138 and Chapter 4.60 (nonresidential linkage fee) apply to mixed-use projects on both the residential and commercial components. County inclusionary ordinance (Title 22 Section 22.12.080) was repealed in 2022 and the County's Title 29 fund is now residual, so the City fund is the only growing in-lieu pool in the county. slocity.org returns 403 to automated access; the ordinance text was read on the zoneomics code mirror and the program history in the HCD-hosted 2020-2028 Housing Element. Confirm current fee rates on the City's inclusionary page before underwriting.

program_name: City Affordable Housing Fund (AHF) grants and loans (in-lieu fee fund; award criteria Resolution 9263, 2001 Series; Housing Element Program 2.5)
administering_agency: City of San Luis Obispo Community Development Department, Housing Programs (Council awards)
typical_award_size: Gap grants and below-market loans at Council discretion. History: $10,450,954 committed to 464 deed-restricted units from 1999 to 2020; Bishop Street Studios (34 units) received $1,595,500 combined AHF loan, impact fee deferral loan and CDBG loan; $2 million approved January 2020 for a 108-unit project; $330,000 grant to TMHA for a 6-unit acquisition-rehab; a 2023 Council resolution (eScribe DocumentId 8320, blocked to scripts) approved $3.2 million to HASLO for 736 Orcutt Road ($2.0 million) and 279 Bridge Street Family Apartments ($1.2 million), each paired with a fee deferral loan. HCD Prohousing Incentive Program funds ($750,000, 2024) were routed through the AHF. Housing Element target: support at least 4 new affordable developments during 2020-2028.
affordability_requirement: Extremely low, very low, low and moderate income; deed restrictions of 55 years rental and 45 years ownership under City Affordable Housing Standards. Housing Element Program 2.5 directs the fund to projects that would not be feasible without AHF support and to production efficiency.
next_deadline: unknown, verify with agency. No formal NOFA; developers request awards through the Housing Programs Coordinator (housing@slocity.org) and awards go to Council by resolution, usually timed to TCAC or CDLAC rounds.
layering_notes: Largest city-controlled housing fund in the county. Revenue is the Chapter 17.138 in-lieu fee and Chapter 4.60 commercial linkage fee plus shared-equity recapture; the City also receives its own CDBG share through the Urban County (county record: Urban County Action Plan NOFA, due October 30, 2026 for the 2027 program year) and has layered CDBG loans with AHF awards. Typical stack for a City of SLO LIHTC deal: AHF grant or loan, City impact fee deferral loan (separate record), County Title 29 or Regional Housing Fund, HASLO project-based vouchers, SLO County Housing Trust Fund predevelopment loan, then state sources. HCD-hosted Housing Element was the only agency document that could be opened; slocity.org (403) and the City eScribe agenda host pub-slocity.escribemeetings.com (filestream 403, JS-only listings) could not be read, so current fund balance and 2025-2026 awards are unconfirmed.

program_name: Affordable Housing Incentives and local density bonus (Municipal Code Chapter 17.140; Ord. 1705, 2021)
administering_agency: City of San Luis Obispo Community Development Department (Director approval; review authority resolution for alternative incentives)
typical_award_size: Requirement-based entitlement, not a subsidy. Density bonus of 20% to 50% per Tables 8-3 and 8-4 (10% low income earns 20%, rising to 50% at 24% low income; 5% very low earns 20%); the Director may approve a bonus above 50% at the developer's request. One to three incentives or concessions on the state schedule, and alternative incentives listed in Section 17.140.070 include deferral of application and development review processing fees, deferral of park land in-lieu fees or dedication, mixed-use zoning, reduced site standards and parking. Housing Element Program 2.14 commits the City to support bonuses above the 35% state base; the City approved more than 15 density bonus requests in 2018-2020.
affordability_requirement: State density bonus thresholds (5% very low, 10% low, 10% moderate for-sale, 100% senior, 10% transitional foster youth, disabled veterans or homeless); affordable units covenanted per state law through an affordable housing agreement (Section 17.140.080). Applies to projects of five or more units including mixed-use.
next_deadline: Not applicable; requested with the planning application.
layering_notes: Local enhancement beyond state law: Director can approve bonuses above 50% and fee deferrals count as incentives. Projects using a density bonus are exempt from Chapter 17.138 inclusionary requirements. Base densities in the City's high-density zones are 24 or more units per acre before bonus, and the Downtown Flexible Density Program (Chapter 17.141) allows small units (150 to 600 sq ft) outside the inclusionary ordinance. Stack with AHF awards and the City impact fee deferral; the County's Regional Housing Incentive Program (Title 22 Section 22.12.010) applies only to unincorporated land. Read on the zoneomics mirror because slocity.org blocks automated access.

program_name: Development services fee waiver and citywide development impact fee deferral loans for affordable units (Housing Element incentives table; Chapter 4.56 impact fee deferral)
administering_agency: City of San Luis Obispo Community Development Department and Finance Department
typical_award_size: Residential projects meeting City affordable housing standards for extremely low, very low and low income households are exempt from all planning, engineering and building review, processing and permit fees and water and sewer meter hook-up fees; mixed-income projects receive the waiver per affordable unit. Citywide development impact fees are deferred (as a deferral loan) for affordable units that exceed the inclusionary minimum or are built, owned and managed by HASLO, other public agencies or nonprofit housing agencies. Example: Bishop Street Studios received an impact fee deferral loan as part of $1,595,500 in City assistance; 2023 HASLO awards for 736 Orcutt and 279 Bridge Street each included a fee deferral loan. HCD's Prohousing release describes the impact fee relief as a waiver for qualifying affordable housing.
affordability_requirement: Deed-restricted affordable units at City Affordable Housing Standards (extremely low, very low, low for the fee exemption; any inclusionary-exceeding or nonprofit or public agency affordable unit for impact fee deferral).
next_deadline: Not applicable; requested with the building permit or through the AHF award resolution.
layering_notes: Local cost-reduction layer that stacks with AHF awards; the City routinely packages an AHF loan plus an impact fee deferral loan in one resolution. Fee exemptions and deferrals are public subsidies and may trigger Labor Code 1720 prevailing wage unless the project already pays it under LIHTC or state funding. The Chapter 4.56 ordinance text and current deferral terms (interest, repayment at permanent loan closing versus residual receipts) could not be opened because slocity.org, codepublishing and the City eScribe agenda host all block automated access; the HCD-hosted 2020 Housing Element incentives table is the source. No comparable county program exists for unincorporated land beyond the Title 22 incentive program.

program_name: Prohousing Designation (HCD, announced January 2024) and Prohousing Incentive Program award
administering_agency: California HCD designation; City of San Luis Obispo Community Development Department administers the incentive funds
typical_award_size: Designation gives City-sponsored or City-located projects extra points in HCD competitive programs (AHSC, IIG, MHP and others). The City received $750,000 from the Prohousing Incentive Program in 2024, deposited to the City Affordable Housing Fund for affordable projects, with final awards to individual projects subject to Council approval. HCD lists the City (and the County, designated October 2025) among designated jurisdictions as of August 10, 2026.
affordability_requirement: Not a direct subsidy; the PIP dollars follow AHF affordability rules (55-year rental, 45-year ownership covenants).
next_deadline: Not applicable; benefit is realized in state NOFA scoring. PIP rounds are announced by HCD (round 2 closed March 15, 2024).
layering_notes: Both the City and the County of San Luis Obispo are Prohousing (county record: Prohousing Designation, October 2025), so any site in the City qualifies for Prohousing bonus points in HCD programs regardless of which agency sponsors. HCD credited the City's hillside program, objective design standards and the waiver of citywide impact fees for affordable housing exceeding inclusionary requirements or built by HASLO, nonprofits or public agencies. The HCD newsroom release and designated-jurisdictions page were opened; the City's own news page about the $750,000 award could not be opened (slocity.org 403).

program_name: Density Bonus (Municipal Code Chapter 21.61; Ord. 1144 N.S., adopted October 1, 2024) and Urban Dwelling Units (Chapter 21.65)
administering_agency: City of El Paso de Robles Community Development Department, Planning Division
typical_award_size: Requirement-based entitlement, not a subsidy. Chapter 21.61 adopts state density bonus law by reference (Government Code 65915 to 65918) with no local enhancement: bonus amounts, incentives and concessions, parking reductions and waivers are as specified in state law and state law prevails over any conflict. Chapter 21.65 implements SB 9 urban dwelling units for individual owners. Both were part of the 2024 comprehensive Zoning Code Update.
affordability_requirement: State thresholds (5% very low, 10% low, 10% moderate for-sale common interest, senior, transitional foster youth, disabled veterans, homeless). Replacement housing requirement of Government Code 65915(c)(3) applies.
next_deadline: Not applicable; requested with the planning application.
layering_notes: Paso Robles has no inclusionary ordinance, no local housing trust fund and no in-lieu fee fund (see separate closed/inactive record), so state density bonus plus fee deferral loans are the only local tools. The 2020-2028 Housing Element Program 10 set a quantified objective of 25 density bonus units. Recent projects: a 79-unit senior low-income development approved February 16, 2021 with fee deferrals, and Highland's Senior Affordable Apartments (30 units, 298 Niblick Road, CEQA notice January 2026) using a density bonus. The County's Regional Housing Incentive Program (Title 22) does not apply inside the City. Read on the zoneomics mirror; prcity.com itself is accessible but municode is blocked.

program_name: Affordable housing fee deferral loans (deferral of development impact, water and sewer connection and building permit fees; Housing Element Programs 8 and 9)
administering_agency: City of El Paso de Robles Community Development Department and City Council (case-by-case resolution)
typical_award_size: Case-by-case Council approval of long-term deferral of City fees, structured as low-interest General Fund loans repaid several years beyond occupancy. Track record: Oak Park Public Housing redevelopment (Paso Robles Housing Authority) phases one through four received fee deferral loans of $1.018 million (2012), $889,000 (2014), $999,423 (2017) and about $1.44 million (2018); a 79-unit senior low-income project at Woodland Plaza II received City fee deferrals in February 2021. News reports (not agency sources) describe a 2026 Council resolution authorizing deferral of water, sewer, development impact and building permit fees for affordable housing, a 30-year deferral of about $1.2 million for Highland's Senior Affordable Apartments (298 Niblick Road), a 30-year deferral of about $1.8 million for Sunrise Villas Apartments, and a roughly 50% impact fee waiver for a nine-unit Habitat for Humanity project on Vine Street. The City also cut development impact fees for studios and one-bedroom units (about $6,226 and $9,343 per unit).
affordability_requirement: Units affordable to lower-income households including extremely low income; 55-year affordability has been required on senior projects receiving deferrals.
next_deadline: unknown, verify with agency. Requests go to Council with the entitlement or before building permit; contact Community Development at (805) 237-3970 or planning@prcity.com. A development services fee update was before the Housing Constraints and Opportunities Committee on February 12, 2026 and then Council.
layering_notes: This is the only City-controlled financial tool in Paso Robles; it substitutes for a housing trust fund. City fee deferrals have been the local match for Paso Robles Housing Authority tax credit deals (Oak Park) and are expected to pair with County Title 29 or Regional Housing Fund awards, HASLO or Paso Robles Housing Authority vouchers, SLO County Housing Trust Fund loans and the Urban County HOME NOFA (county record). The City receives about $165,000 per year of CDBG through the Urban County, which cannot fund new construction or impact fees. The 2026 resolution and project-specific deferrals were found only in local news; the City's eScribe agenda host (pub-pasorobles.escribemeetings.com) renders listings in JavaScript and returns 403 on document downloads, so the HCD-hosted 2020-2028 Housing Element is the agency source. Paso Robles is now preparing its 7th cycle Housing Element (consultant RFP due September 8, 2026).

program_name: Inclusionary housing ordinance and local affordable housing fund (none adopted; Housing Element finding)
administering_agency: City of El Paso de Robles Community Development Department, Housing Programs Division
typical_award_size: None. The 2020-2028 Housing Element states the City of Paso Robles does not have an inclusionary ordinance, and the City holds no inclusionary in-lieu fund, local housing trust fund or RDA successor housing fund for development. The Housing Programs Division's development support is limited to CDBG (about $165,000 per year through the Urban County), applying for County-administered HOME funds, fee deferrals and liaison with the Paso Robles Housing Authority. A November 2025 townhouse proposal offered a voluntary in-lieu payment tied to the County's Title 22 point system for use in a future tax-credit project, which indicates ad hoc negotiated contributions rather than a program.
affordability_requirement: Not applicable.
next_deadline: Not applicable. Watch the 7th cycle Housing Element update (consultant RFP due September 8, 2026) for any inclusionary or impact fee program.
layering_notes: Negative finding recorded so the gap is visible: Paso Robles is the largest North County city and offers no local gap funding beyond fee deferrals. Developers must rely on County Title 29 and the new Regional Housing Fund (county records), HASLO and Paso Robles Housing Authority vouchers, SLO County Housing Trust Fund and state programs. The 2020 Housing Element workshops listed a possible local housing fund (General Fund, TOT, in-lieu fees) as an option but none was adopted. prcity.com pages and the HCD-hosted Housing Element were opened; the 2025 Annual Progress Report could not be located on prcity.com.

program_name: Community Development Block Grant (CDBG) city allocation through the San Luis Obispo Urban County
administering_agency: City of El Paso de Robles Community Development Department, Housing Programs Division (County of San Luis Obispo is lead agency)
typical_award_size: About $165,000 per year to the City. At least 70% must benefit low income persons (80% AMI or below), no more than 15% for public services, up to 30% for blight elimination; projects must complete within about 1.5 years. CDBG cannot pay new housing construction costs or development impact fees; eligible uses include land acquisition for low income housing, street improvements serving low income housing, rehabilitation and public facilities.
affordability_requirement: Beneficiaries at or below 80% of county median income; HOME and CalHome recipients must be low income.
next_deadline: City CDBG requests run on the Urban County Action Plan calendar (2027 Action Plan NOFA applications were due October 30, 2026; next round expected fall 2027). Contact Housing Programs at (805) 237-3970.
layering_notes: The City recommends use of its own CDBG share but the County Board adopts the Action Plan (county record: Urban County Action Plan NOFA). HOME and ESG are not allocated to the City; the City may apply to the County for HOME annually, and County HOME has funded Peoples' Self-Help Housing projects in Paso Robles (Canyon Creek, Creekside Gardens). Useful only for acquisition, site work or rehab components and must be paired with other local or state sources for construction. Davis-Bacon applies.

program_name: Interim Inclusionary Housing Policy (Council policy adopted June 24, 2003, amended November 25, 2003) and inclusionary in-lieu housing fund
administering_agency: City of Atascadero Community Development Department (fund and resale administration by Administrative Services, affordablehousing@atascadero.org)
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Applies only to residential projects needing legislative approval (planned developments, subdivisions, rezones). 20% of units affordable; in multifamily and mixed-use areas split 20% very low, 37% low, 43% moderate (single-family areas 100% moderate). Projects of 1 to 10 units may pay the in-lieu fee or build; 11 or more units must build unless Council approves fees. In-lieu fee equals 5% of the construction valuation of the market-rate units; fractional units up to 0.499 pay fees. Collected fees sit in the City's inclusionary (in-lieu) housing fund, which has helped Peoples' Self-Help Housing (Atalaya Street 24 homes, Triangle parcel 11 units) and Corporation for Better Housing (60 very low and low income units). Housing Element Program 2.C commits the City to adopt a policy for using the in-lieu funds.
affordability_requirement: Deed restriction of 30 years under the policy (County Affordable Housing Standards used for income limits, rents and prices); inclusionary units are treated as density bonus units not counted against maximum density. Projects using the state density bonus and second units are exempt.
next_deadline: Not applicable. The 2022 EPS nexus study recommended replacing the policy with a citywide affordable housing impact fee (nexus-justified maximum $38.71 to $75 per sq ft, adopted fee to be set well below) and lowering inclusionary to 10% to 15% for large discretionary projects; no ordinance had been adopted as of the pages read.
layering_notes: Still an interim policy more than 20 years on; it only reaches discretionary legislative projects, so most by-right multifamily pays nothing. A 100% affordable LIHTC project is effectively exempt and can request the in-lieu fund as gap money; the fund balance is not published and should be requested from Administrative Services at (805) 470-3428. Pair with the City's impact fee deferral program and state density bonus (separate records), County Title 29 and Regional Housing Fund awards, HASLO vouchers and the Urban County HOME NOFA (Atascadero is a participating city). atascadero.org opens to scripts; the policy PDF, Housing Element and EPS nexus study were read directly.

program_name: Affordable Housing Impact Fee Deferral Program (Municipal Code Section 3-14.070 as amended by Ord. 666, September 26, 2023, and Council deferral resolution)
administering_agency: City of Atascadero Community Development Department and Administrative Services
typical_award_size: Development impact fees and wastewater capacity charges, normally due at final inspection, may be deferred under a Council-approved agreement for residential units affordable to low, very low or extremely low income households. Staff reports and local coverage describe the program as a 17-year interest-bearing deferral loan for projects with five or more affordable rental units, with up to about $3 million in fees eligible; the City cites multifamily impact fees of roughly $12,000 to $15,000 per unit. Intended to improve TCAC competitiveness by lowering upfront cost.
per_unit_cap: About $12,000 to $15,000 per high-density multifamily unit in impact fees is deferrable, not waived.
affordability_requirement: Units affordable to low, very low and extremely low income households under a recorded agreement; deferral terms set in the agreement approved by Council.
next_deadline: Not applicable; request with the entitlement or before building permit issuance. Contact Community Development at (805) 461-5000.
layering_notes: Deferral, not forgiveness: fees are a City loan repaid over the term, so underwrite as soft debt. Implements Housing Element Program 2.E. EPS advised the City against outright impact fee waivers for fiscal reasons, so a waiver is unlikely. Stacks with state density bonus (Article 30), the inclusionary in-lieu fund, County Title 29 or Regional Housing Fund, HASLO vouchers and Urban County HOME. The ordinance text was read on the ecode360 code mirror (atascadero.org links to the September 26, 2023 resolution on records.atascadero.org, which returned a scanned PDF with no extractable text).

program_name: Density Bonus (Municipal Code Title 9 Chapter 3 Article 30, Sections 9-3.801 to 9-3.806; Ord. 570, 2013, updated by Ord. 671, June 25, 2024)
administering_agency: City of Atascadero Community Development Department
typical_award_size: Requirement-based entitlement, not a subsidy. Adopts state density bonus law (Government Code 65915 to 65918) by reference: bonus amount, incentives and concessions, parking reductions and development standard waivers as specified in state law; state law prevails over conflicts. No local enhancement beyond state minimums. Market-rate senior projects get the bonus but no other concessions. Projects that use the density bonus are exempt from the City's Interim Inclusionary Housing Policy.
affordability_requirement: State thresholds (5% very low, 10% low, 10% moderate for-sale, 100% senior); replacement housing requirement of Government Code 65915(c)(3) applies.
next_deadline: Not applicable; requested with the planning application.
layering_notes: The 2024 update (Ord. 671) fulfilled Housing Element Program 2.A. Atascadero also adopted objective design standards and SB 330 and SB 9 code changes in 2024 as Housing Element deliverables. The density bonus exempts a project from inclusionary units, so for mixed-income deals the bonus is usually the better path; 100% affordable deals use it for up to 80% bonus and unlimited density near transit under state law. The County's Regional Housing Incentive Program does not apply inside city limits. Read on the zoneomics mirror; the City's March 2023 draft ordinance PDF on atascadero.org was also opened.

program_name: Inclusionary Affordable Housing Requirements (Municipal Code Chapter 16.80; Ord. 595, 2007) and in-lieu fee
administering_agency: City of Arroyo Grande Community Development Department (City Council decides units, fee or land on each project)
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Applies to new residential projects of two or more units, substantial rehabilitation of two or more units and condo conversions. Options: 5% very low income units, or 10% lower income units, or 15% moderate income units (rental or non-common-interest projects), or an equivalent combination; or an in-lieu fee set by Council resolution (the Housing Element reports the fee was raised from 1% to 5%, applied to construction valuation); or land dedication. Projects of two to four units may always pay the fee. Fees go to the Inclusionary Affordable Housing Trust Fund (Sections 16.80.070 and 16.80.080). Through 2020 only two very low income units had been entitled; nearly all applicants paid the fee.
affordability_requirement: Rental units restricted at least 55 years, ownership units at least 45 years, at affordable housing cost per Health and Safety Code 50052.5 and 50053; units dispersed and comparable to market-rate units; affordable housing agreement required before map approval or building permit.
next_deadline: Not applicable; fee paid before the first ministerial permit (grading, demolition or building). Housing Element Program E.1-1 called for amending the requirements and fee within two years of the January 26, 2021 adoption; the fee methodology was still preliminary when the element was adopted.
layering_notes: Low threshold (two units) means almost every multifamily project pays into the trust fund, which is the City's only local gap source (separate record). Chapter 16.80.110 coordinates with the density bonus chapter; inclusionary units can count toward density bonus thresholds. Incentives listed in the Housing Element for inclusionary projects include density bonuses, fee waivers or reductions and modified development standards, but no standing fee waiver ordinance was found. County inclusionary ordinance was repealed in 2022, so this is one of only two active inclusionary programs in the county (with the City of SLO). Read on the zoneomics mirror; arroyogrande.org opens but its housing pages are thin and the eScribe agenda host renders in JavaScript.

program_name: Inclusionary Affordable Housing Trust Fund (In-Lieu Affordable Housing Fund) grants to affordable developments (Housing Element Program C.1-1)
administering_agency: City of Arroyo Grande Community Development Department and City Manager; awards by City Council
typical_award_size: Small fund, awarded by Council to specific projects. Balance of $928,000 as of 2020 per the Housing Element. News reports (not agency sources) state the Council granted $448,370 in July 2023 and a further $630,000 on October 22, 2024 from the Affordable Housing Trust Fund to HASLO's Arroyo Terrace, a 63-unit (reported as 63 to 65 units) 100% affordable project at 700 North Oak Park Boulevard that also received a 2024 TCAC 9% reservation of about $2.2 million in annual federal credits and County Title 29 funds. Housing Element quantified objective: assist three extremely low, three very low and twenty low income units during 2020-2028.
affordability_requirement: Extremely low, very low and low income units with long-term covenants (55 years rental under Chapter 16.80); criteria for allocating the fund were to be adopted under Housing Element Policy C.1.
next_deadline: unknown, verify with agency. No NOFA; requests are made to Community Development and the City Manager during the budget cycle or when a project needs gap funding. Contact (805) 473-5420.
layering_notes: The fund is likely close to depleted after the two HASLO grants (about $1.08 million against a $928,000 2020 balance plus later fees), so treat it as a small top-off source replenished by in-lieu fees. Arroyo Terrace shows the local stack: City trust fund grant, County Title 29 and Urban County HOME or PLHA (county records), HASLO vouchers, SLO County Housing Trust Fund and 9% LIHTC. The City also controls a small CDBG share through the Urban County. The Council staff reports for the 2023 and 2024 grants could not be opened (pub-arroyogrande.escribemeetings.com listings are JavaScript-rendered and documents return 403), so the HCD-hosted 2020-2028 Housing Element is the agency source; confirm the current balance and award history with the City.

program_name: Density Bonuses (Municipal Code Chapter 16.82; Ord. 596, 2007)
administering_agency: City of Arroyo Grande Community Development Department
typical_award_size: Requirement-based entitlement, not a subsidy. Local codification of state density bonus law: one density bonus per project for 10% lower income, 5% very low income, senior housing, qualified mobilehome park or 10% moderate income for-sale units, with specified bonus percentages, incentives and concessions, waivers of development standards, parking incentives and land donation provisions. Section 16.82.130 defers to state law amendments, so the larger bonuses and lower thresholds in current Government Code 65915 apply even though the chapter text dates to 2007.
affordability_requirement: Chapter text requires 30-year affordability for low and very low income bonus units (state law now requires 55 years, which governs); equity sharing for moderate income for-sale units.
next_deadline: Not applicable; requested with the planning application.
layering_notes: No local enhancement beyond state law; the chapter has not been comprehensively updated since 2007 and relies on its state-law amendment clause. Inclusionary units under Chapter 16.80 can be used to qualify for the bonus (Section 16.80.110), which is the main local layering point. Arroyo Grande has no fee waiver ordinance, RDA successor housing fund or NOFA; its tools are the inclusionary trust fund and this chapter, plus County and HASLO resources. Read on the zoneomics mirror.

program_name: Salinas Local Housing Trust Fund (Fund 2603) and Multifamily Housing NOFA gap financing (FY 2025-26 round, Resolution 23358)
administering_agency: City of Salinas Community Development Department, Housing and Community Development Division (City Council sits as the Salinas LHTF Board of Directors)
typical_award_size: The June 24, 2025 Multifamily Housing NOFA offered about $8 million of gap financing; five proposals requested $17,981,000 and four were conditionally committed on November 18, 2025 (Resolution 23358) for $8,460,220: Vista de la Terraza rehabilitation (CHISPA, 40 units) $960,000 (CDBG $400,000, HOME $560,000); Saint George Apartments (CHISPA, 36 senior units) $3,017,699 including $1,432,000 LHTF, $397,000 HOME, $543,699 PLHA and $645,000 PLHA for land; Casentini Street Family Apartments (HACM and Milestone Housing, 88 units plus daycare) $3,837,000 ($570,000 LHTF, $3,267,000 HOME); Republic Cafe (City-owned, Chinatown) $1,290,521 LHTF. The Local Housing Trust Fund was established May 2, 2023; HCD awarded $3,807,248 in January 2024 against a $4,526,562 local match, and the City applied again in September 2024 for $1.5 million with a General Fund match of about $1.5 million. HSA, PLHA and PIP funds supply at least $100,000 a year of ongoing trust fund revenue.
per_unit_cap: None published; awards sized to the gap shown in the applicant pro forma.
affordability_requirement: LHTF-funded units restricted to 60% AMI or below (extremely low, very low and low income) under the City's LHTF program design; federal HOME and CDBG layers carry their own rent and income limits; 55-year covenants used on City loans.
next_deadline: unknown, verify with agency. The FY 2025-26 round closed in 2025 and awards are still being documented (October 20, 2026 update: NEPA clearance and covenants pending; Casentini awaiting a November 2026 tax credit award). The City also keeps an open application for shovel-ready HOME projects and expects a new round once HOME, LHTF and PLHA balances are known; contact Francisco Brambila, Management Analyst, (831) 758-7334 main line.
layering_notes: Largest city-controlled pool in Monterey County. Stacks City HOME, CDBG, LHTF, PLHA and HSA money into one commitment that is then paired with 9% or 4% tax credits (Casentini applied September 8, 2026; Saint George applies after the City commitment). The County's Monterey County Housing Trust Fund (county record) is a separate pool that has not lent inside Salinas; County PLHA is also separate from the City's own PLHA (Salinas is a direct PLHA entitlement, see City PLHA record). The County-owned 855 East Laurel Drive Eden Housing project (county record) is in Salinas and may seek City gap funds in a future round. Blocked: cityofsalinas.org and salinas.gov return 403 to scripts; all material was read from the Salinas Legistar web API and legistar2.granicus.com attachments (staff report of October 20, 2026, Legistar file 26-494, and the September 10, 2024 LHTF staff report, file 24-480).

program_name: Inclusionary Housing Ordinance (Salinas Municipal Code Chapter 17, Sections 17-8 to 17-13), rental housing impact fee, inclusionary housing trust fund and 2026-27 ordinance update (EPS study)
administering_agency: City of Salinas Community Development Department, Housing and Community Development Division
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Current ordinance (2017 amendment and guidelines): on-site inclusionary units apply only to for-sale developments of ten or more units, with three standard options (20% with 4% very low, 8% low, 4% moderate and 4% workforce at 160% AMI; 15% with 6% median, 6% moderate and 3% workforce ownership units; or 12% with 8% very low and 4% low rental units). Rental developments instead pay a per-square-foot rental housing impact fee set by fee resolution and must offer 12% of units to Housing Choice Voucher holders, unless they voluntarily provide affordable units in exchange for a City benefit. For-sale developers may pay a per-square-foot in-lieu fee at building permit. All fees go to the inclusionary housing trust fund. Exemptions include 100% affordable projects with 30-year restrictions and the Downtown (Central City Overlay) exemption added in 2022 (Section 17-8(d)). The City hired Economic and Planning Systems on February 1, 2026 to update the ordinance with a nexus and in-lieu fee study, a Technical Advisory Committee and a cost-recovery review fee; draft ordinance targeted for May 2027.
affordability_requirement: Very low (50% AMI), low (80%), median (100%), moderate (120%) and workforce (160%) tiers depending on option; inclusionary units must be comparable to market units and dispersed; first preference to Salinas residents and workers.
next_deadline: Applies at entitlement; fees due at building permit at the rate in the fee resolution then in effect. Housing and Land Use Committee received the update report October 20, 2026 (file 26-506); TAC outreach runs through spring 2027 and a draft ordinance is expected May 2027. Developers with pending projects should track the Phase 2 Zoning Code Update (mid-2027) as well.
layering_notes: Fee revenue feeds the inclusionary housing trust fund that, with the state LHTF award and HSA money, capitalizes the City's multifamily NOFA (record above). Salinas is the only Monterey County city that charges a rental housing impact fee instead of requiring on-site rental inclusionary units; the County's Chapter 18.40 ordinance (county record) does not apply inside city limits and the County's 2026 move to a fee-based program could influence the Salinas update. Density bonus units are excluded from the inclusionary count (Section 37-50.060). The ordinance text on municode is blocked to scripts; terms above come from the City's 2017 Inclusionary Housing Guidelines PDF (salinasca.prelive.opencities.com) and the October 2026 staff report read through the Salinas Legistar API. Verify current per-square-foot fee amounts in the FY 2026-27 master fee resolution.

program_name: Permanent Local Housing Allocation (PLHA), City of Salinas five-year plan (direct entitlement)
administering_agency: City of Salinas Community Development Department, Housing and Community Development Division
typical_award_size: Standard Agreement with HCD (June 2021) for up to $6,041,082 over the first five years; Fund 2951 Financial Assistance - Multi Family Housing appropriation $3,322,776.95 as of November 2024. Fourth plan amendment (November 19, 2024) set years three to five at 41% to 55% affordable housing development, 14% ADU production in year three, 40% homeownership in years three to five and 5% administration, and allocated $390,000 to CHISPA for three ADUs (138 Carr Avenue, 615 and 617 Fremont Street, rented up to moderate income) and $645,000 to CHISPA for land at 98 Kip Drive for 36 senior units. Earlier uses: Parkside Manor (2021), Fairview (Salinas Inn) Homekey acquisition with HACM ($2,500,000 of PLHA and PIP in 2025, 45 PSH units), SHARE Center homeless services. In January 2026 Council approved a PLHA-funded Mortgage Down Payment Assistance Program (deferred loans up to 150% AMI).
per_unit_cap: None stated; ADU awards averaged $130,000 per unit.
affordability_requirement: PLHA rules: rental development for extremely low to moderate income, ADUs up to moderate income, homeownership up to 150% AMI; City covenants recorded on assisted properties.
next_deadline: unknown, verify with agency. Plan amendments require a 10-day public notice and Council hearing; the 2024-2028 cycle allocations are being programmed alongside the Multifamily NOFA and the down payment program adopted January 27, 2026.
layering_notes: Salinas receives its own PLHA formula allocation and does not share in the County PLHA plan (county record), which covers the unincorporated area plus Carmel-by-the-Sea, Greenfield and Soledad. PLHA pays land and predevelopment costs that HOME cannot (Saint George land $645,000), so it is usually the first City dollar in before a HOME or LHTF commitment. PLHA was also used as the local operating match for the Fairview Homekey PSH site now owned by HACM. Read through the Salinas Legistar API (file 24-570, November 19, 2024) because the City website blocks scripts.

program_name: CDBG, HOME and ESG entitlements, FY 2026-27 Annual Action Plan (PY 2025-2029 Consolidated Plan and Alisal Neighborhood Revitalization Strategy Area)
administering_agency: City of Salinas Community Development Department, Housing and Community Development Division
typical_award_size: FY 2026-27 resources $3,308,936: CDBG $2,196,140 plus $37,000 program income; HOME $844,248 plus $40,000 program income; ESG $191,548. CDBG recommendations: administration $446,628, Habitat for Humanity housing rehabilitation $440,000, Alisal NRSA sidewalks and streetlights $460,000, Chinatown neighborhood improvements $220,000, playground equipment $366,512, ECHO housing rights $100,000, Salinas Outreach and Response Team $200,000. HOME: $669,185 reserved for a shovel-ready affordable housing project (agency to be determined), $126,638 CHDO set-aside, $88,425 administration. ESG: $177,182 rapid rehousing. HOME-ARP $2,918,774 (2023) funds supportive services at Fairview Homekey ($1,190,337 to HACM, February 2026). The City is also the HCD ESG Administrative Entity for the Monterey/San Benito CoC.
per_unit_cap: HOME subsidy limits per HUD; no local cap.
affordability_requirement: HOME and CDBG income limits (80% AMI and below) with HOME rent and period-of-affordability rules; City loans typically carry 55-year covenants.
next_deadline: FY 2026-27 plan: public comment May 2 to June 2, 2026, HLUC May 21, 2026, HUD submittal by August 16, 2026. The FY 2027-28 cycle should open with a NOFA in winter 2026-27; HOME requests for shovel-ready projects are accepted at any time.
layering_notes: Salinas is the only HOME participating jurisdiction in Monterey County besides the Urban County (county record covers unincorporated Monterey plus Gonzales, Greenfield, Marina and Sand City; Salinas is not in it). HOME and CDBG are usually committed through the City's multifamily NOFA (Vista de la Terraza $400,000 CDBG and $560,000 HOME; Casentini $3,267,000 HOME over several years) and require HUD NEPA clearance before covenants are signed. The Alisal NRSA designation (adopted June 17, 2025) relaxes CDBG public benefit rules in East Salinas. Section 108 loan guarantees are listed as a possible future tool. Read through the Salinas Legistar API (file 26-214) and the draft AAP PDF on legistar2.granicus.com.

program_name: Housing Successor Agency (former Salinas Redevelopment Agency) Low and Moderate Income Housing Asset Fund loans
administering_agency: City of Salinas as Housing Successor Agency; Community Development Department, Housing and Community Development Division
typical_award_size: Gap loans from the HSA Affordable Housing fund awarded through the City's annual housing NOFA. Example: $500,000 at 0% for 55 years to Sun Rose Housing, LLC (Interim, Inc.) for the 11-unit Sun Rose Apartments at 439 Soledad Street (8-bed transitional unit plus 9 permanent supportive units), approved December 6, 2022 after an $800,000 construction cost gap; the same site earlier received an $80,000 RDA grant (2000) and $500,000 CDBG (2021). HSA funds are also pledged as part of the $100,000 a year ongoing revenue for the Salinas Local Housing Trust Fund.
affordability_requirement: Very low and low income (HSA law caps use at 80% AMI with at least 30% of expenditures for extremely low income over five-year periods); 55-year deed restrictions on assisted projects.
next_deadline: unknown, verify with agency. HSA funds are offered through the same annual NOFA as HOME, CDBG, LHTF and PLHA (last round opened June 24, 2025); the fund balance is reported in the annual Housing Successor report filed with the Housing Element APR.
layering_notes: The former RDA housing set-aside is the most flexible local layer (no NEPA, 0% long-term loans) and has been used to close inflation gaps on projects that already hold CDBG or HOME. Combine with Monterey County Behavioral Health (MCHOME program) services funding for PSH, and with County HHAP for operating support (county records). Fund balance was not published in the documents opened; confirm with the Housing Division before underwriting. Read through the Salinas Legistar API (file 22-560, December 6, 2022 staff report) because the City website blocks scripts.

program_name: Prohousing Designation and Prohousing Incentive Program (PIP) awards, Fund 2958
administering_agency: City of Salinas Community Development Department, Housing and Community Development Division
typical_award_size: Salinas holds an HCD Prohousing Designation (application authorized November 29, 2022). PIP Round 1 award $1,650,000 funded an Affordable Housing Program and a First Time Homebuyer Down Payment Assistance Program; Rounds 2 and 3 applications (2024) were not funded; Round 4 application for $1,250,000 authorized March 24, 2026 (deadline March 31, 2026) proposing $1,000,000 to rehabilitate the City-owned El Rey Motel (bought with ARPA funds in 2024) as transitional and emergency housing and $250,000 for the Mortgage Down Payment Assistance Program. PIP funds were also matched with PLHA ($2,500,000 combined) for HACM's Fairview Homekey acquisition in 2025.
affordability_requirement: PIP allows rapid rehousing, rental assistance, shelters, new construction, rehabilitation and preservation of permanent and transitional housing, and homeownership assistance up to 150% AMI.
next_deadline: PIP Round 4 award decision pending as of November 2026 (HCD NOFA released September 30, 2025; about $8 million statewide). Designation also gives Salinas scoring bonuses in state programs (AHSC, IIG, MHP) and HCD PLHA flexibility.
layering_notes: The designation is a scoring layer for developers applying to state programs for Salinas sites, and PIP money has been redeployed locally to PSH acquisitions and down payment assistance. Pairs with the City-County MOU to pursue Encampment Resolution Funds Round 5 for the El Rey Motel. No other Monterey County priority city held the designation in the documents opened; Marina submitted a draft application in August 2025 and Soledad states it is pursuing one. Read through the Salinas Legistar API (file 26-111, March 24, 2026 staff report).

program_name: Density bonus (Zoning Code Section 37-50.060) and Zoning Code Update Phase 1 housing law amendments (2026)
administering_agency: City of Salinas Community Development Department, Planning Division
typical_award_size: Requirement and incentive, not a subsidy. Section 37-50.060 implements Government Code 65915 to 65917 with density bonuses, concessions (listed in subsection (k)) and parking reductions for very low, lower and moderate income, senior, day care and land donation projects, and adds a City density bonus for affordable senior housing (a 2014 senior project received a 100% bonus and 29% parking reduction). The Phase 1 Zoning Code Update ordinance (Planning Commission July 15, 2026; Council adoption August 2026, file 26-378) amended the density bonus, employee housing, two-unit development, ADU and emergency shelter provisions to match current state law and Housing Element Programs 4, 6, 7 and 14, and removed covered parking requirements for some residential uses. Phase 2 (objective design standards, General Plan consistency) is due mid-2027 and Phase 3 (new code) by end of 2027.
affordability_requirement: State density bonus law thresholds (5% very low, 10% lower, 10% moderate for-sale, 100% affordable), 55-year rental covenants; affordable rent defined at 30% of 50% AMI (very low) and 30% of 60% AMI (lower).
next_deadline: Not applicable; by-right with the planning application. Watch the Vision Salinas 2040 General Plan draft (summer 2026) and Phase 2 zoning amendments (mid-2027) for new objective standards and West Area and Central Area Specific Plan sites (five tentative maps totaling 3,206 units in process in 2025).
layering_notes: No local trust fund money attaches to the bonus; it is the entitlement layer that is combined with the City's LHTF, HOME, PLHA and HSA loans. Bonus units are excluded when computing inclusionary obligations, and the Downtown inclusionary exemption plus the 2026 SB 423 streamlining (467 and 479 East Market Street hearing September 2025) make Chinatown and downtown the easiest sites. Code text read on the zoneomics mirror because municode and the City site block scripts; the Phase 1 ordinance staff report was read through the Salinas Legistar API.

program_name: CDBG entitlement and PLHA, two-year Notice of Funding Availability FY 2026-27 and FY 2027-28
administering_agency: City of Monterey Community Development Department, Housing Programs (Colton Hall, 570 Pacific Street, (831) 646-3995)
typical_award_size: CDBG entitlement about $250,000 a year ($242,234 in FY 2026-27) plus unusually large program income (estimated $1,023,166 in FY 2026-27; $493,697 from Hotel Pacific loan repayments and English Avenue rents and $729,609 from resale of inclusionary units in 2025), total CDBG resources $1,265,400. FY 2026-27 uses: Affordable Housing Opportunities $940,000 (inclusionary unit acquisition, rehabilitation and resale, minor and major homeowner rehabilitation loans), public services $207,400 (eleven nonprofits including shelters at about $20,000 each), administration $118,000; backup projects include a MidPen project ($1,500,000). PLHA (about $180,952 in 2025) goes to homeless services (PLHA Activity 6) for Gathering for Women, Shuman HeartHouse and Casa de Noche Buena. The two-year NOFA released October 2025 covers public services, public facilities and infrastructure (CDBG) and homeless services (PLHA).
affordability_requirement: CDBG low and moderate income benefit (80% AMI); inclusionary resale units sold to low income first-time buyers; PLHA homeless services for extremely low income households.
next_deadline: The FY 2026-27 and FY 2027-28 NOFA (CDBG and PLHA) was released in late October 2025; FY 2026-27 Action Plan adopted and reduced in June 2026 to match program income. Next two-year NOFA expected fall 2027. Rental Assistance Program (General Fund, $250,000 a year) opens monthly application windows.
layering_notes: The City of Monterey is its own CDBG entitlement and is not in the Monterey Urban County (county record), but it does not receive HOME directly. Its CDBG money is mostly recycled program income used to buy back, repair and resell inclusionary ownership units rather than to fund new multifamily; multifamily developers should instead look at City-donated land (36-unit MidPen project behind City Hall, Van Buren Senior Housing at 669 Van Buren Street) and the $1.5 million MidPen backup line in the Action Plan. Former RDA housing funds built the Monterey Hotel Apartments and the City owns 8 units at Casa de la Estrella. Water allocation is the binding constraint (Housing Element Program 2-J prioritizes affordable projects for new supply). The NOFA flyer PDF link on the City page returned 404; figures come from the FY 2026-27 Annual Action Plan PDF and the 2025 Community Development Department Annual Report, both opened on monterey.gov.

program_name: Inclusionary Housing Program (City Code Section 8-1.00 et seq.), in-lieu fees and inclusionary purchase and resale program
administering_agency: City of Monterey Community Development Department, Housing Programs
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. The City Code (Section 8-1.00 et seq., Ordinance 3346 C.S. of 2004 requiring permanent affordability) requires 20% of units in new residential projects to be affordable, with payment of in-lieu fees allowed; the 2023-2031 Housing Element Program 2-I directs the City to codify the requirement in the Zoning Code. The City holds a first right to repurchase deed-restricted ownership units and resells them to low income buyers using CDBG program income ($729,609 generated from such sales in 2025). Portfolio: 531 restricted units (100 inclusionary ownership, 431 deed-restricted rental) plus 42 in development; 2300 Garden Road delivered 13 inclusionary units in a 91-unit project in 2025.
affordability_requirement: Low and moderate income units with permanent affordability covenants (2004 ordinance); rental inclusionary units monitored by the Housing Office (about 533 deed-restricted units).
next_deadline: Applies at entitlement. Zoning Code codification (Program 2-I) and the density bonus update (Program 2-F, completed by Ordinance 3713 in December 2025) are Housing Element actions due during the 2023-2031 cycle; the Monterey 2031 General Plan update is under way.
layering_notes: Section 38-112.5(G)(4) lets on-site inclusionary units also qualify a project for a state density bonus, but payment of in-lieu fees does not. In-lieu fee amounts and the current fund balance were not in the documents opened; the City's municipal code host (municode) blocks scripts, so the ordinance text itself was not read. Program description comes from the FY 2026-27 Annual Action Plan and the zoning code cross-reference on the zoneomics mirror. Monterey County's Chapter 18.40 (county record) does not apply inside the city.

program_name: Affordable Housing Density Bonus (City Code Section 38-112.5, Ordinance 3713, December 2025) with local density bonuses, and Regional Housing Needs Assessment Overlay District (Ordinance 3688, 2024)
administering_agency: City of Monterey Community Development Department, Planning Division
typical_award_size: Incentive, not a subsidy.
