Section 38-112.5 adopts State Density Bonus Law and adds local bonuses in subsection (J) that are independent of and additional to the state bonus: 10% for consolidating two or more parcels into a lot of at least 0.50 acre; 10% for projects with 70% two- and three-bedroom units (plus one extra story in the Alvarado District and the Pacific, Munras and Cass MF2 overlay); 10% for projects with 40% moderate income units; and 50% for 100% affordable projects under Government Code 65915(b)(1)(G). Rental affordability agreements run 55 years. The RHNA Overlay District (Sections 38-99.9 and 38-99.10) allows multifamily on nonvacant commercial sites carried over from the fourth and fifth cycle inventories, and the Multifamily Residential Overlay sets 60 units per acre.
affordability_requirement: State density bonus thresholds; local bonuses require 40% moderate income or 100% affordable (80% AMI and below with up to 20% moderate) as applicable; 55-year covenants for rental units.
next_deadline: Not applicable; requested with the first planning application on the City form. Coastal zone projects must also meet the Local Coastal Program except for density.
layering_notes: The stackable local bonuses (up to 50% extra for 100% affordable) are the strongest zoning incentive among Monterey County cities and can be combined with the state bonus, inclusionary unit credit and the RHNA overlay sites. No local fee waiver program was found; the City's main constraint is water allocation (Housing Element Program 2-J). Code text read on the zoneomics mirror (Chapter 38, Articles 16E and 17) because the City's municode host blocks scripts.

program_name: Affordable Housing Requirements (Zoning Code Chapter 17.32, 20% inclusionary), in-lieu fund and Campus Town Affordable Housing Agreement
administering_agency: City of Seaside Community Development Department, Planning Division
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Every residential development and condominium conversion must provide at least 20% of units as inclusionary units for moderate, low and very low income households (first third low, second third very low), calculated before any density bonus; equivalents allow one very low unit to count as two moderate units and one low unit as 1.5. Affordability 40 years for rental and for each sale of ownership units. Alternatives (17.32.060): off-site units, land dedication, or any combination of on-site, off-site, in-lieu fees and land dedication equal to the on-site cost. Exemptions: government-built housing, second units, replacement after disaster. The fifth cycle Housing Element reported about $2.6 million in the inclusionary in-lieu fund as of 2017, used for grants to nonprofits. Campus Town (KB Bakewell, Fort Ord, 1,485 units) carries an Affordable Housing Agreement for 225 affordable units (74 very low, 78 low, 73 moderate), equivalent to 350 units, with 161 affordable units in Phase 1 including off-site very low and low income units and land dedicated for a nonprofit rental project.
affordability_requirement: Very low (50% AMI), low (80%) and moderate (120%) households; 40-year covenants; tenants may be drawn from the HACM Section 8 waiting list.
next_deadline: Applies at tentative map, use permit or building permit. Campus Town Phase 1 final map approved and ground broken in 2025; the City bought a 1.62-acre MST parcel in Campus Town in December 2025 and streamlined Campus Town review in February 2026. The 2023-2031 Housing Element (draft May 2023) and Seaside 2040 General Plan were still being finalized in the documents opened.
layering_notes: Seaside's 20% requirement with no ten-unit threshold is the broadest in the county, but the code sets no fee schedule; in-lieu payments are negotiated case by case. The in-lieu fund (about $2.6 million in 2017, about $9 million across two restricted housing funds in 2018 per candidate statements, unverified) plus former RDA successor agency land in the Long Range Property Management Plan are the City's local layers for a nonprofit partner on the Campus Town dedication site or Seaside East. Blocked: ci.seaside.ca.us AgendaCenter is JavaScript-only and the CivicClerk portal only lists meetings from October 2026; code text read on the zoneomics mirror, program history from the fifth cycle Housing Element PDF on hcd.ca.gov. Confirm the current fund balance and any 2024-2026 fee resolution with Planning.

program_name: Affordable Housing Incentives (Zoning Code Chapter 17.33, density bonus)
administering_agency: City of Seaside Community Development Department, Planning Division
typical_award_size: Incentive, not a subsidy. Chapter 17.33 grants density bonuses by Council determination on the state sliding scale (10% lower income units earn 20%, rising to 35% at 20%; 5% very low income units earn a 20% bonus on a parallel scale), with incentives and concessions, reduced parking (17.33.050), child care bonuses (17.33.060), processing rules and a recorded density bonus agreement (17.33.100). Bonus units do not count toward the 20% inclusionary requirement. The fifth cycle Housing Element (Program 13) acknowledged the chapter had not been updated to current state law and committed to do so in the comprehensive zoning update.
affordability_requirement: State density bonus thresholds; affordability terms per Government Code 65915 (55 years rental).
next_deadline: Not applicable; state law controls where the local chapter is less generous. Check for the Seaside 2040 zoning update adoption before relying on local tables.
layering_notes: No local fee waiver, trust fund NOFA or city NOFA was found for Seaside beyond the inclusionary in-lieu fund and CDBG (records above and below). Seaside is a CDBG entitlement city (about $365,000 a year per the fifth cycle Housing Element; FY 2026-27 funding plan adopted March 2026 with about $581,000 including carryover, unverified) and is not in the Urban County. Water connection moratorium relief (Council July 2026) matters more than zoning for multifamily feasibility. Code read on the zoneomics mirror because the City site is JavaScript-only for agendas.

program_name: CDBG entitlement, Inclusionary Housing In-Lieu Fund and Successor Agency properties (Housing Element funding resources)
administering_agency: City of Seaside Community Development Department (Housing and CDBG administration); Successor Agency to the Seaside Redevelopment Agency
typical_award_size: Fifth cycle Housing Element (HCD review draft, March 2020): CDBG entitlement typically about $365,000 a year, allocated annually to public and supportive services and eligible for acquisition, rehabilitation and at-risk unit preservation; Inclusionary Housing In-Lieu Fund balance about $2.6 million as of 2017, historically granted to nonprofit developers to buy existing housing or build new affordable units; Successor Agency Long Range Property Management Plan sites identified for residential and mixed use sale to private developers. Press summaries report a March 2026 Council CDBG funding plan of about $581,000 for FY 2026-27 and an Annual Action Plan to follow HUD's final allocation (not verified on a City page).
affordability_requirement: CDBG 80% AMI benefit; in-lieu fund projects serve very low, low and moderate income households under Chapter 17.32 covenants.
next_deadline: unknown, verify with agency. CDBG public service applications run each winter for the July program year; FY 2026-27 Annual Action Plan had a 30-day review in spring 2026. In-lieu fund awards are ad hoc by Council action.
layering_notes: Seaside controls three small local layers (CDBG entitlement, in-lieu fund, successor agency land) but has no standing NOFA; a developer should approach Community Development with a site on the Campus Town dedication parcel, the North 40 (county land transferred for affordable housing, 2022 work session) or the Parker Flats and 1620 Broadway sites. County HHAP, County Housing Trust Fund and HACM project-based vouchers (county records) are the larger sources. Could not open the City's housing or CDBG pages: ci.seaside.ca.us returns only JavaScript shells for Search and AgendaCenter, the RSS feed is empty, and the CivicClerk API only holds October and November 2026 agendas (no housing items). Figures therefore come from the fifth cycle Housing Element PDF hosted by HCD and need confirmation against the FY 2026-27 Action Plan.

program_name: Inclusionary Housing (Municipal Code Section 17.48.030 as amended by Ordinance 2025-07) and Affordable Housing Trust Fund (Section 17.48.090)
administering_agency: City of Marina Community Development Department, Planning Services Division; City Manager's Office, Housing
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Ordinance 2025-07 (May 20, 2025, implementing Housing Element Program 2.4 with General Plan Amendment Resolution 2025-48) lowered the threshold from 20 to 5 or more units and set a citywide 20% requirement for new or substantially rehabilitated for-sale or rental housing: 6% very low, 7% low, 7% moderate, plus a voluntary incentive-based 10% middle income (up to 135% AMI for-sale) tier; existing occupied housing on the former Fort Ord also 20% (6/7/7), down from 40% (15/15/10). Market-rate density bonus units are exempt. Alternatives approved by Council (17.48.030(D)): land dedication, acquisition and rehabilitation, preservation of at-risk units, conversion of market-rate units, special needs housing, or a tailored program for 500-unit specific plan projects. No in-lieu fee is codified; the Affordable Housing Trust Fund (17.48.090) receives only enforcement recoveries. Rental units restricted 55 years (in perpetuity if allowed), for-sale resale restrictions 45 years, rents capped at 90% of comparable market rent.
affordability_requirement: 20% of units: 6% very low (rent at 30% of 50% AMI), 7% low (30% of 60% AMI rental), 7% moderate (30% of 110% AMI rental); middle income tier voluntary.
eligible_project_types: market-rate rental and for-sale projects of 5 or more units (compliance)
next_deadline: Applies with the first discretionary application (affordable housing plan required). Housing Element objective: 200 lower income units through inclusionary and density bonus by 2031; APR accepted April 1, 2025 reported 93 Dunes BMR units occupied May 1, 2024.
layering_notes: Marina has no in-lieu fee revenue and therefore no local gap fund; its contribution to affordable deals is land and entitlement through specific plans (The Dunes, Sea Haven, Marina Heights, Cypress Knolls each at 20%) and the Affordable Housing Overlay (record below). Marina is in the Monterey Urban County for CDBG and does not receive PLHA directly (county records). Lightfighter Village received a County Housing Trust Fund loan of $500,115 (county record). Ordinance 2025-07 and Resolution 2025-48 were read as PDFs from cityofmarina.org Archive.aspx; the current code text was read on the zoneomics mirror because marina.municipal.codes returns 403.

program_name: Affordable Housing Overlay fee waivers and deferrals (Municipal Code Section 17.48.130, Ordinances 2023-01 and 2023-12) and state density bonus adopted by reference (Section 17.48.040, Ordinance 2023-07)
administering_agency: City of Marina Community Development Department, Planning Services Division
typical_award_size: Projects on Affordable Housing Overlay (AHO) sites mapped for Housing Element opportunity sites receive ministerial administrative approval by the Community Development Director (no hearing), AHO development standards instead of the base zone (42-foot height, 48 feet on Reservation Road and Del Monte Boulevard), and one of three incentives: waived, reduced or deferred planning, plan check or construction permit fees; deferral of City construction and impact fees to completion or occupancy; or payment of construction and impact fees over twelve months or longer after completion. Section 17.48.040 adopts Government Code 65915 to 65918 by reference and caps bonuses, concessions, waivers and parking at the state maximums unless a development agreement provides more. Approvals lapse after two years with a one-year extension.
per_unit_cap: Not applicable; fee relief sized to the project's actual City fees.
affordability_requirement: AHO projects must meet the overlay's affordability requirements (very low and low income emphasis) and the inclusionary ratios in Table 17.48.030-1; density bonus target units restricted 30 years (55 years when also counted as inclusionary units).
next_deadline: Not applicable; ministerial on AHO-mapped sites. Housing Element Program 2.3 committed the City to evaluate its incentives by end of 2024 and strengthen them by end of 2026 if 200 lower income units are not on track.
layering_notes: The AHO is the only fee relief program found among Monterey County priority cities and was cited in Marina's August 2025 Prohousing Designation application (Enhancement Category 3). Fee deferral to occupancy helps construction-period cash flow on tax credit deals such as Lightfighter Village (EAH and Veterans Transition Center, 71 units) and future Dunes and Downtown Marina AHO sites. It does not waive school, water (Marina Coast Water District) or Fort Ord Reuse Authority successor fees. Code read on the zoneomics mirror (Title 17, Chapter 17.48) because marina.municipal.codes returns 403.

program_name: Below Market Rate housing program and project affordable housing agreements (Lightfighter Village, The Dunes BMR, Sea Haven BMR; BMR Administrative Policies adopted March 1, 2021)
administering_agency: City of Marina City Manager's Office, Housing Program Division
typical_award_size: Program, not a cash subsidy. The City records affordable housing agreements under Section 17.48.080 for each project: Lightfighter Village (Veterans Transition Center and EAH Housing, 229-239 Hayes Circle, 71 permanent supportive units, Resolution 2023-34 of April 4, 2023) must keep 40% of units affordable with at least 15% very low income; the agreement restricts 11 units to 30% AMI and 18 units to 50% AMI at TCAC rents for 55 years and the project is securing 17 project-based vouchers. The Dunes BMR site 1 delivered 93 affordable units (occupancy May 1, 2024) and Sea Haven BMR for-sale homes were sold through a 2023 lottery. Housing Element Program 2.5 reserves 30% of BMR units for Marina workers and residents under the BMR Administrative Policies and Procedures (2021).
affordability_requirement: Project-specific: Lightfighter 30% and 50% AMI for 55 years; BMR ownership units resale-restricted 45 years; rental inclusionary units 55 years or perpetual.
next_deadline: Agreements are approved by Council before building permit on each project. Housing Element objective: assist 60 lower income Marina households through the BMR program and facilitate 200 affordable units by 2031.
layering_notes: Marina's role is regulatory and site-based; the money for Lightfighter Village came from County Housing Trust Fund ($500,115), HHAP, state and tax credit sources (county records), and the City contributed entitlements, the AHO process and the 40% affordability agreement. Marina also submitted a draft Prohousing Designation application in August 2025 (draft read on cityofmarina.org) which, if approved, adds state scoring points for Marina sites; designation status not confirmed. The Housing Element APR for 2024 is posted only as a SharePoint link that could not be opened. Documents read: Resolution 2023-34 with the Lightfighter agreement (Archive ADID 13198), Resolution 2025-18 (ADID 14723), the certified Sixth Cycle Housing Element (DocumentCenter View 13793) and the Housing page (cityofmarina.org/190/Housing).

program_name: Inclusionary Housing (Municipal Code Chapter 17.41, Ordinance 620 of 2005 as amended by Ordinance 757 of 2023), in-lieu housing fee and Affordable Housing Fund (Section 17.41.080)
administering_agency: City of Soledad Community and Economic Development Department; Finance Director administers the Affordable Housing Fund
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Applies to residential projects of five or more lots or units and commercial projects of 2,500 square feet or more; the percentage of affordable units is set by the Housing Element (20% is the figure applied to the Miramonte Specific Plan). Compliance by on-site units, land dedication, in-lieu fees or a combination approved by Council; affordable units built concurrently with market-rate units unless an affordable housing developer takes them under an affordable housing agreement (2023 amendment). The in-lieu fee amount and payment method are set by Council case by case (17.41.070) and deposited in the Affordable Housing Fund (17.41.080), which Council may spend only on affordable housing. Exempt: 100% affordable projects, projects of four or fewer units, public and nonprofit service projects. In June 2025 Council voted 3-2 to revise the 132-unit Miravale agreement to replace moderate income units with in-lieu payments and a parcel contribution (press report, about $25,000 a unit proposed), and a Miramonte Affordable Housing Advisory Subcommittee reviewed the ten-phase Miramonte Affordable Housing Plan on May 20, 2026.
affordability_requirement: Per Housing Element affordability policies; incentives in 17.41.100 and real property dedication in 17.41.090; eligibility screening and anti-overconcentration rules in 17.41.140 and 17.41.150.
next_deadline: Applies at tentative map or permit; obligations due before first certificate of occupancy or final map. Miramonte Affordable Housing Plan expected back to Council in 2026-27; confirm the Miravale in-lieu fee resolution.
layering_notes: Soledad's Affordable Housing Fund will be capitalized by Miravale and Miramonte in-lieu payments and could pair with the County PLHA workforce housing set-aside the City requested (record below) for a moderate income for-sale project. Soledad delegated its PLHA to the County in 2024 and is in the state CDBG non-entitlement program, not the Urban County (county records). Blocked: cityofsoledad.gov timed out or refused every connection and cityofsoledad.com fails TLS; the code was read on the zoneomics mirror and the Miravale and Miramonte actions are known only from press and a meeting-aggregator listing, so confirm with the City Clerk.

program_name: Density Bonus (Municipal Code Chapter 17.39, Ordinance 753 of October 4, 2023)
administering_agency: City of Soledad Community and Economic Development Department, Planning
typical_award_size: Incentive, not a subsidy. Chapter 17.39 restates Government Code 65915 to 65918 section by section (state law controls on conflict) for projects with affordable components, child care, senior housing, land donation, 100% affordable, transitional foster youth, disabled veteran or homeless housing and student housing, including the no-minimum-parking rules for lower income rental projects near major transit, senior and special needs projects. No local enhancement beyond state law.
affordability_requirement: State density bonus thresholds and 55-year rental covenants.
next_deadline: Not applicable; by right with the development application. ADU Ordinance 777 (April 1, 2026) and the Housing Element rezonings are the other recent zoning actions.
layering_notes: Soledad has no local trust fund NOFA, fee waiver program or city-run housing NOFA; its tools are the inclusionary Affordable Housing Fund, the County PLHA request and city-owned land (records above and below), plus state non-entitlement CDBG and HOME rounds administered by HCD. Benito Farm Labor Center (HACM) and Senderos transitional housing (14 modular units built with state Encampment Resolution Funds) are the recent affordable projects. Code read on the zoneomics mirror because City hosts were unreachable.

program_name: PLHA delegated to Monterey County and City request for the $1.68 million affordable owner-occupied workforce housing (AOWH) set-aside for a moderate income land purchase
administering_agency: City of Soledad (requesting agency) with Monterey County Housing and Community Development Department (Darby Marshall, Housing Program Manager, (831) 755-5391)
typical_award_size: Soledad delegated its 2019-2023 PLHA allocation to the County in 2024 (with Carmel-by-the-Sea and Greenfield, adding about $1.74 million to the County plan). On March 16, 2026 the County Health, Housing, Homelessness and Human Services Committee considered Soledad's request to use the County's reserved AOWH funds, about $1,680,063, to buy land in Soledad for homes sold to moderate income households under a 45-year resale restriction, with the City selecting a developer; staff would amend the County PLHA plan with HCD and memorialize the City's obligations. The City receives RHNA credit for the units.
affordability_requirement: Moderate income (up to 120% AMI) owner-occupied units with 45-year deed and resale restrictions under PLHA AOWH rules.
next_deadline: unknown, verify with agency. Committee recommendation to the Board of Supervisors was pending in spring 2026; the County's PLHA balance was $1,191,927 in September 2026 (county record) so the AOWH reserve may already be partly committed.
layering_notes: This is a County-controlled dollar (see county PLHA record) directed to a Soledad project; it would pair with Soledad's inclusionary Affordable Housing Fund and a developer's for-sale product in the Miramonte or Miravale areas. Soledad's own 2024-2028 PLHA allocations also flow to the County (about $289,000 a year across the three delegating cities). The Monterey County Housing Trust Fund (county record) has lent in Greenfield and Marina but not yet Soledad. Read through the Monterey County Legistar web API and the staff report PDF (file 26-261) because cityofsoledad.gov could not be reached.

program_name: City land for the Soledad homeless youth housing campus (federal Community Project Funding grant B-22-CP-CA-0157, $2 million) and Prohousing Designation pursuit
administering_agency: City of Soledad with Monterey County Housing and Community Development Department, Housing Authority of the County of Monterey and CHISPA
typical_award_size: The County holds a $2 million HUD Community Project Funding grant (2022, sponsored by Senator Padilla) for a south county housing campus for unhoused parenting youth aged 18 to 24. The City bought a lot next to Vosti Park on Monterey Street with City funds, is demolishing the dilapidated house and remediating the site, and will sell the site to the project using CPF funds; CHISPA will install four to six two-bedroom manufactured homes as permanent supportive housing owned and managed by HACM, with a City, County and HACM services financing plan. Status report to the County 4HS Committee March 26, 2026 (file 26-251). The City's housing web page also states Soledad is pursuing an HCD Prohousing Designation (page not reachable this pass).
per_unit_cap: About $333,000 to $500,000 per unit of CPF grant depending on final unit count.
affordability_requirement: Permanent supportive housing for transition-age parenting youth experiencing homelessness (extremely low income), consistent with CPF grant terms.
next_deadline: Not applicable; single earmarked project. NEPA review and site transfer pending in 2026.
layering_notes: Illustrates Soledad's model: city-owned land plus County-held grants (CPF, HHAP youth set-aside in the county HHAP record) and HACM ownership. The County HHAP-6 plan includes $277,969.56 for a permanent supportive housing project with a city partner with a youth set-aside, which likely attaches to this campus. Prohousing Designation would add state scoring points but was not confirmed because cityofsoledad.gov timed out and refused connections on every attempt (fetch helper, WebFetch and curl). Read through the Monterey County Legistar web API and staff report PDF.

program_name: City of Madera HOME Investment Partnerships (new participating jurisdiction) and CDBG entitlement, 2025-2029 Consolidated Plan
administering_agency: City of Madera Grants Division (Finance), Grants Administrator Marcela Zuniga, (559) 661-3692
typical_award_size: HOME: about $353,555 per year (5-year estimate $1,767,777). The first allocation, in 2024, was $372,065, plus a one-time City match of $127,935, for $500,000. Over 2025-2029 the ConPlan housing goal budgets HOME $1,590,999.90, CDBG $322,982 and PLHA $1,361,913. CDBG: about $989,791 per year. The PY 2027/28 tentative allocation is about $990,000 (up to 20% admin, up to 15% public services, about $643,500 capital).
per_unit_cap: HOME federal per-unit subsidy limits (24 CFR 92.250); no local cap published.
affordability_requirement: HOME rental rules (24 CFR 92.252): HOME rents for households at or below 60% AMI, with 20% of HOME units at 50% AMI in projects with 5 or more units. CDBG must benefit households at or below 80% AMI.
application_cycle: annual NOFA (CDBG application window opens early November; no open developer NOFA found for HOME)
next_deadline: CDBG PY 2027/28 applications opened November 2, 2026 and are due January 29, 2027 by 5:00 p.m. via grantsinfo@madera.gov. No HOME rental NOFA found; request HOME gap funding directly from the Grants Division ahead of tax credit rounds.
layering_notes: Madera became a HOME participating jurisdiction in June 2024, so HOME is now the City's only recurring federal source that can fund new rental construction. The ConPlan lists owner rehab or new affordable housing as HOME uses. The amounts are small (about $354K per year), so the City would likely save several years of HOME for one gap loan, as the City of Merced does. Stack with PLHA (separate record), Housing Authority of the City of Madera project-based vouchers (county record) and 4% or 9% credits. Federal Davis-Bacon wages apply at 12 or more HOME-assisted units. HOME also requires NEPA review, and grants from 2024 on carry Build America Buy America requirements. The CDBG NOFA mostly funds public services and public improvements, but CDBG can pay for acquisition and site work for new housing. Sources read: 2025-2029 Consolidated Plan, PY 2027/28 CDBG Notice of Funding (media-001-us.cdn.govstack.com/madera-003-us/media/guann5xv/notice-of-funding-final.pdf) and the 6th Cycle Housing Element.

program_name: City of Madera Permanent Local Housing Allocation (PLHA), 2019-2023 five-year plan
administering_agency: City of Madera Grants Division (Finance)
typical_award_size: 2022 PLHA award of $1,801,097 (FY 2019, 2020 and 2021 allocations), notified February 15, 2023. The ConPlan lists $1,361,913 remaining for housing. The 2026 Housing Element estimates $1,455,181 available from award years 2021-2023, earmarked for housing construction and rehabilitation.
affordability_requirement: The plan funds affordable rental development or rehabilitation (generally at or below 60% to 80% AMI under HCD PLHA guidelines) and homeless services. The City has not published its own income targets.
application_cycle: rolling (no City NOFA found; Council approves commitments)
next_deadline: unknown, verify with agency. No open City solicitation found as of 2026-11-08. The 2019-2023 plan period has ended, so check whether a new five-year plan has been adopted for later allocations.
layering_notes: The largest uncommitted local pool identified for the City of Madera (about $1.36M to $1.46M). Pair it with City HOME (separate record) to form one local gap layer. Madera County has its own PLHA allocation (county record), so a project in the city could in principle seek both. State-source funds generally count as public funds under Labor Code 1720. The City web page describes only the 2022 application and award; no commitment to a specific project was found this pass.

program_name: Affordable Housing Density Bonus (Madera Municipal Code Chapter 10-3-5.1) with Housing Element incentives: fee reductions (Program B-7), impact fee waivers (MMC 10-8.17) and fee waivers or deferrals (Program A-4)
administering_agency: City of Madera Community Development Department, Planning (Planning Manager David Brletic, (559) 661-5433)
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. The density bonus follows state law; the chapter was amended in February 2025 to track recent state changes, including parking for 100% affordable projects near transit. Program B-7 fee reductions: downtown projects and vacant or aging buildings get up to 100% off Engineering fees and 75% off Planning and Building fees. Non-profit buildings get up to 50%, with building fee reductions capped at $4,000. MMC 10-8.17 lets the Community Development Director approve impact fee adjustments, waivers or exemptions. Program A-4 offers fee waivers and deferrals for affordable projects as technical assistance.
affordability_requirement: State density bonus thresholds (for example 10% lower income or 5% very low income units); 55-year affordability for bonus units.
next_deadline: Available at entitlement, no deadline. The Housing Element commits to local density bonus standards beyond state law by Q1 2028 and to fee reductions for at least 20 qualifying projects by Q3 2026.
layering_notes: Madera has no inclusionary ordinance or in-lieu fund. These fee tools are the only local cost reductions beyond HOME and PLHA. Program B-7 targets downtown revitalization, so it fits best for an affordable rental project downtown. Elsewhere, use the Director's waiver authority in MMC 10-8.17 and ask for a deferral under A-4. A fee waiver is a public subsidy and, depending on its size, can trigger state prevailing wage. The 6th Cycle Housing Element was adopted February 4, 2026. Madera County's density bonus (county record, Chapter 18.114) applies only in unincorporated areas.

program_name: Successor Housing Agency to the former Madera Redevelopment Agency (Low and Moderate Income Housing Asset Fund)
administering_agency: City of Madera as Successor Housing Agency (Resolutions MRA-1498 and CC 12-09)
typical_award_size: Unknown. The City kept the former RDA's housing assets in January 2012, but the latest SB 341 annual reports posted are for FY 2014-15 and FY 2015-16. The FY 2015-16 report is a scanned PDF and its text could not be extracted. No current fund balance found.
affordability_requirement: Housing Asset Fund rules (HSC 34176.1): over each five-year period, at least 30% of development spending must serve extremely low income households and no more than 20% may serve households at 60-80% AMI.
next_deadline: unknown, verify with agency. Ask the City for the latest SB 341 report or the Housing Successor section of the Annual Progress Report.
layering_notes: Recorded so the asset fund is not overlooked. The 2026 Housing Element says losing redevelopment has limited the City's housing work, and it dropped one program for lack of funding, so little uncommitted cash likely remains. Any balance would add a small City layer next to HOME and PLHA. Confirm the fund balance and any housing successor-owned parcels before relying on it.

program_name: Chowchilla state CDBG and HOME small-city grants (non-entitlement applications with Self-Help Enterprises)
administering_agency: City of Chowchilla Community and Economic Development Department, with Self-Help Enterprises as grant writer and program administrator
typical_award_size: CDBG, HOME and CalHome awards of over $2,000,000 combined between 2018 and 2020, for owner rehab, first-time homebuyer and sweat equity programs. A further HOME grant with Self-Help Enterprises was awarded in 2023. Infrastructure goal: at least $120,000 per year to extend water and sewer service to infill housing sites.
per_unit_cap: State HOME and CDBG program limits apply.
affordability_requirement: Households at or below 80% AMI under state CDBG and HOME rules.
application_cycle: annual NOFA (City applies to HCD state CDBG and HOME rounds)
next_deadline: Set by the HCD state CDBG and HOME NOFAs; unknown, verify with agency.
layering_notes: Chowchilla is a non-entitlement city with no local trust fund, inclusionary ordinance, in-lieu fund or city-run NOFA. Its housing money comes from competitive state CDBG and HOME rounds that the City enters with a developer or with Self-Help Enterprises, so a multifamily project would need the City to apply as the sponsoring jurisdiction. Program 2 commits the City to letters of support for AHSC, LHTF, PLHA and HOME applications, expedited processing and possible land write-downs. The Housing Element also says a HUD moratorium stalled the 2018-2020 owner programs. County-level layers: Madera County PLHA and HHAP and the Housing Authority of the City of Madera (county records).

program_name: Housing Density Bonus and Other Incentives (Chowchilla Municipal Code Chapter 18.58) and Housing Element Program 3.e impact fee deferral
administering_agency: City of Chowchilla Community and Economic Development Department
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Chapter 18.58 implements State Density Bonus Law (Gov. Code 65915) with no local enhancements. Program 3.e (adoption targeted for Q1/Q2 2025) would let developers pay a small portion of impact fees at permit and defer the rest for up to 30 years as a recorded note. The note would be due on sale, refinance or loss of affordability.
affordability_requirement: State density bonus thresholds. The deferred fee note becomes due if multifamily rents stop being affordable.
next_deadline: Available at entitlement, no deadline. Program 3.k will amend Chapter 18.58 to match current state law. Confirm whether the Program 3.e fee deferral resolution was adopted.
layering_notes: Chowchilla offers nothing beyond state density bonus law and a proposed fee deferral. The adopted 2024-2032 Housing Element says the City has no inclusionary, affordable housing or other local housing ordinances, and there is no local trust fund, fee waiver fund or NOFA. If adopted, the deferral works like a soft second loan that can sit under tax credit financing. A deferral may count as public funds for prevailing wage purposes. ADU builders can use free pre-approved Cottage Home plans (funded by SB 2). cityofchowchilla.org opened directly; the code was read on the zoneomics mirror.

program_name: City of Merced HOME and CDBG entitlement gap financing (Housing Division, Annual Action Plan and conditional commitment reservations)
administering_agency: City of Merced Development Services Department, Housing Division (Housing Program Supervisor Kimberly Nutt), 678 W. 18th Street, (209) 385-6863
typical_award_size: HOME is about $350,000 per year, with 15% set aside for CHDOs. On April 6, 2026 the City reserved up to $1,756,934 of pooled 2021-2023 HOME (2021 $378,634; 2022 $557,068; 2023 $821,233) for Linc Housing's 54-unit I Street project. PY 2024-2025 HOME of about $886,000 remains. The PY 2026 Annual Action Plan shows $800,355.66 HOME and $1,360,072.38 CDBG available, including $287,991 of HOME carryover.
per_unit_cap: HOME federal per-unit subsidy limits (24 CFR 92.250); no local cap published.
affordability_requirement: HOME rental rules: HOME rents for households at or below 60% AMI, with 20% of HOME units at 50% AMI in projects with 5 or more units. City regulatory agreements run 55 years.
application_cycle: annual NOFA (funding applications in winter, scoring and first public hearing in March, Annual Action Plan adopted May; large rental awards by conditional commitment letter)
next_deadline: The PY 2027 cycle should open in winter 2026-27, with the first public hearing about March 2027; verify dates with the Housing Division. Developers have also been pre-qualified through the City's April 2021 affordable housing developer RFQ.
layering_notes: This is the City's main federal gap source and is usually saved over several years for one tax credit project. The I Street commitment was made to raise Linc's 9% TCAC tiebreaker for the April 7, 2026 round. Linc declined the 2024-2025 HOME because Build America Buy America would have added about $700,000 in material costs. Expect BABA on any new HOME award. Caution: HUD's 2021 environmental monitoring found $700,507 of ineligible CDBG and HOME costs on Gateway Terrace II. In late 2024 the Council weighed voluntary grant reductions of future allocations against repayment from local funds; the outcome was not confirmed this pass. HUD compliance corrections in 2024-2025 also delayed access to grant funds, so allow time for NEPA (AUGF) clearance. Stack with PLHA, Housing Successor land and funds, Fund 1020 (separate records) and Housing Authority of the County of Merced PBVs (county record). Legistar client is 'cityofmerced'; cityofmerced.gov and cityofmerced.org returned Access Denied.

program_name: Merced Housing Successor Agency Low and Moderate Income Housing Asset Fund (Fund 2513) and former RDA housing parcels
administering_agency: City of Merced as Housing Successor to the former Merced Redevelopment Agency (Housing Division; consultant RSG)
typical_award_size: Housing Asset Fund balance was $9,553,758 at June 30, 2025, but most of it is the portfolio of 5 properties and 19 loans receivable ($7,653,072). Unencumbered beginning cash was $2,056,382, with no excess surplus. FY 2024-25 deposits were $147,185 and spending was $316,895, including a $200,000 grant to CC915 Merced for 73 South R Street (extremely low income container units). Staff cited about $1.8M available in January 2025.
affordability_requirement: HSC 34176.1: over each five-year period, at least 30% of development spending for extremely low income (30% AMI) households and no more than 20% for 60-80% AMI. Administration is capped at $382,654 per year.
application_cycle: rolling (Council awards case by case; parcels offered by RFP)
next_deadline: unknown, verify with agency. The FY 2024-25 SB 341 report was received January 2026. The HSA parcels at 1815 and 1823 I Street, 205 and 211 W. 18th Street and 202 W. 19th Street are in escrow with Linc Housing.
layering_notes: This is the only true local cash pool in Merced County found this pass (about $2M liquid). The fund made no development spending in the first five-year compliance period, so new awards should lean toward extremely low income units to meet the proportionality targets. The City has used HSA land as its main contribution (the Linc I Street site and the 73 S. R Street Homekey site), adding PLHA and HOME on top. The 626 W. Main Street RFP involves a former RDA non-housing asset, not this fund. County-level layers are separate (county records).

program_name: City of Merced Affordable Housing Fund (Fund 1020) under the Affordable Housing Fund Policy (Council Resolution 2023-55)
administering_agency: City of Merced Development Services Department, Housing Division, and Finance
typical_award_size: Balance was $881,017 at June 30, 2024. In October 2025 the Council moved $218,000 to cover Housing Division administration, and staff expect more draws for FY 2026-27 administration. The fund was also one option for repaying $700,507 of HUD-disallowed costs (the outcome was not confirmed). Usable balance is likely well under $650,000.
affordability_requirement: Policy eligible uses include predevelopment and development of multifamily rental housing for extremely low to moderate income households (including operating subsidies) and soft costs. Soft costs cover design, water and sewer connection fees, permit and application fees, development impact fees and environmental review.
next_deadline: unknown, verify with agency.
layering_notes: Useful as a local source that can pay or reimburse impact fees and connection fees, which HUD funds cannot easily do; it is the closest thing the City has to a fee waiver fund. It is shrinking because it backfills Housing Division staffing. The revenue source was not confirmed; the scanned Resolution 2023-55 attachment could not be text-extracted. The Housing Element notes advocates commenting on a proposed in-lieu fee by Council resolution, but Merced has no inclusionary ordinance. Confirm whether in-lieu or annexation-related affordable housing payments feed this fund.

program_name: City of Merced Permanent Local Housing Allocation (PLHA), 2019-2023 five-year plan (Resolutions 2021-113 and 2021-114)
administering_agency: City of Merced Housing Division (Fund 2018 Permanent Local Housing)
typical_award_size: About $3,112,314 over 2019-2023. The 2019 carryover ($518,719) and 2020 allocation ($806,250) went to Mercy Village (UPholdings and Self-Help Enterprises, 65 permanent supportive units on Park Avenue). 95% of 2021-2023 (about $1,608,830, including 2021 $887,254 and 2022 $444,694) is committed to Linc Housing's I Street project.
affordability_requirement: 55-year regulatory agreement. In Mercy Village the PLHA-restricted units are 6 at 30% AMI, 5 at 50% AMI and 11 at 60% AMI.
next_deadline: unknown, verify with agency. No new five-year PLHA plan for 2024 and later allocations was found this pass.
layering_notes: All current PLHA is spoken for, so a new project would depend on a future plan amendment or new allocations. The City has used PLHA as a matching layer for Homekey (Mercy Village) and 9% credits (I Street), alongside HOME and Housing Successor land. Merced County's own PLHA (county record) is separate and covers the unincorporated county.

program_name: City of Merced Density Bonus Ordinance (Merced Municipal Code Title 20) and 2024-2032 Housing Element incentives (Programs 2, 6 and 7: fee deferrals, reductions or waivers; 50% senior bonus; UC Merced Student Housing Plan)
administering_agency: City of Merced Development Services Department, Planning Division
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. The ordinance was adopted in 2005 and amended in 2016; it caps the bonus at 35% and lags current state law, which the City commits to fix. The Housing Element commits to: amend the Zoning Code by July 2026 to allow a 50% bonus for senior housing with at least 50% very low income units; offer expedited processing and fee deferrals, reductions or waivers for affordable units on large inventory sites (with extra incentives by July 2028 if needed); scope a UC Merced Student Housing Plan; and require 5% affordable housing plans in annexations around UC Merced.
affordability_requirement: State density bonus thresholds; senior enhancement requires at least 50% very low income units.
next_deadline: Available at entitlement, no deadline. The 6th Cycle Housing Element went to the Planning Commission in April 2026 (Resolution 4181), and Ordinance 2594 (RHNA rezones) had its second reading in July 2026. Verify whether the density bonus update and senior bonus amendment have been adopted.
layering_notes: Merced has no inclusionary ordinance or commercial linkage fee, and the fee deferrals and waivers are Housing Element commitments, not an adopted program. Fund 1020 is the practical way to cover fees today. The UC Merced items are planning commitments, not funding. Merced does not appear to be a Prohousing jurisdiction; the HCD list page returned 404 this pass, so this was not confirmed. The code chapter was not opened directly: zoneomics has Title 20, but the density bonus section was not isolated. The Housing Element was read as a City Legistar attachment.

program_name: Density Bonuses and Other Affordable Housing Incentives (Los Banos Municipal Code Title 9, Chapter 3, Article 34, Sections 9-3.3401 to 9-3.3415) with Housing Element Program 7 fee deferrals
administering_agency: City of Los Banos Community and Economic Development Department, Planning
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Article 34 implements Gov. Code 65915-65918 and adds a commercial development density bonus (9-3.3415), parking modifications and a required density bonus housing agreement. Program 7 offers possible fee waivers, reductions or deferrals until final occupancy, reduced parking, expedited review and city-built off-site improvements as capital projects case by case.
affordability_requirement: State density bonus thresholds; continued affordability per 9-3.3404 and the housing agreement.
next_deadline: Available at entitlement, no deadline. Program 7 committed to revising the ordinance to match state law by the end of 2025 and to adding AB 1287 bonuses; confirm adoption.
layering_notes: Los Banos has no inclusionary ordinance, local trust fund or city-run NOFA for multifamily. Fee deferral until final occupancy is the main local cost tool. The City also reviews impact fees annually to stay competitive. Code was read on the zoneomics mirror; the Housing Plan (September 2025 MJHE version) was read on the MCAG mercedmjhe.com site.

program_name: Los Banos Affordable Housing Projects Developer RFQ (homeless housing, open continuously) with City-owned parcels and PLHA
administering_agency: City of Los Banos Housing Program Division (Housing Program Manager Christy McCammond, (209) 827-7000 ext. 2441)
typical_award_size: No set dollar amount. The City seeks a partner for about 45 to 60 units for people experiencing homelessness. It may convey City-owned parcels or motels to the developer and will co-apply for PLHA (formula and competitive), Encampment Resolution Fund and other state and federal grants.
affordability_requirement: 55-year affordable housing deed restriction. Units must meet HUD HQS so Section 8 vouchers can be used; studios and one-bedroom units with on-site service space.
next_deadline: No deadline; responses reviewed continuously. Qualified respondents go to a pool for later RFPs. Submit by email to christy.mccammond@losbanos.org.
layering_notes: This is the main route into City land and City-sponsored state applications in Los Banos. The City's current PLHA funds operate a second bridge home, so little PLHA is free for capital. Los Banos is not a CDBG entitlement city; it applies to the state CDBG NOFA (code enforcement in 2015, planned 2025 rehab application) and does not fund multifamily development. A related RFP for a joint homeless housing applicant closed April 26, 2024. Merced County CoC CA-520 HHAP and Housing Authority of the County of Merced vouchers (county records) are the other layers.

program_name: Atwater Housing Element Program 7 (Facilitating Affordable Housing Development): density bonus ordinance to be adopted, fee waivers, reductions or deferrals, and city-built off-site improvements
administering_agency: City of Atwater Community Development Department, Planning Division
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. The Housing Element finds the Atwater Zoning Code does not address density bonus and is not in compliance with State Density Bonus Law. The Code was to be amended by January 31, 2026 (end of 2026 in the Program 7 timeline); state law applies directly in the meantime. Incentives: possible fee waivers, reductions or deferrals; expedited review; and off-site improvements (traffic, street, sewer) built by the City as capital projects, case by case.
affordability_requirement: State density bonus thresholds.
next_deadline: Available at entitlement, no deadline. Density bonus ordinance due by end of 2026. A water and sewer priority policy for affordable housing (SB 1087) is due by end of 2026, and the infrastructure fee study and fee schedule update by June 2026; verify status.
layering_notes: Atwater has no local density bonus ordinance yet, and no inclusionary ordinance, trust fund or city NOFA. The goal is entitling at least 100 subsidized units with nonprofit partners during the planning period. The City-built off-site improvements are the most tangible local subsidy and would count as public funds. Source is the July 2026 MJHE version of the Atwater Housing Element on the MCAG mercedmjhe.com site; adoption status not confirmed.

program_name: Atwater PLHA allocation (ADU loans and rental assistance) and state CDBG and HOME grants (non-entitlement)
administering_agency: City of Atwater Community Development Department
typical_award_size: PLHA ADU loans of up to $40,000 per qualified applicant. PLHA mortgage, rent and utility assistance of up to $5,000 per household (up to six months). The City received no CDBG in the 5th cycle but by 2026 had state CDBG and HOME awards for owner-occupied rehab. No multifamily allocation identified.
affordability_requirement: Lower income households under PLHA, CDBG and HOME rules.
application_cycle: annual NOFA (City applies to state CDBG, HOME, CalHome and PLHA; Program 7 commits to annual applications starting 2026)
next_deadline: Set by HCD state NOFAs; unknown, verify with agency.
layering_notes: Atwater's housing money is small and aimed at owners, ADUs and tenants, not multifamily gap financing. A multifamily developer should treat Atwater mainly as a co-applicant for state CDBG or HOME and a source of letters of support. Merced County's surplus land at Castle Commerce Center in Atwater (county record) is the relevant site lead.

program_name: Atwater Housing Successor to the former Atwater Redevelopment Agency (Low and Moderate Income Housing Asset Fund)
administering_agency: City of Atwater as Housing and Non-Housing Successor Agency
typical_award_size: Unknown. The City elected to be the housing successor, but the successor agency page lists only 2012-2015 ROPS and oversight board documents. No current SB 341 report or fund balance was found.
affordability_requirement: Housing Asset Fund rules (HSC 34176.1).
next_deadline: unknown, verify with agency.
layering_notes: Recorded so the asset fund is not missed. The page lists no housing awards or reports, so do not assume any cash. Ask the City for its latest SB 341 report and any housing successor-owned parcels. atwater.org opened directly; a site search for 'housing successor' returned no reports.

program_name: Affordable Housing Development and Substantial Rehabilitation NOFA (HOME, HOME-CHDO and HOME-ARP), City of Fresno PY 2026-2027
administering_agency: City of Fresno Planning and Development Department, Housing and Community Development Division (Housing Finance)
typical_award_size: PY 2026-27 Annual Action Plan programs $2,804,486.73 HOME for affordable development or rehab (entitlement $2,766,057.28 plus $500,000 program income and $229,944 prior year) and a $414,909 HOME CHDO set-aside. Recent awards: $3,000,000 HOME to Sarah's Court II (120 units, 11 HOME units, January 2026). City HOME-ARP allocation was $11.9 million (HOME-ARP supportive services NOFA closed April 13, 2026). Five-year Con Plan years 3 to 5 HOME estimate $8.3 million.
per_unit_cap: HUD HOME maximum per-unit subsidy limits apply; no separate City cap published.
affordability_requirement: HOME rents and incomes (at or below 80% AMI, with HOME rent limits on assisted units); 55-year City regulatory agreement typical for rental loans; priority for projects in areas of opportunity.
next_deadline: 2026-2027 AHD NOFA (PlanetBids No. 2026/12602307) closed August 31, 2026. Next round expected mid-2027 after the PY 2027 Action Plan; verify with HCDD at (559) 621-8300 or HCDD@fresno.gov.
layering_notes: City of Fresno is its own HUD entitlement (CDBG $6.9M, HOME $2.77M, ESG $624K, HOPWA $1.27M in PY 2026) and is not part of the Fresno Urban County, so City projects do not compete in the County HOME/PLHA NOFO and vice versa. The AHD NOFA is separate from the Consolidated NOFA (CDBG, ESG, HOPWA public services and infrastructure, due January 23, 2026). City HOME is usually layered with City PLHA, LHTF and Housing Successor funds and with 4% or 9% LIHTC; HOME triggers Davis-Bacon at 12 or more assisted units and federal NEPA review before choice-limiting actions. Fresno Housing (county record) PBVs and bonds stack on top. The PlanetBids NOFA document itself could not be opened by script; figures come from the City HCD page and the PY 2026-27 Annual Action Plan.

program_name: City of Fresno Local Housing Trust Fund (LHTF), Resolution 2021-201 and Revised Program Guidelines 02
administering_agency: City of Fresno Planning and Development Department, Housing Finance Division
typical_award_size: Dedicated $1,500,000 per year from the City Real Estate Transfer Tax, plus General Fund contributions, Prohousing Incentive Pilot Round 1 ($2,064,891) and State LHTF matching grants (about $8.5 million received to date, including $1,797,373 appropriated January 2026). Recent loans: $5,000,000 Cesar Chavez Apartments (54 units, 2024 commitment) and $3,727,000 The Park at South Stadium (15 LHTF units of 174, approved June 18, 2026; includes $156,800 Housing Successor funds). City applied for PIP Round 4 (up to $2,000,000) to recapitalize the fund.
per_unit_cap: None published; South Stadium works out to about $248,000 per LHTF-restricted unit.
affordability_requirement: Local funds (Guidelines 02) serve households at or below 80% AMI (State match dollars follow State LHTF rules, with at least 30% to extremely low income); 55-year affordability covenants on rental loans. Eviction Protection Program uses are exempt from income verification since July 1, 2025.
next_deadline: LHTF Multi-Family New Construction Affordable Rental Housing NOFA (PlanetBids No. 12601837) released April 24, 2026 and closed May 25, 2026. Next NOFA depends on the FY 2027 transfer-tax allocation and any PIP Round 4 award; verify with Housing@fresno.gov.
layering_notes: One of the few city-controlled flexible local sources in the Central Valley. Loans are 3% simple interest, 55-year, residual receipts, and accept third or fourth lien position behind construction/permanent debt and other public loans, so they fit as gap under 4% LIHTC and tax-exempt bonds. Guidelines 02 were rewritten in 2025 (Resolution 2025-270) and a technical amendment in April 2026 restored multifamily new construction as eligible after it was inadvertently dropped; check the current guidelines before applying. Competes for the same transfer-tax dollars as the Eviction Protection Program. County has no equivalent trust fund (see Fresno County PLHA and HOME records).

program_name: Permanent Local Housing Allocation (PLHA), City of Fresno 2024-2028 Five-Year Plan and PLHA development loans
administering_agency: City of Fresno Planning and Development Department, Housing Finance Division
typical_award_size: Estimated $14,949,413 over 2024-2028 (first allocation $2,391,906, second $2,562,083). 45% of each year to multifamily rental development, 50% to owner-occupied rehab and down payment assistance, 5% admin. Recent award: $1,600,000 PLHA to Helm Lofts (9 restricted units of 98, conditional award February 9, 2026).
per_unit_cap: None published; Helm Lofts was about $178,000 per restricted unit.
affordability_requirement: Rental activity up to 120% AMI under State rules, with a portion of units reserved at or below 60% AMI; 55-year regulatory agreement; loans are low-interest deferred (Helm Lofts: 3% simple, 55-year term).
next_deadline: Last PLHA NOFA ran August 1 to August 29, 2025. The draft 2024-2028 plan had public comment September 21 to October 10, 2026 and a hearing November 5, 2026; Council adoption and the next PLHA NOFA (possibly folded into the AHD NOFA) are pending. Verify with Housing@fresno.gov.
layering_notes: Separate from the Fresno County PLHA (county record covers the unincorporated area and participating cities, not the City of Fresno). The City plan devotes only 45% to rentals, so expect roughly $1.1M per year available for multifamily. PLHA is used as soft gap alongside City HOME and LHTF and with LIHTC; it was also paired with the market-rate-oriented Revolving Loan Fund on Helm Lofts. State PLHA funds count as public funds for prevailing wage purposes.

program_name: Housing Successor to the Redevelopment Agency of the City of Fresno, Low and Moderate Income Housing Asset Fund (LMIHAF) program income and FHS-owned sites
administering_agency: City of Fresno in its capacity as Housing Successor (FHS) and Fresno Revitalization Corporation
typical_award_size: FY 2026-27 budget $4,188,073 (carryover $4,138,073 plus about $50,000 program income); unencumbered and available for development $2,523,599, all restricted to units at or below 30% AMI because FHS exceeded the 20% cap for 60-80% AMI. LMIHAF assets under management $28.9 million; FY 2024-25 ending balance $6,856,360. Historic per-unit contributions range from about $25,000 to $331,000; recent uses include Heritage Estates ($1.2M), B Street ($836,200 encumbered) and 33 E Atchison ($275,000).
affordability_requirement: HSC 34176.1: at least 30% of funds for extremely low income (30% AMI) rentals, no more than 20% for 60-80% AMI, remainder at or below 60% AMI; 55-year covenants for rentals.
next_deadline: No standalone NOFA. Funds and FHS-owned parcels (for example Fulton Street, Chinatown sites) are committed through City NOFAs, RFPs and disposition agreements; FY 2026-27 budget approved June 11, 2026. Contact the Housing Successor (Marlene Murphey, Executive Director).
layering_notes: Small cash pool but useful for deep (30% AMI) targeting and as a match: PLHA allows LMIHAF dollars to be matched into a housing trust account. FHS land is being paired with LHTF, RLF and PRO Housing applications in Downtown and Chinatown (South Stadium used $156,800 FHS plus FHS parcels at 829 and 835 Fulton). Excess surplus test is met (unencumbered $4.08M versus $6.24M threshold at FY 2024-25), so there is no pressure to transfer funds to HCD.

program_name: Downtown and Chinatown Housing Development NOFA, City Revolving Loan Fund (RLF) construction loans
administering_agency: City of Fresno Planning and Development Department
typical_award_size: Construction gap loans of up to $8,000,000 per project from the City Revolving Loan Fund (Round 2 awards: Helm Lofts $8M, Uptown Apartments $8M, The Park at South Stadium $8M). 60-month term, variable rate estimated at 4.81%, secured by deed of trust.
per_unit_cap: None published; awards to date have been a flat $8M regardless of unit count (48 to 174 units).
affordability_requirement: None required for RLF dollars; market-rate projects are eligible (Uptown is 48 market-rate units). Affordability comes from layered sources or Surplus Land Act terms (South Stadium 70 of 174 units restricted to very low and low income for 55 years).
application_cycle: rolling (round-based NOFA, awards on a rolling basis)
next_deadline: Round 2 NOFA (PlanetBids No. 12601560) opened February 13, 2026 and closed April 14, 2026; conditional commitments expire December 31, 2026 unless financing closes. No Round 3 announced as of 2026-11-08.
layering_notes: Short-term construction money, not permanent soft debt: it must be taken out at conversion, so it suits 4% LIHTC or mixed-income deals with a permanent loan sized to repay. Pairs with City PLHA, LHTF and FHS land in the Downtown/Chinatown area, and with the TOD height and density bonus. Source of the RLF capital was not stated in the staff reports reviewed; confirm before relying on it for federal cross-cutters.

program_name: HUD Section 108 Affordable Housing Development Loan Pool (Substantial Amendment 2025-02)
administering_agency: City of Fresno Planning and Development Department, Community Development Division
typical_award_size: $15,000,000 pool (City borrowing capacity $15,494,680) for land acquisition and acquisition of manufactured housing units; no minimum or maximum loan; loans generally forgivable at end of affordability term. City repays HUD over 20 years from future CDBG (estimated 3.94% rate).
per_unit_cap: None; sized to demonstrated financing gap.
affordability_requirement: Nonprofit developers only. At least 51% of units on land acquired with the pool for low and moderate income households (80% AMI), or at least 20% for non-elderly multifamily rental where CDBG share is proportional; 100% LMI for manufactured units; up to 55-year covenants. Borrower must secure outside senior financing and commit up to 10% equity.
next_deadline: Council hearing to adopt Substantial Amendment 2025-02 and authorize the HUD application scheduled November 12, 2026 (ID 26-1506). If approved, a NOFA will be posted on PlanetBids; timing unknown, verify with the Community Development Division.
layering_notes: Land acquisition gap, so it fits early in the stack ahead of LIHTC applications, and can help secure site control for TCAC/CDLAC rounds. CDBG/Section 108 rules apply (Davis-Bacon at 8 or more units for assisted construction, NEPA, URA relocation). Competes with future City CDBG public infrastructure spending because CDBG is pledged for repayment. Separate from the City's earlier $20M Section 108 loan for the Senior Activity Center.

program_name: City-owned and surplus land contributions with conditional City funding commitments (Surplus Land Act RFPs, Land Bank)
administering_agency: City of Fresno Planning and Development Department
typical_award_size: Land at nominal cost plus conditional funding. Examples: Vantage Blackstone senior modular (100 units) gets a 1.21-acre parcel on a 55-year ground lease at $1 per year plus $4,300,000 loan/grant (approved October 22, 2026); Parkview Apartments (98 units, Cesar Chavez Foundation) gets three Parkway Drive parcels plus $10,500,000 conditional commitment (December 2025); Ventura Family Apartments land contribution.
affordability_requirement: Per SLA and Gov. Code 37364 exempt-surplus terms: at least 40% of units at or below 80% AMI with half at or below 50% AMI, regulatory agreement of at least 30 years; recent deals carry 55-year covenants and 30% to 80% AMI targeting.
application_cycle: rolling (site-specific RFPs and SLA notices of availability)
next_deadline: Site by site; Vantage Blackstone commitment expires September 30, 2027 if financing is not secured. Watch City SLA notices and RFPs on PlanetBids.
layering_notes: City land plus a conditional funding resolution is the standard Fresno package for TCAC 4% and HCD MFSN applications (commitments are reissued each round, as with Parkview since 2024). Funding sources behind the commitments vary (CDBG-acquired land on Blackstone carries CDBG national objective requirements). Below-market ground leases count as public subsidy for prevailing wage. The City also adopted a Land Bank program to acquire sites for future reuse.

program_name: Infill Incentive Program development impact fee waiver (FMC Article 12-4.16, Ordinance 2021-029) and Residential BUILD Act waivers
administering_agency: City of Fresno Public Works Department (Traffic and Land Planning), with City Manager approval
typical_award_size: Waives City park, police, fire and street facilities impact fees and reimburses up to 50% of curb, gutter and sidewalk costs. Backfilled from the City budget, first come first served. Cumulative waivers since 2014: $10.19 million across programs ($3.62M Infill Incentive, $659K Residential BUILD). FY 2025 waivers totaled only $45,825 (five single-family homes).
per_unit_cap: Equal to the waived fee amounts; not a fixed cap.
affordability_requirement: None; the waiver is location-based (Infill Opportunity Zone, outside the South Industrial Priority Area, sites up to 6.5 net acres or commercial-to-residential conversions of any size).
next_deadline: The 2025 application form states the waiver is not valid on building permits issued after June 30, 2026 and only when backfill funds exist; extension past that date not confirmed. Verify with Public Works before underwriting.
layering_notes: Market-rate and affordable infill both qualify, so it is not affordable-specific, but it lowers impact fees for downtown and BRT corridor projects that also use the TOD bonus. Applied at certificate of occupancy, not at permit, so the full fee must be carried in the construction budget. Use near zero in FY 2025 suggests limited backfill funding. Fee waivers backfilled with City funds may be public subsidy under Labor Code 1720.

program_name: Affordable housing development impact fee deferral to certificate of occupancy (uncodified Ordinance 2008-51)
administering_agency: City of Fresno Planning and Development Department and Public Works Department
typical_award_size: Defers payment of all adopted City development impact fees (street, water, sewer and others) on qualifying affordable units from building permit to certificate of occupancy. Deferral only, no reduction.
affordability_requirement: Inside the Central Area (bounded by SR 180, 99 and 41): any unit in a development with at least 15% of units restricted; outside the Central Area: restricted units only. Covenants of at least 55 years for rental and 30 years for ownership.
next_deadline: Ongoing; request at building permit.
layering_notes: Construction-period carry savings only; fees are still due before occupancy. Stacks with the Infill Incentive waiver where both apply and with density bonus concessions. Ordinance dates from 2008; confirm current implementation with Public Works since it is uncodified.

program_name: Affordable Housing Density Bonus (FMC Chapter 15, Article 22) with TOD Height and Density Bonus (Article 21) and Housing Element Program 9 by-right approval
administering_agency: City of Fresno Planning and Development Department
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Article 22 implements Gov. Code 65915 for projects of 5 or more units (State law governs on conflict). Article 21 adds a discretionary TOD bonus of up to 100% more density and 25% more height in MX or CMS districts within 500 feet of a BRT station or half mile of Manchester Transit Center, combinable with the affordable bonus. Program 9 text amendment (P26-01326, 2026) makes projects with at least 20% lower-income units by-right on reused housing element sites.
affordability_requirement: State density bonus thresholds (e.g., 5% very low or 10% low income for a 20% bonus); covenants per Article 22 (at least 30 years in local text, 55 years under current State law for rentals). Fresno has no inclusionary requirement; FMC 15-2201(E) bars adopting one until the 2014 General Plan is superseded.
next_deadline: Not applicable; applied with entitlements.
layering_notes: Local text predates recent State amendments, so the State statute controls bonus percentages and concessions. TOD stacking is a Fresno-specific advantage on Blackstone and Ventura/Kings Canyon BRT corridors. No density cap on mixed-use zones since 2022. No inclusionary fund exists to tap. Code read on the zoneomics mirror (City code host not used).

program_name: Clovis Affordable Housing Trust Fund (Martinez v. City of Clovis Judgment Action Item 2)
administering_agency: City of Clovis Affordable Housing Program (Planning and Development Services)
typical_award_size: Initial $1,000,000 (FY 2023-24) awarded to a senior housing project in planning; City sets aside $100,000 per year for seven years. City also holds its State PLHA formula allocation and releases it through the same webpage when available.
affordability_requirement: At least 30% of HTF funds requested must assist extremely low income households (below 30% AMI); the rest at or below 80% AMI; deed-restricted units.
next_deadline: No open RFP as of 2026-11-08 (last RFP August 2024). Check the City affordable housing financial incentives page or email housing@clovisca.gov.
layering_notes: Small fund created under the March 2024 court judgment (Martinez v. City of Clovis); about $100K per year is only useful as a local match or to show local support in TCAC scoring. Future MIZO in-lieu fees ($2.80 per square foot) are expected to feed affordable housing gap funding. Clovis is a CDBG entitlement city, but its CDBG goes mainly to home repair, public services and streets. County HOME/PLHA NOFO records cover the urban county; confirm Clovis eligibility with the County before relying on it.

program_name: Clovis Affordable Housing Development Impact Fee Deferral Program (2025-2026 NOFA, Judgment Action Item 6)
administering_agency: City of Clovis Affordable Housing Program
typical_award_size: Defers 40% (80% AMI units), 45% (50% AMI) or 50% (30% AMI) of City major facility sewer and water fees per restricted unit, up to 120 affordable units per fiscal year. Deferred amount becomes a 0% residual receipts loan, 17-year term for multifamily (30 years single-family) or as senior lenders require.
per_unit_cap: Percentage of each unit's major facility sewer and water fees; no dollar cap.
affordability_requirement: Units restricted at or below 80% AMI; recorded development agreement, deed of trust and declaration of restrictions; units must be built after July 1, 2024 and receive certificates of occupancy by December 31, 2031. Units required by MIZO are ineligible.
application_cycle: rolling (first come, first served, annual NOFA)
next_deadline: 2025-26 NOFA dated August 28, 2025 accepts applications year-round until the 120-unit cap is used; a 2026-27 NOFA has not been located. Priority to senior and multifamily projects with site control and entitlements.
layering_notes: Only sewer and water major facility fees are covered; other City impact fees remain due. The residual receipts note sits behind senior and tax credit financing. Clovis states development fees cannot be waived. Pairs with Clovis density bonus and the R-3 density increase to 20 to 30 du/ac.
source_url: https://www.clovisca.gov/documents/Services/Affordable Housing/Housing Settlement/City of Clovis - NOFA - Development Impact Fee Deferral Program - August 28 2025.pdf

program_name: Clovis Mixed Income Zoning Ordinance (MIZO, Ordinance 26-02) inclusionary requirement and in-lieu fee
administering_agency: City of Clovis Planning and Development Services, Affordable Housing Program
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. 5% of units in new residential projects of 11 or more units must be deed-restricted affordable, or pay an in-lieu fee of $2.80 per square foot of net livable area of all market-rate units; alternatives include off-site land dedication, off-site construction and acquisition-rehab.
affordability_requirement: Rental MIZO units: half at 50% AMI, half at 80% AMI, 55-year deed restriction. For-sale: 100% at 80% AMI, 45-year restriction.
next_deadline: Approved by City Council April 13 and 20, 2026; applies to projects not deemed complete before it took effect.
layering_notes: New for Clovis; required by Action Item 5 of the Martinez judgment (Keyser Marston feasibility study, October 2025). In-lieu revenue should grow the Housing Trust Fund over time, a potential future gap source. Affordable developers partnering with market-rate builders on off-site compliance may find site or fee opportunities. MIZO units cannot use the fee deferral program. The adopted ordinance PDF is a scanned image; terms were read from the City MIZO page, FAQ and December 2025 presentation.

program_name: Clovis Affordable Housing Incentives: Density Bonus (Development Code Chapter 9.26)
administering_agency: City of Clovis Planning and Development Services
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Tracks Gov. Code 65915 as amended through Ord. 21-06 (2021): up to 50% bonus (Tables 3-5 and 3-6), 80% and height increases for 100% affordable projects; projects of 5 or more units.
affordability_requirement: State thresholds: 10% lower income, 5% very low income, senior, 10% moderate for-sale, 20% student, or 100% lower income (up to 20% moderate); 55-year restrictions.
next_deadline: Not applicable; applied with entitlements.
layering_notes: No local enhancement beyond State law found in the chapter. Combined with the June 2024 R-3 and High Density Residential minimum density increase to 20.1 du/ac and the infill rezone program under the judgment. City also offers expedited entitlements and a citywide Cottage Home program. Code read on the zoneomics mirror because codepublishing is blocked.

program_name: Reedley Density Bonus and Concessions for Affordable Housing (Zoning Code Section 10.50.050, Ordinance 2024-001)
administering_agency: City of Reedley Community Development Department
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Section 10.50.050 adopts State Density Bonus Law by reference (Gov. Code 65915 as revised), replacing the prior outdated ordinance; no local enhancements.
affordability_requirement: Per Gov. Code 65915 thresholds and 55-year rental restrictions.
next_deadline: Not applicable; applied with entitlements.
layering_notes: Reedley has no local housing trust fund, inclusionary ordinance or in-lieu fund, no city NOFA and no city-controlled HOME or CDBG entitlement. It is a participating city in the Fresno Urban County, so HOME, CDBG and PLHA flow through the County records (County HOME rehab of Reedley Heritage is the model). Housing Element Program 7 also offers a minor deviation process, reduced parking and frontage improvements and streamlined CEQA. reedley.ca.gov failed TLS handshakes to scripts and WebFetch; code read on the zoneomics mirror of the 2024 zoning code.

program_name: Reedley Impact Fee Reduction Incentive Program (Resolutions 2019-009 and 2022-060) and affordable housing fee deferrals (Housing Element Programs 7 and 17)
administering_agency: City of Reedley Community Development Department and City Council
typical_award_size: Location-based reduction of development impact fees: Infill Area 25% below Expansion Area and City Center 50% below. 2022 multifamily fees per unit: $17,569 Expansion Area, $13,177 Infill Area, $8,785 City Center. Housing Element also commits to fee deferrals and case-by-case reductions for affordable and special-needs projects and to reduced water and wastewater connection fees as flexible standards.
per_unit_cap: Equal to the reduction; City Center saves about $8,785 per multifamily unit versus Expansion Area.
affordability_requirement: Area-based reduction has no affordability requirement; deferrals and further reductions are for lower-income and special-needs projects (details not codified).
next_deadline: Housing Element Program 17 called for a fee review with multifamily developers by December 2024 and a revised fee schedule by December 2025; outcome not confirmed.
layering_notes: Source is the City's adopted 2023-2031 Housing Element (Appendix 1L, adopted April 9, 2024, found in substantial compliance by HCD April 24, 2024), not the resolutions themselves. reedley.ca.gov could not be opened (TLS handshake failure), so the current fee schedule and any 2025 fee update were not verified. City Center sites stack the 50% fee reduction with State density bonus and County HOME/PLHA (Urban County) and Fresno Housing PBVs.

program_name: Sanger Density Bonus (Zoning Code Article XXX, Sections 90-1131 to 90-1138, Ordinance 2025-04)
administering_agency: City of Sanger Community Development Department (Planning Division)
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Adopted May 15, 2025 to implement Gov. Code 65915; Table 90-1138 tracks State percentages (20% bonus at 5% very low, up to 50% at 15% very low or 24% low income, 80% for 100% affordable). Reviewed concurrently with other entitlements; approved if State law is met.
affordability_requirement: State thresholds; covenant approved by the City Attorney ensures continued affordability (55 years for rental under State law).
next_deadline: Not applicable; applied with entitlements.
layering_notes: Sanger has no local housing trust fund, inclusionary ordinance or in-lieu fund, and no city NOFA. It is a participating city in the Fresno Urban County (HOME, CDBG, HARP, rental rehab and homebuyer programs run by the County), so gap funding comes from County HOME/PLHA and Fresno Housing PBVs (county records). Housing Element Program 7 targets 100 units through density bonuses. Code read on zoneomics; gocodebook returned 403.

program_name: Sanger affordable housing impact fee deferrals and reductions (Housing Element Programs 7, 15 and 19)
administering_agency: City of Sanger Community Development Department
typical_award_size: Case-by-case deferral or reduction of City development impact and permit fees for affordable, special-needs and farmworker projects, with priority processing on large sites. Baseline City impact fees (2021): about $18,600 per 1,000 sq ft multifamily unit (sewer $2,724, treatment $5,780, collection $1,356, water $1,397, storm drain $2,290, traffic $1,592, recreation $631, police $1,230, fire $1,270, solid waste $330), plus Sanger Unified school fee $4.79 per sq ft.
affordability_requirement: Lower-income, special-needs or farmworker housing; terms negotiated per project (not codified).
next_deadline: Program 19 called for meeting multifamily developers by December 2024 and revising fees by December 2025; Program 15 incentives for large sites by mid-2025. Outcomes not confirmed.
layering_notes: Source is the City's 2023-2031 Housing Element (Appendix 1N, adopted September 5, 2024, found in substantial compliance by HCD October 4, 2024), not a fee resolution. ci.sanger.ca.us opened but no fee deferral policy page or council resolution was found; confirm terms with the Community Development Department. Sanger's prior cycle reports deferrals evaluated case by case (for example Unity Estates expansion).

program_name: Oxnard Inclusionary Housing Program and Affordable Housing In-Lieu Payments (Uncodified Ordinance No. 2980, as amended by Ordinance No. 2999)
administering_agency: City of Oxnard Housing Department (Housing Director) and Community Development Department
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. In-lieu payments are allowed only if City Council grants the request at pre-application. The April 8, 2020 Harris and Associates nexus study proposed per-unit fees of $36,000 (single-family for-sale), $35,000 (multifamily for-sale) and $28,000 (multifamily rental), replacing 2006 fees of $7,000, $5,500 and $7,735; fees are indexed every July 1 since 2021 to the ENR Building Cost Index (Los Angeles). Current indexed schedule not opened.
affordability_requirement: Projects of 10 or more units. For-sale: at least 10% of units sold to lower income (80% AMI) households, affordable units at least 3 bedrooms. Rental: at least 5% very low income (50% AMI) plus 5% lower income (80% AMI), proportional by bedroom size. Covenants of at least 20 years; Oxnard-resident preference list required. Inclusionary units are figured on the pre-bonus unit count and do not count toward density bonus.
next_deadline: Ordinance applies at entitlement; in-lieu fee due per unit at building permit. An update of the Inclusionary Housing Ordinance is underway (discussed at the April 20, 2026 Housing Element and Prohousing workshop, including possible location-based percentages); no adoption date set as of 2026-11-08.
layering_notes: Ordinance 2980 (adopted June 2, 2020) replaced Ordinance 2721; specific plan areas with equal or higher requirements are exempt. Off-site units or land dedication (MAI appraisal) can substitute for the payment with Council approval. Payments go to the City's Affordable Housing Trust Fund (see separate loan record). Projects in the -AHP/-AHD additive zones must provide units and cannot pay in lieu. The 20-year covenant is far shorter than TCAC's 55-year term, so a tax credit deal on the same site carries the longer restriction. Ventura County has no adopted inclusionary ordinance (postponed June 2026), so Oxnard's requirement is local only. Oxnard's Prohousing application was pending as of April 2026. oxnard.gov HTML pages return 403 (Cloudflare) to scripts, but wp-content PDFs open directly.

program_name: Oxnard Affordable Housing In-Lieu Fund (Affordable Housing Trust Fund) developer loans, with Housing Successor and PLHA funds
administering_agency: City of Oxnard Housing Department, Grants Management Division
typical_award_size: In-lieu fund balance about $1.8 million (FY 2026-27 Annual Action Plan, approved May 5, 2026). Used for developer loans that leverage other sources.
