The City also lists Housing Successor Agency funds and Permanent Local Housing Allocation (PLHA) funds as local investment available to projects; amounts not stated.
affordability_requirement: Housing affordable to lower and very low income households (Ordinance 2980 Part 13). Term and income mix set in loan documents; HOME-layered projects follow HOME rules.
next_deadline: No standing NOFA for the in-lieu fund found; local funds are committed alongside the City's annual HUD funding applications. Contact the Housing Department, Grants Management Division.
layering_notes: Small pool relative to Oxnard's pipeline, so it works as gap filler paired with HOME and HOME-ARP (see CDBG/HOME record). The City's HOME match surplus was $21.5 million at September 2025, so local funds are not needed for HOME match. Housing Successor (former Oxnard CDC) LMIHAF funds are subject to SB 341 income proportionality (at least 30% of development spending to 30% AMI); the City's SB 341 report was not located this pass. County-level sources (HTFVC loans, County NOFA) stack on top. The fund balance figure comes from the HUD Action Plan, not a fund statement.

program_name: Oxnard CDBG, HOME, ESG and HOME-ARP entitlement funds (FY 2026-27 Annual Action Plan)
administering_agency: City of Oxnard Housing Department, Grants Management Division
typical_award_size: FY 2026-27: CDBG $2,064,353 plus $445,685.51 carryover ($2,510,038.51); HOME $610,559.44 (less $61,055.94 admin) plus $1,446,538.38 carryover, $1,996,041.88 available for affordable housing development; ESG about $182,351. HOME-ARP conditional loan awards issued to Cypress Place at Garden City Phase II (People's Self-Help Housing, 60 units) and Aspire Apartments (Many Mansions, 88 units, with HOME and CDBG loans).
per_unit_cap: HOME per-unit subsidy limits (24 CFR 92.250) apply.
affordability_requirement: HOME rental units at HOME rents and incomes (80% AMI cap, 20% of units at Low HOME rent in 5+ unit projects); HOME-ARP qualifying populations. City conditions awards on securing all other funding and Council approval.
application_cycle: annual NOFA (HUD grant cycle, fall to winter)
next_deadline: Annual Action Plan adopted each May; FY 2027-28 HUD funding NOFA expected late 2026 or early 2027, unknown, verify with agency.
layering_notes: Oxnard is a direct HUD entitlement for CDBG, HOME and ESG and is outside the Ventura County HOME Consortium, so county HOME is generally not available inside Oxnard. HOME triggers federal Davis-Bacon at 12+ HOME units and CDBG at 8+ units; state prevailing wage may also apply. HOME-ARP is one-time money. Pair with in-lieu fund loans and the Housing Authority of the City of Oxnard (budgeted $36.6 million for HCV in FY 2026-27) for project-based vouchers. Policy H-4.2 allows fee waivers for affordable projects consistent with state law; no standing fee waiver schedule was found.

program_name: Oxnard Density Bonus and Related Incentives and Concessions Program (City Code Chapter 16, Division 7A, Sec. 16-410 et seq.)
administering_agency: City of Oxnard Community Development Department, Planning Division
typical_award_size: Density bonus, incentives, waivers and parking modifications per Gov. Code 65915; no direct funding.
affordability_requirement: Per state density bonus law; rental affordability at least 55 years; affordable housing agreement and equity sharing agreement for for-sale units (Sec. 16-410.19). Units dispersed, phased proportionally and architecturally consistent (Sec. 16-410.17).
next_deadline: Applied with the qualified housing development application.
layering_notes: Local procedural layer on state law (Ord. 2912, 3002, 3035); includes land donation and child care bonuses and a condominium conversion bonus. Inclusionary units are counted on the base count and do not count toward the bonus (Ordinance 2980 Part 15), which is stricter than cities that allow overlap (City of Ventura). Coastal zone projects also need Coastal Act consistency. Read from the zoneomics code mirror because the city's code host blocks scripts.

program_name: Oxnard Affordable Housing Additive Zones, -AHP (by-right) and -AHD (discretionary) (City Code Chapter 16, Division 7C, Ordinance No. 2999)
administering_agency: City of Oxnard Community Development Department, Planning Division
typical_award_size: Zoning entitlement, not a subsidy: adds the right to build multifamily or mixed use at up to 30 units per acre on Housing Element sites; ministerial site plan review in -AHP; lot merger fees waived when merging parcels under 0.5 acre. The FY 2026-27 Action Plan cites an inventory of 2,466 potential units in these zones.
affordability_requirement: At least 20% of units affordable to extremely low, very low or low income households; 55-year rental and 45-year ownership restrictions; no in-lieu payment option; Inclusionary Housing Ordinance also applies; Oxnard-resident preference list.
next_deadline: Available now on designated Housing Element Supplement 1 sites.
layering_notes: Commercial or office space capped at 15% of floor area for by-right treatment. Impact fees still apply (Sec. 16-420D(D)), so fee relief must come from Policy H-4.2 waivers negotiated separately. State density bonus (Division 7A) can be layered for more density. Useful for 100% affordable tax credit projects seeking ministerial certainty on smaller sites.

program_name: Thousand Oaks Affordable Housing Trust Fund (Municipal Code Title 9, Chapter 10, Article 2, Ord. 1506-NS as amended by 1719-NS)
administering_agency: City of Thousand Oaks Community Development Department
typical_award_size: Special revenue fund for very low, lower and moderate income housing, funded by inclusionary in-lieu fees, loan repayments, grants and Council appropriations. Nonresidential linkage fee proceeds go to a separate subaccount, but the linkage fee is set at $0 per square foot (Council direction 2023). Fund balance not published in the documents opened.
affordability_requirement: Units assisted are subject to an Affordable Housing Agreement under Article 6; funds may only be spent within city limits.
next_deadline: No City NOFA found; the 2024 APR says the County administers the City's HOME and PLHA and that developers were expected to request funding in 2025. Contact Community Development (Senior Planner Iain Holt).
layering_notes: Revenue has been thin because the in-lieu fee was set at zero from 2009 until the November 2023 update. The City has used land instead: it donated Hillcrest area land to the Housing Land Trust Ventura County for a 78-unit for-sale townhome project with People's Self-Help Housing, provided City land for a 50-bed navigation center, and partnered with the County on Step Up (77 extremely low income PSH units). A PLHA grant went to HTFVC as Local Housing Trust Fund match in FY 2021-22. For rental gap, look first to the County PLHA plan (which covers Thousand Oaks), the County HOME Consortium and HTFVC.

program_name: Thousand Oaks Inclusionary Housing Program and in-lieu fees (TOMC 9-10.301 et seq., Ordinance 1719-NS effective November 24, 2023; Resolution 2023-056)
administering_agency: City of Thousand Oaks Community Development Department, Planning Division
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Staff-recommended in-lieu fees (September 11, 2023 Planning Commission report): $25.70 per leasable sq ft for apartments, $14.60 per saleable sq ft for townhomes, $16.80 per saleable sq ft for detached homes, indexed annually; adopted by Resolution 2023-056 (resolution text not opened).
affordability_requirement: Projects of 10+ units. Apartments: 10% at low income, covenant 55 years or as long as residential use. Townhome/condo: 10% moderate; detached: 5% moderate, 45-year resale covenant. Off-site option: 15% of units at very low income within 1 mile (or in TCAC moderate or higher resource areas), with overconcentration limits. Land dedication at Council discretion (15% of units at very low income).
next_deadline: In-lieu fee due before first building permit. In-lieu allowed for fractional units, for-sale projects, and rentals of 20 or fewer units; rentals over 20 units only on an extreme hardship finding.
layering_notes: Off-site rental and land dedication options let a market-rate developer partner with a tax credit developer, creating a site or capital source for a 9% or 4% deal. Projects that build inclusionary units on site may request one Gov. Code 65915(d)(2) incentive even without a density bonus (9-10.307). Density bonus units are excluded from the inclusionary count. toaks.gov opens; agenda documents were read from the PrimeGov host (toaks.primegov.com).

program_name: Thousand Oaks Density Bonus Program plus Incentives for Small and Underutilized Parcels and Lot Consolidation (TOMC 9-10 Articles 5, 7 and 8)
administering_agency: City of Thousand Oaks Community Development Department, Planning Division
typical_award_size: State density bonus with local add-ons: small and underutilized parcel projects at 20+ units per acre may request any two extra incentives beyond density bonus incentives (Art. 7); lot consolidation projects get a pre-application with no Planning Division fees and waivers of listed Mixed-Use standards such as ground floor height, retail depth and some setbacks (Art. 8).
affordability_requirement: Density bonus per Gov. Code 65915 with 55-year rental covenants; lot consolidation incentives on MU, MUOZ or R-3 sites outside the sites inventory require 20% of rental units affordable to lower income households.
next_deadline: Applied with the entitlement application.
layering_notes: Council may grant more density than state law (9-10.502(b)), but the code states the City need not provide financial participation such as fee waivers or land. November 2024 zoning amendments (Housing Element Program 8) updated density bonus, lot merger and SB 35 streamlining provisions. Stack with inclusionary compliance and the impact fee deferral program.

program_name: Thousand Oaks Development Impact Fee Deferral Program (temporary Council resolution, October 2023)
administering_agency: City of Thousand Oaks Community Development Department and Finance Department
typical_award_size: Deferral, not a waiver: City development impact fees paid at certificate of occupancy instead of building permit. Dollar value depends on project fee load.
affordability_requirement: Housing Element Program 7 called for fee deferrals for affordable projects; the 2024 APR describes the October 2023 resolution as a citywide temporary deferral in effect until a date uncertain.
next_deadline: In effect as of the 2024 APR (March 25, 2025 Council report); sunset date not set. Confirm it is still in effect before underwriting.
layering_notes: Improves construction-period cash flow and reduces construction loan interest; does not reduce permanent sources needed. School district and non-City fees are not covered. A pure deferral is generally not treated as a public subsidy under Labor Code 1720, but confirm with counsel if paired with other City assistance.

program_name: Thousand Oaks Housing Successor Agency Low and Moderate Income Housing Asset Fund (former Thousand Oaks Redevelopment Agency)
administering_agency: City of Thousand Oaks as Housing Successor (Finance Department)
typical_award_size: Fund balance $845,021 at June 30, 2024; no excess surplus.
affordability_requirement: SB 341 rules: housing for households at or below 80% AMI, at least 30% of development spending to 30% AMI over each five-year period, no more than 20% to 60-80% AMI; homelessness prevention and rapid rehousing allowed within statutory caps.
next_deadline: No NOFA; request through Community Development. FY 2024-25 report expected with the 2025 APR, unknown, verify with agency.
layering_notes: Small pool, best used as predevelopment or a modest gap loan alongside County HOME Consortium and HTFVC funds. Income proportionality pushes spending toward extremely low income units, which aligns with PSH and 30% AMI tax credit set-asides.

program_name: Thousand Oaks CDBG entitlement (HOME and PLHA through Ventura County)
administering_agency: City of Thousand Oaks Community Development Department
typical_award_size: Annual CDBG entitlement from HUD; current dollar figure not shown on the page opened. The City's CDBG Action Plan has been included in the Ventura County HOME Consortium Action Plan since 2020.
affordability_requirement: CDBG low and moderate income national objective (80% AMI).
next_deadline: 2027-28 CDBG applications and comments accepted November 2, 2026 through January 13, 2027 at 5:00 p.m.; needs assessment hearing November 2, 2026.
layering_notes: Mostly public services and rehabilitation; the County Action Plan states Thousand Oaks' priority is preserving existing affordable units through rehab. HOME and PLHA for Thousand Oaks are administered by the County (see County CDBG/HOME and PLHA records), so new construction gap money comes from the County, not the City. CDBG triggers Davis-Bacon at 8+ units.

program_name: Simi Valley Density Bonus, Incentives and Concessions, Waivers (Municipal Code Chapter 9-31)
administering_agency: City of Simi Valley Environmental Services Department, Planning Division
typical_award_size: Density bonus per state law (code table shows 20% to 35% tiers; current state law governs where higher). Council may grant extra density for low and very low income projects with added benefits such as LEED Silver, capped at 45 units per acre (non-age-restricted) and 50 units per acre (senior).
affordability_requirement: Per Gov. Code 65915; units secured by Affordable Housing Agreement (Housing Element Policy HE 3.2).
next_deadline: Applied with the entitlement application.
layering_notes: Code chapter (Ord. 1157, 2010) predates AB 2345 and AB 1287; state law prevails where more generous. The local 45/50 du/ac caps apply only to the discretionary extra-density path. Housing Element Program 8 provides by-right approval for projects with 20% lower income units on reused sites. Read from zoneomics because simivalley.org returns 403 (Akamai) to scripts and WebFetch.

program_name: Simi Valley Affordable Housing Agreements and Local Housing Fund development loans (Housing Element Program 6)
administering_agency: City of Simi Valley Environmental Services Department, Housing Division; Affordable Housing Subcommittee of the City Council
typical_award_size: Negotiated case by case. Track record: $500,000 City development loan to Camino Esperanza (31 senior units, 2015) alongside a $500,000 HTFVC loan; 25 existing Affordable Housing Agreements. Current Local Housing Fund balance not found.
affordability_requirement: Set by Affordable Housing Agreement; priority for projects with extremely low income and disability set-asides. Objective: 200 lower income units in 2021-2029.
next_deadline: No NOFA found. Nonprofit developers get up to two rounds of Affordable Housing Subcommittee review at no fee. Contact the Housing Division; unknown, verify with agency.
layering_notes: No inclusionary ordinance; the Housing Element says the City is exploring one (Program 6). Affordability is negotiated through density bonus and Affordable Housing Agreements. A development agreement amendment for Runkel Canyon (adopted October 2025) reportedly includes an in-lieu affordable housing fee; seen only in a news aggregator, not confirmed. HOME comes through the Ventura County HOME Consortium. Marked needs_confirmation because simivalley.org (pages and showpublisheddocument PDFs) returns 403 and the only City source opened is the 2021 Housing Element on the HCD site.

program_name: Simi Valley CDBG entitlement and Home Rehabilitation Program (HOME through Ventura County Consortium; PLHA)
administering_agency: City of Simi Valley Environmental Services Department, Housing Division
typical_award_size: CDBG entitlement about $640,000 per year (Housing Element); FY 2026-27 estimated at about $650,000 per a March 11, 2026 advisory committee item seen in search results only. PLHA award $290,357 (2020 allocation) for homelessness and PSH uses. Home Rehabilitation Program: deferred 2% loans to income-qualified owners of detached homes (CalHome and HOME).
affordability_requirement: CDBG 80% AMI; PLHA per state guidelines.
next_deadline: FY 2027-28 CDBG application window not confirmed; unknown, verify with agency.
layering_notes: Limited value for multifamily new construction; CDBG goes mainly to public services and rehab. HOME for Simi Valley projects is allocated by the County HOME Consortium (see County CDBG/HOME record). Section 8 is run by the Area Housing Authority of the County of Ventura (676 Simi households in 2019-20). Needs confirmation because City documents could not be opened (403).

program_name: City of Ventura Inclusionary Housing Program and Inclusionary Housing Fund (Municipal Code 24.445.100 to 24.445.180, Ordinance 2025-003)
administering_agency: City of Ventura (San Buenaventura) Community Development Department
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. In-lieu fees per Council fee schedule, indexed annually to Ventura County new home prices and apartment rents (an in-lieu fee update was heard September 10, 2024; schedule not opened because the city site blocks scripts). Fees deposit to the City of San Buenaventura Inclusionary Housing Fund for extremely low to moderate income housing; balance not found.
affordability_requirement: Projects of 7+ units: 10% of for-sale units at moderate income; 15% of rental units (10% low, 5% very low); or 20% if met through acquisition, rehab or preservation. Inclusionary units count toward density bonus eligibility (24.445.030(C)).
next_deadline: Ordinance 2025-003 adopted June 24, 2025, codified August 2025. In-lieu allowed for fractional units, for-sale projects, rentals of 20 or fewer units, and larger rentals on an extreme hardship finding; paid before first building permit.
layering_notes: Replaced the interim program that covered ownership only and the former Merged Redevelopment Project Area 15% rule; now covers rentals citywide. Overlap with density bonus is allowed, which lowers the cost of compliance compared with Oxnard. Off-site units must be rentals for very low income households. Inclusionary Housing Fund money could become a local gap source, but no NOFA or loan program was found. cityofventura.ca.gov and sanbuenaventura.municipal.codes return Cloudflare 403; code read on zoneomics.

program_name: City of Ventura Density Bonus Regulations (Municipal Code 24.445.010 to 24.445.090, Ordinance 2025-003)
administering_agency: City of Ventura Community Development Department
typical_award_size: State density bonus, incentives, waivers and adjusted parking ratios; no local funding.
affordability_requirement: Rental units 55 years minimum; for-sale 45 years; affordable housing agreement required.
next_deadline: Applied concurrently with the entitlement application.
layering_notes: Updated in 2025 to match current state law (the Housing Element had targeted 2023). Coastal zone projects must stay consistent with the certified LCP (24.445.050). The Downtown Specific Plan has its own standards; not reviewed this pass.

program_name: City of Ventura affordable housing fee deferral and partial fee waiver program (Housing Element Program 29)
administering_agency: City of Ventura Community Development Department
typical_award_size: Program called for a fee deferral program and a Director-granted partial fee waiver for 100% affordable projects by the FY 2022-23 budget, plus expedited plan check. Implementation status and amounts not confirmed.
affordability_requirement: Partial waiver limited to all-affordable projects; deferral for affordable housing projects.
next_deadline: Unknown, verify with agency.
layering_notes: Before this program, fee waivers required City Council approval case by case, which was hard to use because housing projects do not otherwise go to Council. Fee waivers are local public funds and can trigger state prevailing wage. Needs confirmation because the city site (Cloudflare) blocked budget and Council documents; only the 2021-2029 Housing Element on the HCD site was opened.

program_name: City of Ventura City-Owned and Publicly Owned Land for Housing and Affordable Housing Overlay (Housing Element Programs 23 and 24)
administering_agency: City of Ventura Community Development Department
typical_award_size: Land disposition or long-term lease of City sites (e.g., parking lots) via development agreements; no dollar figures.
affordability_requirement: Per disposition terms and the Surplus Land Act.
next_deadline: Housing Element targets: identify properties by end of 2023 and study disposition or lease by 2025. Current status unknown, verify with agency.
layering_notes: Ventura is near build-out, so public land is a main site source. The Housing Element also commits to continued funding of Housing Trust Fund Ventura County (Program 13; see County HTFVC record) and to exploring a business or parcel tax for housing. Needs confirmation because the city site blocked access.

program_name: City of Ventura CDBG entitlement and Successor Housing Agency (former San Buenaventura Redevelopment Agency) housing funds
administering_agency: City of Ventura Community Development Department; Successor Housing Agency of the City of San Buenaventura; Housing Authority of the City of San Buenaventura
typical_award_size: CDBG entitlement (FY 2026-27 amount not confirmed; a search snippet of an April 14, 2026 supplemental report cited $722,425 plus $235,182 carryover, not opened). Successor Housing Agency set-aside funds may support preservation of at-risk units; balance not found (SB 341 reports are posted on the blocked city site).
affordability_requirement: CDBG 80% AMI; LMIHAF per SB 341 income proportionality.
next_deadline: Unknown, verify with agency.
layering_notes: Ventura is a CDBG entitlement within the regional Consolidated Plan but is not a member of the County HOME Consortium (Camarillo, Simi Valley, Thousand Oaks), so confirm HOME eligibility with the County. CDBG uses include the Mobile Home Rehabilitation program run by the Housing Authority. The Housing Authority of the City of San Buenaventura (about 1,550 Section 8 households) is the PBV source. Needs confirmation because city documents were blocked; sources opened were the Housing Element and the County FY 2026-27 draft Action Plan.

program_name: Camarillo Density Bonus and Other Incentives, including Commercial Developer Partnership bonus (Municipal Code Chapter 19.49, Ord. 2018, 2024)
administering_agency: City of Camarillo Department of Community Development
typical_award_size: State density bonus; Council may grant more than state law. Commercial developers that partner on affordable housing (partner project at least 30% low income or 15% very low income, in the city and within 1/2 mile of a major transit stop) can get up to 20% more intensity, FAR or height, up to 20% less parking, or other exceptions.
affordability_requirement: Rental units 55 years; for-sale 55-year resale restriction that resets on each sale, with City equity sharing.
next_deadline: Applied at entitlement application.
layering_notes: The commercial partnership path (Gov. Code 65915.7) lets a commercial developer contribute land or cash to an affordable developer, a possible capital source for a tax credit deal. Camarillo has no inclusionary ordinance; Council Policy 7.09 sets guidelines for affordable units in density bonus projects (see separate record). Managed growth limits residential allocations to 400 per year. Camarillo city site opens; code read via zoneomics.

program_name: Camarillo Housing Successor Low and Moderate Income Housing Asset Fund (former Camarillo Community Development Commission)
administering_agency: City of Camarillo as Housing Successor, Department of Community Development
typical_award_size: Fund balance $453,283 at June 30, 2025 ($176,421 cash, $275,000 KDF loan receivable, $1,862 interest); FY 2024-25 deposits $9,131; no excess surplus; no development spending in FY 2024-25.
affordability_requirement: SB 341: 80% AMI or below; at least 30% of development spending to 30% AMI in the July 2024 to June 2029 compliance period; homelessness prevention up to $500,000 per year allowed.
next_deadline: No NOFA; report dated November 17, 2025. Contact Community Development, (805) 388-5360.
layering_notes: Small pool; useful as predevelopment or a local commitment. The City has used City land and tax-exempt bond proceeds for affordable housing: it bought 2800 Barry Street in 2018 and selected the Area Housing Authority with Many Mansions for Vista Campanario (60 rental and 8 for-sale units, tax credits approved September 2022, near completion FY 2024-25). The former CDC exceeded its production obligations by 179 units, so no outstanding obligations.

program_name: Camarillo CDBG entitlement (Affordable Housing Acquisition Program) and PLHA first-time homebuyer revolving loans (FY 2026-27 Annual Action Plan)
administering_agency: City of Camarillo Department of Community Development
typical_award_size: FY 2026-27: CDBG $345,293 estimated plus $49,803.23 prior year, $395,096.23 total; $224,246.23 to the City's Affordable Housing Acquisition Program (buy a home with a General Fund bridge loan and resell to a low or moderate income buyer with a CDBG write-down) and $50,000 to Habitat home repair. PLHA $782,232 used for a first-time homebuyer revolving loan program since FY 2024-25. Temporary Homes Project (six units on City land for homeless individuals) funded with about $610,000 in CDBG.
affordability_requirement: CDBG 80% AMI; homebuyer programs low and moderate income.
next_deadline: FY 2025-26 CAPER review ran August 24 to September 9, 2026; FY 2027-28 application dates unknown, verify with agency.
layering_notes: Not a multifamily gap source; Camarillo's CDBG and PLHA go to ownership and small projects. Multifamily HOME comes through the Ventura County HOME Consortium (Camarillo is a member) and County PLHA/NOFA. The FY 2024-25 acquisition activity was cancelled and moved to Temporary Homes, so confirm the FY 2026-27 activity proceeds. Section 8 by AHACV (576 Camarillo households, November 2025).

program_name: Camarillo Council Policy 7.09 Inclusionary Housing guidelines (no inclusionary ordinance, no local trust fund contribution)
administering_agency: City of Camarillo Department of Community Development
typical_award_size: No inclusionary ordinance, in-lieu fee, local housing trust fund or commercial linkage fee. Affordable units arise only through density bonus and negotiated Affordable Housing Agreements under Council Policy 7.09 (adopted 2006, amended 2015).
affordability_requirement: Design and dispersal guidelines for affordable units in density bonus projects; affordability per Affordable Housing Agreement.
next_deadline: Not applicable. In April 2021 staff recommended against adding an inclusionary program and against a $25,000 per year HTFVC contribution; the Housing Element certified April 14, 2023 did not add one.
layering_notes: Recorded as negative information: Camarillo relies on state density bonus, City land deals and County sources. Developers should not expect a City NOFA. HTFVC and County PLHA/HOME are the main local gap sources for Camarillo deals.

program_name: Ukiah Housing Trust Fund (UHTF) NOFA, funded with PLHA, Prohousing Incentive Pilot (PIP) and housing successor funds
administering_agency: City of Ukiah Community Development Department, Housing Services Division (Housing and Grants Manager, housing@cityofukiah.com, 707-463-6708)
typical_award_size: Most recent round: June 10, 2024 NOFA for about $1,000,000 to acquire infill parcels for affordable housing, combining a $455,000 Prohousing Incentive Pilot award (October 2023) with up to $617,000 of the City's 2019-2022 PLHA allocation. Loans at 0 to 3% simple interest, 55-year term, repaid from residual cash flow after operating costs, senior debt, reserves and deferred developer fee; due on sale or refinance. Commitments last 24 months from Council approval (one-year extension possible). Earlier UHTF capital came from former RDA housing bond proceeds; the 2019 Housing Element notes a $500,000 NOFA in 2018. Acorn Valley Plaza (DANCO, 74 units, opened March 2025) was built with UHTF funds.
per_unit_cap: None published; sized as gap funding after all other sources.
affordability_requirement: Units affordable at or below 60%, 80% or 120% AMI with a recorded 55-year rent or resale covenant; bonus points for units at 0 to 30% AMI. Funding-source rules (PLHA, PIP) add restrictions.
application_cycle: annual NOFA (irregular; issued when state funds are awarded)
next_deadline: unknown, verify with agency. The 2024 round closed July 8, 2024 and no newer NOFA is posted on the Housing Services page as of 2026-11-08. Projects must deploy UHTF funds and start construction within two years of award.
layering_notes: Ukiah is the only priority city in Mendocino County with a standing local trust fund and was the first rural Northern California city with a Prohousing Designation (April 2023), which earns state Prohousing points on AHSC, IIG and similar applications. The 2024 round targeted parcels in TCAC High and Highest Resource areas and favored scattered-site or non-traditional infill. The Housing Element says the fund exists partly to supply local match points for tax credit applications. Stacks with County HOME program income (about $351,767, for example the Marigold Villas request in Ukiah) and the City's own state HOME awards; County PLHA is a separate formula pool. Local public funds trigger state prevailing wage under Labor Code 1720.

program_name: Ukiah Housing Successor Low and Moderate Income Housing Asset Fund (LMIHAF)
administering_agency: City of Ukiah as Housing Successor to the former Ukiah Redevelopment Agency (Housing Services Division)
typical_award_size: Former RDA housing bond proceeds deposited in the LMIHAF and used to seed the Ukiah Housing Trust Fund in 2017. The City Council authorized $500,000 for affordable housing activities in FY 2019-20 (2019 Housing Element). Current balance not published on the City site; check the annual Housing Successor report (Health and Safety Code 34176.1).
affordability_requirement: At least two-thirds of LMIHAF spending must serve households at or below 60% AMI (Mendocino County); eligible uses include rental rehab, acquisition-rehab and new construction.
next_deadline: unknown, verify with agency; funds are offered through Ukiah Housing Trust Fund rounds rather than a separate application.
layering_notes: Treat as part of the UHTF capital stack, not a separate window. Housing successor income targeting (two-thirds at 60% AMI or below) is stricter than the UHTF NOFA's 120% AMI ceiling, so the City will steer LMIHAF dollars to lower-income units. Balance and five-year expenditure deadlines should be confirmed from the City's latest Housing Successor annual report, which was not located on the City site this pass. Source is the adopted 2019-2027 Housing Element hosted by HCD.

program_name: City of Ukiah state HOME and CDBG awards (City as State Recipient), including the Summercreek Village HOME application
administering_agency: City of Ukiah Community Development Department, Housing Services Division
typical_award_size: City applies to HCD as a non-entitlement State Recipient and relends to projects. Track record: $5 million State HOME grant (2018) for Ukiah Senior Apartments; a $5 million HOME application for a 32-unit project (FY 2019-20 budget narrative); 2026 application of up to $5 million in HOME for rehabilitation of DANCO's 64-unit Summercreek Village Apartments (East Gobbi Street: roofs, pool, energy efficiency, parking). CDBG currently funds a Housing Conditions Survey (3,000-plus units) and First Time Homebuyer loans; the owner-occupied Housing Rehabilitation Program has no funding for 2026.
per_unit_cap: HCD HOME per-unit subsidy limits apply; State Recipient multifamily request cap was $4.5 million plus soft and admin costs in the FY24 NOFA.
affordability_requirement: HOME rental units at or below 60% and 80% AMI with 55-year state affordability (20-year federal minimum); CDBG benefits households at or below 80% AMI.
application_cycle: annual NOFA (HCD HOME and CDBG rounds; City sponsors one application per round)
next_deadline: unknown, verify with agency; Summercreek HOME award decision pending as of the January to March 2026 newsletter. Developers must ask the City to sponsor before the HCD HOME deadline.
layering_notes: Federal HOME triggers Davis-Bacon at 12 or more HOME-assisted units, plus state prevailing wage. City-sponsored HOME is distinct from Mendocino County's HOME program income pool, and both can sit in one project. HOME repayments recycle into City program income. City CDBG is not currently used for multifamily construction.

program_name: Ukiah density bonus (Zoning Code Section 9253) and development fee deferral for affordable housing
administering_agency: City of Ukiah Community Development Department, Planning Services
typical_award_size: Incentive, not a subsidy. Section 9253 (Ord. 945, 1993) grants at least the bonus and incentives in Government Code 65915 and lets the City deliver them through Planned Development zoning regardless of parcel size or a Council variance waiving development standards. The 2019 Housing Element reports a fee deferral program for housing developers (water and sewer hookups are the largest fees; typical multifamily fees about $12,500 per unit, 9.5% of development cost) and that affordable developers may receive funding and fee deferrals for infrastructure.
affordability_requirement: State density bonus thresholds (Gov. Code 65915); deed restriction per state law (55 years for rental).
next_deadline: Not applicable; requested with the project application.
layering_notes: Ukiah has no inclusionary ordinance or in-lieu fee; the 2019 Housing Element removed the inclusionary program and the nexus study, relying on the trust fund and by-right zoning instead. The 1993 code text predates recent state amendments, and the zoneomics mirror may lag the current Ukiah City Code (codepublishing.com is blocked to scripts); state law controls where it is more generous. Fee deferral terms were not found in a current resolution, so confirm amounts and timing with Planning (707-463-6268). A deferral of City fees is likely a public subsidy under Labor Code 1720(b)(4) unless repaid at market terms. The County density bonus ordinance (Chapter 20.234) does not apply inside city limits.

program_name: Fort Bragg Inclusionary Housing Requirements and Inclusionary Housing Trust Fund (Coastal LUDC Chapter 17.32 and Inland LUDC Chapter 18.32; Ordinance 1029-2026)
administering_agency: City of Fort Bragg Community Development Department
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Non-subdivision projects of 5 to 10 units (rental or for-sale) must make 20% of units affordable by design; for-sale projects of 11 to 20 units 10% inclusionary and 21 or more units 15%; rental projects over 10 units owe inclusionary units only when they request a density bonus or incentive. Alternatives: land donation, small secondary units (two per inclusionary unit in 11 to 30 lot subdivisions), in-lieu fee set by Council resolution. In-lieu fees and resale equity recapture go to the Inclusionary Housing Trust Fund (17.32.090), restricted to affordable housing acquisition, construction and reimbursement of excess affordable units. Fund balance not published.
affordability_requirement: Rental inclusionary units: half at 80% AMI and half at 120% AMI, with priority for essential public service employees; rental affordability term 25 years. For-sale units: 15-year resale control with equity sharing back to the Housing Trust Fund. Affordable projects restricted at least 15 years are exempt.
next_deadline: Ordinance 1029-2026 (coastal zone amendments to 17.31 and 17.32) passed in September 2026 and takes effect upon California Coastal Commission certification; verify certification date with the City.
layering_notes: A 2023 City Attorney memo notes Fort Bragg's 20% requirement for 5 to 10 unit projects and no requirement for larger rental buildings without a bonus. A November 12, 2024 hearing on an inclusionary in-lieu fee resolution and nexus study is referenced in a City notice, but city.fortbragg.com returned 502 errors and timeouts this pass, so the adopted fee amount was not confirmed. Trust fund money could serve as local gap funding for tax credit projects but no NOFA or award process was found. The County repealed its inclusionary ordinance; Fort Bragg runs its own. Ordinance read from the City's Legistar attachment host (Legistar web API client 'cityfortbragg').

program_name: Fort Bragg Density Bonuses and Affordable Housing Incentives (CLUDC Chapter 17.31, ILUDC 18.31) and Council preliminary pre-approval of inclusionary incentives (17.32.070)
administering_agency: City of Fort Bragg City Council and Community Development Department
typical_award_size: Incentive, not a cash subsidy. State density bonus implemented locally, with a voluntary pre-application step: a developer can ask Council to pre-approve density bonus, incentives and waivers at a public hearing within 90 days, before filing entitlements. Examples: Hazelwood Senior Apartments (49 units, 30 to 60% AMI) received pre-approval on February 24, 2025 for a height incentive (7 feet 8 inches over the 35-foot limit), reduced parking (75 stalls versus 114) and a 9% density bonus; Fort Bragg Apartments (1151 South Main, 83 units with 8 very low income) received pre-approval in November 2024.
affordability_requirement: Per Government Code 65915; regulatory agreement under 17.31.060.
next_deadline: Not applicable; letter of request may be filed any time before the entitlement application.
layering_notes: In the coastal zone every bonus or incentive must also be consistent with the certified LCP and avoid adverse impacts on coastal resources, a constraint beyond state law; Ordinance 1029-2026 updates 17.31 to current state law pending Coastal Commission certification. Pre-approval is non-binding but de-risks tax credit applications. Hazelwood was approved May 2025 but missed 2025 tax credits and planned to reapply in 2026. 1151 South Main is in CEQA litigation after the Coastal Commission denied an appeal.

program_name: City of Fort Bragg state HOME, PLHA and CDBG applications (City as State Recipient), including Hazelwood Senior Apartments HOME request
administering_agency: City of Fort Bragg Economic Development Department (Grants Coordinator)
typical_award_size: May 12, 2025 Council authorized a $4,600,000 FY24 State HOME application ($4,500,000 loan to AMG Associates for Hazelwood Senior Apartments, 49 units at 30 to 60% AMI, $25 million total cost; $50,000 soft costs; $50,000 admin). Repaid HOME loan proceeds stay in the City Housing Trust Fund. PLHA: formula allocation committed to Housing Mendocino Coast (community land trust); 2021 competitive PLHA award with DANCO for the Plateau project; 2024 competitive PLHA considered for homeless services because no development project was ready. The 2025 CDBG application targets sidewalks, not housing; $570,000 of CDBG program income is encumbered for business loans.
per_unit_cap: HCD HOME per-unit limits; FY24 State Recipient cap $4.5 million per multifamily project plus soft and admin costs.
affordability_requirement: HOME: 55-year state affordability for new construction (20-year federal); PLHA competitive rental: at or below 60% AMI for 55 years.
application_cycle: annual NOFA (HCD rounds; City partners with one developer per round)
next_deadline: unknown, verify with agency. HOME award status for Hazelwood not confirmed; 2025 CDBG applications were due April 3, 2026 with awards expected around September 2026.
layering_notes: City sponsorship is the practical path to state HOME for small coastal projects since Fort Bragg is not a HUD participating jurisdiction. HOME triggers Davis-Bacon at 12 or more HOME units. AMG planned 9% tax credits after HOME. County PLHA and HOME program income are separate County pools; Fort Bragg holds its own PLHA formula share. Staff reports were read from the Legistar attachment host because city.fortbragg.com was down.

program_name: Housing Mendocino Coast community land trust partnership (ARPA housing funds and PLHA), 251 S. Franklin Street
administering_agency: City of Fort Bragg City Manager's Office with Housing Mendocino Coast (501(c)(3) community land trust)
typical_award_size: Council obligated $800,000 in ARPA funds to housing (Resolution 4859-2024); about $50,000 went to the Prohousing Designation application. June 22, 2026 staff recommended $350,000 of remaining ARPA housing funds for HMC's acquisition of 251 S. Franklin Street (about 1 acre, 12 to 13 workforce units) and working capital, under an MOU to be drafted in summer 2026. HMC reports about $1.39 million in existing funding. The City previously used SB 2, LEAP, REAP and PLHA funds to form HMC.
affordability_requirement: Households up to 120% AMI; CLT ground lease (typically 99 years) with resale restrictions; possible priority for City employees and local workforce.
next_deadline: MOU and funding documents were to be prepared in summer 2026; ARPA funds must be expended by December 31, 2026 under federal rules, so verify status with the City Manager.
layering_notes: Not a general NOFA; the City routes funds to its incubated CLT. Useful as a land and ownership partner for small workforce projects rather than a gap lender for tax credit rentals. The staff report states $300,000 in the recommendation and $350,000 in the discussion; confirm the final amount. Fort Bragg also references a Prohousing Designation application funded with ARPA; designation status was not confirmed this pass.

program_name: Willits Density Bonus ordinance (Municipal Code Chapter 17.67) and Housing Element affordable housing incentives (Program HE-2C and related)
administering_agency: City of Willits Community Development Department
typical_award_size: Incentive, not a subsidy. Chapter 17.67 (updated September 2018) implements Government Code 65915 for projects of five or more units, with concessions that can include City fee waivers or publicly owned land. The 2019-2027 Housing Element commits to project-by-project fast-track processing, density bonuses, flexible standards, reduced parking, fee subsidies when feasible and fee deferrals for mixed-use projects with affordable multifamily units, plus water allocation priority for lower-income projects (HE-1.G).
affordability_requirement: Per Government Code 65915.
next_deadline: Not applicable. Willits must adopt its 7th cycle Housing Element by 2027.
layering_notes: Willits has no local housing trust fund, no inclusionary ordinance (Program HE-3.D only committed to study feasibility by spring 2020) and no city-run NOFA for multifamily. Fee subsidies and deferrals are discretionary and General Fund dependent; if granted they likely count as public funds for prevailing wage. Multifamily gap money must come from County HOME program income, state programs and tax credits. Code text read from the zoneomics mirror; Housing Element read from the HCD-hosted copy (willits-6th-adopted121719.pdf).

program_name: Willits Owner-Occupied Housing Rehabilitation Program (PLHA and CDBG funded)
administering_agency: City of Willits Community Development Department
typical_award_size: 0% interest deferred loans of $25,000 to $50,000 per home (current application packet), with the program page citing up to $100,000, funded by the City's PLHA allocation; Council authorized a CDBG application in November 2022 for about $554,000 to seed a revolving housing rehabilitation loan program. The City also holds CDBG business loan program income.
per_unit_cap: $50,000 to $100,000 per home depending on source.
affordability_requirement: Owner-occupants at or below 120% AMI (household of four $108,500).
next_deadline: Open intake by appointment with Community Development (707-459-7112); subject to funding availability.
layering_notes: Shows that Willits commits its PLHA formula share to single-family rehab rather than multifamily gap financing, so no city PLHA is available for affordable rental projects. Recorded as negative information for multifamily layering. Developers should look to Mendocino County HOME program income and the Community Development Commission of Mendocino County for project-based vouchers.

program_name: Truckee Inclusionary Housing (Development Code Chapter 18.214) and Affordable Housing In-Lieu Fee (Section 18.210.100; Resolution 2024-65) with dedicated in-lieu fee account
administering_agency: Town of Truckee Community Development Department and Department of Neighborhood Services and Sustainability (Housing)
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. 15% of all new units in residential projects (and subdivisions of seven or more lots) must be affordable, built no later than the market-rate units; density bonus units are excluded from the base. Alternatives: off-site units in the Truckee region, land dedication, purchase of inclusionary credits, or deed-restricting existing units. In-lieu fee by Council resolution with annual update: $136,851 per required affordable unit under Resolution 2024-65 (up from $115,517 under Resolution 2023-63); projects of six or fewer units or lots pay a scaled fee (Exhibit A1) at the developer's option. Larger projects may pay in lieu only if the review authority finds it furthers affordable housing equally or better. Fees go to a separate interest-bearing account and must be used for Town affordable housing programs that create housing in the Truckee region, not studies (Resolution 2024-65 Exhibit A).
affordability_requirement: Ownership inclusionary units: 100% moderate income, or one-third each low, moderate and above moderate. Rental units: 100% low income, or one-third each very low, low and moderate. Affordability controls under Chapter 18.210 with locals preference; in perpetuity per the Town's Housing Resources page.
next_deadline: Fee is reset annually by resolution; a November 2025 staff report reportedly recommended not adopting an update, so confirm the fee in effect for 2026 with the Town before underwriting.
layering_notes: Inclusionary units can receive Homegrown Housing payments only where the project qualifies for the new Chapter 18.213 non-monetary incentives; otherwise required units are ineligible. In-lieu fee revenue supports Town housing programs (Homegrown Housing, THAP, Lease to Locals and similar) rather than a traditional tax credit gap loan NOFA; no Town multifamily NOFA was found. Separate from the Western Nevada County Regional Housing Trust Fund, which Truckee does not belong to (members are the County, Grass Valley and Nevada City). Code text from the October 12, 2023 Article VII PDF on the Town site.

program_name: Truckee Workforce Housing Ordinance for non-residential development (Development Code Chapter 18.216)
administering_agency: Town of Truckee Community Development Department
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy (commercial linkage). Commercial, industrial, institutional, recreational, residential resort and other non-residential projects must build workforce housing for a share of the full-time equivalent employees they generate (Table 7-7; commercial projects of 3,500 square feet or less and industrial of 7,000 square feet or less, or under 7 FTEE, are exempt). Fractions and approved cases may pay the same in-lieu fee ($136,851 per required unit under Resolution 2024-65) or use alternative equivalent actions such as land dedication.
affordability_requirement: Workforce units restricted under Chapter 18.210 affordability controls; occupancy by employees in the Truckee region.
next_deadline: Not applicable. Draft 7th cycle Program H-2.E calls for reviewing the ordinance and an affordable housing credit bank by December 2029.
layering_notes: Creates partnering opportunities: commercial developers needing workforce units can buy inclusionary credits from, or dedicate land to, affordable projects. The Edmunds Lofts site came to the Town through a land dedication by High Altitude Fitness under this ordinance. No county equivalent exists.

program_name: Truckee Homegrown Housing Program, Monetary Incentives (formerly Deed Restriction for New Housing Development)
administering_agency: Town of Truckee Housing Division; program operator Sierra Business Council (info@sierrabusiness.org, 530-582-4800)
typical_award_size: Per-unit payment for a 55-year deed restriction on newly built units, paid at certificate of occupancy after recording: studio $100,000, one bedroom $150,000, two bedroom $225,000 for units restricted to 180% AMI; studio $116,000, one bedroom $174,000, two bedroom $261,000 for units restricted to 120% AMI. Guidelines approved June 23, 2026. Town Council has committed $3,600,000 to deed restriction payments, after moving site-acquisition funds into the program in September 2025.
per_unit_cap: $261,000 per two-bedroom unit at 120% AMI; studios through two bedrooms only.
affordability_requirement: Occupants must work within the Tahoe Truckee Unified School District boundary; household income at or below 180% AMI (rent or price capped at 120% AMI affordability) or at or below 120% AMI (capped at 80% AMI affordability); 55-year non-renewing restriction; no short-term rental; one dedicated parking space per unit.
application_cycle: rolling (first come, subject to available funds)
next_deadline: Open; apply after a complete Planning application. Milestones: building permit application within 9 months of entitlement, permit issued within 18 months, first inspection within 24 months, certificate of occupancy within 30 months, or the award is cancelled.
layering_notes: Designed for missing-middle workforce units, not tax credit deals: projects entitled under State Density Bonus Law are ineligible, and funds cannot be combined with other assistance that imposes an equivalent 55-year income and workforce restriction. Eligible only in VMT Exemption Areas. Payment at C of O means it works as permanent-loan paydown or equity replacement, not construction financing. A January 27, 2026 BAE valuation analysis informed the revised amounts. Town funds count as public funds under Labor Code 1720.

program_name: Truckee Deed-Restricted Housing Incentives (Development Code Chapter 18.213, Ordinance 2026-06) and Density Bonus (Chapter 18.212)
administering_agency: Town of Truckee Community Development Department, Planning Division
typical_award_size: Non-monetary incentives, not a subsidy. Ordinance 2026-06, adopted April 28, 2026 and effective about May 28, 2026, implements 2040 General Plan Action LU-2.B: a Town-specific workforce and affordable housing bonus with streamlined review and flexible design standards for projects with deed-restricted units, with income criteria set by Council resolution. Chapter 18.212 separately implements state density bonus law, including a Development Bonus for Partnered Commercial Projects (18.212.160).
affordability_requirement: Deed-restricted units meeting the Council-adopted income criteria (workforce levels up to 180% AMI under the companion Homegrown program); state density bonus thresholds for Chapter 18.212.
next_deadline: In effect; requested with the Planning application.
layering_notes: Choose one path: projects using State Density Bonus Law cannot take Homegrown payments, while projects using Chapter 18.213 can also draw Homegrown payments, even for their inclusionary units. Draft 7th cycle Program H-3.D adds fee deferrals, land write-downs and incentives beyond state density bonus for acutely and extremely low income, senior and disability housing. The Housing Development Incentives page text says the ordinance was introduced April 7, 2026 with second reading April 28; the Council work plan page reports adoption on April 28, 2026.

program_name: Truckee existing-stock deed restriction programs: Truckee Home Access Program (THAP), Lease to Locals, Rooted Renters and Short-Term Rental Workforce Housing Token pilot
administering_agency: Town of Truckee Housing Division
typical_award_size: THAP pays buyers up to $150,000 (maximum $937,500 purchase price), sellers and local businesses for permanent workforce deed restrictions on homes (cap 245% AMI). Lease to Locals pays owners up to $18,000 to convert homes to long-term local rentals; Rooted Renters pays up to $26,000 to lock in below-market rents. The STR Token pilot gives short-term rental certificates in exchange for 15-year workforce deed restrictions (150% AMI average per adult; applications closed June 20, 2024). Results to date: 871 deed-restricted units (6.2% of stock), 33 THAP homes, 276 Lease to Locals conversions, 76 Rooted Renters units, 37 ADUs created through grants and loans.
per_unit_cap: THAP $150,000 per home; Lease to Locals $18,000; Rooted Renters $26,000.
affordability_requirement: Occupants must work locally; income caps vary by program (THAP 245% AMI; Token 150% AMI per adult).
next_deadline: Open; THAP parameters under review with revisions targeted for Q4 2026.
layering_notes: Not a source for new affordable multifamily, but signals the Town's local revenue priorities: its housing dollars go mainly to deed restrictions of existing stock and middle-income production. The Town's goal is 10% of housing stock deed restricted by 2032. The Council work plan lists a potential housing revenue measure and draft Program H-2.F targets at least $300,000 per year of added local funding (additional TOT, business, sales or transfer tax). Mountain Housing Council of Tahoe Truckee (Tahoe Truckee Community Foundation) is the regional partner for AMI tiers above 120%.

program_name: Truckee Town-owned land public-private partnerships (Edmunds Lofts) and Railyard Master Plan affordable housing obligations
administering_agency: Town of Truckee Planning Division and Town Manager
typical_award_size: Edmunds Lofts: Town-owned 0.5-acre site (APN 018-580-052, dedicated by High Altitude Fitness) to be conveyed to Paradigm8 / Sagemodern under a Development and Disposition Agreement for 12 deed-restricted workforce units; entitlements granted in 2025 and building permits under review (75% complete at December 31, 2025). Railyard: Council work plan item 6.3 will move inclusionary and workforce housing obligations from the Railyard Development Agreement into the Railyard Master Plan (late 2026 to early 2027); the Town made a significant financial contribution to the earlier 66-unit Truckee Artist Lofts in the Railyard. Draft 7th cycle Program H-2.H directs annual review of all Town-owned and partner-agency land (TTUSD, Caltrans, Tahoe Forest Hospital, Truckee Donner PUD) for housing.
per_unit_cap: Land contribution; no cash figure published.
affordability_requirement: Deed-restricted workforce units per the DDA; Railyard units per the Development Agreement.
application_cycle: closed/inactive (no open solicitation; RFIQ issued October 16, 2024)
next_deadline: No open RFIQ as of 2026-11-08. Council removed the pilot to find another site from the 2025-2027 work plan on September 9, 2025. Watch the Railyard Master Plan amendment (late 2026 to early 2027).
layering_notes: Land write-downs of public land are public subsidy for prevailing wage purposes and trigger Surplus Land Act review. Coldstream Commons (48 units at 60% AMI, nine HUD 811 units) is an existing affordable project in the Coldstream Specific Plan area; no new Coldstream affordable commitment was found this pass. Prohousing Designation status for Truckee was not confirmed.

program_name: Grass Valley Affordable Housing Density Bonuses and Incentives (Development Code Chapter 17.32)
administering_agency: City of Grass Valley Community Development Department
typical_award_size: Incentive, not a subsidy. Local chapter tracks Government Code 65915: one incentive at 10% lower income, 5% very low or 10% moderate (common interest) units, two at 17% lower or 10% very low, and so on; parking reductions (17.32.050) and childcare bonuses (17.32.060); Council grants requested incentives unless it makes written findings. The 2024 Annual Progress Report says no density bonus has been requested and the City planned updates to the ordinance.
affordability_requirement: Per Government Code 65915; density bonus agreement under 17.32.100.
next_deadline: Not applicable; requested before or with the project application.
layering_notes: Grass Valley has no inclusionary ordinance, no city housing trust fund of its own and no city NOFA; its local money flows through the Western Nevada County Regional Housing Trust Fund and the regional PLHA plan administered by Nevada County HCS (see county records). Code text read from the zoneomics mirror; grassvalleyca.gov returns a JavaScript shell to scripts, so the City's meeting-host attachments were used for the APR.

program_name: Grass Valley Housing Element affordable housing programs: fee deferral on request (Program 28), state and federal funding support (Program 13), tax-exempt bonds (Program 14)
administering_agency: City of Grass Valley Community Development Department
typical_award_size: Fee deferral for affordable housing is available on request, but the City reports it has received no requests. Program 13 commits the City to apply for grants and support developers seeking funding (objective 25 very low and 40 to 60 low income new units in 2019-2027); Program 14 supports tax-exempt bonds and mortgage credit certificates. The City won a $2 million DTSC Equitable Community Revitalization Grant in 2024 to clean up a brownfield site of interest to affordable developers, and expedited a Habitat for Humanity SB 9 lot split for three deed-restricted homes.
affordability_requirement: Lower income units per the funding source; Program 28 targets units at or below 30% AMI with Nevada County and the Regional Housing Authority.
next_deadline: unknown, verify with agency. The 7th cycle Housing Element is due in 2027.
layering_notes: Deferral terms are not codified in a published resolution; negotiate case by case. City sites have historically attracted County-sponsored supportive housing (Brunswick Commons, 41 units) and RHA projects. The City joined the October 30, 2025 regional housing workshop with the County, Nevada City, Truckee and HCD. Source is the 2024 General Plan Annual Progress Report (March 2025) on the City's meeting host; a 2025 APR was not located this pass.

program_name: Nevada City density bonus and affordable housing incentives (Housing Element Program 24; Zoning Code update pending)
administering_agency: City of Nevada City Planning Department
typical_award_size: Incentive, not a subsidy. The City grants density bonuses and incentives per state law; Cashin's Field (51 units, opened 2023) used an 80% density bonus and reduced parking. The 2025 Annual Progress Report says the City will update its density bonus regulations in 2026 to match current state law. Nevada City has not raised development impact fees since 1993 and is considering a fee study in 2026.
affordability_requirement: Per Government Code 65915.
next_deadline: Not applicable; 7th cycle Housing Element (2027-2035) update underway with workshops July 30 and September 10, 2026.
layering_notes: Nevada City has no city housing trust fund, no city NOFA and no city-run CDBG or HOME program; the 2025 APR states the City's limited resources preclude its own rehabilitation program. Local gap money comes through the Western Nevada County Regional Housing Trust Fund and regional PLHA (the City allocated PLHA to Cashin's Field). Zoning code density bonus chapter not found on the zoneomics mirror; source is the City's 2025 Housing Element APR.

program_name: Nevada City subdivision affordability requirement (30% of homes 1,500 square feet or smaller; Section 17.80.220 lower income share)
administering_agency: City of Nevada City Planning Department
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Since 2009 new subdivisions must make 30% of homes 1,500 square feet or smaller and affordable to moderate and lower income households, via deed restriction or an affordable housing plan approved by the Planning Commission or Council (size limits, rental units, second units). The APR cites Section 17.80.220 as requiring 20% lower income units in developments. 34 lots approved to date under the affordability-by-design rule.
affordability_requirement: Moderate and below income through deed restriction or approved affordable housing plan.
next_deadline: Not applicable.
layering_notes: Functions as a light inclusionary rule without an in-lieu fee or fund. Section 17.80.220 text was not opened this pass (not on the zoneomics mirror), so confirm the 20% lower income requirement and its thresholds with the City before relying on it.

program_name: Nevada City fee waiver for deed-restricted low income ADUs and reduced ADU impact fees (Municipal Code 17.72.026)
administering_agency: City of Nevada City Planning Department
typical_award_size: Waiver of mitigation fees and utility hook-up fees for deed-restricted low income accessory dwelling units; reduced AB 1600 impact fees for all ADUs and none for ADUs under 750 square feet. Pre-approved ADU plans available. Objective of 8 affordable second units in the cycle.
affordability_requirement: Low income deed restriction on the ADU.
next_deadline: Not applicable.
layering_notes: Small-scale tool only; no equivalent waiver is codified for multifamily. Recorded so the market's lack of multifamily fee relief is visible.

program_name: Riverside Local Affordable Housing Trust Fund (LAHTF), created by Council resolution March 12, 2024
administering_agency: City of Riverside Housing and Human Services Department
typical_award_size: Construction and permanent loans at simple interest of no more than 3% per annum, with repayments recycled into the fund. Seeded with a $1,500,000 transfer of PLHA funds; ongoing revenue from HOME, NSP, CalHome, PLHA and ARPA affordable housing program income (ARPA affordable housing allocation was $1,388,797) plus 50% of future sale proceeds of City-owned land bought with General Fund money. City applied for a $1,000,000 HCD Local Housing Trust Fund match (August 2024). Staff cite typical gap requests of $3M to $4M for 65 to 80 unit projects.
affordability_requirement: Low to moderate income households. Committee recommendations at creation: 99-year affordability term, priority for seniors and justice-involved people, and eligibility for market-rate developers that restrict 10% of rental units (or 5% of for-sale units). Loans funded with PIP Round 4 money require 55-year first-position covenants at or below 50% AMI.
next_deadline: No LAHTF NOFA issued as of 2026-11-08. The March 24, 2026 PIP Round 4 staff report says residual receipts from PIP loans will flow to the trust fund and staff will issue a NOFA once enough has accumulated. Contact Housing and Human Services (Agripina Neubauer, Housing Project Manager).
layering_notes: City-controlled gap layer that sits ahead of County HOME/PLHA (the County CDBG/HOME record covers the Urban County, which excludes the City of Riverside as its own entitlement grantee). Stacks with the City's own HOME, PLHA and PIP loans (separate records) and with 4% or 9% LIHTC. Capitalized mainly from recycled program income, so the balance is small relative to need; expect it to be combined with HOME and PLHA on the same project. If the LHTF state match was awarded it carries HCD LHTF regulatory terms. City pages on riversideca.gov are thin; staff reports were pulled through the Legistar web API (client riversideca).

program_name: Housing Authority of the City of Riverside, Housing Successor Low and Moderate Income Housing Asset Fund (LMIHAF)
administering_agency: Housing Authority of the City of Riverside (Housing Successor to the former Redevelopment Agency)
typical_award_size: FY 2023-24 (latest report found, dated April 1, 2025): $9,403,323 deposited, $2,899,271 spent ($1,597,196 on housing development across ELI, VLI and low income units), ending cash balance $2,547,069. Portfolio $35.6M ($34.9M loans receivable, $685K real property). The Housing Authority also owns 104 units managed by RHDC under a 2024 operating agreement.
affordability_requirement: LMIHAF rules (HSC 34176.1): at least 30% of spending for ELI (30% AMI) and no more than 20% for 60 to 80% AMI over each five-year period; 55-year rental covenants typical.
next_deadline: No standing NOFA. Funds and Housing Authority land are committed project by project through Council and Housing Authority actions; contact Housing and Human Services.
layering_notes: Separate from the County housing successor (HACR) record; only for projects inside city limits. Used alongside City HOME/PLHA and land write-downs (see Housing Authority land record). Ending balance is modest, so treat as a supplemental source. A FY 2024-25 report was not found on the City site (404) and should be requested.

program_name: Housing Authority and Successor Agency land write-downs and surplus land dispositions (e.g., 2882 Mission Inn Avenue DDA, 11049 Bogart, 8733 Indiana)
administering_agency: Housing Authority of the City of Riverside; Successor Agency to the Redevelopment Agency of the City of Riverside
typical_award_size: Land conveyed at or near $1. Example: September 1, 2026 DDA conveys 2882 Mission Inn Ave (0.22 acre) to Grapevine Development for $1, a $245,861 write-down counted as HOME match, for 10 affordable units in a 64-unit mixed-use project; that project also pairs $900,000 City HOME and $250,000 City PLHA with LIHTC. Other Housing Authority sites: 11049 Bogart (DDA with NPHS, 22 PSH units), 8733 Indiana (RFP with adjacent Successor Agency parcel), 2348 University (duplex redevelopment).
affordability_requirement: Surplus Land Act: at least 25% lower income on the notice of availability, 55-year covenants; Grapevine DDA requires 2 units at 50% AMI and 8 at 60% AMI for 55 years.
next_deadline: Sites are offered through SLA notices and RFPs as they come up; watch Housing Authority agendas. The University Avenue Density Transfer Pilot (separate record) also targets City surplus parcels.
layering_notes: Land write-downs count as HOME match (City reports excess HOME match of $16.4M). Successor Agency parcels need Countywide Oversight Board approval and HCD SLA sign-off, which adds months. The County land program (county record) is separate.

program_name: City of Riverside HUD entitlement funds: HOME Infill Residential Development Program and CDBG (FY 2026-27 Annual Action Plan)
administering_agency: City of Riverside Housing and Human Services Department
typical_award_size: FY 2026-27 HUD allocations total $9,050,906: CDBG $2,749,768, HOME $981,735 (of which $883,561 to the Infill Residential Development Program, plus about $200,000 HOME program income), ESG $250,428, HOPWA $5,068,975 (City is the HOPWA EMSA grantee for both Riverside and San Bernardino counties). Recent HOME loans: $1,508,234 Sunrise at Bogart (22 PSH units), $1,550,443 Mulberry Gardens Family (11 HOME units). HOME-ARP also used ($3,000,000 Mulberry Gardens Senior).
affordability_requirement: HOME: at or below 80% AMI with HOME rent limits; 20-year minimum HOME period for new construction, City typically records 55 years.
next_deadline: Public notice of funding availability released each December (last one December 2025) for the following July program year; FY 2027-28 notice expected about December 2026. Action Plan due to HUD by mid-August.
layering_notes: City is its own HUD entitlement and is outside the Riverside Urban County CDBG/HOME pool in the county record. HOME is small (under $1M a year), so it functions as a slice of the local gap. Federal Davis-Bacon applies at 12 or more HOME-assisted units. The draft Action Plan says the City dedicates its direct PLHA allocation to affordable housing development as additional leverage.

program_name: City of Riverside Permanent Local Housing Allocation (PLHA) direct formula allocation, development loans
administering_agency: City of Riverside Housing and Human Services Department
typical_award_size: Five-year PLHA plan (adopted July 7, 2020) estimated $9,732,750. CY 2023 application $2,456,509 (March 2025). Development loans to date: $1,000,000 Golden Pierce (79 units), $1,053,907 The Aspire (32 youth PSH units), $380,562 Sunrise at Bogart (22 PSH units), $250,000 proposed for Grapevine (10 units). A large share also goes to homeless case management ($1,384,134 City Net).
affordability_requirement: PLHA rules: rental units at or below 60% AMI (up to 120% AMI for owner units), 55-year covenants.
next_deadline: Awarded through Council-approved loan agreements; uncommitted amounts may be transferred to the Local Affordable Housing Trust Fund ($1.5M already moved). Contact Housing and Human Services.
layering_notes: City receives its own PLHA formula share separate from the County PLHA record, so City projects can carry both a City and a County PLHA loan. Commonly stacked with City HOME and PIP on the same project (Sunrise at Bogart used PIP $1.44M, PLHA $380K and HOME $1.51M).

program_name: Prohousing designation and Prohousing Incentive Program (PIP) loans, City of Riverside
administering_agency: City of Riverside Housing and Human Services Department (designation by HCD)
typical_award_size: City has received $2.44M in PIP to date: $1,000,000 loan to Mulberry Gardens Family (149 units) and $1,440,000 to Sunrise at Bogart (22 PSH units). Council authorized an application for up to $1,440,000 in PIP Round 4 (March 24, 2026); loans come back to Council project by project.
affordability_requirement: PIP-assisted units at or below 50% AMI; 55-year covenants in first position.
next_deadline: Prohousing designation (awarded March 30, 2023) expires January 1, 2027. The Housing and Homelessness Committee took up reapplication on August 31, 2026; a reapplication resolution and HCD submittal must happen before January 2027 for the City to keep PIP eligibility and Prohousing scoring points.
layering_notes: Designation also gives Riverside projects Prohousing points or preference in HCD competitive programs (AHSC, IIG and others), a meaningful edge for City sites. PIP residual receipts flow to the LAHTF. Risk: staff estimate 16 confident and up to 23 uncertain points against a 30-point threshold under the stricter 2024 criteria, so the designation could lapse. Recorded at city level because the City selects and lends to projects, although the money is HCD's.

program_name: Riverside density bonus, Municipal Code Chapter 19.545
administering_agency: City of Riverside Community and Economic Development Department, Planning Division
typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Implements state density bonus law with a concession table (1 to 4 concessions; 100% affordable projects get 4 and, within half a mile of a major transit stop, up to three extra stories or 33 feet) and reduced parking ratios (1 space for 0-1 BR, 1.5 for 2-3 BR; 0.5 per unit near transit with at least 11% VLI or 20% low).
affordability_requirement: Eligibility per Gov. Code 65915: 5% VLI, 10% low, 10% moderate for-sale, 10% special populations, 20% lower income students, or 100% lower income with up to 20% moderate.
next_deadline: Applied through entitlement review. Zoning Code amendments (PR-2024-001746 and the 2025 omnibus PR-2025-001793) updated Chapter 19.545 for 2024 state law changes.
layering_notes: No local enhancements beyond state law found; the chapter tracks Gov. Code 65915. City has no inclusionary ordinance or in-lieu fee fund, and no adopted citywide affordable housing fee deferral program was found. Pairs with the University Avenue Density Transfer Pilot (separate record) on eligible sites.

program_name: University Avenue Density Transfer Pilot Program (Housing Element Program HE-EJ-7-2)
administering_agency: City of Riverside Community and Economic Development Department, Planning Division
typical_award_size: Not a cash subsidy. Creates a unit bank seeded with residential capacity from City-owned surplus parcels in the University Avenue Specific Plan; receiver sites (City surplus and Housing Element sites) can withdraw extra units first-come first-served, with priority to City surplus sites, and may combine withdrawals with Chapter 19.545 density bonuses.
affordability_requirement: None specific to the transfer; affordability comes from density bonus, SLA covenants or funding sources used on the receiver site.
next_deadline: Land Use Committee recommended approval; the Council item (Legistar 52587, March 2026) showed status Agenda Ready with no recorded vote in the API. Verify adoption with Planning before relying on it.
layering_notes: Most useful when paired with a City surplus parcel disposition (see land write-down record). Pilot limited to the University Avenue Specific Plan area; may expand if successful.

program_name: Moreno Valley Housing Authority, Housing Successor Low and Moderate Income Housing Asset Fund (LMIHAF) and housing successor land
administering_agency: Moreno Valley Housing Authority (Housing Successor to the Community Redevelopment Agency), Financial and Management Services
typical_award_size: FY 2024-25: cash $6,494,846; total fund balance $38,030,093 (mostly loans and interest receivable); deposits $595,276. Excess surplus of $3,238,065 in FY 2024-25 must be spent or encumbered within three fiscal years or transferred to HCD; the prior FY 2023-24 excess was to be spent by June 30, 2026. Land: Fir/Heacock site going to the Linwood Rose 36-unit special needs apartments; Eucalyptus/Heacock to Lantana Court (7 ownership homes); JFK/Elm and Sheila/Perris dispositions starting; the Action Plan also lists Day/Alessandro (8.15 acres) as available.
affordability_requirement: LMIHAF income and ELI spending tests (HSC 34176.1); 55-year rental covenants typical.
next_deadline: No NOFA posted. The excess surplus creates a spend-down deadline (FY 2024-25 excess by about June 30, 2028), so the Authority has a strong incentive to commit funds to a ready project. Contact the Financial and Management Services Grants Division.
layering_notes: Best near-term local cash in Moreno Valley. The City has no Section 8 authority (HACR administers about 1,100 vouchers and 66 RAD PBV units in the City), so HACR PBVs (county record) are the rental subsidy layer. Stack with City HOME (separate record) and County PLHA/HOME-ARP. moval.org and moval.gov both served documents without blocking.

program_name: Moreno Valley HOME Investment Partnerships Program and CDBG annual application round
administering_agency: City of Moreno Valley Financial and Management Services, Grants Division
typical_award_size: FY 2026-27: HOME $623,617 (CHDO set-aside $93,542; $467,714 for other activities; 10% admin), CDBG about $1.9M, ESG about $172,000. The adopted Action Plan (July 2026) also carries $2,265,372 in unencumbered HOME funds with activity TBD, available for a rental project.
affordability_requirement: HOME rent and income limits (at or below 80% AMI; 20-year minimum affordability for new construction).
next_deadline: FY 2026-27 HOME applications were due January 30, 2026 (PlanetBids, opened December 12, 2025). Expect the FY 2027-28 round to open about December 2026 with a late January 2027 deadline; ask the Grants Division about the $2.27M unencumbered HOME balance now.
layering_notes: HUD classifies Moreno Valley as fiscally distressed, giving a 50% HOME match reduction. Moreno Valley is its own entitlement city, outside the County Urban County pool. The Action Plan also lists PLHA, Prohousing Incentive Pilot and former RDA housing funds as leverage. Davis-Bacon applies at 12 or more HOME units.

program_name: Moreno Valley density bonus program, Municipal Code Section 9.03.050 (with impact fee reductions)
administering_agency: City of Moreno Valley Community Development Department, Planning Division
typical_award_size: Implements state density bonus law plus a local fee incentive: 50% reduction of the development impact fee and parkland impact mitigation fee for VLI units and 25% for lower income units (Section 9.03.050.I.2). Up to four concessions; projects within half a mile of a major transit stop also get up to three more stories or 33 feet.
affordability_requirement: Gov. Code 65915 thresholds (5% VLI, 10% lower, 10% moderate for-sale, 100% lower income with up to 20% moderate, and special populations); 55-year affordability agreement for rental units.
next_deadline: Applied at entitlement; last amended by Ord. 1035 (December 16, 2025).
layering_notes: The fee reduction is a real local enhancement beyond state law and can be requested as an additional incentive. A City fee reduction may count as public funds under Labor Code 1720. No local housing trust fund, inclusionary ordinance or in-lieu fee fund was found for Moreno Valley. Code read on the zoneomics mirror.

program_name: Corona Housing Authority Housing Fund (Fund 291) loans and Housing Authority land (Corona 2nd Street Family Apartments DDA)
administering_agency: Corona Housing Authority (Housing Successor), Community Services Department, Housing Services
typical_award_size: Example August 21, 2024 DDA for 115 family units: Authority cash loan $7,535,280 (Housing Fund 291) plus a land loan at the higher of appraisal or $2.8M; City loans of $529,875 HOME-ARP, land at the higher of appraisal or $1.2M, and up to $2,000,000 in deferred development impact fees. Local subsidy about $99,731 per unit, 18.5% of a $62.0M total cost ($539,301 per unit). Loans amortized and repaid over 55 years.
per_unit_cap: None published; about $100K per unit local subsidy on the 2nd Street deal.
affordability_requirement: All units except the manager unit affordable in perpetuity at 30%, 50% and 80% of median income (rents at 30 to 60% with caps to 70% under tax credits); 20-unit preference for homeless families.
next_deadline: No NOFA cycle; the Authority uses RFQ/RFP for its sites. A second phase of about 25 PSH units on the same site is planned. Housing Fund balance was not found; request the latest SB 341 housing successor report from Housing Services.
layering_notes: Corona's main local gap source. Layered with 4% LIHTC, City CDBG and HOME-ARP and a DIF deferral note. Land was bought from RCTC under the SLA with $600K CDBG and $1.4M Housing Fund; repayment splits 30% to CDBG program income and 70% to the Housing Fund. Corona's Legistar (client corona) has no matters after August 2024, so newer Council items were not reachable through the API.

program_name: Corona development impact fee waiver or deferral for affordable housing
administering_agency: City of Corona (City Council; Housing Services and Planning)
typical_award_size: Case by case. On the 2nd Street Family project the City deferred up to $2,000,000 in development impact fees into a promissory note repaid over 55 years.
affordability_requirement: Tied to the affordability terms of the project's DDA or density bonus agreement.
next_deadline: Requested at predevelopment and approved by Council resolution with the project agreement. The FY 2026-27 Action Plan commits staff to educate affordable developers on how to request a waiver or deferral.
layering_notes: No standing fee deferral ordinance was found; treat as negotiable. Deferred fees held as a City loan count as public funds for prevailing wage. Useful to reduce the gap at construction closing.

program_name: Corona CDBG, HOME and HOME-ARP (FY 2026-27 Annual Action Plan)
